title: All In the Mind with Sana Qadar - ABC listen
description: All in the Mind is an exploration of the mental: the mind, brain and behaviour — everything from addiction to artificial intelligence.

episodes.title: The psychology behind our moral outrage
episodes.description: Politics, war, abortion, gun control — why do some topics make us so outraged? One theory is that our preoccupation with preventing harm is to blame.

episodes.title: Staying sane in space
episodes.description: In the last couple of weeks, a lot of people have been getting excited about space exploration thanks to Artemis II.

episodes.title: Mind Hacks with Dr Billy Garvey: "being a bit kinder to myself"
episodes.description: Welcome back to All in the Mind's little sister: Mind Hacks.

episodes.title: Tantrums, sleep training and anxiety: Dr Billy Garvey answers your parenting questions
episodes.description: How can I help my child with anxiety? What's the deal with sleep training? Are we supposed to ignore tantrums?

episodes.title: The psychology of masturbation
episodes.description: This week we're talking about something intimate… and sometimes taboo: masturbation.

episodes.title: Mind Hacks: Casey Beros
episodes.description: Welcome back to All in the Mind's little sister: Mind Hacks.

episodes.title: Tough conversations and anticipatory grief: being a carer
episodes.description: When Casey Beros' dad was diagnosed with mesothelioma, she knew her entire world would change.

episodes.title: Family estrangement and infidelity: Esther Perel answers your questions
episodes.description: How do you grieve a dying parent you're estranged from? Do cheaters ever change? People say love should feel 'easy', is that true?

episodes.title: Mind Hacks: Joel Pearson
episodes.description: Welcome back to All in the Mind's little sister: Mind Hacks. In this episode, cognitive neuroscientist Joel Pearson tells us how he manages his own stress (clue: it involves saunas!)

episodes.title: Is AI making our brains lazier?
episodes.description: Social media gave us brain rot; will AI give us cognitive atrophy? How can we possibly learn to cope with the sheer amount of uncertainty and change heading our way?

title: Background Briefing - ABC listen
description: The Background Briefing podcast brings you true stories not everyone will want you to hear, told by trusted reporters across Australia.

episodes.title: 02 In Search of the Missing Artist | The Plastic
episodes.description: The only clue to Jean Paul Mangin's true identity is hiding in his art.

episodes.title: 01 In Search of the Missing Artist | The sculptor
episodes.description: The sales pitch goes that Jean Paul Mangin is a reclusive Parisian sculptor whose works are internationally acclaimed. His pieces sell quickly through one particular Australian gallery, sought after by trendy interior designers.

episodes.title: Introducing | In Search of the Missing Artist
episodes.description: For years, art buyers have been told that this man is an internationally acclaimed, intensely private Parisian sculptor. His bold, brightly coloured plastic works are available through one Melbourne gallery, and they're selling fast.

episodes.title: 03 The Road to Bondi | Deepfake
episodes.description: How did a wounded Bondi survivor become the face of a global deepfake conspiracy in less than 24 hours? Arsen Ostrovsky was celebrating Chanukah at Bondi Beach when the first shots rang out.

episodes.title: 02 The Road to Bondi | A Test of Character
episodes.description: This man fled Iran after being imprisoned and tortured for protesting the regime. Known only as AB, he came to Australia hoping to start again — and, in many ways, he did. He found love and started a family.

episodes.title: 01 The Road to Bondi | Father and Son
episodes.description: You think you know the story. You know how it ended. But you don’t know how it began. In the first episode of The Road to Bondi, reporter Josh Robertson traces the decades-long path that led a father and son to carry out their plan.

episodes.title: TRAILER — Introducing The Road to Bondi
episodes.description: In an ordinary Australian suburb, a father and son are secretly planning something terrible. One fateful summer evening, their path brings them crashing into the lives of strangers from around the world whose own stories haven’t yet been told.

episodes.title: 06 Hometown Boys | Not the only one
episodes.description: Insiders from the Harrow-Balmoral football club decide to break the code of silence. For Elise, it’s time to rebuild her life. But her story inspires other women to emerge with their own troubling accounts of the town’s club culture.

episodes.title: 05 Hometown Boys | 'Luke, Maybe'
episodes.description: A key witness submits a startling new statement that topples the guilty verdict and forces a retrial. This time, the men accused will not give evidence. But Lisa Hutchins, the trusted bush nurse will take the stand again — now for the defence.

episodes.title: 04 Hometown Boys | The Trial
episodes.description: As the criminal trial unfolds, witnesses from Balmoral waver on the stand, and the judge is "taken aback". The courtroom is heaving with supporters of the accused but the verdict is not what they're expecting.

title: Bludging on the Blindside with Rampaging Roy Slaven and HG Nelson - ABC listen
description: The master of midfield mayhem Rampaging Roy Slaven and the leading light of long shots HG Nelson cast a collective eye over the world of sport.

episodes.title: Are pervs and sickos penetrating the Newcastle Baths?
episodes.description: This week more great moments from the past 12 years from under the SCG vaults. They're stuffed full Bludgers! There's also previously unheard content that appears as part of this 'Best of Bludging on the Blindside.' Enjoy Blindsiders!

episodes.title: Shark Meltdown - 30 year celebration.
episodes.description: This week on Bludging on the Blindside, Roy and HG discuss the Kevvie-ists parallel world view, the six again rule is out of control and funky Jason Day's walking cool.

episodes.title: Happy Easter, happy Rugby League!
episodes.description: This week on Bludging on the Blindside, Roy and HG discuss the small mindedness of a Manly fan, Wayne Bennett's chooks at the Easter Show and listening to a podcast in your dreams.

episodes.title: Win, Win, Win! Thank you ABC
episodes.description: This week on Bludging on the Blindside, Roy and HG discuss the Kevvie-ists movement at the Broncos, how rugby league could bring peace to the world, and Papenhuyzen's new career as a golf caddy.

episodes.title: Rooting King vs Alex Johnston in a race
episodes.description: This week on Bludging on the Blindside, Roy and HG discuss the poor maintenance of our stadiums, whether Wayne Bennett needs to celebrate rather than sulk, and if Gorden Tallis has become a problem for the Broncos.

episodes.title: Heritage Toilet Lager - Easy drinking
episodes.description: This week on Bludging on the Blindside, Roy and HG discuss a possible Rugby League opening ceremony, Rugby League happiness differs from everyday happiness and do we understand the Rugby League expansion master plan?

episodes.title: Celebration of rubber
episodes.description: This week on Bludging on the Blindside, Roy and HG discuss applying logic to rugby league, teams must solve their problems on the field and is Rugby League supervised violence?

episodes.title: Mongrel downstairs, pole in the hand
episodes.description: Bludging on the Blindside is back for 2026! In this week's episode, Roy and HG discuss the return of Rugby League to Las Vegas, the feral pig problem in the country, and whether wisdom is the greatest enemy of Rugby League.

episodes.title: 2026: Can't wait!
episodes.description: This week on Bludging on the Blindside, the last show for 2025. Roy and H.G discuss the you beaut ute boot sale, Sydney's celebration of rubber and when is Four Corners going to do a gambling story about the winners?

episodes.title: The race that stops the world
episodes.description: This week on Bludging on the Blindside, Roy and H.G discuss the new player in the Australian car industry, Hastie Car Corporation. Gus Gould takes a selfie in the toilet and Bunnings Island is a reality, Loloata Island in PNG.

title: Conversations with Richard Fidler and Sarah Kanowski - ABC listen
description: Conversations draws you deeper into the life story of someone you may, or may not, have heard about — someone who has seen and done amazing things.

episodes.title: Surviving White Island and what happened next — Stephanie Browitt's story
episodes.description: At 23 years old, Stephanie Browitt willed herself to stay awake long enough to survive a volcano eruption on New Zealand's Whakaari / White Island. More than six years later, her resilience and sanity remains as strong as ever.

episodes.title: Sandi Toksvig's bright side
episodes.description: The Danish-British author, broadcaster and comedian recalls her unusual early life with glee, including how she came to be holding the hand of Neil Armstrong’s assistant at NASA’s headquarters on July 20, 1969. (R)

episodes.title: My year with the real Rudolf Nureyev — a volatile but vulnerable genius
episodes.description: When the world's most famous dancer offered a young sailor a job as his assistant, Blue Robinson thought it was a joke at first. But what followed was the most fascinating and formative year of Blue's life.

episodes.title: Encore: How I came to work with the lions who live in trees
episodes.description: Alex Braczkowski is a big cat expert and for years he's been following a rare group of tree-climbing lions, including the charismatic, enigmatic, three-legged Jacob.

episodes.title: My best friend was killed by her ex-husband — this is the message I want men to hear
episodes.description: Hannah Clarke and her three children were killed in an horrific attack that shocked Australia but for Dave Kramer their deaths were personal, he was friends with Hannah and had witnessed her relationship up close.

episodes.title: The story behind Sydney’s Luna Park and its impact on the city
episodes.description: Author Helen Pitt has written a history of the iconic fun park and it's a tale bound up with con men, crooked cops, and developers who have long wanted to snatch up the prime piece of waterfront real estate.

episodes.title: Encore: What I learnt about Australia as an Outback GP
episodes.description: When Sonia Henry signed up to work as a GP in a remote mining town in the Pilbara, the experience changed almost everything she believed about Australia.

episodes.title: Why my father was abandoned and the empathy I now have for his mother
episodes.description: Jane Messer grew up with a loving father who never really understood why as a child his mother left him and his older sister at a boarding school, so she decided to find out the full story and prove that he was in fact, loved.

episodes.title: Encore: The hidden corners of Emma's Hong Kong — fishing villages, beaches and ancestral graveyards
episodes.description: Novelist Emma Pei Yin ran away from Hong Kong as a teenager to start fresh in Australia. But she found herself repeatedly drawn back home whenever she put pen to paper.

episodes.title: 'The century of foundlings'—what Cynthia found when she went looking maternal family secrets
episodes.description: Writer Cynthia Banham on discovering the shocking truth about her great-grandmother, reckoning with buried family secrets, and the criticisms mothers face from others and sometimes most harshly, from themselves.

title: Expanse with Dominique Bayens - ABC listen
description: In 1999 a young American dumped his bicycle and walked out into the Great Sandy Desert in remote northern Australia. He was an Alaskan firefighter, seemingly with everything to live for. So why did he risk it all to go into the wilderness alone? And how do you search for someone who doesn't want to be found? New episodes released each Wednesday

episodes.title: BONUS | Inside the Nannup Four police investigation
episodes.description: It has been months in the making, but police are opening up the files on the missing Nannup Four for Expanse host Dominique Bayens, and there's news on another search.

episodes.title: BONUS | Who was Tony Popic?
episodes.description: Since the podcast started rolling out, a lot of people have got in touch with information. Two people have been able to shed light on some previously unknown parts of the story.

episodes.title: 06 Expanse: The Nannup Four | Northcliffe
episodes.description: A family friend and former policeman continues to search for answers for Jim and Cath McDougall decades after the Nannup four vanished. The family and friends of Chantelle McDougall try to find their own answers, as one last glimmer of hope emerges.

episodes.title: 05 Expanse: The Nannup Four | Simon says
episodes.description: Jim and Cath McDougall are left reeling as the true depth of Simon Kadwill’s deception is revealed.

episodes.title: 04 Expanse: The Nannup Four | A question of belief
episodes.description: Tony Popic is talking about an end of days, Simon is seeing spirits and Chantelle is forced into a difficult decision as increasingly troubling hints something's not right come to light.

episodes.title: 03 Expanse: The Nannup Four | Down the rabbit hole
episodes.description: Dominique travels across the country to meet the two people who might be able to help her understand how Chantelle came to be living a reclusive life in a hidden corner of Western Australia, alongside a self-styled spiritual guru 18 years her senior.

episodes.title: 02 Expanse: The Nannup Four | Selling snake oil
episodes.description: A chance encounter in the streets of Melbourne in 1998 leaves a friend wondering what Chantelle McDougall has been pulled into. Dominique hears about the escalating pattern of control Simon Kadwill exercises over Chantelle.

episodes.title: 01 Expanse: The Nannup Four | The people in the blue house
episodes.description: When three adults and a child disappear without a trace from the isolated bush community of Nannup in 2007, it sparks disturbing theories about what might have happened.

episodes.title: Expanse: The Nannup Four
episodes.description: When four people disappeared from a blue farmhouse on the outskirts of the Western Australian town of Nannup in 2007, they left behind the scatterings of a life, a note pinned to their door and a question: was the disappearance a choice... or murder?

episodes.title: BONUS Expanse: Nowhere Man | Gunslinger
episodes.description: The search for Robert Bogucki brought together a cast of colourful characters, including a cigar-toting, moustachioed American named Garrison ‘Gunslinger’ St Clair.

title: Global Roaming with Geraldine Doogue and Hamish Macdonald and Kylie Morris and Latika Bourke - ABC listen
description: Award-winning journalists Geraldine Doogue and Hamish Macdonald are joined by two new hosts, former foreign correspondent Kylie Morris and journalist Latika Bourke in London. Every day, they'll be discussing the biggest world events and how to make of sense of them.

episodes.title: Is a global recession inevitable?
episodes.description: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz is sending shock waves through the global economy. Supply chains are in disarray, inflation is surging and oil prices remain high. With no end in sight to the US-Iran war, is a global recession inevitable?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm David Ma, host of Late Night Live on Radio National, where nothing's off limits. You know, part of being an adult is dealing with discomfort. We gather the sharpest minds around to hash over what's shaping this crazy world. Both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party succumbed to big money. Late Night Live, four new shows a week on ABC Listen, or wherever you get your podcasts. Well, the Middle East war is sending economic shockwaves, along with other shocks, around the globe. Fuel prices skyrocketing, supply chains in disarray, inflation surging. And the question is, is a global recession inevitable? And why doesn't the stock market seem to care? On today's Global Roaming, we look at what's happening to the global economy in the shadow of war and what it will mean for all of us. I'm Geraldine Dugue. I'm Latika Burke. Let's go roaming. Geraldine Dugue. Geraldine, it has been such a confusing situation trying to monitor what is going on with the Strait of Hormuz. One minute the Strait was open, the next is closed. It's becoming difficult, dare I say it impossible, even though it's my job, to keep up with what the situation actually is. Yes, I've sort of made a little decision. You know, you have to sort of audit yourself in terms of how much time you can give to reading and listening. I'm just not going to know all the little granular permutations of what's happening in the Strait. I'm not going to know. You know, I know we'll be bombarded with this and that and the other sort of extraordinary bit of audio between the Iranian Central Command or whatever they are. That's the trouble. We don't know who's in charge there now and various ships. To me, I'm looking now beyond those details in a way. I think it's really interesting to watch what's happening in Australia. So obviously, I'm watching the politics very closely because Jim Chalmers is about to hand down a budget. And I think this is the mother of all budgets for Jim Chalmers. This is a huge test for him and he is essentially now being held hostage to a global situation outside of Australia's making. And this is a really different set of circumstances, even compared to the pandemic and the war in Ukraine, I think, just because of how widespread this is, but also the policy responses it demands. So we saw last week the Australian government increasing defence spending. What are they going to do going forward? Because this, I think, is about to open up a real live debate across the world. Europe and the UK, for instance, there were similar calls to cut the fuel excise like Australia did when that happened. They haven't followed suit. The Americans haven't followed suit on that. In fact, if you look at the European way now, what seems to be coming out is actually we need our consumers to start feeling a bit of this pain. So they adjust their behaviour. They're starting very openly to now talk about if you can work from home, if you can use the public transport, do that more. I know there's been a bit of that in Australia too. It's true, but I also think there's another context to apply here and that's decarbonisation. These jurisdictions that made a call to get to decarbonisation now can use this to accelerate that path and say, look, here is another reason why we've got to do it. And I think you'll see that. OK, well, look, it all makes it just a perfect time to introduce Justin Wolfers, bring him back to the program. He's a very prominent Australian-American economist, a very well-regarded commentator. He's also a professor of public policy and economics at the University of Michigan. Here he is now. Justin Wolfers, welcome back. Mate, it's a pleasure. How do you read the world economy right now? I mean, there's uncertainty everywhere. And if you look at the next few months, it does make for sobering reading. What particular measures do you keep your eyes on as a guide for what might come next? So where are we? We were poised to enter 2026 and for the world to be something only economists could love, which is boring. And it turns out that the script writers over here in the US, in the writer's room, don't like boring. So they decided to punch it up. And obviously, we're looking at the war right now. What the IMF has said so far, and I think they've got it right, is that means for the world as a whole, 2026 will be less good than it otherwise would have been, moderately weak even. So what indicators am I looking at? I am looking at very, very closely at financial markets. And I don't want to sound like an economist who's like, well, stocks up, life good, stocks down, life bad. There's more to life than the stock market. But what I really care about at a moment like this, a time of immense uncertainty, and particularly where we care a lot about where we're going to be in six months time is I want an economic indicator that is forward looking. So if I look at the latest unemployment report, it tells me how many people didn't have a job last month. It's not very helpful for a war and an oil shock and potentially a global shock that's still playing out. And so that's the reason I'm focused very much on financial markets. And Justin, what are the financial markets making of it? They don't seem to have freaked out just yet. Why? Well, it's because I think actually they care deeply. Let me put it this way. You're right to say that, you know, global stocks haven't plummeted. But actually, if you watch it day to day, you'll see a very different play. The play is every time the president escalates, the US market tanks. And as bad as it is for the US, actually, it's even worse for our friends in Europe and Asia, which are much more energy dependent. And every time the president de-escalates, stocks go back up. And it turns out this is the old two-step, which is you escalate, de-escalate. And that's why the level over all is not at sort of terrible, horrible, no good, very bad places. But what it is telling you is, were the president to land on the escalation square, markets are saying they think it would be very, very bad for the world economy. The trouble with watching this soaring stock market, as you're saying, from what I read, there's a lot of people on their phones jumping in retail investors, really who are using it as a true speculative tool, plus the rallies that are occurring, which sort of seesaw up and down on a very narrow range of stocks. So watching from Australia, I wonder if, quite frankly, I'm watching a bunch of amateurs jumping in. So Geraldine, my first ever job was working on the Sydney racetrack. I used to be a bookies runner. And it sounds like you were just criticizing financial markets for being a bunch of degenerate gamblers who can't help but just keep betting, betting, betting. And I tell you what, Ramwick Racecourse definitely is that. And if you think Ramwick's bad, you should go out to Warwick Farm. But it turns out, actually, that the wisdom of that crowd, each of whom you might think of as maybe someone you don't want to invite over for Christmas dinner, that crowd turns out to be remarkably good at picking the winners of horse races. Again, not perfect, but better than the alternative. And here, it's actually altogether different. I want you to maybe back off of thinking about these folks as betting on the stock market as chain-smoking degenerates. And remember that an investment house like Goldman Sachs has dozens of PhDs pouring over the data, that they're getting people on the ground in Iran, that they're looking at satellite photos of what's still working and what's not. Because the thing is, if you can figure out where this war is going 10 minutes a day, a week, a year ahead of the rest, there's billions of dollars in that. And so, these folks, again, a million ways you can criticize them, but there's a lot of people betting a lot of money based on very serious advice. And really, the most important thing is that this is a forward-looking indicator. So, Justin, the phrase I keep reading, and I may have even included it in some of my reports myself, is global recession. Are we heading for a global recession? So, the answer is less, it's more likely we avoid it than we go into one. A slightly better answer, I understand, Lutika, why you'd use that framing, and I've been drawn into it as well. Who cares? Now, by that, I don't care if people lose their livelihoods. What I mean is, I want to move away from the binary thinking towards more continuous thinking. Are we doing worse as a result of this? Yes. War is really, really serious business. And the economic consequences of this war are absolutely first order. I don't want to deny the humanitarian, the ethical, the legal, the foreign affairs implications of it either. But I speak a language, economics, which somehow resonates with people, maybe more than it should at moments like this. But in the US, I get asked day in, day out, what's going with fuel prices, and am I going to have to pay more at the pump? That's only a small part of the economic story. If you force a generation to have to spend more on defence, that fundamentally changes government finances. It changes how much families have left over at the end of the week. The economic, the ways that wars filter through to economies are much broader than the very narrow questions, at the very least, I'm often getting asked in the US. How will increased defence spending affect the global economy, in your view? If we spend money on guns, we're not spending on other stuff. Simple as that. And every member of your audience knows what it means to have a dollar less in their pocket. And it may be we'd spend that dollar on social cohesion. It may also be we spend it on beer and Skittles. Either way, you're doing without something you value and all you're getting is bombs in return. So let's take seriously that and try and figure out how big it is. So we just saw the president submitted his budget for next year. Now, this is a very arcane thing. The president's budget actually turns out not to mean anything. I know that sounds weird, unlike the prime minister, the treasurer's budget back home. But the president is asked to move the American military spend from $1 trillion a year to $1.5 trillion. The difference there is $500 billion. There's roughly 100 million American households. So therefore, the difference is about $5,000 per household. And that's next year. So that's the president's assessment of how much more expensive this increasingly dangerous world will be for Americans, right? And the thing about you don't just spend extra next year and then just, you know, go back to normal the year after. First of all, whatever risks it is he's worried about, presumably stick around. And secondly, once you start doling out money like that, you create a, I believe the term is a military industrial complex. And they hire a ton of lobbyists who come down and tell you that if you spend a dollar less on defense, everything will go terrible. So if it's $5,000 per household and that sticks around for 10 years, now we're talking about $50,000 per household. So in Australian dollars, we're talking about $75,000, $80,000. That's the effect over here. Now, how big would the effect be for Aussies? Well, it depends on what Australia's defense response is. So obviously, energy has been the big immediate shock of this war and its immediate effects for countries like Australia. We've had service stations running out of fuel. We've had the Prime Minister jetting around to Asia and the Middle East shoring up energy supplies. How do you see this global shortfall affecting global economic demand and also supply? Here's the thing. Demand for oil is what economists call inelastic. What does that mean? It means you need it. If I'm going to drive to work tomorrow, I have to get there. So I can't go without. So what we have now is a whole bunch less oil. And how does a market, this is not done by governments, and it's not done through jetting about. It's done by a market. How does a market help us make sense of that? And the answer is, if we've got 12% less oil, we've got to get people to buy 12% less oil. The way we do that is we'll let the price rise. And the thing is, even if the price were to double, I'd still buy enough petrol to get to work. And that's why what sounds like a relatively small disruption to the quantity of oil, 12% of global production, could actually cause the price to double. It's because you need prices to rise a lot before anyone starts to do without. And that's what happens here. So the answer is, if there's less oil, there'll have to be some doing without. How do we decide who does the doing without? Usually, we let prices adjust. So therefore, who does without? It's the folks who get priced out when oil is twice as expensive. There are some ways to adjust that are pretty straightforward. So in the US already, people are reporting families are less likely to go on vacations, three states over. So that's a form of adjustment people can do. Another is, I have an electric bike. I ride my bike to work. And in the short run, which is what we are right now, it's very hard to persuade people to use less petrol. But if we were to enter a world in which petrol would always be expensive, it becomes a lot easier. What do you do? I'm going to buy an electric vehicle next. And the longer this goes on, the more people can make adjustments. And therefore, the less painful the adjustment will be. So the pain that we have at the moment is the peak pain. And you've already seen, I think, electric vehicle sales. There's reports from Europe, electric vehicle sales are up pretty sharply over the past couple of weeks. And so it might lead people to make some of those adjustments. Some of those adjustments, by the way, my environmentalist friends would be very pleased with. We're talking to the Australian-American economist and commentator Justin Wolfers about the state of the global economy. You might remember he made a very considerable contribution to the recent Boyer lectures, particularly about whether Australia's resilient enough to withstand any future shocks. So we keep hearing from our leaders. So in Australia, the government is preparing to hand down the budget. And we've had both the Treasurer, Jim Chalmers, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese repeatedly say, look, even if this war ended tomorrow, the tail, the economic tail is still going to be long. How long? And are we still just talking about oil at that point? Or are we talking about all those other supplies that we've been trying to get through from the Middle East, such as helium and some really important ingredients for things we don't even realise necessarily that we're using? What is it that defines that, Talwin? And how long do you think it really is? So right now, markets are suggesting the tensions could remain high for weeks or months, not years. Now, by the way, we have a long history of underestimating the duration of wars. So don't take optimism too seriously. But if you look at oil price futures, they seem to suggest that oil is going to be high through 2027, 28 and 29. Not as high as it is right now, but higher than it was before the war, substantially higher. So, you know, the shock that persists will be maybe a third as large as it was. We're doing really rough arithmetic, but it'll be about a third of what we're suffering right now for a couple of years. Now, some of that might be because there's been some literal destruction of ports and drilling infrastructure and so on that literally takes time to rebuild. But I also suspect part of what's going on there is, well, actually, if they just get together and they hug it out, lots of things get back to normal, that would be good. But it's also possible they hug it out in a year's time, they're back at it. And all of a sudden, the Middle East feels more dangerous. And what markets are pricing is not this shock, but the possibility that the world has revealed itself to be more dangerous and there'll be future shocks. So that's the lookout for the future part of this. The defence spending that comes out of this, which, as we discussed, I think could be very, very large. It would be realistic to think of that as being high for a decade. The rewiring of global power and of global influence, if, for instance, the American security umbrella becomes unreliable for the Australians, that's incredibly expensive, right? Do you really want to go and set up a military for a country of our size? And do you want to try and do that quickly? We're not there yet, but we've also seen things like the president sort of half walk away from NATO, which does sit and train a lot of really important military spending. And then there are sort of harder things, which is sometimes revealing a vulnerability is just as bad as creating one. And this exercise has revealed the global economy is vulnerable to attacks on the Strait of Hormuz. And it is not the only choke point on the globe. And so now that Iran understands its strength, how will it use it? Now, my guess is one of my favourite things about being Australian is often the rest of the world forgets about us. And that would be marvellous. I mean, it hurts our feelings, but it would be marvellous because if they're in the business of extracting concessions and they come after the Americans and they come after the Europeans and they simply forget that we exist, that would be great. It could be they come after the developed world in a way that really has an effect on Australia. Justin, what is your assessment of the US economy and its ability to withstand these shocks? Issue for who wins a war is a function of how much you can damage the other side, for which the United States is clearly overwhelmingly the world's greatest power and how much damage you can withstand. And that, I think, is a very telling part that the administration refuses to talk about. But the extent of suffering in the United States is A, real and B, substantially less than anywhere else on earth almost. I mean, the Middle East countries that are all rich, they think this is great. But we are roughly speaking, the United States is roughly speaking, energy independent. episodes.title: Is Israel using Lebanon to sabotage peace in the Middle East?
episodes.description: The ink hadn't even dried on the initial US-Iran ceasefire last week when Israel launched an unprecedented bombardment on Lebanon's capital, Beirut.

episodes.title: A Matter of Facts: Wikipedia co-founder on freedom of speech vs disinformation
episodes.description: Is Wikipedia a relic of a more utopian version of the internet? Or is it the citizen-led antidote that we need?

episodes.title: Could Australia and Asia supply our own energy and cut out the Middle East?
episodes.description: The Middle East conflict has triggered a reckoning in global energy supplies.

episodes.title: Can Cubans survive under Trump's fist?
episodes.description: The war in Iran has aroused worldwide fears: what happens if a country runs out of oil? Because of severe US restrictions, Cuba has faced that reality, having been without oil for three months.

title: Health Report with Norman Swan and Dr Preeya Alexander - ABC listen
description: Covering the health stories that make a difference. Dr Norman Swan and Dr Preeya Alexander dissect the latest and breaking news in the medical world.

episodes.title: Can ChatGPT Health tell when you should go to hospital?
episodes.description: Can you trust the advice ChatGPT Health gives about whether you should go to the hospital or not? Who is using GLP-1 weight loss drugs and how common are they? New guidelines for supporting young people with suicidal ideation or who self-harm.

episodes.title: Treating a medical emergency ... in space
episodes.description: When a medical emergency happens in space, how is it treated? And what does life in Antarctica have to teach us about staying healthy on a spaceflight?

episodes.title: What to expect this flu season
episodes.description: Which flu strains are likely to be dominant this flu season - and what's the story with the new nasal spray vaccine? Speaking of sprays ... there's a simple saline spray that might help kids with sleep apnoea avoid surgery.

episodes.title: 3D printing in healthcare
episodes.description: 3D printing is becoming an incredibly versatile modern tool - with scope to apply it to engineering, manufacturing, architecture and design challenges. And it's increasingly being used in ... healthcare.

episodes.title: Ultra-processed foods and behaviour in kids
episodes.description: There's been major buzz in recent years over ultra-processed foods and whether they may be harmful to our health.

episodes.title: MDMA therapy's side effects
episodes.description: MDMA psychotherapy was approved in Australia three years ago. Who's using it and what do we know about treatment side effects? Vaccine reminders can help nudge people back on track, but how the message is framed matters.

episodes.title: Are Australian kids eating too much salt?
episodes.description: Are Australian schoolkids eating too much salt? And does it put them at risk of high blood pressure? A new approach to breast cancer screening based on risk could reduce the number of screens needed for some women.

episodes.title: Can AI chatbots be good therapists?
episodes.description: We know many people are turning to generative AI for health advice, including tips on how to manage stress, anxiety and low mood.

episodes.title: Wait, does exercise help osteoarthritis?
episodes.description: A paper has suggested exercise has minimal, short-term effects on osteoarthritis. But experts are warning people with the condition that they shouldn't stop moving.

episodes.title: Prescribing exercise for mental health
episodes.description: Researchers have pin-pointed the best exercise routines for depression or anxiety symptoms, and they might be equal to medication and talk therapy. Also, why states and territories are making changes to their maternity care guidance for doctors.

title: If You're Listening with Matt Bevan - ABC listen
description: The world is on fire. There’s a coup. Inflation is through the roof, and AI is taking our jobs. What does it all mean? Each week, Matt Bevan explains the biggest story in world news while hiding in his basement from assassins and authoritarian regimes.

episodes.title: When will Australia run out of fuel?
episodes.description: Until now, Australia has been relying on oil that passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war began. But the last tankers to leave the Persian Gulf before the conflict are set to arrive in Australia this week.

episodes.title: How the Iran war exposed Australia's energy mistakes
episodes.description: When the Strait of Hormuz closed, global gas prices doubled seemingly overnight. As one of the world’s biggest gas exporters, the spike should have meant a big payday for Australia.

episodes.title: Trump’s on-again, off-again negotiations with Iran
episodes.description: Matt spent a week camping entirely out of internet reception, so Kara does her best to get him up to speed on all the latest of the US-Iran war negotiations.

episodes.title: The brutal scam compounds of Myanmar
episodes.description: Over the past few years, industrial scam compounds have surged throughout Myanmar, buoyed by the resources of powerful criminal networks, and hidden by the chaos of civil war.

episodes.title: Growing up fighting apartheid
episodes.description: Sisonke Msimang from the new ABC podcast Boycott! joins Matt to share her father’s journey as a revolutionary in the fight against apartheid. Follow If You're Listening on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: What happened last time we ran out of oil
episodes.description: Turn on the tv and you’ll see no shortage of concerned journalists standing at fuel bowsers, shaking their heads at the rising prices.

episodes.title: When Iraq accidentally bombed a U.S. warship
episodes.description: In 1987 the USS Stark became the first U.S. ship sunk by missile fire since World War II. The missiles were fired by Iraq, America’s ally at the time, who claim they did it by mistake. Follow If You're Listening on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: We were warned about the Strait of Hormuz
episodes.description: While governments scramble to find a way around the Strait of Hormuz, a pipeline sits half-finished in the desert that would have solved the problem. So why was it never completed? Follow If You're Listening on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Why Iran is building their own internet
episodes.description: As we’ve been looking into Iran over this month, we’ve had a lot of trouble finding out what is really happening on the ground. That’s due to the concerted and deliberate internet shutdowns carried out by the Iranian regime.

episodes.title: Iran is running out of water
episodes.description: Water is the lifeblood of all civilisations. In Iran, the water is drying up. That disappearance is becoming impossible to ignore, and after decades of mismanagement, the country’s water system is approaching a breaking point.

title: Late Night Live with David Marr - ABC listen
description: Incisive analysis, fearless debates and nightly surprises. Explore the serious, the strange and the profound with David Marr.

episodes.title: Bruce Shapiro's USA, Chernobyl's wildlife thriving and the great convict escape on the Catalpa
episodes.description: Trump contemplates his next move on Iran as the ceasefire deadline looms, while at home his administration is dealing with yet more scandal, this time in the FBI.

episodes.title: Anna Henderson's Canberra, how best to commemorate war, plus Lake Eyre tourists need fuel
episodes.description: Our regular Canberra correspondent on the latest polling, and Independent David Pocock's new focus on taxing gas.

episodes.title: A Jewish Australian lawyer reckons with state violence. Plus, can corporate scandals be good for the world?
episodes.description: The Melbourne legal scholar Marika Sosnowski spent many years researching violence and the law in Syria. Now she reckons with her own family's proximity to state violence in 1950s Palestine.

episodes.title: Ian Dunt's UK, the Colombo plan, and AI publishing scams
episodes.description: Ian Dunt examines what Viktor Orban's loss in Hungary means for the EU and looks at questions around Donald Trump's mental capacity.

episodes.title: Jon Lee Anderson on Trump's Cuba threats, plus how chokepoints like Hormuz have shaped history
episodes.description: Cuba's leader is defiant in the face of the country's worst humanitarian crisis in decades, while President Trump hints at inflicting more pain.

episodes.title: Australia's fuel import dependency, gay conservatives backing Trump, plus damaged treasures in Iran
episodes.description: Professor Mark Kenny reflects on Australia's record fuel price hike and the Australian government's unfolding response.

episodes.title: The making of poet A.D. Hope, Australian literary giant
episodes.description: Alec Derwent Hope (1907–2000) was one of Australia's most acclaimed poets. His first collection was not published until he was 48 years old, but its release cemented his reputation as the pre-eminent Australian poet of his time.

episodes.title: Attacks on culture in the USA, plus the secret life of famous author Daniel Defoe
episodes.description: Pulitzer prize-winning art critic Sebastian Smee, looks at the state of the arts in Trump's America, and the story of Daniel Defoe's secret life as a spy, against Scottish independence, in the early 1700s, before he became the author of the famous…

episodes.title: Bruce Shapiro's USA, antibiotic resistance in India, plus Marralwanga's bark paintings
episodes.description: Bruce Shaprio on the US President's latest ultimatum for Iran. Prof.Assa Doron reveals how India has become the global epicentre for the world's antibiotic resistance problem.

episodes.title: Henry Reynolds turns Australian history upside down
episodes.description: The writing of Australian history has tended to focus on the south-eastern corner of the continent, but the story of colonisation north of the Tropic of Capricorn paints a vastly different picture of this country, its people, politics and ambitions.

title: No One Saw It Coming with Marc Fennell - ABC listen
description: The bit players, the unexpected twists, the turning point you missed. Join Walkley award-winner Marc Fennell as he uncovers the incredible moments that changed the course of history.

episodes.title: Clogged sink doomed a space mission
episodes.description: It’s 1926 and two men are working in a lab trying to create antifreeze. Instead, they make a thick, black goo that stinks out the lab and blocks the sink.

episodes.title: Ancient Greek built a steam engine for dinner parties
episodes.description: Long before steam trains, before factories, before the Industrial Revolution, someone figured out how to turn steam into motion.

episodes.title: She gave her son smallpox. Her bet paid off.
episodes.description: It was one of the deadliest diseases known to humankind. And just 50 years ago it was officially eradicated. But there’s someone missing from the story of smallpox.

episodes.title: Cocaine wine: The Pope’s energy drink
episodes.description: If you looked at it, you wouldn’t bat an eyelid, but this red wine had something in it that today could land you in jail. It was drunk and endorsed by presidents, royalty and even popes and made its maker a millionaire.

episodes.title: A horse race and a murderer invented cinema
episodes.description: Before cinema, before Hollywood, before we even understood how to make pictures move, there was a man constantly reinventing himself. He was a bookseller, a photographer, an alleged fraud and eventually, a killer.

episodes.title: Starving for freedom: The prison death that changed Ireland
episodes.description: As the Irish Revolution raged year after year, there was a space that the British didn’t expect to become places of revolution - prisons.

episodes.title: Let slaves dance: The secret of New Orleans jazz
episodes.description: When you put on a jazz record, what do you hear? Beyond the trumpet and the sax of course... Well etched into that vinyl and living in that music is a long story that dates back 300 years to a dusty public square where slaves would sing and dance.

episodes.title: She faked insanity. Then became a star.
episodes.description: She was put into an insane asylum at the age of 20. Ten days later she was a celebrity and two years later she had cemented a legacy that would last centuries. But Nellie Bly was not insane. She faked it all. But why?

episodes.title: The mafia bar riot that sparked gay pride
episodes.description: 28 June 1969 was a regular Saturday night at the Stonewall Inn. Until it wasn’t.

episodes.title: The royal roots of French fries
episodes.description: ‘Would you like fries with that?’ It’s a question you’ve likely been asked countless times. But what if the only reason French fries are so popular throughout the West today is because of a Queen who lost her head during the French Revolution?

title: Not Stupid with Julia Baird and Jeremy Fernandez - ABC listen
description: Julia Baird and Jeremy Fernandez chat about the stories you're obsessed with, the stuff you've missed and the things that matter.

episodes.title: Trump's oil advice and a legal ruling on social media
episodes.description: As Australia and many other countries continue to feel the effects of fuel shortages due to the closure of the straight of Hormuz, US President Donald Trump hits out in a Truth Social post at American allies saying: "Go get your own oil!"

episodes.title: Let them eat cake
episodes.description: Jules and Jez chat about dinner table etiquette, the correct way to eat cake, random acts of kindness and Lisa's antidote to the manosphere, the nannasphere.

episodes.title: Could China benefit from the Iran war?
episodes.description: Many countries around the world are feeling the effects of fuel shortages due to the war in Iran.

episodes.title: The bikers helping abused kids feel safe

episodes.title: Fuel panic, the manosphere and the truth about Banksy
episodes.description: As people panic buy petrol, questions are being asked about whether Australia has enough fuel stockpiled and how we can secure our future.

episodes.title: What's Chalamet's beef with ballet and opera?
episodes.description: As the Oscars get underway, the internet is still in outrage mode following actor Timothée Chalamet's comments about 'no one caring about' ballet and opera anymore.

episodes.title: Iranian soccer players escape minders to stay in Australia
episodes.description: In the middle of the night five members of the Lionesses, the Iranian women's soccer team, escaped their minders to stay in Australia.

episodes.title: Boredom, phones and electric shocks
episodes.description: Would you give yourself an electric shock to stave off boredom? Or do you never get bored anymore because you're too busy doom-scrolling? Jules and Jez chat about boredom, phones and the highs and lows of raising small humans.

episodes.title: Trump's war, Kyle and Jackie O and Quiet Queers
episodes.description: As Trump continues to flout international law and doubles down on the war on Iran, the regime names Ayatollah Khamenei's successor. But the question is can regime change actually be achieved?

episodes.title: The "fertilization president"
episodes.description: Trump wants to boost the US birth rate and is the self-proclaimed “fertilization president"... if that's enough to make you shudder, keep in mind that his government has approved paid parental leave, which is a positive step.

And so when we divide things into fruit and vegetables, because I went and looked, I went down a bit of a rabbit hole. I looked at the Australian healthy eating guidelines. I looked at some research that looked at intake of fruit and vegetables, and it's very much self-reported and kind of like, it's like a cultural interpretation of what a fruit is in Australia based on the way we eat them. Going back to the Australian guidelines for healthy eating, we are recommended to have five serves of vegetables and two serves of fruit every day. Almost no one meets those guidelines. More people meet the fruit intake guidelines than the vegetable intake guidelines, which is probably a volume thing as much as anything else. Fruit, in our cultural perception of what a fruit is, is often a little bit more portable. You can chuck an apple in your bag. I guess there's nothing stopping you chucking a cucumber in your bag and nibbling on that throughout the day. But that's the recommendation. What we tend to ignore in the nutritional guidelines is the fact that you cook vegetables. There's a cuisine attached to them. So you shouldn't necessarily think of vegetables as being raw because in the cuisine, particularly the Mediterranean cuisine, probably just by accident through time, it produces very important bioactive compounds, which help your immune system, et cetera, et cetera. I knew you were going to say that story. I knew you were going to talk about tomatoes with olive oil because you always do. And I love that you're consistent. In other words, the mind diet's not helping my mind because I'm repeating things. I'm forgetting I told you that story. This is good stuff that bears repeating. But I was cooking some fruit on the weekend. I had some stone fruit that was going to go off. I love stewed fruit. I have it on my yogurt in the morning. Well, I had it on my yogurt this morning. Because generally, when you cook fruit for the purposes of, I'm not going to put all the caveats around it again, when we cook what we usually think of as fruit in Australia, sweet, we'll often cook it with a bit of sugar, a bit of vanilla. Like you're cooking it to be a sweeter dish. You're still taking in all the fiber and presumably the antioxidants and whatever that it's in that fruit. But what you're likely to have done by cooking fruit, particularly if it's at a high heat for longer, is you're going to be destroying the vitamin C in it. I think that the evidence is stronger for vegetables, different colored vegetables. But there is evidence, for example, that the redness in watermelon is pretty good for you and has bioactive compounds in that. And you don't often stew watermelon. That's true. And so we kind of went through, this is not exhaustive, things that we usually think of as getting from fruit, vitamin C, potassium, antioxidants, bioactive compounds, natural sugars, if that's something you want or not. Fiber is a big one. And for all of the things that you can get from fruit, so vitamin C, obviously we think of citrus fruit, strawberries, guavas. You can get that in spades from things like kale, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, basically every vegetable. We think about bananas as a source of potassium. You can get that from potatoes, sweet potatoes, baby spinach. Antioxidants basically taste the rainbow. As you and Priya are always saying on the Health Report, Priya loves talking about eating rainbows. If you're having that variety of colours in the foods that we're eating, whether it's fruit or vegetables, that's good. title: ABC Business Daily with Carrington Clarke and Alan Kohler - ABC listen
description: The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. Analysing the stories moving share markets, shaping industries and affecting the Australian economy. Monday to Thursday, ABC Senior Business Correspondent, Carrington Clarke, examines the biggest business news with ABC's specialist reporters. From finance to AI technology and politics, the team will break down what happened, why it matters and what it might mean for you and your financial future. On Fridays, trusted Australian financial journalist Alan Kohler hosts an in-depth interview with the decisions-makers, innovators and strategists who are shaping the economy. 'That’s Business with Alan Kohler', invites well-known CEOs, entrepreneurs and politicians in for a deep dive into the tough lessons learned and unspoken rules driving Australian business. Host Carrington Clarke is a former economist, ABC North America correspondent from Washington DC and East Asia correspondent from Seoul, He previously worked as a Sky News Journalist and Fairfax Media editor. He has also reported for ABC Investigations’ flagship current affairs television program ‘7.30’ and ‘The Business.’ Host Alan Kohler AM is a former editor of The Age, The Australian Financial Review (AFR) and a columnist for The Sydney Morning Herald and Chanticleer in AFR. He was also the business editor for ABC Investigations’ flagship current affairs television program ‘7.30’ and the host of ‘Inside Business.’ For more sharp insights, clear explanations, and business news coverage you can trust, hit follow or favourite to add new episodes of ABC Business Daily and That's Business with Alan Kohler to your playlist, on ABC listen app, or wherever you get your podcasts.

If it's viewed that he's installed this guy and, you know, he's one of his sort of cronies, then that kind of reduces the impact of him having a scapegoat, someone he can criticise and say, well, I want lower interest rates, it's not my fault.
So that kind of relationship between the government and the central bank, I think, in a way can give the government a potential scapegoat if the central bank is considered to be independent.
Donald Trump has, unlike other politicians, doesn't pretend that he doesn't have a strong interest in the way interest rates go.
And most politicians are careful to not step over those traditional boundaries between the political side, the U.S. administration and the independence of the Federal Reserve.
But yes, I think it would be very difficult for Kevin Walsh to walk that line without upsetting Donald Trump.
And again, context is important here.
Jerome Powell was Donald Trump's pick.
You know, this is a guy who he appointed to the role and he still felt very free to criticise.
And yes, there is this personal connection between Donald Trump and Ronald Lauder.
But yeah, it remains to be seen whether or not that personal relationship will be more important than having someone who he can blame if he's unhappy with the way the economy is performing.
Steph, one to watch and we'll see whether or not he's approved.
But thank you so much for joining us on ABC Business Daily.
That's it for today's episode of ABC Business Daily.
We'll be back with another episode tomorrow.
And if you haven't listened to it already, remember that our latest Fuelcast episode is already in your feed for this morning, right before this one.

episodes.title: Fuelcast: A shipment secured
episodes.description: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Energy Minister Chris Bowen have announced four additional cargoes of diesel have been secured for Australia. It’s an additional 200 million litres of diesel, coming from South Korea, Brunei and Malaysia.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. Welcome to FuelCast. I'm Carrington Clark and this is your source to stay on top of the numbers behind the ongoing energy crisis. It's Wednesday, April the 22nd. We're recording mid-morning. Let's dig in. The price of Brent crude has risen to US$99 a barrel. And since we last checked in, the national average price of unleaded has dropped to $1.98 per litre. And the national average price of diesel has dropped to $2.88 per litre. Today I'm joined by Ian Verinder to dig into today's major energy headlines. Good morning, Ian. Good morning, Carrington. Ian, we've just been watching the Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Energy Minister Chris Bowen. Tell us about these four additional cargoes of diesel being secured for Australia through BP, Viva Energy and Export Finance Australia. They say it's an additional 200 million litres of diesel and the cargoes have come from South Korea, Brunei and Malaysia. Ian, does this fill you with any optimism? Well, it's better than not having it, let's face it. And, you know, we as a nation have the highest consumption of diesel per person than any other country on the planet. And the reason for that is we're, you know, a massive mining country and a huge agricultural country as well. So we require vast amounts of diesel to keep our industry going. And it's a big continent with a relatively small population, which requires a lot of transport, intercity transport, all run by diesel. There's a percentage of cars around about, I think, 10% of passenger vehicles run on diesel as well. And those vehicles, they're subject to what's known as what economists call elasticity of demand. You know, if the price gets too high, you don't drive your car. You catch the train, you walk, you ride a push bike. But when you're, you know, driving a Mack truck from one city to another, or you're running BHP's, you know, iron ore division up in the Pilbara, you have no option but to keep using the same amount of fuel regardless of the price. And so we need supply. And that's what we're concentrating on at the moment. Supply, not so much price. Yeah, that's right. So it's good to not be obviously caught short. The worst nightmare would be for the Bowsers to run dry or there not be enough supply of diesel, as you say, to fuel our mining industry or our agricultural industry. But we don't actually know how much is being paid for this diesel. And so we don't really know what that means for the price of diesel here at home, do we? Well, we don't know anything really. It's totally opaque and look at the moment and quite rightly, the government is focused on supply, just making sure we've got enough fuel to keep the country running. And the price factor, well, that's being pushed into the background. But there's broader implications than simply, you know, how much it's going to cost to fill up the truck or fill up the tractor or whatever it is. I mean, this is going to have a really large effect on the Australian economy down the track because it is going to really feed into the inflationary forces that will probably push the Reserve Bank into raising interest rates and really detract from our growth. So, you know, at the moment, we don't really even know what the price of the spot price of oil is. You know, everybody keeps talking about, oh, the price of Brent is now, what is it today? About $100 a barrel. But if you wanted to buy a barrel of oil on the spot market, like you wanted it right now, you'll probably be paying $140 to $145 because that contract that we keep talking about is for delivery down the track in a couple of months' time. And most markets are pricing in a resolution of the conflict at that stage. But the price of oil right now is actually much, much higher than the price we're quoting. And now on top of this. I believe, so Citi did some analysis of this, which was quite fascinating, suggesting that Australia is paying, they think, between $15 and $25 a barrel above that Brent crude price, which is a much bigger price premium than we would usually be paying. Oh, absolutely. And, you know, as we're saying, this is all about securing supply and forget the price. And the reason why we can secure the supply is because we can afford to. You know, firstly, we've got that leverage in terms of gas. You know, we can say to these countries that with liquid fuels that are producing liquid fuels, you want our gas, we want your liquid fuels, you better reciprocate. But the other factor, of course, is that we're a rich nation and we can afford to do this. If you're not a rich nation and you can't afford to do this, this is going to lead to enormous economic problems for, you know, particularly through Southeast Asia. Yeah, because unfortunately, it is a bit of a zero-sum game at the moment. If Australia is getting this diesel, it means someone else can't get the diesel. Yeah. And if those other places, for example, Southeast Asia or South Asia, which seem to be experiencing this very acutely already real shortages when it comes to refined fuels, that means they're not going to be able to produce the things that they would otherwise produce. That might be agriculture. It might be manufactured goods. And those things are going to flow through to the broader economy, aren't they? And that's going to force up inflation elsewhere. Australia is part of the global economy. That's also going to have repercussions here. Yeah. And, I mean, I think it's one of the issues the IMF was worried about, you know, that they articulated last week about a global recession, a downturn. I mean, this is clearly going to have a major impact on global growth and on inflation as well. And, look, we are in the fortunate position that we can afford to do this. But what do you do? I mean, if you're the prime minister of Australia and you've got the opportunity to try and save your constituency, well, that's what you're going to do. And it's, you know, really, you know, forget about everybody else. It's kind of every man for himself at the moment. How does this fit the messaging? On one hand, the government has been at pains to say Australia doesn't have a shortage of fuel. We still have as much fuel in the country as we had before this situation unfolded. But now that they are going out and doing live press conferences about the arrival of ships with extra supply, does that create a bit of confusion in the eyes of people about exactly how big a crisis is this? I think what they're trying to do is to avoid what we saw in the early part of this conflict where people were panic buying. This is all about, you know, calming down the community. Don't go out there and buy more than you need. There's plenty coming in here. Look at these ships that are about to arrive. And we're seeing that at prices at the Bowser as well. You know, the less demand that we've got. And there's numbers that were released last week essentially showing that Australians are now buying fuel less often. So I think what was happening was people would fill up their tank, drive for 10 minutes down the roads. If they saw another petrol station, put more in. So there's less transactions going on. So I think people are starting to feel a little more comfortable that there is enough to get by, that we're not going to run out. But, you know, at what price? Ian, thank you so much for joining us on Fuelcast. Pleasure. And we'll have another episode of ABC Business Daily for you later today. Make sure you're following the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts so you never miss an episode. And we'll be back in your feeds with all things Fuel on Friday. Bye, Ian. Thanks, Kerrickson. Thank you.
