episodes.title: Why hasn't the price of natural gas spiked?
episodes.description: When Russia launched its full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it sent the price of natural gas soaring - and Australian consumers faced steep hikes in their electricity bills.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. What would you do if someone you loved vanished and you discover the person she's been living with isn't who they said they were? I'm Dominique Bayens, host of Expanse, The Nan Up 4. Is he, you know, a murderer? A self-styled cult leader. It's just not knowing the emptiness, really. That just kills you. This is the bizarre story of The Nan Up 4. Binge all episodes now. Search Expanse on ABC Listen and iView. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine back in 2022, it sent the price of natural gas soaring and Australian consumers faced steep hikes in their electricity bills. But this time around, when once again war has sent the international price of gas skywards, Australia has remained relatively insulated. So what's the difference this time around? And a major tech announcement with long-serving Apple CEO Tim Cook stepping down and anointing his successor. Welcome to ABC Business Daily. I'm Carrington Clark. And I'm the ABC's Chief Business Correspondent, Ian Verinder. Ian, thank you so much for joining us. We've been very focused, obviously, on the soaring price of petrol and diesel. But here in Australia, we're not as focused on the soaring international price of gas. This is something that's obviously preoccupying people, both in East Asia and in Europe, where they have seen a real impact on the price that they're paying for their gas. Why aren't we paying increased prices here in Australia in the way that we did during that Russian invasion of Ukraine? Well, I think it gets down to the amount of power that the gas exporters actually have. And if you've cast your mind back to 2022, I mean, what everyone was focused on, the cost of living crisis. And what was really underpinning that cost of living crisis? I mean, everyone was just up in arms about electricity bills that were doubling each year. Extraordinary rises. I know. And what really drove that was the price of gas. And the reason for that is, even though a lot of our electricity is generated by coal, a lot of it by renewables, and only a smallish part by gas, gas is the swing factor. Gas is what economists would term the marginal cost producer, right? So essentially, when you can't generate anything more from coal, when your renewables are offline, you switch on the gas to generate that last little bit. And because it's the marginal cost producer, it actually sets the price. And so as a result of that, our electricity bills soar. Now, if you look to across the country, New South Wales and Queensland use a lot less gas than they do in, say, Victoria, right? So Victorians use a lot of gas for household heating, for cooking. And so they were getting the double whammy. They were getting huge electricity bills, plus these massive increases in price for their gas supply. Now, this time around, it's suddenly not happening. Not only are we not getting the price hikes that you would have expected if you use the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine as a base model, we're not getting those price hikes, we're actually getting cheaper gas than we had just a few months ago. So this does seem strange. Back in 2022, there was a lot of kind of political pressure and public pressure about gas companies extorting, it was some of the language used, the Australian consumer, because they were making huge profits by selling gas from Australia into this global market. And they were instead sending that gas offshore, even though there was huge demand for it here. Why hasn't that played at this point? Well, they were actually siphoning gas out of the domestic system, right, and then sending it offshore because the prices they could get offshore were just extraordinary. And so as a result of that, you've got massive price rises here. But even before the Russian invasion of Ukraine, I mean, we had, you know, there was uproar across the country because gas prices, you know, before on the East Coast we're talking about here, before the export market opened up and around about 2010, 2012, gas prices were about $3 a gigajoule. We're now just, you know, in heaven because they're $10, right? But during that war, they went up to above $20 a gigajoule. So just massive price hikes. And that had, you know, three successive prime ministers try to intervene to stop this. Now, you had Malcolm Turnbull with his ADGSM, I think it was, what is it, Australian Domestic Gas Supply Mechanism. You had Scotty Morrison with his big stick. Do you remember the big stick? And then you had Anthony Albanese with price controls. None of it worked. None of it worked. But suddenly it's all working now. Taking one step back, because I think this is a thing a lot of people struggle to understand, because we have a situation where prior to Australia becoming a major exporter of gas, we actually had less gas supply. We weren't getting as much gas out of the ground. But yet then when we started exporting gas, so there's more supply, people think, well, if you've got more supply, don't the fundamentals tell you that you should actually have lower prices? But the issue was by Australia becoming a gas exporter and having these facilities, we actually became a price taker for the international price. So whatever was kind of the international price, and when we saw a big spike, suddenly Australians' consumers were paying that price instead of just having whatever the domestic supply and demand curve gave you. That's part of the problem. And that's absolutely right. So we've gone from having an oversupply in the domestic market to we're now hooked into the global market and we're paying their prices. But there was a fundamental fault in the whole process. And that was we had three exporters out of the East Coast market. And the Santos-led consortium decided to double the size of their processing plant on Curtis Island, which is just off the coast of Gladstone in Queensland. They were going to have what's known as a one-train plant. And then they decided, nah, the other two have got two-train plants. We're pretty sure we've got enough gas in the ground to cover this. We'll do a two-train plant. And so they doubled the size of their plant. To justify that, they then sold export contracts to Asian buyers. And then when they started, actually after the plant was built, or while the plant was being built, they tried to source the extra supply of gas and they failed. So they didn't have the supply of gas to justify the size of their plant. And they'd sold far too much in the way of forward contracts to Asian buyers. So that left them with a shortfall. And how did they fill their export contracts? They went into the domestic market and bought gas out of the domestic market. So they essentially raided the domestic market, took gas out, and that forced the price of Australian domestic gas much higher. So let's cut to today. You would have expected, as you said, if you're following the playbook of how this worked last time around, last time we saw a war cause the price of gas to spike linked to the oil price spike that we've seen. This time it doesn't happen. And it doesn't appear to have been explicitly because of government telling them they couldn't do it. Why is it that we haven't seen a massive rise in the price of gas for Australians? Well, it's one of those extraordinary events, I guess, where a threat, right, that's overhanging everything, has more impact than the actual law that's about to be imposed. So after years of just, you know, outrage and uproar, particularly from domestic manufacturers here who use a lot of energy, but also from households across the country, the government last year threw caution to the wind and went, right, okay, East Coast, we're going to have a gas reservation policy. It works on the West Coast. Why can't it work here? And by that stage, the three exporters basically threw up their hands and went, oh, okay. So late last year, the government said, we're imposing this. We've gone through the whole consultation process, which of course was, I think the decision was made before the consultation process started. We're going to impose this tax. Now, here's the general model that we're going to impose, which will be that each of the three exporters will have to be providing gas into the domestic system. That's going to be very hard for Santos, which has got the shortfall. The other two, one's run by Origin, the other one's run by Shell. They have consistently provided gas into the domestic system. It's the Santos consortium that sucks it out. So they've said, this is going to be the general model, but we've got to work out how the whole thing works. Now, because that's probably not going to be worked out until later this year, each of the exporters is really just walking on eggshells at the moment because they don't want to be penalized or hit with some massive model that is going to really stop them from making money. And right now, you've got this shortage around the world because of what's happened in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz being closed. So they don't know what to do. Now, on top of that, there is also the Greens, which have forced a select Senate hearing into the tax arrangements around our big gas exports. The fact that, you know, this is a huge industry that exports multiple billions of dollars worth of gas each year and pays, well, what a lot of people would argue would be an insignificant amount of tax on that. So they've got this double whammy of here's the gas reservation policy, which is yet to be properly formulated, and the potential for windfall profits tax. So you mentioned the fact that there's already a reservation system in place for the West in Western Australia. There isn't on the East Coast. How did that come about? Why do we have two different systems operating within Australia? I think people always find that kind of confusing, the role of the state versus the federal government. And how is it working in Western Australia? And these concerns raised by people about a reservation policy and what that potentially means to the viability of these export projects, just give us how, what the experience in Western Australia has shown actually occurs if you reserve a certain amount of the gas. Well, firstly, I mean, everybody thinks that resources in the ground belong to the Commonwealth and belong to the people of Australia, which is kind of true, but it actually gets down to a state basis because Australia is a federation of states. And so it's the, not Australians per se, but the people who live within the states. Those resources belong to the states and shouldn't be governed for people who are just currently alive, but for future generations as well. Now, how does it work? Well, and how did that come about? Well, the East Coast gas exports come from gas that's supplied out of Bass Strait, out of New South Wales, out of Queensland. So the gas all gets, you know, comes from all the, each of those three states. So obviously there was difficulty in trying to come to some kind of arrangement between the three states. To get some kind of policy there. But it was actively explored and decided, this is the Gillard government. They were already under pressure from iron ore taxes and the resources rent tax on iron ore. We've seen how effective a campaign can be from resource companies when there's ever a suggestion that there might be a higher rate of tax imposed on their exports. And they very successfully managed to force the then Labor government to junk that resources rent tax, come up with a second best option, which was then completely thrown out when Tony Abbott became prime minister. So the Labor government at the time looked at it and said, no, we're not going to have a reservation policy here. Now, interestingly, over in the West, I have spoken to the then Premier, Alan Carpenter, who was the person who imposed that tax. And he told me this story about how he was sitting in a room with, you know, the chief executive, senior executives from the biggest resources companies around the world about, this is really around Northwest Shelf and all of the offshore gas projects that happen there. And apparently at one stage, you know, he said, look, we're going to have this gas reservation policy just to ensure that there's enough gas for Western Australians into the future. And so for every bit of gas you export, there's going to be 10% of that reserved for Western Australians. He said somebody thumped the table and said, there will not be one molecule of gas that will be reserved for domestic use. If that's the case, the deal's off. And he said, well, if that's the situation, ladies and gentlemen, I'm sorry to have wasted your time. Meeting's over. Next day, there's a knock at the door. We've gone through the numbers again. We can make it stack up. We can make it work, yeah. And so it's worked quite well for Western Australia. And you've only got to look at that Ukraine crisis a few years back and gas prices in the West, despite it exporting far more than we do here on the East Coast, gas prices in the West were substantially below what the East Coast gas prices were. And unfortunately, there's no pipeline between Western Australia and the East Coast, which would have equalized the prices somewhat. You point out in your article, this is a great kind of, I guess, microcosm of how this has played out within Australia, between the East and the West, where we used to have on the East Coast of Australia, a fertilizer production business fed by gas, urea, which is one of the things that we're now struggling to get enough of because of the interruption to global supply. And they weren't able to get the gas at a price that could make it still stack up on the East Coast, which is obviously a major, creates sovereign risk for Australia if we can't produce it here at home. How has that now played out with the different policies about gas reservation in the East Coast versus the West? Look, I think it's going to be a lot easier for businesses to source domestic gas supplies at a reasonable price. You know, during the period when I think it was when the Labor government had imposed that price cap of, say, $12 a gigajoule, and particularly through the Ukraine crisis, I think gas prices went to about $23 a gigajoule if you're a business trying to lock in long-term supplies. So it was just uneconomical for most big industrial users. And you're talking about smelters. You're talking about all sorts of, you know, massive uses of energy here. But, you know, the urea example is just a great example of where everything went wrong. I mean, here we are, one of the world's biggest agricultural exporters. So we have, there's a ready home market for fertilizer. And we've got the key ingredient to make it as well. So why wouldn't you be making it here for your own market and then exporting, you know, whatever is left over? But nothing. This is the whole idea of value adding on the kind of resource. You've got the gas on the ground. You're also trying to produce agricultural goods. Why would you be sending the gas overseas to a river? You've got the market and the ingredients. I mean, it's just a no-brainer, really, isn't it? And yet it went broke because they couldn't source the key material to make it. Because, you know, urea is essentially nitrogen and hydrogen combined. And you use nitrogen out of the air and hydrogen out of the gas. You combine that and, Bob's your uncle, you've got urea. And, you know, so there's all these other countries that can make it. But we surely should have been the country making more than anybody else and exporting it. And, I mean, you know, you think the Middle East is now a major producer of urea. And this is where we're getting most of ours from. There's not a lot of agriculture around that part of the world. It's a bit dry. And, you know, so it's just extraordinary that that plant in, what is it, Gibson Island in Brisbane, that it shut down at that point. What do you make of this current inquiry into the gas industry here in Australia? Coming ahead of the budget, is there any chance that the government, given the scar tissue involved from previous attempts, which we've spoken about, of taxing the resource industry? Do you think there's the political will for the Labor Party to actually impose a higher tax on the gas industry? Or do you think they would be scared off doing that because of the likely fierce opposition? Until now, there's always been a real problem with trying to increase tax on miners. And, you know, we saw that during the Gillard era when, you know, the tax on iron ore, which should have been, again, a no-brainer. And even in the past few years, we've seen attempts to modernise the resources rent tax on petroleum. Australia was a groundbreaker in doing that when Paul Keating, as Treasurer, introduced that. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine back in 2022,
it sent the price of natural gas soaring
and Australian consumers faced steep hikes in their electricity bills.
But this time around, when once again war has sent
the international price of gas skywards,
So what's the difference this time around?
And a major tech announcement with long-serving Apple CEO Tim Cook
stepping down and anointing his successor.
And I'm the ABC's Chief Business Correspondent, Ian Verinder.
Ian, thank you so much for joining us.
We've been very focused, obviously, on the soaring price of petrol and diesel.
But here in Australia, we're not as focused on the soaring international price of gas.
This is something that's obviously preoccupying people, both in East Asia and in Europe,
where they have seen a real impact on the price that they're paying for their gas.
Why aren't we paying increased prices here in Australia in the way that we did during that Russian invasion of Ukraine?
Well, I think it gets down to the amount of power that the gas exporters actually have.
And if you've cast your mind back to 2022, I mean, what everyone was focused on,
And what was really underpinning that cost of living crisis?
I mean, everyone was just up in arms about electricity bills that were doubling each year.
And what really drove that was the price of gas.
And the reason for that is, even though a lot of our electricity is generated by coal,
a lot of it by renewables, and only a smallish part by gas, gas is the swing factor.
Gas is what economists would term the marginal cost producer, right?
So essentially, when you can't generate anything more from coal,
when your renewables are offline, you switch on the gas to generate that last little bit.
And because it's the marginal cost producer, it actually sets the price.
And so as a result of that, our electricity bills soar.
Now, if you look to across the country,
New South Wales and Queensland use a lot less gas than they do in, say, Victoria, right?
So Victorians use a lot of gas for household heating, for cooking.
And so they were getting the double whammy.
They were getting huge electricity bills,
plus these massive increases in price for their gas supply.
Now, this time around, it's suddenly not happening.
Not only are we not getting the price hikes that you would have expected
if you use the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine as a base model,
we're not getting those price hikes, we're actually getting cheaper gas
than we had just a few months ago.
Back in 2022, there was a lot of kind of political pressure and public pressure
about gas companies extorting, it was some of the language used,
the Australian consumer, because they were making huge profits
by selling gas from Australia into this global market.
And they were instead sending that gas offshore,
even though there was huge demand for it here.

Well, they were actually siphoning gas out of the domestic system, right,
and then sending it offshore because the prices they could get offshore
And so as a result of that, you've got massive price rises here.

there was uproar across the country because gas prices, you know,
before on the East Coast we're talking about here, before the export market opened up

So whatever was kind of the international price, and when we saw a big spike,

I mean, when you think of the size of these companies, we almost have lost sight about how massive they now are.
I think Apple's now the third biggest company in the world.
It's worth $4 trillion, around $4 trillion US dollars.
I mean, this is, there are many, there are not many countries with that kind of GDP, right?
This is such a massive operation.
And now you've got this new 50-year-old taking the helm.
It'll be fascinating to watch how it goes.
Ian, thank you so much for joining us.
That is it for today's episode of ABC Business Daily.
We'll be back with both a Fuelcast episode with Ian Verinder, the man sitting with me right now,
and another episode of ABC Business Daily tomorrow.
To make sure you don't miss out, make sure you're following us on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts,
and I will catch you later.

episodes.title: Will the budget bring us 'back to the future?'
episodes.description: After a brief window of hope that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz would start to normalise, a harsher reality has kicked in. With both Iran and the US firing on vessels, the oil price is surging once again.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. I really am. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. After a brief window of hope that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz would start to normalise, a harsh reality has kicked in, with both Iran and the United States firing on vessels and causing the oil price to surge once again. Meanwhile, there's fevered speculation about what the government could unveil in this year's federal budget due to be released in early May. Could the capital gains discount be in for a major overhaul? Welcome to ABC Business Daily. I'm Carrington Clarke. And I'm the ABC's Business Editor, Michael Yander. Michael, we've seen another major shift in the energy markets. At the end of last week, we saw oil prices plunge because of declarations about the Strait of Hormuz from both the United States and Iran that it was open once again. And now the price has bounced back up because of multiple incidences around the Strait. That means it's basically closed off. What do you make of it? And what does it mean for the global economy? Well, the first thing I'd say, Carrington, is I was surprised how little the oil price bounced. I mean, it's up 6% as the time we're recording about 11 a.m. in Sydney. I would have thought the rise would be much bigger given that very few ships have still made it through the Strait of Hormuz. I mean, there is no oil and gas really coming out or certainly not much more than there was before this apparent ceasefire. Yeah. Does that indicate that actually people think this is once again a temporary blip and that we will see enough desire to actually get the Strait open up again, that this is only going to be closed for a temporary period? Yeah, it does seem like markets continue to bet on hope and faith, hope that the Strait will reopen soon in the next two or three weeks before the oil crunch gets really bad, and faith in, I don't know, President Trump and the Iranian regime to come to a settlement when they seem poles apart on certain key elements. Disarmament around the spoils of the Strait of Hormuz and whether there will be a toll and who would get it. Yeah, and including whether or not Iran is actually going to show up and be part of these negotiations. But you're right to point out we saw what a 9%, 10% fall in the price of oil when Donald Trump declared the Strait would be open. That was backed up by Iranian statements. And yet we've only seen the price increase about half that amount. And that is despite the fact that we've seen live firing by Iran on those ships it considers to be connected to the kind of Western alliance, even though we haven't actually seen a Western alliance really come together on this particular war. And America actually seizing an Iranian flagged ship, which is quite an extraordinary development. It would seem to be a major escalation from where we're at. And yet, as you say, the oil price today at 11am is about $96 US a barrel for those Brent futures. I mean, it's actually been over $100 for a lot of this conflict. So it's still lower than it has been and well off those peaks, close to $120 a barrel. We saw that extraordinary drop in the price of oil on the announcement that the Strait of Hormuz was open, although that appears to have been a very small window. A bit premature. Premature or very short window. But we've also seen over recent weeks this extraordinary rally in the stock market. We're at record highs in the United States, just off record highs here in Australia. What is it about the current situation that is giving so much confidence to investors? And is it divorced from the reality that's happening with the war? Or is there other factors at play? To be honest, it puzzles me and it puzzles a lot of market analysts. There are a lot of quite rational people out there who are saying, well, markets are trading on the hope and the upside. And there is an upside. Look, I think a lot of sensible market analysts do acknowledge that artificial intelligence profits are starting to show up. And that's, you know, lowered fears that AI was a bubble and getting ahead of itself. At least some of the big companies involved are actually starting to make money out of it. So maybe those valuations are justified. But we're still facing a huge tail risk that the entire energy system of the world is going to be undermined over the coming months if this strait doesn't open and 20% of the world's oil and gas supplies struggle to get out of the Middle East. In recent times, we obviously have seen the price of petrol come down. Here in Australia, there has been a pretty good downward trend since the government announced- I saw unleaded for less than $2 a litre over the weekend. Which is an important psychological level for a lot of people. It would appear that that's going to be relatively short-lived if we don't see the strait-off humus opened up. But the other thing that obviously this brings to mind is the fact that we actually have a budget about to be handed down. So the government isn't getting as much tax revenue from fuel excise as they would have been if they had kept the excise where it was. But it does look like there might be some other adjustments to the revenue base, including a suggestion that we could finally see the end of the CGT as we currently know it. Now, I've been slightly confused. There's been different reporting coming out, and maybe it is just the fact that the government is trying out different options about how they could change the capital gains discount. Do they change the rate? Do they change which houses it's applied to? And Jim Chalmers, again this morning, and he said it before, said it hasn't been decided yet. So if you take him at face value, they are still weighing up these different options. Michael, it does look like it might be okay. So back to the future when it comes to the way the capital gains discount works. Take us through some of the current options that are being looked at. Yeah. So a quick history lesson. Back in, I think it was September 1999, basically overnight, then Treasurer Peter Costello handed investors a windfall gain, or many investors, by changing what had been the original system of capital gains tax implemented by Paul Keating back in the mid 1980s, where you were only taxed on the real gain, which means for non-economists or financial people out there that you got to deduct inflation, the inflation rate from the actual gain you made. And as you mentioned, Shane Wright, he gives the example of how much tax you might pay if you'd only been able to duck that inflation rate instead of the current 50% that Peter Costello brought back in. So people talk about not making tax changes retrospective. Well, Peter Costello retrospectively handed a lot of investors a very juicy discount overnight back in 1999. Now, what the government's looking at doing is unwinding some of this somehow. And what Shane Wright from Nine Newspapers has reported is that they're looking at going back to that indexation system. So instead of a blanket 50% discount, you'd only be able to discount your capital gain by the inflation rate over the period you'd held it. So if you hold it for only two years and inflation was 2.5%, which is the middle of the RBA's target for those two years, instead of a 50% discount on your capital gain, you'd only get 5%. So that's a big difference. The longer you hold the asset, those discounts start adding up because over time inflation compounds. So, you know, Shane Wright gives the example of someone who bought a property back in 2015. If they make a $750,000 capital gain, currently under the discount system, they'd only pay tax on half, $375,000 if they sold it last year. But if the old system had been in place, they would have paid tax on about $420,000 of the capital gain. So they would have paid a little bit more tax, but it's not a massive difference for long-term investors. If the government chooses this model, what it will hit is flippers. So people who buy a property do it up and try and flog it off after a year or two for a quick profit. And arguably in the property market, those are exactly the people you do want to discourage. If what you're trying to do is ensure that first home buyers aren't competing with people who are just looking to turn an investment in a property in a quick way and make money. Yeah, exactly. And then obviously there's the interaction with negative gearing, and we haven't heard as much noise about that. So from what we've heard out of Canberra, including from the Commonwealth Bank's chief economist who used to work for Treasury as a very senior official less than about two years ago, he left for CBA. So he's pretty much convinced that capital gains tax will be on the agenda. That's certainly the noises coming out of Canberra. That's what Shane is reporting in his article. There will be some change. This may be it, or it might be something slightly different. Interestingly, a lot of experts want a more far-reaching change. So the Grattan Institute has long argued to halve the capital gains tax discount. So instead of going back to indexation, just to say instead of 50%, you can have 25%. The impact on investors would be much bigger, particularly long-term investors, from doing that. The tax revenue that could be raised would be a lot more. So they're talking in their submission to the Senate last year of the government potentially being able to raise $6.5 billion a year more in revenue by halving the capital gains tax discount. Currently, it doesn't look like where the government's heading. So one of the arguments for the change that was made under Treasurer Costello during the Howard administration was that they wanted to simplify it. Instead of people having to work out what the inflation rate was for each year that they held that asset, it was very simple. It was very clean, 50%. Do you think that argument with the benefit of hindsight has worked out? And has that been a strong enough argument to keep it in place? Even in 1999, we had computers. Computers are very good at these kind of calculations. You just plug in the date you bought the asset. A computer program sucks in the ABS consumer price index data over that period and spits you out the answer of how much your capital gains are and how much tax you should pay. I mean, the ATO can do it for you on their MyTax system online. So that's a bit of a spurious argument. The other argument back at the time was that this would boost investment, particularly in shares and startup Australian companies. We're obviously in the midst of the tech boom in the late 1990s, just before the big dot-com bust. And so there was a lot of push to get the tech industry fired up. But there's not really much evidence that it seriously increased foreign investment in Australia from other levels. What it has done, though, is interact with the longstanding policy where you can claim losses against a rental property in most cases, mostly fueled by the loan and the interest on that loan that you pay for the rental property. And you can claim that against your income from other sources, like I'm a surgeon and I earn a million dollars a year, but I lose $30,000 on my property investment portfolio because of the home loan on it. And I can take that off my income. And I'm saving tax at the rate of $0.47 in the dollar, the top marginal tax rate plus the Medicare levy. And instead, when I sell that investment property and make a gain on it, I'm paying tax currently on half of the profit. So I'm paying tax on $0.23.5 in the dollar. So it's a good deal if you can shift your income from now. And it's an even better deal, as Grattan pointed out, if I'm that surgeon and let's say I'm in my late 50s and I know I'm going to retire in 10 years and then I'm going to be living on tax-free superannuation or having a much lower taxable income. And so not only do I get the capital gains tax discount, but in the year that I sell the property and recognize my gain, maybe I'm not on the top marginal tax rate of $0.47 in the dollar, but because I'm getting tax-free super income, maybe I'm on a 30% tax rate or even less. And then you really get a great deal out of this capital gains tax discount. So as you say, if we take the treasurer at his word, it appears that this has not been cemented in yet. And the other options would be potentially to look at, well, maybe there isn't a capital gains discount or a different capital gains discount when it comes to existing property versus new property because of an argument that you don't want to see lower investment in new property because Australia needs a greater supply of property. Maybe you differentiate the two. Maybe there's a bigger discount if you buy a new property versus an existing property or maybe no discount at all. Do you think at the moment the modeling or this process of deciding on the policy is more about how is this going to play politically or is it about what will actually create the biggest supply of housing or solve whatever problem you think you're trying to solve? There's been so much work done on this from a modeling perspective by Treasury. Labor, of course, took this kind of policy to the 2019 election and lost an election they're expected to win with Bill Shorten as leader. So they did a lot of work around those proposals. Grattan Institute and other think tanks have done work around it. And from Grattan's modeling, this whole new housing argument's a bit of a furphy as well because their estimate is that it might reduce new housing construction by 10,000 over five years, so 2,000 homes a year, which in the context of what Australia builds is not that much. They say it might increase rents by 1%, but that could be offset if the government used the tax savings to actually build more social housing or community housing. So they say in all, there wouldn't be a big impact even from their more drastic proposal to halve the capital gains tax discount. They reckon it could take about 1% off property prices. If you did that along with curbing negative gearing, so preventing deductions against your other income or perhaps limiting negative gearing to one property only per investor, they reckon at most you're looking at 1% to 2% off property prices. Some other estimates put that at up to 4%, but that's lower than the impact we're seeing on property prices from something like interest rates going up. So there's a lot of experts for a long time who've said this is not that hard. At the margins, it will help first home buyers compete against investors and discourage speculative investment in property, and it won't do too much to discourage genuine long-term investment in rental properties. It'll be very interesting to see exactly how fierce the opposition plan or opposition campaign against this will be. Another one that could be a case of back to the future is the standard or instant tax deduction. Now, Michael, you've got some history with this as well. I don't know if it's scar tissue or how you would describe it, but explain to us what it is and what it could mean and how it might impact people out there when they do their tax returns. So the reason we're talking about this today, Carrington, is that Jim Chalmers has released the draft legislation for a $1,000 standard or instant tax deduction for your personal income tax. So we all know at tax time, you go and try and find your receipts of what are my work-related expenses, and you put in the number, and your taxable income gets reduced by that amount. So what they're saying here, and it had already been announced, but it's now going to Parliament for debate, is if you want, you can just tick a box and say, I'll have a $1,000 deduction for work-related expenses. No receipts needed. No calculations required. No accountant involved. So unsurprisingly, the certified practicing accountants have already come out very strongly against this proposal, because it will put some of their members out of a lot of their bread and butter work. But you can still claim charity and non-work deductions on top of the $1,000, and if your work-related expenses are more than $1,000, and I don't know about you, Carrington, but just my union fees alone are over $1,000, so I won't be ticking that box myself, but you can claim those deductions. You just have to use the old system and have the receipts to back them up. So you talked about the history of this, goes back to 2010, which was one of the first budgets I covered at the ABC, and then-treasurer Wayne Swan, who had a staffer at the time by the name of Jim Chalmers, who is, of course, now our treasurer, had proposed in the 2010 budget to bring in a $500 standard tax deduction, which had been broadly recommended by the Henry Tax Review, and that was going to go up to $1,000 in the next financial year. So that was supposed to come in in 2012-13. Never happened. Announced, but not enacted. And so much for inflation, Carrington. I mean, it was supposed to be a $1,000 standard deduction back then, and the government's still proposing a $1,000 deduction now, and $1,000 buys you a lot less work-related expenses than it did back in 2013-2014. Yeah, but a very round number, and people like round numbers often, and maybe it won't be so onerous on the budget at a time when they are trying to look for extra revenue. Yeah, and look, going back into more of the history of this proposal, back in 2021, Stephen Hamilton, a tax economist who was then at the Blueprint Institute think tank, proposed a $3,000 standard deduction. That would have cost the budget back then about $5.1 billion, but it would have resulted in about $4 billion in compliance savings, both some to the tax office, but also a lot to individuals. So their estimate- So this is the argument, right? This is one of the main reasons that we're even discussing this, because people might say, well, why should you have an automatic deduction? You should have to explain what your deductions are. But it's about simplicity, and basically the government's saying it costs so much to actually check to make sure that people are being compliant with the legislation. It's actually going to be maybe net-net if you just allowed, or somewhere around there, and just a fairer system for most people. Yeah, well, back then, the estimate from the Blueprint Institute was that Australians spent $2.3 billion a year on managing their tax affairs. Now, some of that's high-wealth people who are going to keep spending that money, because they will still keep claiming their deductions. But a lot of that is people going to their local suburban accountant and getting them to do their tax return to try and find the extra receipts and get them a few hundred dollars extra. And if you just have a $1,000 blanket deduction, the government's estimate now is that that would cover about 42% of taxpayers. About 6.2 million people would be better off just ticking the $1,000 box, not worrying about their receipts and claiming that back. And it is actually a progressive tax cut for many of those people, because they tend to be people on lower incomes who don't have as many work-related expenses. So you're basically giving a backdoor tax cut to a lot of low-income people at a relatively minimal cost to the budget and some savings in both individuals and the tax office compliance. What's the argument against this? It seems to be in some ways a no-brainer. Why did it not get brought in originally? And why might people argue against it at this point? Yeah. So the basic reason it didn't get brought in originally is that Wayne Swan back then was desperately trying to get the budget back into surplus or at least balance because he was copying stick from the other side of politics about having persistent deficits after the global financial crisis. And as the blueprint modelling shows, and of course that's a much bigger deduction, but there is a substantial cost associated with this kind of policy because you are giving some people who are not entitled to this deduction a free ride. Like they may have spent nothing on work-related expenses that they could claim, but they still get to claim the $1,000. So it's basically just a tax cut. But if you're on the top marginal tax rate, that can be a tax cut of $470. Most of those people claim their deductions anyway. So the reality is for the average person, this could be a boost of about $205, the government's estimating. But $205 times more than 6 million workers covered, and you can see why there's a budget cost associated that in the past they've decided not to pay. Yeah, fascinating. Well, we'll wait to see what other speculation we get over coming weeks about what's actually in this budget and when the government actually settles on what potential changes might be made to that capital gains discount as well. Michael, thanks for joining us. Thanks, Carrington. That is it for today's episode of ABC Business Daily. We'll be back with another episode tomorrow. And if you haven't already listened to it, remember we have our latest Fuelcast episode in your feed this morning, right before this one. Make sure you're following us on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. And if you'd like to send in a question, email abcbusinessdaily at abc.net.au. Catch you next time, Michael. See you, Carrington.

in new property because Australia needs a greater supply of property.

Do you think at the moment the modeling or this process of deciding on the policy is more
about how is this going to play politically or is it about what will actually create the
biggest supply of housing or solve whatever problem you think you're trying to solve?
There's been so much work done on this from a modeling perspective by Treasury.
Labor, of course, took this kind of policy to the 2019 election and lost an election they're
expected to win with Bill Shorten as leader.
So they did a lot of work around those proposals.
Grattan Institute and other think tanks have done work around it.
And from Grattan's modeling, this whole new housing argument's a bit of a furphy as well
because their estimate is that it might reduce new housing construction by 10,000 over five
years, so 2,000 homes a year, which in the context of what Australia builds is not that
They say it might increase rents by 1%, but that could be offset if the government used the
tax savings to actually build more social housing or community housing.
So they say in all, there wouldn't be a big impact even from their more drastic proposal to halve the
They reckon it could take about 1% off property prices.
If you did that along with curbing negative gearing, so preventing deductions against your
other income or perhaps limiting negative gearing to one property only per investor, they reckon at most you're looking at 1% to 2% off property prices.
Some other estimates put that at up to 4%, but that's lower than the impact we're seeing on property prices from something like interest rates going up.
So there's a lot of experts for a long time who've said this is not that hard.
At the margins, it will help first home buyers compete against investors and discourage speculative
investment in property, and it won't do too much to discourage genuine long-term investment in rental properties.
It'll be very interesting to see exactly how fierce the opposition plan or opposition campaign against this will be.
Another one that could be a case of back to the future is the standard or instant tax deduction.
Now, Michael, you've got some history with this as well.
I don't know if it's scar tissue or how you would describe it, but explain to us what it is and what it could mean and how it might impact people out there when they do their tax returns.
So the reason we're talking about this today, Carrington, is that Jim Chalmers has released the draft legislation for a $1,000 standard or instant tax deduction for your personal income tax.
So we all know at tax time, you go and try and find your receipts of what are my work-related expenses, and you put in the number, and your taxable income gets reduced by that amount.
So what they're saying here, and it had already been announced, but it's now going to Parliament for debate, is if you want, you can just tick a box and say,
I'll have a $1,000 deduction for work-related expenses.
So unsurprisingly, the certified practicing accountants have already come out very strongly against this proposal,
because it will put some of their members out of a lot of their bread and butter work.
But you can still claim charity and non-work deductions on top of the $1,000,
and if your work-related expenses are more than $1,000,
and I don't know about you, Carrington, but just my union fees alone are over $1,000,
so I won't be ticking that box myself,
but you can claim those deductions.
You just have to use the old system and have the receipts to back them up.
So you talked about the history of this, goes back to 2010,
which was one of the first budgets I covered at the ABC,
and then-treasurer Wayne Swan, who had a staffer at the time by the name of Jim Chalmers,
who is, of course, now our treasurer,
had proposed in the 2010 budget to bring in a $500 standard tax deduction,
which had been broadly recommended by the Henry Tax Review,
and that was going to go up to $1,000 in the next financial year.
So that was supposed to come in in 2012-13.
And so much for inflation, Carrington.
I mean, it was supposed to be a $1,000 standard deduction back then,
and the government's still proposing a $1,000 deduction now,
and $1,000 buys you a lot less work-related expenses than it did back in 2013-2014.
Yeah, but a very round number, and people like round numbers often,
and maybe it won't be so onerous on the budget at a time when they are trying to look for extra revenue.
Yeah, and look, going back into more of the history of this proposal,
back in 2021, Stephen Hamilton, a tax economist who was then at the Blueprint Institute think tank,
That would have cost the budget back then about $5.1 billion,
but it would have resulted in about $4 billion in compliance savings,
both some to the tax office, but also a lot to individuals.
So this is the argument, right?
This is one of the main reasons that we're even discussing this,
because people might say, well, why should you have an automatic deduction?
You should have to explain what your deductions are.
But it's about simplicity, and basically the government's saying it costs so much to actually
check to make sure that people are being compliant with the legislation.
It's actually going to be maybe net-net if you just allowed, or somewhere around there,
and just a fairer system for most people.
Yeah, well, back then, the estimate from the Blueprint Institute was that Australians spent
$2.3 billion a year on managing their tax affairs.
Now, some of that's high-wealth people who are going to keep spending that money,
because they will still keep claiming their deductions.
But a lot of that is people going to their local suburban accountant and getting them to
do their tax return to try and find the extra receipts and get them a few hundred dollars extra.
And if you just have a $1,000 blanket deduction, the government's estimate now is that that
About 6.2 million people would be better off just ticking the $1,000 box,
not worrying about their receipts and claiming that back.
And it is actually a progressive tax cut for many of those people, because they tend to be
people on lower incomes who don't have as many work-related expenses.
So you're basically giving a backdoor tax cut to a lot of low-income people
at a relatively minimal cost to the budget and some savings in both individuals and the tax office
It seems to be in some ways a no-brainer.
Why did it not get brought in originally?
And why might people argue against it at this point?
So the basic reason it didn't get brought in originally is that Wayne Swan back then was
desperately trying to get the budget back into surplus or at least balance because he was
copying stick from the other side of politics about having persistent deficits after the global
And as the blueprint modelling shows, and of course that's a much bigger deduction, but
there is a substantial cost associated with this kind of policy because you are giving some
people who are not entitled to this deduction a free ride.
Like they may have spent nothing on work-related expenses that they could claim, but they still
So it's basically just a tax cut.
But if you're on the top marginal tax rate, that can be a tax cut of $470.
Most of those people claim their deductions anyway.
So the reality is for the average person, this could be a boost of about $205, the government's
But $205 times more than 6 million workers covered, and you can see why there's a budget
cost associated that in the past they've decided not to pay.
Well, we'll wait to see what other speculation we get over coming weeks about what's actually
in this budget and when the government actually settles on what potential changes might be
made to that capital gains discount as well.
That is it for today's episode of ABC Business Daily.
We'll be back with another episode tomorrow.
And if you haven't already listened to it, remember we have our latest Fuelcast episode
in your feed this morning, right before this one.
Make sure you're following us on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts.
And if you'd like to send in a question, email abcbusinessdaily at abc.net.au.

episodes.title: Fuelcast: A Strait choked once again
episodes.description: Petrol and diesel prices have been falling in recent days - but the Strait of Hormuz is once again under pressure. Iran has fired on multiple ships attempting to pass through it, and the US has seized an Iranian-flagged container ship.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. Welcome to Fuelcast. I'm Carrington Clark, and this is your source to stay on top of the numbers behind the ongoing energy crisis. It's Monday, April the 20th. We're recording mid-morning, so let's dig in. The price of Brent crude is currently around $96 a barrel after a significant rebound after a renewed confrontation in and around the Gulf of Hormuz. And since we last checked in, the national average price of unleaded has dropped to $2.04, and the national price of diesel has dropped as well down to $2.97 per litre. Today, I'm joined by Alan Kohler to dig into today's major energy headlines. Good morning, Alan. Good morning, Carrington. Alan, petrol and diesel prices had been falling in recent days, but the Strait of Hormuz is once again choked off. Iran has fired upon multiple ships that attempted to travel through it, and the US has seized an Iranian-flagged container ship. So what happens now? Well, as you say, the Strait of Hormuz is closed again. It was open for 24 hours after Iran said on Friday morning New York time, it was actually Friday evening our time, that the Strait was completely open, but it's closed again because America refused to remove its blockade of Iranian ships. So there you go, it's closed. And of course, Brent crude and the benchmarks, West Texas and Brent, having fallen sharply 10% on Friday, are now rising again because of that. The price of petrol has come down, but that seems mainly to be because of the normal petrol price cycles that we see in Australia, which last about 30 days. And, you know, price goes up and down, sort of random, not randomly, but certainly of its own accord. And that's the reason they fell. The Melbourne radio got very excited this morning about there were four petrol stations in Trugger Niner at less than $1.80 per litre, which was unleaded $91.95 is still all above $2, $2, $2.13, $2.20, that sort of price. And that's the national average is kind of on the rise again. And we'll probably keep going up as, unless the Strait of Hormuz opens again. Alan, are we approaching a major pinch point for global supply? There are still, it appears, maybe some ships that got through that strait before the beginning of the war that are arriving at refineries, but are refineries going to start running out of crude input? And is that going to mean a real crunch in supply in coming days or weeks or months? Yes, definitely. Of course. I mean, the Asian refineries that we import our diesel and petrol from rely on Middle Eastern crude, in particular to make diesel, and they aren't getting any. They've still got some on hand, and there are still some ships on the water, but already the Singapore refinery has reduced its output by 20%. As I understand it, other refineries in Korea and Malaysia and Brunei are doing the same. Anthony Albanese has done deals with these countries to sort of guarantee supplies of gas in return for guaranteed supplies of petrol and diesel and jet fuel, but there's a limit to how far that can go. I mean, that doesn't mean we'll necessarily be at the front of the queue. We'll be somewhere near the front of the queue, I think, as supplies dwindle. But even, obviously, if supplies go completely to zero, then there's none for anybody. And at some point that will happen unless they can keep it going. They are able to get some crude from somewhere else. I think they are getting some from America, and elsewhere, perhaps Venezuela, but that's not entirely suitable for making diesel. So, there's a bit of a problem with that. Yeah, I think we saw, even though the estimates were around 20% of the world's usual supply of crude came through that choke point, the Strait of Hormuz, in normal times, even though we've seen that completely choked off, that hasn't been a complete 20% reduction. Maybe some people have estimated maybe 5% because we have seen some offsetting by the ramping up of production in other parts of the world, including the United States, in part because the price has gone higher and some of those ones that were marginal at lower prices became economical. But there does seem, there is a limit on that, isn't there, about how much that production can be ramped up. And as you say, a lot of these refineries are set up to deal with a particular type of crude oil, and if that crude oil is not coming through, they just can't produce in the way that they were beforehand. Correct. So, you know, I'm not an expert on any of this stuff, but it does seem to be that there's a limit to how adaptable those refineries are to crude oil from other reservoirs around the world. I mean, it does seem to be that they're pretty particularly geared for that particular crude oil, has to do with the amount of sulfur in it and the amount of other impurities they're able to deal with. So as to exactly what happens if this, if Australia for Meuse stays closed for, you know, like a month or three months or something, exactly what happens to those Asian refineries that we rely on is a bit hard to know. I mean, whether they completely stop producing or whether they just produce less, I just don't know. Alan, as we start this next week, I'm concerned about asking you, but are you more or less optimistic about the outlook for this energy crisis? Well, I'm obviously less optimistic than I was on Friday night. I woke up on Saturday morning and, you know, everything was fine. So that was an optimistic moment. Return to normality. That was an optimistic moment. And now it's less so. I mean, what seems to be going on in the talks between America and Iran that are taking place in Islamabad, which is what it's all about now, is the same sort of discussion that was taking place between 2013 and 2015, which led to the joint comprehensive agreement that was between Iran and six other countries, including the United States, which ended up with this agreement that Donald Trump cancelled in 2018. But they did sign an agreement in 2015, which was a pause in Iran's uranium enrichment for 10 years in return for freeing up Iran's frozen assets abroad. So they seem to be negotiating the same thing again. It's worth noting that for that 2015 agreement, that took 20 months to negotiate. They started off in Geneva. They ended up in Vienna. They went for 20 months and eventually came up with a deal, which Trump cancelled in 2018. And now here we are negotiating again. I mean, Trump reckons that this time the negotiations will take, will be really quick. I don't know. Well, we know Donald Trump doesn't have a lot of patience for long-term negotiations. But as you say, this has proven to be a tricky problem to solve. And the first challenge will actually be getting them all into the same room again, because Iran at this point, at least, seems to be suggesting that they're not open to that possibility. Alan, thank you for joining me for Fuelcast. Not at all. Thanks, Carrington. And I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like,
