The timing almost couldn't be worse.
At the moment, there is no seeming link to any sort of ramp-up production.
It seems to be an accident.
They're not treating it as suspicious.
Viva has suggested that they're not going to be passing on any costs of repair to customers.
But I found that a kind of interesting comment because surely in a competitive market, the price is being set by all the players and it shouldn't be about Viva alone setting what the price should be.
But does this potentially mean we're going to have an interruption of supply domestically?
If they're at 80% diesel and jet fuel and 60% petrol, then obviously it will have an impact on supplies.
You know, and it isn't possible really for imports to fully replace them because imports are in short supply as well.
That's why Anthony Albanese is travelling around Asia because there clearly is a shortfall in imports which needs to be bolstered in some way by promising to secure the supplies of gas.
I mean, the thing is that he doesn't actually own the gas, right?
And the people he's talking to, which is the heads of state, prime ministers and so on, they don't own the petrol and other fuels.
So all they're doing really is promising not to cut it off.
Do you think there will be any lasting impact from this petrol diplomacy?
Do you see the agreements that are being struck, as you said, if it's – these are company to company, usually transactions that are occurring.
Is there anything that can be done at the political level or does it have to be some sort of declaration of emergency in order to actually change the status quo?

I think we can assume probably that the companies involved, the gas companies here and the fuel companies in Asian refineries, that they are selling as much of the product as they can because they want to make as much money as they can.
So I don't think it's within Anthony Albanese's power to increase those supplies.
What he's promising to do is to not reduce them if things get dire, you know, as a result of the closure of the Straits of Hormuz.

He's saying to the Sultan of Brunei and the Prime Minister of Singapore and so on that we will not cut off your gas or, you know, you'll be at the last – you'll be the last country we cut off or whatever.
I'm not sure exactly what he's saying, but that's kind of what's going on.
They're modifying the Singapore Free Trade Agreement, for example.
So there are actual – there's not just verbal assurances, there are actual changes taking place to documentation.
And the messaging does seem to be from most countries that what they're going to do is prioritise their own domestic consumption.
But if there's fuel left over, then that they will prioritise Australia in that queue.
But obviously, for all countries, domestic considerations will trump any sort of agreement that they're signing with other countries.
They're not going to allow their own supplies to be in question, are they?
And that goes for Australia as well.
I mean, what – I mean, what Anthony Albanese is talking about is the possibility of a domestic gas reservation kicking in,
which he's saying we won't allow that to affect those other countries that are buying our gas if they kind of keep the supply of fuel coming to the extent possible.
So, I mean, obviously, he's got to make sure that there's enough gas in Australia first.
Alan, we're finishing the first week of fuel cast.
This week we've had the double embargo put into place, a fire at one of Australia's two refineries.
Are you feeling more or less optimistic about the state of the energy market?
Well, the energy market is a mess, let's face it, particularly for Australia.
We've learnt this week how much successive Australian governments have messed it up.
You know, allowing eight refineries to close over several decades was a bad idea.
Allowing oil exploration to decline to be replaced by gas exploration.
I mean, that's what the companies did.
There was no kind of guidance, no kind of central decision making going on in Canberra.
Is that a good idea or not?
So here we are with almost no oil coming out of Australia and two refineries.

I think that, you know, I mean, I think it's very interesting that around about the time these refineries were closing and Australia was making these decisions to not pursue renewable energy and not to electrify the Australian economy.
China was making the opposite decisions 20 years ago to electrify its economy, to invest in EVs, high-speed rail and renewable energy.
And now we're seeing the difference.
And we'll see whether or not this proves to be an inflection point for the uptake of electric vehicles here in Australia.
Alan, that's all we have time for on this episode of FuelCast.
Alan, you'll have another episode of That's Business later today.
Daniel Wood, the Chair of the Productivity Commission.
We will be back in your feeds with all things fuel for FuelCast on Monday.

episodes.title: Australia has two refineries. One's been on fire
episodes.description: It was a shocking scene for most Australians to wake up to - the Viva Energy refinery ablaze. The fire has raised further questions about Australia’s vulnerability to cuts in fuel supply. Could biofuels be part of the answer?
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. For years, our buyers have been told the same thing. He was an internationally acclaimed artist. Whose work is available in Australia through only one gallery. His works were selling really well. But workers start to notice something unusual. He's not contactable by any means. They couldn't find any presence of him online. In Search of the Missing Artist, a new three-part series that investigates the strange business of making art. Search Background Briefing wherever you get your podcasts. It was a shocking scene for most Australians to wake up to. The Viva Energy Refinery in Geelong ablaze. Thankfully, no one was hurt, but it's raised further questions about Australia's vulnerability to cuts in fuel supply. Could biofuels be part of the answer? Meanwhile, in the US, markets have surged, leaning hard into the hope that the war with Iran soon could come to an end. Hanging on the latest words from Donald Trump. Welcome to ABC Business Daily. I'm Carrington Clark. And I'm ABC Business reporter Daniel Ziffer. Dan, you're down in Victoria. These scenes were shocking even from Sydney where I am. What was the feeling like when you woke up and saw this massive refinery engulfed in flames? So Corio is just outside of Geelong. It's a strange place. It's one of the most economically depressed suburbs in Australia. It has this massive refinery and also next to it, probably the most expensive school in Australia, Geelong Grammar, where King Charles was a student. Fascinating juxtaposition, isn't it? It really is. It's a very big facility. You can see it because like most refineries, it has a candle. It has a lit exhaust going all the time. So it's always lit. This is obviously one of only two refineries we have. It is obviously going like the clappers at the moment as it refines more fuel than usual because we are importing to try and deal with our current shortages. So a real shock. Fantastic to hear that no one has been injured. We have already had press conferences and information from the company, Viva Energy, directly as well as the fire services this morning. We are speaking around 11.30am. I'm in Sydney. So there will be further updates. But obviously a huge amount of attention on the two refineries we have left in Australia. It does seem like very crazy timing. We don't yet know exactly what has caused this. They say it isn't suspicious. But given that we are in the middle of this fuel crisis, it does seem particularly unfortunate. And it has once again raised those questions about Australia's own sovereign ability to fuel ourselves. So this refinery relies on imported oil coming in from overseas. But then we're able to turn it into fuel here. But if there is a substantial cut in its ability to actually produce that refined fuel, then that would, all other things being equal, mean that we will see prices rise. At this point, they're suggesting it's petrol, high-octane petrol, that's a concern. Jet fuel, diesel aren't affected. But how do you think this will potentially play out, Dan? So the units that we're talking about produce petrol. The other parts of the refinery do diesel or make aviation fuel. And they mix this stuff around. In fact, when I was at the refinery about a month ago, they were converting excess jet fuel into diesel because that's where the demand was. So they do, as the name suggests, refine products, refine crude oil and other products into stuff. And they have the ability to move that around. Whilst the pictures are absolutely spectacular and terrifying, we will find out in the coming days just how much damage there is. These plants are built knowing that they deal with explosive, highly damaging substances. So, you know, they are built with remote-controlled fire hoses, you know, all these ways to isolate different bits. It's not as though this hasn't been thought about in the construction of these facilities, which are decades old. So we'll find it from the company a couple of days what the damage is and how much there is to fix. But it is certainly still going. You know, even today, whilst they're down to their absolute minimums to keep things ticking over, they're still producing jet fuel and aviation fuel today in different parts of the refinery. This will obviously flow in. It makes it harder to refine fuel. It makes it harder to get into the system. So you're going to think that there's definitely an impact on price. But how that plays into what are already sky-high prices amongst a global increased demand and shortages, that will be hard to see. And we're not going to see that for some time. One of the difficulties, of course, is the government, on one hand, is trying to assuage concerns at the consumer level that there is adequate supply of fuel coming through. And we talk about how the ships have kept arriving throughout this global crunch and that Australia still has basically the same amount of fuel that it had before this crisis. This is now something unusual. This is kind of like we've got a global supply crunch happening. Now we've got this domestic supply crunch happening at the same time, particular to Victoria as well. The suggestion 50% of Victoria's fuel comes from this particular refinery. Do you think there is appetite for people to start looking at cuts in fuel use that we could start to see rationing of some description? Is that now a much more real possibility because of this interruption? Again, at the moment, we still don't have the full detail about exactly what is damaged at this facility and what it means for supply. So we have two fuel refineries in Australia. One of them is currently on fire. So there is a very obvious flow on effect from that, which is it is not going to be operating at full capacity for some time. Now, the fire hasn't affected the tanks, which store the stuff they've already done and the ingredients that are going to go in to make more refined products. But it is undeniable that there will be some impact, even if it is just on the process and the flow of juice. If we were to get to rationing, it was always going to be for diesel first. That is the fuel that powers our military emergency services, every facet of business and agriculture. That's always the fuel that is going to be under the most pressure. So if you- And Australia is a world leader in the use of diesel. We are gold medalists. We are gold medalists. We are the per capita winner when it comes to the use of diesel because we're such a big country. We're so spread out because of our massive mining and agriculture industries. We need the stuff more than anyone else. So if you have an extremely large Toyota Prado or Ram that you use to take the children to sporting events, it's not a great time to be you. And certainly if there is rationing, it will affect you first because diesel passenger cars are going to be very low down on the priority list if things get spiky. However, as I've talked about before, we have the ability to convert fuels and to move them around the system. People are already having their conversations. Now, I get information from, say, the financial sector union who are saying, well, all the banks and the financial institutions are not doing enough to get rid of their be-in-the-office-a-certain-number-of-days mandates. People who can stay home should stay home. I think probably what's happening more broadly are conversations between employees and employers saying, it is now costing me X dollars to get to the office every day, so I'm going to do it less frequently. You know, subcontractors, people who are working on jobs where they are travelling every day, are saying to their employer, you're going to have to pay more if you want me to come. Otherwise, we will find other employment. There's a case in front of the Industrial Umpire, the Fair Work Commission, at the moment about the per kilometre rate that is paid to people like in-home carers, where car use is an unavoidable part of the job. Normally, it is indexed annually. The ACTU, the peak body of the unions, wants it done monthly for the next period to deal with these fluctuations, to deal with these high prices. So these conversations are happening. I think these changes are happening, whether they get talked about or they're done in a kind of legislated fashion. I think they're actually happening in the kind of real politic of the actual world. So, Dan, we have had a lot of questions in from listeners about how can Australia potentially have more of its own sovereign capability when it comes to the production of fuels. Bruce wrote in to the ABC Business Daily inbox saying, how does Australia's potential ability to produce biofuels impact on our ability to be self-sufficient in petrol and diesel? Dan, you've been doing some investigations into this. You're the man to ask, does Australia have the capability to do it? And what potentially would it mean to the price of fuel here in Australia? Biofuels are created here using waste matter or organic material that we are otherwise exporting to make biofuels in other countries. It is a low carbon solution that would employ a ton of people in regional areas and could completely flip our fuel sovereignty issue. So 20 years ago in California, they had the impact of the Gulf War and they changed their fuel mix. They pushed the mass electrification of light transport and they got heavily into biofuels. Now, at the moment, they control in California about 80% of their fuel and the imports are about 20%. We are completely flipped. We're the other way around. We are so tapped out of fuel that near where I grew up in Gippsland, they're decommissioning the rigs. There's no more to get out of the basin. We are reliant on imports when we could be literally growing this stuff here and spending our money here. Most Australians, I think, would probably know about biofuels to kind of E10 fuel, which is a mix of traditional fuel with this kind of organic component. Australians do seem somewhat reluctant, though. I remember reading that actually Australians, the uptake of E10 is lower here than in a lot of other places, including America, where I previously was, that people are concerned about it and whether or not it's actually worth the discount or whether they feel safe about putting it into their car. What's your view on that? So about 30 years ago, ethanol wasn't as well put together and cars weren't as well calibrated for it. From the people I've been speaking to, every modern car kind of built in the last 20 years, and Australia does have a reasonably old fleet, is more than capable of taking E10, which is a blend of petrol with a tiny bit of ethanol, largely produced from sugarcane. Biodiesel is a different product. It can be used to power heavy machinery. There are also biofuels that can be blended in to create more sustainable aviation fuels. We have ignored this industry. We haven't pushed it to the extent that not only do we export the feedstock, being the ingredients that other people need to make biofuels in other countries, the biofuels refineries that we have in Australia aren't even operating at capacity now. So even though we're in the middle of a fuel crisis, they're not operating at capacity and a lot of what they produce is being exported. So is the issue with that, that there isn't the demand for these products here in Australia, that people don't want them because it has a bad reputation? It hasn't been mandated to have demand. So what the industry says is you can't really build the supply until you mandate the demand. For a long time, it wasn't as price competitive, right? So you'd need a mandate that you need a certain percentage or you need to, in the same way you have with climate change, kind of ratchet down over time to force this to happen. Now, obviously, at this particular point, they're more than price competitive. But to really build out these ventures, you know, you're looking at decades-long timelines. You need the certainty that mandates provide saying there will be this much demand. So the issue hasn't been on the supply. We've got the ability to ramp that up. We've got refinery capacity right now. The issue is mandating demand. Now, there will be a cost, right? Of course there is. This is how things work. But it's estimated that, say, for a general long domestic flight in Australia, it would be between $2 and $3 per passenger initially, right? That's initially. Over time, as you build capability and you get closer to your California levels where you have a large biofuels industry, you know, you've changed that mix. You've changed the demand pattern. So, you know, this crisis will focus the mind of consumers, of business, of politics. But we need that demand-side mechanism if we're going to make the long, big bets to get this thing happening. So when we're comparing biofuels to using traditional oil sources and they talk about it being lower carbon, why is it lower carbon? Even if you're – because you are still burning things, right? You're still using an internal combustion engine in order to travel around. This is a kind of electrification. How is it lower carbon than traditional oil? Well, it produces less carbon, but also it's absorbing carbon through its growth process. So if you are getting biomass, which is kind of waste vegetation or waste, or if you're even using really high-grade stuff like canola, which is used heavily in Europe because it's very good in cold temperatures, they are absorbing carbon through the growth process. They create lower carbon fuels. It is not the same as electrifying the passenger fleet and getting that electricity from renewable sources. All of these things have to happen at the same time. It's not a one or the other. But people involved in biofuels say that instead of, you know, us controlling kind of 10% to 20% of the fuel we have, importing 80%, we could be controlling 50% to 60% of our fuel needs from biofuels. Others who are even more optimistic say that if you do everything, right, if you electrify the light car fleet, the light transport fleet, you make big changes. We could be exporting energy. We could cover all of our fuel needs from biofuels, particularly from kind of marginal farming land that we have in Australia from biomass and growing things there and then turning them into these kind of fuels and exporting it as well. So the potential is massive. We certainly have the land, but it's about whether we have the will. Yeah, I think that's right, isn't it? That, yes, the longer term goal for those people who believe that we need to be going to net zero is that you want the electrification of the light vehicle fleet as quickly as possible. But one of the lessons from this crisis is still how vulnerable we are to particularly liquid fuel interruptions. And what the argument from the biofuel industry is, is that this isn't going away anytime soon. And so what you're trying to do is to increase your ability to produce fuel locally as much as you possibly can. And that does come at a cost. And that's going to be up to politicians to debate whether or not it's worth that cost. But the idea is that that would help you on that transition. And that's going to be up to people who are thinking, well, hold on, we can just, you know, like New Zealand, store more oil. I'll give you an example. At the Viva refinery in Corio that is currently still on fire, they built a 100 million litre tank in 2017. Cost about $50 million. Obviously, a very big enterprise to do so. So enormous tank. You can see it from the road. Like it is really, really big. It can store enough fuel for Victoria for three days. Yeah. Not Australia for three days. It can store enough fuel for a quarter of the population for three days. And it took them a year to build almost 10 years ago. So like we can't build bigger tanks to get out of this supply crisis or to change our fuel sovereignty. What we need to do is to change the mix of fuel we have and reduce our reliance so that we keep diesel in particular and aviation fuels for the sectors that are really hard to shift, that are really difficult to abate. Big machinery, big trucks, planes, things where it's going to be harder and harder to turn electric. Now, I will say my experience in the US was where this is also a debate and there is a massive agricultural industry built around ethanol, biofuels, is that the difficulty is if you get into a situation where you might be subsidizing those industries, the argument being, again, perhaps that it helps you to remove your reliance on foreign oil, is that you're building up that industry artificially. And then there will be vested interests actively working against any transition to electrification because they've now got this market there for them. They're making a lot of money off it. How do you think you work out that tension to ensure that you don't create artificially an industry that then doesn't want to see that full transition to electrification? The tech is doing it for them. So BYD, the world's largest carmaker, has released, not in Australia, a car that can travel for 1,200 kilometres on a single charge. That is more than the distance between Australia's biggest cities. If you're driving a petrol car between Melbourne and Sydney, you'd have to stop twice or three times in that trip. The internal combustion engine is amazing and has powered the world's development for 150 years. But we are getting fractional improvements from it every year, right? From every F1 team down to mass carmakers, you've got some of the smartest engineers in the world trying to get these things more efficient. They're getting them like little, little, little percentages. Electric vehicles have been around for a couple of decades. What is happening in battery storage and the conversion of electricity to movement is more akin to like Moore's law, which deals with data and the ability that can be stored in a certain space. It is just exponential. So much like, you know, you can't build, even with the world's best technology, a more efficient coal-fired power station, even if you started now, that could produce power cheaper than renewables and battery storage. The tech is just going to do it. So whilst, yes, there is an argument that you are potentially displacing agricultural farmland to create biofuel, the technology explosion in electric vehicles is so substantial. You're already seeing it moving into trucking. You're seeing the start of tiny, tiny aeroplanes that are electrically powered. This stuff will just keep going, whereas the internal combustion engine, amazing device, has really reached the end of the road of what can be further squeezed out of it in terms of efficiency. Dan, before I let you go, I want to check in with what we're seeing overseas, because despite the fact that we are still being warned that the economic consequences of this war are going to continue for a long time, because there's already been damage to oil and gas infrastructure in the Gulf region. There's also a major risk premium being added onto shipping around the world. We're seeing the US stock markets hit record highs, the S&P 500 up above 7,000 points, the NASDAQ up a further 1.6% today. How do you kind of square this circle? Why are we seeing investors seemingly happy to bet on further increases in company values while we're being warned that we are going to see a hit to global growth and a rise in inflation? I've rarely seen a better illustration of the fact that the stock market is an indicator of the economy. It's not the economy. People are hoping that things will be rosy. Trump will get this sorted. It'll be back to great business conditions. We won't have a global recession. There's a lot of hope in pushing indices to record highs at a time where geopolitically the world is on fire. It doesn't seem to make sense. I am not a financial advisor and man, I'm glad about that right now because it wouldn't seem to make sense to an observer. But for the people that are investing, they are finding others who are happy to sell to them at that high price. Yeah. What seems to be happening is any positive news is being seized upon by markets. And there is an argument that the valuations are starting to look relatively healthy, but it does seem to fly in the face of all the advice from experts. You know, we just heard from the IMF that there is a severe scenario where the global economy goes into a recession if we see elevated prices of energy for a prolonged period. Well, my massive red flag for today is that Allbirds, which is the American sneaker company that kind of went viral on Instagram and sold really nice sneakers, they kind of went under. But then they made the really clever move to, despite being a sneaker company, rebrand themselves as an AI infrastructure company. And their shares are up 580% today. So, this makes sense. There are a lot of divergent markers at the moment of what is going to happen. And it is a delicate balance of no one really knowing. Yes. And on that note, let's wrap up today's episode of ABC Business Daily. Thanks for joining us, Dan. Thanks, Carrington. We will be back in your feeds with another episode of Fuelcast tomorrow morning. And on Friday afternoon, be sure to catch That's Business with Alan Kohler, who will be sitting down with Danielle Wood. She's the chair of Australia's Productivity Commission. Remember to never miss an episode. Make sure you're following ABC Business Daily on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. If you'd like to send in a question like Bruce did today, email abcbusinessdaily at abc.net.au. Catch you next time, Dan. Talk soon.

Bruce wrote in to the ABC Business Daily inbox saying, how does Australia's potential ability to produce biofuels impact on our ability to be self-sufficient in petrol and diesel?
Dan, you've been doing some investigations into this.
You're the man to ask, does Australia have the capability to do it?
And what potentially would it mean to the price of fuel here in Australia?
Biofuels are created here using waste matter or organic material that we are otherwise exporting to make biofuels in other countries.
It is a low carbon solution that would employ a ton of people in regional areas and could completely flip our fuel sovereignty issue.
So 20 years ago in California, they had the impact of the Gulf War and they changed their fuel mix.
They pushed the mass electrification of light transport and they got heavily into biofuels.
Now, at the moment, they control in California about 80% of their fuel and the imports are about 20%.
We are so tapped out of fuel that near where I grew up in Gippsland, they're decommissioning the rigs.
There's no more to get out of the basin.
We are reliant on imports when we could be literally growing this stuff here and spending our money here.
Most Australians, I think, would probably know about biofuels to kind of E10 fuel, which is a mix of traditional fuel with this kind of organic component.
Australians do seem somewhat reluctant, though.

I remember reading that actually Australians, the uptake of E10 is lower here than in a lot of other places, including America, where I previously was, that people are concerned about it and whether or not it's actually worth the discount or whether they feel safe about putting it into their car.
So about 30 years ago, ethanol wasn't as well put together and cars weren't as well calibrated for it.

From the people I've been speaking to, every modern car kind of built in the last 20 years, and Australia does have a reasonably old fleet, is more than capable of taking E10, which is a blend of petrol with a tiny bit of ethanol, largely produced from sugarcane.
It can be used to power heavy machinery.
There are also biofuels that can be blended in to create more sustainable aviation fuels.

We haven't pushed it to the extent that not only do we export the feedstock, being the ingredients that other people need to make biofuels in other countries, the biofuels refineries that we have in Australia aren't even operating at capacity now.
So even though we're in the middle of a fuel crisis, they're not operating at capacity and a lot of what they produce is being exported.
So is the issue with that, that there isn't the demand for these products here in Australia, that people don't want them because it has a bad reputation?
It hasn't been mandated to have demand.
So what the industry says is you can't really build the supply until you mandate the demand.
For a long time, it wasn't as price competitive, right?
So you'd need a mandate that you need a certain percentage or you need to, in the same way you have with climate change, kind of ratchet down over time to force this to happen.
Now, obviously, at this particular point, they're more than price competitive.
But to really build out these ventures, you know, you're looking at decades-long timelines.
You need the certainty that mandates provide saying there will be this much demand.
So the issue hasn't been on the supply.
We've got the ability to ramp that up.
We've got refinery capacity right now.
Now, there will be a cost, right?
But it's estimated that, say, for a general long domestic flight in Australia, it would be between $2 and $3 per passenger initially, right?
Over time, as you build capability and you get closer to your California levels where you have a large biofuels industry, you know, you've changed that mix.
So, you know, this crisis will focus the mind of consumers, of business, of politics.
But we need that demand-side mechanism if we're going to make the long, big bets to get this thing happening.
So when we're comparing biofuels to using traditional oil sources and they talk about it being lower carbon, why is it lower carbon?
Even if you're – because you are still burning things, right?
You're still using an internal combustion engine in order to travel around.
This is a kind of electrification.
How is it lower carbon than traditional oil?
Well, it produces less carbon, but also it's absorbing carbon through its growth process.

So if you are getting biomass, which is kind of waste vegetation or waste, or if you're even using really high-grade stuff like canola, which is used heavily in Europe because it's very good in cold temperatures,
they are absorbing carbon through the growth process.
It is not the same as electrifying the passenger fleet and getting that electricity from renewable sources.
All of these things have to happen at the same time.
It's not a one or the other.

But people involved in biofuels say that instead of, you know, us controlling kind of 10% to 20% of the fuel we have, importing 80%, we could be controlling 50% to 60% of our fuel needs from biofuels.
Others who are even more optimistic say that if you do everything, right, if you electrify the light car fleet, the light transport fleet, you make big changes.

We could cover all of our fuel needs from biofuels, particularly from kind of marginal farming land that we have in Australia from biomass and growing things there and then turning them into these kind of fuels and exporting it as well.
We certainly have the land, but it's about whether we have the will.
Yeah, I think that's right, isn't it?
That, yes, the longer term goal for those people who believe that we need to be going to net zero is that you want the electrification of the light vehicle fleet as quickly as possible.
But one of the lessons from this crisis is still how vulnerable we are to particularly liquid fuel interruptions.
And what the argument from the biofuel industry is, is that this isn't going away anytime soon.
And so what you're trying to do is to increase your ability to produce fuel locally as much as you possibly can.
And that does come at a cost.
And that's going to be up to politicians to debate whether or not it's worth that cost.
But the idea is that that would help you on that transition.
And that's going to be up to people who are thinking, well, hold on, we can just, you know, like New Zealand, store more oil.
At the Viva refinery in Corio that is currently still on fire, they built a 100 million litre tank in 2017.
Obviously, a very big enterprise to do so.
You can see it from the road.
Like it is really, really big.
It can store enough fuel for Victoria for three days.
It can store enough fuel for a quarter of the population for three days.
And it took them a year to build almost 10 years ago.
So like we can't build bigger tanks to get out of this supply crisis or to change our fuel sovereignty.

What we need to do is to change the mix of fuel we have and reduce our reliance so that we keep diesel in particular and aviation fuels for the sectors that are really hard to shift, that are really difficult to abate.
Big machinery, big trucks, planes, things where it's going to be harder and harder to turn electric.

Now, I will say my experience in the US was where this is also a debate and there is a massive agricultural industry built around ethanol, biofuels, is that the difficulty is if you get into a situation where you might be subsidizing those industries, the argument being, again, perhaps that it helps you to remove your reliance on foreign oil, is that you're building up that industry artificially.
And then there will be vested interests actively working against any transition to electrification because they've now got this market there for them.
They're making a lot of money off it.
How do you think you work out that tension to ensure that you don't create artificially an industry that then doesn't want to see that full transition to electrification?
The tech is doing it for them.
So BYD, the world's largest carmaker, has released, not in Australia, a car that can travel for 1,200 kilometres on a single charge.
That is more than the distance between Australia's biggest cities.
If you're driving a petrol car between Melbourne and Sydney, you'd have to stop twice or three times in that trip.
The internal combustion engine is amazing and has powered the world's development for 150 years.
But we are getting fractional improvements from it every year, right?
From every F1 team down to mass carmakers, you've got some of the smartest engineers in the world trying to get these things more efficient.
They're getting them like little, little, little percentages.
Electric vehicles have been around for a couple of decades.
What is happening in battery storage and the conversion of electricity to movement is more akin to like Moore's law, which deals with data and the ability that can be stored in a certain space.

So much like, you know, you can't build, even with the world's best technology, a more efficient coal-fired power station, even if you started now, that could produce power cheaper than renewables and battery storage.
The tech is just going to do it.
So whilst, yes, there is an argument that you are potentially displacing agricultural farmland to create biofuel,
the technology explosion in electric vehicles is so substantial.
You're already seeing it moving into trucking.
You're seeing the start of tiny, tiny aeroplanes that are electrically powered.
This stuff will just keep going, whereas the internal combustion engine, amazing device, has really reached the end of the road of what can be further squeezed out of it in terms of efficiency.

Dan, before I let you go, I want to check in with what we're seeing overseas, because despite the fact that we are still being warned that the economic consequences of this war are going to continue for a long time,
because there's already been damage to oil and gas infrastructure in the Gulf region.
There's also a major risk premium being added onto shipping around the world.
We're seeing the US stock markets hit record highs, the S&P 500 up above 7,000 points, the NASDAQ up a further 1.6% today.
How do you kind of square this circle?
Why are we seeing investors seemingly happy to bet on further increases in company values while we're being warned that we are going to see a hit to global growth and a rise in inflation?
I've rarely seen a better illustration of the fact that the stock market is an indicator of the economy.
People are hoping that things will be rosy.
It'll be back to great business conditions.
We won't have a global recession.
There's a lot of hope in pushing indices to record highs at a time where geopolitically the world is on fire.
It doesn't seem to make sense.
I am not a financial advisor and man, I'm glad about that right now because it wouldn't seem to make sense to an observer.
But for the people that are investing, they are finding others who are happy to sell to them at that high price.
What seems to be happening is any positive news is being seized upon by markets.
And there is an argument that the valuations are starting to look relatively healthy, but it does seem to fly in the face of all the advice from experts.
You know, we just heard from the IMF that there is a severe scenario where the global economy goes into a recession if we see elevated prices of energy for a prolonged period.
Well, my massive red flag for today is that Allbirds, which is the American sneaker company that kind of went viral on Instagram and sold really nice sneakers, they kind of went under.
But then they made the really clever move to, despite being a sneaker company, rebrand themselves as an AI infrastructure company.
And their shares are up 580% today.
There are a lot of divergent markers at the moment of what is going to happen.
And it is a delicate balance of no one really knowing.
And on that note, let's wrap up today's episode of ABC Business Daily.
We will be back in your feeds with another episode of Fuelcast tomorrow morning.
And on Friday afternoon, be sure to catch That's Business with Alan Kohler, who will be sitting down with Danielle Wood.
She's the chair of Australia's Productivity Commission.
Remember to never miss an episode.
Make sure you're following ABC Business Daily on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts.
If you'd like to send in a question like Bruce did today, email abcbusinessdaily at abc.net.au.

episodes.title: A warning from the IMF
episodes.description: The world’s financial and economic elite are descending on Washington DC. The International Monetary Fund is holding a series of meetings and warning that the energy crisis is going to mean (at the very least) lower growth and higher inflation.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily, the podcast that brings you one big story affecting your world each weekday in just 15 minutes. I don't think there's a president in US history that's really presented, you know, such a threat to global efforts to cut pollution as Trump has. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. The world's financial and economic elite are descending on Washington, D.C. for a series of high-level meetings amid warnings from the International Monetary Fund that the energy crisis is going to mean at the least lower growth and higher inflation, but also in a severe scenario, a continued energy supply crunch could see the world stumble into its third recession of this century. Welcome to ABC Business Daily. I'm Carrington Clark. And I'm ABC Business Reporter Steph Chalmers. Steph, thank you so much for joining me. Now, the IMF has set the table, as it were, for these meetings with an update to its economic forecasts. This one makes for some pretty sober reading. How seriously do you think we should take the possibility of the world hurtling into an economic recession? So they've outlined three scenarios. It's worth mentioning as well that this is a regular update. They do. It's not kind of like they said, hey, we need to urgently update these forecasts. It was due to happen anyway. And they flagged that normally they have a kind of base case scenario that they based it on. And they said, that's just not appropriate at the moment. We had to outline three separate scenarios of what could happen, really based on how long this conflict drags on and how severe the resulting energy shock is. So you'd have to say the likelihood of each of the scenarios is highly uncertain, and they didn't put any probability on that. So, you know, they've called the scenario where we would have a global recession the severe scenario. So you could say that's seen as perhaps the outlier, but it doesn't feel all that comfortable sitting here that it's some, you know, real fringe option. Yeah, absolutely. And as you say, these forecasts come out regularly. The spring and fall meetings, as they're called over the United States, occur twice a year. And they invite central bankers, finance ministers, treasurers in our case, to come over and basically have one-on-one time with counterparts from around the world, as well as big group meetings. And the idea is to allow these people who are making economic policy to be working in tandem and to be getting information from each other. And obviously, at these kind of times of great uncertainty, they're particularly valuable for people to try to assess what other countries are doing and to get some insight into what they're planning on doing, because obviously you want the world working in sync. Now, let's go through the severe scenario. As you said, they're not putting probabilities on how likely this is, but this is based on certain factors. And the most important, of course, is where the energy price is. Yes. So they've called the severe scenario where the energy supply disruption extends into next year. So, you know, more than six months to go. And they say oil prices will average $110 a barrel this year and $125 a barrel next year. So the severe scenario, they're not predicting this will happen this year, but if it is at around these levels, this is what they think the result would be. Exactly. And I think it's interesting that they see the oil price rising in the latter part of this severe scenario, which is kind of what we've been hearing from analysts as well, that, hey, even if this wraps up in the next month or so, the real tailwind of this is going to be really long. So you can see that under this scenario as well. So under this severe situation, they warn that growth could slow to 2% this year and 2.2% next year, and inflation would exceed 6% globally. So that's obviously that situation you described where you've got slowing economic growth, rising prices. It's not what anyone wants to see. Yeah. In fact, we heard from Andrew Hauser, who's the deputy governor of the Reserve Bank, that stagflation, which is low economic growth and high inflation, is the worst case scenario, the worst nightmare, I think it was his description, for central bankers. And obviously, he's over in America as well, having a series of meetings in connection with these spring meetings over in the United States. But obviously, this is front of mind for the Reserve Bank about how they're going to try and deal with it here in Australia. And again, that kind of interplay with what central bankers say in Australia are doing and what's happening around the world. Because part of what you're doing when you're adjusting interest rates, as Michelle Bullock, the governor of the Reserve Bank, pointed out quite recently, is you are concerned about what it's doing to the currency. So a higher Australian currency actually insulates Australia a bit from higher inflation, because you're able to buy things cheaper from other countries. But if other countries are pushing up their interest rates, well, then you have to adjust your own settings. And it's kind of this feedback loop. Yeah, you'd have to say it is well-timed to have our central bankers in Washington. Andrew Hauser was in New York yesterday speaking. And it is a good look for, obviously, they were pre-scheduled, but it's good to have the Treasurer on the ground, as it seems, you know, holding these discussions. The IMF also had some, you know, what's been construed as advice for Jim Chalmers, essentially saying that any relief to households or handouts, as we saw on COVID, to try and cushion the blow for households and consumers needs to be very targeted. Because essentially, they were talking about not kind of disrupting the price signals sent by low supply. So if you make it, if you do things like cut the fuel excise, you take away some of that price signal of higher prices saying, hey, we don't have a lot of supply, we need to reduce demand accordingly. So there were some comments in there that are kind of been taken as advice for the Treasurer. That's obviously not how the IMF framed it. But it'll be interesting to see what comes out of this visit and what we hear from the Treasurer, talking to counterparts about what other countries are thinking of doing to help the household sector. Yeah, when I spoke to Ian Verinder about these meetings, he pointed out that people get very excited about the headlines, the updates to global growth, these figures, but they are actually based on the data, the forecasts that are provided to the IMF by individual countries. So in some ways, this is data that we're already aware of, these forecasts, although they have in this case come up with these different scenarios about how they think it could play out globally, although they haven't gone into how those scenarios will translate to individual countries. But this is an unusual moment. These might be regular meetings, but this does feel like one of those points when the global economy is particularly fragile. The IMF is giving some advice to countries around the world. They are concerned that you could see countries taking a response that actually just adds to inflationary pressure. They're always concerned about protectionism rising again, which will interrupt the trade between nations. But again, what they're trying, I think, in part to do is to get people focused on the challenge. And perhaps the person who would be most important to influence is Donald Trump. And I think the threat of there being another recession during a Donald Trump administration will be something that will be top of mind for him. We saw what happened during COVID. He won't want to be a president who sees a second recession on his watch, as it were, particularly because in this case, you can see how his detractors would say, this is your fault. You're the one who caused this spike in the price of energy. And I think, as you say, it really all comes down to Donald Trump and how long this all plays out. And I was just having a look at the baseline scenario. So this is not the severe or the adverse. This is just the kind of what they are saying is most, not most likely, but what they think will happen. And it's actually based on commodity future prices as of March 10. So you have to think that's almost a world away now, you know, a full month ago. And it really feels like we're at the mercy of these decisions from Donald Trump. And you look at the stock market today. It opened moderately higher on the ASX. Global markets really seem to be shrugging a lot of this off. It just feels like a real disconnect from getting a report from the International Monetary Fund saying, you know, there is a possible severe scenario where we see a really close call of a global recession and stocks are going higher. So it feels like markets are betting one way on Donald Trump and the mood around corporates and economists is kind of feeling a little the other way. Yeah, it really struck me as kind of that quintessential split screen moment today. On one hand, you've got Washington, D.C., the home of the IMF and the World Bank, warning of the potential of another global recession. Meanwhile, on Wall Street, you've got the S&P 500 heading towards record highs, almost as if the war never occurred or as if the war has come to an end. Now, at the moment, the ceasefire does appear to be holding, as in there isn't live fire between the United States and Iran. But we now have a situation where there is a double blockade in place along the Strait of Hormuz, limiting the supply of energy to global markets. And yet people seem to be, and by people I mean investors, which is why we are seeing the stock market rally, are betting on these negotiations going well. And yes, the White House is saying Iran wants to do a deal, that they are optimistic a deal can be found, although the vice president is also talking about there being a Trumpian bargain, that he doesn't want just a ceasefire that leads to the status quo or what was in place before these initial Israeli-American strikes on Iran. They want something substantive to change in the region. And Iran has said that they don't think America has earned their goodwill yet. So we're just getting very conflicting messages, but I think you're right. I think investors seem to be taking the optimistic view and that eventually Donald Trump will need to make a deal because it's politically advantageous for him and he doesn't want America and the world heading into a recession or in a recession by the time the midterm elections in the United States come around in November. I think the problem for Australians, Australian businesses, is that this is already kind of coming home to roost in terms of we're already hearing from Australian companies updating their forecasts. So companies listed on the stock market obviously have continuous disclosure requirements to keep investors updated on any changes to what they think is going to happen with their profit or their costs and things like that. So you're starting to kind of see the first wave of the real world impact on Australian corporations having to update the market. So we've obviously had the airlines, Qantas and Virgin, both trim their domestic capacity. Virgin today was quite minor. It was 1% of domestic capacity in the next three months. So that kind of sounds like, you know, flights to capital cities, they're just trimming some of those that might not be full, condensing them into one flight rather than two in the evening or something like that. So we're not seeing huge impacts there yet, but it definitely doesn't paint an optimistic picture and that's with the situation as it is now, assuming that it is going to wrap up in a few weeks. So we're also hearing from the likes of Westpac, a major bank, not saying that it's going to have any, you know, immediate impact on them, but them increasing their provisions for the potential flow through on customers. So, you know, expecting more people to fall behind on their mortgages potentially or, you know, have issues with repayments. So it seems as though this is starting to filter through to how businesses are feeling, how consumers are feeling, and therefore whatever happens now, there's already been a real impact here. Yeah, and it is difficult for, again, the Reserve Bank, because on one hand, they were already concerned about inflation heading into this war, which is why we'd seen that first interest rate hike at the beginning of this year, which caught some people by surprise, but because inflation was already running hotter than the Reserve Bank wanted it to be, they felt the need to hike interest rates to put some downward pressure on interest rates, on inflation, sorry. But the concern, of course, is that also feeds through to consumers feeling worse about their situation if they're already laboring under a big mortgage. And the Reserve Bank doesn't want a situation where people completely stop spending their money because they don't want that to lead to the shuttering of businesses or major unemployment. So it's a very fine line that they are trying to walk. As Mr. Houser says, kind of worst case scenario would be a situation of stagflation. And these consumer numbers are very worrying because people aren't feeling good about the state of their finances or the state of the economy, are they? Yeah, this came through in the Westpac Consumer Sentiment Survey. So this is monthly numbers they put out. So this is for April. They would have taken the survey in that first week of April and we're getting them now. So it does reflect how people are feeling after the outbreak of the war and over the fallout over the last month. So consumer sentiment dropped 12.5% in the month, which is a pretty steep fall. And it's the biggest fall since COVID. So if you're getting kind of crisis COVID era vibes, you're not wrong. That seems to be where we're heading. You've got a lot of peers feeling the same. Yeah, exactly. So near-term expectations have dropped back to how people were feeling in 2022, 23, during that kind of cost of living peak inflation era. So people are feeling as worried as they were then, essentially. And I was listening to the Westpac Chief Economist, Lucy Ellis, speak on ABC News Channel. She's a former RBA Chief Economist as well. So, you know, someone worth listening to and she's predicting three more interest rate hikes this year and kind of outlining that scenario as well, where she sees high inflation and lower growth. She seems a little bit more optimistic than the IMF, it has to be said. But yeah, she was saying they're actually already seeing in Westpac transactions coming through the bank, you know, these banks have really... Well, real-time data of how people are spending. Exactly. So it's super valuable. And she was saying they're already seeing some behaviour shift in response to fuel prices. So they're seeing more, you know, people tapping onto public transport with their cards. People apparently at the beginning of the crisis were topping up on fuel more frequently. So I think those initial supply concerns, but now they're actually seeing people decrease the frequency with which they're topping up fuel. So perhaps that's a sign that something like the excise cut, which created a bit more relaxation around the price of fuel, perhaps, you know, tempering some expectations that it's just going to keep rising and rising unabated has meant people feel a bit more confident to use the fuel till the end of the tank and then know that they can fill up. So it seems like it is having an impact. But she was talking again about higher prices actually lead to you needing even higher prices so then people do reduce their demand. It is such a difficult road ahead, I think, for the Reserve Bank, obviously for individuals as well as they try to navigate their own personal finances. It does feel that investors at the moment, those buying stocks, are betting on a quite quick end to this conflict and then a reestablishment of the kind of norms of energy supply. But that just does seem at such odds with what we're hearing from experts when it comes to oil infrastructure and how quickly that actually can be repaired, first of all. And second of all, of how quickly confidence can be restored. Now, yes, confidence can bounce back quite quickly if people are suddenly feeling like there is no further threat of war. But if you're an owner of a ship and you're thinking about whether or not you want to send your ship into a strait, which had previously seen missiles launched at ships doing that, even if you're told things are OK, surely there's some scar tissue there. That means people are going to be reluctant to do that. And that's just going to force up prices for the longer term. And that's obviously on that real international level. But I think we're going to see similar scarring, as you say, on this local level, because we've got, as you say, even if confidence recovers, if we look at the NAB business confidence survey from yesterday, business confidence fell 29 points. So that's the second largest monthly fall in the survey's history. And it's now at its lowest level since April 2020. So again, that real COVID peak crisis level. So even if things start to improve, if we do get a resolution in the next few weeks, you know, it's now fallen to such a low level that that's where we're rebuilding from. And there's going to be local businesses making decisions in this environment that are then going to keep flowing through for the quarters ahead. So there's a measure in that NAB business survey called the Purchase Cost Index, which the chief economist of NAB essentially described as their input prices. And that had a really sharp rise. It rose 3%, which she described as being very rare. And she said businesses don't have the margins to absorb that. So they're going to have to pass that on to consumers. So if this is all happening now, this is going to then flow through for the next couple of quarters. And based on this business survey, NAB sees not only headline inflation, which can be quite volatile, but also core inflation rising substantially. So they're concerned and they think that this is, you know, the ships, sorry to use the ship word, but, you know, the ships already sailed here now. So even if we do get stuff reopening, you know, in the best case scenario, I think for the next couple of quarters, we're still going to be living with the economic fallout. Yeah, I think that's exactly right. Steph, thank you so much for joining us on ABC Business Daily. Thanks for having me. That's it for today's episode. And we'll be back with another tomorrow. Make sure you're following us on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. And if you're curious about the politics behind the IMF meeting, tune into today's episode from Patricia Carvellis and our friends in the Politics Now feed. We'll also have a link in the show notes so you can jump over and listen. If you'd like to send in a question, email abcbusinessdaily at abc.net.au. Catch you next time, Steph. Bye.

that, hey, even if this wraps up in the next month or so,
the real tailwind of this is going to be really long.
So you can see that under this scenario as well.
So under this severe situation, they warn that growth could slow to 2% this year and 2.2% next year,
So that's obviously that situation you described where you've got slowing economic growth, rising prices.
It's not what anyone wants to see.
Yeah. In fact, we heard from Andrew Hauser, who's the deputy governor of the Reserve Bank,
that stagflation, which is low economic growth and high inflation, is the worst case scenario,
the worst nightmare, I think it was his description, for central bankers.
And obviously, he's over in America as well, having a series of meetings in connection with these spring meetings over in the United States.
But obviously, this is front of mind for the Reserve Bank about how they're going to try and deal with it here in Australia.
And again, that kind of interplay with what central bankers say in Australia are doing and what's happening around the world.
Because part of what you're doing when you're adjusting interest rates, as Michelle Bullock, the governor of the Reserve Bank,
pointed out quite recently, is you are concerned about what it's doing to the currency.
So a higher Australian currency actually insulates Australia a bit from higher inflation,
because you're able to buy things cheaper from other countries.
But if other countries are pushing up their interest rates, well, then you have to adjust your own settings.
And it's kind of this feedback loop.
Yeah, you'd have to say it is well-timed to have our central bankers in Washington.
Andrew Hauser was in New York yesterday speaking.
And it is a good look for, obviously, they were pre-scheduled, but it's good to have the Treasurer on the ground,
as it seems, you know, holding these discussions.
The IMF also had some, you know, what's been construed as advice for Jim Chalmers,
essentially saying that any relief to households or handouts, as we saw on COVID,
to try and cushion the blow for households and consumers needs to be very targeted.
Because essentially, they were talking about not kind of disrupting the price signals sent by low supply.
So if you make it, if you do things like cut the fuel excise,
you take away some of that price signal of higher prices saying,
hey, we don't have a lot of supply, we need to reduce demand accordingly.
So there were some comments in there that are kind of been taken as advice for the Treasurer.
That's obviously not how the IMF framed it.
But it'll be interesting to see what comes out of this visit and what we hear from the Treasurer,
talking to counterparts about what other countries are thinking of doing to help the household sector.
Yeah, when I spoke to Ian Verinder about these meetings,
he pointed out that people get very excited about the headlines, the updates to global growth, these figures,
but they are actually based on the data, the forecasts that are provided to the IMF by individual countries.
So in some ways, this is data that we're already aware of, these forecasts,
although they have in this case come up with these different scenarios about how they think it could play out globally,
although they haven't gone into how those scenarios will translate to individual countries.
But this is an unusual moment.
These might be regular meetings, but this does feel like one of those points when the global economy is particularly fragile.
The IMF is giving some advice to countries around the world.
They are concerned that you could see countries taking a response that actually just adds to inflationary pressure.
They're always concerned about protectionism rising again, which will interrupt the trade between nations.
But again, what they're trying, I think, in part to do is to get people focused on the challenge.
And perhaps the person who would be most important to influence is Donald Trump.
And I think the threat of there being another recession during a Donald Trump administration will be something that will be top of mind for him.
We saw what happened during COVID.
He won't want to be a president who sees a second recession on his watch, as it were,
particularly because in this case, you can see how his detractors would say,
You're the one who caused this spike in the price of energy.
And I think, as you say, it really all comes down to Donald Trump and how long this all plays out.
And I was just having a look at the baseline scenario.
So this is not the severe or the adverse.
This is just the kind of what they are saying is most, not most likely, but what they think will happen.
And it's actually based on commodity future prices as of March 10.
So you have to think that's almost a world away now, you know, a full month ago.
And it really feels like we're at the mercy of these decisions from Donald Trump.
And you look at the stock market today.
It opened moderately higher on the ASX.
Global markets really seem to be shrugging a lot of this off.
It just feels like a real disconnect from getting a report from the International Monetary Fund saying,
you know, there is a possible severe scenario where we see a really close call of a global recession
So it feels like markets are betting one way on Donald Trump
and the mood around corporates and economists is kind of feeling a little the other way.
Yeah, it really struck me as kind of that quintessential split screen moment today.
On one hand, you've got Washington, D.C., the home of the IMF and the World Bank,
warning of the potential of another global recession.
Meanwhile, on Wall Street, you've got the S&P 500 heading towards record highs,
almost as if the war never occurred or as if the war has come to an end.
Now, at the moment, the ceasefire does appear to be holding,
as in there isn't live fire between the United States and Iran.
But we now have a situation where there is a double blockade in place along the Strait of Hormuz,
limiting the supply of energy to global markets.
And yet people seem to be, and by people I mean investors,
which is why we are seeing the stock market rally,
are betting on these negotiations going well.
And yes, the White House is saying Iran wants to do a deal,
that they are optimistic a deal can be found,
although the vice president is also talking about there being a Trumpian bargain,
that he doesn't want just a ceasefire that leads to the status quo
or what was in place before these initial Israeli-American strikes on Iran.
They want something substantive to change in the region.
And Iran has said that they don't think America has earned their goodwill yet.
So we're just getting very conflicting messages, but I think you're right.
I think investors seem to be taking the optimistic view
and that eventually Donald Trump will need to make a deal
because it's politically advantageous for him
and he doesn't want America and the world heading into a recession
or in a recession by the time the midterm elections in the United States come around in November.

in terms of we're already hearing from Australian companies updating their forecasts.
So companies listed on the stock market obviously have continuous disclosure requirements
to keep investors updated on any changes to what they think is going to happen with their profit
or their costs and things like that.
So you're starting to kind of see the first wave of the real world impact

So we've obviously had the airlines, Qantas and Virgin,
It was 1% of domestic capacity in the next three months.
So that kind of sounds like, you know, flights to capital cities,

condensing them into one flight rather than two in the evening or something like that.
So we're not seeing huge impacts there yet,

and that's with the situation as it is now,
assuming that it is going to wrap up in a few weeks.
So we're also hearing from the likes of Westpac, a major bank,
not saying that it's going to have any, you know, immediate impact on them,
but them increasing their provisions for the potential flow through on customers.
So, you know, expecting more people to fall behind on their mortgages potentially

So it seems as though this is starting to filter through to how businesses are feeling,
how consumers are feeling, and therefore whatever happens now,
there's already been a real impact here.

which caught some people by surprise,

they felt the need to hike interest rates to put some downward pressure on interest rates,
But the concern, of course, is that also feeds through to consumers feeling worse about their

And the Reserve Bank doesn't want a situation where people completely stop spending their money

So it's a very fine line that they are trying to walk.
As Mr. Houser says, kind of worst case scenario would be a situation of stagflation.
And these consumer numbers are very worrying because people aren't feeling good about the
state of their finances or the state of the economy, are they?
Yeah, this came through in the Westpac Consumer Sentiment Survey.
So this is monthly numbers they put out.
They would have taken the survey in that first week of April and we're getting them now.
So it does reflect how people are feeling after the outbreak of the war and over the fallout

So if you're getting kind of crisis COVID era vibes, you're not wrong.
That seems to be where we're heading.
You've got a lot of peers feeling the same.
So near-term expectations have dropped back to how people were feeling in 2022, 23, during
that kind of cost of living peak inflation era.
So people are feeling as worried as they were then, essentially.
And I was listening to the Westpac Chief Economist, Lucy Ellis, speak on ABC News Channel.
She's a former RBA Chief Economist as well.
So, you know, someone worth listening to and she's predicting three more interest rate hikes
this year and kind of outlining that scenario as well, where she sees high inflation and
She seems a little bit more optimistic than the IMF, it has to be said.
But yeah, she was saying they're actually already seeing in Westpac transactions coming through
the bank, you know, these banks have really...
Well, real-time data of how people are spending.
And she was saying they're already seeing some behaviour shift in response to fuel prices.
So they're seeing more, you know, people tapping onto public transport with their cards.
People apparently at the beginning of the crisis were topping up on fuel more frequently.
So I think those initial supply concerns, but now they're actually seeing people decrease
the frequency with which they're topping up fuel.
So perhaps that's a sign that something like the excise cut, which created a bit more relaxation
around the price of fuel, perhaps, you know, tempering some expectations that it's just going
to keep rising and rising unabated has meant people feel a bit more confident to use the
fuel till the end of the tank and then know that they can fill up.
So it seems like it is having an impact.
But she was talking again about higher prices actually lead to you needing even higher prices
so then people do reduce their demand.
It is such a difficult road ahead, I think, for the Reserve Bank, obviously for individuals
as well as they try to navigate their own personal finances.
It does feel that investors at the moment, those buying stocks, are betting on a quite quick
end to this conflict and then a reestablishment of the kind of norms of energy supply.
But that just does seem at such odds with what we're hearing from experts when it comes to
oil infrastructure and how quickly that actually can be repaired, first of all.
And second of all, of how quickly confidence can be restored.
Now, yes, confidence can bounce back quite quickly if people are suddenly feeling like there is
But if you're an owner of a ship and you're thinking about whether or not you want to

even if you're told things are OK, surely there's some scar tissue there.
That means people are going to be reluctant to do that.

And that's obviously on that real international level.

And it's now at its lowest level since April 2020.
So again, that real COVID peak crisis level.

know, it's now fallen to such a low level that that's where we're rebuilding from.
And there's going to be local businesses making decisions in this environment that are then
going to keep flowing through for the quarters ahead.

economist of NAB essentially described as their input prices.

Steph, thank you so much for joining us on ABC Business Daily.
And we'll be back with another tomorrow.
Make sure you're following us on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts.
And if you're curious about the politics behind the IMF meeting, tune into today's episode
from Patricia Carvellis and our friends in the Politics Now feed.
We'll also have a link in the show notes so you can jump over and listen.
If you'd like to send in a question, email abcbusinessdaily at abc.net.au.

episodes.title: Fuelcast: Airlines feel the pain
episodes.description: Qantas says its fuel bill could be $600 million to $800 million higher than expected because of the ongoing energy crisis - and it plans to reduce capacity to help offset some of those costs.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. Welcome to Fuelcast. I'm Carrington Clark and this is your source to stay on top of the numbers behind the ongoing energy crisis. It's Wednesday, April the 15th. We're recording mid-morning, so let's dig into the numbers. The price of Brent crude has fallen back under 100 US dollars, currently around 95 US dollars a barrel. Since we last checked in, the national average price of unleaded has dropped 2 cents to $2.19 per litre. And the national average price of diesel has dropped 3 cents to $3.18 per litre. Today, I'm joined by ABC Chief Business Correspondent Ian Verinder to dig into today's major energy headlines. Welcome. Good to be here, Carrington. Ian, yesterday, Qantas announced it expects its fuel bill to be between $600 and $800 million higher because of the energy crisis. And it's going to decrease capacity to mitigate some of the costs. Now, Virgin Australia has also announced it's adjusting its fares to manage its increased fuel bill. What do you make of it all? And is there more pain to come for those wanting to travel? Yeah, Carrington, look, jet fuel seems to be one of those fuels that is really impacted by these shortages coming out of the Middle East. And it's not just the price of fuel. So we always talk about the price of crude oil and what Brent's doing and what West Texas Intermediate's doing. But jet fuel itself is a separate category of fuel. And the price of jet fuel has just gone absolutely ballistic. It's been the worst affected form of fuel since this crisis began. And in our part of the world here, which is called Oceania, jet fuel prices are actually up 150% compared to this time last year. And a lot of it is to do with refining margins, the amount of profit that the refiners are making out of particular types of fuel. So out of, say, diesel and petrol, refining margins have jumped around about two to three times. With jet fuel, the margin is now five times what it was just before this crisis came into being. So you can understand why this is all happening. Now, jet fuel essentially is refined kerosene. And it's made from light crude, which is what America actually produces a lot of. But we get a lot of it out of the Middle East and particularly the Asian refiners where we get our jet fuel from, they get their fuel from the Middle East. And so that's why Oceania fuel supplies, jet fuel supplies have really risen quite dramatically. You know, the interesting thing about Qantas is it's always been really good at mitigating price hikes because of fuel prices, because they've always what's known as hedged their oil contract prices. But they've never been able to hedge jet fuel prices, the refined product. So while they've got some insurance in there to mitigate the higher prices, the higher fuel prices, it's only covering the price of oil. It's not covering that huge increase in the price of jet fuel. Do you think there is a scenario where Australia runs out of jet fuel? Well, some of the airline people are talking in that kind of, yeah, they're using that kind of language. You know, I mean, jet fuel stocks are very low. And there's a reason why, you know, the prices are so high here as well, because it's, you know, essentially running short. You know, and look, this is a big continent with a smallish population. We do rely upon, you know, airline travel to get around, to transport smaller goods and so forth around the country. So, you know, this is quite a critical bit of infrastructure for Australia. Do you think the government will be forced into responding? And is there anything they can actually do? Well, you know, as we were talking about earlier, airlines are always ready and willing to have their hand out to accept a bit of taxpayer relief, aren't they? Just look back at the pandemic where Qantas got about, what, $2.5 billion of taxpayer money. So, yes, they'd be looking to have some kind of government support, I'm sure. Would the government do it? Well, we've had that IMF meeting and report out overnight. And the IMF is essentially saying to governments, and particularly the Australian government, be careful about giving taxpayer relief, because all you're going to do is confuse the price signals here. The prices have gone up because there's a shortage. And you want to make sure that people are aware of that shortage and behave accordingly. For the foreseeable future, though, what is the likely impact for consumers? We're looking at both Virgin and Qantas reducing some of the domestic capacity. Are we just going to see higher and higher prices as this crisis continues? If this blockade continues, yeah, absolutely, I think. So, Qantas has mitigated some of this, I guess, issue by trying to capitalise on the fact that the three Middle East carriers, Qatar, Emirates and Etihad, are kind of out of action. So, they're flying to Europe via Singapore and via Perth, and they're trying to get resources. They've moved aircraft out of America and into Australia to try and pick up on that market there. And they've raised prices on international flights as well. But there's no way you can really do anything to absolutely overcome this incredible rise in fuel prices. I mean, they're looking at $3.3 billion in fuel for the half year. So, that gives you a bit of an idea of the fuel bill. And when you're talking about $600, $800 million in profit hit, well, that wipes out pretty much most of your profit for the year, doesn't it? Yeah, absolutely. I think one of the difficulties as well with the airline industry, as opposed to other forms of transportation, is maybe there's some alternatives when it comes to people getting around, say, in their cars. You might be able to take public transport. If it's an electric train, you might be able to look at an electric vehicle in the longer term. There's no alternative to jet fuel at this point, is there? No. So, if that supply is interrupted, then the airline business effectively goes out of business. That's right. So, look, right at the moment, both airlines are looking at, you know, why run two services between capital cities that are half full? Combine them. So, these are the initial kind of cutbacks that we're seeing. I think you're probably going to see, if this, you know, really deteriorates the situation, you're going to see airlines start to cut services. Ian, we're trying to gauge where we're at in this fuel crisis. Are you more optimistic or less optimistic than we were at the start of the week regarding what's going on? Well, look, at least there's, you know, talk about continued negotiations between the US and Iran. So, that's a positive factor. So, you'd have to say that's a bit more optimism than at the start of the week. Ian, thank you so much for joining us for Fuelcast. Thanks, Carrington. You can catch ABC Business Daily later today and we'll be back in your feeds with all things Fuel on Friday.
