episodes.title: Ryan Harris talks 'rhino rev ups', SACA glory and Australian coach aspirations
episodes.description: It's been a wildly successful two seasons for Ryan Harris in his first head coaching role with South Australia and he sits down with Corbin to talk us through his journey, philosophy and dreams.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast time with one of your boys, Corbin Middlemass with you today. There is no Ed Cowan. One more week. Now I promise Ed will be here next Monday to chop it up with us on the ABC Cricket Podcast. But never fear, I always have a suitable replacement. George Bailey last week joined me for a great chat. And I got a message during the week too, by the way, when I threw it out there basically saying, hey, get in contact with us. We do have an email address, which is abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. That's abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. And let us know who are a couple of the people that you would love to hear from during this period while the IPL was going on, Ed's getting refreshed in some random part of the world, wherever he may be today. And Liam got in touch with me. And one of the first things that Liam said was, Corb, would love for you to have a chat with Ryan Harris if you can bring him on. Well, Liam, I've done exactly that. The all-conquering coach of the South Australian cricket team, Ryan Harris, is my special guest today on the ABC Cricket Podcast. A man who took over 100 test wickets. He's got over 300 first-class wickets. He was an absolute warrior, sending them down for Australia for many years. And now he is taken to the coaching game. And boy, has he had success straight out of the gates. Won three of the last four major domestic titles in Australian domestic cricket with the team that I'll still call the Redbacks, the mighty South Australian cricket team. Twice winning the Sheffield Shield, the drought-breaking title, while then defending it, obviously in the season just gone. And then chucking a one-day title the year before as well to add to the list of accolades. His name is Ryan Harris. And I'm pleased to say he joins me as my guest on the ABC Cricket Podcast. Ryan, firstly, congratulations. Thanks, Torb. Yeah, it's a nice feeling to be obviously sitting here again with a Sheffield Shield sitting in the room next door. It's quite a good feeling. Well, that'd be set the Australian cricket fans thinking we would have just taken one. We had to wait like 30 years or whatever to get a drought-breaking title. And then you go out and you back it up away from home in a Shield final. I mean, what a 12, 13 months for SA cricket. Yeah, it has. It's been three years since I've been back at South Australian cricket. So, Saki here. So, it's been a huge couple of years. And, you know, the reason I moved back is I thought I could see some real growth in this group. And, you know, we've managed, obviously, to have a change in the leadership with myself coming in and Dizzy sort of stepping out. But, you know, the group of – a great group of guys, you know, and they've shown – I think they've shown over the last couple of years what they can actually do. So, and you talk about, you know, the game in the Shield final in Melbourne this year was probably one of the better games of cricket I've been involved in. And it's easy to say that now because we won. But I think for a team to sort of be out of the game the whole game and then fight back in the last day and a half to be able to get the result that we did just show – I think it just shows the fight and, you know, the determination in this group that I've got. And one of the things I tried to do when I moved – when I came in was exactly that. We fight, we fight. And it was a great example of that in the final. They got the result that we wanted. So I'm just going to pick up what you're putting down there, right? Your chat with Ned Hall on the ABC, which was moments after the last wicket fell. And you were quite emotional. Yeah. Can you take us back to that moment? What made you emotional in that moment? That's a good question. I've been emotional at times through the season with the players. I was probably a little bit emotional in the morning of that last day, to be honest. Yeah. I've been asked that a couple of times. I can't really put my finger on exactly why and what. But I just think it was – probably it's just the group of guys I have that work so hard that I have a lot of respect for. And, you know, hopefully they have a lot of strength for me. But I just think to be able to come out and do what they did, as I said, we're behind the whole game. And I think I said the message in the morning, as I got them, you know, at whatever time it was, 9.30 in the morning, is that, you know, today wasn't going to define us as a group whether the result went our way. It was all about – I think what I saw, what I remember saying was that we've already come a long way. We've already done such a great thing this year and being in a position that we're in to compete in the final. Today, you know, if we weren't to go – you know, if it wasn't going our way today, this is not going to define us, us as a group now is a great group of guys who have a crack. And, you know, I had so much respect for it. And I got a little bit of emotion probably saying that in the morning. So I think it's just a group that, as I said, you know, I watch them train. I watch them work so hard to be able to get the result that they did. That's probably the emotional part there. And I just – you know, I've got so much respect for them. I grew up in WA and I feel like I look at some of the issues that WA cricket faces and have done for a period of time and the issues that South Australian face. And it feels like they share a lot of things in common. And in the past, it's been, you know, whether it's past players, you know, that feel like they know the way and they want to do it a certain way. The connection with grade cricket and we want to develop our own players. We don't want to just get people in from, you know, from other states or whatever it turns out to be. And the push and pull of that conversation all the time with every tier of cricket that goes into it. So from a South Australian point of view, I always look at the Shield team and sometimes it looks a little bit like the island of misfit toys. It's guys that have come from other states and all over the place. And yet in a way that no one else has been able to for the last 20 years, Ryan, you've been able to harness that and get the best out of those guys. And you lived a little bit of it in your cricketing journey, obviously happening to change states. How do you go about dealing with that aspect of it when it comes to coaching a complex state like South Australia with all those elements baked into it? Yeah, I mean, firstly, I mean, firstly, ultimately, we want to make sure we want to have South Australians playing in this state. And there's no doubt about that. But I think we just don't have to teleport. And that's no disrespect to any of the club cricketers, but we just don't seem to have that right now. And we're working on that. We're trying to get, and we are getting, you know, some young players coming up through our pathways. We've got a great, a very good pathway system with some very good coaches. So we're sort of adjusting that. But ultimately, we've got a pretty small talent pool. And, you know, being able to, and I have to put it out there as well. It's not me doing it. We've got a guy from Shaw Williams who's been here for 12, 13 years. He's our list manager. He's seen a lot of cricket. He's working in Bangladesh. He's working in India. He's been around the world. When I was coaching under-19 Australian stuff and doing the pathways of cricket for Australia, he was heavily involved in a guy that I would talk to a lot about talent. So we've got a guy that, he knows a lot about talent around the country. He knows just about every cricket and playing cricket. And so he chooses pretty carefully who we want, who we need. Well, firstly, who we need, then who we want. And then also the personality, the person that comes in. So in terms of having a squad that's sort of outside of South Australia, it's, yep, again, we want South Australians playing. But when it comes to these guys not growing up and playing here as, you know, coming through pathways, that the massive advantage for me is that these guys are really, really close and good mates because they hang out a lot. They're really good back at their great clubs, their premier clubs, where they obviously choose to play when they come over. But, you know, they've formed relationships. But what they do is, you know, they've got such a close bond because they spend so much time together outside of training. So in terms of, you know, guys that have sort of missed out in other states, that's the bonus, I guess, we get. Obviously, a few guys from New South Wales. But then when they come here, they hang out. They're really, really tight. And people have asked me over the last week, they just seem to be a really, really tight group. And they are. They literally are. They look after each other. And they, you know, for me, even, you know, not that I have too many disciplinary sort of things to do with this group. But, you know, it saves me having to bark at the guys all the time about this and that. They do it themselves because they're so close and they look after each other. So that, for me, as well, makes it just a great group to coach. And, you know, they're a pleasure to coach. And they're all good mates. And they're all my good mates, too. I guess it's always just the structure of cricket that, yeah, the state selectors or state coaches are always nipping at the heels of the, you know, the national selectors saying, how come our guy doesn't get more attention? Do you get that from grade cricket? People saying, yeah, what about this born and bred South Australian player? And, you know, you should be doing more to try and put those guys in the team as opposed to bringing someone in from elsewhere. I mean, it's proven to be successful. You've done something no one else has done in 30 years. But how do you deal with those conversations from, you know, SA cricket people? Yeah, I mean, I think it's exactly that. It's a conversation that we need to have. So we've got, again, we've got myself as a selector. We've got Sean Williams as a selector. I would, I would try, I would do the bowling meetings and, you know, I'd sort of finish it and go, geez, I felt, I felt like I did that one pretty good. And then Ricky would stand up and say a few other different things. I'd be like, yeah, I probably should have mentioned that. Yeah. Probably should have said that. Probably should have done that. Probably should have said that to him. And it just made me think that, I mean, we know, we all know what Ricky's cricket brains like. It's phenomenal, but it made me think that, yeah, I've still got a fair bit to learn here about the tactical part of the game. So, yeah. So I look back on all those, those sort of examples. That's, that's sort of maybe the coach or making, not maybe making me the coach. I'm trying to be. My next question was going to be influences guys that you've sort of, yeah, helped you along the way. So, I mean, Ricky Ponting, Darren Lehman, a couple there that you both mentioned. Is there any others you, you want to give a little hat tip to? Oh, I mean, Wolf has been, Wolf has been great. You know, from the start, he gave me an option. Obviously my career came to an end abruptly, unfortunately, you know, with my knee. And I was able to travel with him a few times around and actually see, sit on the other side while the boys are playing, how it, how it actually worked. Troy, Troy Cooley is probably the other one. He's, he's one that, you know, I spent the whole time at Cricket Australia with. Obviously he was a coach of mine as well, but he, he got me really going in the art of coaching and he talked about the art of coaching and, you know, another, just another guy with so much knowledge around fast bowling, but also, you know, being a coach and, and, you know, what, what it actually takes. So, I guess those two. The other one was Pat Howard, actually, the other cricket high performance manager at Cricket Australia. Here's another one who I'm still in touch with, a very, very smart guy, you know, came in, got a lot of criticism around being from rugby wise, a rugby bloke doing cricket, but he was really smart guy that, and, and, and, you know, just, he, he, he knew cricket a lot more than what people think, but what he didn't do is he knew he wasn't the expert on cricket. So he'd speak to a lot of cricket people as well. So Greg Chappell was around that time, Darren Lamb and Troy Cooley. So, as well as some ex-great. So he was another guy that taught me, you know, about coaching, but also a lot about business, you know, just about how, how to be, how to be a person that relates to a lot of different other people when, you know, when you're working in an organisation like Cricket Australia. So he was another guy that I guess I'll look back on. And, you know, as I said, I still touch base with him now that it gives me some good, good advice. So I've had, well, that's some really good people along the way that, that, that have been, you know, absolutely, um, give me some great advice. And, and again, I'm still on the journey. I'm not anywhere near finished. Um, so I still have a bit to go. Uh, your passion's obvious and everyone that we run into in Australian cricket talks about that with you. We saw it as when you played and you were just such a warrior in the way that you went about it. And, you know, you don't seem like the modern cricketer in terms of our scans and stress fractures and everything else. It's just, you know, plow on, keep playing and everything else. How do you go with the, I guess the modern player or the younger guys coming through or whatever it turns out to be? Have you had to, have you had to sort of almost catch yourself at different times thinking, right, I've got to have a broader lens here than just, Hey, this is what I did. So this is what's going to work. How challenging has that been as a, you know, to, to, to deal with so many different personalities in the, in a dressing room that obviously coaching would, would, would throw at you. Yeah. Very challenging at times. It has been. There's, there is exactly that. Some of the minds, well, the mindset I've had to change is, you know, especially from a bowling point of view is, you know, some guys are sore. It's like, well, how sorry are you? Can you, can you bowl through it? Or is it actually an injury? You know, if it's an injury, then fine. But if it's not push on. And, and, you know, there's definitely times where I'm a lot better at now. Obviously I can, I've talked to the medical staff quite a lot. I do push, I still push them, the medical staff to push the players a fair bit. But again, it's, you've got to be very careful doing that because if it, if it is wrong, it can cause sort of, you know, longer term injury. So that's, again, I'm still learning how to do that, but, but I, I do, I do push the players quite a lot. And I know, well, when they know, and I think that's the relationship I think I have with a lot of the players, if not all of them, that if there is something that's not right, I will, I won't go through the medical staff. I'll go straight to them and talk to them. And, you know, you know, if, if there is something not right, then they look me in the eye and they, and I know, I know straight away that something's not right. So, yeah, I think we're really good here with, with the way we sort of, I think most Australian cricket, to be honest, the States, I can't, I can't talk for the other States, but, you know, we always talk about, and, and I probably got a little bit caught up in it when I was starting coaching in Cricket Australia around workloads and about this and that, and, you know, about two, bowling not enough or bowling too much or bowling the exact amount of balls that you, that the planner says, and that's it. you know, I did, but coming out of that, even now, I mean, we, we, we, you know, quick, quick, the season is quite a challenging season. So, you know, our bowlers, the, the issue obviously we have is our batters have to face bowlers. And sometimes, you know, we, we, we don't, we don't always do that here because we have to allow the bowls to bowl once a week rather than twice a week, or if they need to bowl, you know, not at all to be fresh for games. And, you know, so we're quite open to, to, to getting what the individual needs. And I think the other, part of that as well is, if, you know, we, we still use the same planner. We still say there's 42 balls to bowl this, this week, this day, or each day, but it's, it's, we, we go on time, you know, and for bowls, again, if a bowl is not bowling well enough, then he keeps bowling until he gets, until he gets the right feel. And, you know, you can't go into, you can't go into a game knowing you bowl the right amount of balls, but, you know, 70, 70% or 80% of those balls have been in the wrong spot. Yeah. You're not going to go into a game feeling good. Right. So, you know, so we're, we're really conscious of that here. And again, I've got a really good group, pretty experienced group now that know what they need and, and how much they need to do before, you know, going, leading into a game. So, um, definitely have changed my tune a bit on that. I was, I was a little bit, um, caught up in, I guess, in, yep, just exactly this, exactly that amount of, and then away you go. But I learned pretty quickly though, that, yeah, the skill level, the only way you get better at bowling is to bowl. And, um, you know, even, even at times we talk about being injured, you know, sometimes you saw, you've got to bowl when you saw, because you're never going to be a hundred percent feeling right. Um, and if you, if you do, if you are, then you're not trying hard enough. Yeah. Um, because you're always going to be sought when you bowl. Two more for you. Um, first of all, that coaching a state team. So, I mean, cricket coaches are relatively new thing in the history of the game, but, uh, obviously these jobs were incredibly popular for a long period of time. There's only six of them in the country. So, um, you know, that they're always highly competitive jobs to have in more recent times, though, it feels like, you know, cricket coaches, the appeal of the T20 franchise scene, for example, and, you know, you go away and essentially make, um, you can make a, yeah, an annual salary worth in basically doing two tournaments or whatever it turns out to be. And that's eight weeks worth of work. And you can jump around and do a bunch of those, but it's, it's in and out. It's not the sort of regular contact like it is to, to be a state coach, for example. What is it that appeals to you about this? Cause clearly you, this, this fulfills a passion for you that, uh, that obviously, you know, you like the idea of, of working with players and player development that goes into it that you don't necessarily get when you just roll up and get a collection of the best players in the world for a, for a two week T20 tournament or whatever it turns out to be. Yeah. I mean, firstly, uh, I, I'm, I look at the opportunity to be able to do that. I, I do, I do like the game of T20. I wouldn't say I love it. I love four day cricket. I love five day cricket. I love one day cricket. I'm still, I'm still growing the love for T20 cricket. I played a little bit of it, but, and I've coached a little bit of it. But, and the other part to that is I don't, and this is going to sound really, I don't know how it's actually going to sound, but I don't think a lot of that is proper coaching. I think you're, you're looking after a group of, a group of men for eight weeks, 10 weeks, you know, you're not, I mean, I've seen Ricky do it. Ricky is really good at it. He does coach a lot. Um, and I've seen snippets of Justin as well, Justin Lania, but I feel as though for me as the bowling coach, it was more, again, looking after what, you know, trying to preach what Ricky would say or, or the head coach. But I just, I didn't feel, and maybe because I haven't head coached in one of those leagues, I didn't feel it was proper coaching. Um, and that's probably, that might be another reason why I'm sitting here, not over there in the IPL as well. I might not have been very good at it, but I just find what I do here. Um, this is a program. You get to run your own program. Um, and I think for, again, for majority of the coaches, there's, again, there's a, there's a few guys that, that, that it just happens naturally. And that is the Pontings and Langers because there's such strong personalities and good leaders and amazing readers of the game that there's not too many that you can just walk out of it. Um, or I guess go to playing or doing what they, what they did into a big coaching role like that. And, and to be honest, my name's probably not big enough either to do that in the IPL, which, which is okay. I don't, I don't mind that. So for me, and the other part of that, as I've said to you before, is I, I had to go back and learn a lot, a lot of the games. I didn't see the game in a technical or a tactical way that, that was, was great. It was just bowl fast, hit the top of off and bowl the occasional bounce. Then when I had an opportunity with the bat, get as many as I could, um, hit the ball to the gaps. That was the way I sort of looked at the game. So I, I, I've had to learn a lot of that as I've been through, but yeah, I think the opportunity to run a program, it really excites me. As you say, and it's funny when you say there's only six of us around that. I hadn't actually thought of it like that. You know, and we, what we do, our jobs are, you know, pretty important in, in, in helping get cricket, you know, Australian cricket strong. And that's the detail of it. I haven't really probably thought of it in, in, in detail like that, but I just, I just love the opportunity to run a program. I'm with God, I work, you know, I work, I briefly did it with Queensland cricket as an assistant and doing different things up there. I've come down here in South Australia and give me opportunity to, to, I guess, fulfill another dream. You know, playing was a dream. Now coaching is a dream. And then they've given that opportunity. And I, and I work, I work at a great organization. I've got great people around me and coaches. I've got a great general manager. I've got a great CEO and I've got a great president and a great board. So I'm very happy with what I do. And they allow me to, um, do what I want to do and, and with the program and run the program. So, and, and from now on, it's, it's, you know, we, we, we set a standard now that yet we've won two, but, um, probably after four or five weeks, once I have a break, we're going to win three and four and five. See, that's what we want to do. And, um, that's, as I said before, I don't coach to lose and the players don't play to lose now. So, um, I think, yeah, long winded answer. Again, I just think having that, having that opportunity to, to work in a, to run your program or a program, uh, I think that's, that's what excites me. Last one for you. And you're going to get this question a whole lot, I'm sure. And it's, it's maybe it's the blessing in the curse of having success. It's, it's great to have success, but often what happens when, you know, people are in successful positions or that they, they achieve well, everyone basically says, you know, what's next? What are you going to do next? Where are you going to go next? It's, do you want to coach the national team one day? Is that the, the, I guess the, the end goal that you look at in terms of, of coaching? Yeah, you're right. I've, I've been asked that a lot in the last week again, or the two weeks. Um, I think ultimately, yes. Uh, I think it's like when, so the way I look at it, and I've said it a number of times publicly as well, is when you get into a job, like in this industry, playing or coaching is that, you know, you, you, you play well, you earn your role, earn your spot, you know, in state cricket, you play well, you earn your spot in the Australian team. You've got to keep earning your role, earning your spot and, and performing. I see that here now. I, I, I sit here and everyone's, oh, he's got to coach straight. Firstly, we've got a pretty good, pretty good coach at the moment. He's doing a bloody good job, Andrew McDonald, um, who I don't think will be going anywhere soon. We've also got another guy, I don't have voters who won three or four state titles. And how many, 15 bloody BBL titles. He's not going, he's going to ride as well. So I've got, I've still got a long way to go. Um, and there's a lot of good coaches around the country that, again, that are lining up for that job. Um, but I mean, ultimately, yeah, I will, I do want to do it, but I don't, I don't expect it to do it tomorrow. I'm still young in my coaching. As I've said to you, I'm still learning a lot about the game. Um, you know, if the opportunity comes up one day to put my name in the ring, then yeah, if it's the right time and right. And the other part of that, if it's the right time for my family, because once I get on that bus, it's, it's a long time away and I've got young kids. So, um, you know, a few factors there, but yeah, bottom line is I'd love to one day. Um, but again, I'll, I'll, I'll, I'll wait, earn my, earn my, earn my spot, earn my, um, the, you know, the, the right to do it. And if that's next year, great. If it's 10 years and that's what it is. So, um, but in the meantime, as I said, I'm working in a pretty good place. I love what I do here and I've got a bit of work to do yet. So. You're a popular man in Australian cricket. It's nice to see good things happen to, uh, to good people and your coaching journey is, uh, is certainly up and to the right. Have you got a holiday planned or anything exciting? What are you going to do in your, your little time, just small time you get before, uh, next season starts? Yeah, I'll, I'll get through this next two weeks of kids school holidays. I'm going to recreate myself from a golf clubs and try and get some nice scores. But just while we've been talking, my wife's been flicking through places for holidays next week. So that's my next part after, after I get off the phone here to go and try and organize it. That's a time with family. So yeah, I'm looking forward to that. We'll let you go and do it. Uh, Ryan, appreciate your time as always. Congratulations on all you've achieved so far and we'll, uh, we'll stay close. We'll chat to you soon on the, uh, on the ABC cricket podcast. Thank you. Nice chatting. Thanks, man. Thanks, man.

segments.text: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more.
ABC Cricket Podcast time with one of your boys, Corbin Middlemass with you today.
There is no Ed Cowan. One more week.
Now I promise Ed will be here next Monday to chop it up with us on the ABC Cricket Podcast.
But never fear, I always have a suitable replacement.
George Bailey last week joined me for a great chat.
And I got a message during the week too, by the way, when I threw it out there basically saying,
hey, get in contact with us.
We do have an email address, which is abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au.
And let us know who are a couple of the people that you would love to hear from during this period
while the IPL was going on, Ed's getting refreshed in some random part of the world,
And Liam got in touch with me.
And one of the first things that Liam said was, Corb, would love for you to have a chat
with Ryan Harris if you can bring him on.
Well, Liam, I've done exactly that.
The all-conquering coach of the South Australian cricket team, Ryan Harris,
is my special guest today on the ABC Cricket Podcast.
A man who took over 100 test wickets.
He was an absolute warrior, sending them down for Australia for many years.
And now he is taken to the coaching game.
And boy, has he had success straight out of the gates.
Won three of the last four major domestic titles in Australian domestic cricket
with the team that I'll still call the Redbacks, the mighty South Australian cricket team.
Twice winning the Sheffield Shield, the drought-breaking title, while then defending it,
obviously in the season just gone.
And then chucking a one-day title the year before as well to add to the list of accolades.
And I'm pleased to say he joins me as my guest on the ABC Cricket Podcast.
Yeah, it's a nice feeling to be obviously sitting here again with a Sheffield Shield
sitting in the room next door.
Well, that'd be set the Australian cricket fans thinking we would have just taken one.
We had to wait like 30 years or whatever to get a drought-breaking title.
And then you go out and you back it up away from home in a Shield final.
I mean, what a 12, 13 months for SA cricket.
It's been three years since I've been back at South Australian cricket.
So, it's been a huge couple of years.
And, you know, the reason I moved back is I thought I could see some real growth in this group.
And, you know, we've managed, obviously, to have a change in the leadership with myself coming in
and Dizzy sort of stepping out.
But, you know, the group of – a great group of guys, you know, and they've shown –
I think they've shown over the last couple of years what they can actually do.
So, and you talk about, you know, the game in the Shield final in Melbourne this year
was probably one of the better games of cricket I've been involved in.
And it's easy to say that now because we won.
But I think for a team to sort of be out of the game the whole game
and then fight back in the last day and a half to be able to get the result that we did
just show – I think it just shows the fight and, you know, the determination in this group that I've got.
And one of the things I tried to do when I moved – when I came in was exactly that.
And it was a great example of that in the final.
They got the result that we wanted.
So I'm just going to pick up what you're putting down there, right?
Your chat with Ned Hall on the ABC, which was moments after the last wicket fell.
Can you take us back to that moment?
What made you emotional in that moment?
I've been emotional at times through the season with the players.
I was probably a little bit emotional in the morning of that last day, to be honest.
I've been asked that a couple of times.
I can't really put my finger on exactly why and what.
But I just think it was – probably it's just the group of guys I have that work so hard
that I have a lot of respect for.
And, you know, hopefully they have a lot of strength for me.
But I just think to be able to come out and do what they did, as I said,
And I think I said the message in the morning, as I got them, you know,
at whatever time it was, 9.30 in the morning, is that, you know,
today wasn't going to define us as a group whether the result went our way.
It was all about – I think what I saw, what I remember saying was that we've
We've already done such a great thing this year and being in a position that
we're in to compete in the final.
Today, you know, if we weren't to go – you know, if it wasn't going our way today,
this is not going to define us, us as a group now is a great group of guys
And, you know, I had so much respect for it.
And I got a little bit of emotion probably saying that in the morning.
So I think it's just a group that, as I said, you know, I watch them train.
I watch them work so hard to be able to get the result that they did.
That's probably the emotional part there.
And I just – you know, I've got so much respect for them.
I grew up in WA and I feel like I look at some of the issues that WA cricket
faces and have done for a period of time and the issues that South Australian
And it feels like they share a lot of things in common.
And in the past, it's been, you know, whether it's past players, you know,
that feel like they know the way and they want to do it a certain way.
The connection with grade cricket and we want to develop our own players.
We don't want to just get people in from, you know, from other states
or whatever it turns out to be.
And the push and pull of that conversation all the time with every tier of cricket
So from a South Australian point of view, I always look at the Shield team and
sometimes it looks a little bit like the island of misfit toys.
It's guys that have come from other states and all over the place.
And yet in a way that no one else has been able to for the last 20 years,
Ryan, you've been able to harness that and get the best out of those guys.
And you lived a little bit of it in your cricketing journey,
How do you go about dealing with that aspect of it when it comes to coaching
a complex state like South Australia with all those elements baked into it?
Yeah, I mean, firstly, I mean, firstly, ultimately, we want to make sure
we want to have South Australians playing in this state.
And there's no doubt about that.
But I think we just don't have to teleport.
And that's no disrespect to any of the club cricketers,
but we just don't seem to have that right now.
We're trying to get, and we are getting, you know,
some young players coming up through our pathways.
We've got a great, a very good pathway system with some very good coaches.
So we're sort of adjusting that.
But ultimately, we've got a pretty small talent pool.
And, you know, being able to, and I have to put it out there as well.
We've got a guy from Shaw Williams who's been here for 12, 13 years.
He's seen a lot of cricket.
When I was coaching under-19 Australian stuff and doing the pathways
of cricket for Australia, he was heavily involved in a guy
that I would talk to a lot about talent.
So we've got a guy that, he knows a lot about talent around the country.
He knows just about every cricket and playing cricket.
And so he chooses pretty carefully who we want, who we need.
Well, firstly, who we need, then who we want.
And then also the personality, the person that comes in.
So in terms of having a squad that's sort of outside of South Australia,
it's, yep, again, we want South Australians playing.
But when it comes to these guys not growing up and playing here as, you know,
coming through pathways, that the massive advantage for me is that these guys
are really, really close and good mates because they hang out a lot.
They're really good back at their great clubs, their premier clubs,
where they obviously choose to play when they come over.
But, you know, they've formed relationships.
But what they do is, you know, they've got such a close bond because they spend
so much time together outside of training.
So in terms of, you know, guys that have sort of missed out in other states,
that's the bonus, I guess, we get.
Obviously, a few guys from New South Wales.
But then when they come here, they hang out.
And people have asked me over the last week,
they just seem to be a really, really tight group.
And they, you know, for me, even, you know,
not that I have too many disciplinary sort of things to do with this group.
But, you know, it saves me having to bark at the guys all the time about this
They do it themselves because they're so close and they look after each other.
So that, for me, as well, makes it just a great group to coach.
And, you know, they're a pleasure to coach.
And they're all my good mates, too.
I guess it's always just the structure of cricket that, yeah,
the state selectors or state coaches are always nipping at the heels of the,
you know, the national selectors saying,
how come our guy doesn't get more attention?
Do you get that from grade cricket?
People saying, yeah, what about this born and bred South Australian player?
And, you know, you should be doing more to try and put those guys in the team
as opposed to bringing someone in from elsewhere.
I mean, it's proven to be successful.
You've done something no one else has done in 30 years.
But how do you deal with those conversations from, you know,
Yeah, I mean, I think it's exactly that.
It's a conversation that we need to have.
So we've got, again, we've got myself as a selector.
We've got Sean Williams as a selector.
And we've got Mark Cosgrove as another ex-player who's a selector who,
you know, what we've done over the last couple of years,
I must admit that the relationship between the SAC and the grade clubs
wasn't great when I first got back here.
So, you know, it was a bit of that.
We're not peaking guys that are born and bred.
But ultimately, you know, what I did, and sorry,
I shouldn't say what I did, what we did when I started was that we,
one of the big things was we had to have a good relationship with our people
Again, we go outside at times.
But so I got all the club coaches in and sat them down.
And the thing about that is if they're inquiring about players that should be
playing for South Australia, then their players are playing well.
It makes the club competition stronger and makes it a better standard.
So we had the conversation about, you know, we understand.
And ultimately, we want a team one day with South Australians in it.
But to go back on what Sean Williams does, you know,
he was saying that we just haven't got that.
So it's the honest conversation about we are looking at players from South Australia.
If there's someone there, we'll pick them.
And if there's not, then we won't.
And we have to go into state.
And that's the way it goes.
But also, what we've done over the last couple of years,
we use our second 11 as well to give guys opportunity to show what they can do,
And I think that's the bottom line is you've got to be performing well
And I want them reading me saying, why isn't this guy picked?
Because if we've got our state players playing well,
if we've got our club players playing well, putting pressure on,
we're going to have great, as I said before, really good competing club.
And then they're pushing our state team, which are going to be playing better anyway.
So it all sort of funnels itself up to make sure that, you know,
we have good, solid cricket that makes it better for the state.
You mentioned the culture of this group and how tight they all are.
You've clearly had this mantra sort of, you know,
we, not me and the whole team aspect that goes into it.
How do you go as a coach that walks in the door,
as someone that spends so much time in dressing rooms,
whether it's as an assistant coach or, you know, as a player, obviously,
and a senior player for the back end of your career,
how do you go about building a culture?
What would you say is that if you were giving advice to a young coach or whatever
about, you know, you walk straight into a locker room and you say,
this is the imprint that we want to put on a team.
How do you go about doing that?
Yeah, it's a really good question to try and put into words.
I mean, I'm quite a passionate sort of person.
So I sort of, I think one thing, if you probably, the way I look at it,
I hope, is if you ask to play that, what makes me, what makes Ryan tick?
And, you know, I'm on, I ride every ball with the guys.
You know, they see me at times during the game,
which I'm obviously very careful of showing too much emotion.
And they know that when, you know, when they're doing or playing
or whatever they're doing in a game or training,
that they know I'm right with them.
I'm riding every ball, every shot, everything with them.
So I think the biggest thing for me is, like I said,
I'm pretty good mates with most of all of the boys.
Most of them be closer than others.
But I just think, you know, the passion that I probably, you know,
I played with a lot of passion.
I coached a lot of passion.
I think that's the way, that's me.
It's how I tick when it comes to this game.
So I just, yeah, I think it's just more that they know that their coach
and their coaching staff, they're really good coaching staff,
that every time they walk up on the field, you know,
11 of them are out there, there's three other coaches sitting up
in the coaching box or four that are absolutely right behind them.
And, you know, and one of the things, as I say,
a lot of the things that I've done in the past, you know,

episodes.title: George Bailey chats relationships with the press, retirements and Ashes reviews
episodes.description: Chief selector George Bailey is one of the most influential figures in Australian cricket and joins Corbin to talk through the life of a selector.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast time with one of your boys, Corbin Middlemass in today. There is no Ed Cowan. He's taking a well-earned break, as we say, in the industry. There's no such thing as a cricket off-season. The IPL obviously ongoing at the moment. But Ed's going to just try and take a little bit of time off and recharge the batteries. During that time, when Ed isn't here, I'll be joined by some of the heavy hitters in Australian cricket. So if there's a special guest in particular that you want to hear from on this podcast, of course, your favourite cricket podcast, you can hit us up at abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. That's abccricketpodcast at abc.net.au. And I haven't forgotten, by the way, about Ed and his all-time ODI team. So we'll hold him to that. First up today, the guests don't get too much bigger than this. A man who we talk about all the time here, along with his two selection buddies in Andrew McDonald and Tony Dottomater. My guest today is the chief selector of the Australian cricket team, George Bailey. We talk about the relationship between the team and the press, which we debate, obviously, ongoing here on the ABC Cricket Podcast. People might have different opinions on whether the documentaries being there or not being there is a good thing. I certainly feel like the access to players and the amount of press they do, and then individually with different podcasts and their own social media accounts, I think you're still getting a tremendous insight as to where players are at. The past player criticisms directed at him and at the team more broadly, how that impacts him. I don't perhaps always say it this way, but it's a strength. We don't get the benefit of hindsight. I guess everyone watching and critiquing, they do get that. Who might be the next cab off the rank for the Australian cricket team? And the contract list, which was released last Wednesday. Who got in, who missed out, and what the team is prioritising over the next 12 months? There's no doubt at times we're going to have to go deeper than that. I think always with those contract lists is trying to strike the balance of rewarding those that have performed well in that men's team, particularly across the test space and with what's coming up with the test schedule. And also trying to make sure that you've got all bases covered and a nice balance across that list. So here it is. My chat with the Chief Selector, George Bailey. Former three-format cricketer for Australia, a man who captained his country on many occasions in the white ball format. He is now the Chief Selector of the Australian cricket team. George Bailey joins me on the ABC Cricket Podcast. George, appreciate your time. Howdy, Cole. Squads out. So we learnt that when it came through on Wednesday. What are your key takeaways from the contract list that Cricket Australia released? I think looking forward and understanding that it's a really busy schedule and the contract list is a starting point. There's going to be no doubt at times we're going to have to go deeper than that. I think always with those contract lists is trying to strike the balance of rewarding those that have performed well in that men's team, particularly across the test space and with what's coming up with the test schedule and also trying to make sure that you've got all bases covered and a nice balance across that list. You mentioned as part of it that you have had a leniency towards a longer format of the game, putting this contract list together, given the fact that there's so many test matches in the next 12-month window. So the only three guys that I'm looking at here that are specifically white ball players at the moment, Mitch Marsh, who of course has played red ball cricket in the not-too-distant pass, Adam Zampa and Nathan Ellis. It means there's no Glenn Maxwell, there's no Tim David. Is that their choice? Is that your choice as to how that comes about? Obviously, with the advent of franchise cricket and so many other options, 12 months of the year, how did it come about to leave a couple of those sort of white ball specialists off the list? I think it's looking ahead with what the 12 months is and clearly, I think it's potentially 20, 21, but 20 tests in the next 12 months. Effectively, the red ball focus is going to be huge, but also understanding that at the back end of that, we launch into a 50-over World Cup and then 28 is a home T20 World Cup as well. No idea where the Olympics fit in that at the moment. I haven't got any information. You might have more on that than me. I'm still chasing up. I guess they're three of the key pillars around that white ball team. There's certainly other very important members of multi-format players in that list as well. Is there actually a cut-off date for the Olympic qualification? Are you guys aware of when that has to be, like when you need to be ranked in a certain position or to automatically qualify? No, no idea. No, no. I'd love to know. It's crazy, isn't it? The whole cricket world seemingly in the same boat with that. Jake Weatherald's part of it. Sam Constance isn't. Is that an indication as to what's going to happen the next time the team rolls out in the white clothing in Darwin, that Jake Weatherald will be the opener as he is the incumbent? He is the incumbent. Obviously, playing a part across the Ashes across the summer, also rewarding his consistent performance across a couple of years of domestic cricket as well. Yeah, not shying away from the fact that I think there were a couple of things technically that were targeted and potentially exposed across that Ashes period. But we think he can play. And I think he's got a good opportunity now. He's going to head across to Leicester and have a little stint over there. And in and around that, a good chunk of time where he can get really busy with the coaching staff and, you know, in particular, Michael DiVenuto in that batting space to focus on that. But, you know, as to I won't lock him into that Bangladesh series. I think we've been pretty consistent. You know, we'll pick a team when we need to pick a team. We've got a number of camps across the winter as well, again, which will, you know, encompass a range of players inside and outside that contract list. And, you know, he'll be a part of that and we'll work to that closer. What should we expect from, I guess, the makeup of those teams? Like people would say, yeah, hey, this is a top end series against Bangladesh. It's an opportunity to get a glimpse into the future. Do you look at it more as, you know, this will be not a development team because obviously when you wear the bag of green, it's never that. But is it likely to be a full strength, fully loaded Australian team for that first test in August? Yeah, well, we treat every test match as that. Now, within that, you know, how that shapes up balance wise. We haven't done a great deep dive into, you know, potential conditions up there. We had a little bit of A cricket in the top end last year, some red ball cricket. And we've obviously been up in that part of the world for some white ball cricket as well. So we know the grounds. But no, I think, you know, I would hate to toy with the idea of treating any test match as a development opportunity. And particularly, you know, I think that would be unfair to the players too who invest so much into, as you said, it's not easy to play test cricket and they need to be rewarded for that. Your coach was on radio in Melbourne a couple of days ago and spoke about Webster and Green and that he can see them both playing in the same team in the middle order. He did also preface that by saying, look, I haven't spoken to my fellow selectors yet. I get the opportunity here to speak to one of them. Is that how you see it, given Usman Khawaj's retirement and the fact that there is a spot at number five? Do you see the potential that, you know, that that middle order includes both Webster and Green? Yeah, absolutely. I think we've been on record of saying that those two can play on the same team in the past as well. Well, yeah, I don't see it as a hindrance, the fact that they both have a skill set across the bat and ball. Again, you know, hopefully they both are available to boot. The ball increase by that stage of the year, that'd be helpful. But again, it'll be striking the balance of what we need. I guess specifically, yes, you know, to Uzi or that number five spot opening up. But yeah, I mean, I think we've seen Cam back across a range of positions. I know he probably wasn't as, probably didn't quite get the output that he would have liked across the Aussie summer. But even thinking back to the tricky wickets in the West Indies and again, not massive scores, but in terms of contributions and percentage of runs in what were winning totals, he did really well. So he certainly got the skill set to do that. You know, Alex Carey is another one, I think, who, you know, he's gone up to six. He's got some flexibility there too. So, yeah, no, I mean, I guess the starting point is they can absolutely both play on the same team. Can he bat five, Alex Carey? I reckon he could, whether, you know, whether it suits the balance and understanding that he, you know, on the back of spending however long he may need to in the field. And most of it up to the stumps now, he seems to be loving that. Yeah, what an incredible summer he's had. Congratulations on the Ashes. I mean, a 4-1 series victory at any time is absolutely worthy of celebration. And certainly I think Australian cricket fans appreciated that. Andrew McDonald spoke about the review. And I think in the radio interview with Gerard Waitley, he even had it in front of him and spoke about the subcategories and the training and preparation, all the different areas. Can you give us a little insight as to how that review went? Yeah, I mean, we review every major series. So it's not like it was a special touch point or anything. So it was just, yeah, going through. And I certainly don't have it in front of me, Corb. Apologies for that, unprepared. But, yeah, going through the same sort of four, five, six sort of major headlines and just reviewing. And no two series are the same. So I think there's always little bits you take out of it. I think that, you know, certainly from my area in the selection management, one of the big thing that we try and look back on is just to make sure we, you know, was there anything we missed? Were there any sort of questions or challenge ourselves sort of moments that we didn't foresee? Yeah. And, you know, the ashes, it was the planning for that would have started 12 or 14 months before. You obviously tighten it up as you go. But even as close as probably a month out compared to how that series played out and the personnel that we ended up having available at different times. Some of the guys to step in, some of the late moving parts, even on the morning of games. So, you know, your best laid plans can often be thrown out. But I think what was most pleasing was, you know, how well guys were able to step in and step into some different roles, step in and perform and step in and help that team win. And, you know, it's probably two summers in a row where, you know, the Indian Test Series and the ashes, just the scrutiny and the interest in it's been phenomenal. And I think, you know, that's awesome. And so to see the players, whether that, absorb that with all the different changes that were happening and then come out the other side with a 4-1 victory was very satisfying. They did well. Obviously, we're part of that in what we do on this podcast and certainly in our analysis of the team. I mean, it feels like certainly coming out of Cape Town, there was this Amazon series and it was about showcasing the personalities of the Australian cricket team and who the guys are. And obviously, we've seen less of that in recent times. And it feels like there's been a conscious decision to try and keep the walls a little bit higher. Is that player driven? Is that led by you guys as a selection panel? What's the, I guess, what can you tell us about that? The fact that, and is that part of it, the way that what you're alluding to there, that the criticism or the scrutiny feels like it's as sharp as it has been? No, not at all. I mean, people might have different opinions on whether, yeah, the documentaries being there or not being there is a good thing. I mean, I certainly feel like the access to players and the amount of press they do. And then individually with some, you know, different podcasts and their own social media accounts, I think you're still getting a tremendous insight as to where players are at. But there's probably a focus at certain times within the team to try and, you know, when you do get a day or two in between tests to try and really protect around that. And understanding that you obviously see the physical output within a game, but then also that for players, it's a home summer. But, you know, you only get to potentially stay at your house once for the majority of players. So just understanding the little connection point there with family and friends is also critical. And just being able to freshen up, knowing that, you know, it's coming again and the opposition's hard. So there's been a conscious effort, I think, at different times to protect a day or two. But I think the access is really high. And I still think players are pretty good. I mean, a lot of that potentially comes down to the individual personalities of certain players and where they're at and what they're willing to share. Is this stuff we can do better, do you think, as the press? I don't know, mate. I hadn't really. I mean, I think internally I always, we always think that it's, you know, your good times, you're never going as well as you sometimes are built up to be externally. And vice versa, when things don't go well and you have a bad game or a bad series, things aren't as dire as they seem to be as well. So it's probably just a keeping of the balance and understanding that like anything, you know, particularly in sport, that there's natural ebbs and flows. And it's not certainly in a player's career or a player's series, it's not linear where there's just this constant performance. And they're always working on trying to perform better and trying to fit their role in the team like we are as staff in terms of constantly trying to evolve with the team as well. We've seen, I think there was an article by Tom Deason recently where he detailed his exchange with Cam Green following that Sheffield Shield game. Is that a concern in the, I guess, the relationship between the player and the press and then also Cam more specifically as how he's going as such an asset for Australian cricket as a guy who's about to embark on a pretty long and sometimes difficult IPL campaign? No, I mean, I haven't spoken to Cam directly about that. I imagine, and you know him, you would have spoken to him many times across his journey. I'm very comfortable in saying it's an out of character reaction from him. So that's something that he will potentially reflect and speak to, you know, at some point. But no, I think for the vast majority, using Tom as an example, we've had a number of away trips. I think generally the guy, the cricket writers, the tour, I think everyone gets along well with them. And, you know, everyone just understanding that players have a job to do, the press have a job to do. And, you know, if that works well in, you know, together, I think everyone benefits. You've copped your fair share of criticism too for, you know, again, I'm not trying to blow smoke here, but it's sort of you've had great results clearly in your time as a chief selector. And yet, you know, former players have been critical as, you know, whether you're able to make hard calls on players. And I guess the nature of your job is we don't get to see the hard calls that you do make, obviously, behind the scenes and the conversations that you have. We only obviously get a chance to judge on what the team looks like when it goes out there. How do you go with that as a former player? You know, often the criticism's coming from guys that either you played with or that are, you know, past members of the Australian cricket team. How do you go handling that while also trying to, you know, follow the vision and continue on the path that obviously you have for this team? I think fundamentally it's a, you know, I don't perhaps always say it this way, but it's a strength. You know, I don't, I can't recall ever being in a situation with this team where it feels like if we don't send this 11 out, we can't win the game. So again, it's probably just not so binary around black and white of this is the 11 that can win. I think the coaching staff and playing group have bought into the, and have built up a system where they like to think that there's different ways that they can win a game. And part of that will be the way your team's structured, part of that will be the opposition and clearly the surface at different times as well and being flexible and being flexible within that. So, you know, we don't get the benefit of hindsight. I guess everyone watching and critiquing, they do get that. And, but, you know, we never, I don't think we've ever been in a situation to say where, I don't want to use specific examples, but player X gets a tight selection call going his way. Now it's not to say that we, that we also don't believe that if we'd gone with player, player wide that we also wouldn't have got the same result. It might've been done differently, but we can still, we can still win the game that way. So I try and see it as a strength that, you know, it's great that there are other options and people are publicly backing other options. You know, I imagine in some cases there's some, there's some bias around why people are certain, you know, have certain fondness for players that aren't in the team. But it's, you know, it's a, it's a strength. Hopefully that continues. And hopefully the Australian cricket team continues to have options when it's picking, picking 11s or picking squads. Just on hindsight, if you had your time again, would you play a frontline spinner in Sydney? No, but you could. I mean, yeah, I mean, that's, that's, I think we can continue to debate that. We debated it right up and right up until the morning of the game. Our starting, our starting position is that we don't like not picking a spinner. We don't, we like picking a spinner. We don't, I think when we're putting a test 11 together, the starting premises, there will be a spinner in it, but not, not trying to fight, not trying to fight the conditions just to prove a point at different times. But again, that, I mean, that's, that's probably a good example of one where, yeah, I think we could have played a spinner and I would like to think that we will get the same result. The game might've played out differently, but, but hopefully you could still execute that. In recent times on the schedule, the, the test summer has been starting in Perth. I noticed as, as one of the subheadings in that Ashes review, it was sort of training and preparation. I think you're a fascinating watch in your team and how it's presented in Perth. So two years in a row, split results, one, one, lost one. I think clearly, if you look back on the, the India series, the team warmed into it and clearly, you know, with a better team by the time the, the five test series ended, ended against India, but it didn't start well and you copped a lot of criticism there. Then also when you look at what happened here, it was a fast and frenetic test match. And ultimately another world leanings from, from Travis had separated the two teams. You had a player breakdown in the match. You had players that didn't get to the start line. There's also the added element of the time difference and the fact it's on the other side of the country and guys are sometimes coming off white ball schedules or whatever it turns out to be. Have you refined that or have you reviewed, like, what's the best way to be able to, to start in Perth to make sure that the best version of the Australian cricket team is the one we get in the, in the first red ball test of the summer? Yeah, it's a good question. I mean, I think, I don't think there is a perfect prep. You know, I think if there was, you'd, you'd just replicate that in every time. So there's a, there's a number of factors. I think it depends what you've got in and around that test series, what guys have been coming up off. Have they, have they got enough body of work to be able to perform their role? You know, particularly the, around the fast bowlers and making sure they've got up to the intensity or, or miles in their legs, if you want to call it that. And yeah, as you said, we, we, we lost a couple in the lead up this year, which is never, never ideal. And then there's other years where on the back of a lot of cricket, you might be trying to, to massage them in. Yeah. I, I, I haven't sort of looked back on that and said that, you know, we won the game. So the preparation for this year was good. And last year's preparation was, wasn't good because we lost the game. I think there's, there's things that happen within a game that, that affect that anyway. And I think both, both games had some individual circumstances that, that blew the game in the directions that they went. But yeah, that, that is part of the review. It's part of the planning process when you go forward is to, well, you know, what, what does it look like? What's it, and we're already looking at, what does it look like for the start of this summer? I think we've got a reasonable block of white ball cricket against England leading into the four tests against New Zealand. So that'll be different again, around how we manage that, the individuals within that and how they're tracking. And, you know, that it is very much making sure that you've got the individuals where they need to be and not just a one size fits all for everyone. So that's constantly been refined. It gets refined late because you get your moving parts. So that's, I mean, that's basically, I think, a good snapshot of what the work that we've been doing over the last month and will continue to do is, is building our camps across the winter with the gap, knowing that once this month, basically from the top end series onwards, it's, it's nuts. And, you know, there's a, there's a period here. We'll still have guys playing overseas. We'll have a group of guys that are getting a little bit of rest and prep time in now. But, you know, individuals are going to be everywhere and doing everything and switching between red and white ball and, you know, or coming in for white ball, coming in for red ball. So just getting that balance right is, is always, always a challenge and, and not always, I guess the outcome doesn't always reflect that. One thing we've debated a lot here has been the selection philosophy around specialized batting positions in terms of, you know, openers versus middle order players. And yeah, some have worked well, some haven't worked as well, but it turns out when you look back on the Australian test team for guys that have come in in various spots and Trevor's head's probably proof the other way that he's a guy that can go from the middle order up the top and have success. The T20 team, Steve Smith, obviously not playing. And a lot of the reasoning given for that is that he's an opener. He's not a middle order player. So I guess from a selection philosophy point of view, do you see batting positions more specific in the T20 game than you do in the, in the test arena? No, not necessarily. You know, I think it's, you're potentially trying to break down a, a long stereotype, but again, that's part of, I think what Pat and Mitch through, through captaining these teams and, you know, in conjunction with the, the coaching staff and management around the Australian team is trying to, trying to build teams that have some inherent flexibility or adaptability. And, and that can change either before a game or within a game that can help you get momentum going your way. And I think that's, you know, I don't think that'll, that'll necessarily happen overnight, but that's, that's a work in progress. Can we develop that as that can? And again, knowing that conditions, you know, we've seen Travis do it for a number of years in the subcontinent where we feel he's best suited at the top. And then when the opportunity was there, it looks like it works quite nicely in Australia as well. And also, I'm seeing, you know, that, that may not suit every player. It may not suit every player's personality as well. But again, it's, you know, how, how does it fit? How does it make the team function as a whole? Well, I think you're always, whenever you're putting a team together, you're trying to play to your strengths. There's always going to be a way, you know, the staff talk about a way that you are prepared to lose the game in a quest to try and win it and win it on your terms. Whose responsibility is it to, and I know this is a buzz term, sort of future-proof the team? I mean, I look at you guys as selectors and the next series always feels like the most important one. And so then naturally you've got an older team. But understandably, if I was picking the team, I would think I want to put the best players together that I possibly can at this particular point in time to make sure that we're going to win. So is it the responsibility of the States? Is it also you guys while sort of keeping one eye on the here and now? Whose responsibility is it to make sure that, that the team's not just good today, but also good in five or 10 years time? Yeah, I think that's always, always a focus. And you, you know, once you, once you go into the crystal ball, I think it's dangerous to assume that it will be perfectly future-proof. And I think it's equally as dangerous to assume that there's going to be this cliff where, when you lose. And I get the narrative because, you know, I think over the last few years, if you put Warner, Smith, Kawaja, Cummins, Hazelwood, Stark, Lyon, you've got guys that are going to come up in, in conversations for, you know, some of Australia's best ever players and in Australia's best ever team. So, so yeah, what does that look like when they aren't there for a game or a series or when they eventually move on from formats or altogether?
