episodes.title: Shield final confirmed but the season batting numbers are grim reading
episodes.description: We know it will be Victoria vs South Australia in the Sheffield Shield final but the real question is, why have the runs been so hard to come by this season?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast time with your boys, Corbyn Middlemass and Ed Cowan for your Monday. My name's Corbyn Middlemass. I'm in my home port, as the Australian cricket team would refer it, here in the beautiful city of Melbourne. Ed Cowan is on the other side of the world, somewhere in a completely different time zone. Hello to you, Teddy. Corby, you're coming through loud and clear though. I might not be close, but I can hear you. Too loud. How are you? No, good. Loud enough. Beautiful. I'm well. I feel like I'm a little bit short on cricket. It's a bit of domestic cricket, sort of kicking around. Obviously, I'm just waiting for the IPL to start, I'm sure, like every cricket fan. Oh yeah, are we all? But not a whole lot of international cricket going on, obviously, for our lads, but no shortage of talking points, which is why we're here to chop it up on a Monday. Where are you? Are you going to tell us where you are in the world? I'm in Canada. Okay. I'll give you that. In Canada. Hopefully. Enjoying the winter, a bit of snow, a little time out. I was about to say. Time out for Teddy before work kicks in again next week. So, a little bit of work, a little bit of play, a little bit of play, a little bit of work. That's my trip. Yeah. More play for you, I think, is encouraged. No, never. I'm pleased that you're having a little bit of downtime and you're a very busy man. You still carved out a little bit of time to chat to me, so I appreciate that. I'll never miss it. I'll never miss it, Corb. We got a final in the Sheffield Shield, so South Australia is going to play Victoria. Bit of an anti-climax, must be said. A huge anti-climax. Yeah. I know the point system, you know, people are a fan of for various reasons, but... Hang on. Whoa. Who's a fan of the point system? I've never met anyone who is a fan of the most unfollowable point system in world sport. So, tell me who's a fan of that. Are you a fan of it? No. I just... I don't know. Oh, so you're not a fan. No. Not that we're 0% of this podcast, but I get what it's trying to do, but, gee, when you think we could have had this perfect end of the season where, you know, you need to win and you're in and everything else, and all of a sudden, after the first 100 overs, gone. Yeah, 10 overs into day two or whatever it is, or four overs into day two. It's... The whole thing's already decided. South Australia are through, and, you know, well done to them. Nothing against them, but it feels like the rest of the round now doesn't mean anything. Totally. Like, there was an opportunity for South Australia, you know, having to win the game if Queensland were pushing hard for a victory, or, conversely, if South Australia was struggling or there was a draw going on, Queensland could have set up a game, and instead, as you rightly called out, it's decided on one, you know, poor innings down at Bell Reve from Queensland not being able to get any bonus points that no one really understands. Anyway, and all of a sudden, after 10 rounds of the Shield and, well, you know, nine and a half rounds of the Shield and excitement building, it's just flat. It's muted. What's the answer? Do we go back to the old first innings points? There's some middle ground for sure. So what this is trying to encourage is positive attack in cricket. Yeah. And so there's a world where, yes, there's first innings points, but maybe you outsize an outright victory. So, you know, way back when you were in Nappies, it was six points for a win, two points for a first innings win, and not an outright win, and obviously not cumulative. So if you won outright and first innings, you only got six points. Yep. So what you, you know, there's ways and means that you could maybe manipulate those points. So it's much more on offer for an outright win to encourage teams to play for it, rather than, you know, this attacking cricket, which is trying to basically say anything after batting for 100 overs isn't really valuable, unless you feel like you can drive massive advantage in the game. Yeah. And incredibly, we haven't got any top order players in the country, and everyone averages in the mid-30s. So work that one out. And the rules are set up to obviously incentivize the, you know, being a glorified limited overs game. So, yeah, I think it needs an overhaul. It's a couple of years in a row that we've seen, you know, the points system obviously play a role in, you know, ladder positions and everything else. I think we had a very similar conversation this time last year. So South Australia were informed of the situation. So Ryan Harris decided to tell his team when they came off at T on the second day. So they had an advantage over Queensland, and as a result, they're going to go through and play in the final. The knock-on effect is interesting. So Brendan Doggett, who'd been ruled out for the year with a hamstring injury, is now in the mix to possibly return and play in the final. So he suffered that fielding against New South Wales last month. It also ends the first-class career of Usman Khawaja without him stepping on the park. So he has not played in this round due to the impending birth of his third child. So unfortunately, we've seen Uzi for the last time. He played round nine, and that's it for Usman Khawaja. So he won't go around again next year for Queensland. But we've got our finalists now. It starts 10 days from now, Victoria in South Australia at Junction Oval. Yeah, that's sad. I mean, it's the right call-out. It's sad about Usman, you know, not being able to... I'm sure he'd probably reconciled it emotionally himself. But, you know, many of his fans and the cricket fraternity would have loved to see one last game, for sure. But you're right. I think the two best teams are playing in the final. The two best bowling attacks are definitely playing in the final. And we know bowlers, you know, bowling attacks win Sheffield Shield. So it feels right the right two teams are playing. And I think it's setting itself up for an excellent contest. Day three of all these games. So this is the final round. We've got a little preview here. South Australia and Victoria. Both teams made almost identical scores in the first inning. So there was three runs between them with Victoria on top there. So Victoria got their 300 largely by committee. So 66 for Callaway, 59 for Peek. Two of their young star batsmen. And then Will Southerl and the skipper also with a half century. Earlier in the match, Henry Hunt topscored with 81. And Ben Menenti made a late little fight in 53. Four for Todd Murphy, which is good to see after he was obviously left hanging as the 12th man. The back end of that test series in the home summer, obviously, in the Ashes. And Scott Boland amongst the wickets again with three for 66. So this is well set up. I imagine both teams will be just trying to keep a few cards up their sleeve before the final at the same venue, obviously, taking place, as I said, in nine days from now. Anything jump out at you from that game? Not really. It's now, I mean, it's just sad that it's going to peter out, no doubt. Who has the better attack? Victoria or South Australia? Victoria. Yeah, I think so. Who has the better batting line-up? Yeah. Victoria have a better spread. South Australia, probably if we're picking in the schoolyard, you might take Sanger and McSweeney pretty high or whatever. Yeah, obviously Carey. Alex Carey. That's part of it. He goes okay. So, yeah, it'll be a fun final. And, yeah, hopefully there's a reasonably good wicket, as there has been most of the season at Junction Oval for that matter. A couple of these other games, just on some individual performances. The 100 for Cam Green obviously stands out. So, it feels like the storyline around Cam Green gets reinforced again. That, yeah, he's struggling at international level, but every single time he drops back and plays domestic level, he proves that he's too good for the grade. And so, he has, again, here with 135. He can't do much more than that. So, it feels like, you know, that's in the absence of anyone else really knocking down the door for his place in the test team. You'd feel like if there was a test starting tomorrow, he'd be hard to leave out again. So, you're right. Either one of two things happen from here. Either he has a breakout series that puts at least to bed the conversation for a moment, or he gets dropped. And until one of those two things happen, we're going to keep muddling around, wondering whether he's the guy or not. And anyone that saw the game or highlights, you know, you watch him bat against New South Wales. Yes, so, and you think he's just too good for this standard of cricket. So, you know, is it technical? Is it emotional? Is it psychological? As to why he's not at his best when he's playing test cricket? Which one of those is holding him back from test cricket? And it's probably a little bit of all three. You know, personally, I still think he has a lot to deliver for this test team, and he will. It's more a question of role. And so, at the moment, you know, trying to perform the role of a top order batsman, it's bloody hard. And so, you just get the sense that he's a number six who bowls a bit. I know he had a little bit of that opportunity during the Ashes, but he's been, you know, all over the place, really. And so, to bed that down, he needs a series. But at the same time, it's pretty hard to look past what he keeps delivering in the level below. So, it is. And then you look at the rest of the field. So, I sort of went through, given the fact we're nearing the end of the Sheffield Shield season. So, the guys that have scored over 600 runs for the year, and by the way, the top end of this is Pete Hanscom, 688 at 36, and then it's in Takam Bancroft, 665 at 35. And then the guy who comes in as the third leading run scorer in the tournament this year, feels like the forgotten man of Australian cricket, who was the spruit player 12 months ago, Sam Constance. So, he got scores of 38 and 31. He's the third leading run scorer. He's got 660 at 33. So, it hasn't been a year where he's had, you know, big gaudy hundreds or anything like that. In fact, it's been a lot of what he delivered in this match. It's been starts, and then hasn't really gone on with it. So, for a guy that's averaged 33, he's made 38 and 31 in this match. And that's about what the summer has amounted to for Sam Constance. So, how are we meant to feel about him? I mean, he's still such a young player. It feels like his name's certainly not as close to the top end of the conversation as it was this time last year or last winter. And yet, he's in and around his peers. It's not as if they've completely, you know, lapped him. He's right there with them. But at the same time, it doesn't feel overly convincing from what we've seen from him. This is an interesting case study because for someone who's a speculative buy, he's been a model of consistency. So, I think he got out for 31 today in the second innings. But, you know, since Christmas, 44, 28, 27, 35, 37, 28, 38. So, no 50s, no real failures. And, you know, to be honest, as an opening batsman, that's kind of criminal. To get yourself in and to get yourself out, that's emotional and mental, not technical. And so, you know, to be able to grind out a 70 or an 80 or 150, you know, that turns your season around. But as you say, he hasn't been lapped by the pack. So, I don't know whether that says more about Sam or less about those around him. But on the upside, this is a kid. This is a kid learning the game. There's a full shield season in his kit bag that he can draw on and his experiences. And he's got better for it. So, again, we're looking for opening batters. No one is screaming out saying, pick me, pick me, pick me. And he's probably only a couple of scores away. So, I think it's a good news story. I just don't feel great about it. Yeah. They're fascinating reading. And this is the problem the selectors are going to have. So, say we next play a test match in August against Bangladesh. You look through the lineup and the incumbents at the moment. You think, well, Head plays. Smith's going to play. Carey's going to play. I think Green plays. I think he comes back and scores 100 here. They're going to stick with him. I think Webster plays. Khawaja drops out. So, there's five of your seven immediately. You need two more players. You need top order positions. The question is, do you stay with Wetherald? And do you stay with Marnas? So, I mean, Marnas scored good runs when he played domestic cricket, particularly against the white ball. But if you look at the top run scorers in domestic cricket, so, as I said, the top end is north of 660 but averages in the 30s. And then you have to go all the way down to 560 runs for a season to get to someone that averages 40. And that's Wetherald. So, 562 at 40. Jake Lehman averages 40 as well, but now he's not eligible to play for Australia, nor is he in the conversation to play as a top order player. And then even if you talk to the data a little bit further, you go, well, who are the 100 makers? Who are the guys that are going to put up big runs or whatever it turns out to be? Matt Renshaw's got 300, so that leads the way. But then two each for Marnas, for Lehman, for Curtis Patterson, for Harper, and for Hanscom. So, they've got 200s, and then everybody else is one or fewer. So, that's what the batting ranks look like in domestic cricket for those that are next up. And I feel like we don't even have the Jake Wetherwood case like we had last summer where we felt like, you know, whoever you want to go with, you can always resort back to, you know, there's a standout in domestic cricket. There's no name there that really jumps off the page to me, Teddy, that says, hey, I should knock out the incumbent, even though the guy in the seat hasn't absolutely batted down his position yet. Yeah. In this case, the incumbent keeps his spot, even despite the question marks. And you're right. You know, like someone like Curtis Patterson, who we've talked a lot about, and I'm sure we will when we come to the one-day tournament, 200s but averaging 34. So, you know, as a high-quality top-order player, that's a middling season. But across the board, kind of scratching my head, is it the player quality? Is it their ability to translate their technique across formats? Or simply is it that the wickets are spicier than they've ever been? I don't know. I've watched enough shield cricket to think, yeah, there's some life in the wickets, but it hasn't at any stage looked horrific or unplayable. It does build up, though. I do have a lot of empathy for the top-order players when consistently every wicket has a little bit in it. You know, historically, maybe the Gabba was a bit of a seeming wicket or Belle Reve, and then you got back to the Adelaide Oval and you just knew that that was a run fest and you could get your confidence back. Like, every single ground around Australia now seems. Every single one. And so, you know, you can get in these little moments of five, six, seven innings where you don't do much wrong. You feel like you're playing well, but you look at the score sheet and you've gone, you know, 10 or 20 or, you know, balls had your name on it. So I do have empathy for that. That's hard work. And that is probably the difference. It's not that there are wickets with life in them. It's the quality of wickets with a bit of juice in them is probably higher, or the quality of wickets on average is lower. And then the balls, obviously, with the prouder seam. And I know the players talk a lot about that. This is where it's sort of, you talk about the sympathy for the top order players. Brings me to one guy who's certainly a forgotten player in test cricket. And I'm not suggesting, you know, for a second that they're going to pick him because when he was scoring big, huge runs, they didn't pick him. So they're probably not going to do it now. But underrated season, all things considered for Cam Bancroft. So 665 at 35, which again, you know, is north of his average when he's at his best, but plays half his games at the WACA. He's batted nine times. He's the only player in the competition, other than Jordan Silk, to have not scored over 56 times. So six of his nine hits, he's gone 50 plus. Yeah. In the end, in a season where runs are hard to come by, it's the second leading run scorer in the competition. On the back of a horrendous summer last year, it's not a bad follow-up. Plus he'll get to play in England as well. So he'll keep his red ball form going, but got a little half century in this fixture while Cam Green went large. That's the sand grabber coming out on you. Yeah. I mean, it's going to be an ongoing conversation though, isn't it? In terms of, you know, where are our batters? Who are the next guys? Who are the top order players? What's it going to look like if not now in the, you know, in the medium term? Just on the last of those games, Tasmania, 198 and then six for 264 batting the second time. They took a 21 lead on the first inning. So effectively 284 ahead. The last time I checked that score, Queensland all out 178. And as a result, their hopes of making the final went with it. Wetherald 39 and 62. So again, sort of same kind of thing as what we're talking about with Constance, with Bancroft, now with Wetherald, sort of getting out at difficult times. 82 for Jordan Silk in this game as well. And in terms of the bowlers, Mick Nisa, who certainly had a fine summer, obviously playing test cricket for Australia, 5 for 37. And Xavier Bartlett had 3 last time I checked that score as well. Teddy, the one-day cup came to its conclusion on Wednesday on a cold night down in Tasmania. And New South Wales have a bit more silverware in the cabinet. There is a whole lot to pull apart from this game. But Curtis Patterson saw New South Wales home with an unbeaten 50. So that gives him 300s and three half centuries, averaging over 100 for the tournament. And appropriately, he led New South Wales to a victory here. They had to beat the number one team in consecutive games on their home patch to get it done. And I think that makes you a pretty worthy champion. Yeah, it does for sure. I mean, in both games, Tasmania batted first. And we know the advantage of chasing runs at Belle Reve. So they didn't do any justice to their season in either of those innings. And in both of them, really, New South Wales kind of chased it down easily. There were a few little moments in the final. A few hiccups, you could say. I mean, it wasn't an easy target on a wicket that was offering plenty, more like a four-day wicket and, you know, 120 in 20-odd overs. But Curtis Patterson looked really like he was playing a different game. He was playing a different sport at times. Everyone couldn't put bat on ball and he didn't miss the middle. So it was a sensational innings. It capped off a fantastic season for him and a great season for New South Wales. And, you know, a great way to send Greg Shippard off as the coach. Well, that's the unmissable talking point, isn't it? So 39 days after he was sacked for essentially not... I thought I'd get it in. I knew you were going to talk about it. So I thought I'd get it in. For not winning titles, which was part of the J-Day. All of a sudden, he wins a title, but he's already lost his gig. I think there were reports coming through that he was in the karaoke singing, I'm still standing. Well, he was for a minute, but obviously this round of Shield cricket will be his last as the coach of New South Wales. I think the question that probably arose was, aside from the titles, is he the coach to bring this next generation of New South Wales players to play Test cricket? I don't know the answer to that. It's a win-at-all-cost attitude. They need to learn to win. And, you know, I'm sure that was probably top of mind for the last couple of weeks as well. Yeah. I think I said this at the time when we spoke about it. It was an error one way or the other. And that was probably a thoughtful stand down. Just one more before we move on from domestic cricket. And then Curtis Patterson obviously leads them in the final and ultimately goes on to become the title winning captain there. Is this a little sign of what's to come? Will Jack Edwards be the captain of New South Wales next year? As far as I know. I mean, he didn't captain. He's injured at the moment. So, you know, all those moments of giving up were for a specific reason. Yeah, there's no doubt being an all-rounder, opening the bowling, batting at six and being captain takes its toll. And when you're a young captain still learning that and you're still trying to play for Australia as Jack is, you can imagine the emotion that goes into these fixtures. So there's no doubt that New South Wales will have to manage that probably a little bit better than they did. But you saw the back half of the season, you know, that toll started to play out in the injury. So I expect him to be the captain, no doubt. But how that plays out might be slightly different. Maybe does the four-day, not the one-day. I don't know. It hasn't been a discussion yet. Sounds like me on this podcast, the way you're running through it. I've got to host the show. I've got to give the sharp opinions and lean on all my cricketing experience and everything else to be able to pull us along on the ABC Cricket Podcast. By the way, one thing we have done, Declan Burns got on board and he's keeping us all in order here. episodes.title: Reckoning with the depth of India's T20 dominance
episodes.description: India thumped NZ to make T20 World Cup history and Corbin and Ed can't see anyone competing with them in the near future.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast. I'm with your boys Corbyn Middlemass and Ed Cowan for your Monday. India, the champions of the world again at the T20 World Cup. We have one round left in the Sheffield Shield. We're down to three teams in contention for the title. Speaking of titles, the one-day cup is coming up. But this Wednesday, the final at Bellwave Oval. Plus, Women's Series comes to a close. Curtain comes down on Elisa Healy's career. We've got a whole lot to chop up. My name's Corbyn Middlemass. Ed Cowan is in Sydney. Hello, Teddy. Corby. Here we are. Big Monday pod. Oh, yeah. I mean, world champions. India. First team ever to go back-to-back, which you weren't big on that stat leading into the tournament. But, hey, it's... First host country to ever win it. First host country to ever win. Oh, didn't you? And the first three-time champions that we've ever seen. So, they've now won the T20 World Cup more than any other team. They were obviously coming off a high after posting 253 in the final. They beat the second-best team in the tournament, England, there. And then took on New Zealand in the final. And what an interesting game we saw last night. A 96-run win. So, 96-run win in front of 100,000 at the Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad. Abhishek Sharma, Sandru Sampson got them off to a great start. The opener's put on 92 in the power play alone. And Sandru Sampson, when this tournament was on the line, boy, did he bring his best cricket. So, 97-not in the Super 8s in that must-win game against the Windies. 89 in the semi, 89 in the final. He was named player of the tournament. Ishan Kishin scored a neat little half-century. 255 India posted. So, they actually beat their semi-final score of 253. And then New Zealand, in reply, they lost Finnell and Early. Lost Ravindra to the first ball that Boomerah bowled. Boomerah finished with four for 15. He struck twice. In the 16th over in consecutive balls. Picked up another one in his 18th. 18th and really apart from a half-century for Tim Seifert. They never got going. The Black Caps, in the end, they were all out for 159 with an over to go. So, all out in the 19th over. Big win for India at the World Cup. This is what you call a real fizzer. A fizzer. As it's not across the Dutch. Yes. But in terms of, you know, the script playing out, it was almost to a tee, wasn't it? You know, New Zealand push hard throughout the tournament. The underdog scrapped their way to another final in a World Cup or Champions Trophy and then can't get over the line. I mean, realistically, this game was done after six overs. I mean, 90 in the power play. Everything's against you at that point in time. You just can't wrestle back momentum for the rest of the game as much as you try. And so, you know, they tried to take the pace off the ball consistently and it kept being taken over the fence. So, the Indian T20 cricket is only accelerating. They have the strongest T20 league in the world. They, you know, their younger players are exposed to the pressure of the IPL, which is probably now far greater than most international T20 games. They have this talent funnel and pipeline for this format of the game like no other nation. And so, it's kind of hard to see how other countries are going to compete with them, really. And that's a bit of a bare case. But these World Cups roll around every two years. And you'd be hard-pressed to suggest India, even though it's in Australia, aren't going to start favourites for that one as well. Yep. I think that's a pretty good breakdown. When you think about they've got the best T20 batsman in the world in Abhishek Sharma, he didn't have a great tournament. So, he was off. Surikuma Yardav gets a golden duck in the final. Wasn't really a huge factor throughout. And in the end, Sandro Sampson was great when he needed to be. Jasper Boomer is phenomenal. I mean, it's nothing that hasn't been said before. But, you know, whatever format of the game it is, he's a cut above the rest. And we saw that, obviously, on display again. You know, key moments in this tournament. Yeah. And we talked about it before the tournament started. But what they have been able to do is identify key white ball players. And so, a lot of these names aren't household names to a lot of the Australian audience, aside from if you follow the IPL or the T20 team. They, the modern way is ingrained into them. And they walk out to bat and they try and hit six from the first ball. They've got change-ups. They bowl, you know, it's great spin. You know, T20 spin. And realistically, they could probably field three teams. And those three teams would all make, you know, close to the semifinals. There is so much depth in this format of the game coming out of India. And, you know, it's very hard to compete with because their up-and-coming players, as I said, are exposed to this and ours, you know, muddling along. I mean, they did lose in the group stage, didn't they? South Africa got them. They had to... That was an aberration, though. That was a real aberration. Yeah. They had to pull it out against the West Indies. And England probably pushed them more than, you know, most teams. I think it's clear to say that England were the second-best team, though, Teddy, in the tournament, given they beat New Zealand in the final by 96 runs and they beat England by only seven runs. So does that prove that, given the fact that England won the head-to-head? No. Even though they didn't get as far, they were the better team? No. You still owe me dinner. Unlucky, Corb. I'm going long on vegetable curry. Look, the other thing about the Kiwis. So fifth white ball final in 11 years. Nothing to show for it. Not a single trophy in the cabinet. So this is their role. They're the other team in your favourite sports movie. They're just there to play the broader role of the opposition. So never won a T20 World Cup, never won a 50-over World Cup. Really the only major global tournament they've ever won was the World Test Championship, obviously. They won a Champions Trophy way back when, didn't they? Sure. Great. Cool. But it's – I don't know. Unfortunately for New Zealand, they didn't really give too much last night and they're a long way second in the end, as 96 runs will prove. I don't know what else there's left to say about that game. I mean, yeah, hats off to India, the best team in the world, undoubtedly, when it comes to T20 cricket. Would you change the World Cup format at all? You know, upon reflection, expanded, 20 teams. They kind of mix and match every couple of years. I'd go 16, top two in the group qualify, and then we can do Super 8s. I don't have an issue with that. That's very cricket. So Super 8s from that point into semifinals, into the final. So probably just four teams get a little bit of a haircut, I think. And that still leaves room for some associate nations more, and the qualifiers probably mean a little bit more. I actually thought the last World Cup we had here was excellent. Like, I liked the little pre-tournament that they had with sort of the – Just about to pitch that. I liked that. The qualifiers at the venues prior to the tournament, and then the big teams turn up. And so that team, you know, like you had a situation this time. I know it was an aberration, but the qualifiers were eight months ago for some of these teams. Then they go through their winter cycle, don't play any cricket, and expect them to turn up and reproduce, you know, great cricket against the best teams in the world, as opposed to they're hot, they're ready, they're warm, they actually, you know, can attack from game one. You know, we had a situation where Scotland hadn't played any cricket. As I said, I know that was an aberration with Bangladesh. It's also a great chance to introduce some of those players. So then by the time the tournament starts, you feel like you know them a little bit, and a little bit of their story, and he's the guy that started in the group stage or whatever, or the pre-tournament. episodes.title: T20 World Cups every two years just don't resonate
episodes.description: The T20 World Cup final awaits but the real question is - should this tournament continue to be staged every two years?!
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Cricket Podcast time with your boys, Corbin Middlemass and Ed Cowan for your Friday. We've got our finalists at the T20 World Cup. It will be New Zealand and India for all the marbles. The penultimate round of the Sheffield Shields underway. There's a women's test match which starts today at the WACA ground. And it also doubles up as the last time we'll see Elisa Healy in international cricket. My name's Corbin Middlemass. I am in Sydney. Ed Cowan is also in Sydney and yet we're not in the same room, which I know my podcast co-host is a little snaky about. But good morning to you, Teddy. Corbin, why don't you just call me and say I'm calling the football, the big game that was on last night, whatever, whoever played, whoever. We've got a Friday podcast. Why don't you come into Ultima? It's just down the road, across City Tunnel. I'd be there and you and I could have hugged it out and done this face-to-face because our chemistry is so much better when we're in person. I apologise. I must admit I'm the sort of guy, I don't like disappointing people as you know. So I'm sort of like late night the night before doing my teams for Friday night. I've got to go to the Gold Coast next. Rush in here, do a footy pod. Then I've got a cricket pod. Then I'm on a plane. So I was like, I didn't want you to come all the way in and then we're, you know, I feel like the only time I get with you is on air and then I'm leaving again. So that was sort of my thinking behind it. I didn't want to give people false hope that I had time, which unfortunately I don't have a lot of that. At the moment I'm here for work. It's a business trip. I could have done with a hug, but anyway. Apologies. Apologies. It's lovely to see you though through the screen as we usually do in the universe online. Have you got something for me off the top? I know you've been keen to spit this out. I mean, not that keen, but I did note that New Zealand have qualified for the World Cup final. And I said New Zealand and you kind of had that little glint in your eye like, that's stupid. And now I'm thinking maybe not so stupid. But Finn Allen, let me buy you a beer. I can't believe how let down I've been here. So I feel like my prediction was more bold on England. And yet England were a better team than New Zealand in the tournament. They beat them in the tournament. They almost pulled off the greatest run chase in just about World Cup history. And yet they fell seven runs short. And somehow the team that you picked is the team that's there waiting for them in the final. And so the team that I picked, who were on this unbelievable Cinderella run, somehow fell a stage short. And now I'm an Indian dinner down as a result of it. I'm going to have to cough up there. I couldn't believe it. Couldn't believe it. And I love it. India took two great catches. England dropped a dolly. And, you know, seven runs was the difference. Anyway, keep going. You can give me a great little description. Same guy involved twice. So Akshar Patel took a blinder running back from the infield to deep cover, looking over his shoulder, somehow took it, sliding, you know, face down, head first towards the boundary rope. title: ABC Jazz Favourites - ABC listen
description: Take our curated collections with you on the go! Let ABC Jazz accompany your day or night with our selection of unique, mood-based music picks.

episodes.title: Blues For Dreaming
episodes.description: Unwind to this relaxing mix of soothing jazz. Drift off with ethereal numbers from the likes of drummer Manu Katche, vocalist Norma Winstone, the Charlie Haden/Keith Jarrett duo and more.

episodes.title: Too Darn Hot
episodes.description: Stay cool with a selection of groovin' tunes from ABC Jazz. Ella Fitzgerald gets this session underway, and you'll also enjoy tracks from Django Reinhardt and Anita O'Day.

episodes.title: Walkin'
episodes.description: Get your kicks on and get moving with a fantastic selection of upbeat tunes from ABC Jazz. Enjoy classics from Nina Simone, Miles Davis and Australia's own Dan Barnett across this hour of groovin' tracks.

episodes.title: Sensational Piano
episodes.description: Immerse yourself in a hand-picked selection of songs that celebrate the finest in jazz piano with a swathe of jazz tunes for every occasion.

episodes.title: Jazz Instruments: Piano
episodes.description: The piano is certainly a grand instrument in jazz, and on this session our presenter Mal Stanley looks back at some of the finest players from yesteryear right up to today.

episodes.title: Jazz Instruments: Drums
episodes.description: Enjoy a selection of music from the hardest hitting drummers in jazz. From the early sessions in Chicago to pioneers like Tony Williams and Terri Lyne Carrington, here are some essential names on the instrument.

episodes.title: Jazz Instruments: Male Vocals
episodes.description: Kick back with a selection of tunes featuring some of the iconic male singers in jazz!

episodes.title: Jazz Instruments: Electric Bass
episodes.description: Eric Ajaye is a master electric and double bass player - and on this session, he's bringing to you tunes from a handful of the leaders who have forged their own sound on the electric bass.

episodes.title: Jazz Instruments: Female Vocals
episodes.description: In jazz, the voice is an instrument much like the tenor sax or the trumpet, and across this session we'll be exploring some of the important artists who have used their voice to further the music.

episodes.title: Jazz Instruments: Trumpet
episodes.description: Enjoy a bright and brassy selection of tunes featuring the pioneers of jazz trumpet! This session kicks off with Louis Armstrong and takes us through to innovators like Miles Davis, Clifford Brown and Clora Bryant.

episodes.description: Donald Trump went into the war with Iran thinking it would be over quickly. More than seven weeks later there’s still no obvious off ramp, with uncertainty surrounding a second round of peace talks in Pakistan.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi News Daily listeners. Just stopping by quickly to let you know about my new pod. One of Australia's most baffling missing persons cases. In 2007, four people vanished. The family lived a bizarre alternative lifestyle. It was dubbed a death cult. But after months of investigation, I don't think this story can be condensed into that simple headline. I'm Dominique Bayans, host of Expanse, the Nanup Four. Binge all episodes now. Search for Expanse on ABC Listen and iView. Donald Trump went into the war with Iran thinking it would be over quickly. Now, more than seven weeks later, with a ceasefire about to end, there's still no obvious off-ramp, with uncertainty surrounding a second round of peace talks in Pakistan. Today, a former Iran negotiator in the Trump administration, Nate Swanson, on what the US president needs to do to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hamus. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Nate, we first spoke to you at the start of the war in Iran on day one. That was more than 50 days ago now. So has it been going as you would have predicted? In some respects, yes. But in most respects, no. I mean, I think it was not totally surprising that Iran escalated so quickly based on the scope and size of the initial US and Israeli attack. But never, I think, would I ever have guessed that it would go this long and that it would be still so messy 50 days in without a clear idea of how exactly this ends and really still even at this point what the objective is. Now, up until July last year, you were on Trump's Iran negotiating team. So just tell me, back then, were you articulating what the risks of going into this war would be? And was he listening? Well, I'm a career civil servant across multiple administrations and, as you noted, with the Iran team at the end. I do not have a personal relationship with President Trump by any measure. Never briefed him, unlike other presidents. But to his team, when I was still there, I think they were genuinely interested in diplomacy. But obviously there was a willingness to use force that was kind of unique from other administrations. I think in his first term, he did the strike that killed Gossam Soleimani. And then before I left, there was the midnight hammer operation that we did in connection with the Israelis. So, I mean, Trump was clearly more comfortable using force than other U.S. presidents. And I think, yeah, he didn't really fully understand the risks associated and how a conflict could go bad so quickly. So that is kind of unique to the president. And I think, you know, he has a very, very small inner circle. And I think they're all fairly confident this would be easy, which was a mistake. Yeah, all right, well, a two-week ceasefire has been in place. But the Strait of Hamuz has been an ongoing problem. And, I mean, events have hardly been peaceful, have they, with the U.S. attacking an Iranian cargo ship. A nighttime mission in the Arabian Sea. U.S. Marines boarding an Iranian-flagged cargo ship after its engine room was fired upon. Vacate your engine room. We're prepared to subject you to an enabling fire. Did you predict any of this in relation to the Strait of Hamuz that has become such a massive problem for the entire world? Yes and no. I mean, I thought Iran would lash out the Gulf and try to shut down the Strait. I think what surprised me was really at the first outset is that Iran was able to get, you know, their own exports out for really up until the last two weeks. You know, so for the first six weeks of the war, they basically kept, you know, traffic from the Gulf out. But, you know, their own exports oil to China were still basically happening. So to me, that was quite shocking and was quite significant. And I think also, you know, the Strait has always been this theoretical threat that, you know, the U.S. and others have been worried about. But it was never a practical reality. And Iran made it a reality, you know, almost instantly in the first, you know, 24 to 48 hours. And I think it's really proven to be, in many ways, much more effective than any of the other means of deterrence. It's quite a bit more effective than the proxies. It's quite a bit more effective than their nuclear program. And really even their missile program to some extent. So, I mean, it's really been a, you know, a huge boon for Iran to be able to utilize this power, this new power, in ways that are really quite unforeseen and quite effective. So, I mean, things can have long-lasting implications, unfortunately. And because of that Strait of Hamuz and Iran's seemingly upper hand in it, it considers that it's winning this war. Yeah, I think there are certainly quite a few within the Iranian administration who believe they're winning the war. And I think there's definitely some merit to it, right? I mean, it's different than the U.S. or a Western definition of winning, right? They don't need to defeat the U.S. or defeat Israel militarily. They just need to survive. And they're fighting an asymmetric war. So every day that goes on that the Iranian regime holds, that the, you know, the Islamic Republic is still the face of the country, you know, that's victory. And so they've done that. And they've shown that, you know, that there's no immediate fall coming. And in some ways, they're stronger than they were. So, yeah, I think that defines them in a victory. And I think they also are, you know, emboldened by the Strait as this new security guarantee that they really have lacked since Hezbollah was, you know, so thoroughly defeated in 2024. So it's a new thing. And you can understand why Iran feels that way. But at the same time, they have been pummeled militarily. I don't think there's any point in denying that. You know, I mean, I can't remember what the total number of strikes between U.S. and Israel were. But, you know, it's like well over, I think, 15 or 25,000 strikes. I mean, so it is, you know, this long-lasting damage that Iran has suffered. But, you know, kind of paradoxically, they've been hit so hard militarily, been pummeled militarily, but they've like reestablished deterrence. So you can understand why some in Iran feel like they've won so far. All right, well, Donald Trump, of course, Nate, has been acting erratically. He keeps switching from saying a deal is possible, negotiations are underway, to then saying he's going to blow up every bridge and power plant in Iran. And now, of course, again, there's these conflicting messages about this latest round of peace talks in Pakistan. What do you make of all of that? Well, the president is unique. I can't say that this is typical U.S. president behavior in terms of how they act. You know, the implications of it on Iran are unclear. I think they don't know how to react to this. I think they ultimately feel, though, that it's a sign of weakness on the U.S. side. You know, if you take the day that he threatened to wipe out, you know, civilization, that very same day then, you know, Iran basically didn't change their position and the president announced a peace deal by the end of the day. So from their perspective, you know, they did nothing. Trump basically folded and basically agreed to Iran's framework for talks. It reinforces their own strategy. And so, you know, and that's to their advantage, I think. Yeah, and Iran says it doesn't trust Trump. It sees these peace talks. It's reported as a way to make it surrender. And the two sides, they're so far apart, right, when it comes to a lasting peace deal and the conditions of that. Yeah, no, absolutely. I think Iran's not going to surrender or capitulate. I mean, that much has been made clear through the history of U.S.-Iran relations, but really even just this, you know, 18 months or so of Trump's administration. You know, the entire premise has been that, you know, the U.S. is the dominant military power, has all the leverage Iran should capitulate, and they haven't. And they didn't before the war, they haven't during the war, and they're not going to at the peace talks now. And so I don't think you're going to ever see in the near future Iran, you know, negotiating away the Islamic Republic. But I don't think that's what these talks in Islamabad are about. I mean, I think it's a much, much narrower scope. And I do think it is in the interest of both parties to end the war, to de-escalate, and maybe find some, you know, mutual ground here. So I think that is possible. But, you know, it's not going to change who Iran is. Just on a side note, Nate, and interestingly, Trump had said that J.D. Vance wouldn't be attending these talks in Pakistan, but then Iran seemed to demand that he had to be there or they wouldn't be there. What do you make of this role that J.D. Vance is playing at the moment? Well, two things on that. So the first is just there's a lot of posturing going on on both sides. Will they be there? Won't they be there? And I think that's mostly noise. For the most part, it's just trying to get the strongest position going into talks. For J.D. Vance's role, I think Iran doesn't trust, you know, Wyckoff in particular, but Wyckoff and Kushner in tandem. You know, twice now Iran has been negotiated with Wyckoff and a war started, or an attack started. So for them, I think they perceive Vance to be less supportive of this war, which I think, you know, I think is probably accurate and it has a lot of U.S. media reporting that, and more motivated to end this because this does not fit with the ideology that he espoused, which is kind of an America first, no, you know, silly wars abroad. So I do think J.D. Vance is uniquely positioned within the administration to want this to end. I think Iran recognizes that, and I think it's also a reflection that they just don't trust Wyckoff anymore. Well, Nate, what's your assessment? Do both parties want an off-ramp at this point, and is there actually an off-ramp that can be offered up? Yeah, I mean, my baseline assessment is that it is in the interest of both parties to end this war, and so I think they should be able to figure it out. There are a couple options for that. You know, I think Iran's perspective, I think they care about three things. I think they care about not getting attacked every six months or so, and I think by establishing the Strait of Hormuz as a deterrent, as a security guarantee, I think they've actually ensured that outcome. So I think that was really important. I think second, Iran wants to monetize the Strait of Hormuz. I think the third thing that they just kind of in the last few weeks decided they care about is Lebanon. So they've basically made those their three key demands. In the U.S., I think our primary goal, which is to open up the Strait of Hormuz. And so, you know, of course, the Strait was open at the beginning of the war, so that's, you know, kind of makes you question what the objectives were. But I do think that is our top objective now. Now, that is a political problem for the president. If the only thing you achieve out of a war for 50 days that's caused a major crisis from the global economy is to say, hey, we ended the war in basically the same spot we started. So I think as a result of that, he wants something different that can help him create this narrative that he's accomplished something. So part of that is, you know, degrading Iran's military. But now I think he's trying to achieve something on the nuclear front. He wants a suspension of Iran's enrichment program, and he wants to deal with the highly enriched uranium that's in Iran. So I think Iran's preference would probably be to not deal with the nuclear program, but I think they're open to dealing with it if they can get more in return. And so I think this is where you see the haggling over the frozen assets, potential sanctions relief, things of that sort. So I do think there is a landing zone ultimately for this. But for me, the president should be judged not on necessarily what he gets, but, you know, hopefully I'm not overpaying. You know, if we end up with a situation where Iran has basically a toll booth running through the Strait of Hormuz, that's a huge strategic loss for the U.S. and for the world. So I think, you know, we really don't want that to happen. And so that, you know, I think you should be careful about what he's trading away to make sure it looks different. But time is running out really for both sides. Like, neither side can do this indefinitely. And so I think Iran's calculus is that he'll blink first. But you never know. So just tell me, Nate, do you think that we could actually be close to the end of this war? Or is there a chance that it could still escalate? I mean, Donald Trump has never ruled out sending troops in. I think both are possibilities. The problem with sending troops in is it really doesn't change the middle. I mean, it's problematic on multiple levels. But the biggest problem is it doesn't really change Iran's calculus. Iran will just respond in kind by, you know, hitting Gulf energy, you know, hitting more tankers in the Strait or in the Persian Gulf. So, like, that doesn't really change anything. There's no military objective. The only thing that really changes Iran's calculus is massive ground troops, you know, like Iraq 2003. But that's incredibly unwise, and I don't think the president will do that. Now, look, are we going to have a deal by Wednesday evening in Islamabad? I'm skeptical. I think there's still, you know, it seems like there's still pretty significant differences and gaps. But I do think you could have something close to a framework and, if needed, an extension on the ceasefire as well, as shaky and rocky as that ceasefire is. He is now a resident senior fellow and director of the Iran Strategy Project at the Atlantic Council. This episode was produced by Sydney Pead. Audio production by Sam Dunn. Our supervising producer is David Coney. I'm Sam Hawley. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: When will the Iran war hit your grocery bill?
episodes.description: Shoppers have been dismayed by grocery price rises for years, now there are warnings that food will cost even more as the effects of the Iran war reach consumers.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Do you ever look at your kids and think, they've got it easy, life was so much harder back in my day? Well, have I got the podcast for you. It's called Wait, They Did What? We take a trip back in time to when kids could buy fireworks, cars didn't have seatbelts and we all had to sing God Save the Queen. They did what? They did what? I can't believe that. Check it out with your kids. Wait, they did what? It's on ABC Listen and ABC iView. COVID, Ukraine, now Iran. For years, the food supply chain has faced severe pressure and the cost has been passed on at the supermarket checkout. So, how bad is it this time? And when will another round of price hikes really kick in? Today, we speak to an expert in the costs around our food supply and to South Australian grain grower Louise Flohr about the increasing pressure on farmers. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal Land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Louise, as a farmer, you're very used to uncertainty, but my gosh, this must feel like next level at the moment. It is, Sam. And it's a lot of decision fatigue at the moment in the grain growing community. We're trying to manage the things that we can and, yeah, just trying to keep an eye on all of the different things that are sort of getting thrown our way at the moment. We're managing high fur prices, high fuel, and we're probably looking at higher interest rates coming at us soon. So, it's a lot to be dealing with at the moment. Yeah, I bet. And for farmers like yourself, you're having to make decisions without knowing, I guess, what is around the corner, not knowing how long this war is going to last for. So, just explain that for me because I know there are farmers who are sort of deciding not to plant crops this year, maybe halving their crops. So, what position are you in right at the moment? Look, it's business as usual here, Sam. We aren't in a position where we can cut down our area. We need to be putting in our whole program. So, there's a few tweaks around the edges with some different crop types. But, yes, it's business as usual and keep calm and carry on because, yeah, we can't afford to halve the input. What's happened with this war, which is really different to what happened in the Ukraine war, was we saw prices go up relatively to the price of wheat. And so, prices were all relative. But this war has been different in that at the moment, we sort of experience high input costs, but the price of wheat's not really changed. So, it's really, you're right, we are going in really blind. We are going to wear these high costs, but we're not seeing the same relative increase in the price of grain at the end of the year. So, we expect it will go up, but, yeah, we can't see it yet. Now, you obviously rely heavily on your farm on diesel. Just explain for me that the machinery you use and how much diesel it requires. So, say per month, what does it cost you and how much of an increase have you seen at this point? So, we've seen diesel go up about 40% and we're lucky we had a bulk 30,000 litre diesel tank on farm. So, we are able to purchase it in bulk. But we are at our absolutely highest peak of fuel usage at the moment. We're seeding, so the tractor's sort of going around the clock. We're trying to ameliorate our soils where we can, which is really high diesel intensive use. So, yeah, we're at peak diesel use at the moment and, yeah, we're using thousands of litres of diesel a week at the moment. I mean, a tank of diesel into a tractor might be 200 litres. So, two by, what are we paying now, $3 a litre? Yes, it's enormously expensive. But also, hay production is a big part of our program. So, we're also, you know, driving trucks on the road. We can't pass those costs on. So, we've had contracts in place and we can't pass those costs on, unlike, say, a Qantas. Yeah, we just simply can't pass those costs on. So, it's, you know, absorb, baby, absorb. We have to absorb these costs. That comes off your bottom line. 100%. Basically. On the back of our patch has had two quite severe droughts. It's tiring. There's a fair bit of grower burnout in our patch. So, it's a really tricky time. Farming is always tricky, but this adds a lot of complexity. And as you said, fertiliser too, right? That's a real problem as well. Are you experiencing any shortfall or is it just that it's costing you more at this point? At this point, we are experiencing price increases only. We are sorting out a fertiliser in January. We are just experiencing those higher prices. Yeah, look, urea, which is what we use to put on our crops after they're emerged and growing. There may be some shortages with that. I'm not too sure, but we've got urea locked in. So, we're feeling okay. We will be putting a bit less out just simply due to the cost. And I suspect that will be happening around the place a fair bit too. Yeah. All right. And in your view, how does this compare to, I guess, the last war that you had to deal with, the Ukraine war? Is this worse to that? Yeah, so far it's worse. Absolutely. Ukraine is a major competitor for growing wheat. They're really good at growing wheat in that Black Sea region. So, when their production is disrupted, price tends to go up. And I'm not saying people benefited out of the Ukraine war, but we saw price of fuel go up, but we also saw the price of grain go up. So, it's a really, it is a pretty awful situation at the moment with those input costs, yet no changes to that grain price. So, yeah, it's, look, it's precarious. We're keeping calm. We're controlling what we can control and just take a day at a time. I'm Stefan Vogel. I'm the general manager of Rabobank's research team in Australia and New Zealand. And it's great to talk today about fuel, fertilizer, and everything that the Strait of Hormuz might mean for our farmers and consumers. Absolutely. All right. Because, of course, the uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz, Stefan, just continues. And that will have, won't it, an effect on the food supply chain. Just explain that for me. Absolutely. And it already does have an impact for sure. Right now, a lot of what is happening is more based on fear than real shortage of supply. But if you look at the Strait of Hormuz, it is a real important bottleneck for many, many goods that we need in Australia. 80% of our beef, sheep, grain move to the world market, but we're actually extremely reliant on imports. So diesel imports, about 80% of the diesel we're using is coming from abroad. But clearly, we are also very heavily importing fertilizers from the world market. So more than 90% of the nitrogen fertilizer that we use in the country is coming from abroad. So the whole supply chain is feeling the impact right now. And the concern clearly for farmers is I need to put a crop in the ground and we're in the planting period right now. Do I have the fertilizer? Do I have the fuel to actually make that crop happen, to harvest? Because prices have gone up massively for both fertilizer and fuel on farm. Okay, why don't we consider how much more we will be paying for things when we do go to the supermarket? Now, Stefan, fresh vegetables and fruit, they're really vulnerable, aren't they? Yes, the fresh produce sector is definitely a more vulnerable one. Clearly, if you think about the timing, you need to get them off the farm at the time when they're ripe. Fresh produce is maybe more vulnerable in terms of prices and seeing those price changes maybe a bit quicker in the supermarkets. And it is, first of all, the transport and the fuel costs that are adding in it from a supply chain perspective and from a food perspective, not so much the fertilizer cost. Yeah, I have seen some reports it's potentially between 15 to 30%. For growers, the damage is already done. The National Farmers Federation warning your groceries could cost up to 20% more. What about meat and chicken? What about dairy products? The meat prices of beef and sheep meat were relatively strong already on farm, given of a local supply shortage of sheep meat, for example. The world market is still in good demand for our meat. So with that, we don't expect that the prices for those products on farm will rise as much as the cost these farmers are facing. While on the supermarket side, the transport side will be part of it. The processing side of it will be part of it. And we also know that when inflation is high and we probably also see that the wages will continue to rise. So with that, also the labor cost will be a part of it. Okay. But we do obviously expect that things will get a lot more expensive, even if the farmers are having to absorb these extra costs. Absolutely. Absolutely. And if you look at packaging, clearly a lot of products that we're buying in our supermarkets are packaged. And once again, a lot of the raw material is crude oil based or is chemical based. So that is produced in those same refineries that also produce diesel and so on. Though a lot of the raw material, once again, comes out of the Strait of Hormuz. So if we're looking at the Southeast Asian and Chinese market for PE plastic, so the kind of thin foil that you see a lot wrapped around food or the more sturdy plastic packaging, those prices have risen quite a bit in those origins. And we expect that those costs will also be passed on and will be faced at some point in time by the consumers. We've had a few shocks, of course, Stefan, in recent history. We had COVID. Then we had the Ukraine war. And now, of course, this war. So how does this, do you think, stack up in terms of this supply chain and the pressures on it? Is this worse? I would think it is worse than the shocks we had in the past. Because of the reason of the time it might drag on. So if you look at the war in Ukraine, we have seen that grain prices went up very, very quickly, but also fell very, very quickly again because the world market feared that Russia and Ukraine might not be able to export at the time because they are in a war. Very quickly, the market learned both sides are able to export. Both sides are still producing good crops. So with that, actually, it normalized relatively quickly the prices. And the consumer faced some higher costs on that food side, but not for a prolonged period of time. If you're looking at COVID, it was the disruptions of the supply chain, containers coming in, ships going out. But also, obviously, can we produce and transport everything? Once again, COVID took a long time, but the food and eggs supply chain were considered essential and very quickly tried to stay at relatively normal pace. With the war here in the Strait of Hormuz, the question really is who can offset the shortfall of supply that comes from that region? And that is very difficult because it is very big numbers. Nobody knows when the Strait of Hormuz will really be open. By as long as it's closed, how long does it take for others to step up and supply more? So with that, Australia is doing one thing right now fairly well. We're trying to get imported goods that we really need from the world market. But the longer that conflict strikes on, the higher the costs will probably be. And the more painful it will get for the whole supply chain, including also the consumer inflation. Yeah. All right. Well, as you say, Stefan, it's very hard to know how long the supply chain will be disrupted. But we can assure everyone that prices will remain high for a rather long time. Yeah. So right now, the farmers basically face the higher cost immediately. So on the first day of the Strait of Hormuz being blocked, fertilizer prices went up, diesel prices went up. So that this cost shock comes very quickly on the farm. The transport sector, it's the same thing. Diesel prices went up. Like all of us go to the gas station and see the high tickets, the transport sector face the same thing. So the costs are immediately pushed up on us. However, the capability of moving those costs further down the chain up until at the end of the day, the consumer is something that sometimes isn't 100%. And second of all, it takes a little bit of time. So with that, I think we will see the second half of the year food prices rising. It might actually be that Christmas is the time when food gets more expensive or is more expensive, even if the Strait of Hormuz opens tomorrow. We're expecting that the flow of goods from that region will take time. Because right now, the import companies are buying for a very high price. It takes them six weeks, eight weeks to originate that product in the world market, ship it to Australia, unload, distribute on farm. So with that, even if the Strait of Hormuz resolves magically tomorrow, which isn't the base case scenario of us, it will take time until we see costs dropping. The other part that gives me confidence is if we look at the supply chains, as you said, we've been tested in the last few years multiple times. Our farmers have done a fantastic job and I'm sure they will do once again a good job this year. We are a little bit prepared and I'm fairly optimistic that as long as we can get the diesel into the country that we need to get everything propelled. And as long as we can find a way that we can get the supplies of nitrogen fertilisers, we will have crops and we will have the food that we need. I'm optimistic that the food and supply chain can manage. Stefan Vogel is the General Manager at Raybo Research Australia and New Zealand. Louise Floor is a grain farmer from South Australia. This episode was produced by Sydney Pead. Audio production by Sam Dunn. Our supervising producer is David Cody. I'm Sam Hawley. ABC News Daily. We'll be back again tomorrow. Thanks for listening. I'm Sam Hawley.

which is really high diesel intensive use.

and, yeah, we're using thousands of litres of diesel
I mean, a tank of diesel into a tractor might be 200 litres.
