But also, hay production is a big part of our program.
So, we're also, you know, driving trucks on the road.
We can't pass those costs on.
So, we've had contracts in place
and we can't pass those costs on, unlike, say, a Qantas.
Yeah, we just simply can't pass those costs on.
So, it's, you know, absorb, baby, absorb.
We have to absorb these costs.
That comes off your bottom line.
On the back of our patch has had two quite severe droughts.
There's a fair bit of grower burnout in our patch.
So, it's a really tricky time.
Farming is always tricky, but this adds a lot of complexity.
And as you said, fertiliser too, right?
That's a real problem as well.
or is it just that it's costing you more at this point?
At this point, we are experiencing price increases only.
We are sorting out a fertiliser in January.
We are just experiencing those higher prices.
Yeah, look, urea, which is what we use to put on our crops
There may be some shortages with that.
I'm not too sure, but we've got urea locked in.
We will be putting a bit less out just simply due to the cost.
And I suspect that will be happening around the place a fair bit too.
And in your view, how does this compare to, I guess,
the last war that you had to deal with, the Ukraine war?
Ukraine is a major competitor for growing wheat.
They're really good at growing wheat in that Black Sea region.
So, when their production is disrupted, price tends to go up.
And I'm not saying people benefited out of the Ukraine war,
but we saw price of fuel go up, but we also saw the price of grain go up.
So, it's a really, it is a pretty awful situation at the moment
with those input costs, yet no changes to that grain price.
So, yeah, it's, look, it's precarious.
We're controlling what we can control and just take a day at a time.
I'm the general manager of Rabobank's research team in Australia and New Zealand.
And it's great to talk today about fuel, fertilizer,
and everything that the Strait of Hormuz might mean for our farmers and consumers.
Because, of course, the uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz, Stefan, just continues.
And that will have, won't it, an effect on the food supply chain.
And it already does have an impact for sure.
Right now, a lot of what is happening is more based on fear than real shortage of supply.
But if you look at the Strait of Hormuz, it is a real important bottleneck for many, many goods that we need in Australia.
80% of our beef, sheep, grain move to the world market, but we're actually extremely reliant on imports.
So diesel imports, about 80% of the diesel we're using is coming from abroad.
But clearly, we are also very heavily importing fertilizers from the world market.
So more than 90% of the nitrogen fertilizer that we use in the country is coming from abroad.
So the whole supply chain is feeling the impact right now.
And the concern clearly for farmers is I need to put a crop in the ground and we're in the planting period right now.
Do I have the fuel to actually make that crop happen, to harvest?
Because prices have gone up massively for both fertilizer and fuel on farm.
Okay, why don't we consider how much more we will be paying for things when we do go to the supermarket?
Now, Stefan, fresh vegetables and fruit, they're really vulnerable, aren't they?
Yes, the fresh produce sector is definitely a more vulnerable one.
Clearly, if you think about the timing, you need to get them off the farm at the time when they're ripe.
Fresh produce is maybe more vulnerable in terms of prices and seeing those price changes maybe a bit quicker in the supermarkets.
And it is, first of all, the transport and the fuel costs that are adding in it from a supply chain perspective and from a food perspective, not so much the fertilizer cost.
Yeah, I have seen some reports it's potentially between 15 to 30%.
For growers, the damage is already done.
The National Farmers Federation warning your groceries could cost up to 20% more.
The meat prices of beef and sheep meat were relatively strong already on farm, given of a local supply shortage of sheep meat, for example.
The world market is still in good demand for our meat.
So with that, we don't expect that the prices for those products on farm will rise as much as the cost these farmers are facing.
While on the supermarket side, the transport side will be part of it.
The processing side of it will be part of it.
And we also know that when inflation is high and we probably also see that the wages will continue to rise.
So with that, also the labor cost will be a part of it.
But we do obviously expect that things will get a lot more expensive, even if the farmers are having to absorb these extra costs.
And if you look at packaging, clearly a lot of products that we're buying in our supermarkets are packaged.
And once again, a lot of the raw material is crude oil based or is chemical based.
So that is produced in those same refineries that also produce diesel and so on.
Though a lot of the raw material, once again, comes out of the Strait of Hormuz.
So if we're looking at the Southeast Asian and Chinese market for PE plastic, so the kind of thin foil that you see a lot wrapped around food or the more sturdy plastic packaging,
those prices have risen quite a bit in those origins.
And we expect that those costs will also be passed on and will be faced at some point in time by the consumers.
We've had a few shocks, of course, Stefan, in recent history.
Then we had the Ukraine war.
And now, of course, this war.
So how does this, do you think, stack up in terms of this supply chain and the pressures on it?
I would think it is worse than the shocks we had in the past.
Because of the reason of the time it might drag on.
So if you look at the war in Ukraine, we have seen that grain prices went up very, very quickly,
but also fell very, very quickly again because the world market feared that Russia and Ukraine might not be able to export at the time because they are in a war.
Very quickly, the market learned both sides are able to export.
Both sides are still producing good crops.
So with that, actually, it normalized relatively quickly the prices.
And the consumer faced some higher costs on that food side, but not for a prolonged period of time.
If you're looking at COVID, it was the disruptions of the supply chain, containers coming in, ships going out.
But also, obviously, can we produce and transport everything?
Once again, COVID took a long time, but the food and eggs supply chain were considered essential and very quickly tried to stay at relatively normal pace.
With the war here in the Strait of Hormuz, the question really is who can offset the shortfall of supply that comes from that region?
And that is very difficult because it is very big numbers.
Nobody knows when the Strait of Hormuz will really be open.
By as long as it's closed, how long does it take for others to step up and supply more?
So with that, Australia is doing one thing right now fairly well.
We're trying to get imported goods that we really need from the world market.
But the longer that conflict strikes on, the higher the costs will probably be.
And the more painful it will get for the whole supply chain, including also the consumer inflation.
Well, as you say, Stefan, it's very hard to know how long the supply chain will be disrupted.
But we can assure everyone that prices will remain high for a rather long time.
So right now, the farmers basically face the higher cost immediately.
So on the first day of the Strait of Hormuz being blocked, fertilizer prices went up, diesel prices went up.
So that this cost shock comes very quickly on the farm.
The transport sector, it's the same thing.
Like all of us go to the gas station and see the high tickets, the transport sector face the same thing.
So the costs are immediately pushed up on us.
However, the capability of moving those costs further down the chain up until at the end of the day, the consumer is something that sometimes isn't 100%.
And second of all, it takes a little bit of time.
So with that, I think we will see the second half of the year food prices rising.
It might actually be that Christmas is the time when food gets more expensive or is more expensive, even if the Strait of Hormuz opens tomorrow.
We're expecting that the flow of goods from that region will take time.
Because right now, the import companies are buying for a very high price.
It takes them six weeks, eight weeks to originate that product in the world market, ship it to Australia, unload, distribute on farm.
So with that, even if the Strait of Hormuz resolves magically tomorrow, which isn't the base case scenario of us, it will take time until we see costs dropping.
The other part that gives me confidence is if we look at the supply chains, as you said, we've been tested in the last few years multiple times.
Our farmers have done a fantastic job and I'm sure they will do once again a good job this year.
We are a little bit prepared and I'm fairly optimistic that as long as we can get the diesel into the country that we need to get everything propelled.
And as long as we can find a way that we can get the supplies of nitrogen fertilisers, we will have crops and we will have the food that we need.
I'm optimistic that the food and supply chain can manage.
Stefan Vogel is the General Manager at Raybo Research Australia and New Zealand.
Louise Floor is a grain farmer from South Australia.
This episode was produced by Sydney Pead.
Our supervising producer is David Cody.

episodes.title: What’s driving soaring rates of adult ADHD?
episodes.description: Over the past eight years ADHD diagnoses among Australian adults have surged, especially among women. You might be surprised to hear where the ADHD capitals are.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. For years, our buyers have been told the same thing. He was an internationally acclaimed artist. Whose work is available in Australia through only one gallery. His works were selling really well. But workers start to notice something unusual. He's not contactable by any means. They couldn't find any presence of him online. In Search of the Missing Artist, a new three-part series that investigates the strange business of making art. Search Background Briefing wherever you get your podcasts. Over the past eight years, the diagnosis of ADHD among Australian adults has surged, especially among women. And you might be surprised to find out where the ADHD capitals are in Australia. Today, Norman Swan, on his Four Corners investigation into data that's never been collated before and whether it shows ADHD is being over-diagnosed. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal Land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Norman, Frio or Fremantle in Perth. It's this old port area, although it's pretty ritzy nowadays. But you have found something really unique about the suburb, haven't you? Because it has a much higher rate of people diagnosed with ADHD than anywhere else in the country. Yep. It's the hottest hotspot. So Four Corners has been looking at ADHD in adults in Australia. And it's very hard to get data. So we commissioned a group at the University of New South Wales, the Medicines Intelligence Research Program, who worked with the Australian Bureau of Statistics, to look at ADHD diagnoses. Now, there's no record of who gets diagnosed with ADHD in Australia. So you've got to infer it from who fills out prescriptions for ADHD drugs. So it doesn't matter how many scripts you fill in a year. You've just got to have filled it at least once. And so we can see for the first time ever, actually, in Australia, the geographic spread and variation of what we infer to be ADHD diagnosis rates. It's a dramatic map. And Western Australia stands out. So to June 2024, 4.4% of adults in Fremantle fill the script for an ADHD drug. This is an extraordinary rise, by the way, over the last few years. And you look at women under the age of 44, it comes up roughly around 6%. But since then, the rate of prescriptions for ADHD drugs have gone up by another 30%, in fact, more than that. So then you're up around 8%. Wow. When you ask the experts what actually is the rate of ADHD in the community, it's between 2.5% and 3%. So something's going on because you've just got these sky-high diagnosis rates. Right. Yeah. So in a suburb like Fremantle, experts would expect a rate of around 2.5% as everywhere else, but it's at 4.4%. On average. On average. So the question is, of course, why, which we will get to. But before we go on, I guess, why don't we just reflect on what the symptoms of ADHD are so we can get a better understanding of exactly what it is. It is a neurodevelopmental disorder, meaning that it's been there probably since birth. In other words, you've got a genetic predisposition. And you cannot diagnose ADHD accurately without evidence of it being there in childhood in some shape or form. School reports, teacher reports, there needs to be correlation because there really isn't any such thing as ADHD which suddenly appears in adulthood. So it's a neurodevelopmental disorder and involves impulsivity. It involves problems with emotional regulation. It involves hyperactivity, which includes this inner restlessness. There are other features of it as well. And the key here with ADHD is that it's not a simple condition. There's no test for it. It's a matter of clinician judgment, which is why this variation may arise. Two clinicians may not agree on whether or not somebody has ADHD. And if you get it wrong, it can be serious because these symptoms could be symptoms of another mental health issue, which if it goes undiagnosed and untreated, means the person could come to harm. OK, well, Norman, let's return to Fremantle because, as you said, experts would expect about 2.5% on average of the population to have ADHD there. But it's far, far higher. But what about other places? Now, you spoke to Dr Michael Folster from UNSW. And he has really been analysing this data, I suppose, to find the hotspots across the country. So what has he found? Yes, he was one of the team that did this analysis for us at the University of New South Wales. Wow, Michael, this looks amazing. What have we here? So this is a map that shows the proportion of adults aged 20 to 65 who filled at least one prescription for ADHD medicine. So this is numbers of people? Absolutely. It's effectively the number of people being treated for ADHD. So one of the first places we went to was Sydney. He asked me to guess what I thought we were going to find in Sydney in terms of the high prevalence areas for filled prescriptions. Well, I would have thought the higher income areas, North Shore, Eastern suburbs. Let's take a look. It's not. No, we actually see a really different pattern. So here in Sydney, we see the highest rates of ADHD medicine use and adults are in the inner West and around Marrickville and around the Blue Mountains. And that's at about 3.4%. And then if you go to Melbourne, it's not the eastern suburbs of Melbourne, Toorak, Armadale and so on. It's the inner northern suburbs. It's like Brunswick and Darabin South by a long way. OK, well, let's unpack that a bit more then and try and figure out with you what is going on. Now, there is much more awareness, first of all, isn't there, of this condition? Yeah. You know, people sometimes show up to a doctor already knowing that they have this or thinking they do. I hesitate to recommend this. In fact, I don't. But you just got hashtag ADHD in TikTok or Instagram. People with ADHD always feel like they have so much to do. They have such a huge to-do list. When they achieve something, they won't feel any sense of accomplishment, only a mild sense of relief that it's done. You know, the algorithm will start delivering you short videos. Here are the typical features. And filling your head with stuff that is, while not inaccurate, it misleads you into thinking this is the only possibility that it's ADHD and convincing you that your symptoms are the symptoms of ADHD. We live in an economy where attention is the currency. So, you know, mobile phone, social media. We're on Instagram the whole time. We have kids to look after. We've got high cognitive load. We've got aging parents. We're the sandwich generation. And therefore, we just feel overwhelmed by the stuff that's hitting us. We feel that we can't cope with all this. We can't pay attention to one thing. I'm not completing tasks. And some of that will be people, particularly women with ADHD who have not been diagnosed. And some will be misleading yourself into thinking that the cognitive load of life is, in fact, ADHD. And you point out in your story that there are actually clinics that are set up just to diagnose ADHD. You go and do some sort of questionnaire. It costs you a lot of money, thousands and thousands of dollars. And then you go and have a telehealth appointment so you can get the medication. Just explain that because there's concern about that, isn't there? So there's been the growth of large telehealth clinics who do a broad range of psychiatry. But in fact, their core offering is ADHD and autism spectrum disorder diagnosis. So there are questionnaires which are well validated, which you can do yourself, which some people are misled into thinking are diagnostic. And there really are only just a bit of help for the psychiatrist. People like Professor David Cockhill at the University of Melbourne, who's one of Australia's leading experts, in fact, an international expert in ADHD, are worried about the quality of assessment. Questionnaires are not accurate enough. And they do lead to what we call a lot of false positive recognition of ADHD. A psychiatrist should not rely on these questionnaires for diagnosis. They are not diagnostic tools. Yet anecdotally, we hear of clinics where the psychiatrist accepts the findings of the questionnaire, gives you a short consultation, and you go away with a script for a psychostimulant. And we don't know the rate at which they say no. We hear a lot of feedback from people living with ADHD and those who suspect they have ADHD that their assessment has been very quick. But it's really consisted of just filling in those questionnaires, having the doctor look at them, and then having a rubber stamp. That's not acceptable. Telehealth is turning out to be a bit of a problem in a few different areas, and it may well be an issue here with ADHD. All right. The other question you had, Norman, was about the influence of the big pharmaceutical companies and the impact, I suppose, they have on doctors and the panel of experts that come up with the guidelines on how these drugs should be prescribed. Now, just to note, you as a doctor, you have received yourself a payment from one of these big companies before. Yes, I gave a speech at a conference sponsored by a pharmaceutical company that produces ADHD medications. So I'm well aware of the issues here. And one of the people we spoke to was Professor Lisa Cosgrove of the University of Massachusetts, Boston, who studied conflict of interest and what can happen when you take the pharmaceutical industry's shilling. People get defensive because the implication is, I've done something wrong. And that's not the case. Identifying conflicts of interest is in no way suggesting that someone has engaged in research fraud or done anything wrong. Rather, the real crux of the issue is that those ties engender inevitably implicit bias. We're all vulnerable to implicit bias and we're blissfully ignorant of the way in which that implicit bias can be manifest. And when you look at the references used to back up what's called the National Guideline for Clinical Practice in ADHD, which is like the Bible for people to use to make the diagnosis, which is not a bad guideline, by the way, but a third of the references that they use to back it up have people on the authorship line who've received pharmaceutical funding. And then when you look at the prescribing guide in Australia, which is advising doctors on the selection of drugs and how they should be used. Again, not a bad prescribing guide, but nonetheless, several of the members of that committee had received pharmaceutical industry funding. And so it just creates a problem of trust. Where does the bias arise? And people could actually argue that with me. You know, my bias in my reporting of the issue, people make that judgment when they see the four corners. All right. Well, Norman, you've had a really good look at this very insightful data. The first we've ever had, as you say, in Australia. I guess the question people are really asking now is why is it then that there are these pockets across Australia in Fremantle, for instance, that have this higher rate? Did you get to the bottom of that? It's complicated, isn't it? It is very complicated and you can only speculate. For those of you who know Australia and they know Fremantle, they know Brunswick, they know Marrickville and Sydney. Very similar populations. So it's a younger population, well-educated. They do have money, but not a lot of money, but they do have money. They are probably more accepting of neurodivergence and there's less stigma around it in those suburbs. And they're more aware and more concerned about their health and well-being. What's hard to explain is why women dominate. That's partly catch-up, but we've probably gone beyond catch-up. And I think it's just the general problem that women have as they reach midlife. They are unfairly squeezed by life. And some of those women do have ADHD and some women probably don't, but they have other issues that need to be dealt with. Yeah. And on the other hand, of course, Norman, so costly to get a diagnosis. There must be people within society that can't actually afford a consultation at this point. That's the other side of our data. There are ADHD deserts and there's huge ADHD deserts in Australia where the rate of diagnosis is far below where it should be. So Fairfield in southwest Sydney is the second lowest area for filled prescriptions in the country. And if you look at where they sit in terms of the prevalence of filled prescriptions compared to the actual prevalence of ADHD, 90% of adults with ADHD in Fairfield are likely to be missed. Right. Well, Norman, of course, people should always speak to their own doctor for specific advice. But what's your message to those who are hearing this and thinking maybe I or someone I know has ADHD? How careful do they need to be to make sure they get the right diagnosis? Everybody should have a GP that they know and they trust. And sometimes that's a bit of a journey. People can get so locked in to the belief that they have ADHD. This is something which you really want to be sure about with your doctor and be open to that there are other possibilities here. And you want to find a psychiatrist or a clinical psychologist who doesn't conduct what they call ADHD assessments. They conduct a proper psychological assessment of your mental health and well-being and come to a diagnosis, one of which might be ADHD, but another might be others. So it's just being careful and slow and not jumping to conclusions and not seeing a clinician who jumps to conclusions. The producer is David Cody. I'm Sam Hawley. ABC News Daily will be back again tomorrow. Thanks for listening.

That's the other side of our data.
There are ADHD deserts and there's huge ADHD deserts in Australia where the rate of diagnosis is far below where it should be.

And if you look at where they sit in terms of the prevalence of filled prescriptions compared to the actual prevalence of ADHD, 90% of adults with ADHD in Fairfield are likely to be missed.
Right. Well, Norman, of course, people should always speak to their own doctor for specific advice.
But what's your message to those who are hearing this and thinking maybe I or someone I know has ADHD?
How careful do they need to be to make sure they get the right diagnosis?
Everybody should have a GP that they know and they trust.
And sometimes that's a bit of a journey.
People can get so locked in to the belief that they have ADHD.

They conduct a proper psychological assessment of your mental health and well-being and come to a diagnosis, one of which might be ADHD, but another might be others.

ABC News Daily will be back again tomorrow.

episodes.title: What Putin gains from the Iran war
episodes.description: What does Russia’s Vladimir Putin make of the Iran war? He’s one of the few beneficiaries, making vast sums of money as the oil price spiked and Donald Trump temporarily eased sanctions.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. For years, our buyers have been told the same thing. He was an internationally acclaimed artist. Whose work is available in Australia through only one gallery. His works were selling really well. But workers start to notice something unusual. He's not contactable by any means. They couldn't find any presence of him online. In Search of the Missing Artist, a new three-part series that investigates the strange business of making art. Search Background Briefing wherever you get your podcasts. What's Vladimir Putin been up to since the start of the Iran war? Well, he's one of its only beneficiaries. He's made billions as the oil prices spiked and Donald Trump eased sanctions temporarily. The world's attention has been diverted from his war in Ukraine. And the thorn in his side, the NATO alliance, is crumbling. Today, international relations expert Rajen Menon on Trump's threats to withdraw the US from NATO. And whether Europe can defend itself against its hostile neighbour. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Music Rajen, it's often been said since the start of the war in Iran that Vladimir Putin is one of the only winners, that Russia has gained and not lost anything. What's your assessment? Well, that is largely correct because oil is an extraordinarily important part of the Russian budget. I think it's about 40% of all budget revenue. So two things have happened. One is that President Trump, to ease oil flows into the global economy, to bring the prices down, temporarily suspended sanctions on Russia. And of course, the price of oil has gone up by about, I don't know, 45% since the beginning of the war. So yes, he certainly has been a beneficiary of this war in that respect. All right. Well, let's Rajen look a bit more deeply at how Russia is actually gaining from this war. Now, one problem for Donald Trump and perhaps a win for Russia is that the military powerhouses in Europe have not come to his aid. Even though, of course, Donald Trump has asked repeatedly for help, they have said no. And he's really angry about that, isn't he, with nations like the UK and Spain and many others. I call up France, Macron. Would love to have some help. If you could, could you please send ships immediately? No, no, no. We cannot do that, don't we? We can do that after the war is won. And so I learned about NATO. NATO won't be there if we ever have the big one. You know what I mean by the big one. We ever have the big one, hopefully we won't. Relationships are very good with the big one. Better than with NATO. It's extraordinary. Now, one should know, and you probably know this, but just to set the stage, if you look at the NATO Treaty of 1949, it says that the collective security provision, Article 5, is operative when any of the members of NATO is attacked. The only time Article 5 has been invoked is 9-11, and it was invoked to defend the United States. But in this instance, no NATO member was attacked. A NATO member, namely the United States, attacked another country. What's extraordinary about this is there's been a sweeping kind of rebellion. I mean, it varies from intensity to country to country, but even Keir Starmer, who kind of looks like a mild-mannered banker, and, you know, like all British prime ministers' values, the so-called special relationship with the U.S., has had it with Trump and said, I'm not going to be bullied into doing this. Whatever the pressure on me and others, whatever the noise, I'm going to act in the British national interest in all the decisions that I make. And that's why I've been absolutely clear that this is not our war, or we're not going to get dragged into it. Incidentally, it's not just Trump, where even people who have been seen to have become quasi-Trump whisperers, or people who've gotten Trump's confidence, like Giorgia Maloney in Italy, for example, have turned against him, most recently because of his attack on the Pope. But even before that, she also took the position that this is not our war, this is not a war we were consulted on. So I think Putin is happy looking at NATO, gripped by crises, that works to his advantage in many ways. Yes, because as you say, NATO members do not have to join a war that they weren't consulted about in the first place. Correct. Now, of course, they've again said no thanks to Donald Trump when he requested they help with this blockade of the Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz. So again, they're at loggerheads with Donald Trump. Yes, and there's a reason for that, because a blockade under international law is an act of war. So if you're enforcing the blockade, you have joined the war against Iran. Trump may not realise this, but anyone with even a cursory knowledge of international law understands it, and certainly people like Starmer and others recognise it. All right. Well, it seems like Mark Rutter, the NATO chief, he's really the only one at this point, Rajan, that is sticking by Trump. You know, he once called him daddy, of course. He says NATO members have been a bit slow to act in helping America. What do you make of how he's handling all of this? You know, to be honest, Sam, he looks really pathetic because he's completely out of step with the alliance that he's leading. And the more he gets behind Trump and tries to take NATO into wars that his members don't want to get into, the less credibility he has, I think, among the members of the alliance. So trying to ingratiate himself with Trump, it's a kind of form of self-abasement. But beyond that, it doesn't lead anywhere because it's not as if Trump is going to look at you next week and say, oh, Mark, you did such a great job. You supported me. Now I'm going to do this, that or the other for you. Friendship's been nothing. I mean, look, for example, what happened after Orban lost the election in Hungary. Trump just completely stopped speaking about Orban. Well, Mark Rutter was asked about this daddy comment quite recently at a Ronald Reagan Institute address. And yes, it appears like he will never, ever, ever live that down, Rajan. I was not calling him my daddy, but saying. But of course, daddy has also a special connotation. And I now have to live as this the rest of my life. And I own it. And the president owns it because he brought out T-shirts. He made a movie. Daddy is home. And he returned to the United States. This is all so funny. And this is why I like him so much. He will not. And he's not going to get any big Christmas present from Trump. But more importantly, even if he didn't directly call him daddy, as he tried to explain, well, in Dutch, it means this, that, and the other, just the use of the word was really politically tone deaf. Yes, indeed. All right. Well, Rajan, Donald Trump has, on numerous occasions, now threatened to pull the United States out of NATO. In recent days and weeks, he's called European allies cowards and NATO a paper tiger. And he has said that Putin knows that too. Now, the Wall Street Journal has reported that these European nations are planning for this US exit. What do we know about that? They're obviously quite concerned that this is a real possibility at this point. Yes. So I'll put my cards on the table and say that I've long been a proponent of European strategic autonomy. I made this argument first in the book I wrote in 2007, and most recently, in an article that I wrote for an outfit called the Institute for Arts and Ideas in London. Having said that, this has been a catalyst, because I think NATO has fundamentally had to realize that the day will come when it cannot rely on American protections. Here are a couple of things that have happened. In 2024 and 2025, in the aggregate, each year, defense spending in NATO went up by 20%. So defense budgets are increasing. The German Bundeswehr, the German army, which was shambolic, they are now putting large amounts of money into it. There is a kind of joint defense production document that's been drawn up to reduce duplication and invest in defense industries. There is talk about, more than talk actually, serious negotiations, about whether it is possible to make the Anglo-French nuclear deterrent an umbrella for all of Europe to replace the American umbrella. There are attempts to base forward many more NATO troops on the eastern flank. And so for the first time, I think NATO is taking steps to prepare for the day when it might not be able to rely on the United States. And there's no case to be made that Europe lacks, whether population or wealth or technology or defense industries, the wherewithal to defend itself, because it has only one significant threat. Russia. It doesn't have to be a global power like the United States with a galaxy of bases all over the world. All right. But let's look then at the ramifications of the US actually pulling out of NATO. First, of course, Ukraine, because, of course, Ukraine has been heavily dependent on arms and intelligence from the United States during the war with Russia. Yes, there has been this dependence. But bear in mind that under Trump 2, the most recent iteration of Donald Trump's presidency, the United States ceased direct military support for Ukraine. An alternative was set up called PURL. I won't take the time to spell it out for you. But under this arrangement, the Europeans could request equipment from the United States that they then had to pay for and transfer to Ukraine. But what was delivered and at what pace and when the deliveries were made were entirely up to the United States. And the Ukrainians have long felt that Trump was kind of slow walking it. So the military dependence on the United States has long ceased and the Europeans have stepped up. So the Europeans may not be entirely able to fill the American gap, but they are stepping up for one simple reason. Donald Trump likes to say this is not our war, that is the Russia-Ukraine war, because we have this, quote, big, beautiful ocean separating us. Well, the Europeans cannot say that. They're joined at the hip to Ukraine in the sense that if Ukraine falls, their security future looks much more vulnerable. And what about beyond Ukraine, though? Should these European nations be concerned that Putin could invade other nations? Estonia, Rajan is worried. Poland, Finland. Right. So let me say this. It's very easy for me as an American sitting in New York City to say what I'm about to say. And I completely understand that a Estonian or a Latvian or a Finn, for example, would feel entirely differently. But here's the way I look at it. The Russians have fought Ukraine, a manifestly weaker adversary, for longer than it fought Hitler's armies. It has sustained 1.1 million casualties, that is dead and wounded. Maybe about 300,000 of those are deaths. This is a country that has a very, very low birth rate and is barely reproducing itself, and maybe even there's a net reduction in population. And then the economic consequences have been enormous, just not to mention that all these destroyed areas that Russia now claims have to be rebuilt. So my view is, given the poor showing of Russian army, given the bad experience of the war, and given the economic cost, Russia will be licking its wounds for some time to come. The Russia that will emerge from the Ukraine war is a Russia that can be handled by a robust European defense posture much more easily than the Russia that was before the Ukraine war. Russia might be depleted, but the threat is still real, isn't it? Because, as we saw, the UK's Defence Secretary, John Healy, he recently revealed Russia had sent submarines to spy on British cables and pipelines in waters north of the UK. And to President Putin, I say, we see you, we see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences. So, I mean, that would be a worry for NATO nations. Yes. Yeah, you raise a very good point because it's not just tanks crossing the border. Russian activity against NATO can be manifested in many, many different ways. Cyber warfare, for example, trying to cut undersea cables, espionage and so on. And that will continue. I had in mind at the moment just the question of, can Russia make a sustained assault against the combined resources of non-US NATO? And I'm skeptical that it can. Now, there are experts here who would disagree with me. And I'm sure, again, I want to emphasize this. I understand that people in East Central Europe will have a different idea, but I think it is a problem that Europe can manage on its own. If it puts its mind to it. What's your view? Do you think Donald Trump will jump? Do you think he will remove the United States from NATO after all of these years, all of these decades? You know, I'd rather bet on seeing a unicorn on Central Park and walk tomorrow than on whether Donald Trump will do X or Y. The behavior has been so erratic that it's becoming increasingly difficult to know what he will do or what he won't do. So, you know, anything is feasible. Nothing would surprise me anymore. Thank you. And Anna John. Audio production by Sam Dunn. Our supervising producer is David Cody. I'm Sam Hawley. ABC News Daily will be back again on Monday. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: The President vs the Pope
episodes.description: What’s behind US President Donald Trump’s attack on Pope Leo? After the leader of the Catholic Church criticised Trump’s threats to destroy Iranian civilisation, the president unleashed.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. When energy costs jump, everyone feels it. At the Bowser, on the Power Bill and across the economy. I'm Alan Kohler. And I'm Carrington Clark. On ABC Business Daily's Fuelcast, we break down the latest in fuel, energy and the forces driving prices. It's a quick, clear update on what's moving, why it matters and what it can mean for your wallet and the wider economy. Find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. Is Donald Trump sane enough to be commanding a war? Debate over the US leader's mental health has reignited since he began verbally attacking the Pope and posted an AI image depicting himself as Jesus. Today, David A. Graham from The Atlantic magazine on what Trump's behaviour says about his ability to govern. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. David, you have noted that Donald Trump has a so-called media crash out, which begins on a Sunday and it ends in the early hours of the next morning. So I gather you've been tracking this for some time, have you? Yeah, we've always sort of been tracking Trump's social media since 2015. Yes. But he does seem to have gotten into this new pattern in the last few weeks. What seems to be happening is every Sunday as he kind of tunes back into the news and prepares for the week ahead, he gets on Truth Social, his social network, and starts posting up a storm. And there will be tirades about whatever he's angry about, you know, targeting the Pope in the latest example, but also Democrats and other Republicans who he's upset with in other instances. And then mixed in with memes and campaign endorsements and whatever else might be on his mind on into the early hours of the morning. Yeah, and very early hours by the look of it. I mean, sometimes it's really, really early, like 4 a.m. It's not clear to me when Trump sleeps because he is often posting very late and will be posting again early in the morning too. Yeah, wow. Okay, well, on Sunday, last Sunday, the president was having a particular moment, wasn't he? Things weren't as he wanted them to be and this is when he launched into Pope Leo. Right, Trump had had kind of a rough weekend, I think it's fair to say. We had seen Viktor Orban, his ally and kind of role model in Hungary lose, and negotiations with Iran had gotten nowhere. And he's been taking some criticism from the Pope over the war in Iran. And he decided it was time to say something about that. And he uncorked his long post, starting with Pope Leo was weak on crime, and then criticizing the Pope for making statements about foreign affairs, saying he needed to mind the Catholic Church, complaining that he met with a democratic strategist, and really just venting whatever frustrations he had. Yeah, wow. And he doubled down on that Truth Social post when he was actually asked about it by reporters later. Do you apologize? No, I don't, because Pope Leo said things that are wrong. He was very much against what I'm doing with regard to Iran. And you cannot have a nuclear Iran. Pope Leo would not be happy with the end result. You'll have hundreds of millions of people dead. And it's not going to happen. So I can't. I think he's very weak on crime. But just remind me, David, what was it that Pope Leo had actually done to offend Donald Trump? What was his crime in Donald Trump's eyes? It seems like the thing that really got Trump is that Leo was out saying that people in positions of power should seek peace rather than war. On this day of celebration, let us abandon every desire for conflict, domination, and power, and implore the Lord to grant his peace to a world ravaged by wars and marked by a hatred and indifference that makes us feel powerless in the face of evil. He also said that, you know, people should not make war in God's name with many people. Took as a swipe at Pete Hegseth, the U.S. Secretary of Defense, who's used a lot of really strong Christian rhetoric to justify and to talk about the war. Yeah, he sure has. Well, it did get worse, though, didn't it, David? Because not long after these truth social posts condemning the Pope, Trump then posts this bizarre image of himself, an AI image, where he appears as a Jesus-like figure. I mean, try and explain that image for me, just in case there are some people that haven't seen it by now. Explaining it is so hard. So it's got Trump with a sort of glowing orb in his hand, putting his hand on and appearing to heal an elderly man, and there's people looking up. Up at him in a sort of prayerful way, and there's all this patriotic imagery of a flag and fighter jets and bald eagles and what seem like maybe angels or maybe gargoyles or something in the sky above him. Very much Jesus-like sort of glow about him. Absolutely. And not surprisingly, it causes this huge stir. And in the end, he does take it down. But then, I mean, unbelievably, he then tells reporters that actually the post was meant to portray him as a doctor. What did you make of that? He did say this. He did? Well, it wasn't a picture. It was me. I did post it, and I thought it was me as a doctor and had to do with Red Cross as a Red Cross worker there, which we support. And only the fake news could come up with that one. So I had just heard about it, and I said, how did they come up with that? It's supposed to be me as a doctor making people better. And I do make people better. I make people a lot better. It seems like the sort of thing that he was really reaching for some kind of spin. I mean, this is an image. I don't know where Trump came across it in this instance, but it has been floating around in some version for a couple months now by fans of his who are very clear that he is meant to be looking Christ-like. episodes.description: The US blockade of Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz could make the fuel crunch in Australia even worse. The government’s urging Australians to do what they can to use less fuel, but when will more severe restrictions kick in?

episodes.description: The peace talks failed, so now US President Donald Trump wants to further disrupt the vital oil shipping route, the Strait of Hormuz.

Music Music Music Music Music Music Marathon peace talks between the US and Iran have failed to reach a breakthrough, raising fears of a reignited war. We've had a number of substantive discussions with the Iranians. That's the good news. The bad news is that we have not reached the agreement. And I think that's bad news for Iran much more than it's bad news for the United States of America. Husayn, J.D. Vance, the Vice President, he has largely been missing from this war. In other words, this is notably the highest level diplomatic face-to-face meeting between a serving Iranian official, the Speaker of Parliament, Ali Baaf, who's effectively their leader at this point, I guess, or at least as far as anyone can tell, and a Vice President of the United States since the 1979 revolution. One is he's certainly of the neo-isolationist wing of the MAGA movement. But also, he cannot be fired uniquely. He's the only person around Trump who Trump cannot dismiss. He was elected independently as Vice President. There's nothing Trump can do. He's stuck with him. So, Vance, in a way, was kind of outmaneuvering Trump by making it clear that he wasn't for this unpopular war that a lot of people think has gone very badly, and in many ways has. Trump, I think, returned the favor by saying, right, okay, it's your file now. Let's see what you can do. And now, this way, if you have a big success, I'll be taking credit for it. And if you don't succeed, you'll be getting the blame. All right. So, Vance didn't want the war, and now he's actually tasked with ending it. Exactly. And that's exactly what Iran has threatened to do and has done in the past. And, you know, they can simply say, look, we're not allowing, we have this whole area under surveillance. So, yeah, as you say, the financial impact for the rest of the world could be very severe. Yeah, it's the great weakness of the policy is that it may be more costly to the global economy than it is the Iranian economy. Well, Hussein, let's have a bit of a look at whether or not further talks could yield a better outcome. The US president said there is only one thing that matters. Iran is unwilling to give up its nuclear ambitions. I think Iran is in very bad shape. I think they're very desperate. We had a meeting that lasted 21 hours. We understand the situation better than anybody. And Iran's in very bad shape. And just so you understand, Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. We'll not have. There is no way that they're going to get it. They still want it. And they made that clear the other night. Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. If that is the ultimate aim, is that feasible? Is peace possible? Well, look, here's what I think. Another thing that Donald Trump has probably convinced the Iranian government of is that they need to get hold of a nuclear weapon as soon as possible. Because they will be contrasting their recent experience at the hands of the US and Israel, plus that of Saddam Hussein's Iraq, plus that of Muammar Gaddafi's Libya, with the way in which Donald Trump and others treat North Korea, which has an independent nuclear deterrent and which does not get attacked like this. So you definitely have an absolute collision course. On the other hand, there are many conflicts that are not resolved. The smaller power then retaliates in whatever way it can. And this happens repeatedly over time. It's the relationship the US had with Saddam Hussein's Iraq in the 1990s. There was that reporting in the New York Times last week, right, that made it very clear that it was the Israeli leader who really convinced Donald Trump to go ahead with this war during that crucial Situation Room meeting. Remind me of that and what insights did it give us? How important was that reporting? The New York Times report, which was very well known, explained how and when Netanyahu and leaders of Mossad and other Israeli agencies kind of approached Trump and said, now's the time. Among other things, they promised him that the Iranian people would likely rebel against the clerical regime. And so based off of that and a whole bunch of fairy tales, the Israelis managed to persuade a particularly credulous American president that this was all a very good idea. And whatever the American president thought he was promised certainly didn't happen. So you have to be, I think, pretty ignorant and pretty dense to fall for it. But I think maybe the guy in the White House right now qualifies. So does Benjamin Netanyahu want this war to end, do you think? No, I don't. I don't think so. The one in Lebanon, he definitely doesn't want to end. Well, I think he's envisaging a conflict that goes on for months, if not years, and years, if not decades. So it's going to be hard to prevent him from getting his way unless he loses the coming Israeli election. And there's a very different government with a different attitude, which is possible. Or unless the United States starts changing its view of the Lebanese conflict. Now, one thing that did happen is that at first, the Israelis sold the Lebanese portion of this as a separate conflict, unrelated to the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran. And the Trump administration basically said, in which case you have a free reign here, just don't attack the airport and don't attack the port. And everything else, we leave it up to you. The Israeli response was to keep bombing Lebanon after the ceasefire began. And that led to this very tense early standoff. And now, apparently, the Israelis have promised Trump that they will lay off Lebanon for a little bit. We don't know how much and we don't know for how long. Well, Hussein, in your view, can a new peace agreement actually be reached before the ceasefire expires on April the 22nd? So in less than 10 days' time. Oh, I think it's extremely unlikely, to say the least. I think the most optimistic scenario would be some arrangement whereby more time is bought. And I think otherwise, we will have either emerging by default a stalemated conflict that becomes a grass-mowing exercise, or a series of ineffective short-term agreements that produce the same result. I think that's not in anybody's interest, and particularly not in the interest of Iran's neighbors, the Gulf of Arab countries. For them, it's a security nightmare par excellence, because they expect to be hit more than anybody else. And they fully expect to be the targets of choice again and again and again. Hussein Abish is a senior resident scholar at the Arab Gulf States Institute. This episode was produced by Sydney Pede. Audio production by Cinnamon Nippard. Our supervising producer is David Cody. I'm Sam Hawley. To get in touch with the team, email us on ABC News Daily at abc.net.au. Thanks for listening. Thank you.

And that's exactly what Iran has threatened to do and has done in the past.
And, you know, they can simply say, look, we're not allowing, we have this whole area under surveillance.
We're not allowing anybody's shipping to pass until such time as Iran agrees to recognise that this is an open international shipping way for maritime commerce open to all.
And once we get that commitment from them again, as we had before the war, then we'll be glad to step back.
But Iran has been letting some ships through, right?
But charging a massive, massive toll.
If people are willing to pay, they've been willing to let them through.
And also, if it's, you know, their own petroleum or oil bound for China and Japan and Korea and India, then, yeah, go ahead.
So you don't think the Iranians can stop this blockade?
I think they could try to run it or organise convoys.

But no, I think the US can probably do as much as the Iranians have done to spook shipping and transport and create the same kind of uncertainty that has impeded traffic for most shippers, you know, on the non-Iranian ledger.
Now, the problem is, how long can the global marketplace endure this, right?
What is the economic ramification for the global markets?
Iran does not care about the global markets.
Washington's allies and partners and trading partners are all very worried about this.
Iran is the kind of outsider here.
And so it's possible that the Iranians will calculate that they can survive a month of a blockaded port altogether more easily than the global economy.
So it becomes another weird face-off.
Well, the threat of the blockade itself, of course, it did send oil prices surging again to over 100 US dollars a barrel.
So, yeah, as you say, the financial impact for the rest of the world could be very severe.
Yeah, it's the great weakness of the policy is that it may be more costly to the global economy than it is the Iranian economy.
Well, Hussein, let's have a bit of a look at whether or not further talks could yield a better outcome.
The US president said there is only one thing that matters.
Iran is unwilling to give up its nuclear ambitions.
I think Iran is in very bad shape.
We had a meeting that lasted 21 hours.
We understand the situation better than anybody.
And Iran's in very bad shape.
And just so you understand, Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.
There is no way that they're going to get it.
And they made that clear the other night.
Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.
If that is the ultimate aim, is that feasible?
Well, look, here's what I think.
Another thing that Donald Trump has probably convinced the Iranian government of is that they need to get hold of a nuclear weapon as soon as possible.

Because they will be contrasting their recent experience at the hands of the US and Israel, plus that of Saddam Hussein's Iraq, plus that of Muammar Gaddafi's Libya, with the way in which Donald Trump and others treat North Korea, which has an independent nuclear deterrent and which does not get attacked like this.
They are going to have to, I think, that they need to focus on somehow figuring out in the next few years how to get to nuclear weapons status.
And it is the American aim to absolutely prevent that.
So you definitely have an absolute collision course.
On the other hand, there are many conflicts that are not resolved.

You can see how the current situation, the war as it's shaping up, is leading almost inexorably towards one of these open-ended stalemates, where the larger power sort of ends the fighting, but reserves the right to come back and does on a routine basis every six months, nine months, a year or so attacks again.
The smaller power then retaliates in whatever way it can.
And this happens repeatedly over time.
It's the relationship the US had with Saddam Hussein's Iraq in the 1990s.
And that's exactly the kind of so-called forever war that Trump said he would never get into.
But it really would bear all the hallmarks of that without actually necessitating boots on the ground.
All right, well, Hussein, as we noted, Israel hasn't been part of these peace talks and it does continue to attack in Lebanon.
Israeli strikes continued on Sunday and Lebanon's health ministry said more than 2,000 people had been killed since the start of this latest war, including 165 children.
More than 1 million people in Lebanon have been forced from their homes by Israel's bombing campaign.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he's keeping his nation safe from Iranian-backed militia group Hezbollah.
I guess one question is, though, does Benjamin Netanyahu want the war to end?

There was that reporting in the New York Times last week, right, that made it very clear that it was the Israeli leader who really convinced Donald Trump to go ahead with this war during that crucial Situation Room meeting.
Remind me of that and what insights did it give us?
The New York Times report, which was very well known, explained how and when Netanyahu and leaders of Mossad and other Israeli agencies kind of approached Trump and said, now's the time.
Among other things, they promised him that the Iranian people would likely rebel against the clerical regime.
And so based off of that and a whole bunch of fairy tales, the Israelis managed to persuade a particularly credulous American president that this was all a very good idea.
And whatever the American president thought he was promised certainly didn't happen.
So you have to be, I think, pretty ignorant and pretty dense to fall for it.
But I think maybe the guy in the White House right now qualifies.
So does Benjamin Netanyahu want this war to end, do you think?
No, I don't. I don't think so.
The one in Lebanon, he definitely doesn't want to end.
Well, I think he's envisaging a conflict that goes on for months, if not years, and years, if not decades.
So it's going to be hard to prevent him from getting his way unless he loses the coming Israeli election.
And there's a very different government with a different attitude, which is possible.
Or unless the United States starts changing its view of the Lebanese conflict.
Now, one thing that did happen is that at first, the Israelis sold the Lebanese portion of this as a separate conflict,
unrelated to the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran.
And the Trump administration basically said, in which case you have a free reign here,
just don't attack the airport and don't attack the port.
And everything else, we leave it up to you.
The Israeli response was to keep bombing Lebanon after the ceasefire began.
And that led to this very tense early standoff.
And now, apparently, the Israelis have promised Trump that they will lay off Lebanon for a little bit.
We don't know how much and we don't know for how long.
Well, Hussein, in your view, can a new peace agreement actually be reached before the ceasefire expires on April the 22nd?
So in less than 10 days' time.
Oh, I think it's extremely unlikely, to say the least.
I think the most optimistic scenario would be some arrangement whereby more time is bought.
And I think otherwise, we will have either emerging by default a stalemated conflict that becomes a grass-mowing exercise,
or a series of ineffective short-term agreements that produce the same result.
I think that's not in anybody's interest, and particularly not in the interest of Iran's neighbors, the Gulf of Arab countries.
For them, it's a security nightmare par excellence, because they expect to be hit more than anybody else.
And they fully expect to be the targets of choice again and again and again.
Hussein Abish is a senior resident scholar at the Arab Gulf States Institute.
This episode was produced by Sydney Pede.
Our supervising producer is David Cody.
To get in touch with the team, email us on ABC News Daily at abc.net.au.

episodes.title: Alan Kohler’s case to nationalise childcare
episodes.description: The ABC’s Alan Kohler thinks the treasurer should nationalise the childcare system and take centres out of the hands of for-profit businesses.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. When energy costs jump, everyone feels it. At the Bowser, on the Power Bill and across the economy. I'm Alan Kohler. And I'm Carrington-Clark. On ABC Business Daily's Fuelcast, we break down the latest in fuel, energy and the forces driving prices. It's a quick, clear update on what's moving, why it matters and what it can mean for your wallet and the wider economy. Find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. The ABC's Alan Kohler thinks the Treasurer should nationalise the childcare system. That is, taking it out of the hands of for-profit businesses. With lingering concerns about the quality and safety of some centres and families struggling to afford the bills, is now the time for a radical shake-up. Today, Alan on the case for change. And a childcare policy expert on whether it could really work. I'm Sydney Peed on Gadigal Land, Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Uncertainty in cost of living pressures. The government claims it'll be its most ambitious budget to date. And Alan Kohler has one late suggestion for the Treasurer. I've got an idea for next month's federal budget, although it's probably a bit too late. Alan, you went on ABC News recently and dropped a bombshell of an idea for the federal budget to nationalise childcare and kindergarten. And make them free. I imagine you had a bit of reaction to that. Did you have any missed calls from the Treasurer? No. No. Jim Chalmers didn't ring me, but certainly got a big reaction. It was certainly... A lot of people called me a communist. But it was pretty positive. I think a lot of people believe there's a problem. And the problem isn't simply that childcare is, in my view, too expensive. Also, the private school sector, both primary and secondary, is subsidised by the government, but the subsidy is only available to not-for-profit organisations, whereas with childcare, three-quarters of them are profit-making businesses, and yet they're subsidised as well. So I think that's an inconsistency that also needs to be looked at. Okay. Well, Alan, we're going to step through this idea with you. Childcare is a huge issue for families. Just getting your kid a spot is hard, and even if you can get in, it's just so expensive. So how big a change would this be? Oh, well, I think it would be massive. And I do think it's connected to housing affordability, too, because the fact that house prices are now more than twice the relationship to incomes that they were 25 years ago, that's changed the whole dynamics of running a household, so that the mortgage is now much more, and quite often, whether or not both partners in a family want to work, they have to work because they need to pay the mortgage. So suddenly, there's been a massive change in the way households operate. And of course, if you both work, then you've got to get childcare if you've got kids under five. There is a subsidy, obviously, and it can be 80% of the cost for low-income families, but the means test tapers off pretty quickly. And so if you're a middle-class family earning a reasonable salary, you're not getting much subsidy, if any, and because you've probably got a million-dollar mortgage, you're in strife. The two costs together are really crippling. Well, let's step through exactly how this scheme would work in your mind. You've done some of the numbers. Let's talk about the big one. The government would have to buy out these operators to get this idea over the line. It would cost tens of billions of dollars, wouldn't it? It would. I sort of had a stab at 50 or 60 billion. That was a pretty wild guess. I took one of the operators, looked at their market share and looked at their market value. I think it's roughly correct. Then the question is, well, how do you finance the acquisition of the childcare operators in the wild and crazy event that it was actually nationalised? And I thought, well, they could issue childcare bonds to super funds. Just explain a bit, how does the childcare bonds that super funds could invest in work? Just explain that a bit more. Oh, well, the government issues bonds now to finance its deficit. They're IOUs, effectively, that pay interest. And the interest rate on those bonds at the moment, the 10-year maturity bonds, is about 5%. That would cover the cost of buying them. And then you've got to run them. You know, at the moment, if you subtract the profits that they're making, there's probably 15 to 20 billion in actual cost of running them. And I'm saying, well, you know, if it was free, a lot more people would use it. So the cost would probably increase to, I don't know, 30 billion. The cost of running them and paying the interest on the bonds would be in the order of 30 to $35 billion a year, half of which is covered by the cost of the subsidy now. And, well, the other half, I'm saying, consider that to be an investment. So the government would run the childcare centres that employ the staff as public servants, I presume. It sounds a bit expensive, but as you say, you think it could be viewed as an investment. So just explain that a bit more. What's the case for that? Well, the case simply is, at the moment, what they're doing is subsidising private companies' shareholders. You know, I don't think that's a very good way to go, but there we go. That's just the way it's grown up. So owning the centres themselves would make it more of a state system. I mean, just simply extending the provision of public education to kids under five. I don't think it's particularly radical to do that. You know, we currently have a state education system for people, you know, between five and 18. I'm just trying to get people's minds a bit focused on this problem. Well, just on that issue of nationalising, you know, what does history tell us about the quality of services that taxpayers receive when something is privatised? Because, I mean, we haven't seen many examples of services that have been nationalised or re-nationalised, really. No, in fact, what we've seen is lots of things being privatised. Obviously, Qantas, Commonwealth Bank, Telstra, are they better now than they were? I don't know. I'll leave that up to their customers to decide. It is generally felt as a truism among economists that private sector does things better than the government. And, you know, that's possibly true. Competition certainly works to improve things. And, you know, there is competition between childcare centres at the moment. But, look, there are problems with safety, child safety in these centres. You know, I think that there are question marks around the quality of the childcare centres as they are. And I think it's patchy. Let's face it. I don't know whether you or people you know have got experience with childcare centres, but my experience with grandchildren is that some of them aren't that great and some of them are fantastic. Right. Well, we know the Prime Minister does want to do more on expanding access to childcare. These are the building blocks of a world-class, universal early education system. Getting fees down for families, getting wages up for workers, getting more places for children, more centres... So what do you think, Alan, what are the chances of Anthony Albanese hearing this idea of yours and getting to work on implementing it? Oh, zero, I'd say. Right. I don't want anyone to get the idea that I think it's going to happen. I think the days of nationalising things are well and truly over. I mean, I suppose I was just trying to draw attention to what clearly is a problem. There has been a Productivity Commission report on it, and they've recommended lifting the subsidy to ease the cost of living problems for people. In a way, that just further entrenches the problem to some extent. I think they're a bit stuck, really. I don't think there is the prospect of a big change. So I do think that probably what will happen is they'll just sort of fiddle with the subsidy a bit and help people out. But there's a limit to what they can do because they're trying to reduce the budget deficit. Well, Alan, we're going to see what a childcare policy expert thinks about this idea. So thanks very much. They'll hate it. They'll hate it. Ah, well, let's see. Thanks so much for stepping us through. Righto. My name's Elizabeth Hill. I'm Professor of Political Economy and Deputy Director of the Australian Centre for Gender Equality and Inclusion at Work at the University of Sydney. So, Elizabeth, that's Alan Kohler's idea to nationalise childcare centres and provide free childcare to all parents. What do you think? Is he on to a winner? Alan coming out on national TV and kind of spruiking his back of the envelope numbers on providing for a nationalised system was a bit of a breath of fresh air. Alan's highlighting an issue that academics and leaders across the sector have long mulled over. And that is, why does Australia expose its youngest and most vulnerable to the vagaries of the free market? For-profit provision of an essential service like early childhood education and care was never a good idea. And it still isn't. We've known that markets are not the best way to deliver public goods like childcare. And yet policy choices made over the past 20 years and before have delivered a radical marketisation of early childhood education and care services that do not deliver high-quality services. And, you know, we've kind of come to this point where rather than having a really strong, high-quality sector that everybody can access and benefit from, governments from both sides of politics have found themselves spending increasing billions of dollars on a service that many families find is just too expensive. It's hard to access. It's got workforce challenges due to historically low wages. And as we've been reminded in graphic detail in recent months, it's often of a quality that's too low and in some instances actually very dangerous for young children. So nationalising the system would finally get us out of this vicious cycle of pouring good money after bad and provide government with an opportunity to spend public money directly on a high-quality service. Well, as you've said, we've seen the childcare industry develop into this very lucrative business. But could this idea actually practically work? Can you unscramble this egg, so to speak? Well, here's the rub, right? The politics of nationalisation is no doubt hard, as are the budgetary implications. Unscrambling the egg would be a huge undertaking. But I guess what I would say is that it doesn't have to be all or nothing. Turning the ship will require some time. There's no quick fixes here. But using the funding lever and the regulatory framework, we can use that to break the business model that's so effectively attracted these large for-profit providers, including private equity, I have to say. You know, private equity companies have no pretense to the public good. So I think reducing that type of business's involvement in early childhood education and care would be a really good starting place and really support moves towards improved quality. Well, many in the childcare industry, I'm sure, would insist that a well-regulated, government-supported, competitive industry can actually lead to better, cheaper services and care for our kids. Do they have a point? Look, education and care is not a regular market. It's a public good that's completely different from running a cafe or running a jeans factory where the profit motive drives outcomes. High quality early childhood education and care is expensive. There is absolutely no way around that. It requires skilled staff who have the time to provide high quality care and education. And parents are not regular consumers when they're looking for early childhood education and care for their kids. If I start to have qualms about my early childhood education and care provider, it's not easy to find another place. And it's certainly not easy, as many parents will attest to, to move your child from a centre where they already have connections with staff and peers to a new one. The profit motive in early childhood education and care does not drive quality up. Instead, it drives quality down. And the evidence on this is very clear with for-profit providers much less likely than not-for-profits to meet national minimum quality standards and also less likely to meet the highest standard. So I think we really need to get away from this idea of early childhood education and care being a market. Many in the industry would also say that the majority of centres are providing great care for Australian children. Oh no, many services do provide really good quality care. They have excellent and very committed staff. But we know that the system as a whole is currently not designed and not operating to deliver that high quality service for all children, for all families, no matter where they live. Elizabeth, we know that there's been a huge scandal over the quality of care and the safety of children in childcare. And a lot of that has been exposed by the reporting of the ABC's Adele Ferguson. In the wake of that, is the industry changing? Is regulation forcing the bad operators out? Look, the initial legislative package that the Commonwealth has put through provides some excellent measures to start really shifting the dial on some very basic levels of child safety. That 15% lift in wages has also played a really important role in promoting that kind of stability and offering some opportunity for stable and decently paid employment. So there's a way to go there. But the investment in early childhood workforce will definitely flow through to higher quality outcomes for kids and their families. So Alan doesn't think this is going to happen. But are you any more hopeful about this, given the political realities that we're faced with? Yeah, no, like Alan, I have no expectations that on budget night we're going to get a big announcement on the government nationalising the ECEC system. I am certainly not expecting that. But the benefit of Alan's intervention is that it really does reconnect people with the need to rebalance it away from the large for-profit providers that are driving down quality. And I have to say, I love his idea of childcare bonds and looping in the super funds. Because it's using working people's savings to invest in a public good whose benefits flow directly back to workers and employers, delivering workforce sustainability and productivity. So it's a neat solution. Thanks, Alan. Elizabeth Hill is a professor in the Department of Political Economy at the University of Sydney. Alan Kohler is the ABC's finance expert and co-host of the ABC Business Daily podcast. Audio production on this episode by Sam Dunn and Anna John. Our supervising producer is David Cody. I'm Sydney Pead. ABC News Daily will be back with Sam Hawley tomorrow. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: What the shaky Iran ceasefire means for fuel prices

I will reiterate the president's expectation and demand that the Strait of Hormuz is reopened immediately, quickly and safely. Right now there's been an average of about five or six ships getting through a day, which is well below the average of between 60 and 100 ships. They're estimating that with the ceasefire, there might be somewhere between 10 and 15 ships getting through. But we're still talking, you know, like 20% of what a normal capacity would be. Well, the International Energy Agency said on Monday that at least 40 energy assets across nine countries in the Middle East have been severely or very severely damaged since the Iran war began. Even if the Strait is open, that infrastructure is not returning to normal output anytime soon, is it? No, you're exactly right. It's going to take months, if not years, to rebuild some of that infrastructure. Plus, even the existing facilities and production areas, which weren't damaged so far, they've really powered down because of all the uncertainty. And, you know, they're not going to produce oil and different fuels just to have it sit there. So that all needs to be restarted. And that doesn't happen on a dime either. So they won't really resume full capacity unless they're sure they can put that oil on tankers. And those tankers can safely leave the region to their final destinations. So you would hope that any price decreases that were coming would happen as quickly, but that's probably not going to be the case. So, you know, it might end up being that we don't see any more price increases, but we also don't see major price decreases for the time being. So we're in a good bargaining position, if you will, to remind Singapore that we should be maintained as a priority market for them and that they can be assured that they're going to still get, you know, the gas and other materials that they rely on from Australia. What's your expectation on the security of our fuel supply at this point? Has anything really changed? Hopefully this reprieve will allow us to stock up on any use that we've already dipped into our reserves. There will be a question about what the optimal level of reserves are for Australia. Maybe there might be some technology breakthroughs that would make production cheaper. But all things being equal, if they start to charge tolls, we'll see at least some of that being passed through in terms of higher prices. You need it to put in your car. As long as that demand is very strong, they'll be able to pass on the majority of any price increases that they have due to tolls. So that would imply that petrol prices would remain above pre-war levels. Yeah, okay. And what if oil and energy prices remain high? What's that going to do to the global economy? In the short term, it's going to make goods and services more expensive. It's going to cost more money to produce them. It's going to cost more money to ship them. It's going to cost more money to go and buy them. It's just going to make things more expensive. But, you know, on the other hand, it becomes more viable for companies to start to think about using alternative energy sources and for companies to invest in R&D to figure out how to make those alternative energy sources more efficient, more available, more dependable. So we saw a big surge in alternative energies after the 1970s oil crisis.
