Have we seen the worst of that yet in terms of the price of goods going up as a result of the oil shock? I don't think so, unfortunately. I think that because what we've been seeing immediately are increases in transport costs. We've seen a lot of companies start putting fuel surcharges onto the transport aspect of goods and services. We've seen, obviously, our own payments in terms of consumer spending. They've been shifting away from other types of goods and services because they have to spend more money every week on petrol. But we haven't really experienced what the increased cost in the production of many goods and services. So to the extent that it costs money to fuel production facilities for everything we consume from cars to clothing to household goods, that hasn't really been reflected because currently businesses are still selling inventories and goods they've purchased pre-war. As those inventories begin to dwindle and they need to be replaced to the extent that the new goods that are being replaced reflect higher production costs, we're going to see higher costs in the price of the goods that we're consuming. What about here in Australia? The oil shock will push up prices. Would a two-week ceasefire ease pressure on the Reserve Bank to further hike interest rates? It's two weeks. So that doesn't really mean much to producers. They're not going to do major ramp up for two weeks because that's just not efficient. It doesn't make sense. It costs them more to ramp up. And that two weeks, we're still looking at maybe 20% of the volume pre-war getting through. And that's not going to move the dial on anybody's production costs. You know, we're not even thinking about things like insurance and other costs that are associated with that or the other goods coming through. And the number one thing people have been talking about is fertilizer. So fertilizer cost remains high. And farmers respond to that by either A, costing them more to plant their crops or B, them cutting back on the amount of crops they plant. That has implications for food prices going forward. So there's still a lot of unknowns in terms of what the cost impact that's going to have, therefore the price impact that's going to have on the Australian economy. And the RBA is going to be watching this closely because if we start to see these prices increasing and staying high, then they're going to be in the position where they need to address that by, you know, raising rates or trying somehow not to let that inflation embed itself in the economy over the long run. Because Australia's inflation was already very high before the war started causing problems, wasn't it? That's correct. Not only was it high, it's above the target rate, but it was increasing the last few months. And that's of concern to the RBA. And that wasn't even being driven by international events. If you look at the amount of inflation coming from what we call tradable goods, those goods that are either imported or exported, those goods that are subject to international prices, that inflation is less than 2%. It was like 1.5% prior to the war. While domestic or non-traded goods, that inflation was closer to 5%. So up until this recent event, our inflation has been driven by domestic concerns or domestic pressures, such as housing and such as domestic travel. And so it was already feeling pressure from the domestic side. If we now add pressure from the international side, the RBA is really going to be forced into action. Right. Right. Okay. Well, there's still a lot of uncertainty. The ceasefire may not last long. Do you think the war, though, has changed the outlook for the global economy? I think so. I keep using the same word over and over again is uncertainty. There's uncertainty surrounding the cost of a major input to the global economy. Firms are going to respond to that by not acting. They're going to wait. They're not going to make major investments. They're not going to make any expansion in markets. They're going to put on hold any hiring decisions. And all of that means a slowdown in an economic sense. And so there becomes real concern that the global economy slows down. The IMF has already come out saying that it's concerned some economies could lose, you know, 1%, you know, or higher of GDP growth if this conflict continues. And if that also translates to higher prices, then we get into the situation of stagflation, which is a real problem. And it takes tremendous movements to get an economy out of that situation. And it's not always a pleasant occurrence. We need higher interest rates to kind of get the economy kind of shocked out of any kind of stagflation that we may encounter. So if all of this eventuates, it means, you know, another very large slowdown for the global economy and, of course, the Australian economy as well. Right. So a recession really is still on the cards here in Australia. It is a possibility for sure. Dr. Susan Stone is the Credit Union SA Chair of Economics at Adelaide University. Audio production for this episode by Sam Dunn. Our supervising producer is David Cody. I'm Sydney Pead. ABC News Daily will be back again on Monday. Thanks for listening. episodes.title: Former South Korean president sentenced to jail
episodes.description: Former South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol is sentenced to five years in jail over crimes relating to his failed attempt at imposing martial law in the country.
episodes.transcript: Former South Korean President Yoon Song-yeol has been sentenced to five years in jail over crimes relating to his failed attempt at imposing martial law in the country. Kyung Moon-hwang is a professor with the Korea Foundation at the Australian National University. What do you make of the five-year sentence? This is the first of four charges against him. Well, I personally think that the seriousness of all of his crimes, of course, they were all centered on his botched attempt to impose martial law and to essentially install himself as a petty little dictator. The verdict was correct, but the sentence was much too light. It was half of what was requested by the prosecution. And given the seriousness and the terrible severity and outcomes and consequences of what he did, it seems to be a very light sentence. Although it is just the beginning, he has many, many trials coming up for countless charges, including the most severe one in about a month, which is his leading the insurrection. And so I doubt that he is going to ever leave jail the rest of his life. But this first verdict, I think it was a bit disappointing in that it was not as large of a sentence as it should have been. Professor, can you take me through what actually happened when he announced this martial law? I recall it happening and it was just, it was so chaotic. I don't think anyone knew what was going on at the time. Well, it was just such a shock that this country that had achieved democratization even more than 45 years earlier, anyway, that it all of a sudden had this man declaring martial law, taking the country back to the battle days of the dictatorship. And so I think it was the shock more than anything else that was the prevailing sentiment at the time. And then, of course, the legislator quickly moved to reject and overturn that martial law declaration within a couple of hours. And that night then was just an extraordinary evening. And everything that has come about afterwards has been really a reflection of the polarization of the country in so many ways. Although it has, of course, also driven that polarization even further. But what has come out in the meantime has been just as concerning as what started the whole thing. And that is this extraordinary, crazy declaration of martial law by Jung. And as you mentioned, four trials all in all, and prosecutors will be seeking the death penalty ultimately. How likely is that? Well, I think that's much more of a symbolic gesture. South Korea, even though it has not formally or legally abolished the death penalty, has not implemented an execution in many, many years. And so it's really not a possibility. But as the prosecutor said a few days ago, the point is that this request for the death penalty is a reflection of the severity, the utmost severity of the crime itself. And so even if he is found guilty and sentenced to death, there's almost no chance that it will be carried out. But most likely he will, of course, spend the rest of his life in jail unless somehow he is pardoned later on. But they're working on ways to prevent that from happening legally. That is Kyung Moon Hwang, who is a professor with the Korea Foundation at the Australian National University. And of course, of course, of course, of course.

episodes.title: How the US seized Russian oil tanker fits into Trump's plan for Venezuela
episodes.description: The US military has boarded and seized a Russian-flagged oil tanker in the North Atlantic Ocean that has been trying to evade a US blockade for weeks.
episodes.transcript: The US military has boarded and seized a Russian flagged oil tanker in the North Atlantic Ocean that has been trying to evade a US blockade for weeks. It's one of two Venezuelan linked oil tankers intercepted by the US within a few hours as the Trump administration pledges to tightly control the country's oil industry and use its blockade to pressure its government to cooperate. To help us get to the bottom of this very fast-moving and complex story, I'm joined by energy analyst Clayton Segal, who's a senior fellow for energy security at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. Now, when it comes to Venezuela's oil, we know that they have some of the biggest oil reserves in the world, but they don't export much because they mainly deal with crude oil. What's your reaction to Marco Rubio's comments on the US plan to essentially take over Venezuela's oil, which the US had said before, but now we're hearing that term indefinitely being thrown around? Well, I think we've reached an important milestone with the new information coming from the Trump administration. After four weeks of this pretty unprecedented naval quarantine that, as the Secretary said, has been blocking Venezuela's exports, and now, of course, with the dramatic events of last weekend, we now have the outlines of a plan, of an approach from the administration on what to do with Venezuela's oil in the short term. And as Secretary Rubio said, the idea is for the United States to basically administer those oil exports and to market Venezuela's oil production to the international market at higher prices than they have sold for during the sanctions program, in which the major buyer of Venezuelan oil, which is China, has enjoyed some very steep discounts. So now the United States apparently is going to be taking Venezuelan oil and on its own volition, marketing it to the international seaborne market. We'll see what kind of demand there is in the marketplace for that Venezuelan crude. What happens to current contracts in place? I know we're talking about the future and how the US will manage this, but Venezuela already has contracts to export oil to a number of countries, I understand, including China, Iran and Russia. What's the status of those contracts now? China has a stake, a footprint in Venezuela's oil sector, and was expecting in the coming years to develop it and to reap the benefits of that position in the Venezuelan oil industry. Now it seems pretty clear that the Trump administration is determined to shut China out of that positioning and the potential benefits from it in the coming years, not only to squeeze the volumes of Venezuelan oil that were added to China, again, at those discounted prices, but also to maybe make them exit their positions on the upstream side in Venezuela in favor of maybe more involvement from American and Western companies. So I think it's a pretty big shakeup that will capture attention in Beijing, first of all, about the volumes that are going to change from Venezuela, and then longer term, looking at the geopolitical balance of power. We're also rattling the saber. We hear that rattling from Washington against other oil producers, Iran, Colombia, maybe even Mexico. So China, which has to import 11 million barrels per day, might be concerned about what's next. Yeah, having a look at what's next indeed. Now, when it comes to these two ships that have been seized, the US is accusing them of breaking US sanctions. Could you explain what those sanctions are and their function for the United States? The United States has sanctioned Venezuelan oil generally. Venezuela, like Iran and like Russia, has had to rely on this so-called shadow fleet to move its oil, to transport its oil to market, and get around those sanctions and get around the enforcement authorities. But in the most part, it has succeeded in choking off those oil exports. And so importing countries, particularly China, which, by the way, was taking a full 80% of those Venezuelan oil shipments before the quarantine, are going to have to make adjustments and probably have to find substitute oil supplies. Clayton Segal, who is an energy analyst and a senior fellow for energy security at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

than they have sold for during the sanctions program,
in which the major buyer of Venezuelan oil, which is China, has enjoyed some very steep discounts.
So now the United States apparently is going to be taking Venezuelan oil and on its own volition,
marketing it to the international seaborne market.
We'll see what kind of demand there is in the marketplace for that Venezuelan crude.
What happens to current contracts in place?
I know we're talking about the future and how the US will manage this,
but Venezuela already has contracts to export oil to a number of countries,
I understand, including China, Iran and Russia.
What's the status of those contracts now?
China has a stake, a footprint in Venezuela's oil sector,
and was expecting in the coming years to develop it
and to reap the benefits of that position in the Venezuelan oil industry.
Now it seems pretty clear that the Trump administration is determined to shut China out
of that positioning and the potential benefits from it in the coming years,
not only to squeeze the volumes of Venezuelan oil that were added to China,
but also to maybe make them exit their positions on the upstream side in Venezuela
in favor of maybe more involvement from American and Western companies.
So I think it's a pretty big shakeup that will capture attention in Beijing,
first of all, about the volumes that are going to change from Venezuela,
and then longer term, looking at the geopolitical balance of power.
We hear that rattling from Washington against other oil producers,
So China, which has to import 11 million barrels per day,
might be concerned about what's next.
Yeah, having a look at what's next indeed.
Now, when it comes to these two ships that have been seized,
the US is accusing them of breaking US sanctions.
Could you explain what those sanctions are and their function for the United States?
The United States has sanctioned Venezuelan oil generally.
Venezuela, like Iran and like Russia, has had to rely on this so-called shadow fleet
to move its oil, to transport its oil to market,
and get around those sanctions and get around the enforcement authorities.
But in the most part, it has succeeded in choking off those oil exports.
And so importing countries, particularly China,
which, by the way, was taking a full 80% of those Venezuelan oil shipments
before the quarantine, are going to have to make adjustments
and probably have to find substitute oil supplies.
Clayton Segal, who is an energy analyst and a senior fellow for energy security
at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

episodes.title: NRL Monday: Dragons drama and what's next
episodes.description: What is doing at the Dragons? On NRL Monday, Andrew Moore runs through a day of high drama at St George Illawarra including the sacking of Shane Flanagan, the club’s handling of the situation, and the appointment of Dean Young as interim coach.
episodes.transcript: It's time for kick-off. Welcome to NRL Monday with Andrew Moore. Insights, analysis and all you need to know in the NRL on ABC Radio and ABC Sport Digital. episodes.title: The Raiders are their own worst enemies
episodes.description: Back to back wins for Canberra Raiders have given great entertainment to the neutral but gun centre Simi Sasagi reckons they're making life harder for themselves than it needs to be.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Sports coverage of the NRL Premiership. NRL Saturday. On your radio, ABC Sport Digital Radio. And ABC Listen. Luke Lewis, Michael Kariannis, I'm Andrew Moore here on NRL Saturday on ABC Sport. We raved about Simi Sasangi in Perth last week. We raved about Simi Sasangi last night. We've raved about him in games. Canberra has lost. He's been outstanding playing in the centres for Canberra. And he's on the line. Simi, how are you going? Hey, guys. How are you? Mate, we're well. And part of the reason why we're having so much fun at the footy is watching you play. It is incredible, the turnaround from sort of Mr Utility, what do you need, Ricky? Okay, I'll fill in there, to becoming the form centre in the competition. How have you found it? No, good, bro. I'm just enjoying my footy at the moment. And it's kind of a, it's pretty, it's a fuzzy feeling, man. You know, did a lot of training in different positions and I found myself in centre. Well, it didn't take long for you to have an impact last night. You scored this try in just the sixth minute of the game. Sanders to Strange. Then away through hands it goes. Making half a break with a one-handed pass. Away to Simi Sasangi for the try. That was brilliantly done by Ethan Strange. And it's a try to Simi Sasangi. Billy Walker blows that horn and Canberra is in front. They did that pretty easily. Great set up by Strange and the finish from Simi Sasangi. episodes.description: Another round, another loss for St George Illawarra. Some were encourage by their performance in the defeat by Manly - but not Luke Lewis. He thought talk of an improved effort was a cop out.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Sports coverage of the NRL Premiership. NRL Saturday. On your radio, ABC Sport Digital Radio. And ABC Listen. Let's get to last night's game. And MC, you and I were having a very intimate viewing of the St George Illawarra Manly Ringer game in your hotel room, watching it off your laptop. Yes. We couldn't get it on the TV. But we saw enough to know that Manly did enough to beat St George Illawarra despite a good effort by the Dragons. That final score in favour of the Seagulls after they trailed at one point, 28 points to 18. They led 16-0, then the Dragons led 18-16. Reuben Garrick scored this his second try. We get back and away from the kickoff of Manly here. Garrick receives a pass on the outside. Dummies. He burns Val Holmes for speed. Over halfway, Garrick. They're all chasing him. Overcomes Sloan. Won't catch him. And they score from the kickoff. Oh, dearie me. Dearie, dearie me, Dragons fans. Garrick scores his second try. And that was dearie, dearie me at that point. Reuben Garrick, three points in the ABC Player of the Year from Matthew Elliott. Two to second rower, Homoli Olukowatu, who has been charged with a high tackle on Jacob Little and been fined. One point to Dragons front rower, Toby Couchman. And, look, there was some easy try scored in the game, actually, for both sides, MC. That Luciano Lelewitt try was ridiculous from a tap. Effort there from the Dragons, but the fact is they've lost 10 in a row. What did you make of it? Yeah, I think you summed it up perfectly. A better effort this week compared to that game that we were at last week where they were just so poor and off the pace against North Queensland. But, again, it was lapses in concentration. Some poor defensive re-tom to Voivich over Kyle Flanagan for one of the first try, I think it might have been. And then from the kickoff, they shift wide and take advantage of some lazy switched-off defense from the Dragons and score again. So that's probably been it. Well, it's definitely a concern for the Dragons, but they were more spirited this week than they have been in the past couple. It wasn't always the best game of footy, to be fair, down there in the gong last night. But for Manly, Louis, that's two out of two for Kieran Foran. Yeah, a big smile on Kieran Foran's face after the game in the press conference. And he knew that it wasn't all going to be the same as the way the week before sort of flowed. But they got the job done and they didn't play their best football. But at the end of the day, it's all about winning and coming up with the right plays at the right time. And they did that. And attention to detail, that play off the kickoff where Ruben Garrick scores that try. That's a play that they had planned. So good research, I reckon, from Kieran Foran during the week where he's seen an opportunity that if we do get a kickoff, just keep an eye up on the defense. They come up and in a lot. Let's play back down the sideline. And it was Saab who comes up with that catch and comes up with a beautiful little play. So really good, smart play there from the Seagulls. I thought they played well. But gee, we talk about effort for the Dragons. I reckon it's a cop-out. I'll be honest with you. Talking about, oh, it's a better effort. It's not a better effort. It's 10 weeks, 10 losses. Horrible football. And the least, I say this all the time, the least a rugby league supporter expects out of his team is effort. Effort. That's the least. I don't reckon there was effort. All right. I've seen bits and pieces of it. Some of the plays, effort's getting thrown in your head into tackles where you know you've got to make them. And sometimes some of the attempts were horrible. I sit and I go, there's no effort in that. I don't know what everyone's talking about. Oh, the effort was better. I find that bizarre. But anyway, so that's my opinion on it and take on it. But I just feel like the Dragons are so, so far behind. Their confidence levels are absolutely shot. And I don't reckon they have an answer for it. They don't look like they have an answer for it. Even when they hit the lead last night, Michael, there's kind of an air of expectancy that that wouldn't last very long. No, it was, they've been poor, no doubt, to start this year. And as Louis said, you know, walking away and talking about effort generally indicates that they're at their lowest ebb. And that's where they're at at the moment. But, you know, they play South next week into the Roosters before the bye. I just don't know where their next win comes from. Yeah. So what about the pressure of Shane Flanagan? Does that get eased by the closeness of the scores last night or what? It does in a sense that, you know, I've made a few calls around it today. I don't think anything's imminent in terms of Shane Flanagan's future. And that's probably, you know, at the 16-0 mark, I think the score got to 16-0 in Manly's favour. And you start to go, oh, this could be 30 points at half-time. And they're going to be left with little options. So, no, I don't think there's anything imminent regarding the coach's future at the moment. Rugby League is on your radio. NRL Saturday here on ABC Sport. ABC Sport Digital Radio. And ABC Listen. NRL Saturday here on ABC Sport with Luke Lewis, Michael Carriannis. I'm Andrew Moore as we look forward to this doubleheader under bright, beautiful, sunny skies. South and Canberra coming up into the Cronulla-Sutherland-Sydney Roosters clash. And we're here to, as I said before, get the vibe of the Perth Bears coming into the competition next year. And they have an immortal in charge there, coach Mal Meninga, who joins us in the box. Good to see you, Mal. How are you going? Very good, Andrew. Thank you. The vibe. That's nice. The castle. The castle. That's right. The castle days. Well, you're old enough to remember that. Well, I'm kind of hoping this can be the kingdom. Oh, nice. There you go. A bit of putt on words there. I tell you what, you've got to work hard, though, to put the crown on your head here. It's a challenge, isn't it? How have you found it so far? No, it's been excellent. The support in general. So from the government, your local, obviously, rugby league community has been fantastic. NREL WA has been great. I just kicked off our inaugural Trax Academy. So that's our Elite Pathways program, which is fantastic. So we had about 25 kids all week. They're coming today watching the game, which is fantastic. It's been going commercially. We're going really well. We launched our mascot yesterday. Ran out of merchandising. Won the race, too, didn't they? Won the race by a country mile, basically. Good omen. Yeah, good omen. Yeah. So the memberships, that's coming out soon as well. So bubble on nicely. We spoke to you when you first accepted the gig. And the fair question was, why? The other side of the country. And tough challenge. I think you're still coming back and forth from Canberra to here. What's been the most challenging aspect of, you know, you're trying to put a roster together, let alone coaching staff and all that sort of thing. What's been the most challenging aspect? It's sort of, you're sort of flying blind a bit because it is unique. We, you know, obviously, we've started from basically nothing, you know. So when we talk about, you know, any, I'll just give an example of the Dolphins as an example. So they've got a pathway, elite pathway, kids program participation from under sixes right through the NRL. And we haven't got that, obviously. We've built some strong relationships, partnerships with North Sydney Bears, which is fantastic. And we're acknowledging the heritage and history of the North Sydney Bears. And also got an affiliation with the Brisbane Tigers. So just sort of, we're sort of working on our pathways and how we develop players. But at the same time, trying to get a competitive roster together. And obviously, as you know, a lot of people signed up, a lot of players have signed up. But in saying, I'm very, very happy with the character of the person and the skill set of the players we've got so far. Now, how do you go about building a roster? Like, do you sit down? Do you come up with, like, goals of who you want? How do you approach them? When do you want to get them here? Like, I was looking the other day, seeing Penrith had, like, 10 players coming off contract on November 1. Like, how does that work for you? Understanding the cycle here. So, you know, over here, there's about 5,000 registered players. So we've got to lift the standard and the quality of players over here, definitely. And then, obviously, in partnership with the North Sydney Bears and the Brisbane Tigers, have a look and see how their depth is going as well. So as far as the roster is concerned, you know, we're looking at a certain type of character. Obviously, that wants to come over here for all the right reasons. You know, we talk about distance all the time, but these players, they want to be here. They want to be trailblazers for our great game of rugby league. So it's more around character and actually wanting to be here and want to come over here and want to be, like I said before, trailblazers for our game. What about culture? But, you know, part of that cultural bit is around having the courage and the boldness to make a decision to come over to Perth with their families as well, which is, you know, it's a challenge for them. Have you got the group together yet?
Is there a plan to get them together before the season starts?

But, you know, part of that cultural bit is around having the courage and the boldness to make a decision to come over to Perth with their families as well, which is, you know, it's a challenge for them.
Obviously, we're taking them out of their comfort zones in the east and in England and bringing them to the west of Australia.
So, you know, on that too, Mal, I spoke recently, and I'm sure this is not breaking confidence, with Scott Sorensen, one of your big signings.
And he was raving about how well already they're being treated, they being the family, by the Perth Bears and the options put to them.
Yeah, well, one of our first appointments was our welfare guy, a guy called Sam Wentworth.
Young fella, similar age to all the players and their wives and partners and families, you know.
So I'm really conscious of the fact that when we do relocate over here, we do it in the proper manner.
They're all happy about their decision.

And then I know that if, you know, they're happy about their decision, they come over and everyone's been looked after, they're going to come to train and they're going to be their best version of themselves.
And then we go from there.
You've already obviously signed a handful of English players already too.
How do you go about getting those deals done and can we expect any more Super League players to be part of your top squad?
I've got a big, I mean, I'm a big fan of the English game.
I've been there, played there for many, many years.
You know, we sort of compare things to the NRL.
You know, that's the beast it is.
I love the skill of the English game.
And I think coming over here can only improve them as individuals.

And, you know, obviously I live in Canberra and I see the way the English players have taken to Canberra and just being in a professional environment, you know, elite performance where they have physically, they've got to build themselves, mindset, all those sort of things.
Just being, come up to speed and everything they do around their game.
I think there's a lot more upside to them than what a lot of people think.
So we'll keep on investigating that, you know, the English Super League.
We feel that, you know, we've got a bit of an asset because we're on the West Coast.
You know, we jump on a plane, it's 17 hours to London.
You know, so I just think that we need to investigate.
We need to have a look at how we can bring teams together.
So not only in the West and trying to create, you know, great synergy over here and pathway programs.
I think we've got an opportunity to go into South Africa and Europe and the UK because, just because of where we are.
Now, just a quick one on the English Super League and the players you've got over there.
We've seen some really good English players in the front row come over and play.
We haven't really seen too many backs take to it yet.
Do you have an eye on any good backs out there that we can keep an eye out?
I looked at him quite a long time ago because Dave Ferner, you know, was the coach leads there for quite a while there.
And he was trying to bring, you know, Harry over, Harry Newman over to, you know, play for, you know, Raiders or whatever the case may be.
So he's had a time and place in his career that he wants to prove himself, which is good.
You know, coming over for the right reasons.
We've got a couple of good players out of the Leeds Club.
But I felt, you know, the Leeds are going really well at the moment.
They've got, you know, Brad Arthur as their coach.
We understand, you know, Brad's coaching mentality all around accountability, which is big over here.
We talk about accountability all the time.
The way we, you know, the way we prepare footy teams and, you know, how we prepare individuals as, you know, as human beings as well.
I'm really confident they come into our systems over here and I think they'll excel.
I understand what you say around the backs, but I think Harry Newman's got that mental toughness that's going to, you know, hold him in good stead.
Now there's been some conjecture, a bit of media speculation around some of your staff and even your own future.
Can you guarantee that you'll be coach of the Bears come round one next year?
Oh, we're over in Perth at the moment.

So you can imagine, you know, I mean, I answered that question, Michael, yesterday in regards to when the Broncos have been under the pump, the Manly's been under the pump, the Dragons have been under the pump.
They still are under the pump.
We've got a beautiful double header here with a beautiful, you know, weather over here in Perth.
And all of a sudden they find some negativity over here.
We had a group, really good board meetings yesterday and it wasn't even raised, mate, to be honest with you, you know.
So we're a start-up club, you know, you're going to get some friction at some stage and, you know, the disappointing part that's got in the media is ridiculous.
So will you be coached round one next year?
And the reason why I'm doing this, you know, we talked about, Andrew, I'm 65 years of age.
I just see, I just see it's a wonderful opportunity, you know, for me to, to help our game, legacy-wise, you know.
So, like I said, we want to, we want to grow the game over here.
And, you know, I don't want to let, let the local community down.
So, I mean, it's all part of all that.
Just, you know, I think I'm doing it for all the right reasons as well.
How, though, the day-to-day growing when it starts, obviously it's very exciting now and you're the perfect person to be the, the figurehead of the club.
And setting up the culture and all of that sort of thing.
But you coached Canberra for a limited amount of time, but then an amazing record with Queensland and the Kangaroos.
And you'll know better than anyone how different this is.
How do you expect to cope once you get to the off-season training and the day-to-day grind of it all?
Is that going to be, do you reckon they'll be tougher than you expected?
What, from an age point of view?
Just having not done it for a while.
I mean, I'm prepared for it, you know.
So, mentally I'm prepared for it.
I've been in the professional game for nearly all my life, you know.
So, you have the right people and you have smart people around you.
I mean, it really is that simple.
I think my skill set complements others, you know.
So, I know my strengths and I know my weaknesses.
And, you know, I'll make sure that all my weaknesses are, you know, fostered by really smart people, you know, assistant coaches, all our staff.
You know, it's a big, it's a big team effort.
And if I can manage that process and system really, really well, you know, we'll do really well too on field.
What is it that you love?
I feel that's, you know, that you need, you need to build relationships and you need to get the best out of people.
So, I've always had that, even had that mindset even through Origin, you know, and Australian.
So, it's not about, it's, you know, obviously, you're going to get success.
But you build success off, you know, how you manage that environment that all those players are in.
You've got to keep them happy.
And, you know, you've got to make sure that it's a trustful, honest environment.
So, you can have those trustful, honest conversations, you know.
So, it's all around that, mate.
And, obviously, having everyone buy into how you want to play, how you want to, you know, how you want to behave.
All the standards you want to set internally.
So, you know, I think the modern player, I mean, they come already prepared for that, you know, through their pathways they've been through.
I think they understand the environment.
Now, you've got more than half your squad, 30-man squad locked in now.
What are one or two key positions that you still want to, you know, invest in for next season?
We're around the 18 mark, you know.
So, we don't only need 24 to start the year, you know, then 28 before the season kicks off.
So, you know, we're looking at a few more forwards.
And we obviously, you know, we know how important it is in the modern game.
How important your spine is, you know.
So, we're looking at more options around all that, you know, your halves, your five-eighths, hookers and fullback.
You know, we sort of just need to get a bit more depth in that.
I think the really important part around the game at the moment and obviously the rules, I think you've got to have a really good depth in your squad.
So, we're really working hard on that.
And every player we've signed at the moment has played NRL.
And I think that's the way we'll continue to have a look at our roster.
It also worth remembering, too, you're not just competing with 16 clubs.
You've got riding your coattails that the following year, the P&G Chiefs, with tax-free money.
It's part of the deal, isn't it?
You know, so we signed up to this now, understanding all that, Andrew.
So, you know, we've got a different sell piece.
It's just a – and I don't think it's been about footy.
You know, I think, you know, rugby league, they'll come over here and they'll play really well, pretty well.
It's actually just wanting to be here.
You could go from Perth Bears coach to tourism minister out here.
All right, Malman Inga, so good to see you, mate.
Good luck with everything that lies ahead.
And I'm sure you're pumped about the upcoming off-season to get into next year.
ABC Sports Coverage of NRL Saturday.
Rugby League is on your radio.
Here it is, MC's Hammer Time.
Time to find out all the latest rugby league news and speculation.
Here's Michael Kariannis with MC's Hammer Time.
See, normally I've got no idea how many stories you're going to bring to the table, Michael.
But I watched you in action while you were munching on your baked beans and your scrambled eggs.
I think it's a race in two for Scott Drinkwater Dragons.
And the Tigers are the smoky, depending on what happens with Dureen Buller.
Obviously, that Dureen Buller's contract situation, they've got a mutual option in that deal.
So there's a little bit to play out.
But I think you'll find the Dragons will formalize a three-year offer to Scott Drinkwater.
And his time at North Queensland will come to an end.
North Queensland don't want him there.
It's not that they don't want him there.
He's got 12 months left on his contract.
They're not going to re-sign Scott Drinkwater.
You think about now, Scott Drinkwater's not in their plans, but they had to pick between Drinkwater and the Hammer.
Now he's just nowhere to be seen.
All right, what have we got next?
Tom Duffy outstanding last night for Brisbane.
He's in talks about a one-year extension with the Broncos.
Obviously, Adam Reynolds next year at Brisbane.
So he's in talks with the Broncos about a 12-month extension.
But after his performance last night, he might have got some interest of some other clubs potentially looking for an NRL starting half.
He was the story until Scott Drinkwater became the story.
And that was great composure to kick the winning field goal against his old team.
It looks like he's picked up a fractured eye socket from last night's game.
So he needs scans to confirm that.
But it looks like Moses Suli will be out for an extended period for the Dragons.
It takes a while to get down there.
You better get down to the sideline, mate.
Well, in the pregame show, we spoke to New Perth Bears coach Mal Meninga.
And there are certainly challenges for the team coming into the comp next year.
What sort of a breakthrough can they have through media outlets?
No one better to ask than ABC Perth Drive Time host Olly Peterson, who is a self-acclaimed rugby league nufty.
Olly, great to see you, mate.
Look how spectacular it is here today at Opens Stadium.
Yeah, we've had some poor weather here for State of Origins in the past.
But you put on a show today.
Not a cloud to be seen.
What is the best sport here?
Because they've had test cricket here for a while.
Now the AFL obviously has a time here with the Eagles and Dockers.
And every now and then we get a league game.
It's pretty good for everything, to be blunt.
But obviously it's a footy field, not a footy AFL field.
And when you do get rectangular sports, obviously like league and union plays here, you're not still too far away.
It's not as though you're sitting at the SCG or the MCG.
You do feel a little closer with this cauldron.
And I think for our listeners right around Australia, this is what they're going to be basing the Olympic Stadium on in Brisbane as well.
So you get a bit of a feel and it does work for rectangular sports, particularly for an Origin when it's a full house.
For all of that, that is not where the Perth Bears will be playing.
They're not going to be here.
And it's been around for a long, long time.
That is a really good place for rectangular sports.
Might need a touch-up or two.
Nick, will that be in for next year?
Look, it's a really good field.
And I would rate it up there as being one of the, again, better rectangular fields because it seats about 20,000, 25,000.
And again, you're close to the action.
As you mentioned, though, Maury, the stadium still needs somewhat of an upgrade, particularly in the corporate areas.
And that is important for the commercial success of the Perth Bears because you're going to be selling sponsorship packages and you're looking to try and entice advertisers.
You need to be able to wind and dime them properly.
And it really needs to come into the 21st century.
How far away is that, Ollie, to having the Perth Stadium ready for that?
So it's still a little way off, Luke.
It was rumoured to be part of the announcement here with the Bears.
But to be blunt about it, not everybody here in Perth is on the same page when it comes to state government investment in the Perth Bears.
And I think the stadium upgrades at Perth Oval have been put on the back burner for a little while.
But it should happen because you've got good tenants, the force, the glory, and obviously the Perth Bears will be the main tenant from 2027.
And what about the training facilities?
So they will train next to the Wacker Ground.
And it's a beautiful location because as you're going across the causeway into the Perth CBD, you're going to see this magnificent field that is being established as we speak.
If you look at the grass now, it looks as immaculate as it does here at Perth Stadium.
They will use the old facilities which the WA cricketers have been using because they've just upgraded the Wacker Ground and they've moved to the other side.
So for the next couple of years, they will be in the old Wacker Ground's training facilities for the players.
It's just a really short walk over the road to the training ground.
And there are currently purpose-built facilities being constructed in Malaga, which is about 40 minutes outside of the Perth CBD in the eastern suburbs.
So they're going to have some of the best facilities of any club in Australia.
So the role of the media fascinates me over here, Oli, because not everyone, as you say, is like you and loves rugby league and comes from different parts.
How are they going to get traction in the media, not just with radio, but with TV?
And obviously there's been some conspiring against the Perth Bears in one of the newspapers in particular and one of the TV networks in particular.
Do you think they will get traction or is that going to be a real battle?
I think having Mal Meninga as the head coach is a game changer for a rugby league market like Perth.
But if Mal Meninga walks down the main street of the Perth CBD, Hay Street Mall, everybody knows who Mal Meninga is.
So the more that Mal does, I believe the more that people will come on board.
I don't think they're going to have any issue filling Perth Stadium or Perth Oval, I should say, for their home games, for at least the first few.
But obviously the team has to win.
In terms of media coverage, I think we're in a really interesting situation.
And you both know this better than anybody because the broadcast rights are up for negotiation.
Obviously, if certain media networks are able to land a particular night of football coverage on their television screens, I think that's going to change rapidly.
But at the moment, certainly the Bears are up against it.
It is an AFL town 1, 2 and 3.
Well, it's funny you say that because last night we were trying to find a game where we could go down and watch and maybe have a feed.
And it was very hard to do.

So is there a plan behind that here in Perth to make sure that there is more games on live in certain pubs and areas where people can actually go and have a feed and sit down and start enjoying our game?
And look, there are a few pubs around that are certainly right on board with rugby league.
And this might surprise a lot of people.
But you only have to go back about 10 years ago.
Origin wasn't even live on television in Perth.
There are a few pubs, and I knew where they were, where they'd take a satellite feed of the Northern Territory off in Paja to be able to show it in a pub in Perth.
So that's how quickly the game's developed.
I think through the COVID years, as the game was sped up with the six again rule, the casual sports fan here in Western Australia all of a sudden went,
hold on a minute, rugby league's really good.
Full credit here to, obviously, the National Rugby League to bring Origin back on a number of occasions.
And to the Rabbitohs, for that matter, because they've been bringing games over here for 15 years.
And they've managed to secure well over 1,000 West Australian fans.
But, hey, the grassroots are there.
So the more and more it's played, the more and more, obviously, it's talked about.
And we're a hungry beast, aren't we, in the media?
Hopefully, we'll be talking about it.
Yeah, you forget how long games have been coming to Perth.
Because Canberra, who we've just called against South Sydney, coming into today, they'd won five out of five.
So that's how far back it goes.
I mean, obviously, the Western Reds were here in the mid-90s.
But that's how far back rugby league goes playing here.
The junior numbers have always been very, very good in WA.
But the time slot is the one that's so interesting, Ollie.
Because for years and years, while we kept hearing about a Perth-based team in the NRL, because it's ideal for TV.
What is the ideal time to attract people, apart from viewers on telly, to the ground?
So we're obviously a market where we're used to turning up on a Saturday or Sunday afternoon or early evening anyway, because of television rights, regardless of what sport it is.
So if you can nail that 5 o'clock, 5.30 local time slot on a Saturday, I think that is what West Australians will get behind.
And it's an advantage we have as well.
Like, if you look at the Big Bash success here in Western Australia of the Perth Scorchers, it's because the games start at 4 o'clock in the afternoon.
So I'm the father of a four-year-old and a seven-year-old.
We don't miss a Big Bash match.
But if it's starting at 7 o'clock as it does in Sydney or Melbourne, it's a bit too late to take the kids because they've got to go to bed.
So there's huge advantages to get the kids involved.
And I think we saw yesterday...
And that's always such a quick process too, isn't it?
Well, I'll tell you what, there's plenty of...
Getting the kids involved and then watching our game from a young age, growing up with it here in Perth, that's what grows the crowd.
At the moment, it's not trying to convert the older guys.
So they're in their way and the mothers, but getting these young kids two games on a Saturday, that's what brings the love and the passion behind the jersey.
And I think that there are enough kids, you saw them here yesterday actually with the mascot race, hundreds and hundreds of kids turned up.
And I think if you see the Perth bear, I don't know if he's grizzly enough to be perfectly blunt, but he's a friendly bear.
So maybe that's what's going to entice the kids.
He needs Billy Morty to just have a few words.
All right, Ollie, before we let you go, you are a fanatical St George Illawarra supporter for your sins.
Now they've lost 10 in a row.
Because you don't just say you follow them, you actually follow them and you travel far to watch them play.
Do you regret that at the moment?
I just wonder in the scheme of what has happened at the football club, the likes of Ben Hunt and Zach Lomax being let go.
Damian Cook comes in at the wrong ends of their career.
And we just seem to be going backwards.
Somebody like Tyrell Sloan even last night.
I thought he was really good.
The slowest team I've ever seen.
It's just so hard to watch at the moment, Maury.
But I will keep the faith with the Red V and I will – does it pass the pub test to have two teams?
Because I'm like 100% getting on with the beers.
I always go with two teams.
You do, but you also had two taboos.
Ollie, we'll let you go, mate.
Great to see you here at Perth Stadium as we look forward to this second game between the Roosters and Cronulla Sutherland.
And hopefully we'll see and hear you a lot next year.
Love to help you here on ABC Sport on Grandstand.
It is going to be fantastic and the Bears are going to be very, very successful.
Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Michael Maguire says the Broncos are "always looking to the future"
episodes.description: Andrew Moore, Matt Elliott and Ruan Sims chat to Brisbane Broncos coach Michael Maguire as Brisbane prepare to blood some new players after injuries to some of their playmakers.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. NRL Thursday on ABC Sport. Rugby League is on your radio. ABC Sport Digital Radio and ABC Listen. The Brisbane Broncos, as we mentioned, battling some injury concerns. Albeit their form has certainly returned after a sluggish start to the season. They've won a few in a row, but so have their opponents tomorrow night. The North Queensland Cowboys and the Broncos coach Michael Maguire. He joins us online. G'day, Michael. How are you? Good, Andrew. Thanks for having me on. I remember talking to Justin Holbrook a few weeks ago after Dylan Brown and Kalen Ponga were injured. And I asked him, how do you cope without them looking ahead? He said, well, we don't have a choice. We have to. We've got to get on with it. And I guess you're in the same boat. Yeah, we are. It is. We've had a bit of practice of this over my journey in the last 12 months where we've lost halfbacks and five eights with Adam Reynolds and Benny Hunt. But we've managed to find the right people to come in and do the job for us. So I think it's just another one of those cases where we get to blood a few of our younger guys coming through. And I'm really looking forward to it, to be honest. You know, they work really hard together. And we've had them in plenty of times with the first grade boys. So it's about now going out and playing. Yeah, that was the question I had. How much time have they spent training with first grade? And young Tom Duffy must be that pumped against his old team. Yeah, as I said, I'm really looking forward. Tommy's come in and he's had an absolute ripper of a preseason. He's had plenty of reps with all our sort of senior boys. So I'm looking forward to seeing how he can just roll in and just do his job. I think that's the one thing that he has come to the club doing. He just plays his part. And, you know, he doesn't need to go outside of what he's capable of. And if he does that for us, well, we'll all be happy for him. Mate, I thought Jesse Arthurs did a really good job at fullback. What do you see him bringing to the team over the next couple of weeks? Yeah, Matty, he did do a great job for us. He's really composed, yes. I think, you know, nothing really bothers you. So wherever you put him, he just plays and plays his role. So, look, you know, he's got a different style than obviously what Ressie has. But also, too, he's got a fair bit of speed. So we've just altered a little bit around what it might look like. But Jesse can slot in anywhere. So he'll come in and just perform the way Jesse does. Mate, I know that you're more than a team coach. You're a club coach. And, you know, when we look at you've got players out injured. But you've got a bit of turnover coming up in the future just related to birth certificates. What's the pathways like going into your team? Yeah, we've got some good kids coming through, Matty. But also, too, you're always looking at how you can bolster your squad. And, you know, internally, like, you know, we've got Billy Walters still there. And, you know, Benny Hunt will come back. Obviously, that's the ageing group that I suppose you're talking about. So we've got options. And it's a matter of just working our way through it. And, you know, each time we go through a game, we're looking at different capabilities. Like Tommy's coming in. We've got Pezzik coming next year. So we're always looking to the future, I guess, through recruitment. But also, too, internally, we've got some good young ones coming through. And what about the opposition, mate? They've got a little bit of confidence coming into this game. What do you see of their key threats? And, you know, what have you got the team really focusing on? Yeah, Matty, their spine's up and about at the moment. But they're just jumping off the back of their forwards. You know, big Jason Tomololo and Cowan Esa, they're sort of rolling forward. And then their spine come to life. So, you know, we're going to have to be really strong defensively. You know, I think they've shown that over the last couple of weeks where they can shift and move together very quickly. So, you know, adjusting your line, you need to be aware of that. But also, too, you know, when it gets a bit quicker, you've got to be able to control them through the middle. So it's going to be a real good test for us defensively. But, you know, the boys have really worked hard over the last month to be able to improve that area. So, you know, they're getting a few results off the back of the work they're putting in. So we're going to have to be at our best tomorrow. Well, Mad, you actually already touched on what I was going to ask you about. Unsurprisingly, the forward pack really interests me. It's unsurprising. But what I really love with your forward pack is the amount, just the work rate they have is absolutely phenomenal. And their ability to be able to switch transition really, really quickly. It's so important as this game speeds up, isn't it? It is, Rowan. I mean, they've worked really hard at that. And, you know, we work hard at that at training. And they're getting the benefits of how hard they want to work for each other. And it's something there that I'm, you know, really proud of them of how hard they want to work in and around their training to be able to make sure they put that in the game because it has sped up. You know, it's – and, you know, you've got to be able to handle those speeds and through Paddy Carrigan and Payne. And then we've got our bench coming on in Xavier and Tolts. You know, they're doing a great job for us up the front there. So it then allows our back rowers to play their part. But, you know, we've got Brendy back now, you know, on our left edge. So we sort of missed him a bit earlier. He was – he did a great job for us at the back end of last year. And he's come in firing. So they were all just working well together. And I think that's, you know, why – you know, the way the game's going with the momentum. You have to. You've got no choice. And to be able to achieve at our level and what we're trying to achieve is a group together. Yeah, and not every day do our listeners get to hear from a head coach. I'd love for you to explain to them briefly on what – you've seen this evolution of this six-player bench and what that's brought in as a coach when it comes to your selections and, you know, how you can utilise tactics throughout the game. Yeah, it is really interesting, Ron. I'm still sort of trying to discover it. I mean, you know, tomorrow, you know, it'll come out in time that we're going to have Hayes, Berriman, and Josh Rogers on our bench. So you can have specific players now as you're 18, 19 to be able to cover certain positions when you want to have the cover around the team. So it does add a little bit of a different dynamic of how you're looking at your bench. And so, look, if all of a sudden you do have an injury to your outside backs, you can move someone into a specific role that can play a specific position. So it does sort of give a bit more of a luxury to a coach, not thinking that you've got to have a back rower that can cover the centres and then who can cover your fullback position because you can have one of those on your bench as well. So that's the sort of evolution of how this man bench is coming around in my eyes. Can I ask you, Madge, if you don't mind about Penrith? You played them in round one. You knocked them over in the prelim last year. And they whitewashed you in game one of the season up in Brisbane. And they're playing footy that I don't think we've seen for a long, long time, if at all, for five weeks straight. And they're going in as obviously a hot favourite tonight against Canterbury. Have you seen something in Penrith from your casual observations, Michael, that you haven't noticed of them even when they went on that run of four straight premierships this year? Not so much, Andrew. The thing I'm seeing is that they've got a lot of players that have played together. I think when you've played a lot of footy together, the cohesion of your team, and everyone talks about time spent together, you understand the habits of each other. I think at the moment they've just really nailed it. They're being able to play a brand of footy. They've got a couple of young guys that came in last year. They've now spent another 12 months with those more senior players. Nathan's on fire at the moment with the way he's playing. And, you know, that's the leadership part that goes on in any team. I think that's just really gelled for them. And, look, you know, there's plenty of twists and turns throughout the season. So they're up and about at the moment, and each team will have their moment in time where it might turn a little bit. But at this present moment, they're playing some good footy, aren't they? Right, mate. It's time for me to cut to the chase. He's standing up for this one. We're getting around to it now. So, mate, you'd be really proud of your team, I reckon, because there was some early season controversy, and that really galvanised them and got them to play well. And I'm just wondering whether you need a little bit more controversy. And I can talk about you not buying a coffee for three years. All right. Just sponging off me the whole time. Would you think that'll get the team? So if they win, can I just take credit for that? Oh, mate, I don't mind who takes the credit for winning that extra, to be honest. Look, it was a challenging period for us, but our group's been through a fair bit of that, Matty, over time. And I appreciate the support that I get out wide. But the one thing I do know about the group and what's going on internally, there's a lot of great things. And when you see that, the external stuff, you sort of just wonder where on earth that does come from. But internally, that's the stuff that really matters. And, you know, I see that as why the team has turned a little bit of a corner, if you call it. But, you know, we've got a long way to go and we've got to keep improving and all the rest of it. But to see some of our younger guys coming in this week, I'm actually really excited for tomorrow. You know, another great challenge for us. But also, too, it gives, you know, Jesse Arthur's playing his 100th game. You know, just different little things like that happen within a team. And we applaud that. And that's the special part of what goes on. And the external stuff will just play its path. It's just great to see. Look, I don't, don't, we're not going to get into the whole Ben Teo thing and what happened there. But all I want to know in relation to that is, did you learn how to deal with friction between a head coach and an assistant coach when you were working with Matthew Elliott? Well, Matty taught me a lot. That's it. A lot of good stuff, Matty. But, you know, I did learn a lot as a younger coach back then. And, you know, and I applaud all the people that I've worked with. And Matty's one of them that's helped me get to where I am right now. He taught me a lot about the game, how to watch the game. You know, I was a naive young coach back then. And I never forget him saying, Matty, you've got to watch more football. And I can now go, I get why he says that. Because you understand, you know, the more you watch, the better you're going to see things. And that's just the art of becoming a coach. Yeah, that took a turn I wasn't really hoping for. But anyway, Michael McGuire always... He knows how to buy coffee now, too. Yeah, yeah. For all your assistants. I'm sure. Matty, so good to have you on, mate, as usual. Good luck tomorrow night against the Cowboys, and we'll chat soon. Nah, good on you guys. Thanks for having us on. Good luck, Matty. Thanks, Matty. Good luck. See you, man. See you. Let's get to Michael Kariannis with MC's Hammer Time. You can't touch this. Time to find out all the latest rugby league news. And speculation. Here's Michael Kariannis with MC's Hammer Time. Michael, of course, rugby league's number one journalist with the Daily and Sunday Telegraph and works with us as well. Hello, MC. Good evening, team. How are we? Very well, mate. Have you finished packing for the Perth trip? I've squeezed all my stuff in. Very much looking forward to seeing you bright and early tomorrow. Not too early, but we've got a few days to spend together. Nah, it was some very, very quality time. So it is going to be interesting, MC, to head over to Perth, bearing in mind the Bears are not far away. Mal Meninga will join us in the box, the inaugural Perth Bears coach on Saturday in the pregame show between 2 and 3 Australian Eastern time. So it will be interesting to get a vibe actually being there and at the massive Perth Stadium to see what the interest level is like compared to previous years. Yeah, no doubt. And see what sort of, you know, are fans walking around in Bears gear or are they walking around in South Sydney gear or Roosters gear, that sort of stuff as well. It's going to be interesting to see what sort of get up the fans are wearing. But you're right, this is, there's another game later in the year, but this is the biggest event in terms of NRL games in Perth this year. So, yeah, it's going to be interesting to see what sort of vibe there is there. Tell you what, injuries have been a massive story since last weekend and all through the week, haven't they? Oh, no doubt. A few long-term ones, you know, Parramatta, you have Bailey Simonson gone for the season. That's a big one, no doubt about that. A couple of returning players as well. Cole Flanagan returns for the Dragons. There'll be much intrigue around that inclusion from the concussion playing him at half-back as well. So, yeah, lots around in terms of, you know, guys in and out of line-ups. I'll bring Matthew into this, and Drew, if you want to, about Daniel Atkinson, because he's obviously a terrific rugby league player, but he has not seemed well adjusted to be playing in the half-back role and sort of that dominant position. Should it make that much difference whether you wear number seven or number six, or does it depend on individual game plans? It also depends on the teams and the structures and the systems of play that they have, Andrew. So, a lot of... I'm just having your... Watermelon. Wow. So, a lot of teams will split their halves left and right side. Daniel Atkinson hasn't done a bad job as a half, but what you haven't seen from him is his dynamic running game that he gets to do and play ad-lib footy when he gets at six, in the old style of six. So, when we watch the Bulldogs tonight, they'll have a left and right half. So, that's... Again, that structure changes from team to team, whereas Penrith don't do that. Cleary drifts from one side to the other, and the 5'8", and the fullback play left and right. So, it's a little bit of a different dynamic from one team to another. So, yeah, it's an interesting one. Daniel Atkinson is a great ball carrier, can really light a game up. Have we seen that from him in five rounds of footy yet? No. No. We have learnt that he can kick a ball okay, but kicking a ball okay doesn't win you a game of footy. And I think it was you on Monday, MC, that let us know and wrote that the Dragons were putting on hold contract negotiation talks with Damien Cook, and in fact, all contract talks were being on hold. What's the week been like at Dragons headquarters? Yeah, it's been busy. It's obviously been in the headlines following that loss. I guess from the moment the fans boot him off the ground, there was lots of phone calls laid on Saturday night into Sunday morning just regarding the future of Shane Flanagan, and not just Shane Flanagan alone, but the makeup of the footballing staff. And then later on Sunday, Monday was the news around the fact that they'd put on hold all extension talks for all those players, headlined by Damien Cook, who they were in advanced discussions for a one-year deal. So look, there's no doubt there's pressure on everyone in the organisation, not just Shane Flanagan alone. It's all his coaching staff. It's his support staff there. And some of these players, you know, a lot of them are going to be on show tomorrow. We're talking about Tyrell Sloan, Blake Laurie, Christian Tupolosu, obviously Damien Cook, Harme Felle. The NRL said no very, very quickly because they're not going to change salary cap rules mid-season, but it's definitely something that clubs will explore in the post-season to see if there is an appetite for that or if you pick up a... In the Super League, if you pick up a player, an injury, a season-long injury for a player within the first three rounds, you're able to replace them. So that might be something that comes to light. Manley, well, Manley would want him long-term, I suggest, Andrew, no doubt. You're on fire, MC. You're making sense again. I love it. Twice. Thanks, Matty. That's a rare praise from you. Thank you. He was due. All right, MC, I'll let you go back to packing. Not while he was off the air. Oh, he'll be listening. Yeah. Well done, MC. That was awesome. Because at home, he's got his wife, Clara. He's got two daughters but the one he always refers to is Max the dog. It's a little bit of a worry. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

segments.text: Rugby League is on your radio.
ABC Sport Digital Radio and ABC Listen.
The Brisbane Broncos, as we mentioned, battling some injury concerns.
Albeit their form has certainly returned after a sluggish start to the season.
They've won a few in a row, but so have their opponents tomorrow night.
The North Queensland Cowboys and the Broncos coach Michael Maguire.
I remember talking to Justin Holbrook a few weeks ago after Dylan Brown and Kalen Ponga were injured.
And I asked him, how do you cope without them looking ahead?
He said, well, we don't have a choice.
We've got to get on with it.
And I guess you're in the same boat.
We've had a bit of practice of this over my journey in the last 12 months where we've lost halfbacks and five eights with Adam Reynolds and Benny Hunt.
But we've managed to find the right people to come in and do the job for us.
So I think it's just another one of those cases where we get to blood a few of our younger guys coming through.
And I'm really looking forward to it, to be honest.
You know, they work really hard together.
And we've had them in plenty of times with the first grade boys.
So it's about now going out and playing.
Yeah, that was the question I had.
How much time have they spent training with first grade?
And young Tom Duffy must be that pumped against his old team.
Yeah, as I said, I'm really looking forward.
Tommy's come in and he's had an absolute ripper of a preseason.
He's had plenty of reps with all our sort of senior boys.
So I'm looking forward to seeing how he can just roll in and just do his job.
I think that's the one thing that he has come to the club doing.
And, you know, he doesn't need to go outside of what he's capable of.
And if he does that for us, well, we'll all be happy for him.
Mate, I thought Jesse Arthurs did a really good job at fullback.
What do you see him bringing to the team over the next couple of weeks?
Yeah, Matty, he did do a great job for us.
I think, you know, nothing really bothers you.
So wherever you put him, he just plays and plays his role.
So, look, you know, he's got a different style than obviously what Ressie has.
But also, too, he's got a fair bit of speed.
So we've just altered a little bit around what it might look like.
But Jesse can slot in anywhere.
So he'll come in and just perform the way Jesse does.
Mate, I know that you're more than a team coach.
And, you know, when we look at you've got players out injured.
But you've got a bit of turnover coming up in the future just related to birth certificates.
What's the pathways like going into your team?
Yeah, we've got some good kids coming through, Matty.
But also, too, you're always looking at how you can bolster your squad.
And, you know, internally, like, you know, we've got Billy Walters still there.
And, you know, Benny Hunt will come back.
Obviously, that's the ageing group that I suppose you're talking about.
And it's a matter of just working our way through it.
And, you know, each time we go through a game, we're looking at different capabilities.
We've got Pezzik coming next year.
So we're always looking to the future, I guess, through recruitment.
But also, too, internally, we've got some good young ones coming through.
And what about the opposition, mate?
They've got a little bit of confidence coming into this game.
What do you see of their key threats?
And, you know, what have you got the team really focusing on?
Yeah, Matty, their spine's up and about at the moment.
But they're just jumping off the back of their forwards.
You know, big Jason Tomololo and Cowan Esa, they're sort of rolling forward.
And then their spine come to life.
So, you know, we're going to have to be really strong defensively.
You know, I think they've shown that over the last couple of weeks where they can shift and move together very quickly.
So, you know, adjusting your line, you need to be aware of that.
But also, too, you know, when it gets a bit quicker, you've got to be able to control them through the middle.
So it's going to be a real good test for us defensively.
But, you know, the boys have really worked hard over the last month to be able to improve that area.
So, you know, they're getting a few results off the back of the work they're putting in.
So we're going to have to be at our best tomorrow.
Well, Mad, you actually already touched on what I was going to ask you about.
Unsurprisingly, the forward pack really interests me.
But what I really love with your forward pack is the amount, just the work rate they have is absolutely phenomenal.
And their ability to be able to switch transition really, really quickly.
It's so important as this game speeds up, isn't it?
I mean, they've worked really hard at that.
And, you know, we work hard at that at training.
And they're getting the benefits of how hard they want to work for each other.
And it's something there that I'm, you know, really proud of them of how hard they want to work in and around their training
to be able to make sure they put that in the game because it has sped up.
You know, it's – and, you know, you've got to be able to handle those speeds and through Paddy Carrigan and Payne.
And then we've got our bench coming on in Xavier and Tolts.
You know, they're doing a great job for us up the front there.
So it then allows our back rowers to play their part.
But, you know, we've got Brendy back now, you know, on our left edge.
So we sort of missed him a bit earlier.
He was – he did a great job for us at the back end of last year.
So they were all just working well together.
And I think that's, you know, why – you know, the way the game's going with the momentum.
And to be able to achieve at our level and what we're trying to achieve is a group together.
Yeah, and not every day do our listeners get to hear from a head coach.
I'd love for you to explain to them briefly on what – you've seen this evolution of this six-player bench
and what that's brought in as a coach when it comes to your selections
and, you know, how you can utilise tactics throughout the game.
Yeah, it is really interesting, Ron.
I'm still sort of trying to discover it.
I mean, you know, tomorrow, you know, it'll come out in time that we're going to have Hayes, Berriman,
and Josh Rogers on our bench.
So you can have specific players now as you're 18, 19 to be able to cover certain positions
when you want to have the cover around the team.
So it does add a little bit of a different dynamic of how you're looking at your bench.
And so, look, if all of a sudden you do have an injury to your outside backs,
you can move someone into a specific role that can play a specific position.
So it does sort of give a bit more of a luxury to a coach,
not thinking that you've got to have a back rower that can cover the centres
and then who can cover your fullback position because you can have one of those on your bench as well.
So that's the sort of evolution of how this man bench is coming around in my eyes.
Can I ask you, Madge, if you don't mind about Penrith?
You played them in round one.
You knocked them over in the prelim last year.
And they whitewashed you in game one of the season up in Brisbane.
And they're playing footy that I don't think we've seen for a long, long time, if at all, for five weeks straight.
And they're going in as obviously a hot favourite tonight against Canterbury.
Have you seen something in Penrith from your casual observations, Michael,
that you haven't noticed of them even when they went on that run of four straight premierships this year?
The thing I'm seeing is that they've got a lot of players that have played together.
I think when you've played a lot of footy together, the cohesion of your team,
and everyone talks about time spent together, you understand the habits of each other.
I think at the moment they've just really nailed it.
They're being able to play a brand of footy.
They've got a couple of young guys that came in last year.
They've now spent another 12 months with those more senior players.
Nathan's on fire at the moment with the way he's playing.
And, you know, that's the leadership part that goes on in any team.
I think that's just really gelled for them.
And, look, you know, there's plenty of twists and turns throughout the season.
So they're up and about at the moment,
and each team will have their moment in time where it might turn a little bit.
But at this present moment, they're playing some good footy, aren't they?
It's time for me to cut to the chase.
He's standing up for this one.
We're getting around to it now.
So, mate, you'd be really proud of your team, I reckon,
because there was some early season controversy,
and that really galvanised them and got them to play well.
And I'm just wondering whether you need a little bit more controversy.
And I can talk about you not buying a coffee for three years.
Just sponging off me the whole time.
Would you think that'll get the team?
So if they win, can I just take credit for that?
Oh, mate, I don't mind who takes the credit for winning that extra,
Look, it was a challenging period for us,
but our group's been through a fair bit of that, Matty, over time.
And I appreciate the support that I get out wide.
But the one thing I do know about the group and what's going on internally,
there's a lot of great things.
And when you see that, the external stuff,
you sort of just wonder where on earth that does come from.
But internally, that's the stuff that really matters.
And, you know, I see that as why the team has turned a little bit of a corner,
But, you know, we've got a long way to go and we've got to keep improving
and all the rest of it.
But to see some of our younger guys coming in this week,
I'm actually really excited for tomorrow.
You know, another great challenge for us.
But also, too, it gives, you know, Jesse Arthur's playing his 100th game.
You know, just different little things like that happen within a team.
And that's the special part of what goes on.
And the external stuff will just play its path.
Look, I don't, don't, we're not going to get into the whole Ben Teo thing
But all I want to know in relation to that is,
did you learn how to deal with friction between a head coach
and an assistant coach when you were working with Matthew Elliott?
Well, Matty taught me a lot.
A lot of good stuff, Matty.
But, you know, I did learn a lot as a younger coach back then.
And, you know, and I applaud all the people that I've worked with.
And Matty's one of them that's helped me get to where I am right now.
He taught me a lot about the game, how to watch the game.
You know, I was a naive young coach back then.
And I never forget him saying,
Matty, you've got to watch more football.
And I can now go, I get why he says that.
Because you understand, you know, the more you watch,
the better you're going to see things.
And that's just the art of becoming a coach.
Yeah, that took a turn I wasn't really hoping for.
He knows how to buy coffee now, too.
Matty, so good to have you on, mate, as usual.
