episodes.title: The Cowboys defence is their best offence
episodes.description: North Queensland's Jaxon Purdue continues to impress on and off the field. He scored a double as the Cowboys smashed the Dragons BUT reckoned their win was all based on hard work in defence.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Well, Louie and I were at Jubilee yesterday where North Queensland absolutely crushed St. George Illawarra with 16 points in each half to win 32 points to nil. And Louie gave three points in the ABC Player of the Year to Tom Dearden. Two points to thrilling centre Jackson Perdue and one point to 5'8", Jake Clifford. Again, the Cowboys dominated and now they've won three in a row. Let's find out how they're feeling about things. Jackson Perdue is on the line. Jackson, how are you doing? Hey, good. Thanks, guys. Thanks for having me. Mate, it's always a pleasure. You were good enough to come on on your 20th birthday last July, I think it was, as you're in the middle of a festive look around town. So we appreciate you very much. And the way things have changed from a probably less than ideal start to the season, the way it's built up over the last three weeks must give you guys an enormous amount of confidence and hope. Yeah, it was a rough start to the season, you know, going down our first two games. And, you know, especially at Leichhardt when we got dusted by the Tigers, you know, that one hurt us. And we sort of had to have a look in the mirror and have a look at ourselves and seeing what we wanted to be as a footy team. And we sort of really come together and connected really well. And then, as you can see, the past three games, yeah, we've been really connected and we've fought our way to good wins. I asked Toby Rudolph this on NRL Monday after the Sharks had lost a couple and then they rebounded with a great win last Sunday over Canberra. Is there a moment where you guys as a team unit, this may not even involve the coaching staff, where you do have a bit of an honesty session when, again, you've lost the first couple of games of the season that you need to really rectify this straight away? Is there that moment where you guys have a team meeting or a few of you get together and talk about how you can fix things? Yeah, definitely. There definitely is. But also, you know, it was only the first two rounds of the season. So we also knew that we had plenty to work on and plenty to build on. But I guess there's units like, as I say, like our left edge, you know, Murray Tualagi calls a meeting and really taking the leadership role with our left edge and sort of come up with some clips and what we want to be known as a left edge defensively mainly. So I guess all the units, you know, the middles, the spine, left edge, right edge sort of come together and talk about what we can do better and what we can improve on each week. Well, Scott Drinkwater set up the first points of the game with a magnificent 40-20 and then an individual try beating a couple close to the line. But then you, Jackson Perdue, scored these tries just before half time. Sends the ball away left through hands and it's Clifford. Getting the pass back to Perdue over halfway. He's over the 40, the 30 beats two. Valhans won't catch him. He's special this young boy. Jackson Perdue scores. A long range try. It was too good for the Dragons. Jackson Perdue, a brilliant individual try. He'll play it right in that far corner to Chester. Comes left to Deirdre. Then away through hands. Drinkwater to Clifford. Left foot kick for Jackson Perdue. Oh, that's in his purview to score brilliant tries. What about the lovely sweet kiss off the left boot? It was a great... I am a gibber, fair to you. That was a great kick from Jake Clifford off his left boot. But that first try, especially, Jackson, a long range job, as we heard, it came after you guys had to defend your own line for set after set after set. And that... Talk about setting or turning defence into attack. You guys pulled it off beautifully. Yeah, I think that try just really showed the hard work that we did, you know. It was, like you said, we defended our own line. And that's what we've sort of been practising in the pre-season. And at training each week. I got told on the Saturday that I would be playing.
There was an injury to, if I'm not mistaken, Chris Patterson,
who was one of our front rowers.
And he went down to training.
And obviously I'm not a front rower, and I never was.
But I got a chance to jump on the bench.
And I wasn't promised anything from Sheenzy,
but I expected to play some minutes.
So I got a bunch of tickets for all my family and friends.
But in the end, I only got the last three minutes of the game.
So it was awesome to get the opportunity and then to get the debut.
But also a bit of an anticlimax because it didn't really contribute much.
It was at Leichhardt, though, wasn't it?
Debut the same day as Robbie Farrah.
And he got on early in the first half.
And I actually remember for him, he jumped, I think, in the first set,
he jumped out of dummy half and put a kick in,
which was, you know, something that a young hooker coming up in the first grade,
his first set, he decided he's going to put a kick in out of dummy half.
I thought it was quite, you know, quite a show of confidence for him.
And as time went by and the score got away from us,
I was, as I said, a little bit disappointed that I wasn't on the field.
so I was keen to get out there as much as possible.
Just 38.30, though, that day to Manly Oringa.
Was it Tim Sheens who told you?
And how did that go down?
Yeah, well, he actually called me up on the Saturday morning
to make my way to training because there was an injury cloud over.
Chris Boutis and another couple of players were carrying them as well.
And then, yeah, I got in the car and went to training
And, you know, he said at the end of that session
when Chris didn't get through that I was going to be playing.
So I was obviously quite excited.
I was excited and then, you know, ready for the opportunity.
But then it was a matter of trying to organise tickets
and get people, you know, close to me
to come and try and celebrate with me.
And who were the first three people you told?
Obviously, I got my mum and dad on the phone and let them know.
And then my siblings, my sister and my brother.
And then I just started texting all my mates.
I had a couple of mates that were lower-grade football players
and sort of were tracking similar paths, I guess,
through the Jersey Fleek and reserve grade system.
So I let them know and some schoolmates
and quickly got as many tickets as I could for them.
Now, your second debut actually came in test match footy
So it came about pretty quickly.
It was in Paris, wasn't it?
It was in Carcassonne, actually, in the south of France.
We were over there for end-of-season tri-nations in 2004.
As you said, it was us, the Kangaroos, and England.
But we had a tour match against France down in Carcassonne.
So we went down there for a couple of days.
And, yeah, I was told before we went down there
that I was going to get a game and a prep that way.
I was actually quite nervous for my first hucker.
That was the thing that was worrying me the most.
Also, you get to where the black jersey was
was something pretty special that I was looking forward to as well.
And starting hooker, if memory serves.
Again, a position that I wasn't, like, at that time really used to.
But we didn't have a lot of depth in the squad at the time.
And, you know, I was just talking to Daniel Anderson,
and he was the coach at the time.
And he brought me on the tour for experience,
but also as a bit of a utility cover.
And because I had that ability to play nine,
Louis Anderson was probably the other option for nine,
but he was more of a back rower.
He'd played nine for most of that tour.
And I sort of subbed on for him.
And in that match, they gave him...
I think they gave him a rest.
So they played him elsewhere in the side.
But they wanted to get me some game time
and then give me an opportunity.
As I say, you played 15 tests for the Kiwis.
What was your number one highlight?
But that whole campaign through 2008 was pretty special
to go through and win the World Cup.
We had a really good group that bought into what the coach was trying to do.
Wayne Bennett was his coaching coach, Steve Kearney.
So, you know, you get a really good chance to learn
from a couple of the brightest minds in rugby league.
And that final up in Brisbane was pretty special.
It was a fairly dominant win for our team.
And as I said, I wasn't on the field for that last game.
But to be a part of it was quite special.
The debut in France was a little bit quiet
because we didn't have any people there from New Zealand
or I didn't have any family there.
But, again, like that first hucker and running out for the Kiwis was special.
I do remember in that first tour in England, a tri-series,
I got called into the team for a test against England after that France game.
So it would have been my second test for the Kiwis.
And at the time, the Tigers decided to try and help get my parents over.
So my parents flew to England on the Thursday and I played on the Saturday.
I think we were playing up in Hull, from memory.
And, yeah, they got my parents into England the day before the game.
They caught a train to the game.
And then they were there standing on the sideline.
And the anthem was to me.
But I actually found out one of my cousins spilled the beans.
So that was quite a special moment to look across and see them there
Yeah, that's when you found out.
Your third taboo came at Canterbury Bankstown in 2010.

very different to when you joined the West Tigers.

And, yeah, I snapped like a spur off my ankle.
I had to have surgery on it.
So it kind of delayed my start.
For the Bulldogs, I missed the first couple of weeks.
And in round three, we played the Roosters.
I got named on the bench.
And I was back and ready to go.
But it lasted about as long as my debut for the Tigers.
I was on the field for only a few minutes.
And I went into a tackle and I ended up busting my MCL in my knee.
It's difficult going to a new club and trying to establish yourself
and get that clean run of a start that you want to try and make an impression on people.
So it was, you know, it was cool.
I was really looking forward to, again, getting on the field with the likes of Luke Patton,
Andrew Ryan, you know, Brett Kamal, who's felt the club sellers.
So keen to get out there on the field with those type of guys.
But, yeah, it was very brief.
And I was, unfortunately, laid up for another six or seven weeks.
Well, your debut also proved really costly for Canterbury as you were supposed to come off the bench.
It was a bit of a comfortable one for the boys.
So, again, like it was, yeah, not like I made a huge difference.
But, yeah, it was, like I said, a studded start.
Hey, I remember the cry, stop Halitau, stop the Bulldogs.
Now, your fourth debut, and the last one we'll focus on here, was right here on ABC Radio in 2017.
What do you remember about your first game as a caller?
Yeah, well, it was, I was quite nervous.
I was up in Newcastle for the All-Stars in 2017.
And it was after a conversation with yourself, Andrew, about wanting to get into the media and do some commentary work.
And you thought it would be a good idea to do a trial run, in a sense, and have my first one as the All-Stars.
And I'm pretty sure Bob Gat was calling with us, and he gave me some words of wisdom.
And then, yeah, it was, I was nervous.
And it's hard to sort of sit down on the sideline and get a rhythm and a feel for what's going on.
But it's probably the highlight, and the thing that sticks out the most was that I got to interview Laurie Daly after the game.
I remember how nervous you were.
Yes, yeah, he was my total hero.
So I was quite nervous trying to interview him.
And when he addressed me by name, straight off the bat, it relaxed me quite a bit.
And I think it settled me down, and I quite enjoyed that.
So that's a memory I have clear as day.
I don't know what I asked him.
It was some pretty ordinary questions, I reckon.
But nonetheless, it was a really rewarding thing for me to stand there and interview one of my heroes.
It's funny, I remember clearly you ringing me back to say, yeah, I'm in.
I was at the MCG in the middle of calling in one day.
And you called in between gigs to say we were sweet, and I was very excited.
As I am that you're still with us.
Dean Hallitow again on our Rugby League coverage.
In the meantime, thanks for sharing all the secrets and details of your debuts, mate.

Melbourne Hampton on the half volley.

Who's wearing the scars of battle as well.

You made 2016 the most memorable year of my life.
For the rest of the Kronk supporters.
Bring back some good memories, Louie.

It was, yeah, that was amazing.
Just saw the little bits and pieces.

And Ben Barber told me last week it was a secret.

But then you hear that last 10 seconds.
And I can understand now what every Cornell supporter, when I speak to them, that last
10 seconds, they were just, they were stuck in the mud.

episodes.title: Craig Fitzgibbon has empathy for opposition coaches
episodes.description: Brett Spriggy and Billy Moore chat to Cronulla Sharks head coach Craig Fitzgibbon. Michael Carayannis joined Brett and Billy for his "Hammertime" segment discussing who will be the full time coach at Manly next season.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. ABC Sports coverage of the 2026 NRL Premiership. On your radio, ABC Sport Digital Radio and ABC Listen. This is NRL Thursday on ABC Sport at the start of a new round of footy. Round five, which gets underway here tonight at Dolphin Oval in Redcliffe, where the Dolphins will host the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles. My name is Brett Sprigg. I'm joined by a couple of internationals and origin representatives in Billy Moore and Corrina Brown. And a warm welcome, if you have just joined us through their favourite state, Queensland, on ABC Local Radio. Kickoff here is just under a half an hour away. But on Sunday, we're back with the two o'clock games. Hallelujah. And it will be two o'clock for all of us on at least the eastern side of the country when Cronulla Sutherland hosts the Warriors at Shark Park. The Sharks have split their ledger so far. Two wins and two losses. The Warriors have won all bar one of their games. And it should be a great contest on Sunday in the Shire. The coach of the home team, Craig Fitzgibbon, joins me now. Craig, appreciate your time. No worries. Thanks for having me, guys. You've had a month so far to assess where things sit for you. What's been your overarching snapshot of the first four games and where you think you've left some improvement? Yeah, I think periods of the way we want to set up and the way we want to play. And some, you know, we've been in some pretty hard contests there along the way. But yeah, definitely consistency is a little bit lacking at the moment. And, you know, you do your intentions to set up and play roughly similar every week. And then not much difference between your best and worst. So, yeah, intentions to improve that. But, yeah, I think a month of footy seems like a lot. But in the grand scheme of things, sometimes it takes a little bit longer. And we're hoping we can get on a bit more consistent form from now on. Yeah, we're about to call the Dolphins here tonight. And we talk about their quest for consistency. And that's a word that people certainly attach to you guys at times in terms of the gap between your very best and your very worst. How far do you think you've gone to improving that? At this early stage, it's really hard to know based on our inconsistent performances. So what we have done, we've shown some capabilities and fantastic game last week and obviously round one. But in between, there's been those periods. So, you know, our intention is always to get better and, you know, this early in the season, I think you'll find in the competition proper, there's always some results that pop out when you least expect it and some ups and downs. And generally, the comp will settle itself out after, you know, probably usually six or eight weeks. But it's an entertaining competition for that very reason because so many teams have improved and where your levels at can change pretty quickly. And Fanua Blake up against his old side, which I know it's not the first time. He's had a whole year with you now. But certainly, he's a player in focus when you look at the Battle of the Ford Packs and some of the guys the Warriors still have. Yeah, absolutely. You know, what a player. And obviously, with that and leaving, the Warriors inherited James Fisher-Harris. So, you know, two fantastic spearheads of a pack. And, you know, the Warriors are a super consistent team. And they've been, you know, even last week, I know they've beaten the scoreboard. Might suggest that it was a little bit of a bigger margin than the actual contest was. So, Adan and the Sharks are under no illusion as to how hard they'll be. But, you know, Adan loves those challenges. And I'm sure, based on his preparation, that he's ready to get into it. We're still a few days away from game time. But can we expect Britton Nickero to make his return from that broken nose? Yeah, I would suggest he's a good chance. He's just got a few more boxes to tick there. His preparation's been really good. He's got through everything we've asked of him so far. And he'd be a handy addition if we can, you know, he can pass the last couple of tests in the next few days. So, he's looking strong without committing just this far out, though. When it's all firing and Trindle and Hines are operating as they did last week and Will Kennedy had one of his very best games, is that about as good as your spine can be? How pleased were you with the impact of those names I mentioned last week? Yeah, look, I think you have periods and moments of where you can see their capability level. And as I sort of mentioned to start the chat there was the consistency. And, you know, some of our best performances we felt last year were actually a lot closer on the scoreboard than what these big performances have been. So, you know, again, marrying up what they can do and what they can look like in a tight contest and steering the team home versus what they can do when they're on the front foot, which is obvious. And what we do love about them, they've learnt that via trial and error. We've been together for a number of years now. So, starting to figure out the most important times of when they can assert themselves on the contest. And, you know, to be honest, I think they're shaping well and they seem to be getting stronger each week. So, give or take a few results, we'd like to see that strengthened as well. NRL Thursday on ABC Sport. Our special guest looking ahead to Sunday is Granola coach Craig Fitzgibbon and Billy Moore is here alongside me. Fitz, when you look at 2026, every year seems to be slightly different. Your take on the speed, the rules, little changes in the nuances, you're talking about consistency. Is that because something like the six again seems to have sped the game up even more? Oh, it can be, Billy. We've been on the wrong end of a few of those momentum shifts and periods and calls. But what I think happens is they bring in, competition brings in new rules. And, you know, just because there's a new rule, it doesn't necessarily mean it has to be enforced. And what I think happened was with the new six again, the referees, and it's not, you know, they're obviously following instructions there to enforce the new rules and make sure it's got a change in the game. However, once they settle in, they start to adjust for the new rules. I think it'll calm down and get back to a more consistent level. But initially, when the whole focus is on a certain area, well, their attention goes to the same area as well. So what I think will happen over time, they'll adjust to that. It'll get back to largely what it looked like last year and hopefully make more entertaining games. Your squad, you talked about it being stable and it has been that. And it's obviously finals bound squad you've got there. What are you asking of the team in 2026 that they learnt from the previous campaigns? Well, we know we've got to get better, Billy. I think it's, you know, you don't know the improvement levels of other teams. And just to assume, because we had a decent few years that that'll happen again, we've got to make sure we get better. And I think the focus and stability there is we know where our level's at. We know what our top level's at. And it's been just short. So we've got to get ourselves back to that certain level and then ultimately earn the right to take another step. But, you know, I'm sure there's 16 other teams left something to say about that. So we've got to make sure we're not, you know, we don't think we deserve anything. We just want to earn everything and make sure we play Abbas footy. Player that's jumped out of the box for you this year inside your squad? Oh, jumped out of the box. It's probably too early to say that. We've got a number of players that... First month in, first month in. Yeah, Sam Stonestrain's done a really good job, to be honest. He played about 10 games last year. Got an opportunity and grabbed that. And I think that this representation of Sam's been stronger than the last one. And, you know, going forward, we're excited to see where he can get us to. And, you know, obviously, you know, it's not an easy position nowadays. It's a lot of tough carries and, you know, last play decision-making that he's got to take on. But I feel like he's probably stepped up in the first month. And to have Tom Hazleton back on a consistent base, of course. He's had injury worries, you know, last year. How good is it to have him back in the squad and really performing? Yeah, really good. Hazel's, you know, we're talking about consistency. He plays the same way every week. And, you know, we know what we're going to get out of Tommy. And we've just got to get the balance of our forward pack right. And where Tommy, whether he starts or whether he's coming off the interchange, he's someone that can make a difference. And it's subtle, but he's got a funny knack of finding the troll on. And he's also, he's a really good team player. He gets off the other forwards and supports them well. And little details, things that may not be noticeable on the eye, but I'm definitely valued by the team. And seems a cult hero for footy fans there in the Shire as well at times, Tom Hazleton. You've won eight out of your past nine at Shark Park. How important is having that, I guess, fortress for teams to come and have to challenge against? I think it's important. You know, everyone loves playing at home. And you want to maximise, you know, your community and your fans and the people that come to watch you play. You want to maximise their entertainment by putting a performance in there. And, you know, we'd had one eight out of nine, but the last one was a little bit disappointing for us. So we've got a bit of work to do to make sure we turn up and put a performance in that they're proud of. So, you know, it won't be easy. It won't be a gift. The Warriors are a top squad and a really good side. And we're excited by that challenge now. And we do want the sort of games you want. You want those hard contests that make you earn everything you get. Just lastly, Craig, I don't expect you to comment on specific examples of fellow coaches, but we've had a reminder in the past week, which was round four, as you said, a very early part of the season, of the sometimes chaotic nature of what you guys do. This time last week, Anthony Seabold was getting ready to coach his side against the Roosters. Fast forward to now, it feels like he got the flick weeks ago and things just move on so quickly. I know that you and other coaches would like to think that their club has more stability, more respect for them and wouldn't be dealt with like that. But does it drive home the pressure of coaching? This is now your fifth year as coach. I know that you have a long-term deal, but do you empathize with what you see other coaches sometimes go through? No, I empathize with all the coaches when they go through periods and we all have them. No one's immune. And definitely empathize with Steve for what happened there. I don't know the inner workings of the club and why they made that decision. But one thing that does happen is, you know, if you've got to be strong enough to deal with what comes your way, and as I said, there's always tough times and good times as well, but you've got to stay the course because, you know, at the moment, one loss, as you can understand the pressure and the magnitude, everyone tries to make that one loss feel catastrophic. And sometimes you've got to plan to get your way out of it. Sometimes you might not, but I can't comment on his situation, but definitely have empathy for him. And all of a sudden, we go through those periods, but it's a competition and we all are all striving to beat each other as coaches. However, you do understand what they're going through. You look at the coaching group, I admire the way you've gone from a great player to a great coach. The learn of that process, do you look at other teams and coaches and watch what they do and how they do it? And somehow, without giving away too much, cut and paste a few things, aka Penrith right now have started this year in startling form. Do you break down what you see there? Or do you go, that's not us, we've got nothing to do with that. We know what we are and who we are. Or do you try and lean a bit on what you watch? Oh, look, a bit of both. But if I had Penrith's formula, I would have put it in a few years ago. It seems to me nailed on. Look, we're all, you know, Penrith are a unique position where, you know, eight to 10 generational players start their career in first grade at the same time and the stability and consistency and cohesion of that. And the players of that quality and calibre to stick together for that long is rare. However, what he's managed to do is stay consistent with losing the play here and there. But no, I don't, to be perfectly honest, you've got to be your own man and your own coach and have authenticity. But the game leaves clues. We always look at other people's games and see what you can pick up there. But if you're trying to coach someone else's style, I think that's, players are pretty clever these days. I'll understand if you're not being true to yourself and the way you coach. But yeah, we'd all love the magic potion if we could find it. Craig, appreciate your time and your insights. All the best for the weekend ahead and the game against the Warriors on Sunday. Yeah, no worries, guys. Thanks for having me. Thank you. The 2026 NRL Premiership. episodes.title: 05 | Boycott! | The streets are burning
episodes.description: The 1980s see South Africa spin out of control as defiance to apartheid and the regime’s crackdown builds.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. It's 1984 and musician Paul Simon is struggling. His marriage has ended, his musical partnership with Art Garfunkel, Simon and Garfunkel, has blown up. And he's floundering in the musical backwaters, trying to revive his career. When someone plays him a bootleg cassette of South African a cappella group, Ladysmith Black Mambazo. People are amazed when they see Black Mambazo because that group is an extraordinary blend of voices. Paul Simon is blown away. Who wouldn't be? And he thinks, hmm, maybe I should make an album with them. But that means recording with the group in South Africa, which means breaking the cultural boycott against the apartheid regime. I knew that there would be criticism if I went. I was told that by people in South Africa and people in America. But I was still encouraged to go. And the artistic opportunity was so exciting that I went for it. I went for the music. Paul Simon secretly flies to Johannesburg to record with Ladysmith Black Mambazo. They spend long days in the studio. The black musicians anxious when sessions run late. This white guy's gonna get them arrested. You see, they're not allowed to be out in the city past curfew. But many of you will be very familiar with the extraordinary result of this recording session. One of the most influential albums of all time. Graceland. Fellow musician Billy Bragg is not happy. The fact of going there and breaking the boycott, I think that always made Graceland a fundamentally flawed project. He didn't really respect the politics of the situation that he was putting himself into. Was that naivety or was that arrogance? It's difficult to say. The African National Congress, the ANC, blasts Paul Simon. Anti-apartheid activists are furious. And a ton of people accuse him of cultural appropriation. If this was now, we'd say, Paul Simon is cancelled. But Graceland is a massive hit. It sells 16 million copies. And his world tour sells out. I have rethought this Graceland thing endlessly. Endlessly. I've been up nights, many nights, thinking, Now, is that, did I, did I screw up here? And I, eventually I end up coming up with this conclusion, which is, musicians and artists have a duty to be musicians and artists. But what if you break a cultural boycott to fulfill that duty? What if, like Paul Simon, your intentions are good? There are no easy answers. But I will say this. Graceland introduces generations of music lovers to the incredible sounds of South Africa. Ladiesmith Black Mambazo's music reaches the world. It touches people. They win a Grammy. And Paul Simon forces a spotlight on apartheid. And I can't hate on him for that. But while people in the West are grooving to Graceland, in South Africa, it feels like the violence under the apartheid regime has no end. People are being assassinated, kidnapped. There's a whole government agency of police who are deliberately targeting black activists. They're disappearing them to a farm called Flakplas, where they are torturing them and then burning bodies and then having a braai or a barbecue on a fire that is made on the site where they have killed black people. This is the kind of violence anti-apartheid activists around the world are trying to get governments and global corporations to condemn with sanctions. It's why rugby players and cricketers refused to play South Africa in the 1970s. And why artists like Billy Bragg are saying enough. But as apartheid enters its final, brutal years and international pressure mounts, the regime doubles down and the violence ratchets up. Cracks are appearing, pushing people to their limit and forcing them to make tough choices. For many, it feels like it all comes down to this. Kill or be killed. How many more lives need to be lost before the West finally cuts economic ties with South Africa? I'm Sisonkem Siman. On ABC Rewind, this is Boycott. The fight to end apartheid. Episode 5. The streets are burning. We all know music has power. And it's in the 1980s when musicians start using it, soundtracking South Africa's bloodiest decade yet. Now, just a heads up that we're going to be talking about a bunch of songs we can't play you. Why? Insanely steep copyright fees. So, you can sing along in your head. The first one is Peter Gabriel's Biko. The poignant tribute to the leader murdered by the regime, Steve Biko. The song still gives me chills. And then, in 1984, Jerry Dammers of the British ska band The Specials writes, Free Nelson Mandela and it becomes the anthem of a movement. episodes.description: It's 1984, and in Dublin, Ireland, 21 year old shop assistant Mary Manning refuses to sell a South African grapefruit. Her action draws world attention to the campaign to hit Apartheid where it hurts, by crippling the South African economy.

I was working in Dunn's Stars and Henry Street, which is an art supermarket in Ireland. Everyone in Ireland knows Dunn's supermarkets. They're as Irish as Bunnings is Australian. So Mary's on the bus, travelling into work, thinking about, well, what most young people are thinking about. My main goal was getting money to go out the following weekend or buy clothes or do something. And travelling to work as normal, not knowing that this was going to be a day that would completely change my life. Oh boy, will it ever. Mary's in a union. And the union's asked its members not to handle any fresh produce that's been imported from South Africa. No unpacking it. No ringing it up at the cash register. And today's the first day of the action. Mary knows what a boycott is. It's when you stop dealing with a company or a country to protest this cruelty or exploitation. But she doesn't know much about what's going on in South Africa. We'd heard the word apart that we couldn't even pronounce it properly. We'd heard a Nelson Mandela and maybe Steve Biko. We didn't know anything about really what was happening in South Africa. Still, she's a loyal unionist. So when organisers call for a boycott, she jumps right in. That first morning, Mary stands at the till. Her manager's watching her super closely. And it's making Mary very, very nervous. When a customer brings a South African grapefruit to her register, Mary makes a decision that will change not only her life, it will change the course of a movement. I could see she had two grapefruit. And I was thinking to myself, don't come to my register. But she came to my register anyway. And I said to her that I couldn't handle them. And had been arrested and detained at one point with Nelson Mandela. He'd managed to leave the country. And eventually made his way to Ireland to live in exile as a political refugee. episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. It's 1976. South Africa. And we are only just emerging from what's called the lost decade. You won't believe that this story actually happened. In the summer of 1978, Australian narcotics agents intercepted a large camper van making its way by ship from India to Melbourne. What they discovered inside that van turned out to be the largest ever haul of an illicit substance, in this case black hashish, to land on Australian soil. The camper van was in the names of US citizens Vera Todd and Fleurice Basir, two women in their 60s who'd come to Australia as part of a months-long overland odyssey, a trip arranged for them, courtesy of Vera Todd's nephew, Vern. After a massive sting operation by narcotics agents, the two women were arrested, convicted and dubbed the Drug Grannies. But were they really guilty or merely unwitting pawns in a global drug importation syndicate masterminded by Vera's nephew? Sandy Logan was a young journalist when the Drug Granny story hit the headlines and he ended up becoming swept up in the case. 40 years on from the events, he's written a book about this extraordinary case. And Sandy's also our guide for this second part of the series, Too Old to Run, which picks up the story in Sydney, February 1978, just as the women have been arrested. And a warning, there is a teeny bit of colourful language coming up. I hated my nephew like I never hated anybody in my life. The news story that I'd torn from a telex machine as a young reporter in 1978, when the Drug Grannies were arrested, was about to dominate my life. I wanted answers to how these two elderly American women had almost overnight become Australia's biggest drug criminals. We understand that 1.9 tonnes, and that's an awful lot of hash, has been found in a camper van, which is at present in the possession of the customs department at their marine centre in Neutral Bay. Undercover narcotics agent Mish Khoury was part of the first formal interview after the women's arrest. On the day that we took Vera Todd Hayes back to the customs house interrogation room. It was here that Toddy learned just how much hash was hidden in their camper van. I showed her a sample of the goods that we found under the floor of the camper van. I said, all in all, the total is 1.9 tonnes, to which, in her own inimitable style, said, and I quote, no wonder that motherfucker wouldn't go up them fucking hills. Now that has stayed with me forever and a day. Malawa Prison, Sydney. With prisoners protesting about conditions. It was a very tough prison indeed. After Toddy's formal interview, she was taken to join her companion Beasy in the remand section of Sydney's Malawa Prison. The women were charged with importing a prohibited substance, almost two tonnes of hashish. Toddy and Beasy had been lifelong upstanding U.S. citizens. Nothing in their 60 years had prepared them for what they were about to encounter behind bars. You wouldn't believe rape amongst women, but there was rape, bashings, hair pulling, shaving of heads, scalding water, anything that you could think of. Toddy and Beasy were convinced by their lawyer the best way forward was to plead guilty, to get the case over and done with, and be deported back home to the U.S. Or so they hoped. We were told that's what would happen if we cooperated. If we cooperated, we would be deported. We cooperated. We told everything we could possibly tell. In April 1978, they went to trial before the chief judge of the New South Wales District Court, James Staunton QC. Florese Marie Beasy, I sentence you to imprisonment for 14 years. Vera Todd Hayes, I sentence you to imprisonment for 14 years, to date from the 2nd of February 1978. Toddy and Beasy had the book thrown at them. 14 years jail with no parole date. The sentence shocked the narcotics agents, the defence counsel, and even the prosecution. The prospect of a jail term horrified the women. Here's Toddy in a radio interview, remembering the shock as reality began to bite. You can't believe what you're hearing. You're scared to death. The trauma has set in. What in the world? A special keepsake among the drug granders' possessions from their jail time included a letter Mish Khoury had written to them, using a pseudonym known only to Toddy and Beasy. Toddy and Beasy's camper van, like the rest of Verne Todd's drug shipments, originated from Germany. In 1981, a West German court specially convened in Sydney to hear evidence from Toddy and Beasy. Their statements were crucial to the overseas court's conviction of Philip Schein. The women's three appeals for early release to the Fraser government's Attorney General Peter Jurak had all been rebuffed. This fellow and his wife and the little boy were sitting back having coffee or tea, whatever, and I hollered in the window. I said, hey, you're a Yank, because I'd read in the paper where a Yank had bought it. And I said, boy, you got a good-looking rig here. And he said, yeah, this rig has got quite a history. And I said, yeah, I know. He looked at me kind of funny. I said, yeah, I rode in it from Stuttgart, Germany to Bombay. He says, you one of the drug grannies? And I said, yeah. And he said, what are you doing, escaping? And I said, no, I'm not escaping. I said, we're just out on a fishing trip. And he says, yeah, but I thought you were supposed to be in prison. episodes.description: In the summer of 1978, narcotics agents discovered the largest ever haul of illicit drugs to land in Australia, stashed inside a campervan belonging to two elderly American women tourists.
episodes.transcript: Imagine if a trusted relative offered you the trip of a lifetime, an overland odyssey in a custom designer motorhome. Well, this was the offer made in late 1977 to two retired American women, Vera Todd and her companion, Floris Bessir. Neither woman had been overseas before, so the offer was just too good to refuse. But five months into the journey, that trip spiralled into a nightmare when the women found themselves at the centre of the largest drug hall ever made in Australia at the time. We understand that 1.9 tonnes, and that's an awful lot of hash, has been found in a camper van. I said, what's silver water? He said, well, that's a prison for women. Hello and welcome to ABC Rewind. Hilary Harper here with an astonishing true story about family, deceit, betrayal and a drug kingpin who got off scot-free. Sandy Logan was a young journalist when the drug granny's case hit the headlines, and he found the story both shocking and intriguing. There was the age of the alleged drug smugglers, the amount of high-grade hashish found in their motorhome, and the criminal conviction handed to them. Sandy's written a book about the case called Betrayed, and in this first episode of our two-part series, he winds the clock back to the late 1970s for the start of this very wild ride. Here's the story of the drug grannies, too old to run. In 1978, a story caught my eye, and little did I know then that it would consume my life for many years after. Well, as you say, your lifestyle, Clarice and I both being retired, worked like 59 years of how old you are. That's Vera Todd Hayes, who everyone, including me, called Toddy. She met her companion, Clarice Basir, whose nickname was Beasy, in the early 1950s on the Douglas Aircraft Assembly Line in Los Angeles. We found a little place back in the Deschutes National Forest in Oregon with a population of about 4,100 people. Together, Toddy and Beasy enjoyed an outdoors lifestyle, traveling around the U.S. in a motorhome. In 1977, Toddy's nephew, Vern, offered his aunt and Beasy what sounded like the trip of a lifetime, to drive his brand-new Mercedes-Benz van from Stuttgart, Germany, all the way to Bombay, today known as Mumbai. Even though Toddy and Beasy didn't know it, their itinerary would follow the classic hippie trail. This was the route for a generation of travelers who trailed flowers in their hair and enjoyed the offerings of the local cannabis cafes and hashish shops. The two women mulled over Vern's offer. I said, well, I don't know. I said, I'd have to ask Beasy first. She said, well, she can go along. She's a travel companion. All expenses paid, and you've never been over to Europe, and driving through all these countries you've read about, because we both have belonged to the National Geographic for over 20 years. And we thought, gee, why pass up a chance like this? Vern Todd was an American-born yachty, actor, handyman, and budding businessman. In 1966, in his mid-20s, he settled in Australia. It was well known in the Todd family that Vern considered Toddy his favorite aunt. So the trip offer was in keeping with their relationship. I love those ladies. They were jovial and kind and decent people. That's Carol Brewer, a neighbor of Toddy and Beasy's. She knew them in Lapine in the 70s, as they were deliberating over the trip. They were so excited about going on this trip. They said, well, when are you leaving? When are you leaving? They said, well, when my nephew gets all the plans made. And, you know, they were really looking forward to this trip. On the 26th of August, 1977, Toddy and Beasy flew to Germany to collect the motorhome and start their exciting overland odyssey. In Stuttgart, they collected the 26-foot, that's 8 meters, long, left-hand-drive camper van. A customs carnet was issued in Toddy's name as she was doing the driving. And this document affixed to her passport meant the women could enter and exit international borders with the foreign-registered van. Their destination over a three-month period was Bombay. At various points along the way, nephew Vern or his business associates would meet up with the women. This was part of a plan to promote his new product, an inflatable tubby bath for babies. Once Toddy and Beasy hit Bombay, they'd hand the van back to Vern and fly home to the U.S. This was the women's first time overseas, and during the trip, they kept diaries of their travels. They also sent postcards to family and friends back home and described the extraordinary events they encountered. There were language barriers, the vagaries of foreign cuisine, and wildly varying driving conditions, which often terrified them. And then there were the bandits. Did they tell you about the time that they were going? I don't remember which country, Iran or someplace, they were going through. That's Nancy Carter, another Lapine neighbor, who received postcards from Toddy and Beasy during their trip. She's speaking to me down a scratchy phone line. And Beasy didn't drive, and Toddy was tired, so they stopped like in the middle of the desert, and Beasy sat up with lights on, and that was the only thing that kept them safe because the nomads or whatever they were there circled that motorhome, I guess, all night long. No kidding. Pretty soon the women and the children all disappeared. Here's Beasy back home in the U.S. years later, remembering that night in the desert. And it got dark, and all of a sudden we did look, and here was the bandits. So we rolled up windows, locked doors, pulled drapes and everything, and they're standing out there making noises, pounding on the thing. First I got all the knives we had in the place, all the tarjacks and tools and hammers, and I laid them all out on the counter. I thought, well, if you're breaking the windows, somebody's going to get hurt. I was trying to think of the word. What is the word that means? Baba. Baba. Baba can mean friend. It can also mean son of a bitch. It depends on the intonation he is. So I would try to make my voice as deep as possible so they didn't think there was a man in there. I said, hey, Baba. And I'm nasty, but like, hey, friend, stop it. But I read all night, and they pounded all night and started getting daylight about, oh, 5.30, 6.25 to 6, and they disappeared. But we found out later that the only reason they didn't break in, the light. They couldn't figure what the lights were on in there, and that's what saved us. Tati and Beesey's 1977 overland journey had taken them from Germany through Austria, the former Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. And once they hit India, they thought they were on the home stretch. But as they were making their way to Bombay, they hit the monsoon season. We get about 30 kilometers out of New Delhi, south of New Delhi. Looks like we got a river that's about four miles long, going right across, I won't say highway, the track that we were riding on. Anyhow, you couldn't tell how deep it was because there's no traffic. We were the only ones there. So I said to Tati, I better get out in front here and look for potholes because it's, I mean, real deep. So I rolled up my pants, which was kind of stupid. I might as well just left them down because I was way over my hips. But anyhow, I started feeling around my feet and walking, and she had to keep the motor going so that the water wouldn't come up the exhaust pipe, you know, just keep them, like sound like an outboard motor. And she's in this big Mercedes in which the water was still running in. That's how high it was. And this is out in what they call Bengal Tiger country and also bandit country. So finally, anyhow, when we get through there, Tati finds out that the radiator and it was showing in red. So we pull off, and we finally get the hood open. And here the radiator had bounced off of the mounting bolts. So she finally got it off of the road, and we went down a gradual incline and settled right there. This mechanical issue with the van was to be the least of the women's worries. When they finally reached Bombay, one of Verne's associates, Philip Shine, an Australian antiques dealer, gave Tati and Beasy an ultimatum. Fly to Australia and pick up the van there. If they didn't cooperate, they were told they'd be hounded for the rest of their lives because Philip Shine told the women that the customs document, the Carnet, required them to stay with the vehicle all the way to Australia or face arrest. He also threatened violence by unnamed people. Because it was Tati's nephew, Vern, who'd organized the trip, the women felt obliged to do as they were told. But Tati and Beasy insisted that once the van was on the dock down under, that was it. They were done. And so on the 10th of November, 1977, Tati and Beasy boarded a flight to Australia. Once on the ground in Sydney, they had to wait several weeks for the ship carrying the campervan to reach port. They made the most of their time in a country they'd never planned on visiting. Taking in Sydney, its harbour, and even attending the Colgate International Women's Tennis Championships, where they cheered on Yvonne Goulagon-Cauley. Tati and Beasy continued writing postcards home, though they didn't utter a word to friends or family that they were in Australia essentially against their wishes. In early December 1977, the two women headed to Melbourne as instructed to collect the campervan. And while Tati and Beasy didn't know it, turns out that other people were also keeping watch on the Melbourne docks for the van's arrival. We had three days' notice that the van was arriving in Melbourne. That's Inspector Bob Drain of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. So folks, what I haven't told you yet in this extraordinary tale is why narcotics agents become involved in the story of two elderly American women and their motorhome. You see, from the mid-1970s, Australian intelligence analysts had detected a pattern of vehicle importations from Bombay, supposedly by tourists planning to drive around Australia. The only thing was, the vehicles turned out to be crammed full of hashish. The women's motorhome fit the profile as a likely drug smuggling operation. Here's Bob Drain talking about Tati and Beasy's van from a 1981 Four Corners program. We knew there were narcotics on board, but we didn't know exactly how much. But we figured there were enough to mount a large-scale operation. So we put cars in this area. We had one parked down the road down here, another one towards the city, and we had an officer on the wharf in uniform to cover anything that happened in that area. As Christmas 1977 approached, Bob Drain and a 12-agent undercover surveillance team swung into action. Part of a larger task force known as Operation Genius, Drain's off-sider was agent Michelle Curie, who we'll know as Mish. In the Bureau, I really got down and got my hands dirty. These busts, some of them actually ended up really sadly. I felt I was doing a bit of a job, really, that I could be proud of. You know, I had friends who actually smoked dope, cannabis, but when it came to the hard stuff, the heroin, morphine, and the cutting compounds that they used, I thought, get this scourge off the streets. heading into work just before her 1977 annual leave, Mish soon discovered she might have to change her holiday plans. I think it might have been the 13th of December. Went into work and just for a normal day's work, which was never normal anyway, and found myself in a surveillance car heading up the highway after being briefed, of course. I recall that our persons of interest were actually some elderly ladies. They were around about my grandmother's age, and I was a bit stunned at that. Agents Bob Drane and Mish Khoury went undercover to monitor Toddy and Beazie's movements in Australia 24 hours a day, following the women on the road, in campgrounds, eating at restaurants, or downing a schooner at the pub. Everything. Their first encounter with Toddy and Beazie was in a laundromat in a Shepperton campground in country Victoria. It was the first night of Toddy and Beazie's Australian leg of their now extended overland trip. We never knew where they were going the following day. We had little clothing. We had the clothes that we stood up in. We weren't actually expecting to start a five or six week surveillance. So I asked my fellow narcotics agents that were part of the surveillance teams, and there were about four or five cars, and about at least ten surveillance people, and I just asked them to give me their socks and their jocks, because the ladies had headed to the laundry. This was the laundromat where we first established contact with the two old ladies. We had a female agent come in here and do some washing alongside them, and strike up a conversation with a view to finding out where they were going next. I found myself doing a wash and hoping that they would come back for their washing, which they did whilst I was still there, and struck up a conversation, and just mentioned that I was heading off, heading north, and during the conversation, they sort of said, oh, they're heading up to, I can't recall exactly where it was, so we thought that we knew exactly where they would be going to the following day, so that we could have enough funds sent to the post office at that particular city or town. And that's how we rolled after that first meeting. As the covert surveillance of Toddy and Beezy continued, the agents had to secretly break into the women's van and install a listening device. It was attached to the van's radio. When the two ladies drove the van from Melbourne to Sydney, agents from the Sydney office were called in to assist with the ongoing surveillance. This is former narcotics agent John Shawbrook, who was part of Operation Genius. Here he is reading from his unpublished manuscript about his time as an agent. From Sydney, the two grannies drove the motor home up the Pacific Highway towards New South Wales Central Coast. It was a Christmas school holiday period, and when we arrived at the coastal township of Gosford, it was crowded. The grannies were fortunate to get a berth for their van in the crowded Gosford Caravan Park. It was decided by the officers in charge to plant a bug in the van, a microphone and transmitter, whilst the ladies were dining at the Gosford RSL. I was chosen as a volunteer to enter the van and conceal and connect a small radio transmitter up underneath the dash. I connected our transmitter to what I believe to be the correct wire, and a dim red light glowed on the transmitter. success. Toddie and Beasy, still oblivious to the surveillance, took a shopping trip in Gosford. They then drove out of the caravan park. We followed them from an appropriate distance up through the township of Gosford and into a slightly more industrial area, where, to our surprise and horror, they turned into the driveway of a car radio repair shop. It was at this point that narcotics agent John Shawbrook had to make a call. As the ladies entered the front door of the shop, I ran to the workshop area and entered by a side door. Whether to jeopardise the entire operation by blowing his cover, or instead, bringing the radio repairman into a secret. So he flashed his agent's badge and leaned in to have a quiet word with the repairman. He told me that they had said that their radio was not working, and could he have a look at it? I decided that he needed to know more. I connected a radio transmitter up to it last night, and that must have killed the radio. When you have a look at it, can you leave the transmitter hidden up under the dash and in a working condition? Yeah, sure, he said. But they said the radio hasn't been working since they first started driving the van in Melbourne. Undercover police work can be routine, even boring. But occasionally it throws up the unexpected. And for Narcs, Bob Drain and Mish Khoury, this meant being welcomed into the very motor home they were surveilling. Mish Khoury takes up the story. The last time we ran into the minute, an undercover capacity, was at the Central Coast Leagues Club, where we over-imbibed the four of us. And I think we had a meal together. That's how over-imbibing we did. And they invited us back to the camper van, and we thought, wow, this is pretty great. Dear me. Anyway, upon entering the van, we sat at their little four-seater table, and I was just totally overcome by the aroma of hash. And I just, I'd already over-imbibed it. I don't think the fumes did me any good either. I actually think, I'll admit, that when we did leave the van, I left my handbag in the van with my badge, said Michelle Khoury, Federal Bureau of Narcotics, all of that. Anyway, I said to Bob, I said, oh, I've got to go back to the van. I said, I've left my bloody handbag there. And to which, Bob, a couple of expletives, and I went knocking at the door of the van. The lights were out, the whole lot. And one of the girls said, who is it? And I said, it's Mish. I've left my handbag there. She said, oh, we would have brought it to the club tomorrow. I said, no. I said, actually, I said, I need it tonight. I said, because, you know, I've got my women's thing. Oh, my God. Oh, my God. So, anyway, I've got my handbag, and there you go. And, well, had they been really nosy parkers, they would have realised that we were onto them. So I was not compromised. Toddy remembers the same late-night drinks with Mish Khoury and Bob Drain. She thought the undercover narcs were simply two down-to-earth friendly Aussies. And we ran into Bob and Mitch again. We gambled, we drank together, we were on first-name bases, and I think it was about the third night, oh, we had too much to drink, so we decided to take a taxi and say goodnight to them. And Bob says, no, don't do that, we'll drive you back. I said, well, fine. So he and Mitch drove us back to Terrigo. I said, well, as long as you're here, I guess it was about 1.30, two in the morning, to come in and have a nightcap. So they both came in, sat down. It wasn't one nightcap, they were there two or three hours. Fed them some sandwiches and more cocktails and more conversation and just good friends having a wonderful time. We thought that they were very, very cool people, inviting us back to the van, regardless of what they knew, what we were or not. A couple of very cool customers. In the back of my mind, I felt that perhaps there was a bit of con man in them, or con woman, if you like. episodes.title: Why David Pocock thinks the new gambling reforms are "infuriating"
episodes.description: The Australian Government has introduced new reforms around gambling advertising in an attempt to shield young sports fans from the negative impacts of problem gambling.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. What's gambling really costing you? For free and confidential support, call the number on the screen or visit the website. If you're a sports fan, I can imagine you've heard that disclaimer before. The Australian government has announced a raft of gambling reforms that come into effect in January next year. The reforms include restricting gambling advertising on broadcast TV between 6am and 8.30pm, ban it completely during live sport and on radio at school drop-off and pick-up times, and a ban of online ads where it can't be verified that the users are over 18. The government says the aim is to reduce the exposure that children have to gambling companies, but many are calling for more action. Given the amount of income that sports betting brings into the major sporting codes in Australia, finding a balance will need more than just taking a punt. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. David Pocock is a former Wallaby and is now an independent senator in the ACT, who has long been vocal about the need for gambling reform in Australia. David, earlier this month, the government introduced stricter regulations around gambling advertising to limit children's exposure to gambling harm. What kind of harm does gambling do in this country? Well, per capita, we're the biggest losers in the world. Gambling has been normalised by gambling advertising to the point where three out of four young Australians now think that gambling and betting on sport is just a normal part of enjoying sport. And this is something that the parliament has been grappling with for a number of years now. We're not doing something radical here in Australia. We're playing catch-up. What's radical in Australia is that we have the greatest gambling losses of anywhere in the world, 40% higher than the nation that comes second. What do you do in a society where you have something that can become a real issue for people in our community, so normalised by the gambling industry, and then raking in massive, massive profits? And so the parliament had an inquiry, and there were 31 recommendations saying, this is a public health issue. This is how we can actually turn this around. And one of the central recommendations was to actually have a phased-in ban on all gambling advertising, saying, if you just make some tweaks, history shows us that this is an industry that finds loopholes. And so we just need to go with a full gambling ad ban in recognition that no one's saying you can't have a bet, but we've got to stop the normalisation of gambling in our community. We are getting the balance right. Letting adults have a punt if they want to. But making sure that our children don't see betting ads everywhere they look. You've been on record in saying that these reforms are hugely disappointing. Why is that? For a number of reasons. The big one being that history shows us that partial bans don't work, and that's why this landmark Murphy report, which was backed by every party in the parliament, and every independent in the parliament, said a three-year phased-in ban on all gambling advertising is the only way that we can actually deal with this. The government, when they announced they were going with a partial ban, then delivered the analysis underlying that. And if you actually read the government's own analysis, it shows that a full ban would be cheaper to implement because there's less regulation involved. It's just a blanket ban that comes in over three years. And it would actually provide more benefits to Australians. So we've got a government that has gone for the option that doesn't actually put Australians first. It's an option that the gambling industry will be happy to live with. Between 6am and 8.30pm, we will cap the number of TV ads for betting agencies at a maximum of three per hour. We will ban all gambling ads on radio during school pickup and drop off. Beyond that, there are huge issues with things like inducements, where people get bonus bets, free bets. And if you talk to researchers in this space, they are the most harmful part of the whole sort of gambling advertising and the way that they hook people. Because we know that it's actually a smaller number of Australians that are losing the most money. And often that is off the back of free bets, bonus bets, where people feel like it's risk-free. And that's where we see a lot of people, particularly young men, getting into a lot of trouble. And the government has just not even gone with that recommendation. And that was the most urgent recommendation that was given three years ago. They said that inducements should be banned immediately. Government's not doing that. So wide sweeping reform would have significant impact on the bottom line of a number of sporting codes and broadcast partners and that sort of thing. If you could pick just one thing to change from these government's reforms, what's the top of the tree for you? Well, the gambling ads is the big one. It's what's normalising gambling. It's what's setting up young people for failure. And if we're going to turn this around as a country, you have to look at gambling advertising. We believe that Australians wanted in particular, and the terms of reference to the Win Sum You Lose Sum report, wanted in particular the reduction of exposure of children to gambling advertising. So the reforms that we have landed, and you would have seen Free TV, who is the peak for broadcast television, come out and say this will have a really significant impact to their bottom line. So this has been difficult. And nonetheless, we have made meaningful reform. Yeah, there is the reality that free-to-air television sports broadcasters are deriving income from this. A couple of our major sports now actually get a kickback, a percentage of each bet placed on, say, NRL, AFL. The report from Peter Murphy and her colleagues actually raised concerns and said, listen, we're losing sight of what sport is actually about in this country, and it's no longer just about the enjoyment, the community, the challenge. It's now just it's becoming the sort of avenue to market gambling. So I would go there as to the impacts, you know, we could put a one and a half, two percent levy on bets in this country and more than compensate free-to-air television and probably invest a lot, lot more money into things like community sport, grassroots sport than is currently being invested. So, you know, this is just about political will. And yet again, we're seeing vested interests being put ahead of the interests of the Australian people. Kids are still going to be seeing gambling ads. So that's what Murphy said to stop. Have you canvassed the Greens and or the Coalition for their support on some of these reforms or what you're proposing? Working on it, I'm concerned that the Coalition will wave these through. I think that's really disappointing given what I hear from a lot of people in the Coalition is the talk of family values and focusing on the family. And I don't see what is more squarely about family values than actually protecting young people from a predatory industry. So I would love to see some pushback from the Coalition to actually say at a bare minimum, we've got to fix some of the loopholes in what's been proposed. And, you know, a big one for me is the PM announced that there'll be no gambling ads on sport before 8.30pm. We all know that a whole heap of games kick off at 7.55, 8pm. And so the second half of these games, there are no rules. And so for the Coalition, I'd say at least go with what your former leader, Peter Dutton, said where at least an hour before and an hour after we're not going to have any gambling advertising if they're not willing to actually go with the full ad van. You mentioned the fact that we know that money from gambling is deeply tied to broadcast deals, which is tied to the game and the promotion and the growth of some of our major sporting codes. Both Andrew Abdo and Gillian McLaughlin are both on the record as saying that it contributes heavily to funding grassroots and the women's game for both of those codes. The fans like the fact that child prices are $5, adults are $27. We like that we're investing $55 million in game development every year. How realistic is it to implement further reform without massively compromising some of those things? I mean, I think you've got to start. You know, I'm a former freshman athlete, so I get what this means for sports. But I think we've all got to step back and say, well, what is sport actually for? And I think at its core, sport is about so much that is good in our society, a place where communities can come together, get to know people that you otherwise wouldn't hang out with, challenge yourself physically, mentally, and be part of something bigger than yourself. We cannot lose sight of that. As to the raw dollars and cents, again, something like a levy could actually ensure that there is more money for things like grassroots sport, for women's sports. So I think it's a real cop-out. So, yeah, I'm a little bit cynical about some of the lines that we get, but I do get the financial side of things. And the thing I say to my parliamentary colleagues is, well, let's solve that. But we've seen the real-life cases come forward in that Murphy report and since, and these are people who have felt the real adverse effects of problem gambling. Have you heard from any of those people in response to these reforms? I have. So many people. It is devastating to hear people talk about either their experience or, in the most tragic cases, talking about a loved one that has taken their life due to gambling addiction. And the thing that often comes up in that is that people who know they have a problem and are trying to deal with it, they say, you cannot escape it. Everywhere you turn, there are ads. When you're on a losing streak, you're getting inducements. It is not working. And so I find it not just disappointing, but actually really infuriating that we have political leaders, well, in some instances won't even meet with those people, but must know that that harm is happening and still puts vested interests ahead of protecting Australians, doing the right thing. And no one is saying that we should make gambling illegal. There's a ridiculous argument that gets rolled out by the Prime Minister and others. All we're saying is let's actually protect young Australians. Let's not put people in a situation where it is so hard to find help. And in the last year or so, Poppy, I've noticed such a big increase in the number of young men who've pulled me aside at events saying, hey, could we just talk privately? And then they say, thanks so much for what you're doing on gambling. I'm struggling with it. And it is so hard because you're just getting smashed with ads. And all the ads portray it as something that is so much fun. You know, you're hanging out with your mates. You're having wins. You're betting on the footy. The reality is, is that I'm staring at my screen in bed by myself at 3am chasing losses. People really wanted that saturation and targeting of gambling advertising reduced. And they wanted the exposure of children to gambling advertising reduced. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Minister for Communications, Annika Wells, are both adamant that these reforms have struck the right balance between allowing Australians the freedom to have a bed, as you say, it's not about making gambling illegal, but protecting children from the harm that it can cause, particularly with some of the advertising. Do you think that there's a possibility that these reforms are, at the very least, a step in the right direction to potentially stronger reforms like the ones that you're proposing? Well, they're clearly better than nothing. I don't think we should settle for better than nothing as Australians. They can clearly be strengthened. But, you know, in terms of striking the right balance, again, this is something that the Parliament grappled with through the Murphy inquiry. And they said, you know, a phased in ban over three years would allow sports to make some adjustments. I think something like a levy could plug that gap. My concern with this is everything I've seen from the Albanese Labour government is that if they make a small tweak to an issue, they then just say, OK, we've done that. And every time you ask a question about, hey, you made that reform, it's not really working or didn't go far enough. They'll just say, listen, we did it. It's working great. Let's move on. And so I really do think this is an opportunity for the Parliament to at least make these reforms a lot better. And I think that that's the test for MPs and senators. Who are you here to represent? And I really hope that, you know, the coalition work with the crossbench in the Senate to ensure that we at least have reforms that don't have ridiculous things like no ads in the first half, but second half there'll be a deluge of gambling ads. That just doesn't cut it. David Pocock, it's an ongoing conversation and we're looking forward to seeing how it plays out. Thanks so much for your time. Thanks a lot, Poppy. Headlines. New South Wales and Queensland have today announced their women's state of origin squads ahead of Game 1 next week. New South Wales will bring back 14 players from the team that won the Series 2-1 last year. Plus, welcome back Millie Elliott, who will make her return after giving birth in September. The Maroons are facing the enormous challenge of replacing Ali Brigginshaw and Taryn Aitken, who are both unavailable for selection and have named five potential debutantes. Soccer and former Premier League champions Leicester City have been relegated to the third tier of English football next season, just 10 years after winning the title. A decade ago, they were champions of England. They lifted the Premier League trophy here, but tonight they are relegated to League One, the fifth club in the Premier League era to suffer back-to-back relegations. This will be the second time in their 142-year existence that they have played in the third tier comp. Netball Australia CEO Stacey West has announced her resignation after less than three years in the role. West was appointed back in December 2023 and guided the organisation through a time where the sport was struggling financially and was in a dispute with players about pay. Mark Falvo will serve as interim CEO. And Rugby Australia have announced that they're back in the black after a successful British and Irish Lions tour, turning $36.8 million in losses last year into a tick over $70 million in profit this year. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily produced by Declan Byrne. Thanks to Sky Channel 9 and BN Sports for the extra audio used in this episode. We'll see you next time.

Kids are still going to be seeing gambling ads.
So that's what Murphy said to stop.
Have you canvassed the Greens and or the Coalition for their support on some of these reforms or what you're proposing?
Working on it, I'm concerned that the Coalition will wave these through.
I think that's really disappointing given what I hear from a lot of people in the Coalition is the talk of family values
And I don't see what is more squarely about family values than actually protecting young people
So I would love to see some pushback from the Coalition to actually say at a bare minimum,
we've got to fix some of the loopholes in what's been proposed.
And, you know, a big one for me is the PM announced that there'll be no gambling ads on sport before 8.30pm.
We all know that a whole heap of games kick off at 7.55, 8pm.
And so the second half of these games, there are no rules.
And so for the Coalition, I'd say at least go with what your former leader, Peter Dutton,
said where at least an hour before and an hour after we're not going to have any gambling advertising
if they're not willing to actually go with the full ad van.
You mentioned the fact that we know that money from gambling is deeply tied to broadcast deals,
which is tied to the game and the promotion and the growth of some of our major sporting codes.
Both Andrew Abdo and Gillian McLaughlin are both on the record as saying that it contributes
heavily to funding grassroots and the women's game for both of those codes.
The fans like the fact that child prices are $5, adults are $27.
We like that we're investing $55 million in game development every year.
How realistic is it to implement further reform without massively compromising some of those things?
I mean, I think you've got to start.
You know, I'm a former freshman athlete, so I get what this means for sports.
But I think we've all got to step back and say, well, what is sport actually for?
And I think at its core, sport is about so much that is good in our society,
a place where communities can come together, get to know people that you otherwise wouldn't hang out with,
challenge yourself physically, mentally, and be part of something bigger than yourself.
We cannot lose sight of that.
As to the raw dollars and cents, again, something like a levy could actually ensure that there is more money
for things like grassroots sport, for women's sports.
So I think it's a real cop-out.
So, yeah, I'm a little bit cynical about some of the lines that we get,
but I do get the financial side of things.
And the thing I say to my parliamentary colleagues is, well, let's solve that.
But we've seen the real-life cases come forward in that Murphy report and since,
and these are people who have felt the real adverse effects of problem gambling.
Have you heard from any of those people in response to these reforms?
It is devastating to hear people talk about either their experience or, in the most tragic cases,
talking about a loved one that has taken their life due to gambling addiction.
And the thing that often comes up in that is that people who know they have a problem
and are trying to deal with it, they say, you cannot escape it.
Everywhere you turn, there are ads.
When you're on a losing streak, you're getting inducements.
And so I find it not just disappointing, but actually really infuriating that we have political leaders,
well, in some instances won't even meet with those people,
but must know that that harm is happening and still puts vested interests ahead of protecting Australians,
And no one is saying that we should make gambling illegal.
There's a ridiculous argument that gets rolled out by the Prime Minister and others.
All we're saying is let's actually protect young Australians.
Let's not put people in a situation where it is so hard to find help.
And in the last year or so, Poppy, I've noticed such a big increase in the number of young men who've pulled me aside at events saying,
hey, could we just talk privately?
And then they say, thanks so much for what you're doing on gambling.
And it is so hard because you're just getting smashed with ads.
And all the ads portray it as something that is so much fun.
You know, you're hanging out with your mates.
The reality is, is that I'm staring at my screen in bed by myself at 3am chasing losses.
People really wanted that saturation and targeting of gambling advertising reduced.
And they wanted the exposure of children to gambling advertising reduced.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Minister for Communications, Annika Wells,
are both adamant that these reforms have struck the right balance between allowing Australians the freedom to have a bed,
as you say, it's not about making gambling illegal,
but protecting children from the harm that it can cause, particularly with some of the advertising.
Do you think that there's a possibility that these reforms are, at the very least,
a step in the right direction to potentially stronger reforms like the ones that you're proposing?
Well, they're clearly better than nothing.
I don't think we should settle for better than nothing as Australians.
But, you know, in terms of striking the right balance, again,
this is something that the Parliament grappled with through the Murphy inquiry.
And they said, you know, a phased in ban over three years would allow sports to make some adjustments.
I think something like a levy could plug that gap.
My concern with this is everything I've seen from the Albanese Labour government is that
if they make a small tweak to an issue, they then just say, OK, we've done that.
And every time you ask a question about, hey, you made that reform,
it's not really working or didn't go far enough.
They'll just say, listen, we did it. It's working great. Let's move on.
And so I really do think this is an opportunity for the Parliament to at least make these reforms a lot better.
And I think that that's the test for MPs and senators.
Who are you here to represent?
And I really hope that, you know, the coalition work with the crossbench in the Senate
to ensure that we at least have reforms that don't have ridiculous things like no ads in the first half,
but second half there'll be a deluge of gambling ads.
David Pocock, it's an ongoing conversation and we're looking forward to seeing how it plays out.
Thanks so much for your time.

New South Wales will bring back 14 players from the team that won the Series 2-1 last year.
