Soccer and former Premier League champions Leicester City have been relegated to the third tier of English football next season,
just 10 years after winning the title.

They lifted the Premier League trophy here, but tonight they are relegated to League One,
the fifth club in the Premier League era to suffer back-to-back relegations.
This will be the second time in their 142-year existence that they have played in the third tier comp.
Netball Australia CEO Stacey West has announced her resignation after less than three years in the role.

and was in a dispute with players about pay.
Mark Falvo will serve as interim CEO.
And Rugby Australia have announced that they're back in the black after a successful British and Irish Lions tour,
turning $36.8 million in losses last year into a tick over $70 million in profit this year.

episodes.title: Tom Boyd on the ‘suffocating nature’ of footy in wake of Elijah Hollands’ episode
episodes.description: Elijah Hollands’ mental health episode against Collingwood on Thursday night has raised many questions, particularly of the Carlton Football Club. How did this happen? Why was he allowed to stay on the ground?
episodes.transcript: Just a heads up before we get into today's episode, it is discussing mental health. ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music and more. We are determined to ensure a considered process, not just an understanding of what happened, but to ensure the key learnings come from this, not just for us, but the broader football community and industry. That's Carlton CEO Graham Wright speaking about the ongoing investigation into Elijah Holland's mental health episode on field against Collingwood last Thursday night. Vision of Holland's in-game has spread like wildfire and the questions of Carlton and their handling of this have come thick and fast. How could this have happened? Why was he allowed to play? And how can we stop this from happening again? I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. Tom Boyd is a premiership player for the Western Bulldogs and since retiring, in 2019 has been an advocate for mental health and wellbeing. Tom, I know your experience and what Elijah Holland's has experienced are different things, but I'm hoping to talk about how this has and might continue to play out through your eyes. How did you feel about what you were seeing on Thursday night in the match between Carlton and Collingwood? Yeah, thanks for having me for starters. I think one of the things that's critically important to understand is that regardless of what's actually happened during these moments when really significant attention grabbing issues pop up within the footy world in particular, these things tend to be extremely polarising and it obviously creates an enormous amount of speculation. And I'm probably one of the few people, I suppose, who's experienced a combination of things, a huge amount of attention and mental health being at the core component of that. And so for me, I think really around the responsibility that we all have and the lifelong impacts that these types of moments can have. And I think there's this naivety in many ways that people have to say, hey, it's just a 48 hour news cycle. It'll go away in two days or a week. That's not really how it works. What happens, and I've experienced this firsthand for the better and the worse, is that your entire life can be shaped by these moments. And it infects every part of your life into the future. And so for me, you know, as a father of two young kids, I put myself in the position of really just looking at it to say, if this was my kid, how would I want them to be treated? And what would I want them to feel from the support of the football public and his friends, family members, and of course, the footy club as well? Carlton have since come out and said that this was a mental health episode for him on the field and that they were aware he was struggling during the game. We were aware that he was struggling in the game and he's had, potentially had anxiety previously and panic attacks. And our guys were dealing with him in the game that obviously he was having some problems. You've been inside the four walls of a footy club and as you say, are really uniquely placed to speak about this. How is it possible that he played three and a bit quarters of footy? Yeah, I've thought about this from both angles, frankly. To look at it through the lens of the actual pragmatic preparation for a game of footy, I can see both arguments, right? I can see the fact that really building momentum for a game of footy is like a wave. You start, you enter the ground, you build up, build up, build up. And everyone's job is one, as a player, to get themselves to the position where they can play their best footy. But for the support staff, the coaching staff, the medical staff, their job is to get their players to the point where they can play the best game. And that really is the number one, two, three, four and five priority. And whilst I can see the concept that people would say, with all of those touch points, did they not notice something throughout the warm-up and the lead-up? And I don't know the answer to that. And again, to your point off the top, I don't really feel the need to speculate. But what I can say is that that heightened pressure as you lead into not just any game of footy, but the game of footy of Collingwood and Carlton at the MCG with 80,000 people is incredibly difficult to pick out moments in time and then go, yeah, there's a trend of an issue here rather than people seeing erratic moments over any course of time. And that's regardless of the issue. And the second thing I would say is that as you do build up to these games of footy, there is a great hesitation from staff and support, staff in particular, to knock people off their game. And the concept that someone would go in and say, hey, you don't see me yourself today as this player goes to put themselves out in front of 80,000 people, I think is a pretty questionable concept. At the risk that they were wrong and then they throw this player off and the player has a bad game. This is quite a severe set of consequences that could exist. And so for me, I think through the lens of the fact that one, as we talk about this topic, I think it's critically important that we don't talk about Elijah, but we talk about the issue as a whole and how in any moment within a game of football, if this injury of sorts was considered to be an Achilles or a knee, they would have been brought off the ground. And the question from my point of view is rather than focusing on the club or the player, if you focus on the issue, how can this be better served and supported into the future? So we use this as a learning moment and a point of improvement rather than something that we continue to regret into the future. Since the game, we have been working through a thorough process surrounding the circumstances both leading into and throughout the match and remain in close consultation with the AFL and the AFL-PA. So as you say, the AFL has strict injury and concussion protocols. If a player hurts their hamstring, they're out for the rest of the game. If they get a head knock and is concussed, they miss the following week. Do we need some kind of similar framework to check in with players around their mental health, both pre-game, post-game and also in-game? Yeah, it's an interesting concept. I think it is a challenging framework to implement. I'm probably not the academic person to talk through around what that could look like. And to be fair, there is a lot of connection, in particular with the assistant coaches, the medicos and those types of things as you progress players to get ready, right? And I think this is one of the interesting parts is you sort of arrive at the ground, you deal with the medicos first. We understand that Elijah's got some mental health issues and he's been very open and honest with that. But I feel like he's got great medical people. We've got fantastic medical staff here who have a long history with Elijah as well and understanding his issues. Then you move to the assistant coaches, then the senior coach, and then you go out with the trainers and you start the game. And I think that broadly speaking, the perspective of all of those people, I mean this as genuinely as I can, is they want the best for everyone there. And that is a really important thing to keep at the forefront of our minds. Whether there was mistakes made or issues that could have been prevented, that's another conversation. The intention of these people is incredibly pure and that's why they're in the jobs that they're in. And so for me, I'm not sure on the practical solution in terms of putting a framework in place to actually vet players. And I'm not sure how that would practically work, whether it's feasible academically or not. But I do think that this sort of overall concept, and this was something, by the way, that came up when I actually took time off the game. My message to the public was, just like any other injury, I need to rehabilitate myself to get back out and do my job. And if we look at it through the lens of that and the safety of our players and our people and our staff and the players that obviously make the game possible, I think that's going to serve us well in how we treat these things moving forward. Elijah himself has spoken about his own mental health battles and he's spoken publicly about a game last season against Sydney where he came off and he felt like he's like he couldn't breathe, he wasn't contributing. He described it himself as a mini panic attack. Have you ever experienced anything like that? What would that be like for him in game? Yeah, and I think it's important to remember that these games are not just one moment in time, right? It's not like the game itself is the episode. And I'm talking from my own personal point of view now, rather than what happened last Thursday night. From my perspective, it was a cumulative effect over a number of years as I continue to have worse and worse issues, particularly around sleep. And by the way, particularly around sleep leading into games. And so the concept of turning up to a game of footy where, and I often say, you know, it'd be great to play in front of 60,000, but I used to play in front of about 25 as a Bulldogs player. Turning up in front of 25,000 people, completely underdone from a rest and recovery point of view, unable to concentrate. And then really trying to use whatever means are necessary to get myself to concentrate and focus and prepare so that I don't end up on the back page of the paper as the person who failed. It's an extraordinary amount of stress to add on to what already is an incredibly stressful environment being an AFL footballer. And so for me, I know a lot of players who have dealt with the challenges of preparation for games. And obviously, this is an example where it spills down into something that's more visual rather than what I would say a lot of players are dealing with under the surface as they prepare for these high pressure environments. Yeah, he sort of feels like he's let people down, but we've just got to keep supporting people through those situations. In your experience, when you did come in feeling maybe like you weren't well enough rested or you weren't entirely 100% mentally or physically ready for a match, did you feel as though you had opportunities to say to someone, I don't feel right, I'm not right to play mentally? Yeah, probably all week up until game day. And this is one of the great challenges of professional sport. It's really the defining factor that says to me, we need to learn how to manage these things rather than hoping. It seems unreasonable to me that we're going to massively prevent every issue. It's a really competitive environment. It's incredibly stress inducing and high pressure. And so for me, like anyone, whether it's mental or physical, most of the players that you see running around on the screen every single week have some significant health issue of some kind, right? Whether they have got an ankle that's hurt or a hamstring that's sore or a back that needs surgery or a shoulder for that matter, as I played with for a long time. The challenge with the mental side of things is that these can be incredibly long lasting issues. They don't get the same treatment because they're not as obvious in terms of how to deal with it. And the rehabilitation, by the way, it doesn't have as clear a milestones, right? When a finger is broken, you can see when it's healed. And this is where I think one of the great challenges for the game is how do we think about the sustainable and long looking approach to our players who are making the game possible? Because often is the case that we look at these things very short term and it is the next game that's the most important. The conversation is getting louder around the competition for some kind of mental health round to shine a bigger light on this issue. Bailey Smith added his voice to that chorus as well. I just want to shout out the Dawson family this week and Elijah Hollins last night. I don't know if I'm out of pocket saying it, but I think it's about time the AFL get a men's mental health round. It just makes me feel sick during the week and hopefully the AFL community wraps their arms around them and we can do something. Is it something you'd like to see? Do you think this is something that could have an impact? Look, my perspective is this. I think that there is a value to bringing attention to an issue in an incredibly specific and heightened way and we do it with every issue. But really what I see is the greatest opportunity for the game of the AFL circles is that they can be the greatest force for improving overall health, not just mental health, in our society today. And the clear goals from the game that they've laid out in their strategy is to grow participation by a huge amount over the course of the next six, seven or eight years as they approach 2030. And by and large, if they just execute on that in an effective way, they're going to make a positive impact in this space. If you layer onto that, that if a concerted effort was made to prioritize the mental health of those communities that they're engaging with anyway, in some way, shape or form through partners, awareness, education, support, funding, you name it, they're going to make an enormous impact. And this is why I see the opportunity for a mental health round, not to be a review of everything that's gone wrong, but actually a great way to celebrate the incredible impact that our game does has as of this day, but equally to encourage that concerted effort over an extended period of time and use that, I suppose, it's a review and celebration point for the progress that we've made in the last 12 months. So I certainly would be behind it. Just finally on Elijah and his family, his dad put up a heartfelt post about his quote, beautiful boy on Instagram today after the news that he's been admitted to hospital. His brother, Ollie, plays in that same team and is potentially in the team for this weekend's game against Fremantle. We saw what Jordan Dawson has been through with his brother in the last week or so. How would you like to see the AFL community, be it fans or footy clubs, wrap its arms around players in times like this? Yeah, I think it's important to remember just the magnitude, as I mentioned earlier, of the suffocating nature of what's going on at the moment. I mean, this is a position I personally have been in where you don't feel like you can leave the house. You don't feel like you can have a conversation with anyone. You have a very, very small circle of trusted people who feel like you actually can rely on and feel like who they support you. And as with this conversation has evolved, obviously, since Thursday night, I think it's critically important to remember the sheer magnitude of what this conversation actually means, not only for Elijah's life, but also for the people who are close to him, the broader footy club and the community as a whole. And if nothing else, if we can put ourselves in the shoes of that person being someone that we care about and realising that the game's ability to impact mental health in a positive way is incredibly important. Tom Boyd, thank you so much for sharing your experience with us. We really appreciate it. Thanks for having me. And if you or anyone you know is struggling, you can always contact Lifeline on 13 11 14. Headlines. The NRL have moved to bring in new safety guidelines for the men's and women's competitions to limit contact training. In season, men's players are to engage in no more than 100 minutes of contact training on a regular seven day turnaround. And for NRLW athletes, that drops to 85 minutes. For both men and women on five and six day turnarounds, that drops to 40 and 50 minutes respectively. During the NRL preseason, the limit is no more than 200 minutes per week. And for NRLW, it's 115 minutes. The changes come in a bid to reduce injuries, including concussion. Staying with NRL and the Dragons have named Dean Young as their interim coach for at least the rest of 2026. The changes continue at St. George Illawarra with assistant coach Michael Ennis parting ways with the club just 24 hours after head coach Shane Flanagan. AFL and Zach Butters has had his $1,500 fine for abusive or offensive language toward an umpire overturned after the tribunal deemed there had been a miscarriage of justice. What was that miscarriage? Tribunal member Jason Johnson was driving his car during final submissions and Port Adelaide successfully argued that he could not have properly considered the deliberations if he was also focused on driving. Long story short, Zach Butters is no longer out of pocket $1,500. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily produced by Declan Byrne.

episodes.title: Shane Flanagan is gone, but do the Dragons’ problems run deeper?
episodes.description: In round 23 of last year the St George Illawarra Dragons were celebrating a win over the Sharks and a contract extension for coach Shane Flanagan.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. This is clearly a significant moment for the club. We understand the disappointment and frustrations from our members and our fans feel and we know that results and performances have not met expectations from this proud club. Dragons CEO Tim Watsford announcing that the club and coach Shane Flanagan have mutually agreed to part ways after a 0-7 start to the year. The Dragons have lost 11 straight matches, their last win over the Sharks in 2025, right after Flanagan signed a contract extension. He didn't make it to that extension. We've only made it through seven rounds this season and we've seen two coaches moved on already. Can the Dragons follow in Manly's footsteps and change their 2026 fortunes with a change at the top or do their problems run much deeper? I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. Michael Kariannis writes about Rugby League for News Corp. And MC, the Dragons have come out today and said they have mutually agreed to part ways with coach Shane Flanagan after just 54 games at the helm, along with the general manager of football, Ben Harren. Can you walk us through this decision from management? Yeah, obviously big news out of the Dragons this morning and I don't think anyone's shocked by it. It had been coming because the Dragons just kept losing matches and 11 straight losses now dating back to last year. So it's been a bit of a horror show for St. George of the War over the past few months and culminated in two big scalps, the head of football, Ben Harren and coach Shane Flanagan. I want to begin by confirming that head coach Shane Flanagan and general manager of football, Ben Harren, have departed the St. George of the War over the Dragons by way of mutual agreement. Flanagan was re-signed the week after they beat the Raiders and before they beat the Sharks in round 23 last season, which actually just happened to be the last two wins he coached them to. Party time at Coggera. What a celebration for the first time in 11 starts after 10 straight losses. It's a drought-breaking derby win in most impressive circumstances for the Dragons. In the week they re-signed their coach Shane Flanagan, this is the players saying, and Flano we trust. It's a big win for them. He didn't actually even make it to that extension. How did we get from those results to today? It's unbelievable. It really is. Who would have thought that he would have been sacked before or parted ways with the club before he won another game after inking that contract extension? It was just unheard of that that was the case. So, yeah, it's a surprise, no doubt about it, back then. But given the way the season transpired, they just can't find a way to win games. Gold Coast 22, St George, Illawarra 14. The Dragons remain winless. That's the issue. The roster's not great. And as a result, their coach is no more. The CEO and chairman were at pains to stress today in the press conference that this was a mutual agreement. Can I make the point, we've already made this statement, you say moving on, that's not what we just said. We talked about a mutual agreement. And as I said, we've been speaking with Shane and the football staff along the way. This is not something that you just do because you choose to on a Monday morning. How mutual do you think it really was? Or is that just a big saving face exercise for everybody? Oh, a little bit of, I think Shane knew his time was up. There's no doubt about that. I think he felt, you know, he'd got the best out of the playing group. And those days, like, of trying to fight his way out because he was, you know, a month ago, he was quite steadfast in his belief that he could turn the tide. All I know is I can just do my best. And that's what I do every day when I go to work. Making sure that we prepare the team the best we can. It hasn't worked so far this year. But, you know, I'm not going to give up. I think he came to the realisation that perhaps this was a task a little bit too hard for him now. He did say a week ago, you know, he thought he hadn't lost the dressing room. Players have taken ownership. We haven't lost the dressing room. We had a good training session today. We're in good meetings. I've got a good relationship with all my players. Do you think that that is the case, that he genuinely felt like that? Or was that a line trotted out by a coach who knew he was in trouble? No, I think he felt like that. I think he felt like that. Whether or not that was the reality is different, right? But, no, he definitely felt like he still had the support of the players and was pretty adamant about that. But the issue has been the players just aren't responding. Tackle made. Over the touchline. Well, here's the answer to your question. Full-time Dragons get flopped. Well, I can't remember the last time I heard that for a home team. It's not the greatest roster in the NRL. It is probably the worst roster in the NRL. And these are the phone effects of it. He said recently as well that if someone better was out of the side, I would put them in. Trust me. What was he dealing with talent-wise on the park? You mentioned their roster is probably the worst in the comp. So, was their problem his coaching? Or was him moving on just sort of a circuit breaker for what is a bigger problem with their talent and depth? Yeah, there's no doubt. Like I was sort of intimated, I don't think it's a very strong roster. I think the roster's quite poor and not balanced properly. And the fact that, you know, he's got his high-end recruitment wrong. And he's much to blame for that Shane Flanagan. No doubt about that. So, was it coaching? Was it the roster? It's definitely the roster. And maybe it's a combination of coaching as well. We keep turning up on Monday, mate. And we just keep working hard. And that's what I'm so lucky as a senior player here that we have such a great bunch of guys that have got a great attitude. These young boys, great head on their shoulders. And we just keep working hard. Keep doing what the coach is doing. Keep learning. And just keep pushing harder. And things will turn, mate. You keep doing the right things, it'll happen. So, in that dressing room is also his son, Kyle. How difficult do you think this would be for him? Because he's going to have to front up on the weekend with this club? No doubt. No doubt. Kyle was one of the first players in through the doors this morning, though. Knowing what he would face, I guess. More than the most. You know, he knew that his dad wouldn't be the coach this weekend. The players were unaware when they came to Wollongong for training this morning. By then, the reports had already broken that he was no longer going to be the coach. But, yeah, it's tough for Kyle. They're a close family. Kyle's a contracted player through to the end of 2027. And, yes, we will provide every means possible to support Kyle. And as we have, we'll continue to support Shane. Kyle's been the brunt of lots of criticism of late. He's a good kid. I know him well. I like him. He's very respectful. So, hopefully, this is a bit of a break for him as well, away from that scrutiny surrounding his dad and selection and these sorts of things. Why do you think the club chose now? They've got the Anzac Day match this weekend and then they have the bye. Do you think that they could have waited the extra week and gone into the bye and dealt with this? Or why do you think now is the time? I think in an ideal world, that would have been the play. But I think it's just too far gone. I think the situation is just too far gone. I think Shane had come to the realisation that he wasn't the best man to coach the club anymore. And once you come to that conclusion, well, there's no other option. When things are going bad, they're going bad. You know, some of the young boys got a chance tonight. You know, they tried hard as well. But we're just not getting it done, you know. We can try hard. NRL's not about trying hard. I think every team, every person in the competition tries hard. And you don't get points for trying hard. They said this morning that they haven't made a decision yet on their interim coach. Do you think they'd be looking across at Manly, who sacked their coach, handed Kieran Fore in the reins for the time being, and just kind of watched them climb up the ladder? Do you think they'd be hoping they have a similar result? What's the bar for them this season? I guess to win a game would be a start for them. But no, I don't think they'd be able to replicate what Manly have had. Because Manly have got this roster that had underperformed, right? Whilst the Dragons have underperformed, I don't think anyone had them as, you know, top eight hopes at all. So that's the way this has played out. Now where Manly have got some really elite talent that can win a game for them, the Dragons don't have that. So, yeah, there's no interim coach yet. We will communicate our interim coaching arrangements following discussions with our coaching staff today. There's a board meeting tomorrow. Hopefully they can work it out before then, because it is a little bit embarrassing to not have anyone in charge of your footy site, even if it is for 24 hours. So what are they looking for in their next senior coach? When they sit down and start this search and they've got the rest of this year to do it, what are they looking for? Well, that's going to be the interesting thing, right? What do they look for? What do they need to do? How it needs to play out? You know, it's probably two options. One's Dean Young, who's the assistant coach at the moment. And, you know, if they do give him the job, he'll be catapulted into the interim capacity in the short term. The other one is Ben Hornby, the 2010 Premiership winning captain, who's now Wayne Bennett's right-hand man at South Sydney. I think whoever takes control of this club understands that there will be a significant amount of pressure and expectation, and rightly so. Our job is to get to the right solution, ensure that we've got the right person and people in charge of this organisation. They're probably the two leading candidates. I wouldn't assume that there would be anyone else really in the mix. So, yeah, they're the two. If you were an assistant coach, say, at another club across the competition, would you be looking at the Dragons and thinking they are a possible destination club for you, or would you be looking at them thinking, geez, that's going to be a hard job? I think the benefit around it is that there's not a lot of players contracted long term, so it's probably only a little bit of pain. Usually when a coach comes in, a new coach comes in, he's got to wear two or three years of pain because of legacy contracts. That's not going to be the case here. The guys that I was probably critical of in terms of their deals, they expire at the end of next year. So it's actually not the worst spot or the worst club to be at. If you're someone like Keon Kolamatangi, who is heading to the Dragons next year, what are you thinking? Well, I spoke to him on the field for ABC after the game on Saturday, and I asked him that question, are you still committed to going to the Dragons? Yeah, I signed a contract. Yeah, I'm going to be there. So I've just got one more year here and no five years there. So obviously a lot can change in a year, but yeah, I've got it. I'm not doing anything. But no doubt he'd be having some thoughts going, oh, would I really be making that same choice again? Where does it leave the club more broadly? They won their last premiership, as you say, in 2010. Do you think that this move has moved them forward closer to competing, or do you think it has set them back? They're no closer to competing this week, without Shane there. So as I said, they need to rejigger the roster. They need to rejigger that roster desperately. And without that, there's no chance of competing anytime soon. I'm going to speak to three groups, to our fans, our supporters and our members, our results on the field, and our performance is not to your expectation. It is not to our expectation, and we are clearly taking steps to address this. What do they need, apart from an upgraded roster, but what do you think that this club does need, on-field or off-field, to be back competing in the pointy end of the season? On-field, it's definitely like I've been banging on is their roster, right? Like they just need to rejigger it, get some top-end talent in, like Calumatangi. Off the back of that, they need a bit more stability. The board is legacy issues with the board from either side of it, which is continued. But I'd say the number one factor would be, or is, some top-end talent. Michael Kariannis, two coaches in seven rounds. The NRL really is a rollercoaster. Thanks so much for picking us through this one. No worries. Anytime. Headlines. Staying with NRL, and we are at the point of the season where injuries draw origin availability into question, and Payne Haas has been ruled out of the opener with an MCL injury that will keep him out for six to eight weeks. Add to that Tom Dravojevic's hamstring injury, and the New South Wales team might have some fresh faces this year. Speaking of injuries, the AFL was no better, with the big news being the Western Bulldogs confirming that Sam Darcy has indeed ruptured his ACL and will miss the rest of the season. Carlton have ruled Elijah Hollands out of their clash this weekend with Fremantle after he experienced what the club are calling an unprecedented mental health episode during their match against Collingwood on Thursday night. The AFL has asked the club to investigate and share their findings with the league. Former NRL star Zach Lomax, who actually once played for the Dragons, had his first start in Super Rugby for the Western Force after coming off the bench last week. It would seem he's adapted well to the code switch, scoring a try in their thrilling comeback over the Crusaders. Here's Donaldson, flips it across, here's the moment, Lomax in the corner, welcome to the West. There has been a lot of chat about sprinting on this podcast recently, and you know what? It's not going to stop. As long as we have Australians running super fast, and Eddie Nkia has added his name to that list. He broke the Australian all-conditions record over 100 metres, covering the distance in 9.84 seconds. But an illegal tailwind means it won't count as a national record. Patrick Johnson's days as the national champion appear numbered. In the Premier League, Man City continue to catch Arsenal, beating them 2-1 over the weekend. It's arriving. Holland! Manchester City have trailed Arsenal in the table for so long this season. Is this resurrection day? Is this when City come back to life? The Gunners are clinging to a three-point lead at the top of the table with a little over a month to go in the season. One to watch with interest. Golf and Australian Hannah Green is on a hot streak in the LPGA, winning the LA Championship, her fourth win in five starts. She came from six shots behind in the final round to push it to a playoff, and birdied the first hole to take the title. I'm Poppy Penny, and this is ABC Sport Daily, produced by Declan Byrne. Thanks to Stan Sport for the extra audio used in this episode.

episodes.title: Peter Bol on winning, parenthood and the joy of running
episodes.description: Peter Bol is a five-time 800m national champion and after winning that title last weekend, next on his list is trying to win gold at the Commonwealth Games later this year.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Pete gets away in the stretch. Can he make it to fifth? Boys won't come away. And April Rahman's coming home hard. Boll stretching away. It's not a big margin, but it's enough. And he celebrated just before the line. To win one national title is impressive, but five is downright incredible. Peter Boll is the 800 metre champion again, and it means he's heading to his second Commonwealth Games, hoping to go one better than his silver medal back in 2022. Since his last appearance at that event, he's spent time out of the sport, become a father and worked a heck of a lot on the mental side of competition. After disappointing results at the Paris Olympics and recent World Championships, Boll is shaping up to return to the global stage. How is he feeling about that challenge? We ask him. I'm Pobby Penny, and this is ABC Sport Daily. Peter Boll is the national 800 metre champion for a fifth time and has qualified for his second Commonwealth Games. Peter, you've held on to your national title. What does that mean to you? Oh, it means, I guess, a lot. I've always wanted to win the national championship multiple times. So to be able to do it five times is quite special. To do it once, it's like anyone can do it twice, you might fluke it. But five times, you're kind of like, yeah, I'm that guy. I can do it multiple times. Yep, Pete, we can count as well. It's a handful. It's five of the best Australian championships. What kind of confidence does it give you? Yeah, I think track and field is all that confidence. So winning at home gives you the confidence to be able to go overseas. And obviously taking that confidence over there, it's a big advantage. So in terms of international, it's a huge confidence boost. And also personally, just to know that you can continue to perform at the track at the highest level consistently is great. We know that your best is among the best in the world. Where do you feel you're at at the moment? I mean, I just came, great question. I just came back from world indoors and I was fourth. I would say probably around the world at the moment, I'd be within that top 10, which is a good place to be. But we always, you know, track is a brutal sport. No one really knows beyond top three. So you got to be in that top three position. So we've got a little bit more work to do. But yeah, definitely, I think around that top 10 in the world at the moment. What does that work look like for you heading into the Comm Games? A lot of physical training, obviously. The physical demand is there, but also a lot of mental training and just making sure that confidence is always there. Mentally sharp, making sure that you're resilient, handling pressure, all those things. As I say, that result on the weekend does mean you're heading to the Commonwealth Games. You didn't have the Olympics you probably hoped for in Paris. You missed the final at the World Athletics Championships last year. How are you feeling about pulling on the green and gold again on an international stage like this one? It's always a privilege to be able to put on the green and gold and represent yourself and your family and everything you can understand for. So despite whatever result that previously happened, you know, that pride is always there, which is just kind of consistent, which is cool. Yeah, maybe the drive is a little bit different sometimes with more disappointments. But no, I'm pretty resilient and I'm happy for the challenge and always looking forward to the challenge. So I'm really excited to be able to go to my second Commonwealth Games. And I was second last time at Birmingham. And to be able to do one better would be incredible. Do you use those performances where you didn't perhaps get the results you were after as fuel? Yeah, use it as fuel and as like just mental prep. You've got to watch those tape. You've got to be able to sit down and watch those bad races and like why did it go that way? What could I have done better? What do we need to work on? And all that. And that's something with your whole team. So that's not just something for me to do alone. I've got my coaches. I've got my manager, you know, because most performances, bad performances happen off the track. You know, the bad decisions you kind of made, the races you didn't do and or maybe training a little bit too hard or the lifestyle was a bit too hectic, whatever it is. So everything kind of has to come in one. The physical part generally is pretty good. It's getting everything else together. How hard do you work on the mental side of what you do? It's really hard. And I think that's why I've been able to be consistent, you know, getting a fifth championship, but also being able to run at a high quality as such for so many different years. Peter Boll and Josh Ralph. And here comes Mason Cohen. So Ralph and Boll finding it out. Boll is holding. Ralph trying to come in. Cohen flashing late. Boll still holding. Ralph's coming. It's going to be a dip. So I've been running for years now and still have the highest quality. And that's credible, but more so the mental side of things. We know you had time out of the sport in 2023 with the anti-doping investigation, which obviously you were eventually cleared of. Are you running with a point to prove? No, I'm never running with no point to prove. I'm just running for the joy of it. And that's what makes it, I guess, inspiring. But that's what gives me purpose. You know, I'm not running to prove anyone or do anything. I'm just running for my own joy and to present myself, my country. And that's what I run for. Do you still get joy out of running? Yeah. I mean, yeah, like when you win your fifth national title, that's pretty exciting. If you don't, I think it's time to hang up the spikes and you will know when that is because I won't be on the track. Well, we hope that's still a little while off anyway. You've become a father in the last couple of years as well. Has that changed your approach to training or competing or what your motivations are at all? Yeah, in a sense, it's like, well, I think it just made it more purposeful. Like, because time is everything. And, you know, literally in our sport, time is everything. But also time away is everything. So if I'm spending time away in training, so it better be something that I enjoy doing and love to do. And that's going to inspire my family and my daughter. So I take it quite seriously. I guess probably more seriously than before. I think before we kind of take it for granted. But now it's like, oh, well, yeah, I really want to do this. Athletes in their 30s, I think it's only natural to start looking at what the future looks like. And we start asking these questions. You mentioned you still get joy out of running. So you're not hanging the spikes up just yet. But what does it look like for you post Commonwealth Games? Is it all eyes on LA in 2028? Yeah, we take it one year at a time. And, you know, Comm Games is the major focus this year. Nationals was just a major focus. And now we shift to Comm Games. And after Comm Games, we shift to the World Championship next year. And then there's LA. So it's always, you know, we take it step by step. Because, you know, to be able to do something great as the Olympics, everything kind of got to work out well. You know, the training at home, the championships at home. There's no point in dreaming for LA without having everything else planned. You know, we don't want to just rock up to LA and say, oh, wow, it's the fourth Olympic Games. Want to be able to be there and be competitive to do that. You've got to focus on smaller projects leading up to that. Have you thought at all about a Brisbane Olympic appearance? When is that? It's the one after LA. No, I haven't gave too much thought about it. I mean, I've seen everything that's going around and how much excitement is around Brisbane and, you know, how much athletics in Australia has picked up. So I'm sure that will be a fantastic Olympics. But I haven't thought too much about it in terms of competition-wise. But, yeah, definitely been seeing everything around the campaign. As you mentioned, it is an exciting time for athletics fans. And in particular, I know everyone is excited about an athlete that you're close to. And that's Gout Gout. You've said previously he's like a little brother to you. How did you feel watching him run that blistering 200 on the weekend? I mean, it's always incredible to share the same track with such elite, elite, elite performance. You know, that's the fastest junior that we're seeing. And he performed on that track like just an hour after I performed. So it's nice to be able to be there to perform and share that track with him. Gout's in front. He's coming away now for Murphy. Can he be as quick as this morning? Incredible. Oh, 19.68. Where's the win? The win's legal. He has absolutely done what everybody thought he might. But he's done it at 18 years of age. You know, just watching him grow physically, mentally, and it's been awesome because obviously we've got a little bit more of a personal relationship. So it's been great to watch that and super pumped and super excited to see what he is able to produce. I think we've still got so much more to go. He's just getting started, really. Have you spoken to him? What advice have you given to him? I actually try not to give him much advice because I think he's just doing his thing and he's got his support team that are wonderful and everything's working. If he needs something, you know, Gout is super sharp. If he needs anything, he'll reach out. And so far, he's got it all under control. The best I can do is just be there. Just be a friend and brother to him. And that sometimes doesn't require any advice. It just requires being there. Peter Boll, congratulations on your fifth national title. We can't wait to see you at the Commonwealth Games. Thanks so much for your time. No, thank you. Thank you for having me. I hope you enjoyed that little Saturday special. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily produced by Declan Byrne. We'll be back in your feeds on Monday. Catch you then. Thanks to Australian Athletics for the extra audio used in this episode.

episodes.title: Fri Fix: LIV Golf's murky future and Netball Australia chooses eyeballs over money
episodes.description: LIV Golf has had a rollercoaster 24-hours. Rumours started to swirl that the league would have to fold due to funding cuts then the CEO poured cold water on that then their broadcast went off air for two hours.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. You know, it was a lot of reaching and grabbing for headlines and clickbait and stories. For us, it's like we're business as usual, but if you want to ask me if this business is tough, I would say absolutely. That was Live Golf CEO Scott O'Neill at the top of their broadcast from Mexico City before it actually went off air for a couple of hours due to power outages. Bad timing for the Rebel Golf League, with rumours swirling that the Saudi-backed public investment fund was going to pull their funding, putting the future of the league in doubt. Is golf's big disruptor about to be disrupted? And Netball Australia has signed a new TV rights deal, putting the sport back on free-to-air. It's an organisation that has been plagued by financial problems in recent times. So how might this help? I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. Dean Bilton is a journalist with the ABC and he's been following this story as it unfolded over the last couple of days. Dean, all the talk yesterday morning was that Live was set to fold. Then there was an email from the CEO essentially saying nothing to see here. And then the event in Mexico City got underway, albeit with a couple of hours off air due to power outages. Can you fill in the blanks for us? I feel like everyone's still catching up on the blanks because it changed hour to hour. It basically started from a couple of like Twitter accounts effectively saying there's some big news coming for Live, hinting at, you know, potential trouble ahead. That kind of spiralled and eventually came through reports from the Financial Times and the New York Times, The Athletic, Golf Digest, like proper reporting from journalists both inside and outside the golf world that, without putting any strict timeframes on it, suggested that the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, which has been bankrolling Live from the start, are effectively going to pull their financial support. You know, having been in private equity now for over a dozen years, this is the process you go through. And sometimes it's not smooth and sometimes it's not easy. But I can tell you, given the momentum of this business, we're really excited about where we are and the position where we are. The reports didn't specify if that was going to happen today, if that was going to happen at the end of this 2026 season. But all the reports were pretty consistent in saying that the PIF is changing direction, moving away from the very heavy investment they've been making in global sport. And that is going to effectively see Live without a financial backer. As you say, Scott O'Neill, the CEO of Live Golf, who took over from Greg Norman about 18 months ago now, sent out a company-wide memo to everybody in Live, which conveniently made its way into the media, into the wider public, basically saying, full throttle, full steam ahead for the rest of this season, nothing to see here. We're changing the game. We're pioneers. Kept referring to Live Golf as a startup, which is very cute. Don't worry about it. We're teeing off in Mexico tomorrow. Everything is going fine. Live has always been very public and open and proud of the long-term backing that the PIF has offered. And they've spoken about, you know, we're totally funded through to 2030 to 2032. They've bragged about this and they've used that as a selling point to sponsors and investors. And now this email comes out in the wake of this reporting and suddenly nine more events in 2026 is the most that they can promise. Scott O'Neill has since spoken after the power came back on in Mexico today on the Live Golf broadcast. And without saying it particularly out loud, kind of admitted that a little bit himself. You know, this notion of, do you have to raise money? Probably. Like, this is business. From my vantage point, it doesn't look like it's going to have a happy ending for Live Golf. So if Live Golf does go under beyond 2026, what does it mean for the players who left the PGA Tour to join Live Golf? Do you think that the PGA would welcome them back or is there going to be a lot more to it than that? It's so hard to tell. And I think it's going to vary player to player. The PGA Tour earlier this year, around about conveniently the exact same time that Brooks Koepka came out and said he wanted to leave Live and return to the PGA Tour, opened up this very brief window, this amnesty period for a select handful of players via this arbitrary list of criteria that the Tour just created themselves. Effectively saying Bryson DeChambeau, John Rahm, Cameron Smith, a couple of others. If you would like to come back, you tell us in the next week and we'll have you back with some financial restrictions placed, but no suspension. In that period, Koepka did return to the PGA Tour, but the others all stayed where they were. Now, if Live Golf is not an entity at all going forward, or if it's not an entity with the same sort of financial backing that drew the players there in the first place, it's hard to imagine, you know, the likes of Rahm and DeChambeau, who's been trying to negotiate an insanely lucrative contract with Live over the last few months. Cameron Smith as well and others are going to want to stick around on this Tour for much, much less money than what they were initially promised. So at that point, the cards, you know, it kind of falls to the PGA Tour. Do they open this amnesty period again and say, all is forgiven, don't worry about it, you guys come on back? It would be great for them to have these sort of players back, but then you definitely risk peeving off the entire rest of the PGA Tour field, who stayed true to the Tour and didn't leave when they were presented with the money in the first place. So that's going to be a delicate balance. It's a bit of an unknown because the PGA Tour has kind of been making it up as it goes along as well. The other interesting thing, Dean, is that Live has made commitments to hosting events around the world, including in Adelaide, which we know is a really successful event, both for the competition and for South Australia. What happens there with those commitments? Yeah, that's a big question. I mean, Live Adelaide is probably the event on the Live calendar. It's by far the most successful. We had 5.5 million people turn into our event in Australia with the great Anthony Kim win, the Rocky Balboa story of today. It was the largest golf event in the history of the country. The question then becomes, does Live still exist next year, either as the same version, if they manage to find the exact same amount of money that the Saudi PIF has put into them, which is highly unlikely, or if it is continued backed by some other investor, which seems the only way that Live will continue beyond this year. Live Adelaide probably does still exist at that stage, but then does Bryson come? Is John Rahm still on the tour to come? Does the event still exist, but with a version of, you know, the bottom rung of Live players, plus whoever else they managed to get in to fill the field? Does Live Adelaide draw the same crowds if Cameron Smith, John Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau aren't there? We know how to put on a show. We know how to grow the game. I've seen the kids on the first tee. It's hard to imagine a world where Live Adelaide next year looks the same as it did this year, which is such a shame for Aussie golf. The biggest losers out of all of this are potentially Aussie golf fans. Dean Bilton, it feels like there is still plenty to play out here. Thanks so much for your time. Thanks, Bobby. Brittany Carter is a netball writer for the ABC, and Britt, broadcast right deals aren't often sexy for sports fans. But for netball, it could be really significant. It will return to Frida Air TV with this new deal. Why is this so important? This is really important, Poppy, because netball has been behind the paywall with Fox for the past five years. The average audience per match isn't that great. So in 2024, netball Australia revealed that audience was at 57,000 on average per game, which, as we know, isn't a lot. And so some of its bargaining power has been lost because of that and its ability to grab commercial deals and go out to tender for this broadcast deal. So the cost of the deal is less than what they would have got with Fox in 2021. So they're getting less cash injection at the time of this deal for 2027 and beyond. But they have to almost take a step backwards, get more eyeballs on the sport from a Frida Air audience and more of a casual fan. episodes.title: The emotional toll of Alexa Leary's traumatic brain injury
episodes.description: You might have seen Paralympian Alexa Leary winning gold medals, dancing on the pool deck and giving the most bubbly and joyous interviews.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Love it. I'm so proud of myself. I'll really tell you that. I am so proud of myself. You might have seen one of Alexa Leary's incredible poolside interviews. She's bubbly, fun, the life of the party and at the Paris Paralympics she won two gold medals and broke two world records. Before all that though, Leary had a serious cycling accident at age 19. Her parents were told to say their goodbyes multiple times. Well, Leary's just released a book called Sink or Swim, which documents her second life. And she joins us today to bring us into her reality of living with a traumatic brain injury for the rest of her life. I'm Declan Byrne. This is ABC Sport Daily. Alexa, firstly, congrats on the book release. How are you feeling about it? Yeah, I'm feeling really good. I'm really happy that the book is finally out. Like it's been a year or so now and I'm like, yes, it's out. It's out. I always imagine the coolest bit is when you get it, you get to see it. It's in your hands. You can smell the pages. What was it like when you got that first hard copy? Oh, I couldn't believe it. I had like a little tear in my eye because I was like, I'm so happy this is finally out. Like it just made me so happy and proud for how much it's taken and time like that. It's amazing. And what about the hardest part? Because I kind of think that's the cool bit, but the hardest part is the actual writing. What was the toughest bit? So like to get it out all on the paper, like to get it all out, to say the truth, to just put out the truth of my accident and even before and after. It was just so much to say that. And also the biggest thing is like bringing in about a traumatic brain injury. There was just a lot of factors in there that it was hard for me to talk about, but I wanted to share it in the book. So it was really incredible putting it on there. Did you have to make a commitment to write something down or to someone to be like, I'm going to be, you know, an open book, all the good bits and all the bad bits are going in. Yeah. So like, I didn't want to put some bits in it, but then I got to terms of going, you know, Lex, it's a good thing to do that because it's going to help a lot of other people. So that's how I felt upon doing it. Was that the goal? Did you have something from the start that it was about helping other people? Yeah, of course. And also bringing awareness of traumatic brain injuries because it's something that I suffer with for the rest of my life. And, you know, it's going to bring out so much awareness. You wrote it with Ali Pascoe. The book features not only your voice, but lots of people close to you. So your parents, your brothers and sisters, doctors. For people who don't know, you had that cycling accident, age 19, resulted in your traumatic brain injury, which is, you know, a lot of what the book is about. But reading those early parts, parts that you don't remember, you say you don't remember anything about it, anything before it, really tiny snippets, but now it's down on paper. What was it like to, I guess you would have heard bits and pieces and you were taken back to the scene, but what was it like to see it written down by these people who experienced it, you know, firsthand? Yeah, no, it was a lot because, you know, after the accident happened, my parents had to like fully sit me down and talk to me and tell me because I wiped all my memory and everything from the day of the accident. Like the neuro doctor said, I won't have four to five year prior, like any memory. So it was really hard for me to process the accident. And yeah, that was just like a hard factor to actually even see the photos and things on paper. It was, it's really hard even reading, reading it in the book. It got me like, I did cry because it was like hard to read my brain. I was so bad in the accident, like in the hospital, I couldn't walk and talk. So I was gone. My brain was out, but in rehab, I had to come to terms with it. I'm living a second life flex. Like you've got to, you've got to realize this. And that's why my parents had to sit me down and tell me exactly the story. Reading it and knowing you from like an outsider's perspective, someone who's seen the videos of you as this like bubbly, fun person, this who's full of life, you know, the way you talk about music and living your life. I just can't hold back. I've just got to let go. I've got to get the, got to get the guns out and go for it. I can't stop myself. And then reading the book, it was really eyeopening. Do you think that's what you want people's reaction to be is to, to see the entire spectrum of what you live with? Yeah. Because like people just think, oh, she fell off a bike. Oh, that's, that's it. It's like, oh no, no, I'm living a full second life. Like I have severe traumatic brain injury, like damage in my brain. It's changed my whole life. And so that's like, it's, it's difficult. It's really hard living with the TBI. I have to be honest with you right now. It's so hard. The heightened emotions is one thing that you hear about. Tell us day to day where that shows up. Yeah. So my emotions go insane. I get sad, happy, angry, depressed in a day, in a second. It's like insane. And my emotions is just, oh my goodness. Like I can't even explain to you. That's why I have a behavior coach to help me guide me into the right direction of my behavior. But honestly, oh, when I wake up, I don't even know who I am sometimes from the memory. It's just, it's really hard. I have to be honest with you right now. It's so hard. How are you doing today? Well, this is a stressful day, you know, telling people about your book and about these hard parts of your life. Yeah. It's actually been a very busy day. And sometimes I don't remember, but it's okay. My brain's like 50 first dates, but it's fine. So when you say you wake up, does it take a second to work out what mood am I in? Like, what is my brain giving me in this moment? Yeah. And like mostly every night before I go to bed, I do write out my notes of what I'm doing the next day. So I'm on board with what I'm doing. So I know that my, to try tame my emotions, to not make them so heightened. So that's a big thing that I have to do, which is it's hard. So after the accident, how long was it before you were again swimming? Because doctors said to your parents, they said a few times, be prepared to say goodbye. They said you mightn't walk or talk again. Yet it wasn't that long before you were swimming again and competitively. Yeah. So like when I got out of the hospital, the neuro doctors literally said to my mom and dad, like we want to get Lex's right side because I'm physically damaged from the brain. So I destroyed my left side, which made my right physically damaged. And so now I'm left-handed. Weirdly. I was always right, but now I'm lefty. Yeah. I'm left-handed now. My right is really hard. I'm always a physio and things like that, but it's hard. Anyway, so the neuro doctors were like, get in, swim, and we want to get her to try work the right side. And that's where it all started. And literally it was just, I had passion and I was like, I want more than just, you know, rehab. I've had a massive accident. I've got to go out there and do something good for myself. So that was the biggest goal. And I don't know, look where it's got me. I'm like, yes, Lex, you did it. Hey. She is on fire. She is not holding anything back for Singapore. Stand by for the world record line to be within touching distance. There it is. Can Alexa Leary hunt it down. Your dad talked about in the book, like channeling that anger that you had. So that emotion into swimming, was that how you saw it? When you got in the pool, you were able to harness all this energy. Yeah. A hundred percent. Like, you know, cause I was frustrated. Like I'm living a whole second life. I was just always like, I want, I want this, I want my old life. But if I think about it, I go, no, I don't. I love who I am now where I'm learning to accept her and understand her. But yeah, no, it's just, I don't know. Life is just hard. It can be like, honestly, it is difficult. And making the Paralympics is extremely hard. It's, it's beyond just living a hard life. So how does your, your TBI affect training that those tough sessions in the pool, which you have to do if you want to be a gold medalist like you are? Yeah. Like, honestly, it's tough because like, especially with like my behavior, like every morning at training and I'm training my little heart out and stuff like that, but it's really debatable on my emotions and behavior. To be honest with you, it's, it's, it's difficult, but like I get through it and it's like, I don't know. I'm very, I'm very determined and passionate person. When I want something, I'm not, I'm going to fight for it. And that's what I've done since getting out of the hospital, even in the hospital. I, I fought to walk and talk again, but I've just had that mindset. You fought all the way to the Paris Paralympics, world records, a couple of golds, a silver. That is crazy. Have you, are you able to fully comprehend just how wild that journey is in the space of three or four years? I know it's incredible. And I'm so proud of myself for how far I've actually come, but it like took me a bit of time to process when I won. Cause like with my brain, it's like the process of things, it takes a long time. And I was literally like, when I want to tap the water, my, like everyone was like, like I won. And I was like a shock. episodes.title: Does the Lance Collard hearing raise more questions than answers?
episodes.description: St Kilda’s Lance Collard has been handed a nine-week suspension from the AFL tribunal for a homophobic slur during a VFL match last month.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. You could argue that the word has been in his vocabulary at some point in the past. You could equally argue that he more than most should deeply know the impact of it, given what he's gone through. That's the CEO of the AFL Players Association, James Gallagher, on some of the intricate considerations surrounding the handing down of St Kilda's Lance Collard's nine-week suspension for using a homophobic slur in a VFL match. The fact this incident went to a disciplinary hearing was unusual in the first place. There was extensive questioning of witnesses and between the hearing and deliberations, it went for three days. It feels now that we might have more questions than answers. What's the balance between punishment and prevention? Could the way this played out be a deterrent for others in reporting things they hear on field? And given how many parties were involved and impacted, were there any winners out of this? Yes. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. Marnie Vinyl is a multi-award winning journalist with the ABC and has been following this tribunal hearing since it started way back on Thursday last week. Marnie, firstly, can you explain to us the penalty that Collard has been handed and the reasoning that the tribunal gave? Yeah. So Lance Collard, 21-year-old player at St Kilda, he has been handed a nine-week suspension with two of those weeks suspended. So basically looking at a seven-week suspension, and this is following his 2024 suspension for using the exact same slur in which he received six weeks. So it was debated a lot what this sanction should look like with the AFL going pretty hard that it has to be more than six weeks, given that was his original sanction. And Jeff Gleeson, the tribunal chair, he did really acknowledge the impact that this kind of homophobic language can have on the community. As he handed down his sanction, he really did stress that Hayley Conway, the CEO of Pride Cup, who gave evidence in that initial hearing, her words where she said that this can have really lasting impacts on the queer community within the AFL. And we know that, you know, there's no openly gay men currently playing within the AFL and a lot of players feel like they have to hide their sexuality through all levels of football. And so homophobic language can be really harmful and also a deterrence to keep those players within the system. So noting that they thought that the slur had to have a pretty big consequence. One thing that was interesting to me in the disciplinary hearing was Jeff Gleeson asking whether a lengthy suspension would serve to simply punish or if it would act as an actual preventative measure or a deterrent to discourage not only Collard, but other players from using this kind of language. Where do you think they landed on that point? It's an interesting point that the AFL and the tribunal are kind of wrestling with because we're seeing these really hefty sanctions handed down in the AFL's crackdown on homophobic language that has spanned the last three years. But then they're wrestling with, well, okay, how do we get the balance right? Preventing the language from being used in the first place. Sanctioning and penalty can't be the only response. You know, it has a role to play, but at the moment it's kind of being seen as the solution and it's not. The solution has to start much earlier. Because Collard was suspended back in 2024 for six weeks for using a homophobic slur. And then two years later, he's back and he's now facing the tribunal for the exact same slur. So how do we make sure that these penalties are actually working? The fact that this even made it to the tribunal, I think is interesting in itself, because if we think back to other instances of homophobic language being used on the footy field, like the Isaac Rankin or the Jack Graham instance, which we saw last year, the AFL made their decision on suspensions and penalties behind closed doors. So the fact that it played out in a tribunal was very interesting. Why was that the case? Yeah, the first disciplinary hearing in AFL history, which made it pretty significant. And like you mentioned, there's been so many cases of homophobic language being sanctioned. Isaac has received a format sanction for using a homophobic slur towards a Collingwood opponent. The language used was offensive, hurtful and highly inappropriate. But in those cases, all those players pled guilty. And one of the reasons that Collards was so hefty this time is the tribunal said, well, he showed no remorse. So in him pleading not guilty, they decided that there should be no discount to that penalty where previously, well, the only kind of statements that players say, or we hear from players around these cases is usually just an apology that feels very put together with the club, where in this particular case, we got to hear from Collard himself. We got to hear from the players who reported the slur in the first place. We got to hear about Collard's background. There were so many elements that were really uncovered during this process that we've just never seen before. When you've got two versions of events, it's not a great place to start from when dealing with really challenging issues that the game is facing. On the first day of these hearings, you mentioned the Frankston players who reported the slur in the first place. They gave evidence to the disciplinary hearing and they were examined extensively. They've also received unsavoury attention on social media in the wake of all of this. Is there a risk that the way that this has played out for them might discourage others from coming forward at any level of footy? I found it very interesting when those two Frankston players were giving evidence in that first hearing because it kind of became very apparent that they did not want to be there. I mean, the second player who gave evidence said that they were told they would just have to make an initial statement on game day and that would be it. And rather it snowballed into, as he put it, this whole thing. He said that he was quite hesitant to give evidence, but when he said that, he was told that he might be compelled to do so, so legally required to attend the tribunal. And as you mentioned, they were cross-examined extensively. There were reports that the cross-examination was quite gruelling and they were really questioned and had their integrity in a way questioned. And because the players had to be publicly named when they gave evidence, it meant that social media could weigh in on the evidence, but also on them as people. And so these two players have now been named across social media in a lot of commentary that is, as you say, unsavoury, but I would argue weighs into abuse. What we've seen again is a process that ultimately has caused harm all over the place. The AFL Players Association have also released a statement today criticising the process. What is their argument about how cases like this one can maybe be better handled in the future? So the AFLPA did come out with a pretty lengthy statement and they really did lament the process. I think we've got a lot of work to do to set up, you know, really bespoke processes that should lead us to the outcome. I think having some clarity about what those outcomes might look like is helpful for the game. I think we saw that through COVID. I think that was really helpful for the game. It meant that we were able to get through issues and incidents quickly with clarity for everyone involved. They want a lot more of a nuanced and I guess compassionate look when it comes to this kind of process. They want things like diverse backgrounds to be taken into account, the harm that these kind of hearings that play out publicly can have on the queer community, but also the First Nations community. We know that Lance Collard is a First Nations man, as is Isaac Rankin. And so all of these communities that are really harmed through such a public case as this, to be taken into account on how these matters are handled. Collard's background and upbringing was actually raised as part of the evidence for this. What were they asking to be considered? And I guess how might the AFLPA want that to be more inclusive in the future? Yeah, it was raised a lot. I mean, this is a 21-year-old Indigenous player who's come into the AFL system. And we know that some Indigenous players can struggle when they're moved away from community and, you know, putting these clubs in the city. And it was mentioned quite a lot during the hearing. I mean, Lance Collard now lives with Nazaya Wanganin-Millera. That's a fact I'm not sure the public knew before this because together they're trying to assert themselves as positive role models on other young Indigenous men. And the Saints lawyer really stressed just how much work Collard had been doing in this particular area. You know, I spoke to people this morning who said, that it is not excusing Collard's use of that language at all. It is unacceptable. And it's a word that he knows is unacceptable because he's been sanctioned before. He's done the training. He's been explicitly told how unacceptable it is. But he's a young Indigenous man who grew up in a community where words like this were said quite a lot. And that is a generational consequences of Indigenous communities across Australia. And I'm no expert at all to talk about that. But it is a factor that played so heavily into this particular hearing. I mean, the Saints lawyer said that when he was arguing for a fine or a lesser sanction, that this could be a sliding doors moment where you've got a kid from a hard background who could slide back on the wrong path and potentially have this sanction ruined his life. My understanding is he's, whether devastated is too strong a word, but like he's deeply impacted obviously by this outcome. He's gone, gone back to WA to spend some time with family. As with any tribunal case, clubs are able to appeal the outcome. What are the options for Collard and St Kilda from here? So St Kilda have five days to decide what they're going to do about this. They've got the five days to assess any appeal options. It'll be interesting to see whether they go down that path. I think if it was a fine or a lesser sanction, they might have accepted it. But nine weeks with those two suspended is a long time. And the Saints lawyer was pretty gung-ho during the hearing about just the toll that that could take on Collard. So I wouldn't be surprised if they decided to appeal. Marnie, broadly, if you look at the way that this played out over the three days fairly publicly, between Lance Collard, the players involved, the queer community and the Indigenous community, there are a lot of parties to consider. Do you see any winners out of this? No, none. I think that that's probably one of the main things is that the AFL have tried very hard to make a very public and loud stance when it comes to homophobia in football. And the way that they are doing that is with these really hefty sanctions when players are reported to say slurs on the football field. Inclusion and respect are key priorities for the AFL. They are central to who we are as a game and as an organisation. I know people in the LGBTQI plus community are hurting when an incident like this occurs. One incident is one too many. And the fact there have been multiple incidents over the last 18 months shows there is still much work to do. But we know that there's a cultural problem of homophobia within Australian sports, not just AFL and not just football. The researchers is there on that. And whether this is the right way to really tackle the issues that are affecting so many Australians. When it's a case like this that is so public, the queer community are further battered and bruised because, of course, you have social media who have an increase in homophobia. I mean, I personally feel like a few years ago, I never saw the F slur anywhere. And now I'm seeing it everywhere because every single time these cases come up, it emboldens corners of the internet to feel like they can use it and debate whether it's OK or not to be saying across social, well, to be saying anywhere. You have a lot of people across social media that are attacking the queer community and saying that they're too soft in all of this. And, you know, it's the queer community's fault that players are going to be sanctioned this particular way and have their careers ruined. And then you have the Indigenous community having a lot of people weighing in on the intersection of race in all of this. And then, of course, the players involved, they're impacted. So it does really feel like there are absolutely no winners when these really high profile cases play out. Is there a better way to handle it? It's a really good question. And I feel like it is far above my pay grade. In the ideal world, the homophobic language that is being used and being embedded in these players' minds is tackled first. So I would love to see prevention over punishment. I would love to see all clubs do more training. I would love to see people take this a lot more seriously. I would love to get to a stage where we have openly queer players in the AFL and we can talk about them without having to assess all the risk that them being open does. So it's a very big question, but I kind of just hope that the AFL are really taking all of this on board and listening to all of the voices that have so much to say about this because we're not seeing these sanctions going away, it seems. Marnie, it's been a big story. Thanks so much for stepping us through it. Thanks, Poppy. Port Adelaide's Zach Butters was also in front of the AFL tribunal last night for an incident between him and umpire Nick Foote on Sunday night. Butters was accused of having asked Foote, how much are they paying you? Which he strongly denied. The tribunal agreed with umpire Foote's recollection of events and Butters is set to pay a $1,500 fine. He spoke after the hearing. Incredibly disappointed with the result tonight. I stand by knowing what I said and what I didn't say, especially what I didn't say. Port Adelaide will have the option to appeal the decision. The Western Bulldogs might be looking for a list spot to bring in Prince Harry after he spent the morning at Witten Oval. He received tutoring from Adam Treloar on handballing and appeared to be quite the natural. He was actually there for a charity partnership, but it would bring a few more international eyeballs to the game. And in Super Rugby, Moana Pacifica are looking for new owners or they risk having to leave the competition entirely. The financially challenged club are currently sitting on the bottom of the table, having won just one game this season. It would make them the second club in two years to dissolve due to financial hardship after the Melbourne Rebels in 2024. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily produced by Declan Byrne. Thanks to SEN for the extra audio used in this episode.
