episodes.title: Patrick Johnson on the Australian sprinters coming for his record
episodes.description: Gout Gout and Lachie Kennedy were the headline acts at the 2026 Australian Athletics Championships and they didn’t disappoint.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Gout's in front. He's coming away now for Murphy. Can he be as quick as this morning? Oh, incredible. Oh, 19.68. Where's the wind? The wind's legal. He has absolutely done what everybody thought he might, but he's done it at 18 years of age. The world will be shaking. That's 18-year-old Gout Gout becoming the national champion in the 200 metres, running sub-20 seconds. Add to that result, Lockie Kennedy becoming the first Australian to run 100 metres under 10 seconds on Australian soil. We've been talking about the sprinting boom that's coming in Australia, and I think it's officially here. For over 20 years, Patrick Johnson has held the 100 metre record, but is it only a matter of time until it's broken? We ask him. I'm Poppy Penny, and this is ABC Sport Daily. Patrick Johnson is the fastest Australian over 100 metres for now. Patrick, you set a time of 9.93 back in 2003, but Lockie Kennedy is closing the gap. How did you feel over the weekend watching Kennedy run 9.96 twice? Oh, it was great to see you. I think it was something that I knew that we've got the talent in this country. I've always said that, and I sent a message out to Lockie and just said, congratulations and welcome to the sub-10 club again. And how's that feel? But I think like anything, this is the standard that we wanted to see in this country. And I'm happy to be the first, but I'd never want it to be the last. And I think there's proof in the pudding now with so many incredible athletes now coming out and running fast and not only in our sprints and our long distance, but our field events as well. So it's great to see track and field particularly getting that opportunity to really be on the world stage, which has always been a world sport. Kennedy clearly in front. Browning's having a really good run. How quick is it for Lockie? It's very, very quick again. It's 9.97. It may come down. It may come down to 9.96. It is spectacular. He's first Australian championship. He's a star. Is there a small part of you that wants to hang on to the record? Oh, not really. I think I was very honored to do it in 2003. And I've always been really clear that records are meant to be broken. And I did that a while ago. And I was really, really want the next generation to take over, take ownership of that. And now leading into Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, it's an incredible time. You've got LA coming up as well, Commonwealth Games. So there's incredible opportunities where the athletes now have something to look forward to and a home Olympics. Of course, I was able to go to Sydney Olympic Games in 2000, but a home Olympics is really different. I think there's a real sense of this country where the athletes see a future where they're all looking at, I want to be in the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. And it's only five years away. Lachie's been pretty clear that he has your record in his sights. The sky's the limit. Like I said, I want to try and go 9-8 this year. I definitely want to break the Aussie record. Do you get the feeling that it is only a matter of time before he gets there? How fast do you think he can go? I think the sky's the limit for Lachie and even some of the other sprinters, you know, Gout Gout and a few others coming through. I think you've got to have the standard. So you've got a standard to look for. Now you set the standard, your own standard, and what you look forward to. So I think there's a reality check here, what we run in Australia, what runs overseas. So there's a real opportunity to level that up, which I think, you know, as Australians, we've always been such a great country competing against the rest of the world. I think now in spritting and some of the other long distance events, we're just elevating where we should be. And it's timely, I think, for us to be a country that not only has a talent ability, but we have the opportunity to showcase it as well. What does it feel like to run sub 10 seconds? What would Lachie have been feeling on the weekend? Well, I think he put it very instinctively where it's very easy. Yeah, it just felt easy, you know, so I think I got a bit more in the tank, but I mean, it's good to see I'm in good form. And I think running fast, I mean, again, you forget the six hours a day of training and the mental strain and the commitment and the pressure, but running is pure connection. I mean, I say it's pure spirituality where you're connected to mind, body and soul. But I think Lachie sort of felt that it was so easy to run fast. The thing is now to duplicate that and be consistent, which is always going to be the reality where consistent, not only in Australia, but also against the international rivalry. You've got a lot of international athletes who can run fast. So the test will come is keep backing that up consistently. And then of course, leading it to Commonwealth Games or major championships or into Olympics, which is where you want to do your best. I want to make a bit of pattern of it. You know, I want to make it routine. I want to make it up to standard. You mentioned the other result that got a lot of sprinting fans talking across the weekend, and that's of course, Gout running 19.67 in the 200 meters. It's the new under 20s world record. It's a new national record by some distance, breaking the previous record, which he also held. What did you think as he came flying towards the finish? To me, it was about, it was great to see him enjoying his running. I think, you know, the expectation, the hype, the pressure on him, his coach and his family and everyone, I wanted him to get back to just running free for himself. And I think it was great to see him enjoying that because again, I think Melbourne showed he, he, he's still in great shape, but he had to work on a couple of technical things. Oh no, that definitely fired me up for sure. Knowing that 200 is my baby and I just had, I didn't put together a race I wanted to. So coming out here, I just want to prove to myself and the rest of the world that I'm here to stay. The best thing an athlete can do is work on himself or herself. And I think that just shows the opportunity where he went out and said, look, I've had that thinking in my head, I'm going to run fast. He's probably already done it in training, but he wanted to do it in a competition. And I think for him, I was more relieved that he was actually going back to him himself, run free, run free from pressure. Honestly, it's, it's good when people, you know, compare you to the best in the world. And then at the end of the day, I know I'm me, I'm doing my own thing. And I mean, there's no pressure for me because as soon as I go down and track, it's just me, the track, my spikes, and I go by myself. Run for who you are. And he came out and exceptionally not only himself, but a lot of the athletes behind him were able to go with him, which is probably the first time that you get the confidence that Aiden Murphy and a few other, Calum Law, that actually went with him and said, look, he's not unbeatable. He's just setting the standard for us. So we want to be able to go to that level as well. And I think that's what happens when you have a few great athletes coming out and performing well, you actually lift up the standard of all the other athletes because they believe they can win or they can be close to you. We have such incredible athletes in Australia and me being able to race these athletes and they've raced me, we push each other to the limits. And as you can see in our race, two Australians run sub 20. I mean, this is amazing. He's chosen the under 20s World Championships over the Commonwealth Games later this year. What did you make of that decision? Did you feel like it's the right one for him? Yeah, he's still young. And I think, you know, again, he's showing exceptional talent as a young age, but I feel there's an element here where you've got to let him be a young person, let him have fun, let him enjoy running. So I think we've got to remember that we put all this pressure on our young people to perform and be the best in the world, but we forget they're just kids as well. And they've got to have fun. And again, I'm really conscious that we do the sport because we have fun and we love it. So never forget that. Yes, there's pressure of yourself and your family and what you think and your sponsors. But when you get out there and run fast, I think you just want to do it for yourself and to your family and everyone else involved. But World Juniors is probably a really just a great stepping stone for him. We're not trying to, you know, it's a smart reality from his coach and his manager to say, look, there's five years. He's already shown exceptional talent leading into these couple of these major championships. Get his confidence up, get his training. He'll have his own growth spurts. He'll have his own technical areas or work on, but let him, let him do that. Tweaked a couple of little things, worked his hands a bit better, you know, just try to get his turnover better. And it worked. And I think this is a great decision by his manager and his coach and his family to say, look, let him just do the succession plan that he wants to do. And that's these races. And then he'll lead into those major, because he's got plenty of time. He's young. Let's let him make sure he enjoys what he does. And that's running fast. He is young and so is Lockie Kennedy. Gout's 18. Kennedy's only 22. Have you had much to do with either of them across the journey? And what advice would you be giving them? Oh, I send a message now and then to them just to, you know, wish him well, but also give them that sort of sense of empowerment and confidence. So I think to me, it's about succession planning or passing on knowledge or advice. And they can take it or leave it, of course. But I think I've proven, you know, even I wasn't young when I did it. I did it when I was 30 years old. So you could say I was totally different spectrums where you've got young people coming out running really super quick. I was a lot older when I did it. Good start by Matt Shervington on the outside. Kristen Malcolm got a fair start as well. Also going okay is Saudi Arabia and further out to Great Britain. Look to be well in front. Good bat in exchange to Dwayne Chambers. The Australians right there. Patrick Johnson trying to move up on the Italians. But it just proves it doesn't matter the age. It matters on who the support you've got around you and what's your plan ahead and your attack ahead around major championships training and whatnot. So for me, I just always send them a quick message usually to them and also their coaches. But yeah, I try to make sure that I have a low key approach to it because again, it's their glory. It's their opportunity. It's their time. I'm really keen to make sure the records I've set, they break it and go beyond and be the next superstars, which they already are. Kristen Malcolm They've both spoken about their friendship and the rivalry and the fact that it pushes each of them to be better and faster. And even though we didn't see them race against each other on the weekend, we know that that's the case. When you were racing, it was you and Matt Shervington sort of duking it out. What was that relationship like? And do you see a bit of that in these two? Matt Shervington Yeah, definitely. And I think, you know, Gowgow told what Lockie Kennedy did in the 100 metres and said, okay, he set the benchmark. And I think that's what we need. Matt Shervington This is what I've been waiting for. You know, right before this final, I went on my notes. Matt Shervington I set up running 1975 and 1967. Matt Shervington I think we've always loved rivalry, but we also love to see Australians winning. And I think if we work together, and I'm a big believer, it's not about them two competing against each other. It's more around us against the rest of the world. So if we push ourselves here in Australia, we're just proving now that Australia's always had the talent. We're just unearthing it and showing the point that we have the talent ability. And we're going to have more than just one or two people. We're going to have a collection of many athletes coming out from this country that are going to really contest it against. And we're already doing that as a small country. But I feel there's an element now in the world stage that they're going to go, what are you guys doing? We're just actually lifting up to the standard that we should have been probably 20 or 30 years ago. Matt Shervington It's unreal. Like the bars gets raised to everyone else. Like you got, you wouldn't have all these people out here running if it was just one of us being super good. episodes.title: Is Rory McIlroy's second Masters the start of his second act?
episodes.description: Because there's only one thing better than one green jacket. Rory McIlroy has made history again by winning consecutive Masters on a rollercoaster Sunday at Augusta and it might signal a second surge from one of golf's greats.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. And here we go. His year again. Rory is a rare repeat winner at Augusta. What's better than one green jacket? Two, obviously. After completing the career Grand Slam in 2025 by winning the one trophy that had eluded him, Rory McIlroy has gone back to back at the Masters. It was a wire to wire win for the Northern Irishman, but that doesn't tell you the half of it. A roller coaster Sunday saw McIlroy's six shot lead heading into the weekend evaporate into a two stroke deficit with a dozen holes to play. It's another legacy win for Rory. And who's to say that he's done with two? I'm Declan Byrne. This is ABC Sport Daily. Nicholas, Faldo, Woods and now McIlroy. The only men to go back to back at the Masters. Andrew Beaton writes for the Wall Street Journal. He walked Augusta National this week and was there to see Rory join some of the titans of the game. Andrew, let's start at the end. Take us to the 18th when Rory clinched a second green jacket. What was it like? Well, Rory McIlroy does not make anything easy. He goes into the final hole with a two stroke lead and all he has to do is avoid disaster to become the fourth player ever to win back to back Masters. And what does he do? He flirts with complete and total disaster. This is trouble. Uh-oh. This could be extremely dangerous depending on where this ends up. He sends his drive completely to the right. He doesn't know if he's going to even have a swing on the ball. And in Rory McIlroy fashion, disaster is on the table. All he needed to do was avoid a double bogey. And he managed to do just that with a bogey on the final hole. And when he looked up and screamed after tapping in the final putt, it might have just been as much relief as it was total jubilation. Last year after putting in on 18, he collapsed. There were tears of joy. It was joy today, but it was also maybe disbelief that he had made things so hard for himself. His parents were there. It was a roller coaster Sunday. How did you judge that reaction after he knew he'd won? Well, I think he talked openly about how he felt less of a burden this time around. Because last year, he wasn't just trying to win the Masters for the first time. He was trying to win the career Grand Slam. I thought it was so difficult to win last year because of trying to win the Masters and the Grand Slam. And then this year, I realized it's just really difficult to win the Masters. When he won, it was this kind of double whammy. It was something he had been chasing for over a decade. And two in one, he ends this major drought. He wins the Masters and boom, one fell swoop. And this year, he was kind of unburdened. He talked about that. But he also talked about how after winning the Masters last year, he struggled a bit with motivation. And then all of a sudden, he races out to this historic six-stroke lead after 36 holes. Then he struggles on Saturday, struggles out of the gate on Sunday. Oh, my goodness. Disaster for McIlroy at the floor. Three putts from five feet leads to a double bogey. And now Cam Young has a two-shot lead at the Masters. And you know what? Once again, even when things looked really rocky, he steeled himself and came out on top. It did get really tight and tense and complex today. There were half a dozen names on the scoreboard that were sort of sliding and rising. How valuable do you think last year was for Rory when that temperature was dialed up? I think he was super valuable. And I think what was also really valuable for him was he talked about how over the last few weeks, he's played this course over and over again. And he even joked that it felt like his home course. This place feels like my home course. I haven't played anywhere else in the last two or three weeks, really. And so throughout the week, even when we saw him struggle off the tee in the first couple rounds, he was almost playing like a wily veteran who understood what to do around the course. And you don't think wily veteran when you think Rory McIlroy. You think about the guy who hits the ball 340 yards and just demolishes a course. His short game has been something. I mean, it saved him. His driving's not been what we're used to, his usual standard. But his short game has been 10 out of 10 this week. This was someone who didn't have his A game off the tee and still managed to win because he navigated the course like just a total pro, like someone who really knew the ins and outs of Augusta National. He talked in Butler Cabin and in the press conference afterwards about being a kid with a dream. He had to take a moment to realize what he'd done with his family there as well. My mum and dad, they weren't here last year to celebrate with us. And surprisingly, I had to convince them to come this year because they thought that the reason that I won was because they weren't here. Glad that we proved that wrong. But mum and dad, I owe everything to you. So he now has six majors. That places him equal 12th alongside Mickelson and Faldo. He's one of only six to complete that career Grand Slam that you talked about. He did that 12 months ago. Where do you think McElroy ranks on the all-time list, Andrew? I think the answer is to be determined because he already has a case. He's in the discussion as the greatest European player ever already. But keep in mind, he's only in his mid-30s and he's won Masters in back-to-back years. And so are we thinking this is it for McElroy or this is him just really getting started on a second act of major runs? And I think the latter is much more likely. And so I think we're better going to be able to answer that question in five, ten years when we see does Rory McElroy have double-digit major wins? And by the way, he's going to be the fourth golfer in the last 40 years to lead or co-lead after every round of the Masters. I don't think that's some guarantee. But is it on the table? It would be crazy to say it's not. And then what about the emotion there? So you touched on it a little bit, but we're all watching through the TV, hanging on every moment. You're there at Augusta. Did you get a sense close up as to what it really meant to go back-to-back? Yeah, I think it felt almost like surreal to him. You know, he was talking about how during the victory ceremony last year, he said his goal was to be putting on the green jacket himself. My parting message last year was, I can't wait to come back next year and put the green jacket on myself. I wasn't quite correct because the chairman did it, but I did want to come back here and prove last year wasn't a fluke. And so I think it was just a sort of surreal experience for him because you go from spending your entire career wanting to win the Masters and being unable to do it, to going to winning it twice in a row. Like, this was the big bugaboo of his career. It wasn't just a major drought, it was that he had a game that seemed like it was built to conquer Augusta National. And 16 times in a row, he failed to do it. And then, twice in a row, he does it. And it was A-man corner where he really shot back into contention after being two shots down. Suddenly, he was in the lead. What did you see as the most crucial shot or hole for him in that path to victory? You know, when he stuck that tee shot on the par three. Oh, wow. He was on the right side of that bunker. What a beautiful kick to the right. Two daring shots by the final duo. It was just a brilliant, brilliant shot. He talked about reading the wind on the hole. He knew exactly what type of swing to take. You know, you think about Rory McIlroy, you're expecting his best shots to be a booming drive that gives him an easy wedge. No, he was the person who stuck a shot within seven feet. And that was the closest shot on that hole all day. And then he drains the putt. Birdie for Rory. Momentarily, two in front. And how many times have there been times when we watch Rory McIlroy over the course of his career and say, ah, he would have been a major champion if he just hit a few more putts. That's a putt that if you give yourself that shot, you have to make that putt. And it's only seven feet. You know, a player like Rory expects to make it. But you still don't hit a seven-foot putt nearly every time. And so I would say even more so than the shot off the tee box, him hitting that putt was really what showed it to me. You mentioned the preparation, not playing tournaments in the lead up, taking his daughter Poppy to school. I did a couple of days where I dropped Poppy to school, flew up here, played, landed back home and had dinner with her. Have we seen a shift in perspective, maybe a new sort of selflessness from Rory over these last 12, 13 months? Yeah, I think so. I think he is showing that, you know, he's not the brash young kid that once burst his way onto the scene. He's starting to learn more and more what it takes to win these types of events. And he's fallen short enough times that he probably has some battle scars and it's forced him into learning what you have to do to win at majors. Because it came so naturally to him when he was young that he probably didn't have to hone all the nuances and all the skills because he was just that talented. Well, especially these days, there are a lot of people who are extraordinarily talented. And so for him, I think what we're seeing is just this growth, this evolution that he's now combining the same skill that he has always had. It's not like he's lost power on his drives like a pitcher who's lost his fastball or something. But this is someone who is now combining all the skills that he's always had with the knowledge and the experience that come with both a lot of triumphs and a lot of failures. Can't believe I waited 17 years to get one green jacket and, you know, I get two in a row. It's just sort of the way. I don't know. I think all of my perseverance at this golf tournament over the years has really started to pay off. It also felt like a Ryder Cup at one point. You had McElroy, Rose, Hatton, even Lowry was there at stages. And then you had the Americans, Young, Sheffler, Henley. It was a bit of a battle. Who was the hard luck story for you? You know, ultimately, the person who came closest was Scotty. You know, he was one stroke back and there's just a lot of shots both yesterday and today where it's just like, oh, he was millimeters away from going even lower. And so is it a hard luck story? No. But Scotty Sheffler was one shot off the lead and again, but somehow felt he was even closer with that between Rory's flirting with disaster on the final hole. But also, Scotty had a lot of close calls that didn't seem to go his way. To move into a time for second. Oh, a most improbable birdie. We wondered last year if getting one for Rory might mean more. We've talked about it a little bit. That has been proven right. Is there a ceiling for Rory at Augusta? Could you see three in a row? He said before this tournament that he felt like he had about 10 more good shots at this. And that sounds about right to me. I mean, you saw Justin Rose almost win this at 45. You know, Jack won at 46. Why doesn't he have another decade to be a serious competitor here? Yeah, I said it at the start of the weekend here. I felt like the Grand Slam was the destination. And I realized it wasn't. You know, and I'm on this journey to, I don't know, I've just won my sixth major. And I feel like I'm in a really good spot with my game and my body. And, you know, I still have things that I want to achieve. And so does that mean he'll definitely win another? No. But is there somebody who, after what he's shown over the last two years, you think is a definitively better vet year in and year out? I mean, it's him and Scotty Scheffler right now when it comes to Augusta. It is super late on Sunday night in Augusta. So, Andrew Beaton from the Wall Street Journal, we thank you for sparing some time and taking us to that historic day for Rory McIlroy. Thanks so much for having me. Headlines. While the greens were fast at Augusta, the Australian sprinters were next level rapid at the Australian Athletics Championships across the weekend in Sydney. The man of the moment, Gout Gout, put the world on notice, running a blistering 19.67 in the 200 metre final. Gout's in front. He's coming away now for Murphy. Can he be as quick as this morning? Oh, incredible. Oh, he has absolutely done what everybody thought he might. But he's done it at 18 years of age. The world will be shaking. To give you an idea, that was the Australian 200 metre record. The world under 20 200 metre record. It makes him the 16th fastest man in history over the distance. And here we go. His year again.
Rory is a rare repeat winner at Augusta.
What's better than one green jacket? Two, obviously.
After completing the career Grand Slam in 2025 by winning the one trophy that had eluded him,
Rory McIlroy has gone back to back at the Masters.
It was a wire to wire win for the Northern Irishman, but that doesn't tell you the half of it.
A roller coaster Sunday saw McIlroy's six shot lead heading into the weekend evaporate into a two stroke deficit with a dozen holes to play.
It's another legacy win for Rory. And who's to say that he's done with two?
I'm Declan Byrne. This is ABC Sport Daily.
Nicholas, Faldo, Woods and now McIlroy.
The only men to go back to back at the Masters.
Andrew Beaton writes for the Wall Street Journal.
He walked Augusta National this week and was there to see Rory join some of the titans of the game.
Andrew, let's start at the end.
Take us to the 18th when Rory clinched a second green jacket.
Well, Rory McIlroy does not make anything easy.
He goes into the final hole with a two stroke lead and all he has to do is avoid disaster to become the fourth player ever to win back to back Masters.
He flirts with complete and total disaster.
This could be extremely dangerous depending on where this ends up.
He sends his drive completely to the right.
He doesn't know if he's going to even have a swing on the ball.
And in Rory McIlroy fashion, disaster is on the table.
All he needed to do was avoid a double bogey.
And he managed to do just that with a bogey on the final hole.
And when he looked up and screamed after tapping in the final putt, it might have just been as much relief as it was total jubilation.
Last year after putting in on 18, he collapsed.
It was joy today, but it was also maybe disbelief that he had made things so hard for himself.
It was a roller coaster Sunday.
How did you judge that reaction after he knew he'd won?
Well, I think he talked openly about how he felt less of a burden this time around.
Because last year, he wasn't just trying to win the Masters for the first time.
He was trying to win the career Grand Slam.
I thought it was so difficult to win last year because of trying to win the Masters and the Grand Slam.
And then this year, I realized it's just really difficult to win the Masters.
When he won, it was this kind of double whammy.
It was something he had been chasing for over a decade.
And two in one, he ends this major drought.
He wins the Masters and boom, one fell swoop.
And this year, he was kind of unburdened.
But he also talked about how after winning the Masters last year, he struggled a bit with motivation.
And then all of a sudden, he races out to this historic six-stroke lead after 36 holes.
Then he struggles on Saturday, struggles out of the gate on Sunday.
Disaster for McIlroy at the floor.
Three putts from five feet leads to a double bogey.
And now Cam Young has a two-shot lead at the Masters.
Once again, even when things looked really rocky, he steeled himself and came out on top.
It did get really tight and tense and complex today.
There were half a dozen names on the scoreboard that were sort of sliding and rising.
How valuable do you think last year was for Rory when that temperature was dialed up?
I think he was super valuable.
And I think what was also really valuable for him was he talked about how over the last few weeks,
he's played this course over and over again.
And he even joked that it felt like his home course.
This place feels like my home course.
I haven't played anywhere else in the last two or three weeks, really.
And so throughout the week, even when we saw him struggle off the tee in the first couple rounds,
he was almost playing like a wily veteran who understood what to do around the course.
And you don't think wily veteran when you think Rory McIlroy.
You think about the guy who hits the ball 340 yards and just demolishes a course.
His short game has been something.
His driving's not been what we're used to, his usual standard.
But his short game has been 10 out of 10 this week.
This was someone who didn't have his A game off the tee and still managed to win because
he navigated the course like just a total pro, like someone who really knew the ins and outs of Augusta National.
He talked in Butler Cabin and in the press conference afterwards about being a kid with a dream.
He had to take a moment to realize what he'd done with his family there as well.
My mum and dad, they weren't here last year to celebrate with us.
And surprisingly, I had to convince them to come this year because they thought that the reason that I won was because they weren't here.
Glad that we proved that wrong.
But mum and dad, I owe everything to you.
So he now has six majors.
That places him equal 12th alongside Mickelson and Faldo.
He's one of only six to complete that career Grand Slam that you talked about.
Where do you think McElroy ranks on the all-time list, Andrew?
I think the answer is to be determined because he already has a case.
He's in the discussion as the greatest European player ever already.
But keep in mind, he's only in his mid-30s and he's won Masters in back-to-back years.
And so are we thinking this is it for McElroy or this is him just really getting started on a second act of major runs?
And I think the latter is much more likely.
And so I think we're better going to be able to answer that question in five, ten years when we see does Rory McElroy have double-digit major wins?
And by the way, he's going to be the fourth golfer in the last 40 years to lead or co-lead after every round of the Masters.
I don't think that's some guarantee.
But is it on the table?
It would be crazy to say it's not.
And then what about the emotion there?
So you touched on it a little bit, but we're all watching through the TV, hanging on every moment.
Did you get a sense close up as to what it really meant to go back-to-back?
Yeah, I think it felt almost like surreal to him.
You know, he was talking about how during the victory ceremony last year,
he said his goal was to be putting on the green jacket himself.
My parting message last year was, I can't wait to come back next year and put the green jacket on myself.
I wasn't quite correct because the chairman did it, but I did want to come back here and prove last year wasn't a fluke.
And so I think it was just a sort of surreal experience for him because you go from spending your entire career wanting to win the Masters and being unable to do it,
to going to winning it twice in a row.
Like, this was the big bugaboo of his career.
It wasn't just a major drought, it was that he had a game that seemed like it was built to conquer Augusta National.
And 16 times in a row, he failed to do it.
And then, twice in a row, he does it.
And it was A-man corner where he really shot back into contention after being two shots down.
Suddenly, he was in the lead.
What did you see as the most crucial shot or hole for him in that path to victory?
You know, when he stuck that tee shot on the par three.
He was on the right side of that bunker.
What a beautiful kick to the right.
Two daring shots by the final duo.
It was just a brilliant, brilliant shot.
He talked about reading the wind on the hole.
He knew exactly what type of swing to take.
You know, you think about Rory McIlroy, you're expecting his best shots to be a booming drive that gives him an easy wedge.
No, he was the person who stuck a shot within seven feet.
And that was the closest shot on that hole all day.
And then he drains the putt.
And how many times have there been times when we watch Rory McIlroy over the course of his career and say, ah, he would have been a major champion if he just hit a few more putts.
That's a putt that if you give yourself that shot, you have to make that putt.
You know, a player like Rory expects to make it.
But you still don't hit a seven-foot putt nearly every time.
And so I would say even more so than the shot off the tee box, him hitting that putt was really what showed it to me.
You mentioned the preparation, not playing tournaments in the lead up, taking his daughter Poppy to school.
I did a couple of days where I dropped Poppy to school, flew up here, played, landed back home and had dinner with her.
Have we seen a shift in perspective, maybe a new sort of selflessness from Rory over these last 12, 13 months?
I think he is showing that, you know, he's not the brash young kid that once burst his way onto the scene.
He's starting to learn more and more what it takes to win these types of events.
And he's fallen short enough times that he probably has some battle scars and it's forced him into learning what you have to do to win at majors.

Well, especially these days, there are a lot of people who are extraordinarily talented.
And so for him, I think what we're seeing is just this growth, this evolution that he's now combining the same skill that he has always had.
It's not like he's lost power on his drives like a pitcher who's lost his fastball or something.
But this is someone who is now combining all the skills that he's always had with the knowledge and the experience that come with both a lot of triumphs and a lot of failures.
Can't believe I waited 17 years to get one green jacket and, you know, I get two in a row.
It's just sort of the way.
I think all of my perseverance at this golf tournament over the years has really started to pay off.

You had McElroy, Rose, Hatton, even Lowry was there at stages.
And then you had the Americans, Young, Sheffler, Henley.
It was a bit of a battle.
Who was the hard luck story for you?
You know, ultimately, the person who came closest was Scotty.

To move into a time for second.
We wondered last year if getting one for Rory might mean more.
We've talked about it a little bit.
Is there a ceiling for Rory at Augusta?
Could you see three in a row?
He said before this tournament that he felt like he had about 10 more good shots at this.
And that sounds about right to me.
I mean, you saw Justin Rose almost win this at 45.
Why doesn't he have another decade to be a serious competitor here?
Yeah, I said it at the start of the weekend here.
I felt like the Grand Slam was the destination.
You know, and I'm on this journey to, I don't know, I've just won my sixth major.
And I feel like I'm in a really good spot with my game and my body.
And, you know, I still have things that I want to achieve.
And so does that mean he'll definitely win another?
But is there somebody who, after what he's shown over the last two years, you think is a definitively better vet year in and year out?
I mean, it's him and Scotty Scheffler right now when it comes to Augusta.
It is super late on Sunday night in Augusta.

episodes.title: Fri Fix: The NRL heads west, will AFL's Wildcard Round do the same?
episodes.description: With the Perth Bears joining the competition next year, the double header in Perth this weekend feels extra important for the NRL.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Burton strikes it, likes it, kicks the goal. Matt Burton is five from six and who would have thought we'd be saying this with six minutes left on this Thursday night? Game set, bingo! The Bulldogs are beating Penrith, they've got it in the bag. The Bulldogs saw Nathan Cleary's 200th match and decided it was actually their night, proving what many thought was not possible. The 2026 Panthers are fallible. The NRL have headed to the big state this round and with the Perth Bears less than a year away, big crowds and keen fans will be vital. And how long until the Broncos' injury toll catches up with them and starts to impact their premiership defence? Plus, we haven't even had a wildcard round in the AFL yet, but is it already up for sale? I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily. Zach Bailey is a rugby league reporter with Channel 9 and Zach, last night was meant to be all about Nathan Cleary and his 200th game, but the Bulldogs spoiled the party. Does this mean the Panthers are fallible? And was this Cameron Sorraldo's best win as Bulldogs coach, do you think? Oh, great question, Poppy. It's right up there as his greatest win. It's definitely the best performance of Lockie Galvin's NRL career. He'd been in the spotlight. A lot of people were questioning whether he was a genuine seven or a halfback and not a five-eight. But he outshone Nathan Cleary in game 200 last night. He was really impressive on the right edge with Jacob Preston. They've got a really good combination there. Two tackles left. The ball played by Salmon. Goes right to Galvin. Short ball, Preston, straight through to Lungy. They must score. They do score. Inside ball with Satili Tuberneuer. It might be good by Penrith time. The Panthers were unbeatable or allegedly unbeatable before that match last night, but clearly the Bulldogs were up for it. I was out there last night. I spoke to some of their players after the match and interviewed them. And they said they couldn't ignore the noise. It said, oh, no one gave us a chance tonight. They definitely used it as motivation. They knew the occasion that was Nathan Cleary's 200th. They really muscled up. They played really good footy. They were quite disciplined. On the flip side, Penrith were out of sorts. Very rarely do you see such a poor performance from Penrith. Their left edge, there was a lot of talk about players potentially playing the Origin Arena. Their coach, Ivan Cleary, after the match said, perhaps their performance was so bad because they were thinking about Origin. Obviously, he said it tongue in cheek. Andrew says the left edge in particular look like that's where they targeted a bit. Yeah, maybe they're getting ready for Origin camp. I don't know. But it's a bit of a wake-up call for the Panthers in the sense that, hey, there are other teams in this competition. They are flying at the moment. They were 5-0 to start the season. This brings them back a peg. I think it makes them even more dangerous. But to answer your original question, yeah, it is right up there in terms of Cameron Serrato's best wins ever as an NRL coach. And just quickly, I know it wasn't a win, but 200 games for Nathan Cleary. There aren't too many who have put together 200 better games of rugby league, are there? No. He's a four-time Premiership winner. I know it's a different arena, but three-time Origin series winner, a two-time Clive Churchill medalist. Kenny, short side left Cleary, steps past one, two, three, scores between the post. Nathan Cleary has turned this grand final. He's picked it up, raised it above his head and flipped it over. Some of the performances we've seen, especially in grand finals and big games, have been up there with some of the greats in the game. I spoke to him after the match. He was really, really disappointed. But the one thing I must say about Nathan is that he is such a good person, away from footy as well, in terms of he spent 30 minutes up in the stands, you know, seeing his family and friends who had made the trek out, all the fans. And I said to him afterwards, hey, why do you still do this? And he goes, I play football, but these guys turn up rain, hail, shine, win, loss, draw to support me and support us. The least I can do is get back there and take selfies and, you know, kind of smile through the paint. So hats off to Nathan Cleary. Scooped up here by Alan Motty. He turns it back to Cleary. Puts in a cross-field kick. Looking for Jenkins. Jenkins a catch! Jenkins a double! He scored a million of them and it's 16-all! What about the precision of the Cleary kick? 200 games down. Who knows how many more ahead? But let's hope he's in the game for a lot longer and perhaps he could break Cameron Smith's all-time record of 430 games. That's a long way off, but as you say, it's probably not out of the question. The Broncos take on the Cowboys tonight and the Bronx Woes continue with Walsh and Hunt out for a period. Reynolds still not back. When does this sort of turbulent start to 2026 actually start to threaten the entire season for the defending premiers? Yeah, good question. I mean, Rhys Walsh, this is a bit of an ongoing situation. He's very brave in the way he plays footy and this is, I think, the third cheekbone or eye socket fracture that he's had in the last couple of years. And he'll get to his feet. Campbell, he plays it to Beryl's. Give him a moron who almost ran over the top. He's out, Walsh! Is he out? Rhys Walsh is on his back. I think he's concussed. He might be out of the game. And they are delicate injuries. The best thing is, is that he's not gun shy. When he does return, he goes into the contest just as hard as previously. But he is their live wire. The big question is around their ageing paths in Adam Reynolds, as you mentioned, and Ben Hunt. Adam Reynolds, a short-term injury. Ben Hunt, potentially out for eight weeks. The best news there is they've got Ezra Mann, who is a solid playmaker to come in. Tom Duffy, who's a former Cowboy, will face his former side tonight. But it's whether they can keep those key players of Rhys Walsh, Adam Reynolds, Ben Hunt, all through the middle, the spine players, fit for long enough so that they are in the top four, essentially, by the end of the year. Because the issue is, no team outside the top four is really a premiership threat. The stats show that. History shows that. If results continue to go ways that nobody expects, then it could be a really close competition battling for those top four spots. I do expect the Broncos to be in and around that top four, top six debate by the end of the year. Two games in Perth this weekend, Zach, as the big state tries to get NRL fever ahead of the Bears joining the competition next year. The Perth Bears talked this week about wanting to sell out every home game in 2027. So how important is Saturday's doubleheader to kind of prove to the NRL world and to West Australians that this expansion will work? Yeah, it's hugely important. Some of the biggest names in rugby league in terms of Malmeninga, the Bears coach, Wayne Bennett, the Rabbitohs coach over there, Ricky Stewart, Raiders coach, Roosters coach, Trent Robinson, some of the biggest names in rugby league are over there at the moment with their teams trying to sell rugby league, I guess, to the Perth and Western Australian audience, which, as you know, are rusted on in the Aussie rules and AFL world. And there's no doubt that it's going to be a real challenge for the Bears to get a stronghold or get momentum over in the West. But the Perth Bears, they launched their academy this week, which is exciting in terms of players that are going to start coming through the system. And that's going to be key for them moving forward. If I'm the NRL and the tickets may be not going, you know, as well as possible, I'd be doing every, I'd be going to local schools. I'd be giving tickets away left, right and centre. So there is a big crowd there. Even if it's at a loss for the game, you want to have a big crowd in the West watching that doubleheader this weekend. The next six months is vital for the Bears moving forward. They want to have momentum. They want to have plenty of supporters. They want people in merch so that when they are in the comp to kick off 2027, as you said, the stadium is filled. I don't know if it's going to be a sellout every game. It's ambitious, but you know, why not? Got to be ambitious in this world when there's so much competition from the rival codes, especially the AFL all over in the West. You got to risk it to get the biscuit, Zach. Finally, here's something I didn't think that I would be saying at the end of last season. The West's Tigers in second take on the third place Knights. Which of these teams can realistically maintain this early positivity and form? Oh, it's a great question. Nobody saw this coming at all, especially given Talyn Ponga and Dylan Brown have been injured since round two for the Knights. Yet they've been able to maintain this really strong form of footy and it's been really exciting. Our players are loving what Justin Holbrook, their new coach, has brought to the Knights, especially after finishing with a wooden spoon and coming through a really tough period over the last couple of years under Adam O'Brien. As for the Tigers, so many eyeballs on Benji Marshall. The club's been the basket case of the NRL over the past decade or maybe longer. And here he is, a young rookie coach, getting a huge extension in the off-season. The CEO walked out. They've got some great players. Jerome Luai has also been injured. But the real impressive aspect of both of these teams is their ability to overcome injuries early on in the year and continue to win. Back to Madden. Field goal! No! It's missed to the right, but it's a penalty! Paramount is inside the 10! Penalty to the West Tigers! They are going to win! It's a huge contest, Campbelltown, on Sunday afternoon to see where both of these teams are actually at when they're against each other. They both play a similar brand of exciting footy. As for who can maintain it? Oh, great question. By the end of the year, I don't know. I really think they're a similar style team that have similar chances of where they'll end up by the end of the year. But this weekend, it's a huge weekend. It's a Tigers home game. Here's a stat. They've lost their last five matches at Campbelltown. Of course, they move around. They play matches at Conbank Stadium, Lycared, and also down at Campbelltown. And they've lost 15 of their last 17 matches at Campbelltown. That is not good at home, right? So that is a stat. But they call it their jungle, but they haven't been kings of the jungle for a while. So the Tigers need to show to their home fans that, hey, we mean business this year, and we mean business in one of our home grounds in Campbelltown. So hopefully for Tigers fans, they get the job done. But a huge test up against the Knights we're in for this weekend. Big weekend in rugby league. Zach Bailey, thanks so much for your time. Thanks for having me, Poppy. Gather Round is underway. And while Adelaide were the winners of the opening match, the talk of the town was actually the wildcard round. ABC's Corbyn Middlemass revealed that it could be up for sale. One thing that has been raised in part of this planning and concept building and everything else is the idea that WA or another state government could bid for the right to host the wildcard weekend. Now, at the moment, as it's going to be the case in 2026, we're all thinking 7th and 8th will host the wildcard games. But that is no guarantee to continue at the end of the season. It feels like WA are playing Monopoly and bought all the good properties and put hotels on all of them. The AFL have been big on the wildcard round being good for fans. Those are the same fans who might have to fork out to fly across the country to watch a match their team would ordinarily be hosting. Our fans love finals games. So we think it provides opportunities and provides hope for our fans. And then 7th and 8th, you'll get to host a home wildcard final. For more, make sure you're up to date with the ABC AFL Daily podcast. While we're talking AFL, the Lance Collard Tribunal into an alleged homophobic slur in the VFL headed into a second day today and a decision is yet to be handed down at the time of publication. Keep across the ABC News app or the ABC Sport website for more details. Soundbites. The Masters are underway and Rory McIlroy has started in ominous fashion with his best Augusta opening round in over a decade. He's currently 5-under tied for the lead with Sam Burns. Australian Jason Day is tied for 3rd. And the talk at Augusta has been about how fast the Greens are. Just depends on what they want. Like, I mean, if they want single digits to win, it'll be baked out and fast. And guys will be, you know, kind of spewing on themselves out there. You know, it'd be really difficult. Yeah, spewing on the Greens is one way to soften them up, I guess. The Aussie women's cricket team have just wrapped up an undefeated tour of the West Indies. How do you think they celebrated that? At the pub, of course. Here's the news tonight. Enjoy. Aussie, Aussie. Hooray, hooray, hooray. Aussie, hooray, hooray. Not just any pub, though. Australian-owned and themed Old Mates in New York. Backyard cricket hits different in the Big Apple. And if your family is anything like mine, you've probably connected with them on more than one occasion over sport. But for the James family, it's a bit more literal. On the drop pass, the steal, Bronny, son to father, LeBron James. How many times have you seen it? They probably worked on that in backyard. That is a backyard 1v1 that could pack an arena. I'm Poppy Penny and this is ABC Sport Daily, produced by Declan Byrne. potentially playing the Origin Arena. Their coach, Ivan Cleary, after the match said,
perhaps their performance was so bad because they were thinking about Origin. Obviously,
he said it tongue in cheek.
Andrew says the left edge in particular look like that's where they targeted a bit.
Yeah, maybe they're getting ready for Origin camp. I don't know.
But it's a bit of a wake-up call for the Panthers in the sense that, hey, there are other teams
in this competition. They are flying at the moment. They were 5-0 to start the season.
This brings them back a peg. I think it makes them even more dangerous.
But to answer your original question, yeah, it is right up there in terms of
Cameron Serrato's best wins ever as an NRL coach.
And just quickly, I know it wasn't a win, but 200 games for Nathan Cleary.
There aren't too many who have put together 200 better games of rugby league, are there?
No. He's a four-time Premiership winner. I know it's a different arena,
but three-time Origin series winner, a two-time Clive Churchill medalist.
Kenny, short side left Cleary, steps past one, two, three, scores between the post.
Nathan Cleary has turned this grand final. He's picked it up, raised it above his head
Some of the performances we've seen, especially in grand finals and big games,
have been up there with some of the greats in the game.
I spoke to him after the match. He was really, really disappointed.
But the one thing I must say about Nathan is that he is such a good person,
away from footy as well, in terms of he spent 30 minutes up in the stands,
you know, seeing his family and friends who had made the trek out, all the fans.
And I said to him afterwards, hey, why do you still do this?
And he goes, I play football, but these guys turn up rain, hail, shine, win, loss, draw
to support me and support us. The least I can do is get back there and take selfies
and, you know, kind of smile through the paint.
So hats off to Nathan Cleary.
Scooped up here by Alan Motty. He turns it back to Cleary.
Puts in a cross-field kick. Looking for Jenkins. Jenkins a catch!
Jenkins a double! He scored a million of them and it's 16-all!
What about the precision of the Cleary kick?
200 games down. Who knows how many more ahead?
But let's hope he's in the game for a lot longer
and perhaps he could break Cameron Smith's all-time record of 430 games.
That's a long way off, but as you say, it's probably not out of the question.
The Broncos take on the Cowboys tonight and the Bronx Woes continue with Walsh and Hunt
out for a period. Reynolds still not back.
When does this sort of turbulent start to 2026 actually start to threaten the entire season
Yeah, good question. I mean, Rhys Walsh, this is a bit of an ongoing situation.
He's very brave in the way he plays footy and this is, I think, the third cheekbone or eye socket
fracture that he's had in the last couple of years.
And he'll get to his feet. Campbell, he plays it to Beryl's.
Give him a moron who almost ran over the top.
Rhys Walsh is on his back. I think he's concussed.
He might be out of the game.
The best thing is, is that he's not gun shy.
When he does return, he goes into the contest just as hard as previously.
But he is their live wire.
The big question is around their ageing paths in Adam Reynolds, as you mentioned, and Ben Hunt.
Ben Hunt, potentially out for eight weeks.
The best news there is they've got Ezra Mann, who is a solid playmaker to come in.
Tom Duffy, who's a former Cowboy, will face his former side tonight.
But it's whether they can keep those key players of Rhys Walsh, Adam Reynolds, Ben Hunt, all
through the middle, the spine players, fit for long enough so that they are in the top
four, essentially, by the end of the year.
Because the issue is, no team outside the top four is really a premiership threat.
If results continue to go ways that nobody expects, then it could be a really close competition
battling for those top four spots.
I do expect the Broncos to be in and around that top four, top six debate by the end of
Two games in Perth this weekend, Zach, as the big state tries to get NRL fever ahead of the
Bears joining the competition next year.
The Perth Bears talked this week about wanting to sell out every home game in 2027.
So how important is Saturday's doubleheader to kind of prove to the NRL world and to West
Australians that this expansion will work?
Some of the biggest names in rugby league in terms of Malmeninga, the Bears coach, Wayne
Bennett, the Rabbitohs coach over there, Ricky Stewart, Raiders coach, Roosters coach, Trent
Robinson, some of the biggest names in rugby league are over there at the moment with their
teams trying to sell rugby league, I guess, to the Perth and Western Australian audience,
which, as you know, are rusted on in the Aussie rules and AFL world.
And there's no doubt that it's going to be a real challenge for the Bears to get a stronghold
or get momentum over in the West.
But the Perth Bears, they launched their academy this week, which is exciting in terms of players
that are going to start coming through the system.
And that's going to be key for them moving forward.
If I'm the NRL and the tickets may be not going, you know, as well as possible, I'd be
doing every, I'd be going to local schools.
I'd be giving tickets away left, right and centre.
So there is a big crowd there.
Even if it's at a loss for the game, you want to have a big crowd in the West watching
The next six months is vital for the Bears moving forward.
They want to have plenty of supporters.
They want people in merch so that when they are in the comp to kick off 2027, as you said,
I don't know if it's going to be a sellout every game.
It's ambitious, but you know, why not?
Got to be ambitious in this world when there's so much competition from the rival codes,
especially the AFL all over in the West.
You got to risk it to get the biscuit, Zach.
Finally, here's something I didn't think that I would be saying at the end of last season.
The West's Tigers in second take on the third place Knights.
Which of these teams can realistically maintain this early positivity and form?
Nobody saw this coming at all, especially given Talyn Ponga and Dylan Brown have been injured
since round two for the Knights.
Yet they've been able to maintain this really strong form of footy and it's been really exciting.
Our players are loving what Justin Holbrook, their new coach, has brought to the Knights,
especially after finishing with a wooden spoon and coming through a really tough period
over the last couple of years under Adam O'Brien.
As for the Tigers, so many eyeballs on Benji Marshall.
The club's been the basket case of the NRL over the past decade or maybe longer.
And here he is, a young rookie coach, getting a huge extension in the off-season.
Jerome Luai has also been injured.
But the real impressive aspect of both of these teams is their ability to overcome injuries
early on in the year and continue to win.
It's missed to the right, but it's a penalty!
It's a huge contest, Campbelltown, on Sunday afternoon to see where both of these teams
are actually at when they're against each other.
They both play a similar brand of exciting footy.
As for who can maintain it?
By the end of the year, I don't know.
I really think they're a similar style team that have similar chances of where they'll
end up by the end of the year.
But this weekend, it's a huge weekend.
They've lost their last five matches at Campbelltown.
They play matches at Conbank Stadium, Lycared, and also down at Campbelltown.
And they've lost 15 of their last 17 matches at Campbelltown.
That is not good at home, right?
But they call it their jungle, but they haven't been kings of the jungle for a while.
So the Tigers need to show to their home fans that, hey, we mean business this year,
and we mean business in one of our home grounds in Campbelltown.
So hopefully for Tigers fans, they get the job done.
But a huge test up against the Knights we're in for this weekend.
Zach Bailey, thanks so much for your time.
And while Adelaide were the winners of the opening match,
the talk of the town was actually the wildcard round.
ABC's Corbyn Middlemass revealed that it could be up for sale.
One thing that has been raised in part of this planning and concept building and everything else
is the idea that WA or another state government could bid for the right to host the wildcard weekend.
Now, at the moment, as it's going to be the case in 2026,
we're all thinking 7th and 8th will host the wildcard games.
But that is no guarantee to continue at the end of the season.
It feels like WA are playing Monopoly and bought all the good properties and put hotels on all of them.
The AFL have been big on the wildcard round being good for fans.
Those are the same fans who might have to fork out to fly across the country
to watch a match their team would ordinarily be hosting.
So we think it provides opportunities and provides hope for our fans.
And then 7th and 8th, you'll get to host a home wildcard final.
For more, make sure you're up to date with the ABC AFL Daily podcast.
While we're talking AFL, the Lance Collard Tribunal into an alleged homophobic slur in the VFL
headed into a second day today and a decision is yet to be handed down at the time of publication.
Keep across the ABC News app or the ABC Sport website for more details.
The Masters are underway and Rory McIlroy has started in ominous fashion

He's currently 5-under tied for the lead with Sam Burns.
Australian Jason Day is tied for 3rd.
And the talk at Augusta has been about how fast the Greens are.
Just depends on what they want.
Like, I mean, if they want single digits to win, it'll be baked out and fast.
And guys will be, you know, kind of spewing on themselves out there.
You know, it'd be really difficult.
Yeah, spewing on the Greens is one way to soften them up, I guess.
The Aussie women's cricket team have just wrapped up an undefeated tour of the West Indies.
How do you think they celebrated that?
Australian-owned and themed Old Mates in New York.
Backyard cricket hits different in the Big Apple.

On the drop pass, the steal, Bronny, son to father, LeBron James.

title: ABC TassieCast with Airlie Ward - ABC listen
