episodes.title: Will land sales future-proof Tassie's only uni?
episodes.description: Tasmania has a long tradition of young people growing up, spreading their wings, and leaving for the mainland - before for some, returning to the island.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Everybody's talking about fuel. Whether you're in need of filling up the tank for the week and you're watching the dollars tick over at the Bowser or you're watching weekend plans, holiday plans, business plans change. To help get your head around the latest, you can find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. Is Tasmania's only university facing its toughest test yet? There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. They've spent hundreds of millions of dollars on a misguided plan and they would not let go of that misguided plan no matter what facts were put in front of them and no matter how expensive it was becoming. I was barely on campus and when I was on campus, people weren't hanging around. Yeah, it was just, you'd go, do your thing, duck off again. Sandy Bay needs to change. The current layout and the condition of existing buildings does not allow the university to deliver for its students or drive the innovation Tasmania needs. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. Did you or your kids go to the University of Tasmania? Maybe you've got fond memories of the now defunct uni bar or O-week shenanigans on top of what you learned, of course. Or maybe you or someone you know is considering ditching Tasmania's only university to go interstate. There is a long history of spreading your wings, becoming independent and finding your feet in the big smoke before maybe returning to the island. But the number of young Tasmanians bailing on UTAS has increased markedly. Local students choosing a uni interstate have increased from around 18% to nearly 30% in the past decade, adding to concerns about a brain drain. We know a growing number of jobs require some sort of tertiary education. But is our university equipped to keep pace and attract the students and staff it needs? After a controversial plan to move from its main Sandy Bay campus to the Hobart CBD was met with massive community opposition, UTAS is now hoping legislation, allowing it to sell some of its land, will help see the Institute realise a vision for a world-class STEM centre to support the next generation of Tasmanian scientists get their skills and stay here. But will it be enough? Following the ongoing debate is our investigative reporter Adam Holmes. Adam, it'd be fair to say between interstate and online competition, low staff morale and a challenging financial situation, UTAS is now at a real crossroads? Yeah, it has been facing this confluence of pressures like you just mentioned. It doesn't paint a particularly easy picture. Some of them are the result of external factors, but others could be described as self-inflicted. For example, the requirement to pay back $21 million in staff underpayment. There's been major changes to its arts and humanities courses, partly due to Commonwealth priorities. There's also the aftermath of COVID and how to manage international student enrolments. There's been a steady decline in international students since 2021, which UTAS has been trying to address through its dealings with the Commonwealth. But at the same time, domestic student numbers have actually deadly increased. This does include students from interstate. UTAS actually has lower entry requirements than many mainland universities, so that could be a factor there. And while all of this is going on, UTAS has been mired in this attempted relocation from Sandy Bay to Hobart CBD and associated property dealings. So a very quick potted recent history. UTAS had planned to move into the CBD and completely out of Sandy Bay. It brought up huge chunks of Hobart CBD. Now they've partly backtracked on that, although a substantial amount of the university is now spread around Hobart CBD. Their initial plan to sell all of Sandy Bay for housing was kiboshed, Adam. Yeah, and that was in the aftermath of the council elector poll that UTAS decided to change its plans. So this idea to relocate from Sandy Bay started in about 2015 under former Vice-Chancellor Peter Rathjen and continued under current Vice-Chancellor Rufus Black. And in 2021, they had a master plan to turn all of the Sandy Bay campus into 2,500 dwellings and neighbourhood amenity and had undertaken hundreds of millions of dollars in property transactions to facilitate this, including buying the old Forestry Building and Freedom Furniture site, the Webster site on Argyle Street in Hobart, the K&D site, or what most people know as the Swishers Basketball Centre, and others. There's also been sales from the purchases, like the Fountainside Hotel, Mid-City Hotel, the K&D as well. A lot of property dealings for a university. But having backtracked on much of these plans now, they've landed on this idea of four campus UTAS in Hobart. So four separate campuses. That's the city campus, a historic campus alongside Glebe, a waterfront campus and a retained Sandy Bay campus. And the Sandy Bay campus essentially has been neglected during this period of wheeling and dealing. And now it requires improvement to get it up to modern standards. Now, it needed the government for this to all kind of come together. Adam, after initially saying no way, the state government has now okayed some of UTAS's plans to sell some of the Sandy Bay estate. And legislation enabling that has just passed Parliament. Yeah, during the 2024 state election, the Liberals promised to introduce laws that require UTAS to get the support of Parliament by vote to sell any of its Sandy Bay campus as an oversight measure, as a result of all of these things that have been going on. This is land, of course, that was originally gifted to UTAS. But then there was the unusual spectacle of the government amending its own bill to slice out two pieces of land above Churchill Avenue and not just like slice them out from that, but also rezone them to inner residential. And this change came about after quite extensive lobbying by UTAS, who engaged the services of former Premier Will Hodgman to help get it done at a cost of $25,000. So, you know, small change for the UTAS. How the bill was amended is still quite unclear. And that wasn't discoverable under right to information. During this period, UTAS was also briefing another former Premier, Paul Lennon, for reasons unknown. Labor has been a vigorous supporter of UTAS's master plan for Sandy Bay and the housing component and all that. So with their support, this amended bill was able to pass the lower house and then the upper house with the support of several independents. People could be forgiven for being a bit confused about all of this, but can you tell us what is it that the uni can do now? Yes, everything about UTAS is a bit confusing and convoluted. In terms of the main Sandy Bay campus below Churchill Avenue, where most of the buildings are, UTAS would need the vote of both houses of parliament to sell any of that. But the bill enables them to sell two parcels of land on the upper side of Churchill Avenue, and that's about 27 hectares. That includes the Student Union building and former UniBar, which you would imagine is probably going to be demolished at some point. The inner residential zoning for this land allows for higher density housing, and having it rezoned already takes away one obstacle for UTAS. Any development on that land would still need to pass Hobart City Council. And as we've seen elsewhere in Hobart, housing development takes a long time to come to fruition, if at all. You have things like land banking going on with developers. There's never a guarantee that master plans and glossy pictures actually come to life. There's a remaining 56 hectares further up towards Mount Nelson that wasn't rezoned, but it also wasn't provided the same parliamentary protection of the main campus. It was somewhat forgotten during this debate, really. It wasn't mentioned in second reading speeches. UTAS is in discussions with the Aboriginal Land Council to hand this land back to the Aboriginal community. I contacted the Land Council, and those talks are ongoing, and there is interest. But the very top of that land was actually slated for housing in UTAS's master plan. So who knows if UTAS might try to at least use some of it in its land sale plans further down the track as well. In the meantime, what's been happening to course delivery? I mean, isn't that the core of the university? Yes, that's right. We're teaching people, the next generation of Tasmanians. So in addition to having, you know, academic staff questioning all these property dealings, there's also been reductions in some courses, largely in arts and humanities. There's a reduction in the languages that have been offered. You can't learn German here anymore. The National Tertiary Education Union estimates there could be up to 150 reduction in staff since 2023. Staff morale has been an ongoing issue. But UTAS did open its new forest building in the Hobart CBD this year, which could be a way of, I guess, improving morale. I've been in there. It's quite modern. But how that transition is managed is part of how UTAS, I guess, manages and addresses some of its staff morale problems. Challenges in the tertiary sector, though, they're not unique to Tasmania, Adam. No. And UTAS does regularly point this out in its annual reports that it's constantly having to adapt to policy reforms by the Commonwealth. This includes impacts on its international student quotas, but also the 2021 reforms by the Morrison government that essentially saw student fees soar, particularly for arts and humanities courses. And that resulted in major changes to student behaviour. This was pointed out by UTAS pro-Vice-Chancellor, Professor Nicholas Farrelly, in relation to humanities and social sciences, or HASS. If I had 15 seconds with the Prime Minister, yes, I'd indicate that the former Morrison government's Job Ready Graduates program has profoundly disadvantaged our Tasmanian HASS students, and it would be great to see some reconfiguration of the pricing. Adam, are lectures delivered in person at all anymore? I've been told there are significantly fewer in-person lectures, which may be a lingering after-effect of the COVID period. We all remember the Zoom meetings. Economist John Lawrence attempted to quantify this data by showing that in 2013, 33% of courses were fully online. That has risen to 73%. And I think the main change is that not all students have a choice as to whether they attend online or in-person, whereas in the past, that choice existed. And that does have an effect on campus life. But UTAS said this year that they have seen a 10% increase in on-campus attendees across its four Tasmanian campuses. Given that move to more online, is it understandable then that UTAS wants to change its physical infrastructure? I mean, are they outdated buildings meant for a different era? In some ways, yes. I mean, I mentioned the Forest Building earlier, and that certainly has those modernist elements, very open plan. It's essentially a large library, really. There's not the usual office-type layout that academics were used to. And I'm studying at UTAS at the moment, and my direct teaching staff are in the forest. They don't have their own offices. It's very small spaces for them, and that can cause some frustration. It's something that they're not used to. But it's this idea that open plan fosters collaboration, I suppose. You see that in other developments UTAS has undertaken. There was also the idea that having centrally located, like the forest, right in the middle of the Hobart CBD, really, that improves access from all of the suburbs of Hobart. But that argument was certainly not bought by the community, as we saw in the elector poll. Going back to the legislation now that's passed Parliament in terms of Sandy Bay, in exchange for getting the go-ahead to sell off some of the land and the sale of a couple of its previous CBD investments, UTAS says it intends to spend somewhere around half a billion dollars on a new STEM facility at Sandy Bay, that's science, engineering, technology and maths. Will they have enough money with all of their various sales? It's difficult, very challenging. UTAS's plan, and it is very to be confirmed, really, is to gain about $100 million from these land sales. And that $100 million figure isn't actually based on any reports or anything. It's a comparison of similar land sales. And it was earlier estimated that it was $35 million. But anyway, it promised it will then take these funds to the Commonwealth, not a legally binding promise, mind you, for the Commonwealth to then fund the remaining $400 million or so as a 80-20 contribution. And again, the $500 million estimate for STEM is also somewhat to be confirmed as well. The numbers there can be a little bit rubbery. The problem UTAS faces with this plan is that the Commonwealth no longer really funds projects like these, especially to this scale. And it also doesn't fund this infrastructure at this 80-20. It's more 50-50 contribution. And the Tasmanian government has repeatedly said it won't fund it other than allowing these land sales to take place. The STEM project isn't on the Commonwealth 10-year infrastructure priority list either. So UTAS would have needed a federal election promise to get the funding, but it didn't have its plans in place in time, so it missed out. But here's Tasmanian Education Minister, Joe Palmer, on that land valuation question. The land was valued based on the experience of land sales in the area. The government agrees that there is further work to do to identify the preferred strategies for the development of the land. The land is, however, highly suitable for development. And Professor Farrelly from UTAS again on the challenges it faces here. There's currently no National Infrastructure Fund for Higher Education and as everybody appreciates, there's also a constrained budget environment here in Tasmania and increasingly also in Canberra. We don't need to be able to find ways to invest in the STEM facilities that Tasmania needs. And Adam, I've seen some projections that three quarters of all future jobs will require STEM skills. I guess you've got to be in it to win it. Adam, we've talked about the South. What's happening in the states North and Northwest, those sort of satellite campuses of the university? It's completely moved in terms of its infrastructure in Launceston? It hasn't completely moved from the Newnham campus in northern Launceston. There are still some functions out there. The Australian Maritime College is still at Newnham but there has been substantial development at Inveresk just north of the Tamar River in central Launceston. That move wasn't without issue either. The state government had a bit of a dispute with UTAS over a covenant on the land at Newnham that only allowed education. Minister Erica Betts actually wrote to Parliament to criticise UTAS for altering its negotiating position multiple times during that but that Inveresk upgrade I guess it did receive substantial Commonwealth and state funding. The main issue though that was a different time than when the Sandy Bay STEM plan has emerged and that was a time when the Commonwealth was open to funding this type of infrastructure development whereas now it's much less so. So how is it that UTAS arrives at its governance decisions? Yeah, the UTAS Council essentially signs off on strategic decisions and is meant to provide oversight but the Council has changed quite a lot over the course of decades. For example almost half of its members were academics or students in the 1990s which has dropped down to 20%. There's also been a substantial increase in the Council essentially appointing its own members which can create this cycle of the same people over and over again. Then there's the increasing use of consultants, an estimated $300 million over the course of a decade according to retired Commonwealth public servant Robert Hogan who has been closely scrutinising UTAS. The consultant question is increasingly coming up in Australian universities. A Senate inquiry recently looked into the corporatisation of universities and Four Corners investigated these matters too in a recent episode and we've had UTAS Vice Chancellor Rufus Black appointed as an independent board member of consultant Deloitte in September last year and that was interesting because UTAS had about $10 million worth of contracts with Deloitte since 2018 at least one of which is ongoing. It also wrote the Sedi Bay STEM business case but the matter went to UTAS Council after Rufus Black had been offered the position and given the perceived conflict of interest there there's a view that it should have gone to the Council before he even applied as from that moment there's a perception that if Deloitte attempted to get work with UTAS that decision making could be impacted in some way even if Rufus Black wasn't directly involved UTAS says it will be managed through its normal conflict of interest processes but there is still these questions about the time that he will spend on preparation and attendance of Deloitte board meetings his promise to donate his six-figure remuneration to the university for philanthropic reasons which is partly tax deductible. Well speaking of perceptions how solid are UTAS finances perceived to be? UTAS describes UTAS's financial position as strong in its annual reporting the most recent in 2024 the Auditor General though has been becoming increasingly concerned at UTAS's financial position it pointed out that it had four consecutive deficits from core operations exceeding $120 million and the Auditor General said this was an unsustainable situation opponents of UTAS's property dealings argue that the attempted shift of a CBD is the cause of this and that without that the university's underlying financial position could be manageable so we're now in this period of I guess relative calm compared to the last five to ten years but that still broadly depends on how UTAS approaches this new land sales front that has now opened up UTAS's plans could be seen to be much less ambitious and controversial than they were previously but it still has this ageing infrastructure issue at Sandy Bay that it will need to address and whether that comes from that STEM funding whether the solution comes from that funding all indications show that that is quite a difficult process for UTAS or if it just has to upgrade its existing facilities you know that remains to be seen well fun fact did you know that before it became the university the land it sits on in Sandy Bay was a rifle range and as you've just been explaining there Adam it's still in the crosshairs for many thank you and we're taking a break for a couple of weeks and you can swat up on any previous episodes you missed in the meantime until next time cheers you've been listening to an ABC podcast discover more great ABC podcasts live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app you

episodes.title: Do we care enough about our pollies' mental health?
episodes.description: In what's believed to be the biggest study of its kind, a staggering 70 percent of almost 300 of our federal, state and local politicians who took part say the job has adversely affected their mental health.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Everybody's talking about fuel. Whether you're in need of filling up the tank for the week and you're watching the dollars tick over at the Bowser or you're watching weekend plans, holiday plans, business plans change. To help get your head around the latest, you can find Fuelcast in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. Are you OK? Seems a lot of our politicians aren't. There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. Social media aggression, which can be deeply personal. I ignore it. My family see it. I've told them to ignore it. The notion that you can only be successful in politics if you're willing to be a head kicker is frankly complete bullshit. Social media is one thing, but also some of the behaviour you see within our council chambers, within our parliament, where in many other workplaces, or most other workplaces, you would not accept that sort of behaviour. The mental wear and tear is a real factor in me deciding whether or not I'd nominate later this year. Often when I talk to school groups who are in to watch question time beforehand, I'll say what you're about to see is not a very healthy display of adult behaviour. This is not a way that would be acceptable for your parents to talk to their colleagues at work or for your teachers to talk to each other at work. Hello and welcome to Tassiecast. I'm Ailey Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. Have you ever listened to question time in state or federal parliament or checked out a local council meeting that's streamed online? To say it can be brutal is an understatement, and that must take a toll. We know it has and does because federal, state and local members have quit because it's caused or contributed to mental ill health. Former Premier Peter Gutwin cited burnout for his departure. Ministers have quit cabinet and gone to the back bench. And local councillors have thrown in the towel because of the toll the job was taking. Now, none of us make good decisions when we're not well. Do we really want our elected representatives making decisions that affect all of our lives when they're not well? I don't reckon we do. There's a new study believed to be the biggest to date on the mental health and wellbeing of politicians in Australia. Almost 300 federal, state and local polis took part, and the results are by any measure staggering. 70% say the job has adversely affected their mental health. Now, I can imagine some people might be saying, yeah, violin, this big. You chose to go into public life, you get paid really well and so on. And while that might be true, does that mean it should be open season? Throw in the social media abuse, including death threats. Are we really going to get the best person for the job? State political reporter Lucy MacDonald sees up close the realities of life in the so-called bear pit. Lucy, were you taken aback by what you saw and heard when you first started covering politics as a journalist? Well, Ellie, we obviously all see snippets on the news, but I think nothing prepares you for that full theatre. I mean, sometimes you're in there and you're just thinking, can you just stop with the personal insults and speak a little bit more about policy? There was a 2022 report into the culture in Tasmanian Parliament that found two thirds of staff had witnessed discrimination, sexual harassment and bullying in the workplace. Now, it was the staff that was surveyed, but it did find that MPs were some of the main offenders. And it was suggested in the study that the vitriol displayed in Parliament, particularly in Question Time, might have contributed to that culture. Now, there was a tripartisan reaction to this and there's been a real effort to change it. When Speaker Michelle O'Byrne quit last year, she spoke about how toxic the Parliament was in 2024, but she did say that she thought it had really improved and she put some of that down to the fact that Parliament was a lot bigger by then. But even with the bigger Parliament, Lucy, some of the worst perpetrators of abuse continue to be the pollies themselves. Totally. I mean, look, Question Time is the worst because they are performing for the media. They want to get their grab. But there's fierce, passionate debate and there's another level. Some of the sledging and heckling in there, I think people would see as crossing a line. One of the incidents that people might remember, I think it was two years ago that Government Minister Erica Bette suggested that Greens leader, Rosalie Wardruff, who was heckling him repeatedly and loudly, but he suggested that she was like Mr Bean because she was better when she kept her mouth shut. And I think the day before, another Liberal member had suggested that she put a sock in it. Now, those ones spring to mind, but it comes from all sides, both in Parliament and through releases, accusing people of being liars, deceptive, weak, wreckers. It's pretty nasty stuff that wouldn't stack up in any other workplace. Lucy, politics, we know, it's not a gig for the faint-hearted. And decisions and statements, though, they should be rightly questioned and criticised. Yeah, absolutely. Politicians have power. They need to be scrutinised. And naturally, people get heated about certain debates. I mean, the Government proposal to ban greyhound racing at the moment is a really good example. It's getting pretty nuts. I think we just saw that Christy Johnson had to put a video up to say that her greyhound was still alive because people online have been suggesting that he'd been injured and died. We saw horrible, sexist, violent things posted about Racing Minister Jane Howlett. Or you might remember during the stadium debate that independent Upper House member, Dean Harris, spoke about the fact that people were saying his father would be turning in his grave if he voted against the stadium. He got quite emotional about that. And there was, of course, awful things coming from the other side of that debate too. And then I've had MPs across the spectrum show me messages they've received or comments that have been hidden. Really violent, sexualised comments, if they're women. One that was like about how someone should have been smothered at birth. It's just horrific stuff no one should deal with. But of course, yes, they should be scrutinised for their decisions and actions. We need to be able to criticise and question them. For example, in Parliament recently, the Racing Minister was asked about when she knew something regarding TAS Racing. It was a pretty straight question, but listen to this exchange between Minister Jane Howlett and Labor's Integrity Spokesperson Ella Haddad. This is nothing but a misogynist attack. How do you feel? It's International Women's Week, Miss Haddad. How do you feel? Are you inspiring women to enter Parliament? To misuse and to weaponise a word like misogynistic actually does a disservice not only to all women, but to men as well. For a word, the word misogynistic to be weaponised devalues the word. It devalues the importance and it actually trivialises the misogyny that we all face every day, all of us, in politics as women, in the media every day as women. So Lucy, how do we make Parliament and local government a better workplace? The mental health survey of our elected representatives. Is that the ultimate aim of this research by the Better Politics Foundation? Yeah, like you might be thinking, I mean, who cares? They have signed up to this, but we should all care, according to the Better Politics Foundation. They say that these are the people making decisions, shaping our lives. Better Politics argues that the mental wellbeing of politicians isn't a private issue, it's a public one. They say that when leaders are exhausted, threatened or unsupported, decision-making suffers, polarisation deepens and our democracy weakens. We need leaders who are equipped to respond to crises and opportunities with clarity, empathy and courage. Now, this Australian study came off the back of a smaller international one that found current politicians have worse mental wellbeing than emergency service employees. Wow. Yeah, look, that's dealing with politicians across the world in very different political climates, but it's still pretty shocking. In terms of the Australian study, which, as you mentioned, dealt with all three levels of government, it found that 70% say the job has adversely affected their mental health, 40% felt prevented from speaking out due to their lack of mental wellbeing, 20%, so one in five, have thought about harming themselves due to the pressure of the job, and 73% say gender has influenced their experience as an MP, while 71% say, compared to other workplaces they've experienced, their parliament workplace is the worst. That's like three quarters, almost. Yeah. Wow. I mean, it's probably not unsurprising, right, anything you see in question time. True. Go to HR or anywhere else. You know, one of the leads on this research is former Australian of the Year and psychiatrist Patrick McGorry. He said that the workplace, social media, mainstream media, and the constant pressure and risk associated with their roles is impacting them. This is playing out in these figures of impaired mental health and wellbeing in a significant proportion of politicians, even to the extent that a subset have suicidal thoughts. Now, he thinks it's a real worry and he's concerned that the government is being seen as a problem rather than a cornerstone of our society. He thinks we need to better educate the public about the reality of politics. There are misconceptions around work hours, around decision-making hours, around pay. I mean, people think it's really lucrative, but you can often make more money in the private sector or even high up in a department. And he says there's this sort of attitude that they're, you know, they're all their pollies, they're all the same, and people forget that they're real people with families and lives and feelings. And it's believed that lack of awareness takes a toll on the politicians. And one of the local reps involved in the study, Lucy, is Central Highlands councillor David Meacham. We heard him at the top questioning whether or not he'll even stand again. Yeah, he's a former academic and first-time councillor. He talked about how rough local government is, the ugliness in the chamber, the abuse they get from members of the public, the anonymous hits on social media, and he said councillors can't even access support. He told me being on council has affected him quite badly, and we know this is not an uncommon story. And of course, then we've got state parliament. I mean, here's Labor's El Haddad on how the social media impacts her. What can only be described as horrendous trolling, which some people would probably say, oh, well, you know, you put yourself out there, you deserve to get whatever's coming your way. But a lot of times, as anyone would see on the internet, the comments that people make are often really very vulgar and expletive-laden and often really personal and unnecessarily hurtful. And I don't think that adds to the political debate. And here's long-term legislative councillor Ruth Forrest, who's involved in the study. But it is concerning that we're seeing it actually negatively impacting so many people's mental health and wellbeing in undertaking what is a pretty important role for our democracy. Lucy, Premier Jeremy Rockcliffe used to be a phone councillor with Lifeline and has spent a long time in public life. What's been his response? Yeah, he's in politics for over two decades now, and he cops a lot of abuse. I think everyone's aware of that. He told me he often wonders if he'll feel the effects when he leaves politics. He spoke about how the social media aggression has really amped up since COVID, but he said he's not worried about it for himself. He is more concerned that it will discourage others from running for politics. And he spoke about the culture within Parliament. He's no fan of the sort of grottiness that you see in media releases or how personal it can get in the chamber. And again, he's concerned it'll put decent people off pursuing politics. We've lost the art of good debate. And people are too quick to point the finger and say awful things without reasonable justification. And so the art of political debate where you actually argue the issues robustly, it's just too easy now to attack people personally. And that diminishes debate. It's not good for democracy. And that would dissuade people. He also spoke about the fact that federal parliament has really good support mechanisms for politicians' wellbeing, but Tasmania doesn't actually offer the same level. Well, as Premier, a lot has to rest on him, surely, Lucy, to provide those better support mechanisms. Like, do they have an equivalent of an EAP, an Employee Assistance Program? Yeah, there is actually an EAP. And that's for stress and counselling. My understanding is MPs weren't previously able to access it. Federal parliament also has another level of support service that can be a bit more long-term, trauma-focused and deal with bullying, harassment and actual complaints. You could argue it's on the Premier to change things. And he certainly did say he wants politicians across the chamber to be well-supported. But of course, he's not governing alone. He's part of the broad church that is the Liberal Party. So I guess you could argue it's on the entire government to fix things. If there was one good thing that came out of the COVID pandemic, Lucy, it'd have to be more open discussion about mental health. The increased stress and anxiety that that pandemic induced. Premier Rockleaf's predecessor, Peter Gutwin. I mean, he quit citing burnout. Yeah, that was a pretty huge moment. And I think it sort of made great strides in destigmatising mental health. But unfortunately, the general feeling amongst politicians is that mental illness is still seen as a weakness in the walls of parliament. That politics is not a place for people to be vulnerable. We spoke about supports before, but the politicians I've chatted to for this story all told me they felt some politicians would choose not to access support because of the stigma, which is not ideal when these are the people we want to be setting an example. I think, though, every time someone stands up and speaks about their issues, their mental health, that's really powerful. Nick Street, the former government minister, is one that stands out for me. Late in 2024, he came out at a press conference with the Premier and announced that he was going to be moving to the backbench to focus on his mental health. I was there. I remember it was it really moved me to see him speaking so openly about his struggles. And it was clear how supported he felt by the Premier. Our mental health, just like our physical health, I mean, it's not a constant. It can change depending on a range of factors, including obviously the workplace. And we've heard about the stats of politicians. But according to a recent report by Primary Health Tasmania, one in five of us experience a mental health condition in any given year. And in just over a decade between 2009 and 2022, the proportion of Tasmanians diagnosed with anxiety or depression increased from 21 to 37 percent. Now, some people would say we need to be more resilient or to toughen up. Look, resilient expert Dr. Justine Gatt says it's a misconception that resilience is about being tougher. She says mental health and well-being is about our state, but resilience is about how we deal with adversity or trauma. And it's something we can learn. She says it's not about avoiding stress, but learning how to adapt to it. There are quite a lot of techniques. And she thinks we should be taught about building resilience in school. But it's not just about the person. It's also about the environment they're in and the support around them, which is where politics gets messy. Politics combines sustained high workload. You've got the public scrutiny, adversarial environments, and you've got limited recovery time. So there are a lot of conditions that are happening there that can erode your mental health over time. We've been talking about how politics is tough on everyone. But I mean, if you've already got a pre-existing mental health condition, the idea of entering a workplace that doesn't appear particularly safe is going to be very daunting. The politicians I've spoken to, though, were adamant that they wanted people with mental health issues to feel safe to run and not to be deterred because they want the best people. And they also believe parliament needs to be reflective of society. And we know that it's not like that for many minorities at the moment, including mental health. Lucy, mental well-being is something very close to your heart. A marathon you ran recently was to raise money for the Black Dog Institute. Yeah, I've struggled with mental health issues since I was in my late teens, early 20s. But it wasn't until I was 28 that I was actually diagnosed with bipolar type 2. It answered a lot of questions, but it certainly didn't fix things. It's been it's pretty rough at times. I mean, you know, you've been there every step of the way, pretty much. You know, sometimes my life can be perfectly fine. And then my brain decides that I'm, you know, just going to be overwhelmed by crushing sadness that's at times debilitating. And then other times I'm too happy. I'm too impulsive. I'm making the wrong decisions. And look, you know, for a long time, only a few people knew sort of like knew about this. And I think I was generally pretty good at masking at least the sadness. Like I could, you know, go to work. I'm pretty outgoing and bubbly. And I could sort of put on that show and then get home and fall apart. Or I could sort of, you know, I'd be just crushed by the weight of depression. But then I would perform for camera. I was nervous about speaking out because I guess I felt like a bit of a freak. But look, I wanted to do the run anyway, because I'm a runner and I wanted to run a marathon on the Great Ocean Road. Often those runs come where you can sort of sponsor money for a charity. It made sense to me to sort of raise money for mental health. And then I kind of started thinking about, well, do I suddenly, you know, do I speak about it? And I remember speaking to you about this and I drafted a long message. And then I sat on it for ages because I still wasn't sure. And then, yeah, I did. I chose to sort of share that on a public Instagram post. And there was just this outpouring of support. Like I was flooded with comments. People messaged me, people I didn't know well. People in person said something. It was just, I was sort of wrapped in love. It was pretty incredible. And I'm so glad I did it. And I guess it taught me that people are better than we think they are, except for maybe internet trolls and that you don't know what anyone else is going through. So choose kindness. Thank you, Lucy. And if you're listening to this and you or someone you know is struggling, please do seek help. Until next time. Cheers.

episodes.title: Easter plans under the pump as Tassies shell out for fuel and choccy
episodes.description: Many of us are already feeling the pinch ... We've got massive fuel prices, TT Line has added a surcharge, farmers are worried about future production capacity add to that the Easter Bunny is more expensive than ever.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm Alan Kohler and I want to take you straight to the source. Every Friday I sit down with the people running companies, shaping industries and influencing the Australian economy to talk risk, power, profit, pressure. Not just their success, but their strategy and what it means for the rest of us. Because that's business. Search, subscribe and stay ahead. Find That's Business with Alan Kohler on the ABC Business Daily feed. On ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. Fuel and chocolate, two Easter essentials taking a bigger than usual chunk out of our wallets. There's a lot of hardworking Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. We're looking at going away on a trip at the end of May and we're not real sure whether we're going to go there or not now to the mainland. Probably going to cost me twice what it would. Towing a caravan. I'm not going to have as much for the things that I want. But just the ones just go out the window and you just have to do what you've got to do. I really think we'll just have to cancel. It's not just the cost of the fuel. It's whether it's going to be available. What we want to say to the market is we're still here. We're open for business and come out and see us. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. How are your plans going for the Easter break? Have you ditched the long drive for a catch up with friends or relatives because it's just too expensive to fill up? If so, you're not alone. According to the Tourism and Transport Forum, more than 40% of Australians have abandoned their Easter plans or reduced them to stay closer to home. You know the saying, think global, act local, and you're thinking every little effort such as remembering your keep cup does matter. I guess we're seeing the consequences of global events having real local impacts. We all know the issue, the Persian Gulf, more specifically the Strait of Hormuz. It's been shut by Iran since Israel and US military strikes, disrupting global oil supply. And at the moment, there's no end in sight. The Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, warned of uncertain times in a rare address to the nation. Our 7.30 reporter, Adam Langenberg, has been looking at the havoc the crisis is wreaking. Adam, many of us might be staying put for Easter, but the price and availability of fuel is a moving feast, isn't it? It certainly does feel like that, Ellie. Every day, it feels like there's another announcement or something shifting. Obviously, at the federal level, we saw the halving of the fuel excise. We also saw that address from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, sort of urging people to remain calm throughout this crisis. And then at the statewide level, we've had operators like the Tuller Lakeside Lodge impose a surcharge on visitors. We've had a 15% levy on new Spirit of Tasmania bookings. And then also from the state government, we've seen them make public transport free in a bid to ease that cost of living crisis that's going on at the moment. And then we had legislation rushed through state parliament as well, giving the state government extra powers in an emergency, including setting a maximum price for fuel. So there's been lots of things happening and it feels like every day you wake up and find out what's the latest with fuel. Well, Easter's a really important period for our tourism operators. And for many, it's kind of seen as a bit of like a last gasp before the quieter months. Yeah, you're right. I think for Easter, which is a really big time, lots of that demand's already been locked and loaded, whether it's locals or domestic visitors. Most operators are saying that they're expecting a pretty strong Easter, although there has been some cancellations. But longer term is where we're seeing those cancellations already happen. Those international tourists who are taking a look at what's happening and going, we don't want to fly through the Middle East right now and cancelling their trips to Tasmania or worrying about fuel availability as well. So that's the concern that we're seeing at the moment. On the upside, though, there are lots of people that were staying and travelling locally and not travelling overseas. So there is some benefit to that local tourism sector. There has been a real campaign, though, to get people here for that off season. And there is a concern that it might not eventuate. Well, dark mofo, though, Adam, it looks like it's on the rise. It is early. Tickets went on sale on Wednesday. I was 10 minutes late to getting tickets myself. I was about 11,000 people in the queue. I did get all my tickets to everything that I intended to go to, but they're all sold out now. So a huge rush on those dark mofo tickets. All up, the stats from the festival are that as of 3 p.m. on the first day of going on sale, over $3.8 million had been spent on tickets. That's up 31% on day one sales the year before. Now, almost two thirds of ticket purchases came from outside Tasmania. That's really good news for a tourism industry that was pretty fearful. So June's looking pretty hot for some, Adam, but holidaying at home, a good idea at the moment. I mean, according to those in the industry, tourism supports around 50,000 jobs in Tassie, both directly and indirectly. I mean, it's a massive contributor to our economy, which, let's face it, can do with all the help it can get. Yeah, that's right, Ellie. Tourism directly contributes about $2.27 billion to Tasmania's economy, which is about 5.5% of the state's gross state product. That's significantly higher than the national average. So tourism is really important. On petrol, or back to petrol, Adam, the last time Australia had a severe shortage was in the 1970s. Now, that too, interestingly, was partly as a result of events in Iran. It was after the revolution. But there was an Australian refinery strike too. And there ended up being rationing whereby a number plate system based on odds and evens for buying fuel was introduced. Yeah, that's right. The big difference this time around, Ellie, is that we don't have many refineries. There are just two left in Australia. They supply less than 20% of the nation's fuel demand. ABC guru Alan Kohler wrote a really interesting article about this recently. It was 2013 and 2014 where there were these two big refinery closures that really tipped the balance from Australia being self-sufficient with its fuel supply to being entirely reliant on overseas imports. So how close do you think we might be to rationing again? That's the million-dollar question, Ellie. Certainly, everyone's waiting and watching to see what happens next. And things are moving at a dramatic pace. So we'll keep seeing things develop in future days and weeks. I think the message in that address from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was catch a bus or a train, if you can, to ensure that reserves of fuel remain high. But there was no talk about rationing or real crisis just yet. But there's a... It was a bit sort of keep calm, but also be careful. Absolutely. It did sort of really straddle that line, didn't it? I think everyone's watching and waiting and there's a real chance that we do head towards that the longer that this situation continues. Adam, we've talked about the importance of Tassie's tourism industry, but what about critical services, our emergency services? Is there like a quarantine supply to ensure they're able to continue? Yeah, so there's federal government legislation that basically allows the government to take over fuel supply in an emergency crisis and then quarantine and ration it. And under those provisions, there are a whole number of people who are exempt from that. So taxi services, emergency services. The whole idea of it is to ensure that they're able to continue to receive fuel during a crisis. I was talking to the owner of a small electrical business, Adam. He's got around 10 employees and all of their vehicles run on diesel. His fuel bill has gone up by around $1,000 a week. I mean, that's just not sustainable, is it? No, it's not. And it's not just fuel that's going up. There's a volatility of prices across a whole spectrum of things that are made with petrochemicals. Lots of them that you mightn't have realised. We've heard about PVC pipe, but then there's also electrical cabling. Here's Ben Shaw from the National Electrical Communications Association talking about how the rising price of petrol means cost estimates for work keep changing. When you get a cable quote, so electrical cable, so whether it's fitting out your house or whether it's an underground sub-main, you generally get a quote at the time of quoting from a cable manufacturer or cable supplier. They will hold that quote for normally a period of time. In normal circumstances, it'd be 14 days, 21 days, 30 days. At this stage, cable manufacturers are only holding quotes for 24 hours or 48 hours as maximum. Well, that really shows the volatility, doesn't it, Adam? What about farmers? They're also being hit hard. They are. And obviously, the rising price of diesel is a huge concern for the farming sector. But then there's lots of concern about the availability and supply of fertilisers too, coming up to a really crucial planting season. Here's Nathan Cox from TAS Farmers talking about that uncertainty that's crippling the farming sector. At the moment, we need to get some visibility on fertiliser supply, particularly nitrogen-based fertilisers. Here in Tasmania, we've only got a few months before we'll start to be putting crops in for the spring and the summer. We need to know that there are boats on the water with fertiliser coming in so that we can have certainty of planting, so there can be certainty of harvest. Adam, I've seen some projections that the shortage and consequent surge in the price of fertiliser could lead to a rise of nearing 20% in global food prices. Yeah. So margins are really tight for the farming sector, as we know, Ely. And the lobby groups say that if there is this big rise in fuel, but also the cost of fertiliser, that prices just need to shift. Suppliers will have to pay them more, even if they've got locked-in contracts, just because that's going to be the cost of doing business. And then there's the reality of supply as well. If there's fewer crops in the ground, then inevitably prices go up. And a lot of Tassie farmers are already grappling with the consequences of drought. I mean, parts of the state have recently had their driest conditions in over a century. And it's not just homegrown produce, Adam. Chocolate, a staple for many at this time of year in particular, is really expensive. Yeah, Ely, I'm a bit of a chocolate fiend and I've been walking the grocery store aisles this year and noticing that it's pretty expensive. Although the price of cocoa has now dropped, there's been supply shortages from major producing nations in West Africa, which drove up the prices. And your sweet treat manufacturers had already bought those cocoa beans in advance. So even though cocoa's down, Easter eggs are still really expensive. Adam, on a slightly different note, I really do wonder what the thieves of 12 tonnes of Kit Kat have done with their loot. Late March, the truck left a factory in Italy en route to Poland. And kind of kudos to Nestle, who in a statement said, we've always encouraged people to have a break with Kit Kat, but it seems thieves have taken the message too literally. Yeah, putting a pretty positive spin on a negative situation there, Ely. It's not quite 12 tonnes of chocolate, but just recently hundreds of litres of diesel was stolen from a property in Tasmania's southern Midlands. And police are urging people to store their vehicles and fuel storage tanks in secure buildings. There's also been a rise of thefts from service stations all around Australia as well. Have you noticed a certain smug look on the face of EV drivers during this time? I don't know about smugness, Ely. I might get some noses out of joining the office if I call EV owners smug, mightn't I? But certainly I think the manufacturers and people who sell them are in for a bumper Easter period and maybe beyond that as well. Thanks, Adam. And thanks to you too for joining us on TassieCast. Let us know your plans, whether you've truncated them this Easter break. Until next time, cheers. Cheers. Cheers. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

There's also been a rise of thefts from service stations all around Australia as well.
Have you noticed a certain smug look on the face of EV drivers during this time?
I don't know about smugness, Ely.
I might get some noses out of joining the office if I call EV owners smug, mightn't I?
But certainly I think the manufacturers and people who sell them are in for a bumper Easter period and maybe beyond that as well.

episodes.title: The manosphere creeping into Tassie classrooms
episodes.description: The manosphere - the online world considered responsible for the rise in anti-social behaviour and fuelling misogyny is reaching Tassie classrooms. So how and why are men, particular young men getting caught up in this manosphere web?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm Carrington Clark. And I'm Alan Kohler. In 2026, business big and small is moving at a rapid pace. And ABC Business Daily is here to help you cut through the noise and spin. Monday to Thursday. And on Friday, I sit down with business leaders, founders, creators, changemakers and those in the know to ask them how they see the world because that's business. All in the ABC Business Daily feed on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. Heard of the Manosphere? There's a lot of hardworking Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. We have allowed to settle an impression that more for women always means less for men, that this is a zero-sum game. Whereas actually, the research clearly shows, my own life experiences show, that when we rise, we rise together. A gender equal world would be a better world for men too. There's things that I think all of us can do, both as individuals and as a society and as a government, to make sure that our boys have access to the kind of information that balances out the negativity and the destructive and incredibly misogynistic content that they're getting fed online. As a mum of two teenage daughters, to hear that our sons are on average showing more conservative attitudes to relationships and to women than our father's generation does, it's really scary. And it tells us that the great strides that have been made by decades of the women's movement and movements for equality are being undone and being undone really quickly. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward, coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. This week's pod is slightly shorter than normal as a result of industrial action taken by union members at the ABC in the quest for better wages and conditions. OK, Manosphere. It sounds like it should be pretty innocuous, right? Like maybe just blokes connecting with blokes like men's sheds or something. But it's much darker than that. It's an online world considered responsible for a rise in anti-social behaviour, fuelling misogyny. And we've heard from Tassie teachers about the increasing threats and violence in schools. The bus service is cancelled. I mean, bus company Metro's reported massive increases in reports of abuse, violence and vandalism. That's not to say it's all perpetrated by males, but they are, according to the figures, the main offenders. Maybe you've seen Manosphere by renowned documentarian Louis Theroux, where manfluences promote harmful views in opposition to feminism and gender equality, which it blames for disenfranchising men and in severe cases can lead to violence. So how and why are men, particularly young men, caught up in the ugly Manosphere web? This isn't about shrinking away from the digital world. That's here to stay. But how do we handle the darker side? The ABC's Families reporter, Fiona Blackwood,'s been taking a look at what's being done to combat it. Vee, can you outline at the start, though, what do we mean when we say Manosphere? It's funny, isn't it? Because if you're not in it, you're not in it. And lots of people I spoke to when I was starting to do this story had never heard of it. Even some of the young people I spoke to who might actually be consuming some of the content had no idea about what the Manosphere was. But I think it's becoming more well known, particularly after the release of Louis Theroux's documentary. So basically, the Manosphere describes a community of online influencers and content creators who see men and boys as victims of gender equality and aim to reassert traditional gender roles. If you've been watching the latest series of Married at First Sight, Ellie, you might have heard one of the contestants saying that he wanted a submissive wife. Now, this has sparked debate with commentators talking about how that sort of language is coming directly from the Manosphere. So to go back, these are influencers, podcasters that promote traditional masculinity, male supremacy, misogyny, and in extreme cases, violence. At its most basic, it's a type of thinking that includes negative attitudes towards gender equality and feminism. So blaming women and girls for social and personal problems, dehumanising women, and believing that men should be self-reliant and show no emotion. Indigenous rights activist Thomas Mayo said at a recent No to Violence conference that he's worried that the attitude of boys and men towards women is going backwards. He said the social media algorithms are pretty good at saturating the feeds of boys and young men with this kind of stuff. We mentioned the online and you mentioned Married at First Sight. I'm not sure how that relates to the real world, but is it spilling over into the real world? Yeah, well, this is no longer just a fringe internet issue. These are harmful ideas and they're impacting directly, particularly on Australian classrooms. A recent report by Monash University heard from teachers who are saying that things are getting worse for them. And that process sort of started post the COVID era. I guess more people being online. Female teachers have reported being taunted by students with messages like, make me a sandwich, to imply that a woman's place is in the kitchen. There have also been reports of boys in classroom using hand signals made popular in the manosphere to symbolise male supremacy. And some teachers might not even know what these are or what they mean. She said teachers are also being baited by students to enter into debates about equality. And in serious cases, some female teachers have described in this report being circled by boys in the schoolyard, as well as reports of direct physical and sexual assault. It also found that the rise in the manosphere is impacting on the education of girls, with the guide reporting that one in four girls felt unsafe at school due to boys' behaviours. I think it's important to raise a point here that not all boys are attuned to the manosphere content and not all of them support it, of course. So those boys are sitting in the classroom and they're seeing their teachers being severely disrespected or the girls around them being belittled. And that can have an impact on those boys as well. A lot of what you mentioned there, Fee, is incredibly intimidating. But you mentioned some physical threats there as well. Yeah. I mean, for some teachers, the situation can become intolerable and they might consider moving schools or leaving the teaching profession altogether. And we all know there's a shortage of teachers. So Monash University and the Australian National Research Organisation for Women's Safety have put together a handbook and that's designed to help teachers identify the influence of the manosphere and how to manage it in the classroom. It's about trying to understand the pathways into the manosphere and its appeal to young men. It's also about helping young people develop critical digital literacy. It talks about whole school, consistent response to incidents of sexism and misogyny, making sure that teachers and students who have experienced these behaviours feel supported and that boys who have caused harm are held accountable. We heard at the top, Fee, from former Prime Minister Julia Gillard in a recent interview with the BBC, let's face it, moving through adolescence is often a really difficult time. You know, you're trying to find your tribe, as it were. But this rise in harmful attitudes being seen in classrooms is also being seen in the political sphere. I mean, Julia Gillard's misogyny speech, it's gone down in the annals of history. But we've got the current President of the United States calling female journalists derogatory things based on their looks. Julia Gillard is Chair of the Global Institute for Women's Leadership at King's College in London. And that recent research to mark International Women's Day was so eye-opening. More than 20,000 people across 29 countries, including Australia, were surveyed and 31% of Gen Z men agreed that a wife should always obey her husband. And one third said a husband should have the final word on important decisions. I mean, they're pretty staggering figures. But it's not just girls and women who are impacted by this toxic behaviour perpetrated by the so-called manosphere. That's right. And for some influencers, key beliefs of the manosphere overlap with other far-right groups. So there are links to homophobia, transphobia, white supremacy and racism and anti-immigration views. As Thomas Mayo said in his speech, it's not just about misogyny, but it's about division. What is the advice then to not just teachers, you know, there's a handbook for teachers on how best to try to tackle this. What about parents and carers like at home? Yeah, well, I mean, this guidebook could be handy for parents too, particularly if you have no idea about the manosphere. It sort of gives a bit of an overview of what it is. Parenting experts also say it's important for parents to understand why some boys might be attracted to the manosphere and talking to them about it. It's crucial to help them identify harmful content. Experts say parents need to emphasise that it's normal to be curious, but also to provide other perspectives. They say it might be a good idea to explore a specific piece of content with your child, trying to understand the world they're engaging with, what resonates with them, what doesn't. And also really key is exposing boys to different versions of masculinity than what they're seeing online. So real role models, dads, uncles, brothers, coaches, friends, people in their lives who are healthy male role models and finding ways to connect with them. Well, the non-healthy role models, that's certainly something that our politicians in Tassie have also been raising. Here's what Labor's Ella Haddad and the Greens' Vicar Bailey told TassieCast. Part of the danger of how these algorithms work and they push this content into the feeds of young men is that it's completely pervasive and it can take over so much of the content that they are seeing. And these types of views, I think, were always there, but they used to lurk in the shadows a bit. But now they are on tens of millions of screens of tens of millions of young men every day. We need to accept that Tasmania is no exception. Just because we're an island at the bottom of the world doesn't mean we're immune from these kind of influences because the internet, you know, straddles all people, basically. Fee, Man Cave, a mental health charity that works with young men, have weighed into this. What have they got to say? Yeah, I spoke to Ben Vassilou, who runs the Man Cave. They hold workshops for young men right across Australia. Here he is unpacking a bit more in depth about what the Manosphere looks like. The Manosphere is promoting content that's about getting jacked, getting ripped, getting rich quick. It's very anti-women. It's anti-gender equity. It's anti-gay and queer community. And what it's doing is sucking this vacuum and this opportunity where boys feel either lost, disconnected, or simply just need to be heard and feel belonging into this conversation and this content that's actually quite damaging. It's not all bad news, though, Fee. Ben Vassilou says things might be changing. That's right. The Man Cave has worked with over 100,000 boys over the last decade. He says it can't just be on teachers and parents to deal with this issue and that sometimes schools need to bring the experts in, like his organisation. He says they hold workshops without screens, without PowerPoint presentations, and they talk to boys. And he says the key is being able to have messy conversations that might not be politically correct, that go to the undercurrent of the language and hopefully shift and change behaviour. It's about getting boys to open up, talk about what's going on in their lives, what's happening in the world around them, and bringing up some hairy topics that teachers and parents might struggle with, and then showing them a different way. Here's a bit more of what he had to say. And we're seeing pretty significant impact across those workshops, and we're actually seeing boys reverse behaviours, reverse feelings of hopelessness, reverse misogynistic or homophobic behaviours. We're seeing that in real time, and also longitudinally, we're seeing thousands of boys actually change their view from what they've seen online. Fee, you've got young men in your life. What conversations have you had with them? I mean, I just spend a lot of time asking my son to clean his room, which doesn't really apply to this. But I would say for me, the best time to have these sort of conversations is in the car. So when they're kind of trapped, they don't have to have direct eye contact with you. I mean, I'm no parenting expert, but I guess it's all about trying to keep communication open, which can be really hard when they're teenagers. Let us know what you do with the young men in your life. Is it a chat around the dinner table or with that captive audience in the car like Fee does? Thanks very much, Fee. And thanks to you too for joining us on this truncated version of TassieCast. Until next time, cheers. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Kunanyi/Mt Wellington: A mountain of a debate
episodes.description: Kunanyi/Mt Wellington is Tasmania's most visited natural asset but is a cable car the answer to getting more people on the mountain?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily. The podcast that brings you one big story affecting your world each weekday in just 15 minutes. AI is changing not just how we work, but it's also changing how we fight war. And we see that on our screens. We see what's happening in Iran. We see what's happening in Gaza. We see what's happening in Ukraine. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. It's a mountain of a debate. There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. I just love the rocks, the flora, the fauna, the whole aesthetic of the place. It's just such an amazing park just on our doorstep. I'm committed not only to the Cradle Valley cableway, but also a cableway on Kunani, Mount Wellington, and I've sought advice on developing a pathway to support this to happen. The pipe dream of a cable car, it stymies a proper conversation and real progress on credible solutions to the challenges that faces the mountain. A road that was built in 1930s that has been designed to accommodate traffic in 2030. We'd like to see Kunani return to Aboriginal ownership, but at least it's important that Aboriginal people are given the opportunity to have a say in its protection. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. When was the last time you went up Hobart's Kunani, Mount Wellington? Is it one of the first places you'd take visitors? Or maybe you just look out the window of a morning to have a look to help you decide what to wear by gauging what the weather's going to do that day. Depending on where you are in Tassie South, chances are you have a view of some sort. Home to a vast array of native plants and animals, it's also of major cultural significance for many of the state's First Nations people. Although by no measure Tassie's tallest mountain, Kunani does dominate the Hobart skyline, providing an imposing backdrop to the city. And views from the summit are without doubt spectacular. In good weather, that is. It's already Tassie's most visited natural asset at around half a million people a year. But the government reckons it's still too hard for many to access it. And as we heard at the beginning, Premier Jeremy Rockliffe wants to see a cable car on it. Reporter Adam Holmes has been looking into the various reviews around its future management and access and whether those reviews might make that development easier. Adam, a government review of how the mountain and the surrounding park is managed began around about two years ago. Now, the final report is due soon and access is expected to feature heavily. Yes, due soon. And the report is actually overdue. And it's being delivered by the Department of State Growth, which is soon to be building Tasmania, apparently. But when this review started in 2024, access was just one of a broad range of matters to be looked into. So there were things like governance issues, values management like flora and fauna and Aboriginal cultural values. There's been concern about this not being core to what the government is doing here. And then there was a category user experience. And that's where access came into it. But as the review has progressed, this access question has become one of the main focuses. And that might be because that's what like dominates the public debate. What people seem to get most worked up about is this idea that access to the top of the mountain is restricted when there's adverse weather conditions and so on. And this focus on access has now created a few differences of opinion, it's fair to say. Well, before we get to the potential outcomes of the reviews, and there are a number of reviews underway, can we look at the current management? It's under the auspices of the Wellington Park Management Trust. Yes, the trust is the overarching authority for the park. It has representatives from government agencies like Parks and Wildlife, Tazwater. Also Hobart and Glenorchy Councils, they kind of all jointly fund it. Essentially, their role is to make sure that whatever happens in the broader Wellington Park is in line with an agreed Wellington Park Management Plan. And that's an incredibly important document that we'll probably return to later. But there is a fair bit of overlapping interest when you think of all the different bodies that have ownership there. So Hobart Council owns and manages the summit and the eastern slopes of the mountain. So that's what you see from Hobart, essentially. And that's where the vast majority of the visitor infrastructure is. And the council is spending close to $5 million a year to maintain that. And that's quite a lot more than any of the other bodies are spending on the park, including the state government. Glenorchy Council owns and funds a smaller part, Tazwater as well, Parks and Wildlife and so on. In the Tasmanian context, having so many different landowners and management interests happening. And it probably adds to a lot of the challenges that you see with the mountain. There are already a hell of a lot of people that use the mountain. And that's forecast to increase significantly, Adam. Has something got to give? I mean, you talked about all those different bodies involved. And also, is it sustainable to continue, you know, in this way? I mean, the road to the Pinnacle was finished being built, what, almost 100 years ago. And it is narrow and pretty hairy at times. Yeah. So on that demand question, the most recent forecast was that visitor numbers could increase from 500,000 to 700,000 by 2030. So all these different bodies are in agreement that changes are needed. Because as you say, Pinnacle Road, it was built in a completely different era. The government's review is taking a look at the options there, whether it actually is feasible to widen the road. Even if any of the fire trails leading up to the summit could somehow be developed into new road access as well. I feel like that's probably not going to happen. But interestingly, in the last 12 months to July, there was a 25% increase in the amount of people who enter the shelter at the Pinnacle.
