We know that the two Labor MPs, Sarah Lovell and Luke Edmonds, are on the other side.
So then there's seven swing votes, and you need three of them on side for greyhound racing to be banned.
I think it's fair to say that the government and anti-greyhound racing campaigners are targeting five key independents.
They're Ruth Forrest, Mike Gaffney, Rosemary Armitage, Beck Thomas, and Dean Harris.
What are those five telling you?
I think they're legitimately trying to work out how this is going to work.
Lots of the upper house members would like to see compensation included in this bill, and they expect that the government might meet them halfway on there.
So we're going to see some key independents meet with Jeremy Rockliffe next week with their concerns.
I don't think that this can pass without compensation amounts being part of the legislation.
So it'll end up having to go back to the lower house.
There will be some amendments you anticipate if it gets through at all.
And the pressure's on pretty hard here.
The MPs that I've spoken to have all received lots of emails and texts, but nothing of the scale like the stadium debate that we've talked about before.

It's much more muted than that, but there is pressure, and they are receiving messages from members of the greyhound industry locally who are all telling personal stories about how long they've worked for.
What about the greyhound industry interstate?
I mean, what's the sort of the feeling, and is there pressure as well from interstate not wanting to see a state have a ban?
There 100% is pressure from the industry.
I think they've largely left it to the local industry to lobby politicians and tell their stories as the way of doing that.
I think that that's the coordinated campaign here.
But 100%, we've talked about Australia being one of those big last bastions of greyhound racing.
If one domino falls and says, right, we're out of greyhound racing, does that set a national precedent?
That's the fear of the national greyhound industry.
They're going to fight this as hard as they can.
We've talked about some of the tactics they're employing.

I think that amplification of local voices is part of it, whereas some of the upper house MPs that I was speaking to say they're getting lots of pro forma default templates from people who are against the industry.
So I think that that's a tactic that's maybe having some sort of impact.

And I spoke to MPs who are concerned about the impact on lower paid people from regional Tasmania who've been doing this for the love of animals and racing for a long time and are concerned about the impacts that it's going to have on them.
They feel like the Premier is targeting vulnerable working class Tasmanians.
So it'll be really interesting to see how the government addresses some of those concerns.
And I don't think that case got made any easier when the Premier talked about cashed up mainland thugs in the greyhound industry lobbying against this bill.
I know a few people with adopted greyhounds, Adam.
They're big sloths apart from the occasional Zoomy.
Oh, they're much too energetic for me, Ellie.
Although I have been really surprised at press conferences with large packs of greyhounds over the years.
They've managed to perform better than lots of children I interview.
I'm certainly an admirer from afar.
A shocking pun, I know, Adam.
But there is a lot riding on this vote.
Thanks very much for joining us.
And thanks to you too for joining us on TassieCast.

episodes.title: Inside a Hobart community needle exchange program
episodes.description: When you imagine someone using a needle exchange program, who do you picture? Chances are, it’s not always who you’d expect.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily. The podcast that brings you one big story affecting your world each weekday in just 15 minutes. The idea of regime change being affected from the air, it's got no precedent. Netanyahu and Trump's theory that Iranians will see the weakness of the regime and rush to replace it. I'm sceptical of all of that. I really am. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. When you think of someone using a needle exchange, who comes to mind? Odds are it's not always who you'd expect. There's a lot of hardworking Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. What happens in this room stays in this room. I see a lot of people in the wider community and they're just regular people. I say g'day and I say g'day and we go on our way until I see them next in here again. Hello and welcome to ABC Tassiecast. I'm Selina Bryan, filling in for Airlie Ward for this episode, where I'm taking you out to Bridgewater Community House, where a state-funded needle and syringe exchange program runs out of the Jordan River Service. A recent study found that hundreds of former Queensland prisoners may have been exposed to hepatitis C and HIV after an inmate shared injecting equipment behind bars, sparking debate over harm minimisation and drug use in Australian prisons. And while Senior Harm Minimisation Officer Shane O'Sullivan does see local prisoners who've recently been released, this program here in Tassie is used far more broadly than you might expect. Thanks for joining us, Shane. So can you tell us what happens here? Well, it's basically an outlet to provide clean injecting equipment for people who use drugs. And what's the benefit of that kind of service of having a needle exchange? The benefit for the wider community is that we're minimising harm to everybody else and plus for the person who's actually using drugs. So by providing all the clean equipment, we can ensure that they're practising safe injecting methods. So what are the services that you have here? Can you talk us through that? We have basically a good range of injecting equipment that they could use for any type of opioid, methamphetamine, steroids. We also have naloxone and pranoxad, which are overdose medications, which have actually saved a few lives. So we do get feedback and it saves some people from overdosing. And we have a disposal, a 24-hour disposal method that safe bins that they can put their used equipment into. When you say it also helps harm minimisation in the broader community, how does that benefit come? Well, I suppose it's by not spreading things like Hep C, Hep B and HIV. So by ensuring that they're using clean equipment and they're disposing of it here in a safe manner, the wider community is much safer. And who do you see coming through this centre? A broad range of people. I must admit I was preconceived at what a drug user would be. They're ordinary people and sometimes have just had extraordinary things happen in their life, usually traumatic. And there's always a background story. It takes a very long time for them to trust you and tell you what the background is. So what happens in this room stays in this room. I see a lot of people in the wider community and shopping and that sort of thing. And they're just regular people. I say g'day and I say g'day and we go on our way until I see them next in here again. What addictions are people most commonly struggling with here? Methamphetamine. Methamphetamine. It's the drug of choice by probably 90%. A little bit of morphine use, the occasional heroin and cocaine. But yeah, methamphetamines are the big, big drug that's used in this area. Have you seen that change over your time here or has it stayed pretty steady? No, it stayed pretty static. I think it's easy to produce, it's cheap and it's readily available. So yeah, that's the drug of choice, unfortunately. And has pretty serious side effects for those who are addicted to it. Yeah, it's definitely hard to get off once they start. It's sort of hard to judge. Some people have got an addictive nature, I guess. Some come in here and they say, that's it, I'm not using anymore. And they quit that day and you don't see them again. But others try and they continually come back. So yeah, it must be very hard. Can you talk us through the numbers that you see coming in here each year? In 2025, we saw 1,054 people. 778 were male and 276 were female. So it's usually the same group of people, so it's the same cohort. They'll come in sometimes daily, sometimes weekly. Often you don't see them for quite a period of time and you wonder what's happened to them. Have they overdosed? Have they moved? Have they not used anymore, which is the best case scenario? Yeah, so we saw a broad range of people and most of them are working, functioning people in the community. You wouldn't know unless you actually dealt with them. And so there is quite a high percentage of men there. There are couples who come through as well, is that right? Yeah, there's definitely couples. Not a great deal of couples. There's usually a domineering one of the two. So I think sometimes one of the partners may not want to use, but they're pressured by the other person to use drugs. So yeah, that's always a bit of a difficult one to handle. And there are times where you almost form an unofficial counsellor role then as well? You do. Yeah. Sometimes I come in and shut the door, just cry on your shoulder. Just need somebody to talk to. You deal with a lot of people who have come out of prison as well, is that right? How soon do people come to you once they've been released? Sometimes it's straight out that morning. This is their safe place to come to. Some are homeless, some don't have family. So they know that they can come here, they can get something to eat, they can have a coffee, they can have a chat. And if they really need injecting equipment, yeah, we can provide that too. We saw news that more than 80 prisoners used a single needle to inject illicit drugs in one day inside a Queensland jail. That was according to a study published in the International Journal of Drug Policy. No Australian prison has a needle or syringe exchange program. Do you think that needs to change based on what you see? From what I see, yeah, it would definitely benefit. I read that same thing, sharpening needles on the concrete to use it again and again. Yeah, scary stuff. The damage that they would do to their veins plus the risk of spreading viruses between sharing that same noodle. Yeah, it's something, just personal opinion, yeah, I think it needs something to happen. How do you think that could benefit people who are incarcerated? I guess by testing them and helping them whilst they're incarcerated. Maybe when they come out, they've got a clean slate to start with again. We do see some here. We run regular Hep C clinics here the first Thursday of every month. So I encourage any of them that I know have just been released to come along. There is an incentive, a voucher that we give them for groceries to go and get some food at least. And that incentivizes them to come and get tested. We haven't had a huge amount of positive comeback. So that's been really good. Most of them test negative. But yeah, it's a very good way to do it. And do you see most people do follow through on that then? Like that you encourage people to come to that clinic. Do you see that they do? Yeah, well, it's an eight-week program or 12-week program on a pill. So basically all they've got to do is get tested if it's positive. They take the pill for 12 weeks and, yeah, they're cured again. And they can keep doing that. If they happen to get Hep C again, it's a repetitive thing. You can just take the pill and become cured again. There are other, as you mentioned, risks of needle use like that that they have seen in that study in prisons. Have you seen other people suffer other types of injuries or problems from needle use? I have seen a few. Some people come in and they'll show you their wounds where they're injecting in strange places. Sometimes their abscesses form. Other times some really bad scarring. So, yeah, it is a bit of an issue. But we are fortunate that we also have a medical group that comes here every second Wednesday. So if we happen to spot that at the same time, we can take them straight out and get them some medical attention. What prompted you personally to get involved in this work? Well, I came here as a volunteer teaching driving, of all things. And then all of a sudden they needed somebody to run the needle exchange. And it was sort of something I'd never even contemplated. I've never touched a drop of alcohol in my life. I don't smoke. And I thought ice was what formed in fridges. So to come here and do something like this was totally out of left field. And I wasn't sure what to expect, to be honest, with the people I was going to deal with. But I have, in the seven or eight years I've been here now, I've not had any disrespectful people. They're all extremely polite. They're all very thankful for what you do for them. And is the work here well supported by the community or are there still stigmas around it? No, most people that come in here, we have the regulars that come into the community every day, into the community house every day. I've never heard a bad word spoken about any of the people that come into the NSP. Yeah. I think it's accepted. They realise they're just ordinary people and have been put in bad situations. And unfortunately, some of these drugs, some of these opioids, the synthetic opioids, they're 500 times stronger than heroin. So the tiniest little drop and they're hooked. Yeah. So that addiction does become so hard to keep. Definitely. Thanks for coming out to Bridgewater with me. I'm Selina Bryan. Airlie Ward will be back with you next episode. And if you want to get in touch, you can email us at tassiecast at abc.net.au. Until next time. Cheers. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Is that a side of antibiotics with your seafood?
episodes.description: After its public image took a dive last summer when millions of fish died ... the salmon industry sought regulatory approval to use an antibiotic in a bid to prevent more mass deaths.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily. The podcast that brings you one big story affecting your world each weekday in just 15 minutes. If wealth inequality gets bigger and bigger and bigger, and the super rich, the very rich take a bigger and bigger, bigger share of the wealth, the biggest consequence of that is unaffordable housing. Living standards will fall for ordinary Australians. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. Food is medicine, right? Or is medicine in your food? There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west, I don't care where you live in the state. Well, I just think Tassel's taking the piss, quite frankly. Like, seriously, there's significant concerns around the use of this antibiotic. And public health advice remains that the fish are safe to eat. So I'm not concerned from an environmental health or from a public health perspective about the use of flifenacol. The federal regulator is seeking information because what we don't want to see is an impact on trade relationships and the ability for other really important aquaculture sectors in Tasmania to have access to those markets. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ely Ward coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. Maybe it's your go-to for a healthy family dinner. It's a great source of protein, good fats and other nutrients which can help keep your heart healthy. I'm talking about fish, particularly oily fish such as salmon. It's also a massive shot in the arm to Tasmania's economy. The state's farmed salmon industry is valued at more than $1 billion a year and it employs a lot of people. There are plenty of people championing the salmon industry. But as it's grown, so too have the questions around its social licence, mass fish deaths, other animal cruelty issues, the impact on threatened species, waterways and more recently, particularly over the use of antibiotics. Federal approval to use one antibiotic to treat a bacterial disease in farmed salmon, flifenacol, is probably about to be revoked after traces of it were found in other marine life more than 10 kilometres from the closest farmed salmon pens. ABC Mornings presenter Leon Compton's been following the industry and its impacts on a regular basis. Leon, hello. We have indeed, Ely. We've been doing it over years and this flifenacol aspect of the story really has our audience talking right now. Well, Leon, the industry was left reeling after millions of fish died in their farms last summer. We all know there were chunks of fish washed up on southern beaches and live fish were filmed being put into a bin that was then sealed. I mean, to say it's not been pretty is an understatement, Leon. Absolutely. And we were talking about unprecedented levels of fish death last year. So we're talking literally thousands of tonnes of mortalities or morts as they're known, hoovered up out of the bottom of pens and then the question of where to dispose of them. Ely, we learnt that the industry and the government didn't even have a plan that could cope with the scope and the scale of what they were dealing with at the time. And a lot of where we find ourselves right now is the industry a season on trying to deal with that and make sure it doesn't happen again. Well, after that event, the Premier Jeremy Rockcliffe said in Parliament that the salmon companies were on notice and that the fish deaths were completely unacceptable. He also said he expected the highest degree of accountability and transparency. But in recent days, there have been government briefings and people were told to keep what they were told confidential. And it wasn't just leaders in politics that were told to keep what they heard confidential. We had the Leader of the Greens, Dr Rosalie Woodruff, start our program. And I said, have you been told to keep quiet? And she looked at me and she said yes. Off the back of a briefing in which she was asked not to repeat what was being discussed. And of course, in response to that request, she said no. But the issue about silence goes more widely than that. So as you know, Ely, we work really closely with the newsroom. We were making calls all weekend. You were making calls all weekend. And the level of silence that was coming back was, as they say, deafening. So what have you managed to glean? That there has been a widespread campaign and approach not to talk. But Leon, surely given that these farms are in public waterways and getting back to Premier Rockcliffe's call for transparency, surely there's a public right to know. There is a public right to know. And to give credit to the EPA and to NRE, I think it's fair to say there is more information that is publicly available now in real time in places where people like you and I and our listener can find it. It's better than it was. We're coming, of course, talking about an industry, though, where commercial incompetence can be really important. The industry might not want its competitors to know what it is doing. Some of the declaration rates when it comes to mortality death, for example, Ely, unless 0.25% of a lease dies in a particular period of time over a consecutive number of days, there's no need to declare that. And there are still real issues about whether or not regulations are keeping up with what the Tasmanian public want to know. For example, in that recent time, Meadow Bank, Huon wanted to use an antibiotic and did in a flow-through hatchery. And they decided to tell the EPA that they were doing it, but they didn't actually have to do it, even though that water is part of Hobart's catchment. And that was oxytetracycline. Can we go back to Florphenicol? With the emergency approval permit that was granted in November last year looking increasingly likely that it will be revoked, are the companies trying to get as much treatment into fish as possible? I wonder about that. So this announcement came out at, what was it, four or five o'clock on a Friday afternoon? The APVMA said the use of Florphenicol was under review. And then it was Sunday that the EPA website showed that Tassel, at five sites in the D'Entre Casto Channel, were going to start using the antibiotic. Now, five is quite a lot relative to how much of it has been used since November when it was first approved. And there was a feeling, perhaps, that they were rushing to get this antibiotic into the salmon in case the APVMA revoked the license to use it. Well, there are so many issues to dive into here, Leon. Any potential impacts on human health, the environment and other industries, including the abalone and rock lobster fishes. Now, the rock lobster industry was blindsided late last year because two of its fishing zones were closed just hours after the commercial season had opened because they're within three kilometres of salmon farms that had just started using this Florphenicol. Yeah. Imagine the shock. So Florphenicol can be used in the salmon industry. And then the cray industry was told, hang on a second, you cannot fish in these lease areas. And what we learnt was this was designed to protect the industry in case there was Florphenicol detected in international markets. And particularly China. And here's what James Lawrenson had to say. He's the director of the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology, Sydney. Once it's been detected, you could expect the ban to be overnight. This is not a small, it's not a trivial trade when it comes to Tasmania's trade with China. So it's a significant commercial value at risk. And Leon, we now know that Florphenicol has been found in samples a long way outside that three kilometre radius. And I think this is part of where it's refocused the conversation again, Ellie. Now we know that Florphenicol has been detected 10 kilometres away. In fact, just over 10 kilometres away from where it's been used in salmon pens. And so I think that has triggered actually a lot of the conversation and concern and what the potential issues might be, not just for crayfish, but also for the world's largest wild-caught abalone fishery, where China's also an important market. And what are fishers saying to you, Leon? I spoke to a crayfisher who was in his boat, took my call, has always taken my call. When it was clear that this was the issue I wanted to discuss, someone that the Mornings teams had a longstanding relationship, just started saying, no comment, no comment. And then the call ended. Does that surprise you? It's part of a fear of what might happen if podcasts like this are heard in China. The industry and maybe even our politicians have decided if we stay small and silent, we might minimise the potential harm that this issue does. Let's stay small. Nobody talk. And you know in Tasmania that when people threaten people not to talk, those threats can come with real concern behind them. Nobody talk or else, which when you think about it, Ellie, you've got to ask yourself, what sort of a strategy is that for the people that are part of this, you know, the cray industry, the ab industry, other parts of the economy, politics, regulatory authorities, all of them have shut up this week. Well, we've heard from Rebecca White at the top. Now, she's an assistant minister and she has expressed some concern about the potential impacts on trade. Now, member for Franklin, Julie Collins is Australia's fisheries minister. Have you managed to speak to her? We tried to talk to Julie Collins. You might think that she's our federal fisheries minister, agriculture minister. So you'd think that there'd be that focus on exports as well. Not to mention Franklin. episodes.description: Imagine what you could do with 200 million dollars. That's how much money Tasmanians lost on pokies last financial year,
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. In late 2022, a torso was found in a wheelie bin on a vacant lot in Adelaide's north. Police discovered that it was 55-year-old Geoffrey McLean who'd been reported missing by his partner Cherie Glastonbury a couple of months earlier. Now, Cherie is on trial for his murder. Prosecutors allege that she and her new partner, Mark Murphy, killed Geoffrey with a drug overdose. On the case of the wheelie bin murder, we take you inside the courtroom for this trial. Search for the KSOP podcast on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts. What could you do with $200 million? That's what Tasmanians lost on Poki's last financial year. There's a lot of hard-working Tasmanians out there. My boss is the boss of Tasmania. Tasmanians want us to get on with the job. North, south, east, west. I don't care where you live in the state. I think the government should be really ashamed of what they've put in place. They've bent over to the industry and it's quite clear they've done deals with the industry to not put the absolute gold standard, which is the mandatory pre-commitment card, in place. We're about freedom of choice. We're about supporting people with gambling addiction. We support facial recognition technology. We support gaming care officers. That is a human touch in venues. I refuse to give up. The Poki Barons would love me to give up. Guess what, guys? Not going away. Hello and welcome to TassieCast. I'm Ailey Ward, coming to you from Nipaluna, Hobart. The amount of money Tasmanians lose on gambling is, by any measure, eye-watering. We're a nation of bettors and Tassies no different. I bet. Yeah, you heard that right. Many of us wager in some way, shape or form. Whether that's about if it's going to rain, the traffic lights turning red, or if the bus will be late and so on. And most of it is harmless fun. But for some of us, gambling becomes all-encompassing. Relationships, jobs, and in some cases, lives lost. According to Tasmanian social and economic impact studies, around 2% of the adult population has a serious issue with gambling. And in lower socioeconomic communities, it's almost twice that, around 4%. Now, this doesn't take into account the flow-on effect on partners, families or colleagues. It's bad and been getting worse. In the 2016-17 financial year, Tasmanians lost around $110 million on pokies. Last financial year, that figure had almost doubled. episodes.title: Is it time Tassie declared wild deer a pest?
episodes.description: They might look like Bambi but they're making a big mess. There are tens of thousands of fallow deer trampling across the landscape and they now outnumber some of our most iconic species. Featuring reporter Meg Whitfield.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily. There's a whole raft of other animals that present challenges to farmers. So I think deer are unfairly being maligned in this instance. We're prioritising a species that's been introduced over all of our native species, many of which are highly threatened and endangered and exist nowhere else on Earth. episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. You're listening to A Big Country. I'm David Claughton and it's lovely to have your company as we join our reporters exploring regional Australia. This week we're getting a history lesson into how a summer fruit became a local favourite when we hear the story of how mangoes came to be grown down under. We'll meet a long-time listener to Australia's longest-running radio program as The Country Hour celebrates eight decades of broadcasting. And we're heading into the classroom to meet the young preschoolers learning about the dairy industry. Their lessons cover everything from tractors and cows to making butter in the hope that it might lead to a career in dairy well into the future. Some people might think it's really young to be speaking about careers with three, four, five-year-olds. But we know that young people know what career they don't want to do very early. And if we don't introduce them to a range of careers in the dairy industry at this young age, it's likely that they won't consider that when they are getting to their career-making decision time in their life. First today we start with a remarkable story from far north-western Australia. In 1967, a girl was standing barefoot on the hot sand of the Great Sandy Desert, amidst the low scrub and spinifex grass, surrounded by her family. Her photograph is taken, and her life changes forever. Bougarawoya and her family were removed from their traditional desert life and taken into a Kimberley mission. Now aged 70, she's never stopped wondering about that photo, and never forgotten her connection to her traditional land. Erin Park has the story. It's wet season in the central Kimberley. I'm driving about 300 kilometres inland from Broome, trying to get to a small community called Looma, where there's a woman with a very special, unusual life story that, as far as I know, has never been recorded before. Within minutes of arriving, I'm directed to her house. My name is Bougarawoya. I come from the bush. I've been coming in 1967. Bougarawoya grew up in the desert. The Dowling woman is one of only a handful of surviving elders in Australia who remembers life before contact with white people. Now around 70 years old, her life is one of quiet routines, walking daily to the aged care centre. She's really bossy at times, like most of the time, so yeah. But she's good. I've come from the great sandy desert. I was born in Widdity. What I call Widdity. I've been growing up all my life in the bush. Bougarawoya's ancestors had lived uninterrupted for thousands of years in the vast desert plains. We walk around everywhere. We collect everything. We took it everywhere. What a hole. But the 1960s were a time of great change in northern Australia. Suddenly there were new people moving across the landscape. White people. It was 1967 when Bougarawoya first heard the truck approaching. Do you remember the first time you saw a white person? Yeah, I was seeing a white person walking with shirt and trousers. And my sister, Sally, what was it? She went and ate in the bush. And I told my mummy, mummy, you look like us. Same. Bougarawoya's just told me something pretty crazy, which is that the moment that her life changed forever was actually captured on camera. Apparently that moment in the desert when she first saw white people, there was a woman there taking photographs. And she's got an album with the originals here at her house. So we're just going to have a dig around and try to find them. This is my mum. This is my grandmother. This is my mum. Shall we go outside and have a look? This is my mum. The single photograph shows her family's first interaction with the white fella world. The missionaries and welfare officers handing them clothes and guiding them into the back of the truck. But Bougarawoya says she used to have a whole set of photos that were taken on that life-changing day, including one showing her posing for the camera. But the photo album cannot be found. Maybe lost. Maybe stolen. I've been looking for the photos, but I couldn't find it. I don't know where he was. I promised to try to find the photos. They're irreplaceable. Showing the moment that two wildly different cultures intersected in that hot desert sand. So I'm back in Broome and I think I've had a breakthrough after several months of digging. There's a local historian and author who's passed me on this CD. She's had it in her possession for many years. It's got 23 images on it and she reckons one of them is that missing photograph showing Bougarawoya as a child. Before long, I'm back on the road to Luma. I find Bougarawoya in her usual spot. Hi, look at you. Hanging out with her best friend and next-door neighbour, Polly, who came out of the desert the same year. It's been six months since I came and visited you. You've been well? I've been well. And I look happy. It's time to show Bougaraw the photograph. Is this the photo you were telling me about? How do you feel to see it? See? This is me, Bougaraw. I came with the name of Bougaraw. I had the name because my dad called me the name. The photo was taken as the last of the desert families were moving on to cattle stations and church-run missions along the coast. Some voluntarily, exhausted by drought. Others rounded up reluctantly. The photographer was a nurse who was volunteering at the LaGrange Catholic Mission, where Bougaraw and her family were soon taken. Oh, they've probably been through a lot. A lot of changes. My mother. Bougaraw's cousin is visiting from Perth and seeing the photos for the first time. For her, a young girl, it would have been confusing. That picture says it all right there. Leaving home. You know? And wherever this mob is taking them. It would have been sad at that moment. But it would have been scary. Bougaraw went on to marry a man named Jimmy. And they had three children, two of whom have since died. Bougaraw visits the desert less now. She's getting frail and can no longer drive. But when she closes her eyes, she's back there. I'm sorry for that country. I've been sorry too. I've been crying everywhere I hold for a while. Because I get the memories in that place. They've come far, very far. A long way. And they're still here, you know. Managing both worlds, I guess. At this kindergarten in Victoria's South Gippsland region, the next generation of dairy experts and advocates are being nurtured from a young age. Hi there. I'm Faith Tabaloo-Yan, and I'm visiting the Lee and Gatha Community Preschool here in one of the state's largest dairy farming regions. It's the first time this preschool has run this Dairy in Kinder program, which aims to teach little learners about farming, sustainability and healthy eating. And it seems they're taking the lessons to heart. I've learnt that the milk gets processed. How does it get processed? A big factory. Big factory. What's not in dispute is mangoes were first commercially produced in Bowen.
Queensland DPI Senior Principal Horticulturalist Ian Bally says they arrived from Asia,
where mangoes have been eaten for thousands of years.
In the late 1800s, boats coming to and fro from Bowen used to bring mangoes from Southeast Asia.
Those boats would be travelling from Bowen,
taking horses to India for the remount trade for the British Army.
And as they sort of travelled that India to Australia route,
they would pick up local fruit at local markets and ports along the way.
Quite often those fruit and seed from those fruit were given to local farmers in the Bowen area.
They were often grown on the farm of the harbour master there.
And the better ones of those were then passed on again.
And Kensington Pride was one of those ones that was passed on to a guy.
Harry Lott had a farm at Adelaide Point.
I think the farm was named Kensington.
And from various selections and over time,
the Kensington Pride sort of stood out as being something that was bigger,
better and tastier than all the other selections.
And it began to be grown around the Bowen area.
The Kensington Pride is still the most popular mango in Australia,
and all other varieties developed in Australia have some level of Kensington Pride genetics.
Professor Heather Smyth is a flavour expert
and the Deputy Director of Research at the University of Queensland's
She's helped with breeding programs for most major modern Australian mango varieties.
She said Kensington Pride's sweet, tangy flavour is unique due to a compound called alpha-terpinaline.
So I've been tasting mangoes for a very long time.
which we have come to know is the Australian unique mango flavour that consumers expect.
Mangoes don't taste like that anywhere else in the world.
They taste like that terpini flavour only here in Australia.
And that's because of Kensington Pride or this Bowen style of mango.
A hundred years after the rise of the Kensington Pride,
a second popular mango variety came from Bowen, the R2E2.
It's a large, round fruit with firm flesh and a sweet, fresh flavour.
The original 40-year-old tree still stands at a research centre in Bowen.
Mr Bally worked on its breeding program.
He says research began in the 60s to combat shortcomings with the Kensington Pride.
It was recognised that some of the international overseas varieties were much better producers,
especially some of those from Florida that were in the 1940s sort of were selected over there.
So this is when it was decided that, yeah, some crossbreeding needed to happen.
The introduced varieties seeds were planted in the ground in Bowen.
And as they began to crop, they were assessed for their suitability as commercial varieties for the Bowen area.
And one of those trees was a Kent seedling, which became R2E2.
It was selected because it was quite large, had a very good flesh-to-seed ratio,
and had this great shelf life, much better for travelling than the Kensington Pride.
Today, the Kensington Pride makes up about 40% of mango production,
while the R2E2 makes up about 20% and is the number one export variety.
Other popular Queensland varieties commercialised in the 2000s include the Calypso and Honeygold.
Professor Smyth said they each have their own benefits.
Yeah, Honeygold's got a beautiful, rich, sweet flavour and all that alpha-depinoline.
It's certainly a premium version of mango.
The Calypso can be absolutely gorgeous when it's looking really good.
It is a much, I would say, more delicate flavour compared to the other fruit.
I would say a very clean version of that terpeni, piney flavour that you have from the KP,
you also get in the Calypso mango.
What's the best way to eat a mango?
Under clinical conditions, Professor Smyth tastes mangoes at about 20 degrees to bring out the most flavour.
Just before you want to eat it, put it in the fridge for a couple of hours just to cool it down,
but not to cause the chill injury and make it sort of soft and glassy inside.
And then cut it with your knife, prepare it, pop those cheeks out.
Whether you want to cut off the cubes or whether you want to slice it up and use it in some other way,
it's lovely to have cool mango, but just don't keep it in the fridge for long periods of time.
However, as a child in Darwin, Professor Smyth developed her own favourite style.
I was probably about seven years old and my friend had a swimming pool.
The un-mango season, you could pluck off the tree, climb the tree, plot them into the swimming pool
and then just tear the skin off with your teeth and then just tuck into the mango,
just as it is, no knife, nothing else.
And you saw dripping down your chin, dripping down your arms and then just wash it off in the swimming pool.
That's story from Liam McNally in Mackay in tropical North Queensland.
Before that, we heard from a long-time Country Hour listener and buffalo farmer, Margaret Thompson.
Thanks for listening and bye for now.

episodes.title: Career change to pub owner and new priest turns heads in rural parish
episodes.description: Meet the pint-sized publican granny; motorcycle riding priest shares passion for social justice with rural parish; farming camels for milk and meat; agriculture students get out of the laboratory to taste life on the land.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country. Let's catch up with our reporters on the road in regional Australia. This week, putting theory into practice, we'll meet university agriculture students who are getting out of the lab and onto the land. They're visiting farms to see how their study plays out in practice. We'll visit a church congregation where the new priest is turning heads. Her tattoos, pink hair and motorbike may not be what the parishioners were expecting, but she's using her varied life experience to help others in the community. And we'll meet a pint-sized publican who's proving a drawcard and a social media star. At just 142 centimetres tall, grandmother Barb Parkinson is helping her daughter run a small-town pub on the Queensland coast. And she's posing for photos with passing tourists who come from all over Australia for a selfie. I actually feel like a grommet. Especially when I only, some of them, I only come up to like their waist. I'm getting used to it now, but do have people come out of their way just so they can get their photo taken with a really short grin. We'll meet Barb, the tiny publican. That's coming up. First today, across remote Australia, hundreds of thousands of wild camels are considered feral pests, with many shot and left to rot. But on a farm in south-east Queensland's Scenic Rim, camels are being milked to make cheese, skin care products and vodka, while their meat is being used in a range of cuts, including salamis. And the humped mammals are attracting thousands of tourists to the farm every year. Reporter Jennifer Nichols spoke with Paul Martin of Summerland Camels to hear how the venture came about. Around 2010, we were doing a big camel cull in Australia. The government was throwing a lot of money at it and people were asking, why can't we do something with these amazing animals? And we put a project together and here we are. This was a fully start from scratch project where we go, well, how can we domesticate feral camels for a start? So before we could go and raise capital, we sort of really needed to tick that box. So we brought in about 20 camels out at Lowood where we leased a property, started to domesticate them and then milk them and the yields were reasonable. So we thought, well, OK, we can now expand from here and sort of tap into that dairy intolerant market and that health market for camels. The idea was to sort of try and set something up close to a capital city. So we had the milk and the products that we could make from it. We used some seed capital to start. One of our investors funded a farm that we're at now. We had a crowd behind us, so we raised about $9 million to get to that point where we made our skincare products and cheese and got that into the marketplace. Then we raised probably another $2 million through crowdfunding. And that's sort of a mechanism where you're harnessing your crowd that are following you and like what you do and all the rest of it. And then they'll invest in your company. So it's not floated on the stock exchange. It's still a private company, but they can invest and get shares like you do normally, but then also get discounts for products and stuff like that. What's the good thing about camel milk? It's the only mammal milk that people with dairy allergies can have for a start. So from an environmental point of view, there's this movement sort of looks at a lot of the environmental impacts of nut milks and things like that with their heavy use of water and stuff. So going back to an adaptable animal, which is a camel is the most adaptable animal on the planet, that it can produce a milk for people that is of a health benefit as opposed to just a carrier for a cereal. So that's how we sort of started. Okay. And since then, gosh, I was just listening to your speech, staggered at the products that you can make from a camel. The vodka, for example. Yeah, yeah. It's amazing when you look back at the products we've made, but, you know, all our heads around trying to, okay, what can we make with camel milk that gives it shelf life? So the skincare products and then shelf stability with cheeses. You know, a lot of people say, oh, camel milk, I don't like it. But cheese, you know, you can half rot in a cheese and people still eat it. You know, so, you know, having a cheese. Stinky cheese. Yeah, that's right. Good stinky cheese. So, you know, cheese is an amazing way to get people just interested to go, oh, is that camel really? And then it was like, well, we've got whey left over. What do we do here? What can we do with it? That's where the vodka idea came up. You know, around 800 litres of whey will produce about 110 litres of alcohol. And then that's about 200 litres of vodka. And are you doing that all on site? So we do the brewing side of it, which takes about 14 to 20 days, depending on the time of year. Then we send that 800 litres in to get distilled. How many camels do you have? And how are you running them? And where are you running them? Our farm at Parrisville. So we've got 400 camels there. There's probably 50-odd in our tourism riding team. And then the rest are dairy camels and progeny coming through. So young females that we're keeping. So we're milking probably 70 camels. We've got another 30 that are about to give birth. So, you know, that'll get us up to about 100 by the end of the year. And it's a bit different to cows too, because you allow the calves to stay with the mums. Yes. So the calves need to be at this stage with the mums. Like the camels can hang on to their milk. They've got to express it. So you've got to look after them pretty well. And we take the calves off in the afternoon and we milk them. So we're milking once a day. And then the calf gets the rest of the milk for that day. Your cost of production's higher. How much does it cost at the shops? It ranges anywhere between $16 and $20 a litre. You know, that's a challenging thing for people, especially with the low-cost milk that has been ate for the last few years. But then a lot of your gut health supplements and yogurts, people will pay way more than that per litre for something that actually, that's what traditional people use camel milk for. So it's about a little bit of a branding story that we've got to try and educate people on. Meat and meat products. When did you start venturing down that front? Yeah, probably about three years ago. And our camels go generally because they're so quiet. Once they've spent 14 months in the dairy, they generally go out as pets. But we're also harvesting more females and we get all these other camels. So we really wanted to try and engage other farmers to run these camels. So they'll run them out in Western Queensland to control prickly acacia and Parkinsonia and all that sort of thing if they've got a way to sell them at some point. Overseas camel meat is eaten a lot. What sorts of products are you doing? We're marketing premium cuts to restaurants and supplying what they need. But then what do we do with the rest? So we've got all this trim and all the rest of it left over. So we've got charcuterie products. We've won a gold medal in Sydney with our pepper salami. Congratulations. Yeah, and I think a silver for our beer sticks down there. So we're using Schultz's at Plainlands. Again, another local guys that specialise in preserved meat. And agritourism is a big part of your model too to try to introduce more people to the camel. How's that going? We get 60,000 people a year now through the farm. So it's amazing. And it's a great way to introduce people to a domesticated camel. You know, most people, even if they've had anything to do with the camels, they've probably done it over in Dubai. And some cranky camel that they've had to ride in this desert that's sick of tourists. You know, the camels we've got are just amazing, like grass-eating Labradors. So people come, they feed them over the fence and they can go for a camel ride or go and see some baby camels. And then the view out where we are is quite amazing as well. Pauline Harley takes off her motorbike helmet and walks into church. She swaps her leather jacket for white robes and prepares for the service. I have been stopped once when I've been riding with my collar on. There was a double take from the police officer who was doing the breath test. Reverend Harley's arrival was a bit of a surprise to the more conservative churchgoers at Toowoomba West Parish. Phoebe Mitchell has been attending St Albans for 20 years. We hadn't had a minister for some considerable time. Pauline's arrival was a shock to some people. One, because she was female. And two, because of her hair. And she wasn't as orthodox as everybody else is. So unfortunately one of the upshots of it was that we did lose some of our people who didn't believe in having women as ordained ministers. I think originally in their minds they were getting a man, a male priest, because that's all they've ever had and known. And realised that I was tattooed and pink here. That first service here was a little bit of a shock to some people. I'm not worried about your lifestyle, who you are, young, old, disabled, not disabled. I think a church needs to look like it's community. Welcome Lee to our service. Welcome to St Albans. Reverend Harley didn't grow up in the church. Far from it in fact. I grew up with not a very good family life. So my mum, what I believe now, probably had what's recognised as severe mental illness. Because of past trauma in her life, and she didn't make her a very good parent. She was addicted to all sorts of things. Starting off from cigarettes, to caffeine, to codeine. Because of those obsessions, she neglected us. And she went from boyfriend to boyfriend. And because she swam in those circles, I was abused every which way. So one of her boyfriends, the then boyfriend at the time, decided he didn't want kids around. And I came home one day, and there was a box on the sidewalk of my stuff with a note, don't come back. Pauline spent six months living homeless. Eventually, she ended up moving to Australia with her then husband. And we thought by coming to Australia, we could leave all our problems behind as well. Unfortunately, gambling came with him. And there was casinos here. So as a Kiwi, I couldn't receive any government benefits. So I had to find a way to work. She worked a variety of jobs. In a fish and chip shop, Danish bakery, muffin shop, and then in IT, literally building computers. While studying in TAFE, her teacher mentioned there was work at a local church office. I thought, I've been in hospitality for so long, I'll give it a go. It was there she met Reverend David Cox, a man who became a friend, a mentor, and the person she calls her Aussie dad. So nervous, because I've not been around that sort of person before. And he was just this gentle, kind man. And he saw a broken person, and he was willing to give me a go. Yeah, and next thing you know, I'm at church every Sunday. For the first time, Pauline felt a purpose. A higher calling. There was this little thing in me that voice, I believe to be the voice of God, saying, I want you to look at ordained ministry. And I was going, no way. And tried to run away from that. Tried to get into doing border security for some stupid reason. But every corner I took, God slammed that back, my belief. And I was like, no, you're doing this. At the age of 40, having never graduated high school, she decided to become an ordained Anglican priest. One of my things I say to people is that you can't change your past. You can then make a choice, though, for yourself. And through the healing workshops and through the counselling that I did, my choice was, A, let my past forever dictate me in a negative way, or to use it in a positive way going forward in the future. So in my ministry now, I do have a passion for homelessness and those who are less fortunate. Since Reverend Harley became the priest in charge for the Toowoomba West Parish, there's been some changes. Phoebe Mitchell says they're now more involved than ever in volunteering and social justice. It wasn't an area this parish had ever touched. We're really fortunate to have someone like Pauline, who introduces and challenges us to step outside our comfort zones as well. Pauline's real. Pauline doesn't put herself above anybody else. She's one of us. She's one of everybody. Preaches and teachers through her life experience, which hasn't been easy. The purple bike parked outside St Albans is unique and distinctive, just like its owner, who's happy her married name is so appropriate. I've always loved bikes and I've always, always wanted a motorbike. I've always wanted a Harley, even before I became a Harley. Beyond being known as the motorbike riding priest, Reverend Harley wants her legacy to be one of service to the less fortunate. For me, it's important that I show parishioners actions are just as important in our faith journey. We just pray for our city that more and more people would step out of their comfort zones and help in our community. Thank you. And I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I'm like, I guess, or out of their university classrooms, out into the space. And this is such, I suppose, a diverse region as well. How important is it for that to experience? Yeah, I mean, we get fantastic feedback at the end of this excursion, which we run every year by the way, and we go to a different region in New South Wales every year. Yeah, so a lot of them, as you hinted there, they're stuck in the lab, I shouldn't say stuck, they're in the lab enjoying their biochemistry or their plant pathology for example, or they're doing modelling on a computer. Some of them are doing quite a lot of field work already, but there's no way that they would otherwise be able to access a sheep farm and two beef farms and a research institute, all in the space of a few days. It would be very hard for them to organise that themselves in any way. My name is Damdola Karim, or you can call me Dami. Okay. Yeah, so I'm working with chicken, chicken nutrition, trying to find sustainable ways to produce chickens and also reducing the negative impact of reduced protein diets in chicken nutrition. My name is Kai Sin. I'm from Singapore. And I'm currently doing research on a novel horticultural production system. And I'm very, very happy to be on this trip. Let's just start with this trip. The last two or three days, what you've seen? Oh, it's been a lot. Yeah. And wonderful. For this year, we've been to a cattle farm. So we were able to meet the owners, Juan and Dr. Sabrina, who is also, fortunately, a member of staff at the University of Sydney. So we've been able to learn how the things are done here in Australia, you know, compared to how it is in my country. So that has been a very high opener for me. We also went to the farm where the plants are cottons. So that was a really good one. It's like 1,200 hectares, I guess. Yeah. Which was really huge. And they took us around. So it's really good. And we are here today to see the different equipments of how they do all the seed planting, seed breeding, the technology they're using, making the seed better for us. Because it's really, especially here, I was really interested here. Because, you know, in chicken nutrition, livestock nutrition generally, we depend more on the cereals and legumes. So, you know, to know how the improvement of the breeds have been done is a really good opportunity for me. Kai, what about you? Well, I come from a country with almost zero agriculture production. So more than 90% of our food is imported. So I've been very impressed with the depth of the agriculture industry here in Australia, looking at the various research facilities and the investments that were made to improve the yield or to research into diseases, better livestock. It's just something that just blows my mind because, you know, I've really not come across that kind of research being done in the past. So I think that it's really a very big eye opener for me in terms of the experience, in terms of the exposure. Yeah. Jaime Ruiz Serra. I am doing a PhD in complex systems under the School of Computer Science at the University of Sydney. So I'm Julia and I think you can say it like fate, but it's spelled F like foxtrot, double E-T-H. You've done that before. Yes. Too many times. And what are you studying? I'm doing a PhD in microplastics and soil. Wow. Okay. The last three days. Tell me what you've been seeing and what you've been learning. Really, I think, yeah, something quite impactful to me was the scale of operations compared to the size of labour that's required. Like, for instance, one of the farms, they had 1300 heads of sheep, but it was only the parents and their daughters that looked after the farm and only on the weekends, which to me that was mind blowing because I thought you needed a full time kind of operation. And yeah, to me that was really eye opening. And it kind of made me even more wish that I could have a farm one day. How about you, Julia? Tell me about your experience so far. So two things I would say stood out to me. Yesterday we went to see a sheep farmer and I had no idea that it is so profitable for sheep farmers in Australia. That was really interesting for me to hear. And also the cattle farm we went to first, I had no idea that they make such an effort in terms of animal welfare. And I thought it was lovely to hear about. I really like that. So what were your thoughts? I mean, we all have these ideas of everything in life when we haven't seen it, you know, we have a picture in our head and there's so much in the media that we hear. What did you think about some of those things before you actually got out on the farm? So I've been to the United States before and there you see the cattle like really, like really close together and like really sad looking farms. And I thought no one here cares either. So, but it was nice to see like, cause yeah, I had a more not so animal friendly picture in my head, I would say. But it was really good. Like they tried to not even take the cattle away from the farm for when they, until they sell it really. So it was really good. And they said that they also eat their own meat. So it's very sustainable in that way. And it was great. Yeah. For almost 30 years, Barb Parkinson worked as a nurse on her feet, caring for patients and meeting new people every day. Now at 71 and in semi-retirement, her role is a little different. She is just such a cute little ray of sunshine. The second we met her, I felt like she was my granny as well, honestly. I lost my mother a few years ago and granny is like a mother to me. Oh, she's so cute. As soon as she saw me, she hugged me and like, she's very welcoming. Those are just some of the people who have come to love the 142 centimeter firecracker known as the granny from the Yanni. Barb is the co-owner of the Yandaran Hotel, a short drive north of Bundaberg along the Queensland coast. The nickname came about after a joke with one of the regulars. We've got a local here and his name is Lyle and all the boys are at one end of the pub, like after work. And he turned out and he says, did you hear Barb gets on Tinder? And I says, no, I don't. And he says, oh, yes, she does. And she goes by the name of the granny from the Yanni. And of course, Alicia caught on, so she said, she's going to do a bit of stirring. Alicia is daughter Alicia Smith. And it was her idea to buy this small country pub in the first place. I saw it actually on Facebook. My mother actually, she was working 20 hours a fortnight and she needed to retire as a 69 year old woman. And it was my husband who actually said, it'd be great for your mum to come and buy a pub. At first, Barb wasn't convinced about her daughter's retirement plan. She said to me, have you ever thought of retiring and owning a pub? And I said, no, why would I? I said, I don't even drink. She says, it won't be busy, mum. You'll be able to just come out at the end of the bar and just serve people every now and then. So Alicia and her husband made the move 30 minutes out of town to become co-owners of the pub alongside Barb. And it was a bit of a steep learning curve, especially for Barb, who doesn't even drink alcohol. I used to have to ask people what colour can it was or I had no idea. I don't know some of the cans that have got alcohol in it. I'm not sure what sort of alcohol it is in. I've got to read them up all. And her nursing skills were still being put to use, even as a publican. People come here with cuts and things like that. I've taken a few to hospital. Yeah, they're like an extended family. I worry about them if I haven't seen them. They need to tell me if they go on holiday so I don't fret or think something's happened. Word quickly spread about the granny from the Yanni and now Barb has become somewhat of a social media celebrity, posing with tall patrons who tower over her. It's a little bit overwhelming. Behind the bar, that's my comfort zone. I can talk to anybody. But the other side of the bar, I feel like I'm right out of my comfort zone. The pint-sized publican now has people diverting travel plans to pay her a visit and they come from across Australia and as far away as Europe. I actually feel like a grommet. Especially when I only, some of them I only come up to like their waist. But yeah, no, it's, it's, I'm getting used to it now. But do have people come out of their way just so they can get their photo taken with a really short granny. Barb has her own line of merch, granny from the Yanni t-shirts, coasters and mugs. Hundreds of people attended the pub's 125th birthday celebrations, which included a best-dressed granny competition in honour of the star publican. For daughter Alicia, who had no idea that a retirement plan to buy a country pub in Queensland would end up making her mum semi-famous, she's really proud. She's a little firecracker, that's for sure. Yeah, and hard worker. Like, there's nothing for her on a Tuesday when the delivery of alcohol comes through and she's thrown around cartons. She's a real goer. Like, and you can't stop her. You can't stop her. That's Alicia Smith, new owner of the Yandaran Hotel near Bundaberg in Queensland. She was talking about her mum, Barb Parkinson, who's taken a career change from nursing to help her run the pub. And you can see more on that story, including photos of Barb posing next to some of the pub's taller patrons who tower above her. You'll find that story on the ABC homepage. Head to abc.net.au and search for The Granny Publican. That's the show for today. I'm David Clawton and I'll be back next week with more great stories from beyond the cities. I'll chat to you then. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.description: Turning red wheat and sugar beet into unique spirits, historic cemeteries offer protected habitat for rare orchids, learning from the best at bull-riding camp, country cafe building community.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country. Let's catch up with our reporters on the road in regional Australia. This week, not just a resting place for the long departed. We'll hear how historic cemeteries are providing undisturbed habitat for rare and endangered plants and animals. We'll meet a farmer who's adding value to his crops by turning them into spirits and hear how he's using some less common crops like red wheat and sugar beet to make unconventional alcohol. And we're visiting a tiny border town that suffered a series of setbacks but is now on the road to recovery with the help of a little coffee shop run by local women who see the value in building their community. We live here ourselves. We want a great town. We want a town to be proud of and that doesn't happen by everyone sitting on their bottoms. Like, you've got to get in and do the hard work. That story coming up. But first today, bull riding has a reputation as one of the most dangerous sports you can take up. But it's not proving a turn-off for aspiring bull riders lured by the action and adrenaline of the rodeo scene. Almost 60 up-and-coming riders had the chance to learn from the best at a dedicated bull riding camp in central Queensland recently. And reporter Claudia Sullivan went along to meet some of the talented young riders. There's an art to the popular, if not divisive, sport of bull riding. And the skill set is one that event organisers were concerned could be eroded if not fostered. That's why the organisation Youth of the Nation Rodeo Co organised a bull riding camp in Grace Mears' CQLX Sail Yards. The training day attracted some of Australia's biggest bull riding names, including world number three Brady Fielder. I'm ranked second in the MVP in the PBR Team Series and finished third in the world title race this year for 2025 in PBR and the best bull ride in the world. It's a great feeling. Yeah, incredible. Congratulations. Thank you very much. You know, it's a heck of a journey. I'm just grateful to achieve what I have so far. Yeah, did you ever expect to achieve it? You know, to be honest, I always had a big picture out there far away, but sometimes for sure I didn't know if I could ever do it. But never, ever gave up and just never let up one bit. And I'm grateful for where I'm at now. Are you hoping to keep competing as well? What's the goal? Absolutely, yeah. I plan on riding for the next few years at least and I'd like to become a world champion for sure. It's the main goal, whether I'm in team or individuals. So it's what I'm shooting for each and every time and I know if I do everything right, I'll be all right. Can you paint a bit of the scene for me about what it was like? Where were you competing? Over in America, in the United States. Just I've competed all over the world, really. Just especially in the States, you know, it's the biggest bull riding in the world, from Vegas, all around. It's New York. There's so many cool opportunities to go and visit these places, doing what I truly love. It's really cool. With eager students travelling from as far as the Northern Territory and Victoria, Harrison Prow was just one local future champion in the making, keen to learn the ropes. The best of the best here to coach, so I came here to learn some stuff. What's it like to see some of the best of the best? Oh, pretty cool. I could be just like them one day. So what's something that you've been learning today? Can you walk me through it? So for starters, we went on the drop barrel, which is just like a biking bull, but with a barrel. And then we went and do a shoot procedure, which is what you all do in the shoot, like what you do with your bull rope and that. Is that when you're slowly sitting on the bull? Yeah, it is in the shoot. And then put your hand in the bull rope, just like you do when you're riding one. Do you think you can tell how the bull feels beneath you, if it's like a happy or an angry bull? Not too sure. All the adrenaline rush makes you just like feel nothing really. Sometimes if they're just like running, galloping across the arena, you do sometimes, and it just feels cool and fun. Is it ever scary? Oh, not really. Only when one's chasing you. The sport is also notoriously dangerous. Attending the camp was Sam O'Connor. It was his first time back in the stadium since he broke his back bull riding in 2018. While he was left with a paraplegic disability from the accident, he still loves the sport and was there to help nurture other young riders. Instructing bull riding is, you know, you're starting with a lot of kids that have not learnt anything, so you've got to teach them the basic skills and the fundamentals of riding bulls. So teaching them how to get on them properly, to do the right movements. It's not just crack the gate and hang on for dear life. There's actual skill to it of following the beast, learning how to ride the momentum out of it, and yeah. Can you give me maybe step one, when you're hopping on a bull, like some hot tips? Getting on, just you want to be nice and calm. You don't want to be brain flustered or anything like that. The calmer you are, you're going to keep the beast calm as well. The less energy you use inside the chute, the more energy you've got to get out of the chute with. And can you tell me what makes you experience to do this bull riding training? Can you give me your catalogue? Well, yeah, I rode bulls professionally for about seven years. Sort of rode all over the world, America, Canada, Brazil. It's a sport that took me everywhere, which is what I loved about it. I got to see the world, see all of Australia, meet a lot of great contacts, and in my books it's the best fun you can have with your clothes on, I guess. And you were speaking a bit in past tense there about your bull riding days. Do you mind telling me a bit about how it came to an end? Yeah, so first of the first, so it happened on New Year's Eve. I broke my back at a PBR professional event. It's not ping pong, it is what it is. The true thing about the sport is it is dangerous. You can get killed. There has been people that have been killed. I broke my back and became a complete paraplegic. But the sport of bull riding is what's getting me mind strong, because you have to have a strong mind to ride bulls, and that is dangerous. So if you can get past that, I believe you can get past anything in life. And is there something that, I guess, maybe people don't know so much about your life now that you are paraplegic? What's changed for you? Lots of things have changed. Well, I mean, always run off my feet. It's a bit of a pun there, but yeah. So we had to relearn how to use your body. Once you break your back, you lose certain parts that don't work anymore. Your bowels, your insides and that sort of stuff. So you had to relearn how to use all that sort of stuff again and to get back out there in the world, you know. That's the biggest thing I can say to everybody is the more you can get out there in life, the better you can be. Well, today's your first day back training, isn't it? How does it feel being in the arena? Yeah, no, this is my first bull riding skill since being in a wheelchair. I broke me back here in Rocky. What was that back? Yeah, first of the first, 2018. So seven years ago, I broke me back, and now it's back doing the bull riding skill, helping the younger generation, which is something that I hope I can give them the same life I got they live, you know, getting to travel all over the world and do something you love doing. You're not at work any day. Every day is a great day because you're doing something you love doing, you know, and to hand that back on to young kids and hopefully they can get out there and live the life I got to live. Is there anything that you think people don't know, something you'd like to tell people listening, that they don't know about bull riding? Yeah, so a lot of people think it's cruel, you know. The biggest thing is it's cruelty to animals. A lot of people don't understand, but these bulls are looked after. They're like everybody's pets. The contractors that own the bulls and everything like that, they're their pets. So those bulls, you know, if they get hurt, that's their livelihood gone. So they're not going to put their bulls in any position that's going to hurt them, you know what I mean? And we all love that without bulls, we don't have a sport. No one wants to get out there and hurt the bulls in any kind of way. You know, there's rules against it. The bull gets cut. There's, you know, upper fines up to $1,700 per centimetre. Everything is designed. Our spurs, yes, we ride with spurs, but they're blunt. They're RSPCA approved. To a lot of people out there that looks at it as if it's, you know, cruelty to animals, it's, you know, you've got a bull that weighs up to 900 kilos to a cowboy that weighs up to about 50 kilos, you know. So no way we can hurt them, but, you know, they love to do it as well. A lot of bulls, if they don't want to buck, they'll just gallop down the pen, you know. So they've got to want to buck as well. So they love the sport just as much as the bull riders do, yeah. And there's a bit of action happening behind us. Can you tell me what's happening right now? Yeah, so we just bucked our first one. So one of the young fellas just got on a little potty. Well, it's a steer. I think they rode time too, so that's a good bonus for the young fella. So you've got the bull fighters there parted up with thigh pads, chest pads. You can hear when that young fella just fell off then. You can hear the thump. You will get winded. And that's the part where you find out whether you want to be a bull rider or not. If it's the first time, once you get winded a few times, it's either a full person or it's not full person. The camaraderie behind the chutes, you know, like, yes, it's a one-person sport. No one can help you once that gate's open. But then you've got the boys on the back of the chute. Everyone's out there to help each other to succeed, you know what I mean? Like, yes, we're versing each other in an actual bull ride together, but you'll see everybody on the back of the chutes cheering and trying to get you across the other side. On the outskirts of a small town on the New South Wales mid-north coast, life is blooming in an historic cemetery. Tucked among bushland, the graveyard, more than 150 years old, is home to a critically endangered ground orchid, the pale yellow double tail. It was first discovered at the site in the mid-1990s and since then, the Midcoast Council has carefully managed the area to ensure the orchid species is protected. There's only three or four sites where we know this species occurs, so it's really limited, extremely restricted in its range. I'm here at the graveyard site with the council's senior ecologist, Matt Bell, who regularly monitors the orchids. The orchid does occur in areas that are mown, if they're mown at the right time of the year, when the species isn't flowering. So it really relies on areas that have a native grassy ground cover. So it only appears when it's flowering, so you can only detect it in September or October when the flower spikes emerge. The flower spikes are very small. They're only about 20 centimetres high, but they've got a showy yellow flower on them, a beautiful, delicate, complex flower. But yeah, it's incredibly difficult to find because it's only obvious when it's flowering and it flowers for such a short period of time. So what sort of things do you do to preserve it? So it's essentially protect the flower spikes when they emerge. So it's to safeguard them from trampling or mowing or disturbance. We also look after the habitat. So we treat weeds. And what happens if there is a burial happening at that certain time when it's flowering? Yeah, so it's just the spikes are identified. They're flagged so that the operation can take place respectfully and appropriately, but the orchids are protected from any trampling or inadvertent harm.
