episodes.title: Island community doing golf differently and blossoms turn coffee plantation white
episodes.description: For two days a year, coffee tree blossoms turn plantation white; golf in a stunning setting brings community together on a remote island; lavender grower marks 35 years of labour of love; how conservation dogs are helping with turtle conservation.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, I'm David Claughton and this is A Big Country. Thanks for tuning in for a trip around regional Australia. This week it's harvest time for many Aussie farmers and we'll check in on a pretty special harvest with a lavender grower who's picking the fragrant purple flowers by hand. We'll visit a quirky golf course in a spectacular setting on a remote island that's bringing the community together in camaraderie. And we'll learn about some very clever conservation dogs and hear how they're being used to sniff out freshwater turtle nests to help preserve the native species. They work in short bursts with well-earned rests in between. That sniffing that they're doing takes up a lot of energy. It's not just the physical, as in the legwork of it. It takes a lot of brain power for them to do it as well. They're really focused and on the job. So, yeah, and us handlers probably need a bit of a break as well. Tiring work for dogs and their handlers. We'll hear more about that conservation project coming up. Forget the selfies with pretty purple jacarandas or brilliant yellow sunflowers. White coffee tree blossoms are arguably even more spectacular. But to capture the site, you've got to get in quick as they only last for two days. Reporter Kim Honan was lucky to drop into a coffee plantation at Newry Bar near Barham Bay on the New South Wales north coast, just in time to see the blossom. She spoke to grower Rebecca Senfeldt. It is a beautiful and very special two days. The blossoms are on. You've got to come visit. And why does it only happen like one or two days of the year? The blossoms come in spring after a significant dry spell, which we've had eight weeks or so. And then the rains come, which they did last week. And on the 10th day, the flowers come out. So it has pretty much been on the 9th or 10th day today. And the blossoms on the coffee trees do only last two days. Then they drop. And then that tiny little bud of the next fruit starts to grow for the next 11 months into. It's got to last all the way till next October. The blossoms are white, but can you give a better description of what they look like and maybe what they smell like? Yes, Kim, their coffee blossom is really like a little star jasmine or orange or citrus blossom. And they smell extraordinarily sweet like a jasmine. That's the best description, citrus or jasmine blossom. And as I say, only two days. So it's very special. So you can just go right up to a tree. In fact, we've had people drive by a couple of years ago and have their windows down and come in on the day that the blossoms are out because they could smell the blossom in the air. It is a beautiful, sweet fragrance. So I hope those who visit will come and smell the blossom at least. And the bees are absolutely loving the blossoms. They're everywhere. Yep, they're going crazy. Often what we do is hear the bees first, the hum. They will be out in force. I mean, they're not interested in us, so I'm not worried about being stung. They're just focused in on getting that nectar out of the middle of that gorgeous little blossom. The bees love it. It's a very bee-friendly farm or bee-friendly industry. So I love that for the Australian coffee industry. So a very limited time to come and see the blossoms on the coffee trees. Do you get a lot of people here at the plantation wanting to take selfies with the coffee trees? I think they should. I think it's just marvellous. It is extraordinary. We think this has been the 38th lot of flowering. No, I exaggerate. The trees are 38 years old, so we probably had 34 years of coffee blossoms. And we think this is the best in at least six years. Remember, 2019 was so dry. It was really a drought season for the northern rivers or the north coast of New South Wales, and that's when we had a serious lot of flowers after that dry, and that's what we've got again after only eight weeks. So this amount of blossoming, do you reckon it's going to be a bumper crop next year? Oh, we deserve it to be. We really would hope so. I mean, every flower won't turn into a little fruit. We will allow some to drop and accept that, but it's a really good start. You've got to start with the blossom before you get the fruit. So, yes, it makes sense that we should see a good crop come through next year. Let's hope we can keep the crop on and get a super harvest in 2026. Well, I was hoping to get here for harvest. Turn up, the harvest is just done. Blossoms are out. How was harvest? Harvest was smaller than we wanted. A little bit of sad face here. With that, eight weeks of the dry, it was longer than we thought, and John really likes to let the trees relax with a bit of rain before we harvest. We do use our harvesting machine. If you're handpicking, you could handpick every day for about three months. Well, we're not going to do that. We really can't make money as a professional farm to do that handpicking for the size of our, you know, sort of 40 acres, 16 hectares or so of coffee trees. So, we just had to wait for the rain to come. But meanwhile, you know, some fruits dropping on the ground and then you get a bit of a storm through and more fruit drops on the ground. We were very fortunate to miss the hail that came through a few days ago that, unfortunately for those in southeast Queensland, got it. So, we were very grateful. Fingers crossed that didn't happen last weekend. So, we have only done quite a small harvest on our farm this year. And given the potential bumper crop next year, how good would that be given the demand and the prices for coffee at the moment? Yeah, we need it. Australia needs more growers and we've got a growing industry now. You know, we understand that we've got these new varieties which we're really excited for. So, we've got new growers planting. So, we're coming in each year. I do feel, fingers crossed, we're on a roll now with new growers coming on board and not just a bumper harvest next year. There's demand for it. There's roasters crying out for it. And that's just in Australia. You know, the specialty roasters are really looking for a specialty Australian crop. And they're willing to pay the money for it which is a wonderful thing to keep our growers going and profitable. It's what we want. And we're seeing more growers put in trees further south? Yes, not just northern New South Wales but the mid-north coast, more down Coffs and Port Macquarie Way which is terrific to see. There's interest there along the coast and in their hinterland. And then going right up into Queensland, right up to the tropical coast which is exciting to see. Oh, Western Australia, we're expanding. And are these new farmers to agriculture or are they, you know, are they pulling out other crops to put in coffee or they're just, you know, new to the industry altogether? We're now getting quite a few professional farmers who may have been growing macadamias that have been growing citrus in Western Australia and avocados in Western Australia. Sugar cane in North Queensland. And they've had their issues with industry. Peanut farmers where the local mills have closed down for both sugar cane and peanuts. So, yes, the professional farmer is joining us which is really good because they'll be putting in on scale. You know, they do the maths and they work out that this is a crop that's in demand and should be profitable. And I'm going to really say in demand for the long-term future, not just import replacing as we are but real good chance for export growth. Are the new growers able to put in the new varieties that have been trialled? We've all got access as members of the association just to a small amount because we are excited about the new varieties being available. But we're limited with the amount of supply we've got from the Alstonville trial block and also up in Walkham in North Queensland. So with that limited supply, Joss has been able to allocate just a small amount for each of us who are putting our hand up to be able to purchase, you know, 200 to 500 per variety. But there's four varieties. So at the max is only 2,000 trees per year but each year we'll be able to get more. And after four years, of course, they're open pollinating varieties, open sourced, and they will be self-pollinating, sorry is the right word. So we'll be able to then collect our own fruit and then grow the industry from our own fruit from our farm. And you've got a couple of the new varieties that are four-year-old now that have just exploded with white blossoms. They are a fantastic example. I was very fortunate to receive those as an early gift from our agronomist David Peasley, so I tough see him. Yes, they're an extraordinary amount of flowers. And the Marsalasa, there's Marsalasa and IPR 107. The Marsalasa new varieties out today and the flowers are bigger, the blossoms are bigger than the main two varieties we grow in Australia. So that's going to be interesting to see if that equates to overall bigger-sized fruit or bigger-sized coffee bean inside. Wow, bigger cherry, bigger coffee bean. That'll be interesting. Yeah, maybe. I hope so. I'll look tomorrow. So, you know, on Friday we'll be able to see all the flowers out, so I'll compare flower size and we'll have a judgement and see what happens next year when we get the fruit off the trees in October, November 2026. Go, Carlton! On the fairways of Truana, Cape Barron Island, things are a little unexpected. Go, the brownies! You won't find any tailored trousers or neatly pressed polos here, but you'll score an advantage if a crow steals your ball. And while some players have a decent shot, it's safe to say no-one on this island is turning pro. It's a place to come and nobody worries about anything except the golf because they know me and I want people to relax and we don't have no carry-on or anything like that. That's John Gardner. For this golf course, he's everything. Greenkeeper, the manager, the organiser, player, do everything. A few times a week, you'll find John on the mower, tending the course he's been instrumental in creating. It's called the Marijuana Golf Course. It was a bit of a play on words for me, and it's different. John assures me the club doesn't promote drugs, but it makes for an interesting sign. And John likes his signs. They're dotted around the course, marking the names of holes. Some are funny, like the long drop. Others pay tribute to community members who've died. Trawana, Cape Barren Island sits off the northeast coast of Tasmania. It's home to around 80 people, most of whom are indigenous. The Tasmanian government handed this land back to the Aboriginal community in 2005. Now, the island is run entirely by the community, the only place in the state that's governed this way. Oh, beautiful. Golf is a tourist drawcard for Tasmania. Over on King Island, Cape Wickham Lynx was recently named the best golf course in the country by Australian Golf Digest. A game there will set you back hundreds of dollars in greens fees. The views at marijuana rival that of any prestigious course in the country. You can see beautiful wild hills, clear blue waters, and the mountain range on neighbouring Flinders Island stands on the horizon. But like the land it sits on, this course isn't meant for rich tourists. John made it for locals. And both entry and golf clubs are completely free. It's all set up to not make things too hard for anybody. On the weekend I visit, there's a memorial game for a much-loved community member who died a few years ago. I'm Brooke Burke. So today I was the first female to win the Sharon Shuffle Pairs Championship. I've been coming here for three years doing the championship since my auntie passed away, and we do this game as a tribute to her. And today I won. How's that feel? Great. Every Friday there's a hole-in-one competition. Local Luana Townie is a regular, and like many people here, the first time she played golf was on this course. It doesn't matter if you're good at golf or not. People will support you 100%. People laugh at each other and laugh at themselves, which is the main thing. One of the best players on the island is Tim Maynard. His name holds multiple coveted spots in the shed that serves as a clubhouse. But Tim's not in it for the glory. I reckon it feels better when someone else gets a good shot in celebrating a joint in it. And that pretty well sums up the spirit of this golf course. Everyone has a go, no matter your ability or agility. Unconventionally, John's actually put backboards on some greens to give people a better chance. And he's always there to coach. Even me. Too far. I reckon you're standing too far away from it. That's better. Well, you're on. We're on! Buck Brown is a senior ranger on the island. He says this place is about more than golf. A lot of camaraderie. And it's one of the strongest things I've seen in this community, actually pull the community together, has been this golf club. In a way, I've seen it get a lot of people out of the houses in the community. Well, it's actually got them out of the house and out walking on country. And for John, he's pretty pleased when he sees people enjoying his course. And he gets a lot of joy from being out here too. Especially the day after I've mowed. Because there's a certain smell out here then when you've got fresh cut grass. And especially you come out in the morning and the sun's shining and all the mountains are on. You know, it's beautiful. You can do it! Oh, not all! That's Dory from Louise Moylan on Truana. And there's a great video on that golf course. Search ABC Cape Barron Island and you'll find it. I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country. Still to come, we're meeting a former nurse who stumbled into growing lavender and now runs a flower farm alongside a thriving agrotourism business. And we're heading to the Lower Murray River in South Australia's Riverland region. Where conservation dogs are being deployed to sniff out freshwater turtle nests. The native freshwater turtle population has declined significantly in recent years. And it's hoped by detecting nests, baby turtles can be saved from predators. Conservation dog handler Fiona Jackson told Anita Ward what's involved in training the dogs. It takes a bit of work. But what we're doing with our three dogs here is we're getting substrate from the natural environment and adding some colloquial fluid, some turtle fluid to the substrate and training with the dogs that any time they sniff out that odour, they get rewarded. So any time they sniff out, they get rewarded with either a little bit of food or their absolute favourite thing, which is a ball. Why are they such a good tool in the detection process? Dogs in general as a methodology, because of their sense of smell, it's just so incredible. People say it's, researchers say it's anywhere between 10,000 and 100,000 times better than our sense of smell. So anything that we're struggling to find in the natural environment, like turtle nests, you can deploy a dog. That technology of their sense of smell can be a real aid in finding those nests or anything that's really difficult for us as humans, either as spotters or other methodologies that struggles. How effective are they in finding the nests? I know it's a relatively new process. Yeah, so we are still training. We've just started this week. Actually, in fact, last week we just introduced the dogs to the odour. So the training wheels are very much still on for our three. But that being said, there's other groups around Australia and across the world who have done this successfully. So it can be done. People up in New South Wales, over in Western Australia, and even in Victoria, actually, who have all successfully worked with conservation detection dogs to find turtle nests. So we're confident that once our lot are trained up, they'll be able to do the same and help out here. How long is that training process? In terms of scent imprinting the dog on the odour, it takes a couple of weeks. Then you've got to get the dog out, which is what we're doing this week, is get the dog out in the natural environment, get them used to this environment. And it then becomes very much a process of calibrating the dog across all the different odour possibilities and complexities that there are in the natural environment. So it's hard to say, but in terms of if you have a brand new dog, if you have a dog from PUP, it can take anywhere to 12 months to 18 months to get a dog up and running. But thankfully, the dogs that we've put on this project are already experienced. So they have all their safety and welfare instructions in place. So they're very safe in the natural environment, which is super important to us. So we're hoping after a month or two of training on this odour specifically, that they'll be ready and really calibrated to the odour to help and do searches in the natural environment here. And tell us about the dogs involved. Who are they and how successful have they been so far in getting that imprint? So the dogs, we've got three dogs on this project. Two very experienced dogs who are called Oakley and Rex, who are actually out with us in South Australia at the minute because they're also on the Murray Darling Carpet Python project, which is what we've been doing this morning. And they're super experienced dogs and have quite a few different threatened species odours that they're already on. And they are scent imprinting now to three different turtle species. So the broadshell, the eastern longneck and the Murray shortneck. And then we've got a slightly younger dog, Aaron, who's three years old. This is his first threatened species project, but he's still very experienced and helps us out in our renewable energy projects. And he is also just absolutely nailing his scent imprinting. So we're really excited to take these trading odours that we have and start putting them out here where we are at the minute down by the lake and having him and the other two go out and start searching around here. It's amazing work that you're doing and the dogs are doing. Once they're fully trained for the turtles, what does a day of turtle detection or nest sniffing out look like for them? Yeah, there's definitely, they can go. What we tend to do is we get up at very early. We were actually up at 3.30 this morning to get up, to drive, to sight, to be ready at first light and to do our Murray-Darn carpet python searches. And it will be the same for turtles. It will be up as soon as possible. And they can usually go, dogs can tend to work. It really depends on the terrain and the temperature. But two to three hours is a good time. And then they can have a nice rest and maybe do the same again in the afternoon or evening. And they can probably do that for two, three days. And then they'll require a little rest and then do it again. Because it's a lot of work. That sniffing that they're doing takes up a lot of energy. It's not just the physical, as in the legwork of it. It takes a lot of brainpower for them to do it as well. They're really focused on the job. So yeah, us handlers probably need a bit of a break after three days as well. I can imagine. Once they're ready to go on this turtle project, how confident are you they can help out with the conservation efforts here in the river and along the Murray? I am probably quietly confident. Only because the folk that have done this already in Australia, there's people that have done this and proven it. It's not like we're doing a proof of concept here. So those detection dog handlers that have done this already and we're good friends with them have given us the confidence as well. And they've really helped us in knowing exactly how to train the dogs, how to get the best outcome. So yeah, let's say quietly confident. It's a pristine spring morning when I visit Anne-Marie Manders, a lavender grower from Wandin in Victoria's Yarra Valley. We're going for a stroll through her rows of purple lavender plants. The two main lavenders that we do grow on a commercial basis is an intermediate lavender, which has a gorgeous camphoraceous fragrance and is wonderful for keeping moths and silverfish out of your wardrobe. And it flowers and is ready for picking at the end of December into January. The other lavender that we grow is an angustifolia lavender. And that is a lavender that you can use in food products, drinks, teas, ice cream, scones, biscuits, cakes, herb breads, all those sorts of things. Now with the edible lavender, it is ready for picking at the end of November. So there is a month between when we pick the edible lavender and when we pick the non-edible lavender. Now that was more a matter of good luck rather than good management in my case, because I knew nothing about what I was doing. That's because Anne-Marie never dreamed of becoming a farmer. In fact, she had a whole other career as an operating theatre nurse before she and her late husband decided to buy an old cherry orchard. 35 years later, the property now stands as a thriving lavender farm, attracting flower lovers from across Australia and beyond. And here's what Anne-Marie tells them about the harvest process. Now when we pick the lavender, it's all picked by hand with a sickle, a small sickle, which is what the strawberry growers use. And it's a curved knife with a very sharp serrated edge. We start very early in the morning at the latest at 6am. If it's going to be a really, really hot day, we'll start at 5.30. And that's when the lavender has got its strongest fragrance. Having picked it in the bunches, the bunches are picked by hand, a rubber band is put on the bunch. We then stack all those bunches into big picking bins and then we transport those bins up into the drying shed where they are hung upside down to dry. And in amongst all that lavender, you've got a bit of stick and a bit of leaf and there's also some flower dust. Now you don't want that in your lavender if you're going to be putting it into food or if you're going to be, if it's craft work, you're going to be putting it into little sachets or sleep pillows. So we sift it and we have a series of three sieves and we pour the lavender through and it sits in a big bin, like a rubbish bin and we shake it around. It's all done by hand and people say, oh, this could be much, you could automate this and have it on a shaker table. But it doesn't, it's not hands on and I'm doing it more like the cottage industry, wanting people to see how it was done in the olden days. And I'm a bit olden day sort of in my approach and it gives people a wow factor and then they can put their hands into that stripped lavender, rub it between their hands and smell it. And it is gorgeous. And so now, Emery, you've got about 12,000 plants on the farm? Yes. And you started with how many? 500. 500. Did you expect the farm to get so big? No, I had no idea. I didn't know anything about running a business. I didn't have a tractor. I had no knowledge. And as far as making product, I didn't have a clue. And then I had to learn about how to price it. How was I going to talk to people? Yeah, it started off absolutely at the bottom of the ladder. And so coming back to harvesting and processing the lavender, so the fragrance and the oils, they're actually contained in the flowers themselves? Yes. The actual oil is in the base of every little tiny weenie little flower head. So if you look at the formation of a flower head, it's got a whole lot of little heads within that big head. And every one of those little heads has got a microscopic sack at the bottom. And that's where the oil is. Anne-Marie says most of her customers don't know much about lavender, but she's set on changing that. Some of them want to buy some plants to put in the houses in an indoor plant. That's a definite no-no. So that's where I actually teach them that lavender is an outdoor plant. Secondly, it needs full sun, must have full sun. Thirdly, you do not water it. So you treat it almost with neglect. However, you do need to cut it back once a year and cut off those flower stems and trim it down into a neat, tidy bush. And then it goes into a dormancy. Unfortunately, lavender will not grow in the tropics. It's too humid. And people that come from Singapore or Asia, these countries, and want to grow lavender, I say, no, if you want to grow lavender, sell up and come and live in Victoria. Anne-Marie Manders. She's a lavender grower in Victoria's Yarra Valley, where she spoke to reporter Faith Tabaluyan. And you can read more about that story. You'll find a feature article on the ABC website at abc.net.au. Just search for ABC Lavender. That's the show for today. I'm David Claughton. And I'll catch up with you again next week with more great stories from regional Australia. I'll chat to you then. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. You can discover more ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listener.

So at the max is only 2,000 trees per year but each year we'll be able to get more.

And you've got a couple of the new varieties that are four-year-old now that have just exploded with white blossoms.

So they're very safe in the natural environment, which is super important to us.
So we're hoping after a month or two of training on this odour specifically,
that they'll be ready and really calibrated to the odour to help and do searches in the natural environment here.
And tell us about the dogs involved.
Who are they and how successful have they been so far in getting that imprint?
So the dogs, we've got three dogs on this project.
Two very experienced dogs who are called Oakley and Rex,
who are actually out with us in South Australia at the minute

And they are scent imprinting now to three different turtle species.
So the broadshell, the eastern longneck and the Murray shortneck.
And then we've got a slightly younger dog, Aaron, who's three years old.
This is his first threatened species project, but he's still very experienced
and helps us out in our renewable energy projects.
And he is also just absolutely nailing his scent imprinting.
So we're really excited to take these trading odours that we have
and start putting them out here where we are at the minute down by the lake
and having him and the other two go out and start searching around here.
It's amazing work that you're doing and the dogs are doing.
Once they're fully trained for the turtles,
what does a day of turtle detection or nest sniffing out look like for them?
Yeah, there's definitely, they can go.
What we tend to do is we get up at very early.
We were actually up at 3.30 this morning to get up, to drive, to sight,
to be ready at first light and to do our Murray-Darn carpet python searches.
And it will be the same for turtles.
It will be up as soon as possible.
And they can usually go, dogs can tend to work.
It really depends on the terrain and the temperature.
But two to three hours is a good time.
And then they can have a nice rest and maybe do the same again
And they can probably do that for two, three days.
And then they'll require a little rest and then do it again.
Because it's a lot of work.
That sniffing that they're doing takes up a lot of energy.
It's not just the physical, as in the legwork of it.
It takes a lot of brainpower for them to do it as well.
They're really focused on the job.
So yeah, us handlers probably need a bit of a break after three days as well.
Once they're ready to go on this turtle project,
how confident are you they can help out with the conservation efforts
here in the river and along the Murray?
Only because the folk that have done this already in Australia,
there's people that have done this and proven it.
It's not like we're doing a proof of concept here.
So those detection dog handlers that have done this already
and we're good friends with them have given us the confidence as well.
And they've really helped us in knowing exactly how to train the dogs,
how to get the best outcome.
So yeah, let's say quietly confident.

people to see how it was done in the olden days.

they can put their hands into that stripped lavender, rub it between their hands and smell
And so now, Emery, you've got about 12,000 plants on the farm?

I didn't know anything about running a business.
And as far as making product, I didn't have a clue.

How was I going to talk to people?
Yeah, it started off absolutely at the bottom of the ladder.
And so coming back to harvesting and processing the lavender, so the fragrance and the oils,
they're actually contained in the flowers themselves?

Anne-Marie says most of her customers don't know much about lavender, but she's set on changing

So that's where I actually teach them that lavender is an outdoor plant.
Secondly, it needs full sun, must have full sun.

Unfortunately, lavender will not grow in the tropics.
And people that come from Singapore or Asia, these countries, and want to grow lavender,

episodes.title: Rare shrub thriving and moving fresh milk in kegs
episodes.description: Introduced bumble bees are thriving in Tasmania, researchers are tracking them to find out why; kegs replace plastic bottles to get fresh milk from farm to cup; endangered shrub with a yellow flower showing signs of resurgence; finding the next…
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. You're listening to A Big Country. I'm David Claughton. And it's lovely to have your company as we join our reporters exploring regional Australia. This week we're learning about a study of bumblebees on Tasmanian farms where the pollinators are being fitted with tiny backpacks holding radio transmitters to track their movements. We'll hear about a new way of getting fresh milk from the farm to the cafe or shop without the use of plastic bottles. And we'll meet researchers who are passionate about finding the next variety of one of Australia's favourite summer fruits. At the end of the day I love passion fruit. It's my favourite thing to work with. It tastes good and I eat far too much of it so I feel sick sometimes. I'll be out in the field, every fruit that I say I have to try. It's all good. I love it. A passion for passion fruit. We'll hear why new varieties of the fruit are desperately needed. That's coming up. First today we're heading to the New South Wales Northern Tablelands where a small property is believed to be the only place in the world where a unique and critically endangered yellow shrub grows. Reporter Bridget Murphy ventured into the bush to learn more about the rare plant. After about an hour of walking, ducking and manoeuvring through bushland on Stephen Walkden Brown's property Lomalangi, a bright yellow cluster appears in the distance. We've spotted the critically endangered Astrolasia ripestris, specifically this flower's subspecies, recurva. Here, near Armadale in the state's northern Tablelands, is the only place in the world where this plant grows. Stephen and his wife Yvonne bought the 200 hectare property in 2017. Unbeknownst to them, alongside its almost untouched bushland, it housed the critically endangered species. Ben Vincent is a senior regional conservation officer with the Biodiversity Conservation Trust. He says very little is known about the shrub. There's really little known about its life history, so there's plenty still to learn. It's critically endangered, that's its listing in New South Wales, and to get that listing, you have to be a plant with a very, very restricted geographic location, of which this one has. It's probably about 600 metres in length along a creek line and restricted to the parallel mountains there. And it also has to have very few mature individuals. Although it's a small and relatively simple-looking plant from afar, Mr Vincent says for those with a trained eye, it's striking. The heart-shaped green leaves full of these little star-shaped hairs, which make it kind of a fluffy, light green appearance. And then there's, you know, beautiful, really obvious yellow flower. They really do stand out. Stephen agrees. He says he is proud to consider himself a custodian to the plant. I think it does help that they are quite an attractive plant, a little bit bushy in the wild, but they have a very bright yellow, very distinctive and nice flower. There's a number of conservation efforts in hand. And yes, the fact that it's a lovely plant and where it grows is also nice along the creek banks in amongst some leptospermum over cover in amongst grass and things. So yeah, just walking through it and seeing these bright splashes of yellow when it's flowering. But even the non-flowering plant, it's got a sort of a furry, grey-green leaf that maybe it's an acquired taste, but knowing it's so rare, we think they look quite nice as well. Mr Vincent says despite its critical situation, there could be a prosperous future for the plant with a survey this year showing good signs. We were able to get out and resurvey the existing population and find the mature adults are about the same. So that's great. It means they're persisting well. But the exciting news was to see, I think we counted about over 600. So that's a great outcome. And these guys are, you know, they're probably 20 or 30 centimetres tall. So the point there is that they've been in the landscape now for probably four or five years and persisting well. So it's a good news story for this critically endangered species. It was believed, like so many other Australian natives, fire was needed to break sea dormancy. But it appears in this case, drought was the catalyst. It was thought prior to this resurvey that this plant species, like many astrolasian, needed fire in the landscape to break sea dormancy. And that may be the case. But as it turns out, severe drought like that, which we experienced in 2018 and into the end of 19, appears to also break dormancy. So, you know, the Australian floor is adapted to boom and bust drought situations like we had. Mr Vincent says private landholders like Mr Walkden Brown play a pivotal role in biodiversity and conservation. Private landholders are becoming more aware of what the Biodiversity Conservation Trust does in New South Wales, which is partner with private landholders to achieve conservation outcomes on their property. And yeah, look, I think it is becoming more popular. As part of his work with the state's Biodiversity Conservation Trust, Stephen receives funding to do his part caring for the plants. We do notice that some of them are being nibbled and we do have deer up on this block and there's feral goats as well. And so we're under our contract with BCT. We are obliged to try and control those species, which pose some kind of threat. The population's fairly healthy. We keep a watching brief on it and we're just so pleased that there are so many little seedlings. Because we've had, what, this is probably the fourth, at least the fourth, maybe going on for the fifth year of above average rainfall or pretty good season. So after the 2019 drought, it was terrible up here. But the plant seems to have responded to that run of good seasons. Just like Stephen and Yvonne inherited the beautiful endangered species, they also hope to pass it on, ensuring the plant is cared for in the future. We've got one of our children lives in Armidale and has a number of kids. So, you know, we would like this to pass on through the family after we've gone. That'll be their decision. But we love it. We come up here often. The kids and grandkids come up as well. And it's a very favourite spot. Like many cafes, this busy outlet in the coastal Tasmanian town of Penguin powers through milk on a daily basis. The milk is delivered weekly, in bulk, ready to supply caffeine-starved customers with their daily dose. But unlike other cafes, this milk comes in a keg and it's pulled out of a tap. This pub-like set-up is a deliberate choice. So it's something we've been looking at for a couple of years now. Cafe co-owner Rob Arvia speaking here. He had some misgivings about the system. The main hurdle had been cost at the start. So when we first went to market looking, when we first acquired the shop, the cost was around $12,000 to install a tap, which for a small business was completely unattainable. But fast forward to, I'm trying to think when this went in now, but it's been for longer than a year. The way he describes it is a bit like a vending machine. The cafe is responsible for the daily cleaning and refilling, but the supplier owns the infrastructure and is in charge of all the maintenance and milk deliveries. So that made it accessible for us, which was great. It's more expensive than mass-produced plastic bottles from a large dairy factory, and that's hard to pass on to a consumer. But cafe manager Grace Primrose reckons the benefits outweigh the costs. So we're looking at a fridge, which is hooked up with our kegs inside, and then we've got a milk tap where people can come and bring in their litre refills and refill every day fresh. And you also use this in the coffees? Yeah, definitely. So we fill up separate kegs that are two litres each and go and put them in the coffees, and it just makes the creamiest coffee. What's it like to use, I don't know if you've used a system where you've got milk bottles instead. What's the comparison? It's just fresher, and since we're topping it up every couple of minutes when we go through the litres, you're just getting fresher milk in your coffee. People definitely notice the milk and then come in and want to get the refills, they want to hear the story, they want to hear who's behind it. People really value knowing where the milk comes from. To Grace's point about the story, knowing that it comes from a single farm, people are willing to pay for that privilege. Something we're really proud about is the waste. So over a year, it's about 8,000 plastic bottles that don't come through our store anymore, which is incredible. I've worked in cafes my whole life that have the plastic bottles, and it's quite frustrating. You have to try and get them down small enough to go in the bin, and then you are using so much waste. So it's nice that we can return the kegs washed to him, and then he can refill them for us. And the farmer that does that refilling? Well, about 100 kilometres down the road, Gennaro Velazquez makes boutique Venezuelan-style cheese on what he reckons is one of the smallest dairy farms in Tasmania. We milk our own cows, so we milk 100 cows, and at the moment we produce more milk than what we put towards cheese. The solution? A couple of years ago, he started selling off his fresh milk both directly to customers and to a large nearby milk factory. And so by having milk, like in cakes or pre-filled bottles and plastic bottles, and then we also have skin milk and cream and things like that, it just brings security to our business. So it allows us to value up. Dairy farmers generally sell their milk to these giant, often global, processors, meaning they have little to no say over what price they get. And while Gennaro still sells some milk to a processor, he's been able to cut out the middleman for the rest, processing it on farm, choosing his own prices, and directly receiving profits from sales. Any milk that we are able to process through the factory and sell it as a value-added product, it is milk that we are not relying on what the commodity price or the industry in general wants to say our milk is worth. In a small business scenario like us, like milking 100k hours, to make it viable and to make it profitable and to make it sustainable in the long run, we have to look at ways of, you know, value-adding and doing all the things that are pretty much thinking out of the box. Each week, Gennaro's farm sends out milk to about 20 customers, including popular cafes. Some of it's in glass bottles, some's in plastic bottles, and since introducing it last year, about half is in these reusable milk kegs. It's sort of like a contribution to, you know, looking after the environment, reducing that use of single-use plastic. We started using this system back in April 2024. Not everyone loves them, but his share of customers is increasing. I guess for some people and for some operations, it's easier just to stick to plastic. You just get the plastic, fill up the bottles, they go and you don't have to know about them. As I said, people that care about the environment, that don't want to be using plastic bottles and don't want to be generating more rubbish than what we need to, you know, so we have a number of cafes that are now moving towards that because same thing, like you have the environmental contribution, but you also make it a lot easier for them. Once they're up, like set up and ready to go, it makes it a lot easier for them. And for customers like Rob Arvia at the cafe, there's something charming about having a local farmer come and drop their milk right at the door. Yeah, it's incredible. And obviously we are farmers first and foremost. So to have those connections and also for those people to be directly interacting with the team here, it's just invaluable. So yeah, wouldn't have it any other way. Farmer and cafe owner, Rob Arvia, ending that report from Meg Ferguson. Before that, Brigitte Murphy took us into the bush in the New South Wales Northern Tablelands, where a rare plant is thriving. And you can see more on that story, including pictures of the native shrub with a pretty yellow flower on the ABC homepage at abc.net.au. I'm David Claughton with you for A Big Country. Still to come, the researchers tracking bumblebees in Tasmania with the help of some high-tech equipment. And if you love passion fruit on top of your summer pav, you'll be pleased to know work is underway to develop new varieties to keep the fruit growing in Australia. Jennifer Nichols has this story from the Passion Fruit Research Patch on Queensland's Sunshine Coast. It's a beautiful flower that we're looking at. Yeah. You can see the blue colour here and it is beautiful. And yeah, we use this one. One of the reasons is if we can identify this is tolerant to different stresses like high temperature. Yeah. Hello. I'm Mubashir Alam. So you can call me Mo. I'm leading National Passion Fruit Breeding Program. You're doing some very important work because the plants that growers have been using, there's some problems with them. Yes. For the varieties, yield decline is happening. The size of the fruits are getting reduced. Growers are not making much profit. We want to release new varieties that are profitable for the industry, that can produce optimum fruit size, that have good flavour. What's involved in breeding passion fruit? The first thing is really important. We should have good germplasm. So that's the collection of these different varieties that have different good traits. We probably should have done it 10 years ago when we were a bit younger.
Yeah, I wouldn't recommend doing it now.
But anyway, the aches and pains are, yeah, well, things are improving.
You're fairly urged to get into hospitality and do it bloody 20 years earlier than we do.
Do it earlier than we have, yeah.
This community needs this. Do we need it? Probably not.
But let's give it a crack and see how it goes.
Yeah. What's a town without a pub?
And so this bit of rootstock, because it got damaged, that rootstock's taken off and grown now.
Alan Edwards could talk about lemons all day long. That's because he grew up on his family's citrus orchard in Victoria's Yarra Valley region.
My dad bought this property. He changed the variety of lemons over. And then so they've been in since about 1950.
And you have a lot of memories of picking, growing up, spending a lot of time in the orchard?
Oh, hours and hours. And days and days and months and months.
Today, Alan runs the farm with the help of his son, Michael. When not working on his PhD research, Michael dabbles in growing quirky crops.
But his latest project involves an unusual flower.
On the side, I grow some things for chefs and distillers.
And in talking to distillers and getting to know them, they were interested in getting citrus blossoms.
Initially, it was grapefruit and now it's more lemons.
So we're running a project this year to see how we can, if we can get what they need.
And also basically to reduce the amount of fruit we have by picking the blossom before it becomes fruit.
And so this trial involves one block of lemon trees.
And so just talk me through what your plan is. And it involves renting out that block.
Yeah, exactly. So the distillers will rent that for a year.
They will do the more manual work on this, which is cutting back the trees.
And then we'll apply some fertilizer as a bit of an experiment in certain trees.
And then we can see if that can induce more blossom per tree.
But basically, we want to get the most amount of blossom from that field as possible.
And we've got 300 trees, so I think they'll get what they need.
They've got a year to do it.
So I think it'll be OK.
Michael says it takes a gentle touch to harvest the blossoms.
The actual product is super delicate and, you know, it can be bruised.
You have to pick it fresh because you're picking for aroma.
So it's much like how the fragrance industry would think about growing something.
Yeah, so it's a bit different.
And there's quite a short harvest window as well for these blossoms?
So we have two or three varieties of lemons here.
The main variety we grow is Eureka.
So that will keep just producing blossoms throughout the year.
With some of the other lemon trees that we tested, which was Meyer lemon,
they have a much shorter window, but lots of blossom.
So there's always that as a backup.
But the client really liked the Eureka.
So that's what we'll go for.
Lauren Bonkowski is a co-founder of Marionette,
a Victorian distillery specialising in produce-driven liqueurs.
There was a bit of a gap in the market.
Everyone was making gin and whisky.
And we saw this big hole in the slightly less sexy category,
which was fruit and nuts and these essential cocktail ingredients
that we were using every day.
Ms Bonkowski says they work with farmers across regional Victoria.
The most recent product we've made, elderflower.
That one we've really ran around the state trying to find the right blossoms.
It was quite an adventure because it's not a big industry.
So that led us to the streets of Trantham with a forager.
It's one of our main supplying areas where our oranges and our almonds are grown.
We like to work directly with farmers.
We don't buy it through co-ops so that we can work with the farmers on the season in their schedules.
And we do a lot of work to make sure that we can buy their seconds fruit on farmers' timelines,
which has worked out really, really well for everyone.
Ms Bonkowski says after discovering citrus blossoms, they were hooked.
And they're at the heart of their latest experiment, an elderflower liqueur.

So we went out to the farm and we were lucky enough for them to let us pick a whole lot of different citrus blossoms and decided that the landland blossom is much more gentle and sort of supports the flavour profile of the elderflower putting in the liqueur.
And is this the first time that you're using these blossoms?
Yeah. Blossoms are much harder to work with than fruit.

In different levels of distillation and maceration, the hardier fruits, so the citrus itself, has the most oil and they can really withstand maceration and really high-proof alcohol to draw out flavour.
Whereas blossoms are the complete opposite end of the spectrum, so you have to be really careful.
For Ellen and Michael, this citrus blossom project hasn't always been straightforward.
I think it's a learning curve for both of us.
Well, we have probably little different ways of looking at things, so it's a bit of compromise between the two.
And Michael, what have you had to compromise on since working with your dad?
We do do things a little differently, but I think we understand the logic behind both.
Maybe there's an age thing as well to do with that because I'm willing to experiment more, obviously.
Dad, a little bit less, but it's probably because he has the experience which I really admire and absorb.
And Alan says he's glad to be farming as father and son.
As far as Michael experimenting is concerned, that's exactly what I was like.
When my father was doing this and I was doing it, there was that different way of looking at things.
And so I think it is good to experiment and use a little bit of NEOCE and work it out for yourself what works best.
Yeah, you need to know what fails as well.
Yeah, every experiment has got a failure, but you've got to learn by your failures.
Alan Edwards, a lemon grower from Victoria's Yarra Valley.
He was speaking with Faith Tabuluyan.
Before that, we met the new owners of the Bamboka Pub on the New South Wales far south coast.
You can read more on both those stories.
You'll find articles and pictures on the ABC homepage at abc.net.au.
I'll be back next week with more great stories from the regions.
You've been listening to an ABC podcast.

episodes.title: Shearing record falls and international chefs getting a taste for Australian lamb
episodes.description: Team take out world record in shearing marathon; international chefs learning to love Aussie lamb; promoting flowers that are grown here, over those flown here; farmers transform land with tree-planting over four decades.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. You're listening to A Big Country. I'm David Claughton and it's lovely to have your company as we join reporters exploring regional Australia. This week we're meeting a delegation of international chefs who've gathered in a small town in rural Western Australia. They're visiting the country to learn more about our lamb and how to use it in culinary dishes. It's all part of efforts to get Aussie grown lamb on more plates around the world. We'll meet a couple who've spent more than four decades on the land, not only farming but also transforming the landscape through an extensive tree planting program. And we'll hear about one family's mission to educate consumers about where their flowers come from. With her brother and sister growing flowers on the family farm in Tasmania, when Bec Thomas decided on a career change from her corporate job, she joined the flower industry to promote locally grown blooms. That's coming up. First today to a record-breaking effort. A team of five shearers in southern New South Wales have set a new record for the most Merino lambs shorn over eight hours with five stands. Reporter Emily Doak was in the shed watching the record attempt. It's no ordinary day in the shearing shed at Morvern, south of Wagga Wagga. The five shearers, Lockie Robertson, Benjamin Duncan, Cameron Hicks, Toby Walker and Nick Lehman, are working at a frantic pace, aiming to set a world record. Toby says he's been training for months. It's been about six, seven months of long days of shearing, drive home, smash the gym for an hour and a half, diet, gear preparation. It's been a really long build-up. It's glad to be over, to be honest. People might have seen shearing in a shed during the day. Just how different is it in a world record attempt conditions? As intense as it gets. Today, that's my first experience. It's so mentally straining. I didn't realise how focused I had to be, and that was just all day. It's so dialled in and focused on what we're doing. Good to be shearing with these other blokes alongside you. Great bunch of guys. They were awesome. Everybody pulled through with a mammoth effort today, and it gave me a lot of strength to look around and see the other guys just not backing down an inch all day. It's not just the shearers that need to prepare. We'll grow a James Finlay supplying the Merino lambs, and says making sure there's a nice, even run has been a challenge in the drought conditions. We went through about 5,000, 5,500, and we've drafted that down to 2,650 ready for today for the five boys. And that's because they've got to be a fairly even lot, and they've all got to meet certain criteria in terms of size, weight, wall cut, that sort of thing. Huge logistical challenge. Yeah, it's always a bit stressful when you've got to make sure they average a kilo over everything. That's only about three months old. So when Lockie approached us a few months ago and asked us if we could do the record here, I was a little bit apprehensive with the way the season was going. It was pretty tough fed. We had everything in containment here until sort of July. So yeah, they were well fed. And then, yeah, it started to rain, and we let them out on the grass, and we've had a really good lambing. And we've been pretty fortunate this year. The lambs have actually been really quite even. The World Sheep Shearing Record Society governs attempts like this across Australia, New Zealand, the UK and South Africa. Eight judges are on hand today, and convener Johnny Fraser says this makes sure everyone is on a level playing field. So the lambs had to be one kilo of wool. We had to cut one kilo of wool each. So these did 1.4, which is well over the mark, which is good. So that was a start. And then after that, we're looking mainly out the back. The sheep go down the porthole, and we count out every half an hour. And we have four judges down there, two on each stand. And we are looking at any cuts or any roughness, stitch jobs that they've done and all that. And if there's any more than six sheep that are badly cut, after seventh one, the record will stop. So you've obviously seen a lot of records set, challenged, beaten over the time. How does this one rate here in the Riverina of New South Wales? To be honest, with this merino record, we've never really had a five-stand record before. And these guys aren't your show shearers. These guys are just good old shed shearers that I rate this as probably one of the better ones I've been to. In this high-pressure environment, there's no time for error, and each wriggling sheep can cost valuable seconds. After the first two-hour run, the shearers look exhausted. Smoko, though, is a time to look after the body, as Toby's mum, Sunny Awoko, explains. The ice bath is a rapid reduction of skin temperature, which also reduces the lactic acid build-up, especially in the legs. We've got no fancy plunge pools here. We've got a good old-fashioned bush ice bath. How's it work? Yes, we have an esky out the back. And we did have to shop long and hard because a couple of these boys have got pretty long legs. It's the final run. Hundreds of people are in the crowd cheering the shearers on. The final tally, 2,301. Cameron Hicks has been eyeing off a world record for years, so he's happy to have his name in the books. Glad to see the end of it, but I'm still pretty stoked in my efforts today. Big drain on your body. What do you do to recover? We'll stay hydrated, a lot of stretching and stuff, and just, yeah, monitor things. Can't get too crazy and go out and have too many beers, otherwise, yeah, you end up in a bit of trouble. And I'll tell you what, you Kiwis set a cracking pace, tracking this record as a team of five, but is there much competition between the stands for this special record attempt? Funny enough, there was two Kiwis in the team and they both led the charge, so yeah. We just won't mention that to the Aussies? Yeah, no, we've been living over here long enough that we've been adopted by you lots. Also from New Zealand, Benjamin Duncan was a late call-up, so he didn't have as much time to prepare, but he had the highest tally of 502. I'm probably a bit old to be doing this sort of stuff. You're obviously match fit, though. I think you might have been close to the top. I think I got lucky today. It must have been the pressure. Your first run, pretty good, but then you just built on that throughout the day. Was that something mentally that happened, or did you just get in your groove? Yeah, I sort of wanted to play possum for the first half of the day. Let Cam think he had a win? Yeah, yeah. And then just dragged him back. Nick Lehmans from Dimboola in Victoria. So you've just finished the eight hours. You're clearly exhausted. Did you have a figure in your head that you wanted this year? Not really. I was just trying to get a flow and stick with it. Try and push through the pain. And it's hard, obviously. What's hurting at the moment? Pretty well everything. The event also raised tens of thousands of dollars for charity, and Riverina shearing contractor Lockie Robertson says it's been tough, but worth it. Pretty sore standing near my back's on fire, and I reckon I'm torn my hamstring or something, to be honest. Tough day in the shed or a good day in the shed? I didn't quite hit the 400, which I wanted to, but I was pretty close. So I'm happy with the overall team effort, to be honest, in some sheep that probably weren't what we thought they were going to be. Just not getting a cut. The sheep, yeah, had a bit more dirt in them, and we were changing a cutter every, I don't even know, eight or nine minutes. So that was slowing us down, and took a bit more pushing than we thought, and yeah. I reckon it'll be easier to recruit a few Riverina young blokes to be shearers after putting on this spectacle for them today. Yeah, I reckon there's a few young fellas running around just wanting to have a chat, little kids and stuff, thinking it's all pretty cool, so that's good. This is Freshwater Creek, which doesn't really flow anymore, but the whole length of Freshwater Creek has been vegetated right down to the 90-mile beach where it ends, so we started it, but it's been taken up, which is really good. That's Fergus Irving, a wool producer from Woodside on Victoria's southeastern coast. We've jumped in the ute to check out the property where Fergus and his wife Rosemary have farmed since 1980. Ms Irving says after moving to the farm, they soon realised something was missing. Well, there weren't any trees, and we were running sheep, and sheep need shelter, so we started planting windbreaks, and we've belonged to a local land care group. They had a day on farm planning, and we employed a... Oh, I suppose he was a... A landscape architect. He was a landscape architect, and he came and helped us draw up a plan so as we could do it aesthetically as well as being useful. So that was the start. The start, specifically, of a multi-decade mission to fill their farm with native trees. Step one was to collect seeds. That was Mr Irving's job, and he had a pretty unconventional approach. I had a veterinary practice at the time, so I drove around the district, and I'd be aware of what trees were fruiting and flowering, and we had bags to put dead animals in, so I'd stop the car and pick seeds along the roadside from fruiting trees, and we'd tried to get a good variety, but the backbone of our windbreaks were Melaleuca ericofolia, the local tea tree, Coast Managum, Viminalis. Basically, that was probably... Oh, we'd have apple box and a smattering of all the other local trees, and most of it came from the roadside, although I knew where every patch of remnant vegetation was in the district, the Port Albert Racecourse, the Gifford Rifle Range Reserve, and various other little spots where there were good stands of indigenous trees. To plant these trees, Mr Irving turned to direct seeding. There was a local group, the Gippsland Tree Seeders, who built a direct seeder before they were really commercially available, and we used to mix the tree seed with chicken crumbles. The tree seeder had a disc on the front and a seed box like an ordinary pasture-sowing seeder, and we'd just go along, and we could plant kilometres and kilometres in a day. First of all, we'd use herbicide to flatten the pasture and then just direct seeding. I remember one day with one of my boys, we spent half a day and probably planted 15 linear kilometres of tree seeds, and they grew very well that particular day or that particular sowing period. Mr Irving says planting indigenous trees just makes sense. I want to recreate up to a point the landscape that was here, and also I presume that the local fauna probably prefers to be on local flora. So you're coming up to 40 years of this regeneration project. So how has the farm changed and transformed over those decades? When we bought the farm, there were very few trees on any farms in Woodside, and now most of the farms have got trees, but it's made a huge difference to this place. We have, I think we've just about sown enough trees, but all along our gullies, we have colossal numbers of birds. We've got some species we're not so keen on, like rabbits. We do have the kangaroos, wombats, echidnas, koalas. So we're looking after the local fauna, which gives us a lot of pleasure. Rosemary and Fergus Irving, wool producers from Woodside on Victoria's southeast coast, ending that report from Faith Tabuluyan. Before that, Emily Doak took us to the wool shed for a record-breaking shearing effort, and you can see more of Emily's story on the ABC website at abc.net.au. I'm David Clawton with you for A Big Country. Still to come, we'll meet the chefs who've travelled from around the globe to learn about cooking with lamb, and we're meeting a family working in the flour industry. With more than half the cut flowers sold in Australia imported and no country of origin labelling required, it's tricky for consumers to know where their flowers come from. A Brisbane woman decided something needed to be done so consumers could make informed decisions about what blooms they buy, and she had just the right connections to do it. Pip Courtney has the story. Three years ago, Bec Thomas called time on her 20-year corporate career, bought a van, leased a shop, and became a flour seller. Her mates were baffled, but Bec was on a mission. When buying cut flowers, she wants us to ask, were they flown or grown? I wanted to educate people. I wanted people to be aware of where their flowers are coming from, and I wanted them to get to know their farmer. I wanted them to know Rob grew these. The issue is personal. The reason is on her wall. Bec's brother Rob grows flowers. Rob and sister Pip, she's also on the wall, run one of the biggest oriental lily growing businesses in Australia. Several days a week, flowers from the family farm at Flowerdale, where Bec grew up in northwest Tasmania, arrive in Brisbane. They're pretty much picked, they're cooled, they're packed, put on the boat overnight, and a cool truck meets the boat the next morning, and then zooms up the coast, and then I go and grab the flowers, and then we bring them to market. As well as lilies, Rob and Pip send tulips, delphiniums, stocks, snapdragons, sweet william, and status. There are also flowers grown by several other Tasmanian growers. She wants to start conversations about the downsides of imported flowers, starting with how long they last. Sister Pip says growers want the same transparency for country of origin labelling, like we have for food. You don't know how that's been treated prior to us getting it, who's picked the product, how old is that person, where have they come from, how it's chemically been treated, the residues on the plants, you know, all that sort of stuff. Do you think many people have bought flowers, thinking they're Australian, and they're actually from overseas? Absolutely. Bec's career change came after learning about the impact rising flower imports were having here, especially on rose growers. There's a lot of imported roses that come all the way from, you know, Colombia, Ecuador, Kenya, 12,000 kilometres away. And some of these growers actually went under. As much as Rob said, what are you doing? Can you not find something a little bit easier? But I just had this burning desire to make a difference, because I knew I was actually in a position to be able to do that. Flowerdale is known for its productive volcanic soil. Growing up, there were plenty of farm jobs for the four Sadler kids, as their parents added flowers to milking 700 cows and growing potatoes. Jan and John's diversification into carnations in 1982 surprised many. There was no ag department that could tell us how to grow flowers, because nobody grew flowers. The dairy cows went, new flower varieties were added, and more polytunnels went up. At their peak, there were 86 growing tunnels, and the couple were shipping to most capital cities. Did you ever think that you would have a business this big that could employ three of your children? No, no. And about 30 other people. In 2014, the next generation consolidated the business by importing a greenhouse from the Netherlands. It covers two hectares. Everything is climate controlled, all the fans, the air exchange, everything is done by an algorithm. It'll predict what the weather's going to do. It's very clever. It's been a big investment. For us, it's an insurance policy. It's allowed us to go all year round and to grow really good product that's really consistent, because the consistency is the key. The 800,000 lily bulbs in here will produce about 4 million stems a year. Bulbs are planted every week. The saddlers used to grow in their own productive soil, but problems controlling nematodes forced a move to hydroponics. Rob and Pip have seen the impact imports are having in Australia. As they've grown, others have got out. In the past, there might have been 30 growers. Now there's maybe five to eight major growers that have all invested in technology. They've all got fairly sophisticated setups. I guess that's the future of agriculture as well, to continue to invest, to get the efficiencies. Rob and Pip are proud of Sister Bec and her advocacy for the industry, while Bec's proud of the business her siblings have developed. Jan and John Sadler are proud of all three. And while they know many have tried, they hope Bec's message gets through and people start asking, grown or flown? I make Korean-style bulgogi. Yes, it's like Gangnam-style. Yeah, you know Gangnam-style. Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. A global experience in Western Australia's Great Southern region. Aussie lamb. It's awesome lamb. Recently, 16 chefs, known as Lambassadors, travelled from around the world to the small town of Borden, 380 kilometres south-east of Perth, to cook for local farmers, all bringing their unique flavours and showcasing locally grown lamb. What I'm preparing is we grilled, barbecued lamb neck, beautiful lamb neck from Australia. Then we served the onion soup. Wow. Yeah, something because our team from the Vietnam, USA, Japan. So we tried to put something together on the dish. So what you mean by that is you're trying to bring your own little flair to Australian lamb. Yes, yes, of course, you know, because every country using Australian lamb in a different way. Japanese, they have the Japanese way. Chinese have Chinese way. That was why I tried to align all the flavours and, you know, together on the one dish. Clinton Zhu owns his own cooking school in Shanghai, China, and was one of the many culinary professionals who volunteered their time to come to our country with Meat and Livestock Australia to learn about the red meat supply chain. So I have the culinary school in Shanghai. So we was educated, you know, for 100 and 100 young chefs every year. So I think it's very important to let young chefs and people to know about the quality of the Australian lamb. It's not only about the lamb, it's about this country, the people. So I think this is important why I'm here. Hi. Is this your music? Yeah. Where are you from? I'm from Saudi Arabia. Chefs travelled to Western Australia from 11 different countries and you could really hear it in all the different music and the languages that were being used. Lindsay Noto travelled all the way from America to join this year's delegation, which was the largest group the Lambassador Program has ever seen. It's 27 flight hours and five different airplanes that it took me to get here. I lost an entire day to get here and it was worth every minute. There's a huge opportunity where I'm from in the South in Alabama. You know, barbecue, meat is such a prevalent thing in our cuisines, but lamb is very, there's not a lot of knowledge around it and experience. And so my hope was that I could come here, learn more and then bring that knowledge and information and new techniques from these other chefs back to the States. Obviously there's a lot going on in the geopolitical world at the moment. How do you think that's impacting, you know, what you're able to cook with over there? Well, I think it's really interesting, you know, the primary difference that I've noticed between, you know, Australian producers and the processing facilities as the focus on the ecosystem and sustainability and the emphasis on the product and the quality all the way down to the eating experience for the guests. And that's a huge, there's a huge disconnect. I think no shade to the States, obviously being an American, but, you know, it's all about the carcass, right? And what they eat and then it kind of stops there. And I think that there's such a huge trickle down effect when it comes to the focus on the ecosystem and being fully sustainable that this country puts an emphasis on that we don't as much in the States. How are you going with the flies today? Fly, funny, funny fly. Yeah, but OK. It's OK. And hot, yeah. Over the next couple of weeks, the chefs will tour the country with Meat and Livestock Australia, which this year received $3 million from the federal government's live export transition package. Kazu Mitsuhashi founded the program 10 years ago in Japan. Because in Japan, initially, there's no sheep meat eating habit in Japan, only except up in Hokkaido for skiing area. That's only the culture in Japan. Would that be because a lot of, you know, international people visit there for skiing? Yeah, it is. Very popular, especially from Australian people. Yeah. Yeah, very famous Niseko and stuff. But there is a... Genghis Khan is called, special Japanese sheep meat in Japan. But on the mainland, there's nobody eat lamb for really, really small, tiny consumption in Japan. There's no domestic lamb in Japan. Very, very tiny. So a majority of the sheep meat in Japan is 70% Australian lamb. And New Zealand, it's basically the rest of it. How has it grown in the last few years, though, since you've started this program? Mmm. It's getting popular now, these days, because one of the reasons is just people making more global and then looking for something new. While in Borden, the chefs went head-to-head in a friendly cook-off and then served up their dishes for producers who were in town for the Whamco AGM. I just had the neck chopped, something, made with a neck. It would taste like a bit of miso, a bit of onion. It was pretty good. David Mears is a mixed farmer near Broom Hill in the Great Southern. And he says programs like Lambassada are good for the industry, but with the market shifting, farmers like him have had to adapt. Not as big as what we have been, of course. Yeah, our numbers have decreased a bit due to the, just the sheep market and the way it's gone. But, look, sheep have, haven't, aren't really the big focus on our farm. I guess canola growing has taken over a bit. But sheep are certainly still a good, a good addition to the, to the diversification of what farms need to be. Did you go? Yes. Which one did you go? Thank you. Thank you. There's always a mob. Yes. The chefs will now continue their journey across Australia. And while all of them came from such diverse backgrounds and different cultures, one thing stood out in every conversation I had with them. Their genuine passion for understanding the story behind what Australian farmers do best. We cannot judge just meat. We need to know the back story about the product. When we come here in a beautiful landscape and the very important is the beautiful people behind the industry. It's a good, oh my gosh. And I can't taste any flies. Thank goodness. The Aussie flies are just as good as the Aussie lamb. Reporter Kate Forrester brought us that story from a recent lamb cook-off in the small town of Borden in Western Australia's Great Southern region. You can read more on Kate's story about the international chefs tiering Australia as part of the campaign to promote locally grown lamb. You'll find it on the ABC website at abc.net.au. And that's the show for today. I'm David Claughton. I'll catch up with you again next week with more great stories from regional Australia. I'll chat to you then. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.
