episodes.title: Wetland welcomes new life and rangers on the frontline of fight against coastal weed
episodes.description: Birds and fish flock to farm, as wetland is restored; Indigenous rangers on the frontline of fight against invasive weed on remote Tasmanian island; farming region's community spirit staying strong in the face of shrinking population; couple…
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. I'm David Clawton and this is A Big Country. Thanks for tuning in for a trip around regional Australia. This week we're visiting a wetland on a windy sheep farm in southern Tasmania. The farm's owners are working with conservationists to bring the Ramsar-listed wetland on the farm back to life. It's proving a boon for coastal bird life and local fish stocks. We'll get along to a local footy game in a farming region in western Victoria and hear how sport is helping the community spirit stay strong in the face of a stark population decline. And we'll meet a couple who've made a career change to horticulture. A former science teacher and accountant are growing a tiny variety of citrus that was popular generations ago. We'll learn more about kumquats and how the fruit is being used in everything from marmalade to beverages. That's coming up. First today we're heading to Truwana, Cape Barron Island, off the coast of Tasmania. Indigenous rangers on the island are on the front line of a fight against a weed that's threatening coastal ecosystems right across the southern half of Australia. To battle this weed they're using a fungus. And it's proving so successful that the method is now being rolled out across the rest of the country. Louise Moylan has the story. The beaches of Truwana, Cape Barron Island, off the coast of Tasmania, are pristine. But there's something in the sand that shouldn't be here. Smothering it, burning it, trying to pull it out manually, everything possible. And it's just no matter what you do, it always comes back. Indigenous ranger Shane Hughes is talking about sea spurge. It's a stubborn weed that grows on this island and right across the southern parts of Australia. It grows about half a metre higher and just light green, covers ground everywhere. It's got a milky sap inside if you break it in half. If you get it in your eyes, it can make you go blind. I don't know how much you need of it in there, but it's no good for you. You may well have seen sea spurge's green, squishy tendrils on your local beach in WA, South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales or Tassie, growing from the high watermark into the sand dunes. It looks harmless, but its poisonous toxins can cause temporary blindness. And as CSIRO's Ben Gooden explains, this weed can devastate a coastal ecosystem. It is one of the most problematic species that occurs along the beaches and coastlines across southern Australia, particularly through the impacts that it has on native vegetation, but also how those beaches are utilised by many different shorebird species, particularly some of our threatened shorebird species like the hoarded plover. Many of these nesting shorebirds require particular types of sandy habitats to set up their nesting sites. And when those areas get smothered by sea spurge, hundreds of thousands of plants of sea spurge, it just creates this carpet of vegetation that those birds no longer can nest in safely. Sea spurge is native to southern Europe, North Africa and Western Asia, but not Australia. Its seeds are easily dispersed on land and in the ocean, and it's thought to have arrived to Australia in water carried on ships about 70 years ago. Here on Truana, Cape Barron Island, the Truana Ranges have been working with CSIRO to innovate the battle against sea spurge. Their weapon of choice? A spray bottle full of fungus. Classical biological control. We go to where the weed is native in Europe, and we look at all of the different insects and fungi that are natural enemies of sea spurge, and we identify which one has the biggest impact on the plant and keeps the plant's populations in check. Then we do what's termed host specificity testing, where we bring, in this case, a fungus into Australia in quarantine, and we test to make sure that that fungus is absolutely safe and cannot infect or reproduce on any native plant species in Australia. And on that basis, it is safe and is given approval for release. And the project was to release the fungus into the Australian environment to reconnect with the weed. And when the fungus establishes and it grows on the plant, it reduces how well the plant can grow. Before we tried, it was all sceptical and didn't really want to release it because we didn't know what it was going to do. But we're glad we did because it's done well so far. The fungus is reducing sea spurge on the island. You can see the weeds turning brown, which is a good sign. Now CSIRO is rolling out the sprayable fungicide across mainland Australia. It's already been used on the main island of Tasmania and in Victoria, and WA and South Australia are next on the list. For Ben, the project is about much more than weeds. Weeds are a people problem, and it's through working with people as partnership that we can start tackling these weed threats. It's such a big problem, and that can feel insurmountable and it can feel demoralising. But we have to keep remembering, and it is on a personal level but also a professional level, we achieve really good outcomes for country only through partnership. And for Shane, keeping sea spurge at bay helps protect the land he loves. It makes you feel good in yourself and in what you're doing in your job, and it's going to be better for the future generations as well. So, yeah, it makes you feel very good in yourself. MUSIC PLAYS A thick blanket of fog hangs over Ariambiak, lighting the region in an eerie glow as the sun gets to work, burning off the morning vapour. This local government area in Victoria's west stretches about 100 kilometres from top to tail. Lake Coorong near the north of the region feeds the Ariambiak Creek, which snakes its way from Hopeton until it meets the Wimmera River in Longrenong. From above, the farming region resembles a patchwork quilt, with the land divvied up into squares and rectangles of mostly wheat, barley and sheep farms. On the ground in the small towns that make up the Shire, there is another story playing out. Population is rapidly declining. Since 2001, Ariambiak Shire has lost a quarter of its residents, making it the fastest shrinking region in Victoria. I'm Tamara Clark, and I'm here in the small town of Brim. Brim's football oval and netball courts serve as a reminder of a time when the town once boasted its own sporting teams. These days, the oval and courts are only used occasionally. More than 20 years ago now, Brim was no longer able to find enough players to field its own teams, and it merged with neighbouring Warwick-Nabeel. Mick Gunn once pulled on the boots for the now defunct Brim Eagles, and he's now a life member of the merged team, the Warwick Eagles Football Netball Club. I've lived in Warwick-Nabeel probably 55 years. I had 15 years or 16 years in Melbourne, but returned to Warwick-Nabeel in the late 80s. And my involvement with Warwick-Nabeel Football Club started as a junior back in the early 60s when farms were a lot smaller, a lot more families in the area in those days, and there was a lot of kids playing junior football and netball at the time. Sadly, in the past 50 years, you know, the opposite has happened. Farms have got bigger with less families, with the result, you know, less kids wanting to play sport. Mick Gunn remembers a time when there were seven football netball clubs drawn from the Ariambiak region. Since then, many have struggled to find enough players, and they've been forced to merge. The Wimmera League consists of, well, we've got two teams in Horsham now, Horsham and Horsham Saints, Stahl, Ararat, there was Minyip and Matoa separate, there was Jeparat, Warwick-Nabeel, Nill and Dimboola. Now, Minyip and Matoa merged some 15 years or so, more than that, 20 years ago, to become one entity. Warwick-Nabeel merged with Brim 20 years ago to become the Warwick Eagles. Brim were the Southern Malley side. Jeparat, sadly, they've ended up merging with Hopeton and Bula and Rainbow to form the Southern Malley Thunder. So that's four teams, four towns with one football team. Mick Gunn finished his playing days with Brim and had stints as President and Secretary. Now he's settled into a new role, collecting entry fees at the gate of Anzac Park, the Warwick Eagles' home ground in the region's larger town of Warwick-Nabeel. Football and netball in country towns is everything. You know, it's an outlet for not only the players, but for the adults, the parents and the grandparents. You know, you get together, just not to watch sport, but have a yarn, talk about, you know, the weather, how the crops are looking and all that sort of thing. So that's what it's all about. So social interaction is the main thing about it. Social interaction in these small towns has become more of a challenge in the face of declining population and business closures. But locals in Yariambiak have a history of stepping up to help themselves, and that's what's happened down the road in Mkanya. When the town's pub closed its doors, residents had been struggling without a communal meeting place. The opening of Blacksmith Cafe in the middle of town four months ago has helped. Barista Dylan Walls says it's becoming a meeting place for locals who gather there for hours every day. We're brand new, and the locals have given us amazing support, which is awesome to get to build this little community hub here and get to give people coffee. They love coffee. I mean, we do between 80 and 120 cups of coffee a day so at least 60, 70 people coming through a day, probably more. At least 50 kind of regulars that come in from day to day as well. It's a very welcoming community. People really value that community spirit here. People really help each other out and very neighbourly. We're renovating our house at the moment. If there's anything we need or something we can't do, there's someone in town who'll probably help us out. I'm happy to lend a hand and chuck in some work. On a Saturday in footy season at Warwicknabil Zanzac Park, the human character of the vast rural region is on full display. Warwick Eagles president Paul Rowe is here all day, chipping in where needed, including pulling beers after the seniors' footy is finished. Local towns, small towns, are all sport-minded. And you can see in the surrounding areas of the smaller towns that once they lose their football or netball club, they lose their population. And it's sad to see. This is a sporting club which reflects the ethos of the town and the broader Yariambiak region. Things don't just happen here, people make them happen. Paul Rowe says it's a place where you chip in, not because you're asked, but because you know you need to. I think it's just loyalty. Loyalty. Yeah, I think the people that have been involved, heavily involved in clubs and that realise what it takes to run a football netball club. We have over 100 volunteers positions today to fill. So from scoring, umpiring, water boys, trainers, coaches, you name it, lines people, it takes so much to run a Saturday home club and we just love it. But we also have good volunteers that it doesn't take much to get them to help out. So really appreciate it. That story from Tamara Clark, reporting from the Yariambiak region of Western Victoria. For more on how that region is faring in the face of population decline, you can read an in-depth article on the ABC homepage. Head to abc.net.au. You'll find a link from the Big Country program page. I'm David Claughton, with you for A Big Country. Still to come, wetlands are critical for biodiversity and their role as carbon sinks. But many wetlands on private farming land have become degraded over the years. We'll meet a farmer who's working with conservationists to restore a natural wetland on his property in southern Tasmania. And have you ever tasted a kumquat or kumquat marmalade? You'll rarely find the tiny citrus that's native to China in the supermarkets. And that's partly why when Rosalind and Patrick McCarthy ready themselves to finish their professional careers, a treasured taste of Rosalind's childhood became their anti-retirement plan. Jennifer Nichols says the story. It's lovely how these flavours can take you back to your grandmother's era, which was such a comforting time, wasn't it? I love kumquats. They're a beautiful citrus for anybody who hasn't seen them. And you look like you've got a couple of varieties here. Yes, we've got the nagami at the front there and then the kalamondan. The kalamondans are quite bitter but they're brilliant for marmalade. And the nagami, you can eat them whole. They're very, very popular. And they're just the most gorgeous colour. So where is your farm based? We're located at Toguluwa, which is near Esk in the Somerset region. Yeah, we had cattle there but we've diversified into kumquats and we also grow ginger for ourselves. And how on earth did you decide on kumquats? I just love kumquats and you could never buy them. You can't find them anywhere. So I just thought I'm going to do this and we planted a kumquat orchard and value add to it. And how many trees you had? I've got 600. Okay, so just a few. Yes, yes. A lot of fruit. A lot of fruit. And how old are they now? Probably about four or five years. Yeah, about five years. So they're bearing a lot of fruit now but they're still growing. We are looking at having a farm shop and we're continuing to value add by distilling. So very soon we'll move into distilling and we're looking towards an ODV which in two years time becomes a brandy. I don't think I've heard of that before. The ODV is the liquid that goes into the barrel and it sits for two years before it can be considered a brandy. So that's our focus or our future direction. What have you got already? That's what we call a shrub which is a very, very old-fashioned drink from the 17th century and the story behind that is the sailors didn't have refrigeration so they just put all their excess fruit into an apple cider being good for their scurvy. The cider would then take on the flavour of the fruit and then they drink that with their rum. So this is basically a mixer. We do the same process. with the fruits that we grow on the farm and we have it with soda water but our children will have it with their gin and their vodka as a mixer. The word shrub comes from the Arabic word shirab which means to drink. Ours are based on an apple cider vinegar. My favourite kumquat by far would be the kalamondin. We have two varieties the nagami and the kalamondin. The kalamondin is more aromatic. I just love those aromatics. It looks like a mini mandarin. It does. It does. But they are sour. The other one here is that sweeter. That's a nagami so the skin is sweet. You eat the whole thing like a grape. Really? So the first bite will be a little bit tangy and then when you start to eat the skin it gets sweet. Can we give it a taste test? Sweet and sour lolly. High in vitamin C. Wow that's really interesting. I can see a lot of people actually liking that. I've never seen them in the shops. Yeah they are growing in demand definitely. But yeah it's only your small green grocers that will stock the kumquats. We sell quite a bit into Rockley and then also to Sydney the markets but next year we'll aim towards Melbourne. So now I'm trying the kaffir ginger shrub. Oh yum that's delicious. It's really smart to do a niche product isn't it? Yeah. It seems to be what I do. Things that aren't greatly heard of you know like kumquats like shrub and now an ODV. Is this a career change for you? Yeah definitely a career change. Well we've had the farm for about 18 years and we just had cattle so we've diversified from cattle into more than just one produce. It secures the future or the viability of the farm really. And it's of an interest to us that we're both sort of retired from my profession and Ros has as well so we love doing what we do. What was your previous profession? I was a science teacher and Pat was an accountant. An accountant? Yes. Okay well you know those number skills will come in handy for your small business. Oh we love it. It's great. We've just recently completed a commercial kitchen on the property so a very large shed what's it 14 by 9 metres and a very large kitchen in there so we can start to increase capacity. So you're growing a little bit of ginger too? We'd have about a quarter of an acre of ginger every year and we use those a lot in our products. That's our candied ginger. We process that probably over about a three day period and then cook in its own syrup cold press quite a lot of ginger and then that's the end product. It's got a fair bit of bite to it because it's fresh. Try one of those? Absolutely. That's yummy. Some of our product does go to the Journey Beyond Rail which is served on the Great Southern Train Journey and the Indian Pacific. The relish is a new one and we trialled it quite a lot before we decided to proceed with it and modern it. That sounds tough. It is lovely. Very nice. Like the outside was tangy and then you got that sweet skin and it was it just came together well. Oh that sounds like you're having a tremendous time. segments.text: We'll talk about the biggest production tractor in the world.
Also from a Merino sheep farm to cycling all the way across Australia,
you'll meet a remarkable man who's putting the foot to the pedal
to raise awareness and a million dollars for Dementia Australia.
And a Victorian agronomist has been celebrated with an international peace prize
for his groundbreaking work, helping farmers in West Africa regenerate the land.
And there's an incredible figure for every 10% increase in what's called the green index,
So how green we have this landscape.
For every 10% increase, deaths of women and children in conflict situations reduces 25%.
First today, let's head to Western Australia's southwest region of Carradale,
where Anne and Noel Cochran breed the biggest cows in the world.
Some of these cattle can weigh more than 1.7 tonnes,
and stand about two metres tall.
The ancient breed is called Chianina,
and their genetics come all the way from Italy.
Georgia Hargraves went to the farm to find out more.
We initially had Chianus cattle and an Angus bull,
and then we thought, well, our property's really quite small, it's only 50 acres.
So to do what we kind of dreamed of doing,
we thought, well, we'll fulfil that, we'll fulfil that dream.
And as Noel said before, not go for profit, but for passion.
For people who are listening and can't see them,
can you just describe what they look like?
Well, I guess the signature thing about them is that they are big, white cattle.
They're an Italian breed that's got a very long history.
They have a little black switch on their tail and black hooves.
And the thing about them is that although they're a very big animal, they're elegant.
So to my eyes, they're actually very beautiful.
Maybe not to everybody else, but to my eyes, they are very beautiful.
And they are very elegant to look at, aren't they?
They're known as being the biggest breed of cattle in the world.
Is it difficult to manage cattle that get that big?
In all honesty, I don't manage them.
And he has a really lovely, gentle way of doing it.
They're very respectful of their nature.
We try very hard to be calm with them, to not sort of push them around or yell at them or, you know, force them to do things,
but to find ways that they'll do it by their nature.
And so can you take me back to when you first saw them?
The first time I ever saw Ken in a cattle was at the Royal Show, the Perth Royal Show, during the Grand Parade.
And it was in about 1984, I think.
And I was there at the show with my two young daughters at the time.
And so there's horses and cows and goat sheep and then the cattle.
And at the time, I'm a social worker, working in Perth, married to somebody else, with two little girls.
And when these cattle came around, the Keanina cattle came around, I was absolutely amazed by them, by their size, by their elegance, by their, just their physical presence.
They have quite a magical, physical presence.
And I thought to myself, if ever I have cattle, then I'm having Keaninas.
But it does make me really emotional, actually.
They were majestic to see and to watch them walk.
And it was a bull, a cow and a calf.
And ironically, when we did buy our farm and did decide to go into Keanina, it was exactly that same breeder that we went to, to buy our cattle.
And that was 17 years ago, that we actually went to Doug Corker, who'd been breeding them since the 70s.
Yeah, that was the start of it.
They believe that it's before Roman times, just with the cave paintings and the paintings and that in Italy.
And what were they used for in Italy hundreds of years ago?
And that's why they're so big, because I think Italians over years have selected the biggest animals for the draft.

And then lately they've gone into more of a beef animal, mainly because the beef is, you know, you've got some of the richest beef or the healthiest beef in the world, you know, like with protein levels, cholesterol levels.
And in Italy they call it Bistecca alla Florentina, is that right?
Yeah, that Bistecca is a big T-bone steak, about 1.5 kilograms.
But that Bistecca goes back, you know, back to the 1360s with English knights entering Tuscany.
So that history started for that steak way back then when those English knights would go into town and ask for a beef steak.
That Bistecca came into the Tianling language.
But that history alone is, it's surrounded just one part of Tuscany.
So in a 50 kilometer area you had the English knights, all the counts, all those sort of herds, like the Medici family and all that.
So the history is just all linked together throughout Tuscany and the Italian history.
It's quite incredible when you look back and read it.
There was something big at the Henty Field Days this year, and I had all of the farmers talking.
Yeah, if I had the money I would.
It should be a big price tag for a big tractor.
But yeah, I'd get one if I could.
Dubbed the biggest production tractor in the world, the John Deere 9RX830 was on full display.
To put it into perspective, the average tractor has a horsepower of around 150 to 200.
This tractor has a horsepower of 830.
It's amazing to see how big it is up close.
830 horsepower, that's just insane from where we've come over the last 50 years.
Are you going to climb into the cab and have a look?
Oh, I'm in a tractor more than enough.
I said enough time in there, so on a day off we'd like to stay away from it.
There were plenty of people circling this beast of a tractor.
Kids climbing into the cab, farmers looking under the bonnet.
But Thomas Dewhurst, a group sales manager at Hutchin and Pierce, said not many people were pulling out the checkbooks at Henty this year.
I know if you're standing next to it, kind of well over six feet every track.
Huge footprint, and that's required because the tractor, fully ballasted, is 38 tonnes.
So what would you use a tractor like this for in farming?
A lot of seeding application mostly, and maybe wider tillage application from efficiency and scale point of view.
The wider you go, the more efficient.
So we've seen seeding rigs pushing out past 80 feet recently, and the current horsepower that we have is not necessarily always doing the job.
So, yeah, really great to have another option for farmers that can kind of potentially take them from two machines back to one.
And kind of increase their efficiencies.
Is bigger better in this case?
In this case, bigger is definitely better.
And a lot of people are probably thinking listening to this, and I'm sure you've been asked this already a million times, but what's the price tag on a tractor like this?
Everything from John Deere we're ordering straight from factory, so we can change lots and lots of options depending on exactly what the customer needs.
Probably looking somewhere in the $1.5 million range.
But again, completely dependent on options.
But when you look at it from a dollars per horsepower point of view, it compares really favorably to all current machines in the market.
Have you sold any at Henty this weekend?
None at Henty, but we've plenty of interest, which has been great.
And we do have units in the market already.
I heard someone say before, the bonnet's so big you could almost roll your swag out on the front of it if you needed.
The bonnet opens with one hand.
In terms of, I guess, machinery sales in general, I mean, this is one of the biggest machinery field days in the country, so people coming to have a look.
But what's happening in that space?
It's been an incredibly tough year, especially around here in Henty.
Yeah, it's been a really interesting season, especially in our part of the world here.
I'd say it's probably a bit quieter year, but there's still a lot of interest.
The recent rain has kind of made people interested again, but we just have to see what harvest does.
It's really hard to make any decisions without knowing exactly how the crops are going to come off, and that's probably what we're seeing at the moment.
They're probably a little bit quieter right now, but that's not uncommon at this time of year.
Do you find a lot of farmers buy at a field days, or are they coming to have a look and more of a feel of what's on offer?
No, yeah, it's definitely more to come and see what's available, have a look at the new technology.
We're really lucky with the tech site set up here.
We've got the full technology set up that customers can come and look at.
It's the biggest tractor in the world here at Henty Field Days.
It's really cool to come and have a look at it.
Can tractors get bigger than this, or do you expect them to get bigger?
Everything can always get bigger, but I think this might be the ceiling for a little bit.
Thomas Dewhurst from farm equipment supplier Hutchin and Pearce, speaking to Annie Brown at the recent Henty machinery field days in southern New South Wales.
You can read more about those amazing Chianina cattle online and have a look at just how big they really are.
You'll find it on the ABC homepage at abc.net.au.
Just look for the Big Country program page.
I'm David Corden with you for A Big Country.
Still to come, you'll meet a cyclist on a gruelling journey to fight for a better future for people with dementia.
But first, the verdant hills of Druin in West Gippsland may feel a world away from the barren desert landscape of West Africa.
But it's where agronomist Tony Renato has settled down after decades working with primary producers in Nigeria, regenerating the landscape.
Tony has recently been celebrated with an International Peace Prize.
The ABC's Madeleine Stutchbury went to find out more about his work.
So I studied and we moved to Niger Republic in West Africa in 1980.

And the landscape that confronted us when we arrived there, even though in my lifetime, I was 24 years old, in my lifetime, this had been a biodiverse forest with fertile farms in the clearings, permanent springs and even wildlife.
In my lifetime, that forest had been cleared and it created barren windswept plains.
And there are consequences for that kind of degradation.
The land was at the point of ecological collapse and barely able to support life.
Can you explain to me what is your regenerative principle and how did you deploy that?
So I figured if deforestation was one of the major root causes of all those problems that I listed,
then surely replanting trees would go a long way towards solving those problems.
And the solution actually came as an answer to prayer.
One day I was delivering a ute load of seedlings to the villagers, knowing full well most would die.
And the people thought this was ridiculous anyway.
And I stopped to reduce the air pressure to get through the sandy soil.
And this, what appeared as a useless bush, caught my attention.
And I walked over to take a closer look.
And if you look at the leaf of most species of plants, it's like having a signature that tells you exactly what that plant is.
Immediately, I realised that it's not a bush, it's not a weed, that's a tree.
And if you bend down and brush away the sand, sure enough, there was a stump under those shoots.
Once you were outside of that acute learning period, what was the impact of your work long term in the African context?
If we take the Niger case alone, over the following 20 years, from 1984, when we really had a strong promotion,
from that time on, this method spread at the rate of a quarter of a million hectares per year for those 20 years.
Coming to 5 million hectares, 200 million hectares, 200 million hectares regenerated across that agricultural landscape.
Economic and social benefits were very, very significant.
Farmers in Niger, to give context, it's one of the poorest countries in the world, in
an extremely harsh environment on the edge of the Sahara Desert.
Farmers in Niger, by virtue of now working with the direction of nature instead of fighting
against it, earn an additional gross income in the order of $900 million US dollars every
year without subsidies or incentives to do this.
Farmers in Niger are growing an additional 500,000 tonnes of grain every year, enough
to feed 2.5 million people because their crop yields have increased and that's not including
The award was the Luxembourg Peace Prize and it was recognition that when we restore environmental
conditions it's actually a great precursor to creating conditions for peace.
There's an incredible figure for every 10% increase in what's called the green index,
So how green we have this landscape.
For every 10% increase deaths of women and children in conflict situations reduces 25%.
So what's happening when you degrade landscapes and there's a shortage of food, fuel, fodder,
water, there's more competition for those scarce resources and more likelihood that conflict
As you restore the environment there's an abundance of greater abundance of those elements and less
reason for people to fight over resources.
So it was a recognition for that.
And for me, yes of course I'm honoured, but it highlights the incredible work of millions
of smallholder farmers who took this risk with this crazy white guy and restored their land.
It's a tribute to them and I would say also to World Vision which has now taken this relatively
obscure technique and it's spreading it globally.
When you first started your career in agronomy, did you ever imagine that this would be the
impact of your work and your passion?
I certainly hoped to have an impact, but I could never have imagined the scale that it's taken
off and today, largely through World Vision, it's spread to some 40 countries around the
Cycling more than 40,000 kilometers across the country isn't for the faint-hearted.
And as Nicholas Tremain settles up for another day on the roads, he explains why he decided
to take on this gruelling year-long journey.
Dementia has obviously hit our family quite hard with the diagnosis of my mother and also
I just wanted to do something that might drive more awareness for the disease here in Australia
I thought, what's the craziest thing I can come up with?
And yeah, I thought riding around Australia wasn't just enough.
I thought I'd add a few kilometers to it.
Cycling a distance equivalent to the circumference of the earth isn't just a physical test for
Nick, I've got a lot of time out on the bike to think things over and how I feel about certain
things and what I should be doing and spending the time I can with my mom while she's still
And sometimes trying to remember the times before she had dementia.
Growing up on a Merino sheep farm near Pandana on Kangaroo Island, his mother Marilyn was heavily
involved in farm life and the town's tight-knit neighborhood.
Mom was a very active member of the community.
There's probably not a job that she wouldn't put her hand up to do.
So she was on the local show committee.
She was an umpire for netball.
She always tried to get to my football games as a supporter.
She was on the local Lions club as well, so cooking barbecues at events and doing catering.
She helped in the canteen at the local sports club.
So many different aspects of the community.
His mother first got diagnosed with dementia in 2019.
But her rapidly declining health meant she had to move into a full-time healthcare facility,
as Nick's father, Mervyn Tremain, explains.
She had had a seizure during the night and we had to get the ambulance.
And next morning after the doctors have to, oh well, she's not going home.
Coming to terms with Marilyn having to leave the home has been painful for the family.
Leaving a big gap and heartbreak Mervyn is battling to accept.
When one disappears, the other one is lost.
And I feel that I'm partly lost with not having Marilyn around.
In Australia, dementia has become the leading cause of death.
Dementia Australia's chief executive officer, Tanya Buchanan, explains why the number of people living with dementia is increasing.
There are around 433,000 Australians currently living with dementia.
And of that, 29,000 are living with younger onset dementia.
And of course, around 1,500 children are living with conditions that also cause dementia.
There's a number of reasons that dementia rates are expected to rise.
As we get older, our risk of developing dementia increases.
But it's really important to know that age, getting older, doesn't mean that you will invariably develop dementia.
Dementia is not a normal part of aging.
And there are a number of modifiable risk factors that we can all tackle to reduce our risk of developing dementia.
And there are things about keeping healthy, stopping smoking, having a healthy diet, staying physically active, socially connective,
and of course, doing things that are cognitively challenging on a regular basis.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare's latest data projects the number of people living with dementia
will more than double to over 1 million Australians by 2065.
Dementia Australia's CEO, Tanya Buchanan, is calling for more discussions on brain health.
There's a lot of stigma attached to the diagnosis of dementia.
And so people don't tend to talk about it.
And it's really important that we start this conversation about reducing our risks of developing dementia
and looking after our brain health right across our life.
It's a conversation Nick's been eager to share on his ride,
passing through Australian communities during the past 268 days on the road.
I get a great response from people because they share their story of how they're connected with dementia as well.
And whether it's a loved one, a close friend or a family member,
it affects so many people in Australia and you don't realise how big this issue is.
As an active member of SA Country Shows, he makes sure to call in on the town's big annual agricultural event to share his message.
It's a pleasure and an honour to be here today to open the Mount Barker Show.
2025, I'm on a new mission to raise awareness and money for Dementia Australia.
I'm currently riding my bike around Australia unsupported for the next year.
While the journey has come with highlights like these,
it's also thrown him plenty of challenges, testing his willpower.
I probably shouldn't be stopping today.
It's way too cold for that.
It isn't easy to have to say this, but after 133 days and over 17,000 kilometres,
it might be possible that this coming week might be my last on the bike.
Despite the challenges, he's committed to his goal to create more awareness about dementia
and some of the additional hurdles it comes with for people living with it in remote and rural areas.
The biggest fear is mum wandering off, which did happen on occasions,
and having such a large farm, it's just like, well, which direction did she go into?
And then what hazard we have out on the farm that could potentially cause harm to her if she had an accident?
While people who live in regional Australia experience a higher prevalence of dementia
compared to those living in major cities,
researchers say there's limited scientific understanding about how dementia risk factors
Associate Professor of Healthy Ageing Dr. Ashley Smith and her academic team
from the University of South Australia are working on a study with regional communities to find out.
Our research project involves three phases.
The first phase is to look at the clustering of risk factors for dementia in rural compared to urban participants.
And then in phase two and three, we're going to work with the rural communities
to start to identify where the pain points are for dementia in their communities.
And in phase three, we're interested in working with rural communities to develop a toolkit.
Dr. Smith says they'll focus on the 14 modifiable risk factors of dementia.
Dementia is really a lifelong condition.
In early life, factors such as lower levels of education increases people's risk of dementia.
In midlife, there's factors like physical inactivity and vascular health,
which contribute to people's risk of dementia.
So what we're really trying to do is work with these rural communities
about how can we tackle these different modifiable risk factors.
With more than 33,000 kilometers already clocked up,
Nick's sheer determination to get back on the bicycle is driven by his biggest motivator.
It's just, I can see her if she was able to.
I know she would be at the finish line to see me finish.
And with less than 7,000 kilometers to cross the finish line in Sydney on December 31st,
he wants others to know that you're not alone.
And there's others that are going through the same situation.
So there's always someone to talk to.
Nicholas Tremaine, ending that story by Jessica Schremer.

episodes.description: When local footy fan Clint Rule headed to the Melbourne V Essendon clash at Adelaide Oval, with tongue-in-cheek banner in tow, he couldn't have predicted the colourful night ahead.
episodes.transcript: Now I was a little bit ticked off, a little bit bemused, and I said, actually I'm going to leave on principles because I should be allowed to have the banner. A banner that was controversial. Clint from Cumberland Park, I got the spirit of the banner. I'd love you to share the story and tell me why you took it to the Bombers-Demons game. I love footy, I love gather round. I'm a power guy, but I wanted to go to a true gather round game that's a non-power and I guess a non-Adelaide game. So I got some tickets to the Essendon Melbourne game and I thought I'm going to be a little bit funny, a little bit cryptic, and I haven't done a banner for a long time, so I'm doing a banner today. And that banner had the words, I don't particularly like either side. I thought it might project a bit of humour and a bit of warmth to say that I'm at the game, even though I don't particularly like either side. That's the beauty of gather round. Okay, so you've put it up. Were there people around you that got the joke? Yes, there was. And I spoke to an Essendon supporter who'd driven over and he liked it. And I was hanging out with my mates there and within five minutes the security came over and started to have an elongated conversation with me and about the banner, which I told them that it was tongue-in-cheek and showed in the Facebook post. The guy was very good, number 235, but he had his boss in his ear and he said, just hang on a minute. I turned to my mates and said, decision pending. And then the boss said, sorry, you can't have the banner. You have to go and check it in the cloakroom. Now, I was a little bit ticked off, a little bit bemused, and I said, actually, I'm going to leave on principles because I should be allowed to have the banner. So you decided to leave. Where did you go? So I went outside and started scratching my head and then I saw the Shane Maughan health checks booth and I thought, I'm turning this negative into a positive. And I went and did a health check. It actually told me that my health age was 68 and I'm only 55, so that was a bit of a scare. I had something to do in the evening and I had to kill some time. So I went and had a nap at uni grandstand at my beautiful university oval where I played some footy. Fortunately, my banner also used to be a blanket and it was a tad cold. So I wrapped up a nap and settled in for a nap. I love a nap. Meanwhile, the Premier had heard about it and he gave me a call. Hawks versus Bulldogs. I did get it up to the president's room at Adelaide Oval. And while I had a lovely lamb dinner, the marvellous catering staff went and found one for me. Sat down with a nice swanky end to a curious day for this footy fan.

episodes.title: Government set to announce NDIS reforms
episodes.description: It costs 50 billion dollars a year and it's plagued by rorts, so how can the Government reform the NDIS to protect its budget while maintaining services to those who need it?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Wednesday the 22nd of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. US President Donald Trump says he will extend the ceasefire with Iran, just hours from its scheduled end, despite no progress on negotiations for peace talks. In a social media post, Mr Trump says he will hold off attacking Iran until Tehran's negotiating teams come up with a unified proposal for a peace agreement. Correspondent Rachel Clayton is in Washington, D.C. Rachel, President Trump says the ceasefire is being extended. What are the details? That's right. So there'd been significant uncertainty for the past few hours about whether these peace talks were going to go ahead to extend this ceasefire. We've now heard from the president on social media who says the US is going to hold off its attacks on Iran and that this ceasefire will continue to give Iran more time to come up with a proposal for a peace plan. So he said on Truth Social that based on the fact the government of Iran is what he calls seriously fractured. And because he'd been requested by Pakistani officials, including the prime minister, who asked the US to hold off its attack on the country of Iran until, as he says, until such time as their leaders and representatives can come up with a unified proposal. He goes on and says that he's directed the military to continue the blockade of Iranian ports, but to also extend the ceasefire until the proposal is submitted. So it's interesting that he's extending the ceasefire because days ago he told Bloomberg that he was definitely not going to extend the ceasefire, that if the talks failed, he was ready to bomb Iran. He said as early as this morning to CNBC that the military was gearing up to continue the fight. This is now a complete 180 where he said that the ceasefire will continue and he won't attack Iran. And it really, I think, shows not just how fluid the situation is and how quickly things can change. But the pressure that these Pakistani leaders and officials are under to make sure that the fighting does not continue. They've been under significant pressure to ask Washington to make some concessions to get Iran to the table. That hasn't worked. One of the main things was that blockade. Iran wanted that blockade of its ports lifted. Washington was unwilling to do that. And in this post, we've heard from the president saying that that blockade will continue, but that the ceasefire will also continue. So it seems to have worked. The pressure the Pakistani leaders have been putting on Washington has worked and the talks will go ahead, it seems, just a little later than when we were expecting. But as you say, the blockade continuing and we still have action from the US Navy that boarded another ship as part of this blockade. So what do we know about that? That's right. So this happened overnight in the US. It was a tanker that was allegedly carrying sanctioned Iranian oil towards Singapore, flying the flag of Botswana, allegedly part of Iran's shadow fleet that we've heard quite a bit about from General Dan Kane. He calls it a dog fleet. And it was boarded. It's been taken over by the United States. What happens to it now is a bit unknown. It will be handed over to the Coast Guard. And I've been told that there'll be discussions with various countries around the Bay of Bengal in South Asia, where the tanker was seized to decide what to do with the oil on board. The other development that's happened today is that the Treasury Department has announced new sanctions on 14 people and aircraft from Iran, the UAE and Turkey that the US says are helping Iran obtain weapons or parts of weapons. So the pressure from the United States on Iran has continued all day. And now it's culminated in this extension of the ceasefire, which is giving everyone a bit more breathing room. Rachel Clayton in Washington, D.C. And Iran has responded to the latest announcement by President Trump. A spokesman has said the ceasefire extension is a ploy to buy time for a surprise attack by the US. Back home, the federal government is set to announce major reforms to the $50 billion National Disability Insurance Scheme today, when the minister in charge of the program, Mark Butler, gives a speech at the National Press Club. Changes such as mandatory registration of providers, altering pricing rules and tightening of certain types of support have all been under consideration. For more, I was joined earlier by our National Disability Affairs reporter, Naz Campanella. Naz, why is today's speech so important? Well, today is a really hotly anticipated speech, purely because a lot of the talk in the recent years about the NDIS has been about its cost. So in its original projections, the Productivity Commission said that in its maturity, the NDIS would support about 400,000 participants, and that has now swelled to 760,000 participants, and it's now costing $50 billion, so more than Medicare, and edging pretty close to defence spending as well. Now, the government has had a target of 10%, and it has said in recent time that it is on track to meet that target, but it is now going to be talking about plans to reach a 5% target, and how they will achieve that is what will be unveiled today. So can you talk me through some of the things that are likely to be the key areas of focus if the government is looking to try and further constrain the growth of the NDIS? Well, I have to say the government has been really tight-lipped about what this is, so it's all predictions from me and from conversations with many people, but I think the really key things is firstly, mandatory registration. So it is voluntary for many organisations and providers to be registered. It is not illegal to operate as an NDIS provider unregistered, but some providers, particularly in accommodation and sort of platform providers which connect participants with support workers, will have to be registered by July 1st. That was recently announced, and my feeling is that that will go even further today. Another big thing is what to do with groups outside of the NDIS, and one in particular is people with psychosocial disability. There are about 65,000 of them on the NDIS, but hundreds of thousands still outside the scheme who require support. So what will be done across the states and territories really to support those people? And finally, it's pricing, Mel. There's a quite a, I guess it's described as a flat pricing structure at the moment. So you could be a support worker going in and providing, for example, you know, showering, feeding, or you could be a nurse that goes in and supports someone to have medication or a feeding tube, and the prices are very similar. So people talking about looking at prices of therapies, who can get them, how frequently they can get them. And also looking at, I guess, the price of services according to quality. So maybe perhaps a tiered approach. So that'll be really interesting to see what happens there. So depending on what the government announces today, there could be some big changes coming. What's the feeling in the community? Yeah, it's safe to say the changes will be big. And the feeling in the community, to put it in a word, is anxiety. I know of one particular group that ran an online town hall last night for people to try and quell concerns, have a bit of a sit down with everyone and have a chat and just kind of say, you know, we're all in this together. But, you know, I've heard weekly for years now about people having cuts to plans, being very concerned that they have significant permanent disability, and feeling like a lot of their services are being cut. Everyone has consensus that something needs to change. The trajectory of the scheme cannot continue this way because the community wants this scheme to last into the future for generations. So there's consensus on that. It's how the reforms are done that the community is concerned about. They want it done with transparency and proper communication. Naz Campanella there. Hundreds of parents are already dealing with the impact of earlier changes to the NDIS aimed at reining in its growing costs. A key provider of specialised childcare centres for autistic children, the AEIOU Foundation, went into liquidation last month. The abrupt closure of its 11 sites followed cuts to plans for NDIS recipients. Emma Pollard reports. Hands on the steering wheel. In the garden of a brick home north of Brisbane, five-year-old Dimitri plays with a toy car alongside his father. When he was two, Dimitri was diagnosed with the most severe level of autism. He didn't speak or interact with people. Single dad, Eric Moore, who's a teacher, says Dimitri had to leave three mainstream childcare centres. They asked me to find somewhere else for him because they couldn't manage him. Then early last year, he started at an AEIOU centre, which provided autistic children with high support needs with daycare and therapies under one safe roof. Dimitri was making steady progress. He started being more expressive of his needs and what he wanted. We started learning some basic ways to communicate back and forth. His understanding vastly improved. But last month, their lives were turned upside down when the AEIOU Foundation went into liquidation. All 11 centres in Queensland, Adelaide and Canberra telling hundreds of parents like Eric not to return. We're closed. We no longer have jobs. We're shut down. Don't bring him back tomorrow. So I initially had to take time off work to care for him during the day while we start trying to piece everything back together. For 20 years, AEIOU provided thousands of autistic children with early intervention services. Devastated parents and staff blame NDIS cuts for its demise. Cancer doctor, James Morton started the foundation after his own son's autism diagnosis and was on the board. And in 2024, suddenly packages got dramatically cut. So from six hours of therapy, which they were funded at the time, down to two hours of therapy. And parents were told that they had to have their children in mainstream or look after them at home. Canberra-based Dr Martin Laverty helped design and implement the NDIS and now heads a disability service. He says the AEIOU Foundation likely won't be the last to fold. Right around the country, we are seeing therapy providers who have faced a seven-year freeze in the therapy price, fighting viability challenges to survive. In a statement, a spokesperson for the NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister says the scheme funds individual supports in line with the child's assessed needs, not entire programs designed by providers. Griffith University autism researcher Jessica Painter previously worked for AEIOU. The associate professor says benchmarking shows the centres had positive outcomes and their closure is unacceptable. By cutting funds from one place, such as NDIS, we're only going to increase costs in other places, such as mental health, emergency wards or education settings. The agency running the NDIS says it has worked closely with families affected by the closures to assist children to transition to alternative services. Dimitri's dad says his son's behaviour deteriorated after his centre shut. He's since enrolled the five-year-old in a special school, an option not open to parents with younger children. It is grossly unfair because it is the children, ultimately, who suffer. Queensland father Eric Moore, ending that report by Emma Pollard. The leadership of UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer is under pressure as the fallout over the appointment and subsequent sacking of Peter Mandelson as ambassador to Washington, widens. A senior civil servant was blamed and fired for not informing the Prime Minister Mandelson had failed to pass security vetting. But the controversy has emboldened critics of Keir Starmer, who was already under political pressure. Stephanie Smale reports. The probe into how Labor power broker Peter Mandelson was appointed the British ambassador to the US, despite concerns about his past, continues. And the now former Foreign Office boss says there was pressure to make it happen, coming from the top. I'm afraid I walked into a situation in which there was already a very, very strong expectation coming from number 10 that he needed to be in post and in America as quickly as humanly possible. Sir Ollie Robbins was sacked last week after it emerged his department had granted Lord Mandelson security clearance in January 2025. Lord Mandelson formally took up the role the following month, but was sacked seven months later over his ties to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Sir Ollie has told the UK Parliament number 10 Downing Street wanted Peter Mandelson in the post before Donald Trump's inauguration. So I'm afraid what that translated into for my team in the Foreign Office and certainly the handover briefing I was getting as I arrived at post was what I felt was a generally dismissive attitude to his vetting clearance. The focus was on getting Mandelson out to Washington quickly. Sir Ollie has pointed out that regardless of that pressure, his department completed the vetting process to the normal high standard. He explains Lord Mandelson was considered a borderline case and officials were leaning towards denying clearance, but the Foreign Office Security Department ruled that the risks could be managed or mitigated. I was also told that the risks did not relate to Mandelson's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and that I was told that UK SV acknowledged. I don't know in what way, but acknowledged that the Foreign Office might wish to grant clearance with appropriate risk management. Sakia Starmer says even after Peter Mandelson was sacked over new revelations about his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, he was not told about the vetting results. But the Prime Minister's judgment is under scrutiny after backing a man with a troubled and colourful past with public links to China, Russia and Epstein. In response to Conservative MP Afro Brandis, Sir Ollie Robbins has echoed questions about Sakia's judgment. I regret that this process was not done before announcement. I regret that the due diligence process, which threw up, as I understand it, serious reputational risks, didn't colour the Prime Minister's judgment in making the appointment. The full political impact from the Washington appointment, particularly on Sakia Starmer, is still unclear. Former advisor to UK Prime Minister Tony Blair, John McTernan, doubts he will be dumped as leader yet, but says his party will take a hit. But the appointment was the terrible mistake. The appointment was the original sin. And the Labor Party is going to be punished badly, the polls, in May for that. Former Prime Ministerial advisor John McTernan ending that report by Stephanie Smale. Back home, older Australians getting at-home support will no longer have to pay for showering from October in a major backdown by the federal government. Just six months in, it's dumping a controversial co-contribution decision that saw some older Australians paying $50 an hour out of pocket for basic care like showering. Political reporter Evelyn Manfield has more. Basic care like showering should never have been treated like optional extras. With advocates and providers aligned, the government has been under pressure for months to reverse its decision to charge at-home aged care recipients for basic services like showers. Corey Erlam from the Council on the Aging says the government's decision to now stop that come October is welcome but overdue. This is about dignity. No one should have to choose between affordability and basic personal care. Because of the new fee structure as part of the aged care reforms that passed Parliament in 2024 and took effect in November, the hourly cost provider's charge has shot up. It's meant elderly folk on support-at-home packages have been paying between 5% and 50% of the fee of certain supports, which Samantha Edmond from the Older Persons Advocacy Network says has equaled big out-of-pocket costs. From $50 upwards for showering in particular, certainly unreasonable prices. Some other older people, you know, might have only been having a shower once or twice a week. Tom Simonson from Aging Australia, which represents providers, is also backing the move. It's a common sense, human rights-based decision to hopefully rebuild a bit of trust in the reforms that came in on the 1st of November. With such widespread support, it begs the question why showers weren't fully covered in the first place. Well, Tom Simonson was also on the task force that reviewed the funding of aged care. Providing fee-free or contribution-free services has a cost. The government has to pay the full price of those services through aged care packages, and they had wanted to make the aged care budget more manageable into the future. The backflip just six months into the scheme will be officially announced by Health Minister Mark Butler during a speech at the National Press Club today, where he'll also unveil the government's plans to curb the cost of the National Disability Insurance Scheme, with some of those savings, as the government calls them, to be directed to aged care. It's not yet clear how much this aged care announcement will cost, but it's expected to be north of a billion dollars. The spending demands don't stop there, though. Ahead of the federal budget, providers and advocates are once again united in a push for the government to fund more support-at-home packages to help reduce the waitlist and wait times. episodes.title: Iran and US head back to negotiating table
episodes.description: With negotiators heading back to Islamabad for peace talks, Donald Trump again threatens Iran to make a deal or face devastating consequences.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Monday the 20th of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. The United States is preparing for another round of talks about a possible end to the war in Iran. Vice President J.D. Vance will be in Pakistan later today for more negotiations, though Iranian state media has cast doubt on the regime's participation. But before talks can even begin, tensions have escalated, with President Donald Trump posting on social media that the US Navy has taken custody of an Iranian cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman. The ABC's America's editor, John Lyons, is in Washington. John, realistically, could we be looking at moves towards the end of the war with another round of peace talks apparently about to get underway? Well, Melissa, I think it is possible that there could be a peace deal this week, although obviously nobody can be sure. This situation is very fluid. It's fast moving. There's now the reports that the US Navy has intercepted and seized an Iranian-flared cargo ship coming through. President Trump has talked about that, which is obviously a deterioration in that sense. However, this will be the second face-to-face meeting that Vice President Vance has in Pakistan with Iranian officials. I don't think that Vice President would accept to go unless there's a serious possibility of a breakthrough. It would be humiliating to twice have to return to the United States, having been seen to have failed to come up with any agreement. What's been happening behind the scenes is the Pakistanis, Egypt, Syria, Saudi Arabia have all been trying to broker a deal. In fact, the Pakistani military senior officials have been shuttling between Islamabad, Tehran and Washington DC to come up with this to lay the groundwork for it. So yes, it's a possibility, but of course, we can't assume it's going to happen until it's done. So how much does President Trump want to see the end of the war? What's the level of motivation there on the US side? He very much wants to see an end to the war, but I think the real story of what's happening at the moment is there's a monumental power struggle, an extraordinary military and diplomatic arm wrestle going on between the United States and Iran. Donald Trump had assumed clearly, because he's commander in chief of the most powerful military in human history, that what he said would happen. For example, he said that after Iran and the US agreed that they would reopen the Strait of Hormuz for a period, Donald Trump later, almost as an afterthought, said, but your ships can't come through. Everybody else's ships can. The Iranians had the view, we brokered this deal, therefore we're not going to allow our ships not to come through, and they reclosed it. Donald Trump's not used to not getting his way, and I think he's realising that Iran is a tougher negotiator than he had assumed. What is the latest status of the Strait of Hormuz and the passage of vessels through that strait that is what the rest of the world is keeping an eye on? Well, at the moment, the Strait of Hormuz, which of course 20% of the world's energy goes through is in chaos. Now, the Iranians see this as their single best and perhaps only real negotiating leverage, and so they're guarding that like anything. But the bottom line is that at the moment, nothing of any significance is moving through. So the world's energy crisis deteriorates by the day, and the Iranians know that puts huge pressure on Donald Trump. His polling is going down, for example, with non-college educated whites in the United States. That's one of his strongholds. His approval rating is tanking. They did a joint Fox, CNN and CBS. They put all of those polls together. He's in deep political trouble, and he knows that, and he wants an end to this war quickly. John Lyons in Washington there. Patrick Clausen is the Director of the Iran Program at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. He joined me earlier. Patrick Clausen, thanks very much for speaking to me this morning. Happy to do it. What's at stake for the US with this second round of talks with Iran? Well, the big question is whether or not Iran can be counted on to follow through on commitments that the United States thinks Iran has made. And this whole episode of a foreign minister saying, oh, the Straits of Hormuz is open, and then other parts of the government saying, well, not so fast, suggests that decision-making in Iran is not so clear and not so efficient. And the US has to worry about whether or not Iran would follow through on other parts of any accord that might be agreed to. So what outcome would be acceptable to the Iranian regime, do you think, given that they've now seen the power that they can wield by controlling the Strait of Hormuz? Well, I think the Iranian government's hardliners certainly want to see the US blockade on Iranian ships lifted. And they will also insist that Iran has a considerable say over what happens in the Strait. Maybe not tolls, maybe not permission, but a considerable Iranian influence over what happens in the Strait. And then, of course, there's other issues like the nuclear program, where, again, Iran will want to have things going a considerable way towards what it's demanded. Much has been made of the gulf between what Iran wants out of these talks and what America wants. Do you think there is enough motivation from both parties to be able to bridge that gap? Certainly, there are important voices in the United States and in Iran who want to see that gap bridged. But there are also important voices in Iran who think that the military confrontation was working to Iran's advantage and would like to see it resumed. How that's going to play out in a situation where decision-making in Iran is no longer centralized in the hands of the supreme leader the way it used to be, it's not clear what's going to happen. What is the potential of Iran continuing to have some level of control over the Strait of Hormuz? Unclear how that might play out, but given, as you say, there's a desire from their part to see some level of control maintained, what implications does that have for the global economy? It could be pretty benign if some of the voices in Iran which are saying, oh, well, we have to make sure that there's safety and environmental standards are being met, then that's something that's at the limit when international law kind of allows countries to do about Straits. Or it could be something much more difficult for the world to accept because it would suggest that other countries could also block Straits. The Straits of Malacca, for instance, is something quite interesting to Australia. Patrick Clausen, thank you very much for speaking to AM this morning. Thank you. And Patrick Clausen is the Director of the Iran Program at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. As the future of the Strait of Hormuz remains uncertain, the impact on the global economy continues to mount. The federal government is trying to settle its budget, not knowing how long global shortages of fuel, fertiliser and other goods will last. Katie Gallagher is the Minister for Finance. Senator, thanks for speaking with AM this morning. Good morning, Mel. We've seen over the weekend the Strait of Hormuz open and then pretty quickly close again. What's the best estimate of the impact on the Australian economy of this extended closure of the Strait? So one of the things we've been dealing with as we've been working through the budget over the last few months is this global uncertainty then and particularly the economic uncertainty that's flowing from the conflict in the Middle East. And I mean, Australia, like many other countries, are wanting to see an end to this conflict. And for those peace talks, which are going to resume to be successful. Obviously, you know, we're not immune from the impact on the global economy. We already had an inflation challenge across our economy. This war is making it harder. And, you know, we're working through all of those, that uncertainty as we finalise the budget over the next few weeks. I mean, that must be pretty difficult. The budget's only three weeks away. How are you going trying to nail down those forecasts when the situation seems to change almost every day? Yeah, so budgets are always difficult to put together. I mean, this one has additional challenges. But I mean, our focus has been on what can we do to protect the Australian economy? How do we support businesses and households with some of the impacts that we're seeing here, particularly around the price of fuel and distribution of diesel and petrol? And so, you know, that's been our focus and it'll continue to be as we finalise the budget. So, a range of business and industry groups are pushing for a cut to the regulation they face. They say they want a 25% cut in the red tape they face, that that would help them, particularly at difficult times at the moment. Are they going to be happy on budget day? Well, you know, I'll leave that to them to assess the budget. But, you know, they're right to point out about regulatory reform or better regulation. And we're always interested in hearing from stakeholders, business, industry about their views on that. And so, their input is really worthwhile. I mean, we've done a lot of work. We've had one bill pass the parliament this term on regulatory reform. We've made it clear we want to continue on that. And many of the areas that business are calling for, whether it be in R&D, in, you know, major approvals, in supporting investment and regulatory reform are all things the government is working on. And we'll have more to say on regulatory reform in the budget when it's announced. And are those decisions finalised yet? Or are the suggestions being made by these business and industry groups of where they would like to see some more cuts to red tape? Is there still time in this budget process for more changes? Or have you pretty much settled on what you'll be doing already? Look, we've been, I mean, what they're saying today are certainly views that they've put forward to the government already. So, in that sense, that's not a surprise. I mean, I think, you know, one of the things about regulatory reform is the government's keen to do some where it makes sense, where it improves outcomes, where it delivers better regulation. It's not just a cut-all regulation and, you know, see how it goes. So, we're working with their ideas as well as ideas across government. And we'll certainly have a focus on that through the budget. What about consideration of taxation reform? Has Cabinet settled on changes to capital gains tax or other related areas? Or is that still being worked on in these final weeks? Thank you. Well, the budget will be released in that second week of May. And that will have all the decisions the government has made. I mean, I think the Treasurer and PM have made it clear our tax policies haven't changed. They're focused on delivering tax cuts, which will come in, looking at our instant deductions reform that will also be coming in the next financial year. And I think we've made it clear we want to focus on intergenerational equity. And so, you know, we've been clear about that, but the announcements around that will be made in the budget. And the government's now opened up applications for zero-interest loans for businesses that have been directly affected by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. That was an initiative announced at the start of the month. How quickly can that now get moving for businesses that are struggling with fuel or fertiliser shortages, for example? Look, really quickly. I mean, it's been one of our responses to this Middle East conflict and the consequential impacts here, looking at how we shore up our supply chains and support business at a time when, you know, these consequences are real and happening. So this is a new process for us, but it's all up and running. People can go to the NRF website and have a look. But it's essentially providing, you know, cash flow support for businesses in the manufacturing sector that assist other businesses during this time. And we're really pleased that the banks have come on board and will help. But it's essentially a no-interest loan up to $5 million over a two-year period to make sure that we're doing what we can around supporting energy security resilience across the economy. Katie Gallaher, thank you very much for speaking with AM this morning. Thanks very much, Mel. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, or ADHD, rates in adults have been rising fast for the last eight years, but not evenly across Australia. Four Corners has obtained data which, for the first time, charts adult ADHD medication use by local area. Tonight's program shows that it varies wildly from very low to very high and rising quickly among women. The question is why. Norman Swan has the story. There's no register of people given an ADHD diagnosis in Australia, but you can infer diagnostic rates from the numbers of people filling ADHD prescriptions. Based on that data, one state stands out. Western Australia has 13 of the top 20 areas with the highest rates of adults using ADHD medicines in the country. Associate Professor Michael Foster is with the Medicines Intelligence Research Program at the University of New South Wales. The unit has been working with Four Corners and the Australian Bureau of Statistics to analyse the data based on geographic area. The analysis has also found that WA has the hottest hotspot in the nation. Fremantle here has the highest rates of ADHD medicine use in the whole country. The data reveal that 4.4% of people in Fremantle are filling prescriptions for ADHD medications, but those numbers are from two years ago. Since then, medication use in adults has jumped by at least 30% nationally, which means in Fremantle it could now be around 6%. And in women under 44 in Fremantle, up to 8% of the population filling prescriptions for ADHD medication. That's quite different from what some experts say is the actual rate of ADHD in the wider community. Professor David Coghill of the University of Melbourne is arguably Australia's leading clinical researcher into ADHD. In adults, the figures that I tend to stick with are the published figures between 2.5% and 3%. And it may be that we're underestimating the amount of ADHD in adult females, but 2.5% to 3% is a figure I'm comfortable with. The thing is, an ADHD diagnosis can cost thousands of dollars. So you'd imagine that the diagnosis rates would be highest in the wealthiest areas. But Fremantle isn't the richest area of Perth, nor is Brunswick in Melbourne, or Merrickville in Sydney. But both have the highest rates of ADHD prescriptions being filled in Victoria and New South Wales. And then there are many ADHD deserts. Fairfield in southwest Sydney, for example, has only 7.5% of the level of filled ADHD prescriptions compared to Fremantle.
