episodes.title: Israel and Lebanon agree to temporary ceasefire
episodes.description: US President Donald Trump says the leaders of Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 10-day ceasefire.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Friday the 17th of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. US President Donald Trump says the leaders of Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 10-day ceasefire, starting from this morning, Australian time. It would bring a temporary end to hostilities in Lebanon, with Israel's campaign against Iranian-backed militant group Hezbollah killing more than 2,000 people. It also now removes a major hurdle for possible peace talks between the US and Iran, which President Trump says could happen soon. ABC correspondent Tim Swanston is in Dubai. Tim, talk us through what President Trump said when announcing this ceasefire. Well, Mel, there's been a lot of speculation that some kind of ceasefire could be announced. There's reports that Israel's been pressured by Washington to declare a ceasefire in Lebanon. That's particularly after the historic meeting in Washington earlier this week between representatives from Israel and Lebanon. I guess it's important to note, though, at this stage that Israel has been fighting with Hezbollah, not with Lebanon. At any rate, though, this post on social media by President Trump said that he'd just had excellent conversations with the highly respected Lebanese President Joseph Oun, as well as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, said that these two leaders have agreed that in order to achieve peace between their countries, they'll formally begin a 10-day ceasefire. He also added that he's going to be inviting the pair to the White House for meaningful talks. He says the first meaningful talks between Israel and Lebanon since 1983. But ultimately, this could bring a temporary end to hostilities. Israel launched its attacks on Lebanon after Hezbollah fired on Israel in solidarity with Iran and the start of the war on Iran. But that's led to an extensive ground campaign in Lebanon, which, according to its health ministry, has killed more than 2,100 people. So where does this leave things with the wider war? Because, of course, this flashpoint has been critical in the talks between the US and Iran. Yeah, it really does sort of leave a little bit of clearer air, I guess, between the United States and Iran. You know, Pakistan, the mediator between the US and Iran, had said that this was a crucial sticking point, really, for the US and Iran to come together to achieve a peace agreement to end the war. We have, though, recently heard from United States President Donald Trump that he appears he's quite optimistic, you know, that a deal could be reached in the coming days. He said that the Iran war may be nearing an end. He was speaking just outside the White House and he said that Iran had offered not to have nuclear weapons for more than two decades. He also said that he didn't think that a ceasefire necessarily needed to be extended because he believed that Iran wanted to make a deal. So certainly he's really leaving the door wide open there for there to be a return to Islamabad, Pakistan, for there to be further talks between the United States and Iran. But meanwhile, that blockade continues of Iran's coastlines and ports. We've also heard earlier from US Secretary of Defence that the United States remained locked and loaded if Iran didn't make a deal. So while they're really leaving the door open to an agreement there, they've stepped up the rhetoric that if Iran doesn't make an agreement, that the US is ready to return to war. Tim Swanston in Dubai there. Australia's newly unveiled defence strategy has been heralded by the federal government as a commitment to preparedness and self-reliance in the face of a dangerous decade ahead. But a former chief of the Defence Force is calling for elements of the plan to be overhauled, saying it does not recognise Australia's closest ally could pose the greatest risk. Here's political reporter Lexi Juniwik. Australia's national defence strategy set out to equip the Defence Force of today for the challenges of the future. But a former chief of the ADF believes it's missed the mark. Well, I'm not saying the whole plan goes down the gurgle of it, but I am saying that strategic assumptions which underpin this plan need to be redone to take account of what a changing world is delivering for our security. Retired Admiral Chris Barry, who was also founder of the Australian Security Leaders Climate Group, suspects the government largely constructed the latest national defence strategy prior to the US-Israeli strikes on Iran. The government's plan as delivered talks about risks, but it doesn't talk about the United States potentially being the largest risk. And it then goes on to talk about the foundations of our alliance relationship and how valuable it is and so on. I think that is all now under question and it needs to be redone. Peter Dean is a professor of strategic studies at the Australian National University and worked on the 2023 Defence Strategic Review. He says the newly unveiled plan, which cites the US as Australia's closest ally and principal strategic partner, meets the moment. I think since the last strategy and even in the last six months, we've seen a kind of a poly-crisis moment in the world where strategic issues, geopolitics, economics are all intersecting. The government says the additional investment of $53 billion over the next decade will see defence spending as a proportion of GDP reach around 3% by 2033 in NATO terms. The opposition says it's not enough and has accused Labor of accounting trickery that won't keep Australians safer. But Professor Dean doesn't see it that way. It's not just how much money you're spending, but it's what you're spending that money on. And the government is fundamentally focused on undersea warfare. That includes the AUKUS agreement and our Ghost Shark autonomous vehicles and our blue-bottle uncrewed surface vessels. And of course, our own guided weapons and explosive ordnance, which means building ammunition and missiles in Australia, which makes us more sovereign capable, but also helps us contribute to that kind of collective effort in our region to deter China and to maintain that regional strategic balance. As part of the strategy, the government will redirect $5 billion from existing defence to new key military priorities. Andrew Carr, an associate professor at the Australian National University's Strategic Defence Study Centre, says reprioritising funding is a useful approach. You don't want to just try and fund everything you've already committed to. You always want to keep saying what actually buys us the security we need for the specific strategic problems we face. Associate Professor Andrew Carr there, ending that report from Lexi Junawik. US President Donald Trump has again criticised Australia for not supporting US efforts to open the Strait of Hormuz. His comments come despite the Australian government consistently saying it was never asked by the US to contribute to that action. Mr Trump has also ignored a question about the Australian government's increase in defence spending. Speaking this morning, Defence Minister Richard Miles has reiterated Australia's strong relationship with the US. It is profoundly important to our national security. We have a very close relationship with the United States Armed Forces and that is very central to how we conceive of our own national security and how we build our own defence capability. And it's really important that people hear that message. Our relationship with the US deeply matters. We work constructively with all of our friends and partners, including the United States, in respect of any situation we find in the world. An additional 250,000 tonnes of fertiliser will be imported to Australia with the support of the federal government. Many farmers are facing limits on how much they can grow over winter with fertiliser supplies disrupted because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Julie Collins is the Federal Agriculture Minister and joins us now. Minister, thanks for speaking with AM this morning. Thanks very much for having me on. Minister, just before we get to the fertiliser deal, do you have any updates on the impact of the fire at the Viva refinery in Geelong and what that might mean for Australia's fuel supplies? Well, my understanding is it has affected in terms of particular types of fuel, particularly petroleum, so petrol that people use to fill up their cars. But that Viva is confident that we can mitigate this with imports. But that was certainly the latest that I heard this morning. On the additional fertiliser supply, can you tell me what difference this extra urea being purchased will make for Australia's agriculture sector? Well, we certainly know how important fertiliser and urea is for certainty for farmers in terms of the initial planting season that they are undertaking now and in coming weeks. So we know that certainty of supply is really critical for them, which is why this additional 250,000 tonnes is so important. And this sends a strong message that Australia is working with our international partners to secure additional supply. So this is additional supply coming from Indonesia. And I again want to thank the Indonesian government for their cooperation. And of course, Incitec Pivot and PT Pupuk in Indonesia for this arrangement. This will mean a great deal to Australian farmers and will give them some certainty in terms of going forward with the season. So this was a commercial deal between those two companies. What role did the federal government play here? Well, we've obviously been talking to our like-minded partners and around the Southeast Asian countries. And you've seen that with the Prime Minister's visits, talking to them and working with them about additional supplies. And certainly the Indonesian government have been supporting us and supporting Incitec Pivot and PT Pupuk in terms of getting this deal negotiated to get this additional supply out of Indonesia into Australia. Indonesia is already a very trusted supplier and partner of Australia when it comes to fertiliser. But this is additional supply that we've been able to secure. But it didn't involve the federal government underwriting the purchase or any financial support. It was more a discussion facilitation? It was certainly a facilitation and a discussion about what is available and having those discussions like we are around Southeast Asia. We continue to have discussions with like-minded countries and with the private sector in terms of any underwriting that may be necessary. How quickly will farmers be able to access this additional fertiliser, given many are making decisions right now about whether to sow or how much to sow for the next growing round? Well, as I said, we do have enough fertiliser in Australia, either on the water or in the country at the moment for the initial planting season. But this gives farmers certainty going into the future. So we do expect this additional supplies to come in sometime in June. So that will provide farmers, I think, with some confidence that fertiliser is on its way. Are there distribution problems then? Because many of the grower groups are saying they're not getting the supply and they're having to make calculations about whether or not it's worth them putting in a round of seasonal produce, particularly some of the winter greens and the like. Well, certainly the distribution of fertiliser is very complex and quite different to fuel. And it is commercial. And obviously some companies hold their own fertiliser stocks. They do private deals in terms of their fertiliser needs throughout the year. But this is us working with the industry and securing additional supplies for Australia. So this will give some farmers confidence that there'll be fertiliser in coming months. Do you think it's more of a confidence issue than any actual problem with accessing supply? Well, certainly we know at the moment, as I said, that there is enough either here in Australia or on its way on the water already to be able to deal with this initial planting season. So this is about providing certainty and confidence to our farmers that further supply is on its way. What about in the longer term? What plans is there for the government to ensure that we're not so reliant on supplies out of the Middle East for urea and other products? Well, obviously there is the investment coming from the National Australia Infrastructure Facility into the Purdiman Plant in Western Australia. We're talking around a $220 million loan facility there and they will produce urea. So it will be able to be produced here in Australia from the middle of next year. But obviously, you know, our trading relationships and our relationships with particularly some of our southeast neighbours has been really critical in terms of this supply. As I said, Indonesia is already a trusted supplier of fertiliser to Australia. And this is additional supply that we've been able to secure. Julie Collins, thanks very much for speaking to AM this morning. Thanks very much. And Julie Collins is the Federal Agriculture Minister. Now, some energy analysts say the federal and state governments need to consider some kind of fuel rationing after a fire at Australia's largest oil refinery. Experts warn the incident will likely push up petrol prices, especially in Victoria. Bridget Fitzgerald reports. After weeks of soaring fuel prices and economic uncertainty, the news that one of only two operational oil refineries in Australia was on fire was yet another blow. Probably the worst thing that we could have heard at this moment in time. Sally Curtin is the chief executive of the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry. She says the incident just adds to energy market volatility. Of course, business right now is in the process of budgeting for next year. And imagine trying to, you know, foresee what's going to happen, you know, 16 months away, let alone next week. segments.text: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more.
Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Friday the 17th of April.
I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians.
US President Donald Trump says the leaders of Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 10-day ceasefire,
starting from this morning, Australian time.
It would bring a temporary end to hostilities in Lebanon,
with Israel's campaign against Iranian-backed militant group Hezbollah killing more than 2,000 people.
It also now removes a major hurdle for possible peace talks between the US and Iran,
which President Trump says could happen soon.
ABC correspondent Tim Swanston is in Dubai.
Tim, talk us through what President Trump said when announcing this ceasefire.
Well, Mel, there's been a lot of speculation that some kind of ceasefire could be announced.
There's reports that Israel's been pressured by Washington to declare a ceasefire in Lebanon.
That's particularly after the historic meeting in Washington earlier this week between representatives from Israel and Lebanon.
I guess it's important to note, though, at this stage that Israel has been fighting with Hezbollah, not with Lebanon.
At any rate, though, this post on social media by President Trump said that he'd just had excellent conversations with the highly respected Lebanese President Joseph Oun,
as well as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, said that these two leaders have agreed that in order to achieve peace between their countries,
He also added that he's going to be inviting the pair to the White House for meaningful talks.
He says the first meaningful talks between Israel and Lebanon since 1983.
But ultimately, this could bring a temporary end to hostilities.
Israel launched its attacks on Lebanon after Hezbollah fired on Israel in solidarity with Iran and the start of the war on Iran.
But that's led to an extensive ground campaign in Lebanon, which, according to its health ministry, has killed more than 2,100 people.
So where does this leave things with the wider war?
Because, of course, this flashpoint has been critical in the talks between the US and Iran.
Yeah, it really does sort of leave a little bit of clearer air, I guess, between the United States and Iran.
You know, Pakistan, the mediator between the US and Iran, had said that this was a crucial sticking point, really,
for the US and Iran to come together to achieve a peace agreement to end the war.
We have, though, recently heard from United States President Donald Trump that he appears he's quite optimistic,
you know, that a deal could be reached in the coming days.
He said that the Iran war may be nearing an end.
He was speaking just outside the White House and he said that Iran had offered not to have nuclear weapons for more than two decades.
He also said that he didn't think that a ceasefire necessarily needed to be extended because he believed that Iran wanted to make a deal.
So certainly he's really leaving the door wide open there for there to be a return to Islamabad, Pakistan,
for there to be further talks between the United States and Iran.
But meanwhile, that blockade continues of Iran's coastlines and ports.
We've also heard earlier from US Secretary of Defence that the United States remained locked and loaded if Iran didn't make a deal.
So while they're really leaving the door open to an agreement there, they've stepped up the rhetoric that if Iran doesn't make an agreement,
that the US is ready to return to war.
Australia's newly unveiled defence strategy has been heralded by the federal government as a commitment to preparedness and self-reliance
in the face of a dangerous decade ahead.
But a former chief of the Defence Force is calling for elements of the plan to be overhauled,
saying it does not recognise Australia's closest ally could pose the greatest risk.
Australia's national defence strategy set out to equip the Defence Force of today for the challenges of the future.
But a former chief of the ADF believes it's missed the mark.
Well, I'm not saying the whole plan goes down the gurgle of it, but I am saying that strategic assumptions which underpin this plan
need to be redone to take account of what a changing world is delivering for our security.
Retired Admiral Chris Barry, who was also founder of the Australian Security Leaders Climate Group,
suspects the government largely constructed the latest national defence strategy prior to the US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
The government's plan as delivered talks about risks, but it doesn't talk about the United States potentially being the largest risk.
And it then goes on to talk about the foundations of our alliance relationship and how valuable it is and so on.
I think that is all now under question and it needs to be redone.
Peter Dean is a professor of strategic studies at the Australian National University and worked on the 2023 Defence Strategic Review.
He says the newly unveiled plan, which cites the US as Australia's closest ally and principal strategic partner, meets the moment.
I think since the last strategy and even in the last six months, we've seen a kind of a poly-crisis moment in the world
where strategic issues, geopolitics, economics are all intersecting.
The government says the additional investment of $53 billion over the next decade will see defence spending as a proportion of GDP reach around 3% by 2033 in NATO terms.
The opposition says it's not enough and has accused Labor of accounting trickery that won't keep Australians safer.
But Professor Dean doesn't see it that way.
It's not just how much money you're spending, but it's what you're spending that money on.
And the government is fundamentally focused on undersea warfare.
That includes the AUKUS agreement and our Ghost Shark autonomous vehicles and our blue-bottle uncrewed surface vessels.
And of course, our own guided weapons and explosive ordnance, which means building ammunition and missiles in Australia,
which makes us more sovereign capable, but also helps us contribute to that kind of collective effort in our region to deter China and to maintain that regional strategic balance.
As part of the strategy, the government will redirect $5 billion from existing defence to new key military priorities.
Andrew Carr, an associate professor at the Australian National University's Strategic Defence Study Centre, says reprioritising funding is a useful approach.
You don't want to just try and fund everything you've already committed to.
You always want to keep saying what actually buys us the security we need for the specific strategic problems we face.
Associate Professor Andrew Carr there, ending that report from Lexi Junawik.
US President Donald Trump has again criticised Australia for not supporting US efforts to open the Strait of Hormuz.
His comments come despite the Australian government consistently saying it was never asked by the US to contribute to that action.
Mr Trump has also ignored a question about the Australian government's increase in defence spending.
Speaking this morning, Defence Minister Richard Miles has reiterated Australia's strong relationship with the US.
It is profoundly important to our national security.
We have a very close relationship with the United States Armed Forces and that is very central to how we conceive of our own national security and how we build our own defence capability.
And it's really important that people hear that message.
Our relationship with the US deeply matters.
We work constructively with all of our friends and partners, including the United States, in respect of any situation we find in the world.
An additional 250,000 tonnes of fertiliser will be imported to Australia with the support of the federal government.

Indonesia is already a very trusted supplier and partner of Australia when it comes to fertiliser.
But this is additional supply that we've been able to secure.
But it didn't involve the federal government underwriting the purchase or any financial support.
It was more a discussion facilitation?
It was certainly a facilitation and a discussion about what is available and having those discussions like we are around Southeast Asia.
We continue to have discussions with like-minded countries and with the private sector in terms of any underwriting that may be necessary.
How quickly will farmers be able to access this additional fertiliser, given many are making decisions right now about whether to sow or how much to sow for the next growing round?
Well, as I said, we do have enough fertiliser in Australia, either on the water or in the country at the moment for the initial planting season.
But this gives farmers certainty going into the future.
So we do expect this additional supplies to come in sometime in June.
So that will provide farmers, I think, with some confidence that fertiliser is on its way.

Because many of the grower groups are saying they're not getting the supply and they're having to make calculations about whether or not it's worth them putting in a round of seasonal produce, particularly some of the winter greens and the like.
Well, certainly the distribution of fertiliser is very complex and quite different to fuel.
And obviously some companies hold their own fertiliser stocks.
They do private deals in terms of their fertiliser needs throughout the year.
But this is us working with the industry and securing additional supplies for Australia.
So this will give some farmers confidence that there'll be fertiliser in coming months.
Do you think it's more of a confidence issue than any actual problem with accessing supply?
Well, certainly we know at the moment, as I said, that there is enough either here in Australia or on its way on the water already to be able to deal with this initial planting season.
So this is about providing certainty and confidence to our farmers that further supply is on its way.
What about in the longer term?
What plans is there for the government to ensure that we're not so reliant on supplies out of the Middle East for urea and other products?
Well, obviously there is the investment coming from the National Australia Infrastructure Facility into the Purdiman Plant in Western Australia.
We're talking around a $220 million loan facility there and they will produce urea.
So it will be able to be produced here in Australia from the middle of next year.
But obviously, you know, our trading relationships and our relationships with particularly some of our southeast neighbours has been really critical in terms of this supply.
As I said, Indonesia is already a trusted supplier of fertiliser to Australia.
And this is additional supply that we've been able to secure.
Julie Collins, thanks very much for speaking to AM this morning.
And Julie Collins is the Federal Agriculture Minister.
Now, some energy analysts say the federal and state governments need to consider some kind of fuel rationing after a fire at Australia's largest oil refinery.
Experts warn the incident will likely push up petrol prices, especially in Victoria.
After weeks of soaring fuel prices and economic uncertainty, the news that one of only two operational oil refineries in Australia was on fire was yet another blow.
Probably the worst thing that we could have heard at this moment in time.
Sally Curtin is the chief executive of the Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

We don't really have that option.
And that's why I say that our options are kind of running out.
Energy analyst Kevin Morrison ending that report by Bridget Fitzgerald.

episodes.title: Massive fire rips through refinery
episodes.description: As we deal with a fuel crisis, a massive blaze rips through one of the country's only two oil refineries.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning, welcome to AM. It's Thursday the 16th of April. I'm Rachel Mealy coming to you from the lands of the Turbul and Yaghera people in Brisbane. A major fire is burning at one of Australia's only operating oil refineries. The blaze broke out last night at Viva Energy's Geelong facility, 75 kilometres south-west of Melbourne and is still burning out of control. The facility supplies more than 50% of Victoria's fuel and 10% of Australia's. Our reporter Kathleen O'Connor is covering the story. Rachel, the fire is large and it's been burning since around 11 o'clock last night, producing flames of up to 50 metres in height. There's also been several explosions, according to Fire Rescue Victorian authorities. Around 50 firefighters have been on scene all night putting water on the fire, but with it being an oil plant, it's been difficult for them to bring it under control. Now, the Viva Energy refinery is Victoria's only oil refinery, supplying approximately 50% of the state's fuel. It's one of just two refineries remaining in Australia, employing over 1,100 people. Authorities from Fire Rescue Victoria say the blaze started in the MOGAS plant. Now, MOGAS stands for motor gasoline. So it's the section of the refinery that produces petrol or unleaded premium gasoline, things that motorists can get at the Bowser. I spoke to Fire Rescue Victoria's Chief Assistant Fire Officer Michael McGinnis a short time ago. This is what he had to say. There's been some sort of leak of hydrocarbon, some of the liquids, which had very readily caught fire. And it has now been quite a major fire. It's been burning all night and still is burning. We're likely to be here for several more hours. It depends on how we can continue our combat and firefighting strategies, and that's by slowly isolating pipe work and some of the plant area that's feeding hydrocarbons into this fire. It's also not the first fire at the plant. It had a significant fire last year due to failing pumps. Fire Rescue Victoria's Chief Assistant Fire Officer Michael McGinnis says it's still quite unclear how much fuel is still in there, but it could burn for hours. But the intensity has decreased, which is a good sign. And Kathleen, obviously fuel supply is on everyone's minds right now. Is this likely to impact the country's fuel supply? Yeah, Rachel, look, people are obviously very worried about this, and it could very well put further pressure on the current fuel crisis. We just don't know yet. The company was ordered to boost output by the state government due to supply pressures about a month ago. It's unclear just how much fuel has been lost as a result of the fire, but authorities say they've been told by the company Viva that there's no immediate impact on fuel supply at this point. In terms of the damage caused, it will take some time for fire crews to bring the fire under control before an investigation is launched. Victoria Police will also be involved in that investigation, looking into how this could have happened and what overall impact this will have on the country's fuel supply. And before I let you go, because of those heightened tensions in the world right now, I have to ask, is sabotage something that police will look into? Yeah, Rachel, authorities say that they're not treating it as suspicious at this stage, but investigators will be looking at everything. Kathleen O'Connor. As that fire threatens to worsen the situation, the Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, continues his tour of Southeast Asia to shore up fuel supplies. Here's political reporter Lexi Juniwick. Ben Bennett's dairy farm in southwest Victoria is a world away from the war in the Middle East, but the impact of the conflict is hitting home for the farmer. You know, we're not sitting here swimming in cash, like it's particularly this time of year, coming out of summer, going into autumn, and we're sort of all hanging out for the autumn break. And on that basis, we need fertiliser, particularly in the form of urea, which is quite common for the far majority of dairy farmers. That's gone from $800 a tonne to $1,800 a tonne. In a bid to better equip Aussie exporters and importers with the ongoing shipping and cargo disruptions stemming from the war, the federal government has activated a new service providing real-time logistics advice to businesses. Trade Minister Don Farrell says the initiative will offer up advanced systems used by the government. What this system will do is, in real time, look at alternative ways of getting your products into that market or bringing the products to Australia. Farmer Ben Bennett, who also heads up Australian dairy farmers, isn't convinced the measure will make a difference. Well, I suppose the analogy is, we've got a freight train that's going to run us over, and now he's just giving us a better view of the freight train that's coming at us. But the Export Council of Australia, which represents thousands of exporters and international trade professionals, can see the value. Its CEO is Arnold Jorge. Exporters, what they want right now is straight, timely information about what's happening in terms of the shipping, air routes, sanctions, the market risk. They also want government agencies working off the same page, so the advice is consistent. The National Farmers' Federation's president, Hamish McIntyre, is also welcoming the initiative. We also need the federal government to keep looking laterally and looking for new opportunities that we can obviously enter into and markets that we may be able to start providing for due to what's going on around the world. The Australian government is set to join more than 40 other countries at an upcoming international summit led by the United Kingdom and France, focused on safeguarding shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. As the world grapples with the current uncertainty, the CEO of the Export Council of Australia is urging the Treasurer to provide exporters with targeted support in the upcoming budget. The messaging that's being received at the moment is that the government is focused on budget repair, for example. And unfortunately what that means is that they're now fearful that whatever support that might still exist there is going to be shut or reprioritised or put to something else. And that will actually literally pull the rug from under them. Arnold Jorge from the Export Council of Australia ending that report from Lexi Juniwik. Another interest rate rise is looking more likely for Australians next month. The International Monetary Fund has painted a grim picture, warning of a rise in inflation and a global recession, depending on how long the Middle East war continues. Isabel Massali reports. Asha Golding's life is a little different ever since fuel prices and interest rates started to climb this year. Her partner has a fly-in-fly-out job and used to work the occasional week away. Now he's away two or three weeks at a time. And we work as a team, but the reality is that our family feels that absence and that's the hardest part. The mother of three is juggling her own work as a nurse in regional New South Wales. I've always believed life should be about thriving and not just surviving. This impending interest rate is one expected bill away from everything becoming overwhelming. The public may also be overwhelmed by the International Monetary Fund's latest economic outlook, which considers the impact of the Middle East crisis under different scenarios. National Australia Bank Chief Economist Sally Auld explains. Yeah, so it makes a pretty sobering reading. And, you know, they have done to their forecasts what most economists are doing to their own forecasts. And that in very simple terms is they have cut their growth forecasts for the global economy, but also increase their inflation forecasts. Dr Auld says the Reserve Bank of Australia will also be looking at its own forecasts. They'll be revising up forecasts for inflation here in Australia and inflation globally, and they'll be also revising down growth forecasts domestically and globally. But the IMF is pretty clear on saying that, you know, central banks have got to be vigilant. They've got to be prepared to act clearly and decisively, you know, in line with their mandates. That could mean lifting interest rates. So we're still forecasting an interest rate rise from the Reserve Bank in May. And I think it's fair to say with everything going on in the world, you know, it's hard to have a huge amount of conviction in that view. But I think we anchor back to this idea that for Australia, the starting point for inflation was already a bit unfavourable before the war happened. Paul Bloxham agrees. He's HSBC's Chief Economist for Australia and New Zealand. episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Wednesday the 15th of April. I'm Rachel Mealy coming to you from the lands of the Turbul and Yagora people in Brisbane. A dire scenario predicting long-term scarring of the world's economy. In its latest World Economic Outlook report, the IMF has produced three scenarios that get progressively worse depending on how long Middle East energy supplies are disrupted. Shane Oliver is Chief Economist at AMP. He joined me a short time ago. Shane Oliver, the IMF has warned the war in Iran has turned the global economy upside down and the resulting inflation pressures could take years to overcome. Is Australia headed for recession? Look, it's not my base case, but it's certainly a risk. And I think the IMF is simply reflecting that risk. The reality is that the clock is ticking. There's talk of more talks between the US and Iran. But the key is that the flow of oil out of the Middle East needs to start up again pretty soon to avoid the recession scenario because the reality is it's now starting to bite. Over the last six weeks, countries, including Australia, have still been getting oil because of the ships that had been coming out of the Middle East and got a refinery process and they arrive in Australia. But eventually that will stop. There will be less oil going into refineries in Asia and therefore less refined product available to come to Australia. So that's a serious risk. And the longer the crisis continues, the blockage continues, the greater the risk that we do slide into recession as we have to eventually cut back on fuel usage. The IMF paints a picture of stagflation. What is that and what does it mean for Australians? Well, stagflation is a phenomenon that was quite common in the 1970s. And of course, that was partly related to oil shocks at the time. That's a situation where you have a supply side shock to an economy that pushes up prices and constrains economic activity at the same time. So you end up with both higher inflation and lower economic growth, possibly recession and higher unemployment occurring simultaneously. We have experienced little bits of that over the years, but it hasn't been a common phenomenon like it was in the 1970s. And the reality is that we are heading for some, at least a mild form of stagflation. Economists have already been revising up their inflation forecast. General talkers of inflation going up to around 5% could be higher if the situation in the Middle East isn't resolved quickly. And then, of course, at the same time, as Australians have to fork out more for fuel, they will cut back their spending. And if we get to a point where we're actually restricted in our fuel use, then that could actually cut back economic activity even further. And then you get a combination of higher inflation and weaker growth. With a federal budget now just weeks away, how would Treasury officials be factoring this into their budget this year? Look, I think this is a really difficult time for policymakers like the government and the Treasury, just as it is for the Reserve Bank, because you've got this double-edged sword hitting the economy. On the one hand, higher inflation pressures, and on the other hand, a hit to economic activity at the same time. So, I think the – and, of course, federal government needs to be careful because – as does the Reserve Bank, because you don't know how long the crisis is going to go for. If we overreact and do the wrong thing in the short term, you could damage things in the longer term. I suspect that the budget probably will, and the government seems to be heading in this direction, announce more cost-of-living support. The key is that that support be timely, impacts fairly quickly, temporary, and targeted. In other words, that it doesn't blow budget spending out indefinitely, and that it's also targeted to those who actually need it, particularly low- and middle-income earners and those businesses that are most affected potentially by fuel shortages, along with high fuel costs. So, we probably will see an element of that in the budget, but longer term, I think the government has to continue to focus on ways to boost productivity in the economy because the reality is that the global economy has become more fraught. You can't align at being stable, as we found out over the last few years, and therefore we have to improve our own game, and that means make it easier for Australian businesses to employ people and make things. AMP Chief Economist Shane Oliver. U.S. President Donald Trump has foreshadowed a possible return to peace talks with Iran. His latest comments have come as Israel and Lebanon met for historic talks in Washington, D.C. But even the U.S. mediators have acknowledged it's only the beginning of a long process. The Iran-backed militia Hezbollah was not party to the talks and says it will not abide by any resulting agreement. Shantel Al-Khoury is in our Washington Bureau. She joined me earlier. Well, these direct talks between Lebanon and Israel are highly unusual. They concluded around two hours, but any sort of big breakthrough at this meeting was always going to be highly unlikely. Now, after the meeting, the U.S. put out a statement saying that the talks covered the prospect of future direct negotiations. They said the participants held productive discussions on steps towards launching direct negotiations between Israel and Lebanon. Now, Lebanon went into this discussion wanting a ceasefire for Israel's attacks on the country to stop. Those attacks have killed more than 2,000 people and displaced more than 1.1 million since March. And Israel has been ramping up those strikes and its invasion since the war in Iran began. Israel, on the other hand, says it wants to disarm Hezbollah and says there will be no ceasefire with the group. Hezbollah is not party to these talks that have happened today. In a practical sense, Lebanon wouldn't be able to disarm Hezbollah. It does not have control over the group. I've been speaking to the International Crisis Group, who says that Israel and the U.S. have been aggressively pushing for that disarmament of Hezbollah and for the Lebanese government to take steps that would essentially, potentially trigger a civil war. It also says that these talks today are a useful vehicle for the U.S. to be able to manage the progress between Israel and Lebanon, given Israel's attacks are for them standing in the way of its already fragile ceasefire arrangement with Iran. Now, Hezbollah has responded to these talks. Before they happened, they said that they wouldn't abide to any agreements that came out of the talks. It had been urging the Lebanese government to pull out of the talks as well, and we know that both Hezbollah and Israel have since continued their attacks. So how are people on the ground in both Lebanon and Israel feeling about the prospects of these talks? Well, for many Lebanese people, it's hugely controversial and divisive for Lebanon to be meeting with Israel at all. There was a lot of scepticism because they see little guarantee that a diplomatic agreement would stop Israel's strikes on the country. For people in Israel that the ABC has spoken to, they've said that they're exhausted by the fighting. They want a resolution. We've heard from some of those people in both Lebanon and Israel, from our colleagues who've spoken with them. Here's Michelle Keren, who lives in northern Israel. I hope it will be useful for Israel and for Lebanon. But in my opinion, I can't think that it will help because Hezbollah is more bigger than the government in Lebanon. They are not strong to bring a peace. But I hope they will bring something. We have to finish this. We also heard from many in Lebanon who our colleagues from the ABC have spoken to. This is Loretta Jajour in southern Lebanon. I hope that these negotiations in the end bring us to peace and safety, for us to finish with this war, not to reach negotiations or a ceasefire just for a few days like they did before. We had started to get our lives back, and now we're back to a war that's much harder than before. That's Loretta Jajour in southern Lebanon. And Chantel, Donald Trump is saying negotiations between the US and Iran could resume within days. Yeah, that's right. The US president says that talks with Iran could resume after both parties failed to come to any sort of agreement in Islamabad on the weekend. He told the New York Post that something could be happening over the next two days, and he says we're more inclined to go there. episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Tuesday the 14th of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. A United States blockade of Iranian ports and coastlines is now in effect after US President Donald Trump ordered the operation in response to Iran's control over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has stepped up its threats in response, saying if its ports aren't safe, no ports in the region will be safe. Correspondent Tim Swanston filed this report. Mr President, are another round of talks planned with Iran? Just hours after what the US President described as a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz began, Donald Trump was quite vague about what he wanted it to achieve. Mr President, what's the endgame? Is it to force Iran back to the negotiating table? Is it to open up the Strait so the gas prices ultimately come down? Maybe everything. I mean, both of those things, certainly, and more. We can't let a country blackmail or extort the world. The US military announced in a note to seafarers that the US was enforcing a blockade of the Iranian coastline, including ports and oil terminals, and any vessel entering or departing the blockaded area without authorisation would be subject to interception, diversion and capture. The note said the blockade would not impede ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz to or from non-Iranian destinations. On Iranian state media, a TV anchor read a fiery statement by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps threatening Gulf countries if the US pressed ahead with the blockade. If the security of the ports of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the waters of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman is threatened, no port in the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman will remain safe. It set up a dramatic escalation around the Strait of Hormuz, which is threatening an already very fragile ceasefire. President Trump also claimed that other countries would support the blockade. We don't need other countries, frankly, but they've offered the services. We'll let it be known probably tomorrow. But US allies in NATO, including Britain and France, said they wouldn't be drawn in, instead saying the waterway needed to be reopened. French President Emmanuel Macron has said France, along with the UK, are working on bringing together a range of countries on a mission to restore freedom of navigation in the Strait. In a statement on social media, he said this strictly defensive mission, separate from the warring parties to the conflict, is intended to be deployed as soon as circumstances permit. In UK's Parliament, British Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer elaborated on a proposed summit involving dozens of countries to be held this week. The summit will be focused on two things. First, diplomatic efforts to bring pressure to bear for a negotiated end to the conflict and for the strait to be opened. Second, military planning to provide assurance to shipping as soon as a stable environment can be established. This is Tim Swanston in Dubai reporting for AM. The federal government has reassessed Australia's defence strategy and has decided to spend billions of dollars more on drones and other autonomous technology. A new national defence strategy will be unveiled on Thursday, taking into account lessons learnt from recent conflicts around the world. The Defence Minister joins me. Richard Miles, thanks for speaking with AM this morning. Good morning, Melissa. How are you? Good, thank you. Can you take me through how much extra money there is for drones and other autonomous capabilities and what exactly will it fund? So this, we're spending $12 to $15 billion over the next decade on autonomous capabilities, which is a significant increase, $2 to $5 billion extra relative to what we had in NDS 24. So it is a very big step up in terms of the spending that we're doing on this. And really, it's driven by the way in which modern warfare has changed. I think everyone has been really amazed at how the war in Ukraine has unfolded but evolved over the period in which it's been contested. And clearly, autonomous systems now are really central to how contest happens, how war happens. We can see that also playing out in the Middle East. So it's very important that we are maintaining pace with that and we're very much increasing our focus on autonomous systems as a result. So an extra $2 to $5 billion on top of what had already been planned to be spent in this area. So what's being deprioritised to spare up funding to shift towards drones and other autonomous vehicles? Well, we'll go through all of that on Thursday. But I guess the point I would simply say in terms of the broader picture around the funding of defence, what you'll see on Thursday is a continuation of our track record, which is to increase our investment in defence. And we'll talk about that on Thursday. But clearly, a focus on autonomous systems has to be a part of how we are thinking about the defence force that we are building today. And so be it Ghost Shark, which we announced in the course of the last year, $1.7 billion over the next five years, which is the largest underwater autonomous system in the world today, or Ghostbat, which is really the leading collaborative combat aircraft, which is being developed in Australia. And again, we spent $1.4 billion just recently in terms of the next phase of Ghostbat. These are really critical, cutting edge, world leading technologies that are autonomous, obviously, but which also fit the Australian circumstance. They're at the larger end of that spectrum, given where we are and the distances that we need to deal with. And it's now a very central part of the defence force we're building. Do we need to look more at counter-drone capabilities as well? Or does our geographic situation mean that's less of a priority than the sorts of initiatives you just outlined? No, we definitely are looking at counter-drone technology as well. So it is very much across the spectrum. I mean, I think what would be fair to say is that given our geography, we are becoming specialists in terms of the development of technology here in Australia at the larger end. But in terms of the capabilities that we will need for our defence force, it is across the full spectrum. What you get at the smaller end is mass, lots of units, and that's what we are seeing play out in Ukraine. But if we look at what's happening in the Middle East right now, you need counter-drone technology as well. And that's a critical part of the whole equation of what we're putting together here. Well, we also see that US and Gulf countries have really burnt through years of missiles and interceptors to deal with the threats from drones and missiles. We've even seen missiles meant for Ukraine being diverted to the Middle East. Does that leave Australia a little bit exposed, given we're still in the process of developing our own domestic manufacturing of missiles? Is Australia at the back of the queue now for new missile systems? Well, in terms of missile systems, it has been really clear for some time that for Australia to have the war stocks that we need, we've got to be building missiles in Australia. And that's why we've greatly brought forward the development of a missile manufacturing capability in Australia, which has now actually seen us for the first time manufacture missiles in Australia. episodes.title: US to blockade Strait of Hormuz
episodes.description: Oil prices could soar even higher as Donald Trump announces a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz following the failure of peace talks over the weekend.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning. Welcome to AM. It's Monday the 13th of April. I'm Melissa Clark in Canberra, coming to you from Ngunnawal country and acknowledging other custodians. United States President Donald Trump says the US Navy will begin a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz after negotiations between the US and Iran failed to land an agreement to end hostilities. It comes as the fragile two-week ceasefire holds for now, with other leaders in the region urging both parties to continue talking. Correspondent Tim Swanston filed this report. Boarding Air Force Two with a wave to Pakistani mediators. US Vice President J.D. Vance left Islamabad empty-handed. Earlier in a short press conference, after what he said were 21 hours of negotiations, the Vice President said a deal to end the war hadn't been reached. We've had a number of substantive discussions with the Iranians. That's the good news. The bad news is that we have not reached an agreement. And I think that's bad news for Iran much more than it's bad news for the United States of America. In the wash-up of the meeting, both sides were blaming one another for not reaching an agreement. Vice President Vance said Iran had chosen not to accept US terms, saying the US needed a commitment that Iran would not seek a nuclear weapon. For Iran's part, an Iranian semi-official news outlet said the demands were excessive, and Parliamentary Speaker Mohamed Bakay Ghalibaf, who led the Iranian delegation, said the US had not won his team's trust. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Bagay, said it shouldn't have been expected that a result would be achieved from one day of talks. We reached understandings on a number of issues. That's the reality. However, regarding two or three important issues, the views were distant and ultimately did not lead to an agreement. But if the ceasefire was already looking perilous leading into talks, it became even more fragile hours after. Joining me now live on the telephone with the very latest is the nation's 45th and 47th President of the United States, President Donald J. Trump. Phoning in to Fox News, US President Donald Trump elaborated on a social media post he'd just made, saying he'd directed the US Navy to blockade the Strait of Hormuz. We've got a lot of ships, so we're bringing them up. We think that numerous countries are going to be helping us with this also, but we're putting on a complete blockade. Iran has maintained a stranglehold over the Strait of Hormuz since the beginning of the war, threatening and attacking commercial ships and causing chaos in global energy markets. President Trump said Iran promised to reopen the Strait with the ceasefire and knowingly failed. Taking aim at reports Iran was charging a toll for ships to pass through the Strait and that sea mines had been placed by Iran. Mr Trump described Iran's actions as world extortion and a US blockade of the Strait would begin shortly. Speaking to Fox News, he also said work would begin on destroying sea mines. So we have minesweepers there now. We have highly sophisticated underwater minesweepers, which are the latest and the greatest, but we're also bringing in more traditional minesweepers. And so I understand is the UK and a couple of other countries are sending minesweepers. A lot of countries don't have minesweepers. The US president weighed in on negotiations and said while points that were agreed to were better than continuing military operations, those points didn't matter compared to the single most important issue of Iranian nuclear ambitions. The other issue complicating the ceasefire is Israel's continuing assault on Lebanon and the Iranian-backed militant group Hezbollah. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu crossed into southern Lebanon on Sunday, visiting Israeli soldiers and saying there is more to do. Talks are scheduled between Israeli and Lebanese officials on Tuesday, although crucially, those aren't talks between Israel and Hezbollah. This is Tim Swanston in Dubai reporting for AM. Professor Usha Haley is an international business expert from Wichita State University in the United States. Professor Haley, what's the most likely short-term impact on oil prices if the US Navy continues to blockade the Strait of Hormuz? Well, oil prices are expected to rise when they open on Monday. And so that's what's going to happen right away because, well, there's going to be reduced supply. They're already talking about, I think, maybe a one and a half to two. They've already gotten about 10 billion barrels a day stopped and this is going to be another one and a half billion or so more. And what happens in the longer term if the straits aren't reopened? The International Monetary Fund is expected to meet this coming week and the prognostication is reduced global growth. The global growth projections have varied from half a percent to one percent down. And so that's what we're expecting. It really depends on how long this conflict goes on, how long the blockade of the strait goes on and whether critical infrastructure is damaged. And what's this doing to certainty and the planning prospects for businesses worldwide at the moment as they try and figure out what's happening and how long it might last? Oh, it's just heightened economic uncertainty all around. Can't make projections. People are expecting prices to rise. It's not just oil, but also everything associated with oil. So certain plastics, certain pharmaceuticals and, of course, fertilizer. It's going to hit farmers really hard. And how does this current crisis differ from some of the past oil shocks, particularly in terms of that long-term impact? There's a lot of uncertainty and then one keeps wondering what we're doing in the Strait of Hormuz. This is not unexpected. It's the only card that Iran has, the Strait of Hormuz. episodes.description: Israel agrees to start ceasefire talks with Lebanon, as its continued attacks on Hezbollah sites in the country strain the already fragile 2-day-old ceasefire in the Middle East.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Good morning, welcome to AM. It's Friday the 10th of April. I'm Rachel Mealy coming to you from the lands of the Turbul and Yaghera people in Brisbane. Israel's continued attacks on Hezbollah sites in Lebanon are jeopardising the already fragile two-day-old ceasefire in the Middle East. US President Donald Trump has called on Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to be more low-key in Lebanon as it continues negotiations to bring the war to an end. Iran has threatened to pull out of this weekend's peace talks in Pakistan if Lebanon isn't brought under the terms of the ceasefire. Correspondent Matthew Doran is in Jerusalem. Matthew, what's the latest on the fragile ceasefire in the Middle East? Well, it does seem to be holding as much as it seems weird to describe it as holding when we have seen a considerable amount of disruption, a considerable number of strikes in the last short while since that deal was announced in the very early hours of Wednesday morning local time. The most shocking, I think you could say, part of that was yesterday in Lebanon with Israel launching strikes hitting more than 100 different sites in the course of just a 10 minute window. The death toll as a result of that action being now more than 200 people with many more hundreds having been injured as a result of it. That has really cast a light on whether or not this ceasefire, whether or not this very fragile truce can actually hold. And it goes to this issue which has arisen where there are differing versions of what this ceasefire actually covers. Clearly Israel, backed in here by the United States, says that Israel's bombardment of Lebanon against claimed Hezbollah sites is not included in this truce, whereas Iran, the other major player here, and of course Pakistan, which is the country which brokered this agreement, they both say that Lebanon is covered by it. And as a result, we've seen Israel continue to launch its strikes against claimed Hezbollah targets. episodes.description: One of the greatest tragedies of war is the loss of innocent life, and it’s rightly at the forefront of how we measure the cost of conflict. Against that reality, the protection of buildings and monuments can seem frivolous — even misplaced.

And the trees. So there's a complete kind of reset through this absolute destruction that's going on there. Yeah? Yes. Anthony, it's something that we have witnessed that is extremely new, which is void. So you feel that there is no more energy there. There's no more life there. Beyond emptiness, it's void. These kinds of villages, I mean, they've evolved over generations, haven't they? They've been people's houses, they've been in the family through a number of generations. So these aren't sort of new suburbs. No, no, no. There's absolutely no new suburbs there. We're talking about villages that are old between, some of them will have monuments that are 500 years old. Others will have monuments that sometimes they go back to 700 years old. The ancestral family villages go back to at least 200 years old. So we're talking about historical villages that have organically grown with time, with the family expansion, and the children adding houses to the ancestral family house. We're not talking about anything modern here. We're talking about traditional houses and traditional villages that have been passed on from one generation to the other for the last 500, 600, 700 years. And we're talking about also the historical monuments, such as the mosques, such as the churches, or even the shrines. Everything have been destroyed in southern Lebanon, up next to the border. And the area that is a little bit located, a little bit more further to the border, that's where the destruction is taking place. And it's an uprooting of the population. But because people were able to go back in 2024, before they were able to rebuild some of it. When, you know, they have worked this house, where in one area they have made it impossible to return, and in other areas people were able to return. So amongst all of this, like, systematic destruction that's going on, what is the work you're trying to do here? What's the value that you're trying to bring to this diabolical situation? We work on two different levels. Either we work on antiquities and archaeological sites and storages, which is done with private collections, or with the government institutions, where we try to secure the collections outside of the bombing areas. Or we work on the villages and the communities where we try to document what they had and what they have lost. Because once you know, you cannot unknow. And we want them to know what they have lost, as it being part of the history. So adding the scientific element of architectural history, or the value of the historical houses, it adds another layer of pain that is true, where you even know even more that the house that you have lost is not just your family house, it's also a historical building. But at the same time, it adds also an element of pride that now we know what we have lost. In terms of not just me and my memories, but as a general loss for the nation. So we document what have been lost in order to assess the level of damage assessment or destruction assessment. And we provide this information back to the communities. And we give this to the policy level at the government level for any reconstruction plan that will be worked upon for the South in order for it to include the historical buildings as part of the reconstruction plan and remunerate people accordingly in order to push for the preservation of the history. So there's a kind of an archaeology of resistance going on here. And the uses of this archive that you're, or the work that you're doing, the surveying work and the archaeology that you're doing, is about maintaining that memory, maintaining its access to that memory. Is that right? Yes, absolutely. We see it also as an act of resistance to a war that aims at also eradicating the history of the place. Of course, it's a Pacific resistance, but it's still resistance. What that means to you and me is that it is something that they can do with very little extra staffing or thought. But it is something that can make their job significantly more easy. So it was dead easy for a group of Sunni extremists to walk into the Al-Aqshiri mosque in Samara, the third holiest place in Shia Islam, and blow it up. And I'm not saying there was a simple, direct, and one only link between the destruction of the mosque and the emergence and re-emergence of those two organisations. But there was a very firm, heavily dotted line between the two. That's a strong argument for protecting places of cultural significance during war. They are beginning to understand. That was my next question. Are they starting to listen? They are starting to listen. So there is a thing that most people generically call a no-strike list that the military pull together if they're going into a conflict. episodes.title: Extraordinary Everyday : Gravestones
episodes.description: Gravestones may be stark reminders of our mortality, but they’re also powerful records of history, identity and belief. What can the design of these enduring markers tell us about the people they commemorate — and the eras they lived through?
episodes.transcript: We're always chasing the next big invention, the gadget that promises to make life easier, and it's those new ideas that tend to grab the headlines. But on Extraordinary Every Day, we turn the spotlight elsewhere, focusing on the ingenious designs that have been with us far longer and that many of us use every day. Today, we're exploring the surprisingly fascinating world of gravestones. It's an epitaph meant to endure across generations, your final footprint on the world. Gravestones may be stark reminders of our mortality, but they're also rich repositories of history and memory. So what can the design of these markers tell us about the people they commemorate and, the errors they lived through? And how have these designs changed over time? Satch Killam is a stonemason and heritage specialist who works at Rookwood Cemetery in Sydney. Hi, Satch. Hello. Let's get into headstones and gravestones then. And I suppose the first really obvious question is, what's the difference between a headstone and a gravestone? And why is that a good thing to know about? I think in this space and in stonemasonry, there's often people will say something very definitive, but really, it's all right to have a little bit of difference on this. A gravestone is the wider term, and a headstone is actually quite literally started off being as a headstone. You'd have a headstone and a footstone, or perhaps a headstone, a body stone and a footstone. So you're indicating where the person is. But I think the idea of a headstone is actually quite evocative because we want to know where the person's buried and which is the head of the grave. So we orientate ourselves. We know where the dead person is, which is kind of culturally significant if you think about it, that that's important to us. It's not just a space. It's an exact space. What's the earliest recorded gravestones that we know of then? That's a very difficult question because that's how you define gravestones. So very early peoples often had grave goods. There's different markings. Often shells were associated with burials. Shells are a very good object, and they'll come up into our conversation, I'm sure, later because shells are calcium carbonate. So they have a double diffraction, and they're very bright. They're bright in dusk. They're bright at night. You can see them by the moon. So they're a fantastic way to mark a grave and to be able to find a spot. And really, that's one of the key elements of a headstone, a gravestone, is that you want it to be seen. You want it to be a place that someone knows to come to and a place of remembrance. But it all starts with somewhere that you have to be able to find it. I would have thought that sandstone was too soft a stone to use for a gravestone or a headstone because it does weather, sandstone, more than something like granite. I mean, these must be choices that are being made all the time, I suppose, about the longevity of these markers. Yeah. Yeah. People choose their gravestones based on what's available. So the cemeteries that look the best to us now that are the most accessible are where the stone was actually a good stone for cemeteries. However, masons have known this, architects have known this for a long time, what is a good stone. And Sydney sandstone, there are Sydney sandstones that are fantastic and will last hundreds and hundreds of years, if not thousands of years. So what are the oldest cemeteries in Australia then? I just came from the oldest extant cemetery in mainland Australia, which is St. John's Parramatta, right across from the ABC Studios. And a fantastic place to look at if one is interested in the history and the evolution of gravestones because it's all written there in the landscape. The oldest cemetery that's kind of still active is actually in Norfolk Island and is a fantastic cemetery to go to if you ever have the opportunity. Coral gravestones that have lasted hundreds of years. So a coral limestone. And you work at Rookwood Cemetery, is that correct? Yes.
