episodes.title: Is adaptive reuse worth the investment?
episodes.description: Heritage buildings can be pretty … but are they worth the money? Adaptive reuse advocates argue that reworking existing structures isn’t about nostalgia — it’s about unlocking potential.
episodes.transcript: We're often told heritage buildings should be preserved, carefully protected and left untouched. Don't get me wrong, I love an old building that's been thoughtfully brought back to life. But there's something else that can happen in these spaces, something beyond restoration. I'm talking about reinvention. It can mean giving a building a completely new purpose or reworking its bones in smarter, more sustainable ways. This is Adaptive Reuse and it's what we're diving into today. Hello, I'm Anthony Burke and this is By Design on ABC Radio National. Adaptive reuse takes time. It can cost more. But for those who choose to reimagine existing buildings, it's driven by passion and by a simple truth. The most sustainable building is the one that already exists. The challenge? You can't use a generic plan. These buildings demand patience, detail and creative problem solving. Things designers love and budgets don't. So, how do you update a building without losing its soul? The very first thing that kind of had a big impact on me was the real estate listing and I saw these pictures of this very humble little cottage on this picturesque riverside setting and beautiful stone chimneys and I just thought it looked like heaven. That's Hannah Chapman. We'll come back to Hannah and what it took to revive the old post office and turn it into a living space. But first, let's come to grips with what adaptive reuse actually means. Hannah Louie is a professor in the School of Architecture at Melbourne University and co-author of Adapt, Designing New Lives for Old Buildings. Traditionally, adaptive reuse is a term that means basically a place or a building that undergoes a change of function or use from its original intended purpose. We were really keen to expand this so that we're interested in adaptive reuse across a kind of spectrum of change. And that might be change of use. But it might also be changing the way a building performs, like sustainability measures. It might be changing ownership and changing the way it's valued. And most of those come with inevitable changes of use. But it's a kind of spectrum. And I reckon there's really good examples at either end of that spectrum of change about defining what do you mean by adaptive reuse. And it might be complete change. A good example is turning what was a prison warden's building into a childcare centre in Kovork, which is a really interesting one, or maybe a church into contemporary multiple residential housing. So there's a lot of change of use going on there. And then at the other end, there might be more subtle changes. There's some great fairly recent public buildings. The Broadmeadows Town Hall in Melbourne's one by Kirsten Thompson Architects or the Great Cobb Art Museum is another great one by Dunhillam in regional New South Wales, where it's not a whole lot of change. So it may not technically be a lot of change of use. But in the end, you've really adapted and reused the building to make it work today. And so what's the big difference then in people's minds? How should we separate the idea of adaptive reuse and heritage restoration? Yeah, and they overlap. But at one end, I think the heritage restoration is a faithful conserving and restoring of the authentic fabric of what was there before. And that often does include the use, but not always, because there's an argument that heritage buildings need to be used. So they might change the use. But in changing that use, you're not changing the integral exterior or interior fabric and design and ethos of the building. Whereas at the other end, you might be dealing with historic buildings, but they might not be the sort of capital H heritage, state, national registered buildings. So there's a lot more room for creativity, room to move in how much and how you change things. I do tell my students often, actually, that I think adaptive reuse is where the best designs are happening, because you do have to be so focused on the small things that add up to the single picture. And you're dealing with so much more time and depth. And do you agree with that? Yeah, no, definitely. And I think as educators, I mean, I'm the same in a university setting, but this is the way forward. And I think I'm seeing that generation, the generation of students now, this is what they really want to talk about. And it's not just architects and designers, but it is all these people like quantity surveyors, planners, construction managements, you know, students in training courses in universities that need to be equipped with engaging with that existing context. And that's really different to how 20th century education was, you know, where we valued, say, from a modernist legacy. It's like blank slate, start again. Everything's new. Everything's shiny. Everything's isolated on its own. We've really got past that. And sometimes that's hard. It's hard as a teacher and it's hard as a student to go to go, look what I've done. You know, I've done this wazzy render. In fact, no, you know, you've done all these small but sensitive moves that aren't as showy. That's right. Not as showy, but much more meaningful. Yeah. Yeah. So, okay, let's just take a step back then because there are challenges here, obviously, in adaptive reuse projects. And I'm thinking in particular of updating things like commercial buildings to current commercial standards. You've got a great inventory of examples there. What kind of extra challenges are you coming across time and again in that kind of adaptive reuse? You can't gloss over the challenges because it is really complex. And it's complex in terms of things like meeting current regulations, which is huge in terms of accessibility, fire regulations, dealing with materials that are no longer fit for purpose. And, you know, asbestos is always the big one where if anyone wants to argue to knock something down. So there are huge challenges, I think. But by providing case studies, by providing know-how, by providing just that will to get around them, you know, I think it is possible. And there has been, yeah, there is some really good examples, but there's been a lot of focus on turning office towers, which we may not need in the future, into housing. And that's seen as a bit of a panacea for a housing shortage. And there's been a lot of interesting experiments. There's been some in US cities to varying degrees of success. And it's really difficult because an office tower, you know, there's all sorts of different needs in terms of ventilation, how you access them, the shape of the building floors and the access to natural light if you're going to make them into successful housing. But, yeah, there are good examples. I mean, there's a great tower that's been converted into assisted aged care living apartments in South Melbourne. And I think it's been really popular and the development is continuing. So, you know, I think it's case by case, piece by piece. You gradually build the know-how. So a building doesn't have to be a quaint cottage like Hannah Chapman's in Tasmania. It could just as easily be a pared back modernist office block from the 1960s or a heavy concrete brutalist museum from the 70s. As Carl Elefonte, ex-president of the American Institute of Architects, said, The greenest building is the one already standing, which means adaptive reuse pushes well beyond the kind of houses you might see on Restoration Australia and into far more unexpected territory. And there are plenty of reasons why reworking an existing building can be far more sustainable than starting from scratch. There's embodied carbon, meaning materials and structures, say like a big concrete frame structure that has carbon built into it from when it's constructed. And it has wastage involved in demolition. So and in dealing with waste materials, of which the construction sector is a huge contributor to waste and emissions from that perspective. And then I think there's keeping existing buildings and adapting them to perform better environmentally. That's a real imperative, you know, as easy as putting double glazing in, increasing the insulation. But there's also often historical buildings that actually perform better. They're more climatically suited to our environment that are sort of pre-air conditioning, pre-kind of wholesale cheap energy of the mid-20th century, that we can actually retain and get the benefits from. So there's a whole raft of reasons why an existing or adaptive reuse project is environmentally better for us. And the social argument for adaptive reuse, it seems to me that one of the things I love about adaptive reuse the most is that these layers of story are given a kind of a breadth of new, they're brought back to life, you know, they're brought back into the sort of like the current storytelling of architecture. Is that sort of social side, that sense of building community, something that you feel is very present in the adaptive reuse conversations? Yeah, absolutely. And that's also partly why we're kind of not just interested in those sort of heritage, really high level heritage buildings and things that we would think of as monuments in our places, but more the sort of myriad of valuable but less prominent, less landmark places that communities really embed in individual and community collective memory. And so conserving those, whether that's just the exterior or the whole place, really contributes to sense of place, to identity in suburbs, in regions, in city centres. So they are part of that social fabric, I think. And yeah, there's some great examples of the more socially minded adaptive reuse, I think, as well. Like there was a former hospital in part of Fremantle in Western Australia that's been converted into supported accommodation for men in a hostile situation by space agency. And it's a sort of gentle, yeah, socially minded adaptation of a place. The other part about this, I suppose, the whole conversation, this can be expensive because it does take a little longer. When you're doing this kind of adaptive reuse work, you kind of have to be a little bit forensic about the thing that you're adapting and reusing. So is there an economic argument for adaptive reuse? Yeah, I mean, there's no doubt that keeping existing buildings and adapting them comes with, as you said, with a price tag, and that is time and money. And, you know, in shows like yours on the ABC, you often see that. But I think part of a motivation of looking at this area is to sort of provide some persuasive tools and case studies for clients, building owners, builders, policymakers to see how we might think of some of those short term pain points, but think more in terms of longer term rewards and thinking of buildings more as long term public assets. And how do you add that value into the equation? And I think other countries have or are currently implementing regulations and incentives to get over some of the financial barriers like, you know, making building owners and developers truly account for the cost of demolishing the existing building as part of that financial equation so that starting with a blank slate isn't free. And then also other, you know, carrot and stick approaches like financial incentives for retention through tax breaks, through development incentives and so on, and harder regulations around demolition and accounting for that true cost of both material and embodied carbon wastage. So, you know, people are having to justify why am I demolishing rather than, you know, sort of just carte blanche, basically. Yeah. I mean, actually, what you just said reminds me, like, it's not so much a question of price. Yes, it does maybe cost a little more, but the real conversation there is in values and what do we value. And, of course, that's a much bigger conversation than price alone, which is what you were alluding to, that cultural value that we, it's hard to put a price on. Yeah, yeah. And I think part of it is really re-evaluating value and it can be historic and heritage value that we've already talked about. It can be just ways of rethinking economic value. How do we account for the scarcity of buildings, of craftsmanship, of materials, of that contextual value that those old and existing places bring to make precincts and neighbourhoods and cities vibrant? And there is actually some interesting work being done by quantity surveyors at the moment. How do you actually put a dollar of economic value on the sort of knock-on effects of keeping some old fabric, you know, in an area like, say, I know it's been a real focus in Collingwood, in Melbourne. And then that, in turn, adds value to its neighbours. So there's some interesting, I think, work. And then even also in regional centres, I mean, some great examples of reuse of, say, I know in Western Australia in the town of Catanning, Catanning Flower Mill has been converted into a hotel for some time by Space Agency. And it's really brought economic vibrancy back to a country town. Speaking of country towns, let's head back to Carlton in Tasmania, where Hannah Chapman is staring down a long list of renovations, each with a hefty price tag attached. I asked whether the cost of bringing this little piece of Riverside history back to life ever gave her pause. Yeah, look, absolutely. There were several kind of evolutions of what it might be that we would do once we finally could do anything. And then simultaneously, I think interest rates had been going through the roof and we didn't know how long this period of uncertainty would last. So we actually decided to sort of free up the equity in our family home and sell that and rent so that we could actually, when we finally could do something, first just to relieve the pressure, but then also so that we had options. Restoring the post office and turning it into a genuinely livable home meant Hannah had to stretch herself financially. In the end, a heritage grant helped ease some of that pressure. But beyond the cost of the build, one of the biggest hurdles was something less tangible. Before a single dollar could be spent on renovations, Hannah had to navigate an extraordinary amount of bureaucratic red tape, a process that proved just as challenging as the construction itself. They were considering that it was a commercial building and we would need to do a change of use in order to make it something residential, which would have been an impossible disaster because it would have invoked the modern building code. And as you know, there is basically not a straight line in that cottage, which again is part of the charm, but completely kind of unapproachable if you're going to try to attempt modern standards. So that was a really long protracted battle and a really big barrier. But really in those early colonial days, these very humble, almost huts really with this split slab construction were just put up and they were serving really as a dwelling for the postmaster. So there would be a humble kitchen, there would be, you know, a humble bedroom. Emphasis on the word humble. I'm saying that a lot, aren't I? No, but I'm agreeing with you. Yeah, so and actually eventually we did convince council, the relevant council involved, that that was the case, but it did take two years. And red tape isn't just an issue for small residential projects like the post office in Tasmania. Hannah Louie again. We interviewed a whole raft of design architects in our project and they all talked about that. So that's real. But we also interviewed Australian state government architects and they were really on board to thinking differently about that regulatory framework. But I think also Australia needs to look here. You know, I'm not always saying we need to look over our shoulder at other places that are doing it better. But there are examples in Europe, in the UK and in specific cities that have put forward ways of getting through this regulation burdens. And, you know, that's a balance between fostering good design, about heritage protections, value for money. So it's complex. But I think there are ways in which you might be able to incentivise adaptive reuse and make that pathway quicker and more efficient. And that's partly by, yeah, getting policymakers on board to say, you know, maybe rather than no, I guess. Okay, I'll take a maybe for now over a no. So does that, in your mind, does that red tape sort of land mostly in the planning and zoning kind of area or more in, let's say, the standards of contemporary building versus older buildings? Like, I think it's all of those things. And ironically, also, a lot of the architects are saying that it's actually the sustainability regulation, which is not kind of calibrated right yet here. So that to make a building perform to standard, it's really difficult. And that needs to be rethought so that there's some offsets for say, okay, you get sort of some stars in your rating system for retaining fabric, for retaining materials. And then we'll work to see how we can make it perform. But at the moment, yeah, there's some big barriers in making them to code. I'm hearing also, I guess, that adaptive reuse is becoming more popular. It's certainly becoming more prolific. Do you sort of see it becoming more popular? And how can we help that along? Well, I think it's just by necessity and by desire. You need both of those things. You need the regulation, but you also need the want to, you know, yeah. And so I hope it's becoming more popular. And that's partly, I think, we use the word old in our title of our book of rather than existing. And someone said that we had a book launch the other day and someone said, why didn't you use the word existing buildings instead of old buildings? And I was sort of saying, well, I kind of want to be a bit provocative that Australians need to love old things a bit more. You know, we're quite good at getting rid of old things. And then we mourn them when they're gone. And so we need to rethink obsolescence and make it popular, make it desirable, make it the places to be. And it's already happening in hospitality and in, you know, all sorts of venues that are capitalizing on that. So, yeah, it needs to become more widespread. I was also thinking about it with a stupid analogy because I'm going to the dentist tomorrow. Oh, I can't wait for this. It might be. You know, it's a bit like what dentistry used to be, which is basically too difficult to deal with your old teeth. So they used to take them all out and put in a set of false teeth, which we now know was really bad for the health of the whole body, for all sorts of things. And now we nurse each tooth, or they do in my old mouth, you know, we nurse each tooth along and tinker with it and keep it there. And so I sort of feel like that's our cities as well. Where do you think the major opportunities are for future adaptive reuse projects? The opportunities, like the things that will really make a difference for us? Well, I think we're not bad at valuing 19th century buildings. And when we did this work and seeing a lot of examples, you tend to get the same kind of aesthetic of, yeah, we want to keep old red brick, timber, buildings of that era. We're less good about thinking about 20th century, mid-20th century, late 20th century buildings. But they are so substantial. And again, that's what things like these heritage surveys have happened in the Hoddle Street grid survey in Melbourne as one, but they're happening everywhere. There's all this sort of, yeah, 1950s, 60s building stock. And that embodies so much calm and so much materials. I mean, I happen to really like modern architecture. I know a lot of people don't. But I think there is such opportunities in imaginatively reusing that building stock. Back in Tasmania, Hannah Chapman's post office was finished and is now an Airbnb. For her, tinkering with the old post office in Carlton was definitely worth the time and money. We sort of have this idea that one day we'll retire there and perhaps, you know, build a modern extension. And so long as I can drag my husband away from the city. But it's just, you know, it does bring us a lot of joy. And as much as sharing it with other people might have seemed like, you know, something that we felt hesitant to do, it's actually been incredibly rewarding to see other people also fall in love with it. And to see people really relax there and appreciate the history of the building, the significance of it and the way that it's been conserved. Falling for a sweet little riverside cottage can come with its fair share of headaches. Red tape, rising costs and plenty of uncertainty. But stories like Hannah's make it clear that there are real rewards in investing in our past in this way. For me, it's a space where I think some of our best architectural design is happening. Because you need to think in detail. There is no off-the-shelf solution for taking non-standard circumstances and making them new ones. And after all, you're breathing new life into the stories that give a building meaning and depth, which we know is so important to our sense of belonging and place. If we take the opportunity, as Hannah Louie suggests, to rethink what we've labelled as obsolete and instead see possibility, we're not only making a more environmentally responsible choice, we're opening the door to a whole lot of creative ones too. Do you have a favourite building or home that has been adapted? Write to us and tell us where and why you love it so much. I love getting your emails. Speaking of which, By Design listener Ian emailed in. He says, I enjoyed your program featuring your engagement with the exceptionally vivacious Indonesian artist, Josephine. And I was thinking a nice follow-up might be a show featuring or drawing connection with Australia's northern Aboriginal batik weavers. Great idea, Ian. We'll put that one in our ideas bucket for a future episode. I love getting your thoughts on the program, so keep them coming. You can email me at bydesign at abc.net.au. segments.text: We're often told heritage buildings should be preserved, carefully protected and left untouched.
Don't get me wrong, I love an old building that's been thoughtfully brought back to life.
But there's something else that can happen in these spaces, something beyond restoration.
It can mean giving a building a completely new purpose or reworking its bones in smarter, more sustainable ways.
This is Adaptive Reuse and it's what we're diving into today.
Hello, I'm Anthony Burke and this is By Design on ABC Radio National.
But for those who choose to reimagine existing buildings, it's driven by passion and by a simple truth.
The most sustainable building is the one that already exists.
You can't use a generic plan.
These buildings demand patience, detail and creative problem solving.
Things designers love and budgets don't.
So, how do you update a building without losing its soul?

The very first thing that kind of had a big impact on me was the real estate listing and I saw these pictures of this very humble little cottage on this picturesque riverside setting and beautiful stone chimneys and I just thought it looked like heaven.
We'll come back to Hannah and what it took to revive the old post office and turn it into a living space.
But first, let's come to grips with what adaptive reuse actually means.
Hannah Louie is a professor in the School of Architecture at Melbourne University and co-author of Adapt, Designing New Lives for Old Buildings.
Traditionally, adaptive reuse is a term that means basically a place or a building that undergoes a change of function or use from its original intended purpose.
We were really keen to expand this so that we're interested in adaptive reuse across a kind of spectrum of change.
And that might be change of use.
But it might also be changing the way a building performs, like sustainability measures.
It might be changing ownership and changing the way it's valued.
And most of those come with inevitable changes of use.
But it's a kind of spectrum.
And I reckon there's really good examples at either end of that spectrum of change about defining what do you mean by adaptive reuse.
And it might be complete change.
A good example is turning what was a prison warden's building into a childcare centre in Kovork, which is a really interesting one, or maybe a church into contemporary multiple residential housing.
So there's a lot of change of use going on there.
And then at the other end, there might be more subtle changes.
There's some great fairly recent public buildings.

The Broadmeadows Town Hall in Melbourne's one by Kirsten Thompson Architects or the Great Cobb Art Museum is another great one by Dunhillam in regional New South Wales, where it's not a whole lot of change.
So it may not technically be a lot of change of use.
But in the end, you've really adapted and reused the building to make it work today.
And so what's the big difference then in people's minds?
How should we separate the idea of adaptive reuse and heritage restoration?
But at one end, I think the heritage restoration is a faithful conserving and restoring of the authentic fabric of what was there before.
And that often does include the use, but not always, because there's an argument that heritage buildings need to be used.
So they might change the use.
But in changing that use, you're not changing the integral exterior or interior fabric and design and ethos of the building.
Whereas at the other end, you might be dealing with historic buildings, but they might not be the sort of capital H heritage, state, national registered buildings.
So there's a lot more room for creativity, room to move in how much and how you change things.
I do tell my students often, actually, that I think adaptive reuse is where the best designs are happening, because you do have to be so focused on the small things that add up to the single picture.
And you're dealing with so much more time and depth.
And do you agree with that?
And I think as educators, I mean, I'm the same in a university setting, but this is the way forward.
And I think I'm seeing that generation, the generation of students now, this is what they really want to talk about.
And it's not just architects and designers, but it is all these people like quantity surveyors, planners, construction managements,
you know, students in training courses in universities that need to be equipped with engaging with that existing context.
And that's really different to how 20th century education was, you know, where we valued, say, from a modernist legacy.
It's like blank slate, start again.
It's hard as a teacher and it's hard as a student to go to go, look what I've done.
You know, I've done this wazzy render.
In fact, no, you know, you've done all these small but sensitive moves that aren't as showy.
Not as showy, but much more meaningful.
So, okay, let's just take a step back then because there are challenges here, obviously, in adaptive reuse projects.
And I'm thinking in particular of updating things like commercial buildings to current commercial standards.
You've got a great inventory of examples there.
What kind of extra challenges are you coming across time and again in that kind of adaptive reuse?
You can't gloss over the challenges because it is really complex.
And it's complex in terms of things like meeting current regulations, which is huge in terms of accessibility, fire regulations, dealing with materials that are no longer fit for purpose.
And, you know, asbestos is always the big one where if anyone wants to argue to knock something down.
So there are huge challenges, I think.
But by providing case studies, by providing know-how, by providing just that will to get around them, you know, I think it is possible.
And there has been, yeah, there is some really good examples, but there's been a lot of focus on turning office towers, which we may not need in the future, into housing.
And that's seen as a bit of a panacea for a housing shortage.
And there's been a lot of interesting experiments.
There's been some in US cities to varying degrees of success.

And it's really difficult because an office tower, you know, there's all sorts of different needs in terms of ventilation, how you access them, the shape of the building floors and the access to natural light if you're going to make them into successful housing.
But, yeah, there are good examples.
I mean, there's a great tower that's been converted into assisted aged care living apartments in South Melbourne.
And I think it's been really popular and the development is continuing.
So, you know, I think it's case by case, piece by piece.
So a building doesn't have to be a quaint cottage like Hannah Chapman's in Tasmania.
It could just as easily be a pared back modernist office block from the 1960s or a heavy concrete brutalist museum from the 70s.
As Carl Elefonte, ex-president of the American Institute of Architects, said,
The greenest building is the one already standing, which means adaptive reuse pushes well beyond the kind of houses you might see on Restoration Australia and into far more unexpected territory.
And there are plenty of reasons why reworking an existing building can be far more sustainable than starting from scratch.
There's embodied carbon, meaning materials and structures, say like a big concrete frame structure that has carbon built into it from when it's constructed.
And it has wastage involved in demolition.
So and in dealing with waste materials, of which the construction sector is a huge contributor to waste and emissions from that perspective.
And then I think there's keeping existing buildings and adapting them to perform better environmentally.
That's a real imperative, you know, as easy as putting double glazing in, increasing the insulation.
But there's also often historical buildings that actually perform better.
They're more climatically suited to our environment that are sort of pre-air conditioning, pre-kind of wholesale cheap energy of the mid-20th century,
that we can actually retain and get the benefits from.
So there's a whole raft of reasons why an existing or adaptive reuse project is environmentally better for us.
And the social argument for adaptive reuse, it seems to me that one of the things I love about adaptive reuse the most is that these layers of story are given a kind of a breadth of new,
they're brought back to life, you know, they're brought back into the sort of like the current storytelling of architecture.
Is that sort of social side, that sense of building community, something that you feel is very present in the adaptive reuse conversations?
And that's also partly why we're kind of not just interested in those sort of heritage, really high level heritage buildings and things that we would think of as monuments in our places,
but more the sort of myriad of valuable but less prominent, less landmark places that communities really embed in individual and community collective memory.
And so conserving those, whether that's just the exterior or the whole place,
really contributes to sense of place, to identity in suburbs, in regions, in city centres.
So they are part of that social fabric, I think.
And yeah, there's some great examples of the more socially minded adaptive reuse, I think, as well.
Like there was a former hospital in part of Fremantle in Western Australia that's been converted into supported accommodation for men in a hostile situation by space agency.
And it's a sort of gentle, yeah, socially minded adaptation of a place.
The other part about this, I suppose, the whole conversation, this can be expensive because it does take a little longer.
When you're doing this kind of adaptive reuse work, you kind of have to be a little bit forensic about the thing that you're adapting and reusing.
So is there an economic argument for adaptive reuse?
Yeah, I mean, there's no doubt that keeping existing buildings and adapting them comes with, as you said, with a price tag, and that is time and money.
And, you know, in shows like yours on the ABC, you often see that.

But I think part of a motivation of looking at this area is to sort of provide some persuasive tools and case studies for clients, building owners, builders, policymakers to see how we might think of some of those short term pain points, but think more in terms of longer term rewards and thinking of buildings more as long term public assets.
And how do you add that value into the equation?

And I think other countries have or are currently implementing regulations and incentives to get over some of the financial barriers like, you know, making building owners and developers truly account for the cost of demolishing the existing building as part of that financial equation so that starting with a blank slate isn't free.

And then also other, you know, carrot and stick approaches like financial incentives for retention through tax breaks, through development incentives and so on, and harder regulations around demolition and accounting for that true cost of both material and embodied carbon wastage.
So, you know, people are having to justify why am I demolishing rather than, you know, sort of just carte blanche, basically.
I mean, actually, what you just said reminds me, like, it's not so much a question of price.
Yes, it does maybe cost a little more, but the real conversation there is in values and what do we value.
And, of course, that's a much bigger conversation than price alone, which is what you were alluding to, that cultural value that we, it's hard to put a price on.
And I think part of it is really re-evaluating value and it can be historic and heritage value that we've already talked about.
It can be just ways of rethinking economic value.

How do we account for the scarcity of buildings, of craftsmanship, of materials, of that contextual value that those old and existing places bring to make precincts and neighbourhoods and cities vibrant?
And there is actually some interesting work being done by quantity surveyors at the moment.

How do you actually put a dollar of economic value on the sort of knock-on effects of keeping some old fabric, you know, in an area like, say, I know it's been a real focus in Collingwood, in Melbourne.
And then that, in turn, adds value to its neighbours.
So there's some interesting, I think, work.

And then even also in regional centres, I mean, some great examples of reuse of, say, I know in Western Australia in the town of Catanning, Catanning Flower Mill has been converted into a hotel for some time by Space Agency.
And it's really brought economic vibrancy back to a country town.
Speaking of country towns, let's head back to Carlton in Tasmania, where Hannah Chapman is staring down a long list of renovations, each with a hefty price tag attached.
I asked whether the cost of bringing this little piece of Riverside history back to life ever gave her pause.
There were several kind of evolutions of what it might be that we would do once we finally could do anything.
And then simultaneously, I think interest rates had been going through the roof and we didn't know how long this period of uncertainty would last.

So we actually decided to sort of free up the equity in our family home and sell that and rent so that we could actually, when we finally could do something, first just to relieve the pressure, but then also so that we had options.
Restoring the post office and turning it into a genuinely livable home meant Hannah had to stretch herself financially.
In the end, a heritage grant helped ease some of that pressure.
But beyond the cost of the build, one of the biggest hurdles was something less tangible.
Before a single dollar could be spent on renovations, Hannah had to navigate an extraordinary amount of bureaucratic red tape, a process that proved just as challenging as the construction itself.

They were considering that it was a commercial building and we would need to do a change of use in order to make it something residential, which would have been an impossible disaster because it would have invoked the modern building code.
And as you know, there is basically not a straight line in that cottage, which again is part of the charm, but completely kind of unapproachable if you're going to try to attempt modern standards.
So that was a really long protracted battle and a really big barrier.
But really in those early colonial days, these very humble, almost huts really with this split slab construction were just put up and they were serving really as a dwelling for the postmaster.
So there would be a humble kitchen, there would be, you know, a humble bedroom.
I'm saying that a lot, aren't I?
No, but I'm agreeing with you.
Yeah, so and actually eventually we did convince council, the relevant council involved, that that was the case, but it did take two years.
And red tape isn't just an issue for small residential projects like the post office in Tasmania.
We interviewed a whole raft of design architects in our project and they all talked about that.
But we also interviewed Australian state government architects and they were really on board to thinking differently about that regulatory framework.
But I think also Australia needs to look here.
You know, I'm not always saying we need to look over our shoulder at other places that are doing it better.
But there are examples in Europe, in the UK and in specific cities that have put forward ways of getting through this regulation burdens.
And, you know, that's a balance between fostering good design, about heritage protections, value for money.
But I think there are ways in which you might be able to incentivise adaptive reuse and make that pathway quicker and more efficient.
And that's partly by, yeah, getting policymakers on board to say, you know, maybe rather than no, I guess.
Okay, I'll take a maybe for now over a no.
So does that, in your mind, does that red tape sort of land mostly in the planning and zoning kind of area or more in, let's say, the standards of contemporary building versus older buildings?
Like, I think it's all of those things.
And ironically, also, a lot of the architects are saying that it's actually the sustainability regulation, which is not kind of calibrated right yet here.
So that to make a building perform to standard, it's really difficult.
And that needs to be rethought so that there's some offsets for say, okay, you get sort of some stars in your rating system for retaining fabric, for retaining materials.
And then we'll work to see how we can make it perform.
But at the moment, yeah, there's some big barriers in making them to code.
I'm hearing also, I guess, that adaptive reuse is becoming more popular.
Do you sort of see it becoming more popular?
And how can we help that along?
Well, I think it's just by necessity and by desire.
You need both of those things.
You need the regulation, but you also need the want to, you know, yeah.
And so I hope it's becoming more popular.
And that's partly, I think, we use the word old in our title of our book of rather than existing.
And someone said that we had a book launch the other day and someone said, why didn't you use the word existing buildings instead of old buildings?
And I was sort of saying, well, I kind of want to be a bit provocative that Australians need to love old things a bit more.
You know, we're quite good at getting rid of old things.
And then we mourn them when they're gone.
And so we need to rethink obsolescence and make it popular, make it desirable, make it the places to be.
And it's already happening in hospitality and in, you know, all sorts of venues that are capitalizing on that.
So, yeah, it needs to become more widespread.
I was also thinking about it with a stupid analogy because I'm going to the dentist tomorrow.
Oh, I can't wait for this.
You know, it's a bit like what dentistry used to be, which is basically too difficult to deal with your old teeth.
So they used to take them all out and put in a set of false teeth, which we now know was really bad for the health of the whole body, for all sorts of things.
And now we nurse each tooth, or they do in my old mouth, you know, we nurse each tooth along and tinker with it and keep it there.
And so I sort of feel like that's our cities as well.
Where do you think the major opportunities are for future adaptive reuse projects?
The opportunities, like the things that will really make a difference for us?
Well, I think we're not bad at valuing 19th century buildings.
And when we did this work and seeing a lot of examples, you tend to get the same kind of aesthetic of, yeah, we want to keep old red brick, timber, buildings of that era.
We're less good about thinking about 20th century, mid-20th century, late 20th century buildings.
And again, that's what things like these heritage surveys have happened in the Hoddle Street grid survey in Melbourne as one, but they're happening everywhere.
There's all this sort of, yeah, 1950s, 60s building stock.
And that embodies so much calm and so much materials.
I mean, I happen to really like modern architecture.
I know a lot of people don't.
But I think there is such opportunities in imaginatively reusing that building stock.
Back in Tasmania, Hannah Chapman's post office was finished and is now an Airbnb.
For her, tinkering with the old post office in Carlton was definitely worth the time and money.
We sort of have this idea that one day we'll retire there and perhaps, you know, build a modern extension.
And so long as I can drag my husband away from the city.
But it's just, you know, it does bring us a lot of joy.
And as much as sharing it with other people might have seemed like, you know, something that we felt hesitant to do,
it's actually been incredibly rewarding to see other people also fall in love with it.
And to see people really relax there and appreciate the history of the building, the significance of it and the way that it's been conserved.
Falling for a sweet little riverside cottage can come with its fair share of headaches.
Red tape, rising costs and plenty of uncertainty.
But stories like Hannah's make it clear that there are real rewards in investing in our past in this way.
For me, it's a space where I think some of our best architectural design is happening.
Because you need to think in detail.
There is no off-the-shelf solution for taking non-standard circumstances and making them new ones.
And after all, you're breathing new life into the stories that give a building meaning and depth,

we're not only making a more environmentally responsible choice,
we're opening the door to a whole lot of creative ones too.

episodes.title: Extraordinary Everyday: Pockets
episodes.description: Men expect them in every pair of pants, every jacket, every coat. And yet, for women, pockets have been mysteriously withheld, removed, resized, or declared “unnecessary” for centuries. Why?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. We spend most of our days using ordinary objects that make our life easier, but each one of those objects holds a delightful design story. Welcome to Extraordinary Every Day, where we bring that history back to life. Podcasts, could anything in clothing seem more ordinary? Probably not. I expect every pair of pants or jacket I buy to come with them, but that hasn't always been true for women's fashion. Throughout history, the need for pockets never disappeared, even when designers inexplicably removed them from women's clothing. Even now, the rare dress or skirt with pockets sparks a little thrill of surprise. So, I want to know more. Let's dive into the unexpected and quietly revolutionary story of pockets. And to talk all things pockets, I'm joined by Nicole Jenkins, who's a fashion historian. Hi, Nicole. Hi, Anthony. Thanks for joining me today. Pockets, who knew? So exciting. This is one of those things I guess I've never really given much thought to, but there's a huge history here, isn't there? There is, there is. And you're in a very fortunate position being a man because your clothes will automatically give you pockets, so you don't need to worry about it. I see. So, this has been gendered from the very beginning, yes? Pretty much, pretty much. So, when were the first pockets included in women's clothing then? Well, it's very hard to sort of differentiate because they are a kind of purse, a kind of handbag, a kind of bag that women originally would hang around their waist. And so, it started during about the 15th century, they think. But my feeling, I'm a sewer, and sewers know that when you're a sewer, when you make clothes, you just make clothes that fit your purpose. And so, I'm pretty confident that women would have been sewing pockets into garments or on top of them or, you know, they would have been customising their garments to suit their purposes for a long, long time. So, much earlier than the 15th century. Absolutely. We don't have evidence for it, but I know what people who sew do. So, what did those early pockets look like then? The early ones are called hanging pockets, and they're like little sort of bags that would hang on a cord around your waist. So, I guess in a way, a bit like a sort of waist version of a cross-body bag. Okay. So, they're quite big then, yeah? They're like a little, more like a satchel. Yeah. A small satchel. Well, they're as big as they needed to be. And back in the day, back in the Middle Ages or in the 15th century, 16th century, women didn't need to carry very much most of the time. And so, they didn't, it all depends on what your function is, you know, what you need and use. So, they were probably fairly small. The ones that I've seen are kind of little flat things, pretty much like a pocket with an opening at the top, and you just put in the things that you have. So, I should say men also had bags at this time as well, and also similar pockets. So, in the beginning, they weren't really gendered at all, but people would put them on around their waist and carry them, fill them with what they needed and go about the day. You're describing a very functional address to a real issue, which is where on earth do I put my coins, for example? But was there a fashion side to this? Was there any kind of, I guess, statement being made by having a pocket or not having a pocket? Well, exactly. It's very much a fashion thing because generally, in the history of fashion, menswear tends towards functionality and womenswear tends to fashionability. And womenswear, at any given time, reflects the fashionable silhouette of the time. And depending on your social status, where you are in the class system, the more fashionable you'll dress. And pockets can get in the way of that. You know, they can sort of spoil a nice, beautiful line of a dress. And this is probably why they've fallen foul of the world and why they fell out of favour and why they're only starting to come back again in about the last 50 or so years. Yeah. Wouldn't want any sort of utilitarian kind of, you know, accoutrement to spoil the silhouette of a beautiful dress, for example. Well, that's right. episodes.title: How AI is reshaping architecture
episodes.description: Algorithms are sketching, rendering, optimising, and quietly reshaping who holds creative power. In this episode, we ask the uncomfortable questions: Is AI a tool, a collaborator, or a threat?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. When I look at a building, I don't just see the finished structure. I see the many steps that brought it to life. The creative conversations, the sketches and drawings, the site meeting where ideas are tested, challenged and refined. It's this human collaboration between architects and builders that shapes the world we live in. But what happens to that process and to the buildings it produces when artificial intelligence enters the picture? I'm Professor of Architecture Anthony Burke and this is By Design on ABC Radio National. It's the new kid on the block when it comes to technology and it's changing everything from how we analyse data to the way we communicate. But just how much is artificial intelligence reshaping the way we build? Can anyone now design their own home? James Loder is a partner at Wardle, an award-winning architectural firm based in Sydney and Melbourne. Wardle is known for the texture, tone and handmade materials that bring their work to life. They pay extraordinary attention to detail. Not exactly what you might associate with the output of AI. But James says AI is simply a tool and what matters is how you use it. When we first started using the more image-based tools like Mid Journey, this was probably a couple of years ago, we were having a bit of fun just sort of experimenting with what we could produce. And I think some of the more sort of beautiful conceptual imagery that was pretty unrealistic to ever build was certainly something interesting for us to kind of draw inspiration from or even build into an overarching concept that we would then develop into a model. So sort of inspiring yourselves, sort of, you know, tricking yourself in a way and like opening the box of design a little broader than you ever imagined. Yeah, I think both being expansive in the way we're able to experiment, but then I think as a means of particularly communicating a really early concept, say to a client, you could use some evocative imagery with, say, a diagram that pairs with the potential without having to go the full distance. We found that quite effective. Yeah, right. So there's a sort of a shorthand to some visualisation. It's a kind of a promise, but not an actual design. That's right. And I think the trap is users or architects are trying to create the kind of full final image. For us, it's trying to create something more abstract and evocative that communicates an idea rather than a final potential outcome. So that's one way to use AI. That's the kind of image generation side of things. Do you use it in other ways? Yeah, look, I mean, chat GPT is interesting. It's obviously probably the most broadly used tool sort of as far as AI goes in most industries. I think the challenges around it are its reliability. And I think what we've looked at doing, and I know a lot of other firms are investing in, is kind of creating their own chat GPT chatbot where it harvests all the information and data of a practice. And you can use it to interact with, to pull up old projects or information very, very quickly. The challenge there really is in data management. It's all very dry, but it relies on a really robust back end that I think it's kind of out of reach for most architectural practices. Right. It's a bigger enterprise than you'd imagine. Yeah, very much so. So, I mean, I have heard of that. Like that is practices training their own AIs so that they avoid the trap of firstly intellectual property that's been brought into large models. They can control that content. But then also give it a language, I suppose, cultivate a language that is appropriate to the office itself. Do you see that as something that's going to continue, do you think? Or do you think that's the way forward? I think from a language of a tone of voice perspective or the way in which a practice communicates is certainly also something we've looked to use it for. And the way in which we write for reports and bids and the way we would outwardly communicate inward, though, is a little more complex to pull off. And again, the reliability of the data is one of the biggest hurdles, I think. So can you give me a specific example in your practice where you've used AI? So on a regular basis, we would use it to almost copyright and proofread large bodies of text, whether it's for a design report. It can edit down, reduce content and I think overall review the overall pitch, perhaps. So it's a really kind of useful kind of copywriting tool. What about in the design space, the visualization and so on? Pretty broad. And I'd say from the spectrum of a kind of high level exploration of ideas in a very early phase to the most common tool that everyone's using for is highly polished renderings, which, you know, used to be quite expensive to output and time consuming. Now it is at the click of a button. You can knock it out in 10 seconds and endlessly iterate. I think that's where we're using it kind of on a day to day basis the most. So that super quick response. Super quick response and really high quality renderings that you could just about, you type any prompt in, changing an image, you can change materials, the entourage. It's, yeah, it's sort of really limitless. Are the architects in the office getting a bit nervous about design being, you know, like taken over by the new kid on the block, which happens to be living in the hard drive just under my desk? It's interesting because like at the end of the day, I've always felt that AI really is just a tool for greater efficiency. It's just speeding up a process that used to take us longer to undertake. And with regards to it being a design tool to iterate ideas, I'd liken to, you know, giving a task to a room full of graduates to say, here's my prompt, here's my instruction. Come up with 10 different scenarios, bring it back to me, I'll pick one and we'll go from there. That's effectively how we see the kind of engagement with the tool. And whilst you might worry that it's removing it from the graduate, the notion there is it's the grads, it's the younger generation who are actually most attuned to using the software. So it's actually them really come on board with the kind of processes and workflows of that iterative process. We're still in the early days of AI, but it's already making a noticeable impact on architectural studios like Wardle. James says it's giving designers the freedom to push their imaginations further than ever before, expanding what's possible in the conceptual stage. And it's streamlining data in ways that might sound dull at first, but as James points out, those efficiencies matter. For architect Philip Alsop, AI and access to vast troves of research data represents one of the biggest potential breakthroughs in how we design and build for human health and well-being. Bet you didn't see that coming. Philip is the co-chair of the Royal Institute of British Architects expert advisory panel on AI, and he has a deep interest in how the built environment affects our physical and mental health. If you ask any wildlife biologist, what makes a species thrive? They'll invariably give you a short answer as habitat. But our species has decided to turn its habitat into a kind of a real estate commodity, a line item, a market, a transaction. And yet it is habitat. It is the places that we inhabit that play such a profound role in who we are as people, how we get on in life, how kids learn to explore the world around them and become adults. That being able to analyze all of the information pertaining to the design of environments and the full integration of biodiversity within that, which is so vitally important, becomes something where AI can play a massively important role in helping architects to grapple with the very things they've always wanted to do, which is to know more about how design works and why it works better in certain circumstances than in others. And at the same time, that ability to grapple with complex and very disparate data gives architects a significant leg up in being able to say, well, look, if you come to us and use us for this design work, we can operate almost as if we are conducting gene therapy on the DNA of where you live. And we can do it very well. And we have access to information. And we can manipulate that information to optimize the design solution that is likely to work. And it also gives great agency for clients to become much more engaged with architects in that process. So I think it suggests to me, at least, that there is an opportunity for greater transparency in what it is that architects do and the process of actually creating a design from the very idea of a need of a building all the ways through to the making of it as well. episodes.description: Australia’s surfing story has been influenced from far beyond our shores, from ancient Peruvian reed boards to Hawaiian royalty and the design revolutions that shaped the modern surfboard.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. As humanity keeps chasing the next big leap forward, it's worth remembering that innovation also thrives in the quiet, ordinary things woven into daily life. I'm Anthony Burke and this is Extraordinary Every Day, a weekly segment on ABC Radio Nationals by Design. And today, we're going surfing. Australia's surfing story has been influenced from far beyond our shores, from ancient Peruvian reed boards to Hawaiian royalty and the design revolutions that shaped the modern surfboard. So, how did we get from the earliest surfboards of heavy wooden planks to the sleek high-performance boards written today? Andrew McKinnon is a surf reporter, historian and a surfer for over 60 years. Let's talk about the history of surfing because we all think of it as sort of a fun sport, but it's got this pretty interesting and really long history that I didn't really know about. As I understand it, and correct me if I'm wrong here, surfing actually originated in Peru and not in Hawaii, like I thought, but in Peru. Is that true? Well, the Caballito de Toro, the Peruvian Reed Board, de Toro means reeds, board of reeds. This goes back 3,000 to 5,000 years as part of the Moche civilization, Chumu, pre-Inca. I mean, it's sort of well known now that the Peruvians were the early seafarers. They were getting across the Pacific before anybody else. They had been explorers and they were expert seafarers and they designed this special fishing boat, like a canoe, called the Caballito de Toro. So, we call it the Peruvian Reed Board. episodes.title: Material Cultures: Reinventing Batik in Indonesia
episodes.description: Batik is a material that is both ancient and modern.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Some materials hold stories on their surface. Some keep them buried in their threads. Batik is one of those fabrics. Wax, dye, cloth and of course so much more. A language of pattern and patience. A textile that's made and then often lived in, passed on and protected. This is By Design on ABC Radio National and I'm Professor Anthony Burke. Today we arrive at our final stop in our Material Cultures series. Meeting designers and artisans who think deeply about their materials. And who let those materials speak in ways that feel utterly right for their time and place. Over the last few years, I've spent a fair bit of time in Asia filming for ABC International. Including a TV series called Culture By Design. You can find it on ABC iview. And along the way, I had conversations that stayed with me long after we stopped recording. And I'm so happy to share them here with you. Today we're talking about a fabric with a whole lot of history. Batik. For centuries, it has carried deep meaning. Worn by royals. Used in ceremonies. Even wrapped around newborns for luck. But rising costs and fading demand nearly pushed it to the margins. Now, Batik is stepping back into the spotlight. Welcome to By Design, the ABC Radio National Show exploring the ideas, objects and people shaping the way we live. This is hand spun, hand woven. This is batik. And then embroidered. If you touch the textures here. The lines are embroidered. This is the paddy fields. The paddy fields. And then you have the rivers running. And then you have the current down with your death. This is Indonesia. And this is what it's all about. Josephine, affectionately known as Oban Kamara, uses long-established processes to both champion traditional Indonesian batik and create contemporary stories in cloth. Made into sophisticated cocktail dresses, bespoke tailored shirts or gently draping shawls, batik has become as much a fashion choice as a Chanel or Hermes for many in Southeast Asia and internationally. Walking into Josephine Oban Kamara's workshop, which is also her home and office in central Java, there's an immediate sense of energy and colour and smell. Hey! How do you do? Welcome. Thank you so much. You must be Anthony. I'm Anthony. I'm Bin. Pleasure to meet you. Pleasure to meet you too. This is your showroom, studio? This is where I work and this is where I live. Aha. Come. Yeah. Pick me again. I can see, I can see it's all happening. It's happening. This is all prepared for you. They're batik-ing, they're waxing. This is the skill that I've heard so much about. And the beauty of the fabrics that you produce sort of starts here, yeah? Can you smell the wax? Yeah. Come, sit down. Josephine Obin Kamara didn't have a traditional pathway into weaving cloth and dyeing batik. It's a fascinating story of absorbing the diversity of Indonesian culture. Oh, Bin, this is a remarkable space you brought me into. But tell me, where did all of this come from? Where does your story start? So I was gallivanting around Indonesia when all the children my age were in school. But I saw a lot. I saw a lot. I traveled a lot. I stayed in Java for a while. I was exposed to the culture there. One of my mentors was the late Mr. Harjo Nagoro. He was sort of like the chancellor and the lord of, and the keeper of the treasures of the palace of Solo, Surakarta. He has just passed away. He's a beautiful dancer. Watching him and listening to him talk, I learned so much. I absorbed so much. I could smell the Java solo and its surrounding regions. I could feel the pace and the pulse. The colors, the motifs, the people, the sounds. It's all there. And in Indonesia, it's so diverse. You drive the car for one hour to another city and they're speaking a different dialect. The food is different. You call dialect. It's language. The language different. Sometimes similar. West Java, Central Java. But West Java and East Java, like Surabaya, are very different. And it gets more distinct as you go further on and further on until you go to the outer islands like Flores and Medan. You go to Sumatra. You go to Sulawesi celibacy. What you're describing there is you're opening up to an empathy for beauty and color and texture and senses. The people, the color, the music. The differences. The differences. And for me, they're all rolled into one. So why was cloth or weaving, why was that a natural medium for you to express these things? In 1979. Yeah. Around 1979. How old was I? I was born in 1955. So how old am I? 1979. Not a day over 45. Well, anyway, around that time. By that time, I've been collecting. I love beautiful things. And it just so happens that the antiques are beautiful. They're well made. Indonesia's a treasure trove of culture, for antiques from 9th, 11th, 10th, 13th, 14th century. Weather, whatever it is. Fabrics. Unfortunately for the antiques, the fabrics don't last much. I mean, that long because of the weather. But I collected a lot of things. Beautiful. Because they're beautiful and they're meaningful and they just, my mind goes crazy. I can imagine what it was before. But of all the things that I collected, the jewelry, the ceramics, the furniture, the bronzers, the terracottas, the cloth. It was the cloth that really, I was dealing too because I couldn't pay for everything without selling. But then I started to weave raw silk. Plain. Plain. And then checks. And then stripes. And then ikat. Raw silk is very thick. So it was used usually for interior, like upholstery, curtains and stuff. Maybe I was doing the right thing at the right time in 1979. But the Hilton Hotel was being built. Mandarin Hotel. Arya Dutta Hotel. And the designers, the architects and the designers, they couldn't find any interior fabric. You had to import. So they used, I was making bed covers, curtains, lampshades. So I had a little industry going. You took off. I guess I went crazy. Yeah. I collected all the lampshade makers from Jalan Kebon Siri. There's a little street there. And where all the lampshade makers used to be. And I brought them over to the garage at home. And we made lampshades. And we made this. And we made that. And then I went on weaving and weaving and weaving. And the fabric from very thick got to be very thin. You know, weaving course of yarns are easy. But weaving very thin yarns are very difficult. Because it's so thin. And when you weave, it's white. It's so thin that sometimes when the yarn breaks, you can't see. That's why. The people, the weavers, had to wear very dark. To see the cloth. To see the yarns. Yeah, yeah. So from very thick, we were able to do very fine yarns. And then I got bored. Something happened in around 1985. And I got bored. And I just shut down. I didn't want to do anything. I was divorced. I had Elang, my son. And I'm going to share with you all something that happened. It was called the Big Bang. I call it the Big Bang. It was like 3 o'clock in the morning. And I was having a cigarette and having a glass of wine. And by that time, I had two big chests. Two chests. Two antique chests. One was full of weavings from the outer islands. From Sulawesi. From Batak. From, you know, from everywhere. And one chest was full of antique batiks. Mind you, batiks are only made in Java. Especially throughout the coastal, the Java coastal area. So one day, I spread them out. And I looked at all the weavings. Which I was trying to redo the techniques. And I saw all the batiks. Mind you, by that time, I could already weave very, very fine, thin silk. See-through. Transparent, but very thin. So in my mind's eye, I saw a very thin piece of cloth. Hand spun. Hand woven. With a batik motif on top. So this is the moment where batik... This was the moment. ...walked into your life. Yeah. This was the moment when batik entered my life. I've always loved it, but I've never done it. Yeah. And for me, this is something new. Let me explain. All the vintage batiks that you see. All the old antique batiks that you see are on cotton. Indonesia does not produce cotton. The cottons were a result of bartering with China, India, and England. England, because of Industrial Revolution, they were overproducing. So the companies, the Dutch company and the British company said that we have overproduction of cotton. And the Dutch say, oh, there is a tradition in Indonesia that's called batik. So... And they get their cloths, their cottons from China and India. So from the antique batiks, I could learn. The ones with this width are the ones from China. The ones with this width, that one's from England. The one, the wide ones, are from India. Because in India, it's the men who weave. So they're taller and so it's wider. That's right. I learned so much. I learned so much just by looking at it. Anyway. Every piece of fabric has a story. Exactly. And you have that ability to see all of the stories. Oh, I was just nosy. I was curious. You were nosy. But for me, being able to do the hand weaving, Indonesian, and then doing the batik on it, putting it together. For me, it was like putting Indonesia together by doing this one thing. I'm Anthony Burke, and this is By Design on Radio National, exploring how a material with an ancient heritage is making a comeback. Creating batik with its extraordinary range of distinct patterns that have evolved over time is an incredibly complex and skillful process, as we've been hearing. Josephine Obin-Kamara and her team are a one-stop shop. They spin the thread. They weave the cloth. Each step with its own intricacies. When you look around her studio, the bolts of raw fabric are already full of texture and shape and pattern. And that's even before they've ever touched wax or dye. The final cloth is fine, but rich, layered, deep with meaning and craft. I call myself Tukangkain, cloth maker, because I start from scratch. I spin, I weave, and I do batik, or whatever cloth manipulation that can be done to it. So where did you learn all of those skills? It's not one thing. Watching. My mother used to sew. She used to make her patterns using newspapers. Okay. And she'd roll them. This was her blouse. This was her thing. This was her house coat. I mean, all mothers used to do that. Yeah. I think all the mothers, I don't know. But that's one. And then you see her sew, and you have the sewing machine, the singer sewing machine, you know. I see her darning. And then when the colors are dirty, she likes to change the colors. And I see how she does it. Yeah. So you're just that capacity to see those sorts of things and to take them on for yourself. If I'm a camera, I go in it. You're like a highly tuned design radar. I like to look at things small, you know, microscopic. And then where does design fit into all of this? When you then go into a creative mode. When you talk about design. Yeah. It's actually not so much the visual, but more the technique. Because design is making. You know the antique textiles, the one I told you, the woven ones? Many of them are ripped and torn. And that makes me so happy. One is cheaper. And the other one is also because if it's torn, I can take a loop and I can go in. I can see the steps from the tear. Yeah. This is your magic. You can see it into that process. That's the magic of the cloth. But you can see that, the tradition of making the particular cloth, the issue of the material itself. And then you bring your design sort of approach to things, which this turns it into something new again. But can you imagine the tear in the cloth? Where there is the warp? And then there is the weft and all the funny foot dancing there. You know, the supplementary weaving going up and down. But then you can see all that. And then you do something even more sinful. You take the weft and you pull it. You tear it even more to see where it goes and where it goes up and then it goes down. You're scaring me at this point. It was in the making. It happened. And the batik-ing, I just went to the batik workshops all over Jawa. Like I told you, I lived in Jawa. And I used to sit there for hours watching them with the gamelan music at the back, you know, and listening to them talking between each other and then smelling the wax. And I see the way they were. Then I went to Pekalongan and I saw the famous batik house. I saw that their batiks were different. They were all European colors. They were pinks and blues and more. The patterns were of flowers that were not Indonesian, of peonies and chrysanthemums and everything. Then I realized this was the residential area of the Dutch, the Dutch-Chinese. So the colors were European. And then I asked, why is it the batiks from Pekalongan, they were all in bouquets. One, two, three. And they're all the same and the same format for many of the batiks. I was informed that the Dutch ladies who were residing in Pekalongan region, they would order their embroidery pattern from Holland. And the embroidery patterns were of bouquets and flowers. episodes.title: Extraordinary Everyday: Kites
episodes.description: Kites aren’t just toys—they’re one of the most influential inventions in the history of science. Sure, they look playful drifting across a windy sky, but the humble kite has quietly powered some of humanity’s biggest breakthroughs.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. What secret histories hide in the objects we use every day? Each object carries a hidden story, a design journey shaped by culture, innovation and necessity. I'm Anthony Burke and this is Extraordinary Every Day. Today, thanks to a story suggestion from listener Louisa, we're off to fly some kites. If you saw our next item whipping through the sky on a windy day, you might shrug and think, oh, pretty, fun. But don't be fooled. This isn't just colourful airborne decoration. The kite has been a secret agent of world-shaping science, sparking experiments, discoveries and breakthroughs that shifted the course of history. Not bad for something held together with string. John Murray is the president of the Australian Kite Flyer Society. Thanks for having me, Anthony. Let's talk about the history for a second. Now, as I understand it, traditionally, it's thought that kites came from China. Yeah. Yeah? But you've got a slightly different thesis here. Well, that is the oldest written records about kites are from China. 5th century BC. So, you know, a long, long time ago. But more recently, they've discovered some petroglyphs, rock carvings in Indonesia. And they're about 12,500 years old. And initially, when they were discovered, it was a matter of people just saying, oh, yeah, it's just a rock carving. And I guess what I would be saying is that in Sulawesi in Indonesia and Lampung, they actually use kites to catch fish. Oh, get out of here. Really? Yeah. How does that work? Well, you've got like a leaf off a local plant. I guess the Australian equivalent would be a staghorn, something like that. So you shape the leaf. You then tie a line to the leaf. From the leaf, you then let it drop down into the water. But you've got like a little circular noose of fishing line into which you feed a bait. And that skips across the water. And the fish you're trying to catch is quite, well, it's like a garfish, but it's quite a big garfish with quite big teeth. So the fish says, oh, a live piece of bait, a flying fish, something like that. I'll go and get that. The jaw goes through. It's a noose. And they catch the fish. Hooks, line and sinker, all done from above. All done from above. And I guess personally, I think, you know what? People would look to feed their family before they would look to knock off and go down the beach and fly kite for fun. So amazing. So back to China for a second, though. How were kites used in China? Well, initially for military purposes, because that is this first recorded history is a general putting a kite up in the air, theoretically with someone attached to it. So they could look. Yeah. Like an elevator? Well. Like a lift to get a perspective on the approaching enemy? Yeah. Either a basket or whether they tied them to it. I guess the jury's out on that as well. And that was then used to gauge how far, because they were, the city was, that they were trying to attack was under siege. I thought you were going to say maybe signalling or something like this, but it's actually far more elaborate than that. Yeah. Well, warfare as barrage, you know, to keep wires up in the sky, to try and stop bombers coming through. There was also the Americans in the Second World War used kites as target practice. Oh. And so they could have the equivalent of a Japanese plane on it and they would zoom that around the sky and they would try and shoot that down. And if you were an American that was shot down, in your life raft was a kite called the Gibson Girl, which was a aluminium and cloth kite, which you hoisted up into the sky and came with a little radio transmitter. So people could, you would crank the radio transmitter and send out a signal and hopefully people would find you. And that to me sounds like a great idea, except I guess if you've just been shot down and you're in the middle of a stormy sea and you're going, okay, right now, first of all, I've got to get the kite up. Get the kite up. And now I've got to attach it all. And now I've got to wind. And now I've got to... I suppose any search and rescue in a situation you'll go for though, right? Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. So, okay, that's great. But what about Benjamin Franklin? I've got to mention the famous lightning kite story. Oh, okay. You're going, oh, geez, that's just a myth. It's immortalised. All I would say is theoretically the next number of people who tried it, guess what? Were electrocuted. So if you're going to try and convince me that, okay, I'm going to go fishing for electricity. It's going to come down the line and I'm magically not going to get injured. Okay. Yeah. You know, once again, I don't want to upset historians and I don't want to upset, you know, the stamp that the US have put out, which shows all of that happening. But I guess the more scientific things that I would look at is Marconi lifting a piece of wire up in the sky to be the aerial. So the first transatlantic radio signal came to Signal Hill in Newfoundland, in Canada. So across the Atlantic. So very useful scientific apparatus here. Can I just get you to rewind for a second though and just tell in a brief way the story of Benjamin Franklin? Because it is sort of mythologised so much. Like what's the real story as you understand it? The story is meant to be he's flying a kite in a storm looking to indicate that lightning was electricity.
